Journalist to be crowned king in Uganda after bitter succession dispute
- Published
Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo I, who is set to be crowned king of Uganda's Tooro kingdom later, has long been a familiar face in the country.
For many Ugandans, he was known not as the heir to the throne, but as a storyteller, as a long-serving anchor and editor at the state broadcaster.
But Kijanangoma, 56, has now become the subject of media attention himself - his rise to the Tooro throne sparking controversy and widespread reactions beyond the country.
Tooro is one of Uganda's four main officially recognised historical kingdoms. For the last 31 years, it has been headed by King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who was once known as a "boy king", after ascending to the throne as an infant.
Oyo became king in 1995 at the age of just three, following the death of his father. Then the world's youngest monarch, he ruled until he died last month from cancer, aged just 34.
The coronation is a day for celebration, involving traditional practices starting from midnight. The new king then walks about 4km (2.5 miles) to the official Karuziika royal palace where he is crowned.
A mock fight follows, to signify that kingship does not come easy, and he is then blessed by members of the royal Babiito clan, the Tooro kingdom's Information Minister Charles Mwanguhya told the BBC Focus on Africa podcast.
He performs other ceremonies that signifies his assumption of the throne, before he sits on the throne and an actual crown placed on his head to signify his new authority, his new position as the new Tooro king.
But the selection of Kijanangoma as king was far from straightforward.
According to tradition, a recognised son of the late king should succeed him. Close members of the royal family said Oyo had left a young son and a will with instructions that the child should be next on the throne.
But the son has never been revealed to the public and nor was he recognised by the committee of 21 Babiito clan members who choose the king and eventually selected Kijanangoma.
The late King Oyo was never publicly married, and little is known about his wife or their son.
Nonetheless his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, argued that the late king's will ought to have been respected.
However, the royal succession committee ignored her wishes, insisting their selection process was conducted in accordance with Tooro customs and traditions.
The new king has thus found himself at the centre of a succession dispute, with Kemigisa and her close relatives unhappy with the outcome.
Kemigisa referred to Kijanangoma's selection as the "announcement of a second king" being "made after the will of King Oyo was read to members of the royal family".
"As a mother, that was extraordinarily painful," she said, describing celebrations for the next king taking place "only metres from where my son's body lay".
The queen later said Oyo's son, who was in the US state of Texas, had been due to return home but that could not happen amid a "tense and polarised succession dispute".
"No child should be placed in circumstances where returning to his father's homeland could mean being drawn into hostility and conflict," Kemigisa asserted in a post on X.
But according to the Tooro kingdom's information minister, the son being talked about "hasn't been presented anywhere, which means there is a growing acceptance that sad as it may be, King Oyo didn't leave a son behind".
While King Oyo inherited the crown from his father, Mwanguhya told the BBC "the crown has moved to a different line within the ruling clan".
A king must come from the Babiito clan, specifically the lineage of King George David Matthew Kamurasi Rukidi III, according to royal palace sources.
Kijanangoma and the late King Oyo are cousins. Both are grandsons of Rukidi III, the 11th king, or Omukama, who ruled the Tooro kingdom from 1928 to 1965.
Kijanangoma was among several people who were considered for the role, including Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, who plays football for one of the UK's best-known amateur clubs.
According to the succession committee, the South East Dons captain and goalkeeper declined the offer of the throne, citing other responsibilities.
After he was formally announced, Kijanangoma promised that the palace would be open to the people, while vowing to focus on unity and development.
"I ask you for one thing - they have given me this title as king but I cannot work alone, I have to work with you," he said.
Uganda's traditional kings have no formal political authority, but they retain cultural influence and command significant loyalty in the communities they lead.
The country is home to four main kingdoms, the largest and most prominent being Buganda in the central region, which encompasses the capital Kampala.
The kingdoms were abolished in 1967, but the government under President Yoweri Museveni restored them in the early 1990s.
The government said this was to promote cultural pride and national unity, but the move has also been interpreted as a way of appeasing communities and fostering political loyalty.
Amid the succession dispute, the government backed the Babiito clan's choice of Kijanangoma. Attorney General Sam Mayanja said the Tooro kingdom was cleared to go ahead with the coronation, as there had not been a formal complaint against him.
The date of the coronation was announced by the government and Museveni is scheduled to attend.
The president's son and the head of the military, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has also publicly supported Kijanangoma. "Long may he reign," he posted on X.
Kijanangoma's very name points to his royal heritage.
His father, the first Kijanangoma, was born in the year King Rukidi III became king. The king gave him the name, which means the "one who comes with the royal drum".
The drum of royalty, foretold two generations earlier, is now returning to its bearer.
Kijanangoma was born in 1970 and raised at their family home at Kidukuru village in Fort Portal, about 300 km (186 miles) from Kampala.
He left the village to pursue further studies and graduated with a mass communication degree from Uganda's prestigious Makerere University in 1999.
He worked as a broadcaster in a career spanning more than two decades, including in neighbouring Rwanda and at home, with the Uganda Broadcasting Corporation.
The years spent engaging with the public, the interactions with leaders and the exposure to national affairs in his work as a journalist may yet serve him well as he returns to the community he came from, this time as their leader.
After he was named king, Kijanangoma said he would use the connections he had built up over 21 years working as a journalist "to get good things for our people".
His mother, Assimwe Yusta Kijanangoma, is confident that he is well prepared for his new role. She says his upbringing was deeply rooted in tradition.
"I really raised him with the teachings of the old kingdom of a cane and instructions and scolding. I laugh with him, and other times I scold him," she told the BBC.
She added: "Eddy is well-mannered, he does not fight, or shout, even when wronged, he says a few words and does not go so much into it."
She feels good for her son, although she admits to having mixed emotions, especially as her son is taking over after the death of a "great man".

Supporters of jailed ex-PM Imran Khan march to Pakistan capital
- Published
Thousands of supporters of Pakistan's jailed ex-prime minister Imran Khan are marching to the capital Islamabad as they call for his release.
Concerns over the 73-year-old's health have grown louder in recent months. His family claims he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.
The cricket star-turned-politician, who faces charges in more than 100 cases, was jailed for 17 years over corruption last year. Khan said all the cases against him are politically motivated.
Even behind bars, he remains a force in Pakistani politics, and demonstrations in support for him have led to deadly violence and crackdowns in the past.
Sunday's march, which began in Lakki Marwat, a city 275km away from Islamabad, had paused for the night and is expected to resume around midday local time on Monday.
Originally scheduled for last week, it was postponed to allow for talks between the government and Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party but the talks ended in a deadlock.
Khan, who faces charges ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts, was first imprisoned in August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year.
Sohail Afridi, chief minister for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province ruled by PTI, expects that the march will make its way to a town about 80km (50 miles) west of Islamabad by Thursday.
"[By then] this movement will have reached every corner of the country and every square will have become a centre of activity," he said on Sunday, urging the people to "play an active role in the political process".
Authorities in Islamabad have stacked up shipping containers to block key access routes to the capital city.
The PTI said talks with government failed because authorities rejected the party's request for access to Khan so that its leaders could consult him on national and political issues.
The party also said it had demanded that Khan be given an immediate medical examination and treatment.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi meanwhile accused Afridi of "sabotaging" negotiations, saying the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government had backed out of earlier commitments on counter-terrorism issues, according to Pakistan's local media reports.
In August, Khan was briefly transferred from jail to a state-run hospital for medical examination and treatment following complaints about his deteriorating health. The doctors later deemed him "medically fit".
The intervention was the most significant relief Khan has received from the courts since he was imprisoned in 2023 on corruption charges, which he says were politically motivated.
Khan's family and the PTI, however, criticised the authorities for defying a court order that he be examined by physicians at a specific private hospital.
On 20 September, Khan's sister Aleema Khanum was arrested in the eastern city of Lahore.
The arrest order said Khanum had been mobilising people to "create law and order situations" and "raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the Government".
Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as the country's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.
His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things.
At least eight people died in the protests and the army had to be called in to quell the violence.
Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif urging Khan be accorded proper medical care.

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

EXCLUSIVE: Jim Taylor, the Academy Award and Golden Globe-winning screenwriter known for his longtime creative partnership with filmmaker Alexander Payne on a series of lauded, darkly comedic character studies, has inked with Paradigm for representation.
Payne and Taylor first collaborated on the Laura Dern-led indie satire Citizen Ruth, following that up with the Tom Perrotta adaptation Election, a dark comedy starring Matthew Broderick and Reese Witherspoon that brought them an Oscar nomination for Best Adapted Screenplay and scored Independent Spirit Awards wins for Picture, Director and Screenplay, bringing Witherspoon her first Golden Globe nomination.
Taylor and Payne won the Golden Globe for Best Screenplay for About Schmidt, an existential dramedy whose stars Nicholson and Kathy Bates earned Oscar nominations. Two years later, the duo won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay for Sideways, the celebrated wine country dramedy starring Paul Giamatti, Thomas Haden Church, Virginia Madsen and Sandra Oh, based on the 2004 novel by Rex Pickett. The film earned Academy Award nominations for Giamatti, Handen Church and Madsen for acting, as well as Payne for directing. In addition, Taylor and Payne won a BAFTA Award for Best Adapted Screenplay.
Watch on Deadline
Outside of his collaboration with Payne, Taylor is known for his creative partnership with his wife, Oscar-nominated filmmaker Tamara Jenkins (The Savages). Together, they adapted the Nick Hornby novel Juliet, Naked into the 2018 film starring Rose Byrne and Ethan Hawke.
Taylor was a producer on Payne’s 2011 film The Descendants, starring George Clooney, which was nominated for five Oscars and won two Golden Globes. Together, they’re currently adapting an Election sequel, based on Perrotta’s 2022 novel Tracy Flick Can’t Win, for Paramount, with Hello Sunshine and Bona Fide producing.
Taylor continues to be represented by Untitled Entertainment and attorney John Diemer at Goodman, Genow, Schenkman.

The Pentagon has removed bombers based at the Royal Air Force base in the U.K. that was at the center of a suspected attempted terrorist attack last week.
The New York Times, citing two unnamed U.S. officials, reported that the withdrawal had been carried out with unusual swiftness and urgency after new threats of a plot linked to Iran had emerged.
A Defense Department official said all American bombers deployed at RAF Fairford had now returned to their home bases in the U.S.
American warplanes had used RAF Fairford in the military campaign against Iran that began in late February.
This shift takes critical equipment out of the preferred forward operating base for bomber aircraft in Europe, but the Pentagon official said the personnel who operate the U.S. bomber fleet, including B-1s, B-2s and B-52s, remain prepared to carry out precision global strikes anywhere.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham in July approved the use of the base by the U.S. for “defensive strikes” against Iran, continuing the policy of his predecessor, Keir Starmer.
The Wall Street Journal reported about the bombers’ redeployment earlier Sunday, citing a senior U.S. official as saying that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had recruited Britons in the Fairford plot.
U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said Iran was likely responsible for the thwarted attempt to attack, after police said on Thursday they had arrested a British-Iranian dual national.
The 27-year-old suspect was detained in London on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts and brought the tally of people arrested in connection with the incident up to six. Another man, a British national, was questioned under caution and two properties in the area were searched.
“We’re exploring with our police and security services a range of leads and possibilities, but as our prime minister has stated it is likely that Iran was responsible,” Streeting said in an interview in Iceland, while emphasizing that the U.K. had yet to formally attribute the attack.
Five men were arrested outside the base last Sunday. Police did not find any explosives but recovered a quantity of fuel from the scene. The five were later released on bail, a decision that drew criticism from U.S. President Donald Trump.
Asked about potential Iranian involvement in the Sept. 27 incident, Trump told reporters Thursday “it’s looking like that,” but that he could not say so “with confirmation.”

Uproar escalated on Friday (October 2, 2026) after a video went viral showing a Dalit woman who was allegedly denied admission at the government hospital in Bhadohi district during labour pain and forced to deliver outside the hospital in public.

“The family categorically alleged that hospital staff failed to provide timely treatment and did not admit due to her caste affiliation, this is so sad and inhuman that even after 79 years of independence, untouchability and discrimination prevails in government system, forcing a Dalit woman to give birth on the roadside, outside a government hospital. The feudal elements within the administrative system are emboldened by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government. The fight of the Samajwadi Party (SP) for justice, equality is against such tendencies,” said Sunil Singh Yadav ‘Sajan’, the SP spokesperson.

US Supreme Court wrestles with oil companies' bid to scuttle climate lawsuit
Boulder, Colorado, sued oil companies ExxonMobil and Suncor, accusing them of contributing to climate change through fossil fuel use.
WASHINGTON: US Supreme Court justices wrestled with a bid by oil companies ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy to thwart a lawsuit by officials in Boulder, Colorado, seeking monetary damages for harms caused by climate change, as they opened their new nine-month term on Monday (Oct 5).
US-based Exxon and Canada-based Suncor appealed after the Colorado Supreme Court let Boulder's lawsuit accusing them of state law violations proceed.
"This case involves an unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct," Kannon Shanmugam, a lawyer for the oil companies, told the justices.
Boulder is suing the oil companies under Colorado law, Shanmugam added, "on the theory that their global conduct increased the global use of fossil fuels, which led to an increase in global greenhouse gas emissions, which contributed to global climate change, which resulted in global harms."
"Our constitutional system does not permit state law to be used in that manner. The Constitution bars the application of state law to certain inherently federal areas," Shanmugam said.
"Because of the ambient nature of air and water and the conflicting rights of states, this court has held for over a century that federal law governs interstate pollution claims. That principle applies with even greater force to claims involving global climate change," Shanmugam said.
Boulder's city and county governments have accused Exxon and Suncor of helping drive climate change and misleading the public about the risks of fossil fuels. Boulder aims to hold the companies liable for past and future costs associated with climate change such as infrastructure repairs, environmental damage, emergency management and harms to public health.
US President Donald Trump's administration has backed Exxon and Suncor, arguing that the federal government's authority to regulate air pollution precludes Boulder's claims.
"Interstate air pollution is an inherently federal area," said Sarah Harris, a Justice Department lawyer representing the Trump administration, and Congress has not authorized the Boulder suit under a key provision of the Clean Air Act, the landmark federal anti-pollution law.
"Second, this suit egregiously exceeds constitutional limits on state authority," Harris told the justices.
Conservative Chief Justice John Roberts pressed Shanmugam and Harris on their contention that state lawsuits are barred when such litigation has been allowed in similar contexts.
"I guess I'm not quite sure what makes this situation different from all those other ones where we've allowed (it)," Roberts told Harris.
The top US judicial body opened its new term on the first Monday in October, as is its custom. It also has major cases involving Trump's hardline immigration policies and state-level bans on assault-style rifles, among others, lined up for the term. Before the arguments, the court turned away some appeals including in cases involving bids by real estate platform Zillow Group and Nexstar Media Group to avoid lawsuits.
"SORT OF PREMATURE"
The burning of fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases including carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, trapping heat and raising average global temperatures over time.
Nearly 60 state and local governments have brought similar suits seeking billions of dollars from fossil fuel companies, with more continuing to be filed, Exxon and Suncor told the justices. A ruling by the Supreme Court siding with the companies could lead to many of those cases being dismissed.
Liberal Ketanji Brown Jackson said some of the questions asked by her colleagues during the arguments "make me think that we're really early in this case" and "that this is sort of premature from the standpoint of this court exercising its jurisdiction."
"I understand that you have several other federal issues that you have raised that are still pending in the state court. So why shouldn't we wait and hear all of these claims once the state courts are done with their federal considerations?" Jackson asked Shanmugam.
"I would submit," Shanmugam replied, "that given the extraordinary magnitude of these cases, where in each of these cases plaintiffs are seeking billions of dollars of damages, that we need an answer to this question sooner rather than later."
"And just as a matter of judicial administration, given the number of these cases that are in courts around the country, that the time is really now for this court to resolve these issues," Shanmugam said.
Monday's arguments marked the latest example of energy-sector companies asking the justices to block climate-related liability or limit federal environmental regulation.
Backers of the oil companies argue that if Boulder's most far-reaching claims are allowed to proceed, it could give states sweeping power over conduct occurring far outside their borders.
Energy companies and trade groups, along with states allied with them, have built a largely winning record before the justices over the past two decades in cases involving climate liability and the reach of federal environmental regulation.
The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. Conservative Justice Samuel Alito has recused himself from participating in the case, meaning the ruling will be made by eight justices and not nine. Alito owns stock in several oil and gas companies but not Exxon or Suncor, according to his financial disclosure forms.
The Supreme Court's decision is expected by the end of June.

A video has gone viral on social media platforms, showing two women slapping a man wearing a saffron scarf. Users claim that it shows a Muslim man masquerading as Hindu by wearing a saffron scarf, and that he was allegedly caught stalking college girls in an attempt to snatch their phones.
Right-wing handle @MeghUpdates posted the clip, which garnered more than 116,000 views, and has been shared around 2,000 times at the time of this article being written. (Archive)
A “Peaceful” in a saffron scarf was allegedly STALKING college girls and ATTEMPTING to snatch their phones before the Hindu girls CAUGHT him RED-HANDED and BEAT him up. 👏 https://t.co/EK2q3vkgN1
— Megh Updates 🚨™ (@MeghUpdates) September 25, 2026
In Right-wing social-media discourse, the term ‘peaceful’ is used as a a code word for Muslims as a negative stereotype, while avoiding saying ‘Muslim’ directly.
An X user with the handle @Hinduspirit0 had also posted the viral clip on September 24 with the same claim that a Muslim boy pretending to be Hindu while wearing a saffron scarf had been “caught red-handed and beaten up badly”.
Other users who shared this clip with the same claim included the user ‘Boiled Anda’ (@AmitLeliSlayer), Vishal Deep Singh (@VishalDeep5151), Amitabh Chaudhary (@MithilaWaaala), and (@singh31919). Archives: 1, 2, 3, 4
The readers should note that many of this handles, like ‘Boiled Anda’, Amitabh Chaudhary, and MeghUpdates, have been found sharing misinformation and communal propaganda several times in the past.
Fact Check
To verify the veracity of the claims, we broke down the viral video into several keyframes. A reverse image search on one such keyframe led us to a news report by Aaj Tak, published on August 10.
According to the report, the viral clip is from Gwalior in Madhya Pradesh. On August 8, twin sisters Harshita and Rashita Agarwal, while on their way to college on a scooter, had one of their phones snatched by a miscreant trailing them on another scooter.
A chase ensued, after which the sisters were able to apprehend the man at an intersection and proceeded to thrash him, visuals of which began to circulate on social media soon after. The report identifies the culprit as a resident of Jalandhar, Punjab, named Manpreet. We found another news report published by The Free Press Journal, on August 9, which corroborated this finding.
On using relevant keywords, we also came across a video uploaded by ANI Bharat, in which Gwalior SSP Dharamveer Singh lauded the bravery of the twin sisters in nabbing the motorcycle-borne mobile snatcher.
So, to sum up, the viral claims suggesting that the man being slapped in the clip is Muslim, is false. The man in the viral video was identified as Manpreet.

Tesla sold 486,532 electric vehicles during the third quarter of 2026. That’s a 2.1 percent decrease on the same quarter in 2025, when the company found homes for 497,099 EVs, and one might think that would be bad news for a company valued on the premise of near-constant growth.
But Tesla stock is up this morning; the year-over-year numbers might look bad, but the company still exceeded analysts’ expectations of 456,600 cars, which would have been a larger 8 percent year-on-year decline
Total production at Tesla actually increased year over year; it built 464,391 vehicles—a 3.7 percent increase—457,387 of which were Models 3 and Y (a 4.9 percent increase year over year). The remaining 7,004 were other models, mostly Cybertrucks, with presumably some Semis and Cybercabs, as the Models S and X are now retired; this category saw a 39.8 percent decrease year over year.
But the company couldn’t sell all the cars it made in Q3. It was able to sell 478,237 Models 3 and Y, a 0.6 percent decrease compared to Q3 2025. The decline in other models was severe, dropping by 48 percent to 8,295 units in total.
However, Tesla’s energy storage business had a much better three months. Between the beginning of July and the end of September, Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage products, a 9.6 percent year-over-year increase.
Tesla will publish its Q3 financial results on October 21.

After years of waiting, Apple Pay officially launched in India. Eligible users can add their Visa and Mastercard credit cards issued by supported banks (only Axis Bank at this time of launch) to the Apple Wallet app and make payments using Apple Pay. Apple says Apple Pay is available on iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch at launch, and Mac support is coming soon. You can view the full device support list here.

IPO-bound Razorpay announced today that it has deepened its partnership with AI major OpenAI to help Indian brands advertise on ChatGPT. Under the partnership, the company's growth marketing platform, Razorpay Engage, will enable brands to prepare product catalogues, launch and manage campaigns on ChatGPT Ads. Brands onboarded by Razorpay include Tanishq, Fastrack, Traya, Tata Neu, Rivaah by Tanishq, Shaadi.com, Axis Max Life, Palmonas and Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies (NMIMS). Razorpay Engage To Become ChatGPT Ads Layer Razorpay Engage will provide the technology and operational infrastructure for businesses looking to get started with ChatGPT Ads. Its offering will include assessing catalogue readiness, improving and structuring product feeds, creating and managing campaigns, and measuring and optimising campaign performance. The platform will also use an AI agent built around ChatGPT Ads best practices to help create and manage campaigns across different contexts where consumers may encounter a brand's products. The agent will monitor campaign performance and make ongoing adjustments, while Razorpay's team will provide human oversight where required. “The way people discover products is changing. The next customer may not search for a product or scroll through an ad; they may simply ask an AI assistant for help deciding what to buy. For businesses, we believe that opens up an entirely new moment to be discovered,” Razorpay COO Rahul Kothari said. The Broader Context Behind OpenAI-Razorpay Partnership The partnership comes as consumer discovery of brands is shifting from traditional keyword-based searches on engines to conversational interactions with AI chatbots. An early trend of users describing what they are looking for to an AI bot, comparing options and refine their choices via subsequent conversations is emerging at the moment. As this trend gains more footing, ChatGPT started rolling out ads on ChatGPT in India, with the initial rollout covering logged-in adults on the Free and Go plans at the end of August. Ad agencies WPP and Omnicom are OpenAI’s first agency partners in India. For brands, this creates a new channel where products need to be structured and represented with sufficient information and context to surface across different consumer queries. Razorpay said managing this process manually at scale can be challenging. The advertising push builds on Razorpay's earlier efforts to turn ChatGPT into a commerce channel. The fintech company has been working with OpenAI and NPCI on infrastructure that allows merchants to create ChatGPT-native storefronts, sync product catalogues and eventually complete purchases within the chat interface. In August, Razorpay said it was working with around 50 brands and several ecommerce marketplaces on agentic-commerce pilots. The company has also earlier said that its technology can reduce the time required for a Shopify merchant to set up a ChatGPT storefront from around eight to 10 weeks to roughly 30 minutes by automating catalogue syncing and the submission process. The broader proposition is that merchants need more than visibility on AI platforms: they also need structured catalogues, storefronts and payment infrastructure that can work inside conversational interfaces. Razorpay has been building these layers as it seeks to establish itself as an infrastructure provider for AI-led commerce. This also marks a continuation of Razorpay's partnership with OpenAI and NPCI around agentic payments. The company has been experimenting with UPI Circle and UPI Reserve Pay to enable purchases within ChatGPT, while keeping payment credentials away from the AI model and requiring user consent for transactions. Razorpay's push comes as other payment companies, including Cashfree and Pine Labs, are also building infrastructure for agentic commerce, suggesting that payment providers see the AI interface as a potential new layer between consumers and merchants rather than simply another checkout channel. The partnership also marks another step in Razorpay's expansion beyond its core payments business. Razorpay was founded in 2014 by IIT Roorkee alumni Shashank Kumar and Harshil Mathur and has expanded from payments into a broader suite of business and banking solutions. Razorpay launched Engage in 2023 as a full-stack growth marketing platform, offering businesses customer acquisition, retention and engagement tools. The platform provides personalised incentives, gift cards and targeted rewards across an inventory of more than 5,000 options. Its AI push, meanwhile, extends beyond commerce and advertising. In August, Razorpay launched Vulcan, a proprietary AI foundation model designed to improve payment success, fraud detection and transaction routing, underlining the company's broader attempt to build AI into its payments infrastructure. Razorpay has also been developing Agent Studio, its platform for deploying task-specific AI agents for businesses. Around 200 businesses were using the platform in beta as of August, with use cases including reconciliation, abandoned-cart recovery, subscription recovery and finance operations. The company has previously described this as a broader “distribution layer” across different agentic touchpoints, including merchant websites, independent agent platforms and large language model platforms, rather than a bet solely on ChatGPT. The startup, which has raised over $800 M from investors like Tiger Global, Y Combinator, Lightspeed, is gearing up for a public markets debut soon.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

The zardozi embroidery on a Dior dress, the T-strap leather sandals at a Prada show, the mirror-work technique used on a Fendi bag – for decades, the skill of Indian artisans has been an invisible force behind some of the world’s most coveted fashion.
Now, that work is beginning to claim its own place in the spotlight, and the Mumbai-based textile and embroidery atelier Chanakya International is at the forefront.
Chanakya marked its 40th anniversary this month, celebrating with three exhibitions that trace its journey from an embroidery powerhouse to a present-day craft and cultural institution. The person steering it is 49-year-old Karishma Swali, whose father set up the group’s operations in the 1980s.
“What we have as a country is unique,” she tells me of India’s rich textile and craft heritage. “It’s unparalleled in many ways, and it’s the only place where we continue to practise it.” During the Renaissance, she says, France and Italy had established and varied traditions. “But what we have in India today is [what] other parts of the world have lost.”
Chanakya has a network of 1,400 artisans, and says that some are 13th-generation craftspeople, skilled in hundreds of embroidery traditions and supplying almost every luxury label you can imagine. Among the techniques they have revived is the Mughal-era silver filigree lace, or chaand jaal, reintroduced in a lighter form that has since become a regular feature in couture collections.
In 2023, Dior held a show at Mumbai’s Gateway of India, showcasing its partnership with Chanakya, in a high-profile acknowledgment of Indian craftsmanship. The runway saw sari-inspired skirts, vibrant madras-checks sets and Nehru-collar jackets.
These collaborations are supported by expert craft knowledge passed down and refined over generations, and they need institutional support to survive. The Kalhath Institute, a craft-preservation centre in Lucknow, runs residencies that pair artists from across the world with local artisans.
Kalhath’s co-founder Mohammed Amine Dadda tells me that Indian craftsmanship’s defining quality is “intelligence of the hand” – a sensitive, slow and cumulative process underpinned by patience and dexterity. “Without this technical mastery, and the considerable time required to create the most demanding pieces, haute couture and contemporary luxury simply could not bring their most ambitious creative visions to life.”
This mastery is not limited to textiles. When it comes to jewellery, global luxury brands have long sought Jaipur-based the Gem Palace, established in 1852 by the Kasliwal family, who still run it today. Samarth Kasliwal, 33, says part of the appeal lies in the visual language of Indian artistry itself. “There is something about Indian artistry that is inspired by nature,” he tells me, pointing to the recurring use of floral patterns and animals across Indian art and design. These motifs are universal, and travel across the lines of culture and language.
One recent collaboration Kasliwal is particularly proud of is a collection for Dior featuring green onyx and rock crystals, with engravings of birds, animals and flowers. The combination, he says, is reminiscent of traditional Indian jewellery, while drawing on techniques that remain central to the atelier’s work today.
With increased visibility, the question of credit and appropriation has become harder to ignore. Last week, a Ralph Lauren gown from the designer’s spring 2027 collection attracted criticism after many Indians pointed out that the embroidery the brand described as “embellishments” looked a lot like Indian zardozi, but without any accompanying credit. (Ralph Lauren did not respond to my request for comment.)
Then, Fendi came under fire when people noticed that a baguette bag from its autumn/winter collection featured mirrorwork often seen in Gujarati crafts. In April, Fendi credited Chanakya artisans in a social media video showcasing the same embroidery. But the product description on its site failed to mention any Indian inspiration, and its final label read “Made in Italy”.
After I asked Fendi about the discrepancy, the brand cited its “creative partnership” with Chanakya of more than three decades, saying it “remains committed to supporting and recognizing India’s rich craft heritage”. The website descriptor now reads: “Made in Italy and India with Chanakya”.
A recent Financial Times report noted that under EU rules, garments embroidered in India can still end up with a European label – so long as the final construction and finishing take place in Europe.
Last year, Prada was accused of appropriating Indian culture with Kolhapuri-inspired sandals, a controversy that showed us these debates around recognition can sometimes produce a more structural response. “We acknowledge the sandals … are inspired by traditional Indian handcrafted footwear, with a centuries-old heritage,” Lorenzo Bertelli, the corporate social responsibility chief at the Italian fashion house, had written in a letter to the Maharashtra chamber of commerce at the time.
Prada subsequently partnered with state-backed organisations in Maharashtra and Karnataka to produce a limited-edition collection, Made in India, and committed to a three-year training programme for artisans specialising in the craft.
Might these collaborations, controversies and corrections represent a shift in India’s place in the fashion industry? Anthropologist Phyllida Jay, author of Inspired by India: How India Transformed Global Design, appears to think so, placing the debate in a longer arc. “The stories of the ateliers producing highly skilled Indian craft in the elevated realm of European luxury and high fashion is part of a broader paradigm shift,” she writes, “where over 70 years after the end of colonial rule, India is being looked at in a different way on the world stage.” It is, in a way, a reversal, moving from a colonial history of extraction toward one in which Indians themselves get a voice in how their craft is represented.
Swali is ensuring this visibility also lives on through the Chanakya School of Craft, which she set up in 2016. Its 18-month programme provides free embroidery training and a travel honorarium to dozens of women, some of whom have gone on to work at the main atelier. Others have set up their own independent studios.
I had a chance to visit the space – inside a high-rise in Lower Parel, where those as young as 18 learn intricate needlework alongside grandmothers in their 60s. “Craft in India has never been institutionalised,” Swali says of the ethos behind the initiative. “It’s intergenerational,” she says, adding that women have often been excluded.
India’s culture of craft has always been precious. Growing up, I loved having the choice to affordably create any type of clothing. At one point, I had a small army of tailors, each with a different specialisation, whom I’d go to for different needs. I’d buy ajrakh and mashru silks from Dastkar or Nalli, and hand it to the right Masterji to stitch, embroider and tweak to my size. So, to me, Indian craftsmanship is not just a part of luxury, but a luxury itself.
What else we’re reading about
Travel | Time Out just confirmed what everyone in Mumbai’s Bandra West knows: that it’s one of the coolest neighbourhoods in the world. The other Indian spot to make the cut is Delhi’s food and fashion centre, Humayunpur. The top spot went to Jongno 3-ga in Seoul – my second home!

Ashneer Grover, co-founder and former CEO of fintech firm BharatPe slammed the move, describing it as “tax collection”.
Immigration | An investigation by Scroll’s Rokibuz Zaman has revealed a troubling pattern in West Bengal: since June, at least nine Muslim men and two children have been picked up by the police from their homes over allegations that they are Bangladeshi nationals – without being given a chance to prove their citizenship. Most were picked up and detained in midnight raids, the report said, and family members accused the police of not producing warrants.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Fashion designer Payal Khandwala, whose spring-summer ’26 collection featured handwoven silks, cottons and brocades, recommends the perfect saree weave: “The delicate poetry of a Jamdani saree is definitely my favourite. A 2,000-year-old craft, typically woven in fine muslin and of Bengali origin, it’s somewhat an unsung hero. The weaving process itself is exceptionally intricate. Using a supplementary weft technique, thousands of markings are meticulously mapped on to the warp to recreate the pattern, interlaced by hand with a wooden shuttle and metallic needle to guide the motifs in silver and gold yarn, on fine mulberry silk and organza.”

Vibe check
The true measure of my love for my friends is in the number of memes I send them. One of the accounts I rely on is Bahaish Kapoor’s. The screenwriter-turned-meme evangelist pairs black-and-white Bollywood stills with contemporary gen Z sass, and lets incongruity do the rest. What makes an image meme-worthy? “I always look for people who are in a deep philosophical, romantic, dramatic action moment which I can repurpose to bring in a whole new meaning,” he tells me. “I try to mix and match and see what’s working.” His 340,000-plus followers include Sharon Stone and Hrithik Roshan.
“I just want to make people feel a little better,” says Kapoor, adding that he receives a lot of DMs from people about how his page helped them through a bad day. “People confessing that they are lighter because of this experience is all that I can hope for. I mean, that’s the endgame.”

£800m in, £800m out - Why Man City scandal shines light on Man Utd finances
- Published
The Premier League panel's report laid it out in black and white.
"The club's income was hugely overstated by over £830 million."
In other words, Manchester City's owners circumvented the league's financial regulations over a number of years by pumping money into the club that should not have been recorded as sponsorship income.
The damning judgement landed less than five days after Manchester United's extended filing to the New York Stock Exchange which detailed their end of year accounts to 30 June 2026.
Contained within it was an interest payment of £37m, an increase from £34m the previous year.
And respected football finance blogger Swiss Ramble now estimates that United's net interest payments since the leveraged Glazer takeover of the club in 2005 have risen to a total of £852m.
Without excusing City's owners in any way, it has not escaped the attentions of many fans from both Manchester clubs that while the arrival of one ownership group in the city resulted in money being ploughed in, it meant a similar significant sum being paid out in interest for the other.
Maintaining financial discipline
United's latest accounts included this comment from chief executive Omar Berrada: "While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable."
This came after a third-place finish in the Premier League, which confirmed a return to the Champions League after a two-year absence.
Record revenues of £677.6m, projected to go as high as £760m in 2026-27, is something to celebrate.
Yet Berrada's cautious stance underlined a few home truths.
In confirming they had spent £191.7m on new players; notably Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, and costs associated with them, plus academy players such as England youth international Tynan Thompson, since 30 June, with payments due 'in the next five years'. United also revealed they had borrowed an additional £90m. It took their overall debt to £1.15bn.
To put that into context, in accounts to June 2021, the comparable sum was £667m.
Prior to 30 June, United's transfer debt was £375m. Of that, £218m must be paid before 30 June 2027. United have also said in addition to Baleba, Santos and Tielemans, they are liable for another £122.8m in potential contract payments if players they have already signed hit pre-agreed targets – although presumably the club would be happy if they ended up paying this.
When they restructured their debt in June, United added $125m (£94.36m) to their main debt. On 23 September, they said £63.5m had been spent on land for their proposed new stadium, the precise funding model for which is still to be determined.
Many fans, particularly those who do not want a new stadium, feel that money would have been better invested in Michael Carrick's squad.
Yet, as Berrada said, United are taking a 'disciplined approach' on that.
In 2025, United had the fifth highest wage bill in the Premier League, at £313m. The absence of European football means that sum dropped to £302m in 2025-26. No other clubs have released their figures yet, but it would be a major surprise if United climbed any higher, meaning Carrick over-achieved by finishing third. United's wages to turnover ratio is 45%. No club had a better figure than that last season.
While there are variables and also notable exceptions, including the Old Trafford outfit themselves who over the past decade, have topped the annual salary cost table but not the actual Premier League, and in 2024-25 finished 15th despite those fifth highest wage costs, there is a general correlation between salaries and performance.
Yet, while United were relatively restrained on the transfer front in terms of spending this summer – their £148m outlay was below that of newly-promoted Ipswich and Hull among others – their recent net spend has been high. The reason for this is clear.
When the most recent transfer window closed on 1 September, they had generated £47m from sales. It put them 11th in the Premier League. Only Liverpool of their 'big six' rivals brought in less.
Since they sold striker Romelu Lukaku to Inter Milan for £74m in 2019, United have only generated more than £25m for a player on four occasions – for Mason Greenwood, Scott McTominay, Rasmus Hojlund and Alejandro Garnacho.
It was instructive this summer a series of young players were sold, either for a lower fee than anticipated in the cases of Radek Vitek and Toby Collyer, who joined Middlesbrough and West Brom respectively, or none, like defenders Tyler Fredricson and James Overy. In all cases though, the transfers included significant sell-on and buy-back clauses, which is part of a strategy by United to generate more revenue from player sales.
In June 2023, Premier League clubs voted to cap future leveraged buyouts at around 65% of a club's value. The move seemed to be in response to ALK Capital's takeover of Burnley in December 2020.
Many United fans feel the move was 18 years too late.
The negativity around Manchester City's scandal has indirectly, shone a light on the situation at Old Trafford.
Given there is little realistic chance of the substantive debt being paid off, Berrada and his colleagues must navigate the tricky balance of keeping costs under control, trimming the outstanding transfer fees, not extending the revolving credit limit and funding a new stadium – all while spending enough to deliver on the pitch.
In 2017-18, United made £80m in prize money from their run to the Champions League quarter-finals. In 2024-25, they got £31m for reaching the Europa League final. In their recently negotiated shirt deal with Adidas, a £10m annual reduction is applied if the club miss out on reaching the Champions League.
When Carrick sends his team out against bottom-club Tottenham at Old Trafford on 10 October, they will be attempting to drag themselves up from 12th place in the table.
The overall target is undefined, but it is pretty clear Champions League qualification will be a significant part of it.

Think about what you’re wearing right now. Did you pick it out? Or was it chosen for you by an algorithm you haven’t even considered?
Can thrift shops save us from Shein?
Ultra-fast fashion is everywhere. Thrift shops offer a way out.
You may think it’s the former, but with the state of the fashion industry, it’s likely the latter. There was a time when taste was decided by designers at luxury fashion houses, à la Karl Lagerfeld at Chanel, or Anna Wintour-type magazine editors (think of the famous cerulean sweater monologue from The Devil Wears Prada). Now, in the era of fast fashion, our clothing options are often dictated by computers.
Amy Odell writes the Back Row newsletter and hosts a podcast with the same name. She told Vox that what’s known as fast fashion has been kicked into hyperdrive by companies like Shein.
“I’ve also heard it called instant fashion,” she says. “The way it works is that they use algorithms to track trends and what people are interested in, and then they make a few hundred of a very large number of different items and they test demand.” She says this model has allowed companies like Shein to introduce around 4,700 new apparel styles per day. (For comparison, fast fashion brand Zara produces around 20,000 a year.)
Some are trying to claw back their personal style by hitting the thrift store instead. Traditionally, it’s where people go to find less expensive clothes. But fashion journalist Hannah Marriott says it can be so much more than that.
“For the last probably a hundred years, [the thrift store] has had lots of moments where it’s been cool within countercultures,” Marriott told Vox. “Whether it’s grunge, or the surrealists in the 1920s, or the Rolling Stones in the 1960s, secondhand clothing was cool because of the stigma.”
So how did thrifting go from stigmatized to chic? And are thrift stores still thrifty now that they’re more mainstream, especially in an era of ultra-cheap Shein clothing? We find out that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Marriott, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
There’s sometimes this stigma that’s attached to buying secondhand clothes. How has its perception changed over time?
Secondhand clothing used to be something that there was a real sense that if you couldn’t buy new, you would buy secondhand. At the same time, it has had lots of moments where it’s been cool within countercultures.
People within countercultures — whether it’s grunge, or the surrealists in the 1920s, or the Rolling Stones in the 1960s — secondhand clothing was cool because of the stigma. It’s also been a really important resource for people on lower incomes for a long time.
I think it was a gradual shift by various things that happened in the pandemic, including this absolute influx of apps [like The RealReal and Depop] that got very, very popular during that time, particularly among younger Gen Z consumers.
Thrifting became a social currency on social media platforms, especially on TikTok. It’s a vast ecosystem at the moment, and all of them have slightly different business models, slightly different fees that they charge, and slightly different audiences that they’re reaching. The stigma has really gone away, and it’s almost reversed.
What does that ecosystem look like?
There are different layers to it. There are consignment places like The RealReal where they take quite a big cut, but they will promote your items for you. I think those sites tend to work best if you’ve actually got designer clothes that have quite a big margin, particularly handbags.
Then there are other sites that are a bit more laid-back: eBay maybe skews a bit older, Depop skews a bit younger and trendier. There’s Vinted, which I know from the UK, but is making inroads into the US now. There’s ThreadUp as well. Poshmark.
It’s an absolutely vast ecosystem at the moment, and all of them have slightly different business models, slightly different fees that they charge, and slightly different audiences that they’re reaching.
One of the biggest secondhand shops here in the US is still Goodwill. Can you walk me through how Goodwill has adapted and changed to the secondhand boom?
Neighborhood thrift stores of that kind are the sort of stores that people on lower incomes do rely on more. It’s less trend-led than something like Depop. And it is somewhere that people have often been going for decades to get clothes that they can afford.
Goodwill undeniably has put its prices up. Inflation is such an issue for everyone, so I’m sure that there would be an element of prices going up anyway, but a lot of shoppers feel strongly that they’ve gone up a lot — that you can’t find bargains anymore, that the bargains get sent online to either their website or are bought by resellers who sell them for an inflated price online.
It’s hard to get to the bottom of exactly how true all of that is, especially because Goodwill is run as 150 autonomous [nonprofits], and each of them set their own prices. But what I would say is you are seeing things like the Goodwill branch in Connecticut charging $75 bucks to go on a thrift tour coach to get early access to a Goodwill store, and then you get to go to another store. You used to be able to buy 10 things in Goodwill for $75.
It’s so interesting that thrifting used to be this edgy original thing, but it’s really gone mainstream. Has it sold out?
I remember when I was much younger, people would say, “Ooh, you got that secondhand.” I just don’t think anyone would ever say that now because that’s kind of how we shop.
But I still think it is great if you find something original that you love that no one else has, and I still think you’re more likely to find it secondhand or in certain other under-the-radar brands that aren’t fast fashion.
I think maybe this is a reaction to 30 years of fast fashion just getting faster and faster and faster. I think we’re all feeling a bit tired of that business model, so we’re trying to find other ways to shop and express ourselves.

The CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic have been called to appear at an Australian Senate inquiry on AI, the head of the probe said on Sunday, September 27, 2026, days after the revelation that a rogue OpenAI bot had hacked the country's health-system database.
The Medicare breach, condemned by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the U.S.
OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei have been sent written requests to appear at the inquiry, which is to hold public hearings in the capital Canberra on Thursday, said a spokesperson for Senator Sarah Hanson-Young of the Australian Greens party, who chairs the probe.
OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to requests for comment outside business hours.
The OpenAI agent's incursion on one of the country's most used government agencies may prompt Albanese's Labor government to toughen AI-specific laws it is readying for next year, adding pressure to Australia-US relations already tested by Canberra's ban on social media for teens, tech policy experts say.
The Senate inquiry is examining the potential impacts of AI and data centres on Australian communities, industries, water and energy. It is one of several state and federal probes into AI.
"There are serious questions for Sam Altman to answer about the OpenAI hack of Australian government websites," Hanson-Young said in a statement. Altman and Amodei "must front up, face the Senate's questions and have an honest conversation about what effective, lasting regulation of this industry should look like", she said.
Albanese, who revealed the June breach of Medicare on Thursday, called it "unacceptable", saying he had voiced "extreme concern" to Altman.
OpenAI says it only learned of the breach — one of at least four of Australian government websites — in August. It says the incident was not intentional and did not compromise any private information.

A 1-kg mass of hair was removed from the stomach and small intestine of a nine-year-old girl in a rare surgery at a private hospital in Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam, authorities said on Saturday.
The girl, who was diagnosed with Rapunzel syndrome, underwent the surgery at NIMS Medicity in nearby Neyyattinkara, they said.
She was admitted to the hospital with persistent abdominal pain and vomiting, according to a statement issued by the hospital. Ultrasound and CT scans revealed severe intestinal obstruction, and a subsequent endoscopy confirmed a large mass of hair accumulated in the stomach and small intestine.
The hairball was completely removed through a complex surgical procedure led by Dr Biju I G Nair, senior consultant in the Department of Paediatric Surgery at the hospital. The girl recovered well, resumed eating normally and was discharged, the doctor said.
Dr Nair said a trichobezoar, or hairball, forms when a person repeatedly pulls out and swallows hair. The swallowed hair cannot be digested and can gradually accumulate in the stomach, forming a hard mass that may cause intestinal obstruction over time, he said.
Rare condition
Rapunzel syndrome is an extremely rare condition in which a trichobezoar extends from the stomach into the small intestine. It is usually seen in adolescent girls, according to medical literature. Hospital authorities said fewer than 100 cases have been reported worldwide.

Anthropic vs. the pope
Claude’s creators are worried the LLM could be conscious. The Catholic Church disagrees.
Hi readers, happy Friday! It’s been a big week for the AI debate — not the one about whether it will cause the robot apocalypse, though there’s still plenty to worry about there, but instead about whether the technology is conscious.
The folks at Anthropic, the AI company behind the large language model Claude, certainly seem to think it is — or at least, they’re extremely open to the possibility.
As the New York Times reported earlier in the week, the company has spent the last year grappling with the question by speaking with religious thinkers from many faith traditions in an effort to chart a moral course for the LLM (that is, to keep it from killing us all, so maybe it is all one big debate).
In the process, the Times reports, some of those thinkers observed that members of the Anthropic team were “relating to [Claude] like a conscious being” and even, according to it, a degree of “moral status.”
On the flip side of this debate is Pope Leo XIV, who decidedly does not seem to buy into AI consciousness arguments. His “Magnifica Humanitas” encyclical earlier this year argued that AI will never be able to replace humanity — and reportedly “alarmed” Anthropic’s co-founder, Christopher Olah.
Since then, Pope Leo has continued to emphasize the differences between humans and machines this week. “There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others,” he posted on Friday. “Algorithms lack the spark of humanity.”
Loneliness machines
Conscious or no (and that’s a no from me), it’s hard to argue that tech companies don’t want you to interact with their models like people. That includes OpenAI and Meta, both of whom introduced “cute” new AI agents — called Dots and Muse, respectively — last month.
As my colleague Adam Clark Estes reported this week, though, the promise of a companionable, always-there AI might not be the best idea in the world — especially for children. A new study, still under review, suggests that AI use may be causing loneliness in middle schoolers.
Adam spoke with the lead researcher on the study, UNC Chapel Hill professor Anne Maheux, who explained that “middle school students using AI for emotional intimacy and companionship developed greater loneliness over time.”
According to Maheux, one big point where AI chatbots fail compared to human beings is “friction,” or the complicated push-and-pull dynamic of any connection with a real human being. By contrast, chatbots are “sycophantic, highly agreeable, anthropomorphized,” she says, which can lead to kids “developing expectations or understandings of interactive relationships that are actually fundamentally at odds with a normal human relationship.”
People, in other words, still matter, no matter how much the AI companies want us to build our lives around machines instead.
One link for later
➨ Why is horror so fun? It’s October, which means you might be planning a horror movie marathon or a trip to a haunted house/forest/corn maze/what have you in the near future. It’ll probably be a great time — but why? Terrifying yourself doesn’t intuitively sound like fun, but humans love to seek out frights, whether that means ghost stories or a rollercoaster. In 2024, Vox’s Unexplainable podcast spoke with some researchers trying to figure it out.
