Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beat the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but failed to secure the outright majority he needed to avoid a runoff.
With more than 99% of votes counted, the 45-year-old son of the disgraced former president, Jair Bolsonaro, had won 47.1%, meaning he will now face a 25 October showdown with his 80-year-old rival. Lula received 45%.
Bolsonaro will go into the second round as favourite and is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates, who included Ronaldo Caiado, who secured 2.1%, and Renan Santos, who won 2.2%.
Brazil’s far-right put in a stronger than expected showing, with a succession of Bolsonarista politicians winning congressional or gubernatorial races. They included Jair Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, and his wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who both won seats in the senate. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, Jair Renan, was elected to the lower house of congress. Bolsonaro’s former infrastructure minister, Tarcísio de Freitas, was reelected as governor of São Paulo, Brazil’s most populous and economically important state.
Of the 54 senators elected, 34 were from the right or far right.
Speaking in Sāo Paulo, Lula put a brave face on a difficult night for the left. “We have just had a lesson in Brazilian democracy,” he said. “The result is often unexpected. We can never get everything we wanted. I confess to you that I was convinced I was going to win the election in the first round … But we have a second round.”
Lula said Bolsonaro’s “dark past” would become clearer to voters in the lead-up to that vote. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil.”
Earlier, as he cast this vote, Lula said Latin America’s largest democracy faced a stark choice, highlighting his adversary’s well-documented links to members of Rio’s underworld, including once employing close relatives of a notorious contract killer.
After voting in Rio, where the Bolsonaro political dynasty was born in the late 80s, Flávio Bolsonaro urged Brazilians to end what he called Lula’s “era of backwardness”. “I’m more than ready to lead this country and to give Brazilian families the right to dream once again,” claimed Bolsonaro, who has promised an iron-fisted crackdown on crime, despite his ties to members of Rio’s paramilitary mafias.
Lula, who became Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002 and was returned to office in 2006 and 2022, is hoping to secure a historic fourth non-consecutive term in this year’s election.
Allies of the veteran leftwinger called the election a crucial battle in the fight against a far-right movement that less than four years ago brought chaos to the capital, Brasília, during an unsuccessful attempt to overturn the result of the 2022 election, when Lula beat the incumbent president, Jair Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro hopes winning the presidency will allow him to free his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after refusing to accept he had lost the last election to Lula. Ahead of the election he also called for tactical voting from conservatives who are not supporters of Bolsonarismo, but want to vote Lula out of power.
As well as the president, Brazil’s nearly 159 million voters were choosing state parliamentarians, 27 state governors, 513 members of the lower house and 54 members of the 81-seat senate. Bolsonaro supporters made the senate race a priority because senators are the only lawmakers who can impeach supreme court justices – a demand among Bolsonaristas since the court jailed the former president for attempting a coup.
Hundreds of leftwingers had gathered at the heart of Laranjeiras, one of Rio’s most leftwing neighbourhoods, hoping to celebrate a Lula win to the sound of samba. But the mood soured and tears were shed as the hours passed and Bolsonaro’s lead over Lula held.
“It’s so sad that the Brazilian people … have opted for so much retrogression,” said Marcelo Mac, one of the owners of Miolo, a leftwing bar in Laranjeiras, as the scale of the rightwing advance was confirmed on Sunday night.
Mac, 46, voiced perplexity that the son of the man who tried to stage a coup only four years ago was now in pole position to become Brazil’s next leader. “He’s such an abominable guy that he manages to be even worse than his father,” Mac said of Bolsonaro.
Beside the bar a yellow flag stamped with Lula’s face carried the slogan: “Turn left”. But Brazil had voted for a turn to the far right.
Bolsonaro seemed to have the wind in his sails in the final days before Sunday’s vote, amid public frustration at a cost of living crisis and urban violence.
But opinion polls failed to predict the scale of the rightwing triumph.
Shop assistant Italo Andrade dos Santos, a 31-year-old Bolsonaro voter, had to keep his celebrations restrained behind the counter of the pharmacy where he was working a Sunday night shift. “I was a little disappointed because I expected Flávio to win in the first round. But I’m happy he’s ahead,” said Santos, adding that he voted “more to get Lula out than for Flávio himself”.
Donald Trump became a key election issue, with Lula accusing the US president of trying to swing the vote in Bolsonaro’s favour in order to “colonise” Brazil and appropriate its natural resources. Bolsonaro has vowed to build a closer relationship with Trump, who hopes a rightwing victory will help him further cement US control over Latin America after the election of pro-Trump leaders in a succession of countries, including Chile, Colombia and Peru.

The Supreme Court on Monday (September 28, 2026) questioned the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) over its proposed deadline – of nearly two years — for implementing front-of-pack warning labels (FoPL) on packaged foods, asking why it wanted to “waste so much time” on fresh public and industry consultations when the issue concerned citizens’ health.
The court’s remarks came as it pressed the food safety regulator to expedite the introduction of warning labels on packaged foods high in sugar, salt and saturated fat.
Responding to the court’s September 10 order, which raised several questions over the size, colour, and placement of the proposed labels as well as the timeline for their implementation, the FSSAI said in an affidavit filed last week that the draft regulations would require a four-month process of consultation and finalisation. It proposed notifying the labelling norms by July 1 next year, following which food business operators would be given another 365 days to transition to the new regime to ensure minimal hardship.
“Why voluntary compliance for a year? Why do you need so much time? Why do you want to start afresh with the exercise of hearing and calling for objections? You started in 2022. What did you do in the last four years?” a Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran asked while reserving its order in the matter.
PIL petition
The top court was hearing a public interest litigation (PIL) petition filed by non-profit organisation 3S and Our Health Society, seeking the introduction of FoPL guidelines on the lines of those in force in foreign jurisdictions. The petitioner, represented by advocate Rajiv Shankar Dwivedi, has argued that such labels are necessary to warn children and other consumers about packaged foods containing high levels of salt, sugar and saturated fat, and their potential adverse health effects.
Additional Solicitor-General Brijender Chahar, appearing for the Centre and the FSSAI, explained that the exercise initiated in 2022 concerned the Indian Nutrition Rating (star-rating) system and was based on a different yardstick from the warning-label regime now under consideration.
“Today, the yardstick is completely different. We have set four months for drafting the regulations. The rest we leave it to my Lords — how much time should be given for compliance,” Mr. Chahar submitted.
Public health goal
Justice Pardiwala appreciated the steps taken by the regulator so far, but said much more remained to be done to give meaningful effect to the court’s objective of protecting public health. The Bench also indicated that it would seek to strike a “balance” while fixing a reasonable timeline to roll out the warning labels.
“We appreciate whatever you have done so far, and we appreciate your initiative, but there is a lot which is required to be done to give meaningful effect to what we want to achieve… We are undertaking this entire exercise for the good of the nation, for the good of the citizens, so we expect the authority to accept our order in its true spirit,” the Bench said.
The Bench further made it clear that its forthcoming directions would be binding on the regulator and said it expected the FSSAI to implement them “scrupulously” and in their “true spirit”. The court also indicated that it would keep the matter pending to monitor compliance with its directions.
“We will now pronounce the final order. We will again keep it for some time to ensure due compliance with each and every direction. Do not disappoint us on the day when the matter comes up for reporting compliance,” the Bench told the regulator.
Single-phase proposal
In its affidavit filed earlier, the FSSAI had told the top court that it was prepared to roll out FoPL for packaged foods in a single phase, departing from its earlier proposal for a two-stage implementation based on the number of “nutrients of concern” present in a product.
“The FSSAI proposes to adopt a single-phase approach for the implementation of Front-of-Pack Nutrition Labelling. To finalise the draft regulations, it requires a four-month period, and there shall be a ‘voluntary implementation period of 365 days’ by Food Business Operators (FBOs),” the affidavit had stated.
On the design of the warning label, the regulator modified its earlier proposal for a red hexagon and suggested placing the hexagon against a white, square-shaped background, drawing from the labelling format followed in Canada.
The FSSAI also clarified that the warning requirement would not be confined to products containing high levels of two or more nutrients of concern. Packaged foods exceeding the prescribed threshold for even one such nutrient would carry the warning.
Under the proposed framework, the warning label would be prominently placed on the top-left corner of the front of the package for greater visibility. The warning would also appear in a font larger than that used for the nutritional information displayed on the back of the pack.
Note of caution
Earlier, the top court had also flagged a possible unintended consequence of the proposed regime. It had noted that requiring manufacturers to reduce salt, sugar and fat — ingredients that add to taste, texture, and shelf life — could prompt greater reliance on artificial preservatives, emulsifiers and other additives.
The Bench had therefore asked the FSSAI to examine this possibility and consider corresponding regulatory safeguards to ensure that reducing one set of potentially harmful ingredients does not result in their substitution with other additives that could pose health concerns.
For determining the products that would require such warnings, the FSSAI has proposed adopting threshold values for added sugar, added fat used in cooking, and salt per 100 g/ml, as prescribed in the Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024, issued by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN).

- U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced the creation of an Office of Religious Affairs at the Department of Defense on Sept. 30, 2026, during a speech he called the "State of the Force" address.
- Hegseth suggested the Office of Religious Affairs would address urgent spiritual needs among the troops, which he said had long been neglected. He said the office would report directly to him and that budgets would be guaranteed both for chaplaincy and infrastructure, such as "base chapels."
- Hegseth said that "less than 5% of our force identifies as non-religious," without citing his source for the number. A 2019 congressional report found that while 2.3% of the force identified as agnostic or atheist, the affiliation of 24.4% of active duty personnel fell under "Other/Unclassified/Unknown."
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have reached out to the DOD to ask what concrete actions the office will take. We also reached out to the American Humanist Association and are waiting for responses.
In October 2026, a rumor spread that U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had announced the creation of an Office of Religious Affairs at the Pentagon.
The claim spread on social media, including X. One X post included a video of Hegseth speaking on a stage with a U.S. flag background (archived):
"Today, at my direction, I am establishing the Office of Religious Affairs," Hegseth says in the video. "Starting today, and for secretaries of war after me, the Office of Religious Affairs will report straight to the top. No staff filters. No bureaucratic dilution. A direct line to the secretary."
Meanwhile, several Snopes readers searched the website seeking more information about the supposed Office of Religious Affairs.
It is true that on Sept. 30, 2026, Hegseth gave a speech he called the "State of the Force" address. In this speech, he said he had ordered the creation of an office dedicated to religious affairs, which Department of Defense spokesperson Sean Parnell confirmed in an X post (archived):
We reached out to the DOD seeking more details about the initiative and will update this story if we learn more.
Here's what we know about the new DOD office so far:
Office of Religious Affairs
In his speech, Hegseth said the initiative would address what he described as long-neglected spiritual needs among the troops (starting around the 50:25 mark of the DOD's recording of the speech):
After describing how significant the loss of a religious community could be for military personnel assigned to a new location or deployed abroad, Hegseth said that "political correctness and secular humanism" had allowed budgets for religious support to dwindle and infrastructure such as "base chapels" to go into disarray.
Religious diversity in the force
Hegseth said that "less than 5% of our force identifies as non-religious," without citing his source for the number. A 2019 congressional report found that while 2.3% of the force identified as agnostic or atheist, the affiliation of 24.4% of active duty personnel fell under "Other/Unclassified/Unknown" (PDF Page 51).
Meanwhile, the Military Association of Atheists and Freethinkers, an organization that advocates for nonreligious military members but is not associated with the DOD, said 2.05% of the force identified as "Humanists" in 2018 (Humanism is a non-theistic belief; Humanists believe in a moral and ethical code without believing in God). That report also said the chaplaincy did not represent the religious diversity of the military, with an overrepresentation of evangelistic Christians, when only 13.31% of the troops identified as such.
We reached out to the MAAF for comment on the creation of the office. A spokesperson told us the group was in the process of dissolving and directed us to the American Humanist Association, a nonprofit that advocates for secular humanism. We will update this story if the AHA returns our request for a statement on the possible impact of the creation of the office on nonreligious service members.
In May 2026, the DOD released a list of recognized religions in a memorandum signed by Undersecretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony Tata. The memo included 31 religions, down from 211, according to Military.com, the news outlet dedicated to reporting on the U.S. Military. Twenty-two of those 31 were Christian denominations.
Hegseth then announced the creation of the Office of Religious Affairs, designed to report directly to him in the Pentagon organizational chart. In his announcement, he said (around 52:32 of the video embedded above):
This won't be a paper pushing shop. It will have real teeth. It will protect budgets, demand infrastructure, and strengthen religious support. The experts, our chaplains, will finally have an advocate at the highest levels. Policy and resources will serve the mission, not smother the mission.
'Spiritual readiness' and 'spiritual resilience'
A memo issued on the same day confirmed the creation of the office. It read, in part:
The Department of War is committed to fulfilling its duty to support the Department's Service members, their families, and the Department's civilian personnel in the free exercise of religion as protected by the Constitution of the United States and applicable Federal law. While the Department accomplishes this mission primarily through the chaplaincies of the Military Departments established under title 10, U.S. Code, the establishment of the ORA will ensure resources are adequately provided and, where necessary, policy is properly aligned to prioritize the free exercise of religion and the spiritual readiness across the Total Force.
Still, Hegseth's memo said, this effort to support the spirituality of military personnel should not "be construed to compel religious participation or to diminish the free exercise rights of any Service member, civilian employee, or family member of any faith or no faith."
The memo also said the new office had 90 days to present a plan of action to rebuild the spiritual force of the military:
Within 90 days of the date of this memorandum, the Secretaries of the Military Departments, in coordination with their respective Chiefs of Chaplains, will submit to the Director a comprehensive baseline report of all unfunded and underfunded religious affairs requirements, including, but not limited to, delivery ofreligious ministry, facilities and infrastructure, logistics, chaplain-led programs, chapel youth programs, faith-based homeschool support for military families, programs related to suicide reduction, and contracted services from faith-based non-Federal entities; research, technology, and analytical tools to support spiritual fitness, spiritual readiness, and spiritual resilience; chaplain in-service procurement programs, chaplain and religious support team training and education.
For further reading, Snopes examined another announcement Hegseth made that day, the launch of "Project Meridian," set to study the "future of warfare."

The National Weather Service in the US has issued extreme heat warnings for parts of southern California, including Los Angeles, until Thursday, as temperatures are expected to hit the high 30s celsius. Burbank, a suburb north of Los Angeles, recorded 39C on Saturday, a few degrees shy of the October record for the region set in 1987. A persistent area of high pressure will remain in place this week, leading to further hazardous hot weather and increased fire risk.
Parts of Indonesia are in the midst of an extreme wildfire season, which has peaked over the past month. Western Kalimantan (Borneo) and southern Sumatra have been particularly badly affected. The lack of rainfall has dried the usually water-logged tropical soils, meaning that fires have been able to spread quickly, above and below the surface. Indonesia’s soils are also extremely rich in peat, meaning that the smoke produced from the fires contain higher levels of toxic gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide. Cities in surrounding areas and as far as Malaysia and Singapore have experienced reduced air quality in recent weeks as a result. Drought and wildfires are more common in this part of the world during El Niño events owing to suppressed thunderstorm activity.
On the flip side, El Niño is contributing to an extremely active period for tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean. After recent hurricanes in the eastern half of the basin, Super Typhoon Choi-Wan is now active and a category 4 typhoon to the south-east of Japan, while on a strengthening trend. After developing on 30 September, Choi-Wan moved through the Northern Mariana Islands as a tropical storm, causing power outages on the island of Tinian, forcing the closure of schools and government offices. Choi-Wan underwent rapid intensification after clearing the islands on Sunday, and as of Sunday night has sustained winds of 150mph, and gusts of up to 180mph. The system is expected to curve away from mainland Japan and areas affected by Typhoon Dujuan last month, while steadily weakening over the coming week.

Roughly 200 people are under medical observation, several hospitals are under quarantine, and dozens are in isolation in Russia following the unexplained death of an infectious disease researcher at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia, in the town of Shelekhov, according to early reports of the situation on Sunday and Monday.
Researcher Darya Shipilova reportedly died last week from pneumonia of “unknown” cause, according to Rospotrebnadzor, a Russian public health agency.
Unconfirmed information regarding her death has swirled. Some reports have claimed she accidentally broke a test tube containing the plague pathogen, Yersinia pestis, on September 25. She subsequently fell ill, was admitted to a hospital September 29 with severe pneumonia and died overnight between October 1 and Oct. 2. The head of the Russian region that neighbors Irkutsk, Alexey Tsydenov, initially reported that she had died of plague but later altered his statement to say she “possibly” died of the disease.
Y. pestis can cause several forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic—the latter of which can be aggressive and quickly fatal. However, the pathogen is generally easily treated by antibiotics. In the US, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that anyone exposed to the pathogen should undergo an immediate 7-day post-exposure antibiotic prophylaxis treatment. Additionally, though pneumonic plague is spread via respiratory particles from coughing, it is not considered highly infectious; it requires direct, close contact for the bacteria to be transmitted.

Are there any disadvantages to using IMAX theaters?
Ticket availability and how much they cost can be important factors.
For a cinematic experience that is truly larger than life, you won't find many theater formats that rival IMAX. IMAX movies are among the biggest and loudest you'll ever watch. The entire experience is meant to be premium, a step above what you'll find in a typical screening. Few movies are truly made for IMAX, with Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey one of the most recent blockbuster standouts.
There are disadvantages to IMAX theaters, though. You can expect an IMAX ticket to cost more – if you can get one. The biggest showings are hard to book, if you're close to one anyway, with titles like The Odyssey only playing in IMAX 70mm at just 41 locations worldwide when it came to screens in July 2026. The format isn't automatically the best choice for a movie, either.
A bigger picture isn't always a better one
People go to IMAX movie theaters to enjoy big-screen pictures. IMAX releases feature an expanded aspect ratio compared to standard cinematic movies. Instead of the 2.39:1 widescreen ratio commonly used for blockbusters, IMAX movies can use 1.90:1 or 1.43:1 aspect ratios. The black space above and below a movie that you'll typically see is completely removed with an IMAX screening, with more of the movie filling your field of view.
Productions require specialist equipment to film it. IMAX films use either traditional 65mm IMAX film cameras, which are typically very loud, bulky and incredibly expensive. Movies which are "Filmed for IMAX" — like Tom Cruise's Mission Impossible: The Final Reckoning — use digital IMAX cameras to capture expanded footage, although they aren't shooting on the same large-format film stock. Either way, the effect is much the same: large landscapes end up feeling much bigger, and the action taking place across the entire screen seems much more immersive.
That wouldn't necessarily be a disadvantage for the watcher. You're probably not rushing to complain that a movie is too immersive. The problem is that a bigger frame can show you more without actually showing you anything better.
This is especially true for movies that haven't been made specifically for IMAX. Recent releases like Toy Story 5 and Moana have both screened in IMAX theaters without being classed by IMAX as "Filmed for IMAX." You're getting an IMAX screening, but if the movie wasn't shot with IMAX cameras or created with its aspect ratio, it won't be the same. Sure, it'll be bigger and louder, but you won't necessarily get the expanded aspect ratio and extra picture area that you'd expect from a movie made with IMAX in mind.
That can take away one of the strongest reasons to pay the premium. If I'm spending more on an IMAX ticket, I'll want to watch a film that actually makes use of the format in its truest format, rather than one that's simply been remastered to fit the screen.
You'll pay more for IMAX
Speaking of costs, buying an IMAX ticket will set you back more. IMAX is a premium format, and the cinemas that offer IMAX screenings are pricing it accordingly. Big chains including AMC and Regal explicitly apply surcharges for IMAX and other premium large-format screenings on top of their usual prices. How much you'll pay will vary, depending on the theater, location and screening but if you choose an IMAX viewing, you will almost certainly pay more.
That's easier to swallow if it's a movie specifically designed to take advantage of the grandeur of IMAX. Take The Odyssey, this year's darling of the IMAX world and the first Hollywood movie to be shot entirely on IMAX film. This is a movie that deserves to be seen on the biggest screen. The immersive scale of its production means that watching it in IMAX is part of the experience, rather than just an upgrade. You're not simply paying more to watch the same movie on a bigger screen.
I'm not entirely convinced that watching a showing of Minions and Monsters is quite the same. That's not a criticism of that particular movie: it applies just as much to Moana, Scream 7 or Masters of the Universe, all recent releases that also had IMAX screenings. These are just films that haven't been made with IMAX in mind. Their scale just isn't able to match, and you won't get the same experience from it.
So, if you're expecting to pay more, you want the best. The Odyssey and films to follow it sit at the top, filmed with 70mm IMAX film. IMAX Digital movies like the latest Mission Impossible movie go next. Everything else, it's probably worth just paying less and watching it on a standard cinema screen and not in an IMAX theater.
You won't find many true IMAX screens around
If you're certain you want to go watch a movie at an IMAX theater, there's likely one nearby. According to IMAX, there's 1,876 screens available across 91 different countries, although that number includes screens you'll find in museums and science centers, for instance.
Sounds good? Well, if you wanted to watch The Odyssey at IMAX in its true 70mm IMAX film, you'd have far less choice. Only 41 locations worldwide provided screenings for watching it on traditional IMAX 70mm film. There are far more IMAX-labeled screens, but these typically rely on digital projection rather than the physical 70mm film, so you're not necessarily enjoying the same experience.
So, what are you getting? Your local IMAX might still give you a huge screen and upgraded sound, but it could be a digital setup rather than the enormous 1.43:1, 70mm presentation that the critics are raving about. I travelled to watch The Odyssey for that very reason. I'm not sure I would do so for movies that are simply remastered for an IMAX screen, however.
The best movies mean a fight for tickets
So, you're ready to go to an IMAX theater, but there's a potential problem. You're up against 10,000 other people trying to find a ticket for a less-than-adequate number of screenings. Finding a seat could be tough when booking the biggest blockbusters.
The Odyssey once again proves the point. Tickets for its first IMAX 70mm screenings were put on sale a full year before it was released. 95 percent of the first batch were sold within a day, with many selling within minutes. Once it was released, IMAX claimed that the 41 theaters showing it in 70mm film were recording sellouts well into its run.
A sellout run is great for the movie business. Less so for the cinema-goer who wants to watch it. Likewise, if the best seats are sold out, you're not getting the best experience. Where you sit in an IMAX theater can make a real difference: you don't want to be craning your neck from the second row or sitting right at the edge of an enormous screen. If the best seats are gone, I'd rather choose another showing than pay extra for a worse view.
Booking early can fix that, but who's choosing to book a trip to the cinema far in advance? Yes, IMAX theaters can be worth it for the biggest pictures, but there are too many disadvantages to overcome at the moment for smaller films. With pricing and availability, along with packed screenings to deal with, IMAX theaters have a barrier to entry that, in most cases, makes them more hassle than a standard screening. Whether that's worth it will really be up to you.

Vaxcyte said Monday that its experimental pneumococcal vaccine hit the primary endpoints in a Phase 3 clinical trial, setting up the California-based biotech to compete with Pfizer and Merck.
Vaxcyte’s shot, VAX-31, is designed to protect against 31 serotypes, or strains, of bacteria that can cause pneumococcal disease, including pneumonia, compared to 20 strains for Pfizer’s Prevnar and 21 strains for Merck’s Capvaxive.
In the trial, just over 3,500 adults age 50 and older were randomized to receive VAX-31, Prevnar, or Capvaxive. Investigators then measured the strength of their antibody responses against different strains.

Man City charges: Premier League clubs do not expect City to be in Premier League next season if appeal fails
Man City have lodged their appeal against an independent commission finding them guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules; if it fails, City's rivals believe that a points deduction is not sufficient if they return to the top-flight after one year
Monday 5 October 2026 16:56, UK
Sympathy is in short supply at other clubs after an independent commission laid bare the scale of Manchester City's rule breaking across nine seasons in a devastating decision published last week.
As City's legal team prepare for their appeal and sanctions hearing after being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of the Premier League's rules, their rivals in England and across Europe believe "the punishment should fit the crime".

With the looming prospect of City taking their bid to clear their name all the way to the High Court, rival clubs are becomingly increasingly concerned about the damage that is being done to the image and integrity of the Premier League, the cost of the dispute and what they see as City's failure to take any responsibility or accountability for their actions.
City are adamant they have done nothing wrong, insisting they are innocent and that a "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists" to support their position as they lodged their appeal.
But even a cursory reading of the decision which was published by the independent disciplinary commission puts into sharp focus the scale of the task facing City's lawyers when an appeal hearing takes place before Christmas.
The commission's finding are about as serious as it gets when it comes to financial rule-breaking and the fact that it was carried out over nine seasons and distorted the competition means City's rivals are not expecting Enzo Maresca's team to be playing in the Premier League next season.
Many believe that a points deduction is not a sufficient punishment if it would lead to City spending just one season outside the top flight.
It is only natural for clubs to think of their own self-interest and City's relegation would mean one fewer club going down this season as well as removing one of the favourites from the title race and opening up another European place. Self-interest is not the over-riding consideration though.
The consensus appears to be that rules have to be respected by all clubs, no matter their size or status - and it would not be sufficient to hand City a punishment that would last only one season for rules which were broken across multiple seasons.
City's rival Premier League clubs will not be involved in the sanction hearing, which could be take place while the appeal process runs its course.
The same three-person panel which heard the evidence at the 42-day hearing in 2024 and delivered its core decision last Tuesday will decide on sanctions after the Premier League, as the prosecutors, put forward their recommendation and City's lawyers argue their case.
It will be down to the Premier League board to decide what recommended sanction their lawyers should present to the panel.
In 2023, the Premier League argued that Everton deserved a 12-point deduction for one breach of the Profitability and Sustainability Rules.
Everton, who were in a desperate financial position at the time, eventually ended up with a six-point deduction after they appealed the original 10-point sanction.
With both sides allowed to appeal the sanctions, and City appealing the judgment, Premier League clubs are prepared for this marathon dispute to keep on running until at least next year.
Clubs have been trying to draw a line under the legal disputes which have become a feature of the English game as they try to move towards what some executives call "the NFL model" where the league speaks with one voice.
That will not happen until the final chapter of the 115 charges case is finally written.

Newcastle University is facing a backlash from conservationists over the appointment of the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune who runs a controversial mega-zoo as a professor of sustainability.
The university announced that Anant Ambani had been given a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.
Ambani is the son of India’s richest person, Mukesh Ambani, who made his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and has close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, and firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations to the party. The prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.
Anant Amabani, 31, who is leads on renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn, has set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly has more than 150,000 animals including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.
Conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals were sourced, given many were endangered species. Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing.
The university’s announcement was met with incredulity and derision from academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists.
Ramachandra Guha, a leading Indian public intellectual and the author of the book Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.
“I wonder on whose advice Newcastle University has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”
Bhuvan Mangalore, an Indian investigator into illegal wildlife trade who is completing a dissertation on Vantara at Anglia Ruskin University, asked: “Is this a joke?”
Prof Matt Perry, the chair of the University and College Union branch at Newcastle University, said staff members had objected to the appointment citing environmental concerns.
Prof Lyla Mehta, the head of the climate, environment and sustainability department at the University of Sussex’s Institute of Development Studies, shared concerns that “as public funding for universities falls, there is a real danger that billionaire and corporate money begins to shape academia”.
She said: “Universities are supposed to be places that question power and hold corporations to account, not give them academic legitimacy.”
In April, Anant Ambani launched Vantara University, billed as the world’s first global university dedicated to wildlife conservation and veterinary science.
Lorne Stockman, a research co-director at Oil Change International, said: “At a time when the climate crisis demands an urgent phaseout of oil and gas, we must demand our publicly funded institutions do better.”
In 2025, an investigation by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung found that many animals delivered to Vantara arrived through countries with opaque wildlife trading networks such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United Arab Emirates, raising concerns that endangered species may have been illegally trafficked.
In August last year, an investigation by India’s supreme court, which lasted less than three weeks, cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing. A subsequent fact-finding mission into the zoo by Cites, the UN body that regulates the trade of endangered species, found that some of the permits used to bring animals to Vantara were probably forged.
Its report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”
Cites recommended restrictions on India’s imports of endangered wild animals. However, it subsequently reversed its decision after objections from India, the US and Japan at a Cites meeting after they argued there was not enough proof of illegal imports.
In August, the zoo launched a “reset” in its operations by appointing a former Cites head to oversee its operations and said it would voluntarily pause all wildlife imports until June next year.
Vantara has declined to comment. The Ambani family and Vantara have previously denied the allegations of wildlife trafficking. They have said: “Our mission and focus continues to be the rescue, rehabilitation and care of animals.”
A Newcastle University spokesperson said: “The award of a professorship of practice recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship through his work with Vantara, a wildlife rescue and conservation initiative, and as the executive lead for the Reliance Group’s transition toward a green energy future.”

All six passengers presumed dead after plane went missing off US coast
- Published
Six people aboard a medical transport aircraft that went missing on Saturday while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston are presumed dead, according to a statement from the flight's operator.
On Sunday evening, the United States Coast Guard said it was ending its search for survivors off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island.
"We must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died," Latitude Air Ambulance said in a statement shortly thereafter.
"Our thoughts are first and foremost with their families, loved ones, friends, and colleagues."
The Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Saturday morning.
On Saturday evening, authorities located a "debris field" confirmed to be from the aircraft.
The plane had departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time on Friday night, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT).
Four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals were onboard.
"This is an unimaginable loss for our Latitude family and for everyone who loved the six people aboard Heartbeat 104," said Peter Byl, President of Latitude Air Ambulance, on Sunday evening.
"Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities. We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day."
Latitude Air Ambulance is a Canadian company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home.
Two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, had flown to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News.
FlightAware's tracker shows that the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft).
Radio transmissions show trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported, based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net.
"You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?"
The pilot's response was inaudible.
"You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe.
The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency.
An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue".
The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar".
Latitude said in its statement on Sunday evening that it would continue to cooperate with relevant authorities during ongoing recovery efforts and investigations.
"Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred," the company said.

The disclosure of BJP’s West Bengal election expenditure has sparked a storm on social media after revealing a Rs 2.5 lakh payment to Bengali actor and vlogger Sayak Chakraborty, who was involved in a controversial beef-steak incident at Kolkata’s Olypub in January 2026.
The report, published on the party’s letterhead and signed by office secretary at the BJP headquarters Mahendra Kumar Pandey details the party’s expenditure between March 15, the date of announcement of West Bengal assembly elections, and May 6, 2026, the official completion of the polls. The report shows that the BJP paid Rs 2,50,000 to a person named Sayak Chakraborty.
The payment appears under Schedule 3, titled “Expense(s) on Media Advertisement (print and electronic, bulk SMS, cable, website and TV channel etc.) on General Party propaganda authorised/incurred by Party Central Headquarters”. Chakraborty is listed at serial number 23 under the “electronic media” category.
The disclosure has drawn particular attention because Chakraborty was involved in a beef-related controversy at the iconic Park Street pub, Olypub, on January 30, 2026.
Following the publication of the expenditure report, Chakraborty acknowledged that he had been paid by the BJP, but claimed it had nothing to do with the Olypub incident.
The Olypub Incident & Why the Expenditure Disclosure Raises Eyebrows
On January 30, Chakraborty alleged that he had been served beef steak instead of a mutton dish at the restaurant. He subsequently lodged an FIR against Olypub and the concerned waiter who allegedly served him beef.
Sayak recorded the heated interaction on a live video and posted it on his Facebook page. His page, ‘Sayakk’, has 1.5 million followers. The 3-minute-47-second video has since been deleted from the page but remains available across social media. The clip can be watched here:
According to Chakraborty, while having dinner at Olypub, he and two friends ordered a mutton steak. The server placed a plate of food on their table without telling them what it was. Unaware of what they had been served, they ate it. After they had finished the dish, the waiter returned with another plate and said, “This is your mutton steak.” When they questioned him about the earlier dish, the waiter allegedly said it had been a beef steak.
Trouble started after that.
In the viral video, Chakraborty can be heard saying, “I ordered mutton steak; how could you mess it up and serve me beef instead? How could you hear beef instead of mutton? Do you know I am a Brahmin? I ate beef instead of mutton because of you!”
He also asked the server, Nasimuddin Sheikh, about his religion, before saying, “You made me eat Go-Mata!”
Following the altercation with the server, the actor lodged an FIR at Park Street police station. Kolkata Police arrested Nasimuddin based on the complaint. He was released on bail four days later.
The disclosure of the BJP’s expenditure immediately raised questions about whether Chakraborty had been paid by the party for his role in the Olypub episode. The questions gained further significance given that the incident had the potential to fuel a communal debate around beef, religion and Hindu identity — ideas that could serve the BJP’s broader political messaging.
They also arose because the immediate relatives of another person who was with Sayak during the incident appear in the BJP’s expenditure list.
At Olypub, while the beef controversy was unfolding, Sayak was accompanied by fellow social media influencer Sukanta Kundu and Kundu’s female friend. The BJP’s list includes the names of Sikha Kundu and Subrata Kundu, identified as Sukanta’s parents. Sikha and Subrata were paid Rs 4,50,000 and Rs 3,00,000 respectively.
Sayak Chakraborty’s Disclosure
As social media posts questioning Chakraborty’s association with the BJP gained traction, and media reports on the issue emerged, Sayak made a Facebook post on the morning of September 26, admitting that he had received a payment from the party.
He, however, claimed that his reaction at Olypub was a genuine outburst and not paid promotion.
He pointed to Olypub’s statement apologising for the meat mix-up as evidence that the episode was not scripted to evoke emotions. According to him, the BJP and others who shared his views simply supported him after the incident.
Chakraborty said the BJP and a few other political parties had subsequently approached him to make promotional content. He accepted the BJP’s offer and made several videos, including content on the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), possible reasons behind Narendra Modi’s silence during the conflict, and a congratulatory message for Suvendu Adhikari after he became chief minister.
He reiterated that these videos were made between March and May, the period covered by the BJP’s expenditure report, while the Olypub incident took place in January. Alt News tried calling up Chakraborty on his mobile number, but his phone was switched off.
Kundu, too, shared a Facebook post on September 26, acknowledging that the payment details being linked to him were indeed genuine. At the same time, he asserted that the Olypub incident was not part of his political campaign.

Samoa prime minister apologizes for Nazi gesture and saying 'Heil Hitler' in 2007 video
Samoa’s Prime Minister Laʻauli Leuatea Schmidt has apologized for a 2007 video that showed him saying “Heil Hitler” and making a Nazi gesture
WELLINGTON, New Zealand -- Samoa’s Prime Minister Laʻauli Leuatea Schmidt apologized Monday for a video from 19 years earlier in which he said “Heil Hitler” and made a Nazi gesture during what he described as a family gathering.
His statement published on the government's Facebook page came a day after the Samoa Observer newspaper made public for the first time the existence and content of a seven-second clip that the outlet said was filmed at a Schmidt family reunion in Samoa in July 2007.
In a screenshot from the video, Schmidt holds a microphone in one hand with the other arm lifted, surrounded by others making the same gesture.
The newspaper reported Schmidt was heard saying into the microphone, “Raise your right hand, Heil Hitler!”
Schmidt, who was the deputy speaker of Samoa's Parliament in 2007, didn't dispute the report. He has led the South Pacific island nation of 220,000 people since winning an August 2025 election.
“I recognise that those words and gesture were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt and I apologise for using them,” he said Monday. He added that the video was filmed “at a private family gathering — not intended for the public.”
He rejected “Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism,” the statement said.
What happened immediately before and after the moment depicted was unknown, the newspaper said, and Schmidt's statement didn't explain further.
The episode unfolded as Pacific media groups decried Schmidt's ongoing rancor against the Observer, which has been barred from covering his and other government news conferences and events since November, when Schmidt accused the newspaper of misleading coverage.
On Friday, Schmidt confirmed claims that an Observer reporter's photos of him, taken in front of government buildings during an official event, were deleted from their camera by an aide. He defended the move, saying the Observer, Samoa's largest newspaper group, was flouting its prohibition.
The Observer has called his ban “authoritarian.” Pacific media groups have called on the prime minister for a reversal, with the Journalists Association of Samoa saying it was “deeply disturbed” by the photo deletion incident.
Like a number of other leaders of small island nations in the South Pacific Ocean, Schmidt has voiced vehement support for Israel before.
Since September 2023, three Pacific islands, not including Samoa, have been among a handful of countries to follow the United States in opening embassies in the contested city of Jerusalem instead of Tel Aviv, where most diplomatic missions are located.
Analysts attribute support for Israel in the region to deep Christian traditions woven throughout public life. When Schmidt was sworn into office in September 2025, he wore a Jewish prayer shawl during a ceremony that included the blowing of a shofar.
“Samoa will not withdraw from supporting Israel as the country of God’s people,” he told reporters after the event, according to local news outlets.

- Hegseth named Tesla and Space X CEO Elon Musk, former Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich and Palmer Luckey, founder of defense technology company Anduril Industries, as heads of Project Meridian.

In late September 2026, a rumor spread online that Tesla and Space X CEO Elon Musk and former Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich had joined a new effort announced by the U.S. Department of Defense called "Project Meridian."
Several social media posts made the claim, including on Reddit and X. One X post (archived) said Musk, Gingrich and Palmer Luckey, founder of defense technology company Anduril Industries, had been recruited to lead the project "to focus on developing future warfare and autonomous weapons systems for battlefields 'from under the Earth to beyond the moon'":
The official X account of the DOD's chief technology officer confirmed the story (archived):
"From under the earth to beyond the moon, our warfighters will have technological superiority," the post read. "PROJECT MERIDIAN: THE FUTURE OF WARFARE."
Here's what we know so far about the initiative, its goals and the people involved:
Hegseth's announcement
On Sept. 30, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth delivered what he called a "State of the Force" address — meant to evoke the State of the Union address, which the president delivers annually to Congress — and announced the launch of Project Meridian, which he described as "an effort led by America's best minds to study the future of warfare."
Hegseth began to describe Project Meridian roughly midway through his address (at 34:45 in the video):
Today we are leveraging a unique source of American advantage. One our adversaries do not have: our innovators, our senior leaders and our technologists — big thinkers who will forecast the creative solutions for tomorrow's conflicts. That's why today at my direction I am announcing Project Meridian, an effort led by America's best minds to study the future of warfare. Under the leadership of the department's chief technology officer, Emil Michael, Project Meridian will be co-led by three of our nations best minds. Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich, all of whom are up in the audience with us today.
Shortly after he named them, Musk, Luckey and Gingrich stood up to applause from the crowd.
Musk, Gingrich and Luckey
Hegseth said the three men would lead a group of "subject-matter experts from across our nation's unmatched innovation, academic and policy ecosystems." The goal, he said, would be to develop "absolute technological superiority," by focusing on, among other things, "autonomous warfare" — in other words, weapons and equipment capable of functioning autonomously.
Musk was previously involved in President Donald Trump's administration as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency, which spearheaded drastic spending cuts to government programs. (The Government Accountability Office said in August 2026 that DOGE incorrectly reported or failed to substantiate some of its purported savings.) Musk's xAI technology has reportedly been used by U.S. forces in the Iran war.
Gingrich has consistently defended the war with Iran (archived), which has proved unpopular with U.S. voters, according to polls.
Luckey described himself as a "radical Zionist" during "The Shawn Ryan Show" podcast in February 2025, saying he defended Israel's right to exist. Asked directly by Axios what he thought of the war in Iran, he declined to answer.
Autonomous warfare
During the address, Hegseth also announced the creation of a new combatant command: "Today, with Autonomous War Command — AutoWarCom — we institutionalize and we supercharge the era of SI, robotics, and autonomous systems. All in order to win," Hegseth said. ("SI" refers to "super intelligence," what the federal government began calling artificial intelligence in September 2026.)
Hegseth appeared to present Project Meridian as the way to identify the technologies best suited to arm AutoWarCom. He said the group led by Musk, Gingrich and Luckey would render its first conclusions in 120 days.
The same day, the Pentagon published a memorandum that further outlined the goal of Project Meridian. It read:
Project Meridian will leverage critical perspectives from outside the Pentagon, drawing upon a group of top technologists, innovators, business leaders, policy makers, and national security experts. Project Meridian's primary function will be to map the trajectory of future warfare, identify critical capability gaps, and propose actionable solutions in furtherance of the identified goals in the 2026 National Security Science and Technology Strategy.
For further reading, Snopes has investigated a number of rumors about Hegseth's Defense Department, including a claim that the department spent $93 billion in one month.

UAE had shared details about FlyDubai flight with Israel, including pilots' names and nationalities
Regional officials say authorities in the United Arab Emirates shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of last week's FlyDubai flight on which a pilot attempted to seize control of the Israel-bound aircraft and crash it
TEL AVIV, Israel -- Authorities in the United Arab Emirates shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of the FlyDubai flight on which a pilot attempted to seize control of the Israel-bound aircraft and crash it, regional officials said Sunday, raising new questions over how the attacker evaded detection.
While the investigation continues, preliminary details about the incident have highlighted several major security lapses. Officials already have said the Omani co-pilot had been barred from flying by his own country because of concerns about his extremist views. It also remains unclear how a citizen of Oman, an Arab country that has no diplomatic relations with Israel, was allowed to fly a planeload of Israelis to Tel Aviv.
The United Arab Emirates, which is leading the investigation, said the co-pilot attacked the flight's captain with the cockpit’s crash ax and tried to take control of the plummeting plane in a “terrorist attack” Wednesday. His actions nearly crashed the flight with 182 people on board before the Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and others to rush in and subdued the attacker.
The regional officials said Emirati authorities had shared information about the passengers and crew, including their nationalities. Israel hadn’t raised red flags on any passenger or member of the crew, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters about the probe.
The passengers who halted the attack and helped regain control of the aircraft have been hailed as heroes in Israel.
But officials have begun to raise difficult questions and trade accusations about the security blunders that could have led to a major disaster.
The Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, said the Transportation Ministry is responsible for vetting passenger lists from foreign flights. Transportation Minister Miri Regev told Israel’s public broadcaster Kan that the security agencies are responsible for flight security and that her ministry wasn’t given a list of passengers or any warnings.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday that Israel has long-standing agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don’t maintain diplomatic relations with Israel.
It also remains unclear how FlyDubai, a low-cost Emirati airline that operates flights between Israel and the UAE, had failed to identify the Omani pilot as a security risk. Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England who wrote a book about aircraft hijackings and bombings, said background check systems differ from country to country and there are limits on what types of information can be shared.
“In terms of aviation security itself, obviously we want to have as robust background checks as possible. But there are huge limitations on doing background checks in any case, especially in cross-border checks,” he said.

The women's championship categories will line-up behind the women's elite field for the first time in the London race.

India had the highest number of children with no sanitation service in schools, with 50 million out of the world total of 244 million as of 2025, according to a new global report. Only Nigeria (34 million), Ethiopia (26 million), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (11 million) or Indonesia (8 million) had a comparatively large number of schoolchildren who had no access to sanitation service.
The data from ‘Progress on drinking water, sanitation and hygiene in schools 2015-2025’ shows the progress as well as the challenges India is facing in meeting the water, sanitation and hygiene goals that are part of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) set for 2030.
14% reduction in schools with no sanitation service
The report can also be seen as a decadal report card on the Swachh Bharat Mission, which was launched in India on October 2, 2014. The report cites the achievement of India which saw a 14% reduction in schools with no sanitation service.
Lack of hygiene service
The WHO/UNICEF report that is part of the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) shows that globally, 362 million children still had no hygiene service at their school in 2025. Of these, 20 million were from India.
It is not just lack of access that the WHO report flags about India but also gaps in data. “There is now sufficient data to estimate trends in basic hygiene coverage between 2015 and 2025 for all SDG regions except Central and Southern Asia where there were insufficient recent data to generate estimates for India, and therefore the region, beyond 2024.”
Drinking water
On the brighter side, India is among the 28 out of 62 countries that are on track to achieve universal coverage of basic drinking water in schools by 2030.
As of 2025, there were 258 million children who still had no drinking water service at their school. The number of children from Indian schools made up 12 million of this number or about 1 out 20 children in the world. The report shows that India has made a big progress in basic drinking water services in 2025 and average rates of change between 2015 and 2025. India, Panama, Syrian Arab Republic, Togo and Tuvalu increased coverage by over 4% per year, “demonstrating that rapid progress is possible”.
However, the report found that while gaps in basic water coverage persists between school levels and between rural and urban areas, this did not apply to India, Cambodia and Fiji.

Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
- Published
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators near a school in France, an official has said, as student protests continue across the country.
The "very serious incident" happened in the north-eastern city of Lens on Monday morning, according to the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, François-Xavier Lauch.
"The student's life is not in danger," he said, adding that the teenager was transferred "very quickly" to a hospital nearby.
Around 500 schools were partially or totally closed across the country on Monday amid student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing which have led to clashes with police in recent days.
There are mixed reports in French media about how the boy came to sustain the injury.
AFP news agency, citing a police union source, reported that the student appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which exploded in his hand.
However, regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord quoted a girl who it said was near the teenager as saying he did not pick up the grenade.
"He didn't pick it up. I was there, I saw it. He didn't pick it up, he didn't catch it," she was quoted as saying.
When asked about the incident, Lens Mayor Sylvain Robert said the circumstances still needed to be clarified.
"Like you, and like many others, I have seen some videos showing the aftermath. But I did not see how the operation was organised, either by the police or by the students," he told French media.
A regional prosecutor said an investigation would be carried out by the French police watchdog, the General Inspection of the National Police (IGPN), "so all light can be shed on what happened".
The incident took place close to the Auguste Béhal high school, the prefect said.
Lauch said a "larger gathering" of students than on previous days had assembled outside the school.
"At the start of the morning, they threw various projectiles at the local police officers who were on site initially. When I say projectiles, I mean stones, fireworks, and mortars," he told French media.
"Instructions were given by the interdepartmental director of the National Police, naturally with my approval, to deploy a company of riot police (CRS) here to maintain order, and it was in this context that this event occurred."
The school issued a statement on Monday morning, saying: "In light of the events that took place this morning and in order to ensure the safety of the entire school community, the institution is switching to distance learning from now on.
"In addition, to support everyone during this period, a listening and support unit has also been set up at the establishment."
This is not the first time students have been seriously injured during the recent wave of protests in France. Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck in the head by a tear gas grenade.
The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has announced an investigation.
Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered".
"His jaw is wired shut. He can't eat except through a straw and only liquids," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying.
"It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," she said, adding: "This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study."

‘There is no Lindsey Graham Bill in Europe’: Nirmala Sitharaman on Russian oil, trade talks
The Lindsey Graham Bill gives US president the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from countries identified as major purchasers of Russian oil
Union finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Monday drew a distinction between the US and Europe over pressure on India's Russian oil purchases, saying there was no equivalent of the “Lindsey Graham Bill” in Europe as New Delhi negotiates trade agreements with European countries.
Responding to a question on whether India’s strategic autonomy could be affected by discussions around Russian oil during bilateral trade talks, Sitharaman said the global trading environment had changed significantly, with countries increasingly tailoring agreements around national interests and supply-chain concerns.
“In Europe, as much as I understand till today, there is no Lindsey Graham Bill,” Sitharaman said.
The remark came amid questions over India's continued purchases of Russian crude and whether the issue could feature in negotiations with European countries. India has maintained that its energy purchases are guided by national interests and energy security.
India’s trade strategy amid changing global order
Sitharaman said trade negotiations had become considerably more complicated as countries seek to protect supply chains and reduce their vulnerability to disruptions.
“10 years ago, you wouldn't have had to do this pairing out of details. You would broadly agree on terms and get going with it,” she said.
“Today, you want to be conscious that the supply chains are not going to be disrupted. But where the supply chains have already got disrupted, you're finding a newer partner to ensure that supply chain continues,” she added.
Sitharaman said that in the current global environment, even agreements involving a larger grouping such as the European Union have to account for individual national interests.
“So, in the current reality, bilateral—or I would still call this bilateral, even within a larger body, the EU comes with a cluster of countries. I think, ultimately, you are tailoring the agreement to keep national interest alive, but to survive in a very challenging global environment where no WTO-related laws have been left to be respected,” she said.
“Everybody's broken the law here and there. And so, you're making it up now,” the finance minister added.
What is the Lindsey Graham law?
The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 was signed into law by US President Donald Trump last month after being passed by both chambers of Congress.
The legislation gives the US president the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from countries identified as major purchasers of Russian oil and gas.
India and China, two of the biggest buyers of Russian crude, could potentially face such measures. However, the law does not automatically impose a tariff on either country and gives the US president discretion over whether and how to use the provisions.
The legislation also provides for sanctions targeting Russia’s energy and defence sectors and its so-called shadow fleet of tankers.
The law has become an important factor in India-US relations as New Delhi and Washington continue negotiations for a bilateral trade agreement.
US-India trade talks ‘reached a plateau’
Sitharaman also spoke about the ongoing India-US trade negotiations, describing them as “hard and very rigorously negotiated”.
She said the talks were still underway but indicated that both sides may have reached a point where further concessions could be difficult.
“The agreement's negotiations are still ongoing, although we'd like to believe that both sides have reached a plateau, beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult,” she said.
Sitharaman, however, said there could still be room for movement if both sides found areas where they could compromise.
“But maybe if there are room—if there are rooms to operate from, both sides would do it,” she said.
The finance minister also pointed to the trade imbalance between India and the US as a major feature of the negotiations.
“But what is the predominant feature of the trade relations between India and US? The trade balance is very much in our favor. Naturally, the deficit is there in their side, or the balance is going unfavorably for the US,” she said.
She said the US would therefore want to reduce the imbalance and seek greater access to the Indian market.
“So they would want to reduce that imbalance, and their desire would be to see, as much as possible, get some kind of, from their point of view, making up for all that they've lost over these years...” Sitharaman said.
Why Russian oil remains a key issue
India sharply increased its purchases of Russian crude after Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, when Western sanctions disrupted established global energy flows and Russian oil became available to major buyers at discounted prices.
The purchases have since become a major point of friction between India and the US, with Washington seeking to restrict Russia’s energy revenues that help fund its war in Ukraine.
New Delhi, however, has consistently maintained that it makes energy procurement decisions based on national interest, affordability and energy security.
The Lindsey Graham law has added another layer to that pressure because of its potential to target countries that continue to purchase Russian energy.
For India, the issue has become intertwined with its broader trade negotiations with Washington. At the same time, New Delhi is pursuing trade agreements with the European Union and other partners while attempting to preserve its strategic autonomy.

'I have never felt heat like that' - a survivor on watching 33 cellmates die in Nigeria
- Published
Usman Muhammad pauses by the entrance to a tiny Nigerian prison cell and leans his forehead against the wall unable to speak.
The day before he had been trapped inside the stifling room, measuring roughly 6m (19.7ft) by 3m (9.8ft), with more than 50 other prisoners.
Thirty-three of his cellmates died in the cramped conditions in the prison in Minna, the capital of Nigeria's Niger state - and four died later in hospital.
The mass deaths caused an outcry and sparked protests, including attacks on public buildings, as relatives and locals demanded answers.
Federal officials had initially blamed the deaths on a diphtheria outbreak but exactly what happened is now the subject of an investigation.
"I have never felt heat like that in my life. When we touched each other's bodies, it felt like fire burning," Muhammad tells the BBC once he is able to gather his thoughts.
When he was locked inside, there was standing room only amid humidity levels of more than 90%, which in some circumstances can be dangerous to human health as it prevents the natural cooling mechanism of sweat drying on the skin.
The temperature outside was above 25C and the only ventilation came from a small, high-up window.
"One of us fainted and we started knocking at the [cell] door. When [a guard] came we asked him for water. He looked at the guy that fainted and closed the door. That's how they started dying one after the other," Muhammad says.
Like the others who had been detained, the young man, in his 20s, is an artisanal miner, eking out a living searching for precious metals at mine sites.
The federal government has tried to crack down on this alleged illegal activity as it says it costs the country revenue, damages the environment and can be linked to wider criminal activity.
Officers from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) had arrested a large group of miners near Minna last Tuesday and Wednesday.
The prisoners were held at its detention centre in the city, but the NSCDC has not shared either the names or the number of those it was holding.
As the hours inside the cell wore on, the heat and dehydration became unbearable and Muhammad says some of the detainees began drinking their own urine and collecting sweat from their bodies to try to stay alive.
He describes seeing people in distress and struggling to breathe.
"People were calling for help, some were already very weak."
But no-one came to help, he and others allege.
"While in the cell, we were shouting and telling them that people were dying," another survivor Adamu Isah told the Reuters news agency.
"We tried to break down the door when they refused to open it… At one point, a security officer came to the door.
"We were shouting and telling him that people were dying, but he said it wasn't his problem if people died."
Finally, on Thursday, the cell door was opened and the guards saw the dead bodies.
The NSCDC has not directly responded to the accusations of neglect and maltreatment but has said that 24 of its personnel are now in custody in connection with the deaths, including its suspended Niger state commandant Suberu Aniviye.
"The people who were killed are not flies. How can this go unlooked? We will get to the bottom of this," Niger state Governor Umaru Bago told the BBC.
As the organisation involved is a federal body rather than a force under his jurisdiction, such as the police, the governor is unable to exert direct influence but he welcomes the investigation that has been ordered by the government in capital, Abuja.
A 10-member committee has now been set-up to determine exactly what happened.
It has two weeks to establish the causes of the deaths and identify who was responsible and can recommend legal action against anyone found culpable.
No officer, regardless of rank, would be protected and any attempt to obstruct the investigation would be taken seriously, Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said.
As he leaves the cell after talking to the BBC, Muhammad says he hopes that by speaking out he can help find justice and bring some closure to this traumatic event.

Pakistan-made cosmetics that continued to find their way to Hyderabad more than a year after India shut the door on imports from the neighbouring country have now led investigators to Mumbai’s Crawford Market, pointing to a wider supply chain behind the banned products.
The development comes amid a separate public-health concern over some of the skin-whitening products. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) last month specifically warned consumers against two Pakistan-made creams after tests found excessive levels of heavy metals.
Both ‘Goree Beauty Cream’ and ‘Chandni Whitening Cream’, named in the September 8 CDSCO alert, were among the products found during raids on three shops in Hyderabad this week.
An officer involved in the investigation said the cosmetics seized in Hyderabad were allegedly being sourced from Crawford Market in Mumbai. “Investigators are now looking further up the chain to establish how the products entered India and reached wholesale and retail markets despite restrictions on their import.
Imports from Pakistan prohibited since May 2025
India prohibited the direct or indirect import or transit of all goods originating in or exported from Pakistan on May 2, 2025. The Directorate General of Foreign Trade imposed the restriction through a notification, citing national security and public policy.
The prohibition extends to goods entering India indirectly, meaning routing Pakistan-origin products through another country does not by itself make their import permissible.
Cosmetics imported into India are additionally governed by the Cosmetics Rules, 2020. Products must be registered with the Central Licensing Authority before import and are required to comply with prescribed quality and safety standards.
The CDSCO had stepped up scrutiny even before the latest Hyderabad seizure. In July, it directed its zonal offices, State licensing authorities and officers at ports to maintain enhanced surveillance following instances of imported cosmetics being sold in domestic markets without valid import registration certificates.
Heavy metals found in two creams
The health regulator followed this with a more pointed warning on September 8. After testing Goree Beauty Cream and Chandni Whitening Cream, it said neither had been issued a registration certificate for import and that the products contained heavy metals beyond specified limits, which could pose health risks, including toxic effects. Consumers were advised not to purchase or use them.
The Hyderabad investigation has meanwhile opened another line of inquiry. According to the officer, investigators found that an ointment originating from the United Kingdom was allegedly being mixed with cosmetic products and the resulting preparation sold for skin-lightening purposes.
Samples of the products have been sent for forensic examination, and investigators are awaiting the laboratory findings to establish their composition and determine the substances present in them.
Officials have raised concerns about potentially carcinogenic substances, but the forensic results are awaited. The precise health implications of the seized preparations are therefore yet to be established.
The latest investigation follows raids by the Hyderabad police and CDSCO at Beauty Ladies Emporium, Beauty Queen Shop and S.J. Medical Shop in the Habeeb Nagar and Nampally areas, where cosmetics valued at about ₹7 lakh were seized.
The stock included several Pakistan-made whitening creams, soaps and other cosmetic products. Five persons were identified in connection with their alleged sale and distribution.
The Crawford Market link also comes against the backdrop of enforcement action in Mumbai itself, where Pakistan-made cosmetics valued at about ₹12 lakh were seized during a raid in July.
