Snapdeal parent AceVector’s initial public offering (IPO) is set to provide an exit opportunity to several of its early investors and promoters, with SoftBank-backed Starfish I Pte Ltd set to be the biggest beneficiary of the offer-for-sale (OFS) component. At the issue price of ₹32 per share, Starfish I, a SoftBank entity and the company’s largest shareholder, raked in about ₹88.3 Cr by selling 2.76 Cr shares, representing about two-thirds of the total OFS proceeds. The transaction represents an 0.08X return multiple on the shares being sold, according to AceVector’s red herring prospectus (RHP). Starfish will continue to hold 11.3 Cr shares, valued at about ₹361.8 Cr at ₹32 apiece, after the IPO. AceVector’s ₹420 Cr IPO comprises a fresh issue of ₹287 Cr and an OFS of up to 4.16 Cr shares worth about ₹133 Cr at the upper price band, valuing the company at ₹1,741 Cr at ₹32 per share. Nexus Sees Mixed Returns Across Funds AceVector’s IPO also marks a partial exit for Nexus Venture Partners, although returns vary significantly across its investment vehicles. Nexus India Direct Investments II sold 73.9 Lakh shares for ₹23.6 Cr, representing a 1.03X return multiple. The fund will retain 3 Cr shares worth about ₹96.7 Cr at the IPO price. Meanwhile, Nexus Opportunity Fund Ltd sold 8.4 Lakh shares for ₹2.6 Cr, representing a 0.14X return multiple, while Nexus Ventures III sold 4.6 Lakh shares for ₹1.4 Cr at a 0.07X multiple. Together, the three Nexus entities are selling 86.9 Lakh shares, however, the investor failed to book a positive return across the funds. Other selling shareholders include FIH Business Global, Rupen Investment and Industries and Centaurus Trading and Investments. FIH will sell 17.4 Lakh shares for ₹5.6 Cr, while Rupen Investment and Centaurus will each sell 2.7 Lakh shares for about ₹86 Lakh. Individual investors See Multi-Bagger Returns The sharpest returns in the data were booked by individual shareholders instead. For instance, Kenneth Stuart Glass sold 13.2 Lakh shares for ₹4.2 Cr at ₹32 apiece. The transaction represents a 5.42X return multiple, making it the highest return among selling investors. Glass will still hold 30.7 Lakh shares, worth about ₹9.8 Cr at the IPO price. Meanwhile, Laurent Bernard Amouyal booked a substantial return of investment after selling 2.2 Lakh shares for ₹72 Lakh, representing a 4.38X return multiple. He will retain 5.2 Lakh shares worth around ₹1.7 Cr. On the other hand, former Snapdeal chief strategy and investment officer Jason Ashok Kothari sold 11.1 Lakh shares for ₹3.5 Cr, with a 0.78X return multiple, while retaining another 11.1 Lakh shares valued at ₹3.5 Cr. AceVector had earlier proposed a substantially larger OFS, but trimmed the component by 34.9% to 4.16 Cr shares. Starfish alone reduced its proposed sale from 4.23 Cr shares to 2.76 Cr. The company raised ₹13 Cr through a pre-IPO placement, which brought down the fresh issue to ₹287 Cr. The fresh capital is earmarked largely for Snapdeal, including ₹132 Cr for marketing and business promotion and ₹50 Cr for technology infrastructure, while the remaining proceeds are intended for acquisitions and general corporate purposes. Founded in 2010 by Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal, AceVector started off as ecommerce platform, Snapdeal. Following the collapse of its proposed merger with Flipkart in 2017, it pivoted to a value-focused ecommerce model. Besides Snapdeal, AceVector’s businesses include listed ecommerce SaaS company Unicommerce and consumer brands business Stellaro Brands. The group adopted the AceVector identity in 2022. Ahead of opening the public issue for subscription, AceVector raised ₹189 Cr from anchor investors. Helios Mutual Fund and Taurus Ethical Fund were the only domestic mutual funds to participate, together picking up 93.75 Lakh shares, or 15.87% of the anchor allocation. AceVector’s IPO closed on Tuesday (September 29), receiving 4.93X subscription. Investors placed bids for 36.61 Cr shares against 7.42 Cr shares on offer. On the financial front, AceVector’s restated net loss narrowed nearly 64% to ₹45.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹126.3 Cr in FY25. Operating revenue rose 29.2% to ₹510.3 Cr from ₹395 Cr.

Drones buzz overhead, troops hunker underground in Ukraine's hellish kill zone
KYIV, Ukraine — The front line in the Russia-Ukraine war stretches the entire length of this country, from north to south. It has barely budged in four years and is sometimes compared to the static, deadlocked, trench warfare of World War I.
Yet straddling this front line is the kill zone, dominated by constantly evolving drone technology that's defining this conflict — and the future of warfare.
"This kill zone is a belt of territory which is full of Russian drones, Russian mines and also artillery. It's nonstop reconnaissance and surveillance," said Ukraine's Sr. Lt. Taras Myshak, the spokesman for Ukraine's 59th Separate Assault Brigade. He spoke with NPR on Zoom, just a few miles from the front line in eastern Ukraine.
Ukraine has a similar arsenal threatening the Russian forces that are dug in on the other side of the line.
The most important thing to know about the kill zone is that any sign of movement — just sticking your head out of a foxhole for fresh air — can get you noticed, and attacked, by the drones constantly buzzing overhead.
Myshak says even routine movements, like rotating troops in and out of this zone, is a nightmare.
"Not far from where we are talking today, we have a group that moved through the kill zone, and they will walk four hours just to go 1 kilometer," he said. "Because all the time they hear the drone, and they have to hide and wait. Then the drone passes, and they can move."
Nightfall doesn't make it any safer to move because the drones have thermal cameras that detect body heat and make it even harder to hide.
"In the night, it's even more dangerous," he said.
A front line that barely budges
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it advanced rapidly in conventional fashion with large columns of troops in armored vehicles. Later that fall, Ukraine's counteroffensive drove the Russians back in some places.
Since then, the two armies have settled in, and the front line has moved only incrementally, mostly with limited gains by Russia. This line now stretches more than 700 miles. On either side of the line, the kill zone is a band roughly 10 to 20 miles wide and dominated by drones.
"The kill zone is basically a product of drone warfare," said Rob Lee, a U.S. Marine veteran who now lives in Ukraine and monitors the war for the Foreign Policy Research Institute of Philadelphia.
Because Ukraine has far fewer troops and relies heavily on drones, it has a remarkably small presence on the front line.
Lee said that in many places, Ukraine has fewer than 10 soldiers per mile, in small groups, spaced out hundreds of yards apart.
"Those infantrymen are maybe two positions where it's two to four people," said Lee. "They're underground for the most part. They're trying to remain hidden."
These troops are not really trying to hold back advancing Russian soldiers, he added. They act more as spotters, relaying Russian movements to Ukrainian drone operators behind the front lines, who then track down the Russian intruders from the air.
Lee says the front line is so saturated with drones that it's virtually impossible for either side to pull together a large ground force without being detected and drawing fire.
Military vehicles like tanks and armored personnel carriers are even easier to spot and attack.
"Because of such a high density of drones, it became very difficult to bring vehicles near the front line at all," he said.
Neither army planned to fight this way.
Ukraine had no real drone industry at the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the country will make 10 million this year.
Russia has ramped up its own drone production. It's expected to make more than 7 million this year, including jet-powered aircraft that are often evading Ukraine's defenses.
Starting from scratch
When Dima Putiata joined Ukraine's military four years ago, he knew nothing about drones and didn't think this was a manly way to wage war.
"When I saw that we have drones, I was not smart enough. I said, 'No, we don't need to have it. Let's fight like men.' I was a little bit maybe romantic in this way," said Putiata.
In addition to skeptics like Putiata, few Ukrainian troops were trained to use these new weapons.
"No one had drone operators," he recalled. "It's just, 'Oh, you're a driver? You can use it.' Or, 'Oh, can I use a drone? You can try.'"
By the time he left the military in May, Putiata, a sergeant, was commanding 26 drone crews in and around the kill zone in northeastern Ukraine.
Both sides have rapidly embraced the technology even if they don't know where it's headed next, he said.
"They understand how to use it here and right now, maybe not really understanding how to use it in the future," he noted. "My point is, you just need to keep going and adapting."
Recognizing the role of drones
Two years ago, Ukraine became the first country to establish drones as an independent branch of its military.
This innovation now includes the widespread use of ground drones, which look like trollies and perform a wide range of tasks that have become too dangerous for troops.
The robots deliver food, medicine and ammunition to the front line. The robots can be loaded with machine guns that now carry out regular attacks.
The ground robots are also being used to evacuate wounded soldiers from the kill zone. But drone operators and combat medics have separate skills, and it turns out you need both.
"The drone operator doesn't know how to properly evacuate a wounded soldier, and the medic doesn't know how to operate a ground robot," said Lyuba Shipovich, a Ukrainian American who heads a private group, Dignitas, that trains troops on drones.
"So now we're trying to create combined program that will train both the medic and the robot operator," she said.
Media coverage tends to focus on long-range airstrikes that Russia and Ukraine are inflicting deep inside each other's territory.
But the vast majority of the fighting is in the kill zone, with drones now responsible for 80% of all casualties, according to Rob Lee and other military analysts.
Dima Putiata, the former Ukrainian soldier, says what started in this war has already spread to other conflicts.
"With drones, this is the cheapest flying munition that can be massively produced. You can destroy a lot of stuff," he said. "It's much cheaper than it used to be to have a war, unfortunately."
A kind of war, he predicts, that the world will see more often.
NPR's Hanna Palamarenko contributed to this story.

Chiefs and 49ers remain unbeaten - five things from NFL week four
- Published
Only three teams remain unbeaten in the NFL after two more 100% starts were halted during week four of the season.
Sunday's slate got under way with the Indianapolis Colts beating the Washington Commanders in the first of this season's three London games.
The New England Patriots and Los Angeles Rams then avoided dropping to a 1-3 record by pulling off some big wins on the road.
The Kansas City Chiefs and Las Vegas Raiders were among the five teams who made a 3-0 start to the season and one team's '0' had to go as the divisional rivals met, while the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings marched on.
Here are five things you missed from Sunday's action.
Raiders push Chiefs all the way
Kansas City have dominated their rivalry with the Raiders in recent years, but Las Vegas are vastly improved after winning only three games last season and pushed the Chiefs all the way.
The Raiders led 13-10 heading into the final quarter in Vegas, which featured three lead changes before Kansas City held on for a 30-27 win.
The turning point came as new running back Kenneth Walker maintained his stunning start by scoring two touchdowns in 19 seconds, with the Chiefs regaining possession immediately by forcing a fumble on the kick-off return.
The Raiders gave themselves hope with a Brock Bowers score and stayed alive until the final play, when Kirk Cousins was tackled as he threw and his wayward pass was intercepted.
Walker finished with 177 yards from 22 carries, while team-mate Tyquan Thornton also had two touchdowns and 111 receiving yards.
After missing last season's play-offs, the Chiefs look capable of getting back into Super Bowl contention. They next face the Los Angeles Chargers, who are 0-4 after losing 30-23 to defending champions the Seattle Seahawks.
49ers and Vikings march on
The other two teams who improved to 4-0 were the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings.
The 49ers hosted the Denver Broncos, who overcame Super Bowl favourites the Rams last week, and they were tied 3-3 until late in the third quarter.
Christian McCaffrey's touchdown in the fourth quarter gave the 49ers some breathing space and, although Jaylen Waddle replied, George Kittle scored on a huge catch-and-run down the middle to seal a 24-14 win.
While Cousins and Brock Purdy lead the league with 11 touchdown passes, Purdy has been intercepted only once and has not been sacked in the 49ers' first four games.
The Vikings are the biggest surprise to be 4-0, having ground out another win, this time 15-10 over the Miami Dolphins, with Will Reichard kicking five field goals.
Maye bounces back
Some said Drake Maye's confidence was shot after he was benched during the New England Patriots' blowout loss at the Jacksonville Jaguars last week.
After throwing eight interceptions in the 2025 regular season, the 24-year-old quarterback had six in the Patriots' first three games and only one touchdown pass.
Next up was a daunting trip to the unbeaten Buffalo Bills - led by the 2024 Most Valuable Player Josh Allen - but Maye showed why he narrowly missed out on the MVP award last season, when he led the Patriots to an unexpected Super Bowl run.
After Allen restored Buffalo's lead with a 34-yard touchdown pass to Keon Coleman with four minutes left, Efton Chism made a superb one-handed catch in the endzone to put the Patriots back in front.
They then intercepted a hopeful Allen throw to clinch a 29-26 win, with Maye passing for three touchdowns and 269 yards.
The Bills joined the Rams as Super Bowl favourites last week and they go head to head in LA next week.
Another Eagles injury before London trip
After losing a thriller at Denver last Monday, the LA Rams were 1-2 and faced another stern test on the road this week at the Philadelphia Eagles.
The hosts led 20-10 at half-time after two Darius Cooper touchdowns, but the Rams fought back, with Kyren Williams rushing for two touchdowns in the final four minutes to claim a 24-20 victory.
The fit-again Puka Nacua finished with 125 receiving yards and a touchdown for the Rams, while the Eagles' injury concerns mounted.
Wide receiver DeVonta Smith (hamstring) was ruled out before the game, joining tight end Dallas Goedert (knee) on the sidelines, and Philadelphia lost star running back Saquon Barkley to an early hamstring injury.
That is a big blow for the Eagles and UK fans as they visit Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Sunday to face the Jacksonville Jaguars, who beat the Cincinnati Bengals 22-17 to make it back-to-back wins.
The Baltimore Ravens also have fitness concerns over a key man, with two-time MVP Lamar Jackson (ankle) unable to play during the second half of their 24-18 home win against the Tennessee Titans.

Cowboys continue to entertain
There have been at least 48 points in every Dallas Cowboys game this season, and they played their part in another high-scoring affair at state rivals Houston.
The Texans led 23-13 after Nico Collins' second score in the third quarter and then 30-27 with two minutes remaining.
But Dak Prescott led the Cowboys to a game-winning drive of 11 plays and 74 yards, throwing a touchdown pass to star receiver CeeDee Lamb to claim a 34-30 win.
Lamb had a career-high 17 receptions for 189 yards, while team-mate Javonte Williams rushed for three touchdowns as Dallas improved to 2-2.
Sunday's highest scorers were the New York Giants after Jameis Winston, filling in for injured quarterback Jaxson Dart, threw three touchdowns and two interceptions in a 36-24 win at home to the Arizona Cardinals.

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.

It's been more than four years since the launch of LIV Golf rocked the game.
A brash breakaway league, bankrolled by Saudi Arabian billions, luring top players with promises of big money.
Still it divides opinion in golf, and has split the loyalty of its champions.
But it could all come to an end soon.
After the League's Saudi backers pulled its funding - having spent more than $5bn (£3.6bn) - this week's abortive season finale could be the end.
That's unless a new deal is struck, soon.
BBC Sport visited the final event of 2026 at an exclusive golf club in Indianapolis, and found a strange atmosphere of surface-level optimism, but deep uncertainty.
Get ready for LIV 2.0... or the end?
LIV staff have learnt to put on a brave face. And that was no more necessary than this week at Chatham Hills Golf Club.
Despite endless questions about the future, they still had a tournament to host, and LIV Golf's white knight was in town - "the investor", as he was most frequently described.
The phrase "LIV 2.0" was used on countless occasions by the league's leadership - and that is the dream they are clinging to.
It stands for a new chapter, a second life for LIV.
There did appear to be genuine optimism that a deal could be struck.
LIV Golf chief executive officer Scott O'Neil believes he can pull off the near-impossible, and so do many of those closest to him.
But there was widespread acknowledgement that, if they do achieve it, the process to get there won't be easy.
One insider remarked "it's darkest before dawn". Another said "it will get worse before it gets better".
Work is said to be happening at "breakneck speed" behind the scenes, because of the pressure of players needing clarity on their futures, events needing to be organised, and sponsorships agreed.
However, there were players, caddies, staff and volunteers who shared a more pessimistic view with BBC Sport, with one describing it as the "last hurrah".
One senior figure within golf's media remarked: "We're at the hospice, not the funeral."
What would new era of LIV look like?
Much of the format is expected to stay the same in any new LIV - a shotgun start, team competition, music blaring from speakers and party holes.
But change will be felt in the boardrooms and in players' pockets.
The "free-spending" days are over.
If LIV does get a second chapter, it will need to be run in a more financially-disciplined way, given overall losses of this era of LIV are expected to have run into several billions of dollars.
BBC Sport has had it confirmed by multiple sources that the prospective investor behind plans for LIV 2.0 is Ted Goldthorpe, head of the credit division of international investment firm BC Partners.
Indeed, one insider referred to him simply as "TG", a nickname that suggests he has become a familiar face.
Goldthorpe attended LIV's most recent event in Bedminster, New York, and O'Neil said he was spending time "looking under the hood" of the league.
But in Indianapolis, Goldthorpe kept himself out of public view, even ushered out of a side door of the clubhouse to avoid media huddled by the front entrance.
He did, however, meet players as a group and set out his vision for the future - the primary aim being to make LIV sustainable, and ultimately profitable.
Selling franchises will certainly be part of the plan, and BBC Sport heard from one of the team's general managers about "significant interest" from investors.
O'Neil said the ambition was to set LIV up so it was "built to last".
There would be a reduced schedule of 10 events a year, across five continents.
The final location of those may well depend on which players stick around, with Australia's former Open champion Cameron Smith particularly popular in Adelaide, for example.
O'Neil said the schedule would be aimed at maximising LIV players' ability to be match-fit come the majors.
Players have been promised equity under a deal with a new investor, but quite what that equates to remains unknown.
They will also get key commercial rights back - called 'Name Image Likeness' rights - which means they can maximise their own endorsements.
Prize money was roughly half this week compared to previous events, and that is a sign of things to come.
Over on the American-based PGA Tour - which LIV players are banned from - prize money has increased in recent years, in large part because of LIV.
If the PGA Tour follows through on its plans to have a two-track system - with a Championship Series and a Challenger Series - it is likely that LIV prize money would sit somewhere between those, and higher than the European-based DP World Tour prize money.
'57 players with 57 different mindsets'
If there are no players, there is no LIV 2.0.
So the next few weeks will be critical in providing the specific details players say they're currently lacking to make decisions over their future.
When asked if there was a critical mass of players needed to sign up for the future before a transaction could be done, O'Neil said: "The entirety of our focus is to get to this transaction and get through it.
"Without the players, that becomes very difficult. I have a good level of confidence in my conversation that we'll have a critical mass of the right players to move this league forward."
Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell, who joined LIV in 2022, told BBC Sport the mood among the players was "subdued".
"There are 57 players out here on LIV and there are 57 different mindsets," said the 2010 US Open champion.
"Some guys have some exemptions in other tours, some have nowhere to go [if LIV folds]."
He said he would be "taking a step back" to work out his future after the Indianapolis event.
"If LIV 2.0 goes ahead, we'll look at the schedule and how it all plays out, and see if that suits me and my lifestyle," McDowell added.
"I have an opportunity to go back to the European Tour and play there as well.
"Whether the two of those can happen simultaneously, whether I can only do one or the other, there are questions like that we don't know the answers to. Until I get that, it's very difficult to make any decisions."
When asked by BBC Sport about his future, Smith, who joined LIV just after winning The Open in 2022, said there would be a "little bit of time to think about that once the season is done".
Would he like to stick with LIV? "I really love LIV," he said. "It has done wonders for my family, for golf in Australia, my friends, the people that we've got to meet around the world. It would be a shame for it to be done, but we'll see what happens."
Other players did not feel comfortable speaking on the record.
One senior player said there is an "emotional" feeling among the group as they await clarity.
Another told BBC Sport "it's been great", before quickly adding "it is great".
It was made clear Jon Rahm - whose future is the source of considerable speculation - would not speak to media aside from his tournament obligations.
American Bryson DeChambeau declined an interview request from BBC Sport.
But after Thursday's first round, he said: "We definitely have a lot against us.
"If it works, it works, awesome. If it doesn't, we'll figure things out. Time will move on, and I would say that time heals things.
"I hope people can see that we actually bring value to the game of golf. My wish is that people give us one more shot and be open minded."
Signs of a strange week
Several people over the past few days privately told me this week had been "extraordinary". Here are some examples.
On Monday, Englishmen Lee Westwood and Tyrrell Hatton were sitting side-by-side in the front row of their flight from Dublin to Indianapolis when official confirmation finally came that their season would be ending early this week.
While the Saudi Public Investment Fund had said it would continue funding LIV until the end of the season, the decision to cancel the team event at the end of August in Michigan was necessary financially, and allowed LIV bosses to "focus on the next chapter".
In the press release about the schedule change came significant news regarding the Indianapolis event too - no live music sets on the weekend, which have been seen as a staple at LIV events over the past four years.
Later on Monday it was announced that routine player news conferences the following day wouldn't happen. It was felt, BBC Sport understands, that players would be left fielding questions they simply didn't know the answers to.
There were reports of vendors suing LIV over unpaid invoices, and of prize money being paid more slowly than normal - although BBC Sport understands that latter issue has been resolved.
Then, at 16:30 local time on Tuesday, the driving range emptied, as players headed for a meeting with "the investor". Fifty minutes later they emerged from the clubhouse, with most swerving awaiting media.
A few stopped to chat, but appeared careful about what they divulged. Martin Kaymer said it was "productive and positive".
Sergio Garcia agreed it had been "productive", but when pushed on his future walked away and said "we'll see".
American Brendan Steele was the only player BBC Sport spoke to in the week who has nailed his colours to the mast - he wants to remain a LIV player.
"It feels new life has been breathed into [LIV]. There was a lot of excitement and energy in the room.
"I'm committed to being here, this is where I want to be."
A critical month ahead
When asked by BBC Sport if he had doubts about LIV's existence beyond this week's event in Indianapolis, O'Neil said the "facts are good" and finished his answer by saying "I wouldn't bet against us".
So what's he basing his optimism on?
In terms of uptake of LIV worldwide, LIV said Adelaide attracted a record 115,000 fans - said to make it Australia's highest-attended golf event - and had a global broadcast audience of 5.5m.
Meanwhile, 100,000 fans attended the event in South Africa, and 50,000 went to the recent UK event, according to LIV.
LIV said 30% of its event-goers had never attended a professional golf event before.
O'Neil said that annual attendance in 2026 would surpass that of 2025, with two fewer events.
LIV Golf said revenue grew by more than100% from 2024 to 2025, and the first half of 2026 suggested this would increase again.
O'Neil also said sponsors were not "running for the hills" despite the uncertainty.
Growth is clearly promising. But there will be no doubt in the minds of Goldthorpe and the LIV hierarchy that turning this into a profitable organisation will take a serious shift in outlook, and of course in spending.
Once everyone packs up from Indianapolis on Sunday night, the focus will turn entirely to securing a transaction to give LIV 2.0 a chance of getting off the ground.
There are a few options available - filing for bankruptcy, pre-packaged insolvency, or someone comes in and pays the outstanding bills.
If all outstanding payments were settled, including on player contracts - such as Rahm, who is understood to be owed millions – then players wouldn't be able to break their contracts early.
O'Neil said there was a deadline for players to sign up to LIV 2.0, but wouldn't provide details of what that was.
The manoeuvrings of the PGA Tour and DP World Tour will be crucial.
There are undoubtedly difficult decisions ahead.
This is the end of an era for LIV.
What no one knows yet is whether it is the end full stop.

It’s a regrettable reality that there is never enough time to cover all the interesting scientific stories we come across. So every month, we highlight a handful of the best stories that nearly slipped through the cracks. September’s list includes a tantalizing hint of the elusive dark matter at the LUX-ZEPLIN detector; entangled Z bosons at the Large Hadron Collider; possible use of psychoactive substances in the Late Pleistocene; and an intriguing technical description of a telescope attributed to Galileo.
A hint of dark matter?
Physicists believe dark matter makes up roughly 85 percent of matter in our universe, with the strongest (but not only) candidate being so-called weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs). But directly detecting WIMPs, or other alternative hypothetical dark matter particles, has eluded physicists for decades. We might have our first glimpse, however, courtesy of the LUX-ZEPLIN detector buried deep in a gold mine in South Dakota. Those potentially exciting results were presented in a scientific talk at the 2026 TeV Particle Astrophysics conference in Japan, with a preprint available on the arXiv. (It has been submitted to Physical Review Letters for peer review.)
The announcement came with strong caveats: the signal is just a hint, well below the threshold needed to confirm discovery, and might just be a statistical fluke. Anyone who regularly follows dark matter news knows that past tantalizing anomalies evaporated as more data came in. But the LUX-ZEPLIN team was unable to account for this event and decided to report their result to the broader physics community. They are still collecting data, as is the XENONnT at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory in Italy. And China’s PandaX detector is currently being built.
If it turns out to be a WIMP that struck a xenon nucleus, it’s not what physicists would predict. The event had a higher nuclear recoil energy than expected, which means the detector should have also picked up several lower-energy WIMPs; it did not. That has theoreticians scrambling to come up with alternative models. Perhaps the interaction rate increases with collision energy. Or perhaps WIMPs have an internal structure, like an atom, and only interact if hit hard enough. Or its coupling to ordinary matter could depend on its momentum.
Cornell University physicist N. David Mermin once described quantum entanglement as “the closest thing we have to magic,” since it means that disturbances in one part of the universe can instantly affect distant other parts of the universe, somehow bypassing the cosmic speed-of-light limit. Albert Einstein memorably dubbed it “spooky action at a distance.” Today, entanglement is the foundation for quantum computing and next-generation sensors, among other applications.
Maintaining quantum entanglement is usually a delicate process; any interference can cause entangled particles to decohere quickly. Despite this, in 2023, physicists found evidence of entanglement between pairs of top quarks produced at the Large Hadron Collider’s ATLAS experiment, raising the possibility that large colliders could be used as an investigative tool to study spooky action at a distance. Now ATLAS physicists have observed entanglement in pairs of Z bosons, according to a paper published in the journal Physical Review Letters.
Z bosons are produced when a Higgs boson decays and are themselves extremely short-lived particles, decaying into pairs of electrons and muons. The ATLAS detector precisely tracks those decay patterns. The physicists used that data to reconstruct the angles at which electrons and muons were emitted to infer the spins of the original Z bosons that preceded them. The authors claim that this is the highest-energy example of entanglement observed to date
Dreams of colonizing Mars face many significant obstacles given the harsh conditions (for humans) on the red planet—including housing. Transporting anything from Earth to Mars is costly, and building materials are especially so. That’s why Hong Kong engineers devised a recipe to combine Martian rocks with terrestrial gelatin and yeast, which then hardens into a durable “living” building material on par with cheap concrete, according to a paper published in the journal Chem Circularity.
Co-author Jishen Qiu of The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology drew inspiration from the hardening of freeze-dried fruits, noting that the Martian environment has extremely low temperatures and pressures akin to freeze-drying. The team experimented with various mixtures of sand and glue, the latter made from gelatin and yeast. But it’s a special yeast coated with sticky proteins similar to those mussels use to adhere to rocky surfaces. The gelatin provides scaffolding for the cells to grow, and the sand provides the structure and mass. Qiu et al. tested their concoction in simulated Martian conditions, 3D-printing small domes the size of wine corks.
They found that the mixture freeze-dries after exiting the nozzle, leaving a light, porous foam with a compressive strength of 10 to 12 megapascals. Per the authors, that is strong enough to build a one- or two-story structure on Earth, where gravity is three times stronger than on Mars, so it should be possible to use their material to make much higher structures on the red planet. It’s less energy-intensive than heating and melting Martian rocks or moon dust into bricks, another approach that’s been proposed. And yeast recovered from dismantled structures could be easily recycled to build new ones.
There is ample evidence that humans in many cultures throughout history used various hallucinogenic substances in religious ceremonies or shamanic rituals, at least since the Neolithic period and the advent of farming and fermented alcoholic drinks (like barley beer). That includes not just ancient Egypt but also ancient Greek, Vedic, Maya, Inca, and Aztec cultures. For instance, in 2024, archaeologists found that an ancient Egyptian vase in the shape of the deity Bes showed traces of chemical plant compounds known to produce hallucinations. And in 2022, archaeologists uncovered evidence that an ancient Peruvian people laced the beer served at their feasts with hallucinogens.
Now Griffith University archaeologists have discovered that humans might have been using mind-altering subsances—by sucking and chewing on betel nuts—as early as the Late Pleistocene period some 25,000 years ago, according to a paper published in Science Advances. Betel nut consumption is common in India and the South Pacific, usually by mixing the seed with slaked lime (which releases the psychoactive compounds) and a few other ingredients to make a “quid,” then chewing it. The effects include mild euphoria and high alertness.
The Griffith team discovered two rare early human forager skeletons from the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, concluding that one dated to 25,000 to 16,000 years ago and the other to 7,600–6,300 years ago. Both skeletons had deep rounded grooves in their teeth, apparently caused by constantly sucking on whole betel nuts. By soaking betel nuts in artificial saliva, the authors concluded that this would release enough arecoline to alter brain function, although the psychoactive effects would be milder.
The authors posit that people from that period sucked on betel nuts to relieve tooth pain, given that these populations are known to have had bad teeth and arecoline is a natural analgesic. But the seeds are abrasive and, over time, wore down the foragers’ teeth so much that inner pulp chambers were exposed. “So while this habit may have been a remedy for toothache, years of prolonged nut-sucking eventually caused much worse dental health problems, creating a cycle of continued habitual use,” said co-author Adam Brumm.
Historians generally agree that a German-born eyeglass manufacturer in the Netherlands, Hans Lippershey, invented the first bona fide telescope in the 1590s. Similar instruments made by other inventors soon popped up, and by 1609, people could buy “spyglasses” in local shops in Paris. Within a few months, the phenomenon had spread to Italy and caught the attention of Galileo Galilei, who fashioned his own telescopes to make ground-breaking astronomical observations that helped the Copernican model of the solar system supplant the Ptolemaic worldview that had dominated for centuries.
Galileo swore never to sell any of his telescopes, and he didn’t document any technical analyses of his instruments either; only eight such telescopes survive; none can unequivocally be attributed to the astronomer. But a historian at the University of Limerick in Ireland has uncovered a previously unknown 17th century description of a four-lens telescope attributed to Galileo in a 1666 manuscript written by a Spanish Dominican friar, detailing his findings in a paper published in the journal Annals of Science.
The text in question is De Tellescopiis Stellarum, by Friar Ignacio Muñoz. Author Jose Maria Moreno Madrid was perusing the treatise when he came across the friar’s analysis of the telescope, complete with diagrams and drawings of the instrument. The analysis was specifically requested by the viceroy of New Spain as a test of the friar’s scientific expertise. Muñoz proposed improvements to the Spanish fleet to King Philip IV in hopes of ending his exile to Portuguese India. Muñoz noted in his manuscript that the telescope belonged to the king and was made by Galileo.
According to Madrid, Galileo had presented Philip IV and his wife with one large and two smaller telescopes to curry favor while working on the problem of longitude. So Muñoz’s description could be referring to one of those three telescopes. The first four-lens telescopes appeared around 1643, but if Madrid’s analysis is correct, this would mean the innovation occurred much earlier, in 1630 at the latest, and could be attributed to Galileo. And Muñoz’s 1666 description would be “the most detailed technical analysis of a telescope provenly made” by the Renaissance astronomer.
Peep shows, aka raree shows, were wildly popular in 17th and 18th century Europe as a form of immersive entertainment by traveling showmen. Pictures or objects were mounted inside a box or wooden cabinet and viewed through a small hole or magnifying glass, creating the illusion of depth perception, sometimes illuminated with candles to create special lighting effects. By the 19th century, peep shows had evolved into cosmoramas, collected in galleries housed in urban bazaars across Britain and Ireland. The cosmoramas weren’t just used for entertainment, but also as a real estate marketing tool, according to a paper published in the journal Early Popular Visual Culture.
John Plunkett, a historian at the University of Exeter, was researching the history of cosmoramas and similar visual technology in the UK and Ireland as part of a broader European project. While poring over advertisements and articles in newspaper archives from the 1820s onward, in order to map the emerging use of cosmoramas around the world, he stumbled on a London auctioneer and surveyor, Brooks and Hedger, who were using cosmoramas in the 1830s to market various estate properties for sale, offering views of homes and grounds including “aerial perspectives.”
Their offices were on Old Bond Street, close to the Cosmorama Rooms of Regent Street, so clearly the firm was capitalizing on the current fad. Per Plunkett, producing cosmoramas would have been a costly investment for the firm, requiring an artist to visit each property and create paintings or drawings from different angles, so this strategy was likely reserved for estates and luxury properties. The practice seems to have been abandoned by 1860, but Plunkett likened it to the virtual tours or walkthroughs employed by online real estate listing services like Redfin, Zillow, or Rightmove in the UK.

Florida weighs ditching property taxes and sticking Canadians with the bill
'I don't want to give Canadians a tax cut,' Florida governor says as he pushes to end property taxes for some
Florida voters are weighing whether to scrap residential property taxes and the state's governor has a solution to that potentially huge revenue loss: tax Canadians more.
Canadians who own property in Florida describe the threats to shake them down for more money as just the latest insult in a series of them since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to power last year with a decidedly anti-Canada agenda.
Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis has railed against property taxes, which fund local governments and the services they provide — law enforcement, fire, EMS, disaster preparation and mosquito control, among many others — equating them to a form of modern-day feudalism where homeowners must "pony up money to the government just for the courtesy of using your own property."
To end this, DeSantis is pushing Amendment 3, a ballot measure crafted by his Republican statehouse allies that will be put to voters in the midterm election next month.
If passed, Florida "homesteaders," as permanent residents are called, will see a dramatic increase in an existing property tax exemption.
Any Floridian with a primary residence valued at $250,000 US or less — about 60 per cent of all homesteaders, according to the governor's office, although that figure has been questioned — would pay nothing and those with a home worth more than that would pay much less than they do now. The measure also calls on the state to eliminate homesteader property taxes entirely over time.
This constitutional amendment requires a 60 per cent supermajority, and at least one recent poll suggests it will easily clear that hurdle.
State economists project such a move will cost about $12 billion US annually, forcing local and county governments that depend on these taxes to make deep cuts, find new revenue elsewhere or both.
That's where things could get more expensive for the Canadians who own an estimated $60 billion US worth of property in the Sunshine State. DeSantis has explicitly described them as a resource to tap to close expected budget gaps.
"We need to focus on our Florida residents. And focus on, in this case, Florida homeowners, particularly our homesteaded homeowners, and we need to focus the relief there," DeSantis said at a news conference last year defending his call for lower property taxes instead of a sales tax cut.
"I want Canadian tourists and Brazilian tourists subsidizing the state and making it so Florida residents pay less taxes. I don't want to give Canadians a tax cut."
In an interview with Fox Business in June, DeSantis said that while homesteader property tax revenue will be a fraction of what it once was if the measure passes, Canadian property owners won't see any of that relief, which could help pad local coffers.
"They tax property that is non-homestead: residential, Airbnb, Canadian snowbirds, commercial. That's a lot of money that they have," DeSantis said of local and county governments.
While reducing taxes for Floridians, the ballot measure also dictates that the assessed value of a non-homesteaded property — owned by a Canadian or another non-resident — can increase by up to 5 per cent a year, steadily raising the revenue local governments can collect.
"They are going to start getting more revenue from existing taxes without having to add new taxes and they're going to end up in a very stable situation very shortly," DeSantis said.
Snowbirds 'fed up'
DeSantis has routinely poked at Canada — including its perennially losing hockey teams. He initially mocked the trade war-induced travel boycott, saying he didn't think it would meaningfully materialize, only to see his state tourism bureau report a double-digit drop in Canadian arrivals last year.
Some Canadians who have put down seasonal roots in the state have had enough of the taunts.
Glenn McGill of Wiarton, Ont., has been wintering in North Fort Myers, Fla., a community once well-populated with fellow Canadian sunseekers, for the last 15 years.
But after Trump's second win there's been what he describes as a "stampede" of Canadians out of the park he and his wife Deb long thought of as a second home.
He says there are only four Canadians left in the sprawling retirement community, a fraction of what there once was when he first started going south.
McGill said DeSantis's threat to lean on Canadians to make up for lost property tax revenue will only drive more of them away, including himself — he listed his home for sale.
"They're a greedy bunch of SOBs," McGill said in an interview with CBC News. "They want to drive Canadians out."
"Those who are well off really don't care but we're not rich, we're not broke, we can do the Florida thing comfortably, but starting to pay extra taxes — that would hurt," he said.
"And this political thing with Trump, I've had enough of it."
With so many Canadians leaving or staying away, McGill says the housing market in Florida has been tough to navigate as a seller.
"The market's pretty dry," he said. "It's listed, but it hasn't sold yet."
Canadians make up the vast majority of foreign property buyers in areas along Florida's Gulf Coast.
According to Realtor.com data, Canadians represent more than 70 per cent of international demand in the Cape Coral metropolitan area, which includes McGill's community.
And with Canadian sales nowhere near pre-trade war levels, the firm says local sellers face "real pricing pressure" with properties listed for weeks longer than the national average.
The areas of Florida that have historically attracted the most Canadian interest are projected to see the largest drop in home prices this year, according to the firm's projections.
Edie Ousley, a spokesperson for Vote No on 3, a group opposing the property tax ballot measure, anticipates more housing market shocks given a possible flood of new Canadian-owned home listings if this tax change takes effect.
"Gosh, it wouldn't surprise me if there's an exodus of Canadians — they are going to be hit significantly," Ousley said in an interview.
"Amendment 3 is a train wreck. It's a train wreck for Floridians. It's a train wreck for those who come in the winter. Those Canadian snowbirds are going to be impacted with additional taxes — this is a tax shift, it's not tax relief," she said.
'Everyone is going to lose'
Ousley said a shrinking Canadian population base alone can't replace what will be lost if homestead taxes disappear.
Many municipalities are already warning that a sudden erosion in their tax base will decimate public services, most notably law enforcement and 911 response times.
"Everyone is going to lose with cuts," she said.
John May of Ottawa offloaded his Key West, Fla., condo after getting sick of hearing people he thought were friends parrot Trump's harsh rhetoric about Canada.
He said he felt like he was swimming in "a sea of stupidity" with falsehoods about his country commonplace.
"Trump would say something stupid, Governor Trudeau, 51st state and all that, and they'd stand there and laugh and I'd say to myself, 'Well, I just lost all respect for you,'" May said in an interview.
"And then you start avoiding people because you know what the conversation is going to be. If you try and have a logical discussion with somebody who's a Trumper, just forget about it," he said.
Jo-Ann Rowe, a Canadian who was wintering in Fort Lauderdale for years with no issue before Trump's return, had the same experience.
"The 51st state thing, my American friends all thought that was quite funny. And I really don't," she said.
She left Florida for a rental property in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico. "I found it totally disrespectful. And I just couldn't do it anymore, this was my little part to do," she said.
Lilly White of Almonte, Ont., spent the last 25 years going to Tarpon Springs, Fla., near Tampa and then Flagler Beach on the other side of the state to escape Canadian winters.
White describes her time there in glowing terms, but said things changed dramatically in the Trump 2.0 era and she had to leave.
"It's not that we don't like it. We're just uncomfortable now. We'll always love the U.S. They'll always be our neighbours. They will always be friends. That's a choice we can make. But we can also choose not to fall down the rabbit hole of what's going on over there right now," she said in an interview.
"I don't like rabbit holes."
White said any move to take more property taxes from Canadians is unfair to those who have pumped a lot of money into the state's economy over the years.
The many small businesses that rely on an influx of Canadian snowbirds are surely hurting as visitor figures plummet amid the bilateral bad blood, she said.
Canadians are by the far largest single source of international tourism to the state, and the number of trips dropped by 20 per cent in the prime winter season this year, data shows.
"I can't imagine how much the businesses are losing. I know how many of my friends are not going down anymore. And we were big spenders," she said.

Ola Electric founder and CMD Bhavish Aggarwal has pledged a 4.32% stake in the electric two-wheeler maker to fund his participation in the company’s proposed rights issue of up to ₹1,000 Cr. In an exchange filing yesterday, the company said the pledge was solely meant to finance Aggarwal’s subscription to the issue and that there were no other pledges outstanding on his securities. “No shares are being sold. The promoter will invest alongside all other shareholders on the same terms,” Ola Electric said. Citing the promoter’s disclosures under SAST regulations, PTI reported that the arrangement involves pledging 20 Cr shares in favour of CTL Trusteeship Limited to secure non-convertible debentures issued by Krutrim Data Centre Pvt Ltd. The report described Krutrim Data Centre as a non-operative promoter group entity owned by Aggarwal, separate from Krutrim SI Designs, which operates the AI and cloud infrastructure businesses. The debenture proceeds will fund Aggarwal’s participation in Ola Electric’s rights issue, it added. Ola Electric’s statement did not disclose the amount raised against the shares or the financing terms. According to the draft letter of offer filed last week, Aggarwal held a 26.52% stake in Ola Electric as of June 30, 2026. The 20 Cr pledged shares represent about 16.3% of that holding. The draft document said Aggarwal has committed to subscribing to his full rights entitlement, subject to provisions allowing him to renounce entitlements in favour of promoter group members or specified investors. He may also subscribe to additional shares or any portion left unsubscribed, subject to minimum public shareholding requirements. The disclosure comes after Ola Electric’s board cleared the rights issue on September 28. The issue is part of a broader ₹1,500 Cr fundraising plan approved by the board on September 5. The company has not announced whether or how it will raise the remaining ₹500 Cr. Ola Electric said it chose the rights issue route to enable participation by eligible retail, institutional, and promoter group shareholders. Debt Repayment, Expansion Drive Fundraise Of the proceeds, the company plans to deploy ₹350 Cr towards repaying or prepaying borrowings of Ola Electric and its material subsidiaries, including accrued interest and applicable prepayment penalties. Another ₹400 Cr is earmarked for organic growth initiatives across its electric mobility and energy storage businesses, including manufacturing, R&D, stores, dealerships, service infrastructure, and sales and marketing. The remaining net proceeds will go towards general corporate purposes. The company expects to deploy the funds during FY27 and FY28. As the shares will be partly paid-up, shareholders will pay a portion on application and the balance through a subsequent call. The draft document envisages completing the first and final call by October 31, 2027, although the board can revise the schedule. The proposed issue follows Ola Electric’s ₹780.2 Cr QIP in June. Of the ₹744.9 Cr net proceeds, it earmarked ₹225 Cr for debt repayment, ₹335 Cr for organic growth initiatives, and ₹184.9 Cr for general corporate purposes. Fundraising Amid Falling Revenue, Market Share The fundraising push comes amid continued pressure on Ola Electric’s business. Its consolidated operating revenue fell 45% to ₹455 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹828 Cr in the year-ago quarter, while net loss narrowed 21.5% to ₹336 Cr from ₹428 Cr. For FY26, operating revenue halved to ₹2,253 Cr from ₹4,514 Cr in FY25, while E2W deliveries fell to 1.74 Lakh units from 3.59 Lakh units. More recently, Ola Electric recorded 13,449 registrations in September, down 3.5% MoM, giving it around 6.5% of the E2W market, according to Vahan data as of October 1. The company described FY26 as a “year of structural reset”, during which it rationalised its retail network, cut costs, strengthened service operations, and focused on improving unit economics. It has since opened its first dealer-operated stores across seven states. Last month, it outlined plans to build a network of more than 500 dealerships over the following two quarters, with dealer partners handling local sales and service and company-owned outlets transitioning into product experience centres. Beyond E2Ws, Ola Electric is expanding its battery cell manufacturing and battery energy storage businesses. It also launched the S1Z escooter range in August, powered by its internally developed Bharat Cell LFP technology. At 13:20 IST, Ola Electric's shares were trading at ₹36.76, down 0.89% from the previous day's close.

Rahul Vohra was only 27 when his first startup was acquired by networking site LinkedIn for $15 million (approximately ₹144.47 crore). But behind the success was a period of intense pressure that eventually sent the young entrepreneur to the hospital. More than a decade later, Vohra has spoken about how that experience changed the way he approached work, health and entrepreneurship. His second startup, Superhuman, was eventually acquired by Grammarly for $825 million in 2025. Rahul Vohra is an Indo-British entrepreneur and the founder of productivity-focused email startup Superhuman. Before building Superhuman, he co-founded Rapportive, a browser plug-in that integrated information about contacts into email. Rapportive was founded in 2009 and was acquired by LinkedIn in February 2012 in a deal reportedly valued at $15 million. Vohra was 27 at the time. While the acquisition marked a major milestone in his career, the months leading up to the deal came with a significant personal cost. A few months before the LinkedIn acquisition was completed, Vohra was hospitalised after experiencing severe pain and nausea. “I didn’t think I was stressed, but I think that’s just because when you’re stressed all the time, you don’t even notice it anymore,” he told Fortune. The symptoms began early one morning when Vohra woke up around 3 am feeling extremely unwell. He initially tried to carry on with his normal routine, but his condition deteriorated as the day progressed. By lunchtime, the pain had become so severe that he attempted to reach a pharmacy near his office. He collapsed on the way, outside a McDonald’s outlet in San Francisco. One of his co-founders eventually came to help him and brought him painkillers. Despite the episode, Vohra returned to work rather than immediately seeking medical care. “like an idiot,” Vohra later recalled about his decision to return to the grind. Vohra eventually went to the hospital the next day, where doctors conducted several tests. According to Vohra's account, years of sustained stress, combined with poor eating habits and a lack of exercise, had affected his health. He was diagnosed with gastrointestinal reflux disease. The warning from a nurse made an even deeper impression on him. She told him that his insides appeared to belong to someone 10 to 20 years older and advised him to “re-examine” his life. Vohra spent a week in hospital. He then stayed home with his family for several weeks while recovering. That period gave him time to reconsider how he wanted to balance his ambitions with his personal life. The experience became a turning point for Vohra. Instead of viewing extreme work hours as an unavoidable part of entrepreneurship, he began looking for a different way to run a company. “I personally find it sad and dismaying when founders in their 20s…[are] running themselves into the ground, often much worse than what I did,” Vohra said. “They’re doing what I did plus stupid hours, and they’re wearing that as a badge of honor. I hope that when people read this, that they see that there is another path.” For Vohra, that alternative involved deliberately stepping away from work after his hospitalisation and making more time for his family. One of the biggest changes in Vohra's routine came when he began practising transcendental meditation under the guidance of Laurent Valosek, a wellness coach and CEO of executive coaching firm Peak Leadership Institute. Vohra learnt the practice in the Raj tradition of India, which involves personalised instruction and a mantra. His initial training consisted of sessions lasting several hours over a number of days. Even after years of practising meditation, Vohra continued meeting Valosek in person every two or three months. Today, the 42-year-old entrepreneur starts his mornings with a 20-minute meditation session. He credits the practice with helping him approach the day with a more “calmer” and “clearer” headspace. “When I did finally get back into work, all of the games that the VCs were playing…that were really getting to me, just suddenly didn’t faze me at all,” Vohra says. The lessons Vohra took from his first startup shaped his approach to building his next company. He went on to launch Superhuman, an email productivity company that attracted significant attention in the technology and startup world. Vohra eventually sold Superhuman to Grammarly for $825 million in 2025. Unlike his first major exit, the journey this time did not involve hospital visits. Vohra said the difference was partly down to the lifestyle changes he had made over the years, including regular exercise, meditation and a healthier diet. “I had this new source of grit and resilience. I just straight-up called VCs who were BS-ing me out on their BS, and refused to engage with them because I had this new found source of strength, which was simply this gratitude for being alive.” Vohra's routine today includes dedicated time for meditation and exercise. He also changed his diet after consulting dieticians and nutritionists. Looking back at the Superhuman acquisition, he said the circumstances were very different from his first startup experience. “I think just being older and wiser, having more perspective, having an exercise practice, having a meditation practice, eating way better,” Vohra says. “There was no existential dread. We weren’t running out of money. We were growing faster than ever. I could have raised more money. Selling the company was really more about: Are we going to achieve our mission faster together if we do this?” For Vohra, the journey from Rapportive to Superhuman was therefore not just about two successful exits. His experience of falling ill at 27 ultimately influenced how he wanted to work, live and build companies in the years that followed. While thousands of Indian students head overseas annually for medical degrees, comprising a heavily monitored segment under the National Medical Commission (NMC) and the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS), parliamentary disclosures indicate that centralised tracking of specific discipline-wise student outflows remains complex.
But for many, the journey culminates in a grueling, high-stakes afternoon inside an Indian examination hall. When the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) released the results for the Foreign Medical Graduate Examination (FMGE) June 2026, the pass rate had plummeted sharply to just 12.4%, triggering nationwide discussions, student protests, and scrutiny over what is locking foreign medical graduates out of medical practice.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
The panic after the paper
Dr. Chaynika Soni, a medical intern in a Government Hospital in Rajasthan who cleared the exam in her second attempt after graduating from Belarus in 2024, recalls, “Every single year after the exam, you’ll see the same thing. Students come out saying, ‘The paper was impossible.’ ‘It was too hard.’ ‘Nobody could solve it.’ Coaching centers will upload videos saying, ‘The paper was unexpected.’ Telegram groups will be filled with panic.”
This panic was visible during the June session, where candidates faced sudden structural shifts. Describing his experience with the exam pattern, Dr. Kshitij Anand said, “The questions were relatively long and time-consuming. I felt the questions were completely unrelated to what I studied. There were some questions I could get direct answers for, but it wasn’t much. They give you questions and options in a way that you take time to figure out answers but not enough time to think.”
He adds that the introduction of unfamiliar video modules caught aspirants off guard: “The Board gave us video questions which I agreed were manageable, but it was a new pattern. The FMGE conducted last January was way more image-based, and the options were comparatively easier to tap than this one. Also, the diagrams I have never seen before.”
Acknowledging these pressures, Professor Dr. Karan Juneja, National Convenor of IMA Junior Doctors’ Network, points out that “More video-based questions (this time), clinical-based questions will be tough for FMG’s [as they are] not exposed to Indian setting and less time make the exam tough.”
Inside the recall analysis
As the National Board of Examinations does not release official FMGE question papers, student-reconstructed “recall” papers serve as the baseline for preparation. A look at the high-weightage sections — Community Medicine (PSM), Internal Medicine, and Obstetrics and Gynaecology — reveals distinct hurdles.
Community Medicine heavily tests India-specific public health administration, including domestic health committees like the Bhore or Kartar Singh committees, local staffing norms at Primary Health Centres, and administrative schemes that foreign universities naturally omit. For a student trained overseas, this often translates to unfamiliar civic administration rather than core medicine.
Conversely, Internal Medicine acts as a control case focused on universal clinical reasoning, ranging from ABG analysis to emergency cardiac protocols. Meanwhile, Obstetrics and Gynaecology balances international diagnostic criteria with clinical application, though candidate performance frequently hinges on interpreting embedded clinical images, manoeuvres, or diagnostic scans.
Weighing these system dynamics, Dr. Samar Kumar, National FMG In-charge for the Federation of All India Medical Association (FAIMA), explains, “In departments such as Medicine, Surgery, and Obstetrics & Gynaecology, Indian hospitals generally see a very large number of patients. This gives doctors and students exposure to a wide variety of clinical presentations and allows them to learn how to manage patients even when resources are limited. I would particularly highlight Community Medicine... If an FMG studies Medicine, Surgery, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, and Community Medicine properly, focuses on clinical concepts, and practices clinical and image-based questions, they should find these areas much more manageable in the FMGE.”
Conceptual depth and the gap in coaching materials
Beyond traditional curriculum differences, candidates found that the depth of questioning defied standard coaching modules. Dr. Ruhi Kumari, who appeared in the June session, explains, “We weren’t trained that way. For example, there was a question on cholera; the answer was an increase in cAMP. I knew it was an increase in cAMP (cyclic Adenosine Monophosphate), but the options were given in biochemistry language. Like, you have to know what cAMP is in biochemistry; only then can you answer that. No coaching institute is teaching anyone like this. Only USMLE tutors do. Because USMLE has always asked in-depth questions. Many clinical questions expect you to have clinical experience. But that’s just unfair, because I will only get that experience after I visit the clinic.”
Dr. Kumari further notes the obsolescence of traditional prep material: “Marrow [an online platform) questions were considered the standard before this exam, but I can tell you they are not anymore. There were a lot of questions that weren’t even asked in many previous years' papers, that flustered everyone... Honestly, I am not sure which resource would give me the most apt training, because no institute is teaching you like that at present. Doing INICET papers is not going to help you, or even NEET-PG papers.”
Logistics, exam conditions, and the transparency debate
The academic difficulty was further compounded by severe logistical hurdles on test day. Dr. Samar Kumar outlines the physical toll: “The first issue was related to examination centres. Multiple centres had inadequate facilities. Some did not have coolers or fans, and in some cases, even drinking water was not adequately available. As you know, the FMG examination is five hours, and overall it takes eight hours. Maintaining concentration in such tough conditions, especially during extreme summer, is something beyond the capacity of many students and FMG doctors particularly when they are not provided with adequate facilities.”
He added regarding the sudden format changes, “The second and most important issue was the sudden introduction of video-based questions in the FMG June 2026 examination. FMGs opposed this later as well and conducted protests regarding this issue in Delhi, Gautam Nagar. The demand of the students was to provide compensation for the sudden introduction of video-based questions, but NBEMS denied the demand.”
Adding to student frustration is a perceived lack of institutional accountability. Dr. Kumar said, “Moreover, the FMG examination does not have any kind of transparency. The questions and answers have never been shown to FMGs. Thus, no one knows how they failed by just one mark, five marks, or ten marks... Then why does NBEMS say that they cannot show the questions and answers together? Why can’t the examination questions and their corresponding answers be disclosed?”
FMGE versus NEET-PG and the time crunch
Comparing the screening test to domestic evaluations, Professor Dr. Karan Juneja, National Convenor of IMA Junior Doctors’ Network, notes that “NEET PG exam standard is being given in FMGE exam as the board-making exam is the same NBE.”
While Indian MBBS graduates prepping for NEET-PG sit within a mature ecosystem of shared question banks and peer networks, foreign-trained graduates often experience thinner access to these informal pipelines.
Dr. Samar Kumar contrasts the two exams, “Recently, FMGE has also included video-based and lengthy clinically oriented questions, which adds another dimension to the examination... FMGE continues to have 300 questions, whereas NEET-PG has moved from the earlier 200-question format to 180 questions. Therefore, FMGE tests not only clinical knowledge and application but also a candidate’s ability to maintain concentration and consistency throughout a long examination. NEET-PG, on the other hand, has its own competitive dynamics, including negative marking and a highly competitive selection process. But if you remove these factors from NEET-PG, then it becomes easier than FMGE.”
This time crunch is intensified by structural scheduling. Dr. Anjali Ayappan from Kochi points out, “Two months is simply not enough preparation time for FMG students, especially considering the amount of syllabus and the situation most FMGs are already in. And bringing the next exam forward to October is especially bad for the June pass-outs. They barely get any time to prepare after the result, and then suddenly they’re expected to appear again in October.”
The long road to registration
Clearing the exam is only the first milestone; graduates face a complex administrative labyrinth before they can practice. Dr. Parvathy Sabu, who cleared the exam and works in a Government Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram, said, “Internship posts for FMGs are fewer across almost every State, and protests to increase seats are seen often... By the time you get PR [permanent registration], best-case scenario, approximately 8 years have gone by (including course duration) and a lot of money. Abroad MBBS is a very long-term investment that many don’t realise initially. I think the integration into Indian healthcare and internship issues are the biggest challenges faced by FMGs.”
Reflecting on these cumulative pressures, Dr. Madhavi Gurung, an FMG aspirant who studied in the U.K., concludes, “Many of my friends skipped FMGE and are now doing residency in the U.S., some are working non-training jobs in the U.K., and some are on track to settle in Australia. The struggle doesn’t end after NEET-UG. And with rising competition and reservation quotas, the system is tough. Every year wasted in endless NEET attempts can drain your mental health and confidence. I’m now planning to take AMC Part 1 by the end of this year and hopefully move abroad permanently.”
