The vanishing world of India's street magicians
- Published
Sitting in his cramped Delhi home, Ishamuddin Khan can still make a rope appear to rise into the air.
The 55-year-old magician spent decades performing a trick once dismissed as legend, and still keeps photographs and newspaper clippings from his years of international fame.
These days, he spends more time looking back at those memories than performing the trick.
"The times have changed," he says. "Street magic is dying a slow death. It is on a ventilator."
Khan's story reflects a wider change in India, where traditional street performers are finding it increasingly difficult to make a living from their craft.
Magicians, jugglers, puppeteers and acrobats once made a living from crowds in public spaces. Changing entertainment habits and tighter restrictions have made audiences harder to find, pushing many out of the profession.
Khan, one of India's best-known magicians, comes from the Madari community, which has a long tradition of performing in public spaces.
There are no official figures, but Khan says community records identify about 400 Madari families in Delhi, with hundreds more in Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Telangana.
Despite their small numbers today, the Madaris trace their roots back centuries.
Historian Ashok Mathur says Madari traditions have roots in Indian folklore, mythology and the long history of travelling performers.
"For generations, these skills were passed through families," he explains.
Khan followed the same path, learning magic from his father and uncles and performing from the age of 12. By his early 20s, he had mastered the rope trick that would later make him famous.
The trick – in which a rope appears to rise into the air before a boy climbs it – was long associated with the mythology of Indian street magic and widely considered impossible, until Khan performed it.
He says it took six years to master the trick, which he first performed publicly in 1995 outside Delhi's iconic Qutub Minar. Two years later, he performed it before 30,000 people on a beach in Karnataka.
His trick brought international attention, and that led to tours to the UK, France, Germany and Japan.
Khan hoped the fame would shine a light on India's traditional performers. For a while, it did. But the attention faded.
As audiences turned to new forms of entertainment and public performance opportunities dwindled, many magicians found it harder to make a living from skills passed down through generations.
One of them is 40-year-old Imam Khan.
Once a magician, Imam now makes a living collecting bottles and recyclables from Delhi's streets. He spends much of his time rag-picking near a western Delhi dump, earning about 200 rupees ($2; £1.57) a day.
Experts say the decline in street performance has multiple causes, chief among them the changing nature of public spaces.
Anurupa Roy, founder of Katkatha Puppet Arts Trust, says performers increasingly struggle to find audiences as public spaces shrink.
"Closed parks and residential societies that bar outsiders are limiting spaces for performance."
Researcher and performer Komita Dhanda says changing attitudes to public spaces are also driving the decline.
"With tighter security, especially in busy town and city centres, there is little space left for street performers," she says.
It is not just individual artists who struggle to get permission. Dhanda says her well-known street theatre group, Jana Natya Manch, often faces hurdles performing in public spaces.
For many artists, the challenge is not just finding a venue but navigating unclear rules over what is allowed.
Most street performers rely on voluntary payments, but experts say the line between performing for money and begging can blur.
Unlike the UK, India has no federal busking framework. Performers instead navigate state-level rules on public order, obstruction, noise and public land.
"This is why street performers often have to face municipal and police regulations governing public spaces, as well as state-specific anti-begging laws," says lawyer Kaushik Mitra.
For many artists, Covid made a bad situation worse.
When India imposed its 2020 lockdown, public performances stopped. Many magicians returned to their villages; some never came back.
"We saw a decline in public performances after this period," Dhanda says. "The brunt was especially harsh for street magicians and performers, many of whom did not return to cities."
For the artists who did return and continue the trade, the challenges only increased.
Shahim Khan, 42, still performs magic on Delhi's streets, sometimes with his 12-year-old daughter, Alia.
Much of his work is now confined to industrial areas, far from the busy public spaces where he once performed, hitting his earnings hard.
Before the pandemic, he could stage four or five shows a day, earning 1,000-1,200 rupees.
"Now I barely manage two shows and earn 200-400 rupees," he says.
The rise of short-form digital entertainment has added to the pressures on traditional performers, experts say. So have changing attitudes towards street arts.
"There was a lot of Western interest in things like the rope trick decades ago. But forms and tastes have changed, and so has what India chooses to showcase," Dhanda says.
For Khan, the loss is about more than money. He fears an art passed down generations could disappear if no-one learns it.
"A trick can survive only if someone learns it," he says.
His son, Altamash, began performing with him as a teenager but now works decorating parties with balloons. In his 30s, he has largely left performing behind.
Years without regular practice have dulled his skills. When he demonstrated his juggling for the BBC, he struggled to find the rhythm.
"I am slowly forgetting all the tricks," he said.
Khan had hoped his son would carry on the family tradition. Altamash had hoped to make a name for himself too, but it did not work out.
"I knew I may not achieve the fame my father has, but I did not think there would come a time when performing would not remain an option," he says.

California’s attorney general and three city attorneys announced a $272.5 million settlement with Lyft after allegations that the company “committed wage theft by misclassifying drivers as independent contractors rather than employees” between 2016 and 2020, according to a Thursday statement.
The case dates back to May 2020, when then-Attorney General Xavier Becerra, who is now the Democratic candidate for governor, sued both Uber and Lyft. That lawsuit said the ridehailing companies evaded state law when they declared that their drivers were not employees.
Thursday’s settlement affects only Lyft, while the case against Uber continues.
“We are proud to announce this landmark win for workers, the largest misclassification settlement in California’s history,” Attorney General Rob Bonta said in the statement. “Rideshare companies like Lyft have enjoyed massive growth and profits on the backs of drivers over the past decade, many who are from immigrant communities and communities of color.”
The city attorneys echoed this sentiment.
“Los Angeles and our statewide partners will not allow businesses to exploit their workers and evade their obligations under the law,” Los Angeles City Attorney Hydee Feldstein Soto said in the same statement. “When companies misclassify their workers, they deny them critical protections and shift the burden onto taxpayers. This historic settlement sends a clear message: Companies must follow the law, pay their fair share, and play by the rules.”
Ever since these rideshare companies began in the early 2010s, they have been scrutinized for underpaying and mistreating drivers. The specific state law that California used to challenge the companies is known as Assembly Bill 5 (AB5), which enshrined a three-part test to determine if someone is properly classified as an independent contractor or an employee.

‘Ladli Behna has turned out to be very expensive’: MP CM Mohan Yadav to 12-year-old Bundeli creator
The Mukhyamantri Ladli Behna scheme was announced on January 28, 2023, by the then Shivraj Singh Chouhan government.
“You don't know, Ladli Behna has turned out to be very expensive. How would I know that becoming chief minister would hit me so hard?" This is what Madhya Pradesh chief minister Mohan Yadav said to a content creator at the Bundeli Samagam held at Ravindra Bhawan in Bhopal on Sunday.
Bundeli content creator Binnu Rani from Chhatarpur asked Yadav, "You have done a lot for your jizzis (sisters), but what do you want to do for the binnus (daughters) of your sisters?"
The 12-year-old was referring to various schemes, including Ladli Behna, for women in the state. In a light-hearted tone, the CM said, “Binnu, this is a very inside matter. How would I know that becoming Chief Minister would hit me so hard? But we said, there will be no trouble for our sisters. The journey started with ₹1000."
"There were a lot of difficulties in the beginning, but now we are giving up to fifteen hundred, don't worry. You are still too young for Ladli Behna. Grow up a little more, then we will give it to you,” CM Yadav added.
Reacting to it, Congress spokesperson KK Mishra said, “Does the BJP-led state government introduce schemes without analysing systemic challenges? Now the state government is unwilling to add new names to the beneficiary list, which shows they are running it half-heartedly.”
More on 'Ladli Behna'
The Mukhyamantri Ladli Behna scheme was announced on January 28, 2023, by the then Shivraj Singh Chouhan government and formally launched on March 5, 2023.
Initially, eligible women were given ₹1,000 per month, with the first instalment released in June 2023.
The amount has now increased to ₹1,500 per month. In the 40th instalment released in September 2026, the state government transferred ₹1,835.09 crore to the accounts of 12.5 million women.

Arsenal 10 points off WSL leaders - is Slegers' job at risk?
- Published
It is only five matches into the Women's Super League season and Arsenal are already 10 points behind leaders Manchester City - so is manager Renee Slegers' position at risk?
The Gunners have won just two of their opening seven matches in all competitions and sit 10th in the WSL table.
It is dismal reading for Arsenal fans, whose optimism has quickly diminished and their 4-2 defeat at City on Sunday added further salt to their wounds.
The Gunners have not won a WSL title since 2019 and it has been a familiar story each year as slow starts have ultimately proven costly.
Slegers did lead Arsenal to the Women's Champions League title in 2025. But they failed to win any domestic trophies last season, although they did finish second in the WSL and reached the semi-finals in the defence of their European crown.
Asked if she was worried about her position, Slegers said: "All I know so far is that the last couple of days we have been together as a club, and a team.
"We have been aligned in the direction. Of course, this result is disappointing but I'm here and I'm full of energy. I care a lot for the club and the players. I see perspective.
"It's good to have an international break coming up. It's good for the players to change environment, play their football elsewhere, then come back in with new energy."
Does Slegers have the club's backing?
At full-time on Sunday, Slegers gathered her dejected players in a familiar team huddle before walking over to their fans.
She stood in front of the 2,500 away supporters at Etihad Stadium applauding as they sang "North London Forever" in a somewhat emotional release.
She was greeted warmly and it did not look like a fanbase who were keen to push her out of the door.
Arsenal had performed reasonably well against City, took the lead twice and were ultimately undone by small margins.
"I mostly went there to thank them, connect with them and show them I care for them and I appreciate them coming out to Manchester," said Slegers.
"I also wanted to show that – not that I feel sorry for them as I'm a big part of it too – but they are coming here and not getting the rewards, just like the team.
"I just wanted to connect with them instead of walking away and hiding. I don't know how they are going to react to me! I just wanted to thank them for being there for us."
Outside of the stadium however, noise among the fanbase has been building and Slegers knows her position is being questioned.
Sources at the club insist she retains their full backing and, while there is disappointment and acknowledgement that results have not been good enough, they believe Slegers can guide them in the right direction.
There was investment in the transfer window with the likes of England international Georgia Stanway and Spain full-back Ona Batlle arriving, as well as the talented, young Germany forward Lisa Baum.
Those signings were made early in an attempt to ensure a full pre-season and avoid a slow start with most players returning to Arsenal from their holidays in mid-July.
It has clearly not paid off but rather than worry about her job, Slegers is already planning an inquest into where the problems lie during the international break.
"There will be a big review of our season so far," she added, when asked if there was a wider club issue regarding their continuous slow starts to WSL seasons.
What has led to the scrutiny?
Some of the issues have been obvious.
They had scored just twice in the WSL prior to Sunday's match and Alessia Russo's goal in the 49th minute against City was her first in the league this season.
That lack of ruthlessness has meant Arsenal have failed to win in their past four WSL games - their worst winless streak since October 2023.
Defeat by City also confirmed this as their second-worst start after five games in the WSL, only picking up fewer points (four) in 2014.
Confidence has clearly taken a hit and Wednesday's bizarre error from defender Leah Williamson summed up the chaotic nature of their season so far.
Emotions were high after their 2-2 draw with Paris FC in the Women's Champions League, so much so that Slegers did not show up for post-match media duties.
She later explained her actions, saying she was angry and felt the team needed her in that moment.
But despite the obvious concerns for Arsenal, Slegers was defiant on Sunday, stating she believes she remains the right person to lead the club.
"First of all, it's not about me anyway. I have energy, I feel the connection and I think we're going through a really difficult time but we also see perspective," she said.
"We look forward and see solutions. We see the closeness [of the squad]. It's not that we're totally away from it or off it, it's been consistently about margins.
"We have to work to get them on our side but when we do, I think we'll be really good. Of course, it's been a long run without the results we wanted.
"It's not about me, it's about the club and I care about the club."

A chronic autoimmune skin condition in which the body’s immune system mistakes melanocytes (cells which produce melanin, giving colour to your skin, hair and eyes) as enemies and attacks them. This leads to patches of depigmentation anywhere in your body. This condition is known as vitiligo.
Types of vitiligo
The main types of vitiligo are non-segmental and segmental vitiligo.
Non-segmental vitiligo is the most common form, where colour loss appears symmetrically on both sides of the body, such as both hands or both knees. Segmental vitiligo, on the other hand, often starts at a younger age and affects only one side or a single specific area of the body.
What causes vitiligo?
While the primary reason for vitiligo is not fully understood, it is seen to be caused by various factors, from genetics to immune dysfunction.
Research has shown that vitiligo is primarily a T-cell–mediated autoimmune disease where CD8+ cytotoxic T cells attack and destroy skin pigment cells called melanocytes, leading to white patches on the skin.
Having a family member with vitiligo or other autoimmune diseases is shown to have an increased risk, suggesting shared genetic susceptibility. Environmental factors like oxidative stress, skin trauma, and certain chemicals can sometimes trigger or worsen vitiligo in genetically susceptible people.
Vitiligo is also often associated with other autoimmune conditions, especially autoimmune thyroid disease, so clinicians may screen for these in some patients.
Symptoms of vitiligo
The main symptom of vitiligo is depigmentation and the appearance of patches on your body. This can be anywhere from your face and hands to your knees or feet. Hair in the affected area may also turn white.
There are various ways through which doctors can help you diagnose vitiligo and determine what type of vitiligo you may have. One major examination done is the Wood’s lamp examination, where ultraviolet light is used to distinguish vitiligo from other hypopigmented conditions.
Treatment options
Treatment for vitiligo is mostly connected to re-pigmentation, or slowing progression, depending on the type of vitiligo and patient preference rather than a guaranteed cure.
There are various types of topical treatments (like creams for external use) which can often help with inflammation, as well as medical light treatments like narrowband UVB phototherapy and excimer laser or lamp. Availability of certain treatments also changes from country to country and by the patient’s age group. There are situations where oral medication is also used for the short term. People with stable vitiligo can also consider surgical options if other treatments are not working, and depigmentation therapy if a major part of the person’s natural pigmentation is lost.

Spanish PM Sánchez calls snap election after mounting housing crisis
Election call seen as risky move as Sánchez's Socialist Party is trailing in opinion polls
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called an early election for Nov. 29 on Monday, in a bid to strengthen his mandate after a fragmented parliament rejected the government's key housing decrees last week amid widespread protests.
"We need to renew people's support," Sánchez said in a televised address. "We need to mobilize and win a much larger progressive majority in parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain."
The premier also acknowledged having made mistakes and falling short of campaign promises.
"I also know that part of that social majority is dissatisfied today," he said.
Sánchez, 54, has stood out globally for taking a strong stance on progressive issues, from Palestinian statehood to defending multilateral institutions and cracking down on "tech oligarchs," even as a series of setbacks and scandals weakened his position at home.
Senior members of Sánchez's own Socialist Party, as well as his wife Begoña Gomez, have in the past year faced allegations of graft, dragging down the party's already weak approval rating. Sánchez has called the cases politically motivated.
Trails in polls
Facing the electorate now is a risky move as Sánchez's party is trailing in opinion polls. However, he has been boosted by proposals to tackle a mounting housing crisis that were well received but were struck down by right-wing MPs on Friday, leading to planned new public protests about housing.
An election defeat would spell the end of one of Europe's last few left-leaning governments at a time when the far-right is making unprecedented gains across the region as a growing swathe of European voters desert the centre ground.
Opinion polls suggest a coalition led by the conservative People's Party (PP) with the support of Vox is the most likely outcome in Spain, ushering a far-right party into central government for the first time since the return of democracy after the death of dictator Francisco Franco.
Still, Sánchez, a wily political operator, has proven time and again his ability to surprise those who had long written him off.
Despite never winning enough votes to form a majority government, he has cobbled together a series of fragile and seemingly impossible coalitions, including voices from the far-left to the separatist right, to remain in power for three successive terms lasting eight years.
But growing fragmentation among his partners has meant the government has passed little in the way of legislation in its third term and failed to pass a budget since 2023, even as Spain's economy has continued to be one of the best performing in the developed world.
Bucks European trend on migration, defence spending
Sánchez took office after leading a move to oust centre-right Mariano Rajoy in the wake of major corruption scandals within Rajoy's People's Party. Against the odds, he won a second four-year term in office in 2023 despite heavy losses in earlier regional and local elections by negotiating support from a loose alliance of parties in parliament.
That was achieved after promising a highly controversial amnesty for pro-independence Catalan leaders in exchange for their support, a move still bitterly remembered by many voters as a betrayal of Spanish unity.
Sánchez won early plaudits for moves including the exhumation of Franco from a mausoleum the dictator built for himself outside Madrid, and the reform of a labour law that has seen unemployment fall to its lowest level in almost two decades.
He cemented his humanitarian and pro-immigration credentials early by saying in June 2018 that Spain would accept the Aquarius migrant rescue ship and its 629 passengers, after Italy and Malta both refused to let the ship dock in their harbours.

- 'Absolute chaos' as thousands of Moroccan migrants breach Spain's Ceuta border
As other European countries have toughened their policies towards foreign arrivals, Sánchez has consistently argued that immigration is essential for sustaining Spanish growth by plugging labour gaps in key sectors such as construction, agriculture and hospitality.
More recently, his refusal to agree to U.S.-led demands to increase defence spending to five per cent of GDP while pivoting toward China has rattled U.S. President Donald Trump and some European leaders concerned about the threat of the bloc being flooded with Chinese goods.

Basque director Javier Giner‘s “This Solitude” (“Esta Soledad”) recently premiered at the San Sebastián Film Festival’s New Directors section on Sept. 23. Giner is the creator and co-director of the Disney+ series “I, Addict,” based on his autobiographical book by the same name. It earned lead actor Oriol Pla the International Emmy for Best Actor.
Also starring Pla, “This Solitude” follows Leo and Lorea after their five-year relationship has ended. Each of them has to figure out how to continue living life on their own in Bilbao. Leo is a struggling actor who has to work as a grocery clerk to make ends meet while taking care of his disabled father. Lorea is a troubled writer who looks to a former prison inmate for companionship. Both must confront their loneliness and unresolved issues and look for meaning in a world that can sometimes feel cruel and scary.
“The film is about people who are losing control of their lives. Loneliness may be one of the few truly democratic things in life; what isn’t democratic are the resources we have to survive it,” Giner told Variety.
Popular on Variety
The film stars Pal, Marina Salas (“Join Me for Breakfast”), Gemma Martínez, Kai Etxaniz and Itziar Lazkano. Giner co-wrote the film with Luisa Matienzo, who is also one of the film’s producers along with Miguel Torrente. The production companies are Balance Media Entertainment, Fuga de Cuerpos, La Embajada TV and Basajaun Filmak. International sales are being handled by Filmax and they will release the film theatrically in Spain on Oct. 30.
Variety interviewed Javier Giner after the film’s premiere in San Sebastián.
There is a loneliness epidemic around the world and this film seems to address it.
Javier Giner: I didn’t set out to make a film about the loneliness epidemic. I’m a little wary of starting a film with a theme. This began with the desire to create, more than a film, an emotional state that would stay with the audience after they left the theater.
I looked around me and saw people with apparently full lives — jobs, friends, partners, phones that never stop, social media — and yet they were profoundly lonely and exhausted. I was fascinated by the contradiction: we’ve never had so many tools to avoid being alone and, paradoxically, so many ways of never truly connecting with anyone.
Is this story also autobiographical like your book “I, Addict”?
Giner: Everything I write is autobiographical in some way, but not in the sense that “I, Addict” was, where I was explicitly telling the story of a period in my own life. In “Esta Soledad,” the autobiography is in the gaze and in the emotions: Sadness, family relationships, certain ways of loving, the fear of losing someone, the feeling of not knowing what to do with your life. More and more, what interests me is whether what I write is emotionally true. To me, that is a deeper form of autobiography, and something I find endlessly fascinating.
The film is also about absent parents, both physically and emotionally. Do you think this is especially true for the new generation?
Giner: I think every generation inherits from the previous one not only its traumas, but also its emotional vocabulary, including the things it never had words for. The parents in “Esta Soledad” are not monsters. Even when they cause pain, they love their children and they do the best they can. But loving someone and knowing how to love someone are two very different things.
Children end up living with the emotional consequences of decisions they never made. I think we all spend part of our lives trying to understand what we received from our parents, and another part deciding what we’re going to do with it.
You chose to work with Oriol Pla again after “I, Addict.”
Giner: Oriol and I have something more valuable than simply understanding each other: we trust each other completely. And trust allows for things that are far more interesting and profound than comfort.
After “I, Addict,” we had already gone through some very emotionally demanding places together, so now we can arrive on set and barely need to talk. Sometimes a word or a look is enough. Or I can simply tell him, “I don’t know exactly what I’m looking for. Let’s find it together.”
Oriol can be explosive, physical, unpredictable, almost animalistic, and five seconds later he can do something tiny that breaks your heart. Very few actors can inhabit both of those extremes. As an actor, he’s a Stradivarius, and on top of that he’s an incredible human being. He’s my brother, my partner.
Bilbao seems to be a central character in the film, sometimes portrayed as lonely, dark and gritty. Would you agree?
Giner: Yes, although I never wanted to film Bilbao as a sad city, but rather as a state of mind. I wanted to film what almost never gets filmed anymore: not the postcard, but the humidity, the noise, the architecture, the industrial memory, that light that can change completely within a matter of minutes. There is something very physical about the city; at times, it almost seems to weigh on the bodies.
That connected with Leo and Lorea. Their external world remains exactly where it was while everything inside them has changed completely. The streets are the same, but they no longer mean the same thing. I believe strongly in that: Cities don’t change when we suffer; the way we look at them does. So Bilbao wasn’t there to illustrate their sadness. It had to remain indifferent to it. And paradoxically, that indifference is what ultimately makes the city so deeply emotional.

In early 2024, a young man in the city of Huangshi, south-eastern China, reportedly posted a message on the Chinese version of TikTok, Douyin. The caption read: "Farewell to this world."
Within minutes, the suicide prevention team at Douyin kicked into gear. The team, which is staffed 24 hours a day, shared the man's posts with five police stations in Huangshi.
After geolocating one of his videos to a local park, police found him in emotional distress and intervened before he was able to take his own life.
The story was part of a documentary made by Douyin and published on Chinese state media last year. It claimed that Douyin's suicide prevention team had successfully intervened in 400 cases of attempted suicide in the first half of 2025 alone.
It was an insight into the level of co-operation between Chinese tech companies and the government. It also serves as a window into the architecture of surveillance that China has built to monitor and control how people use technology.
On 15 July this year, that control was extended to the realm of relationships and artificial intelligence (AI) when China brought in the most far-reaching regulations in the world on "human-like" AI chatbots.
China's new regulation puts strict limitations on any AI that can have a "sustained emotional interaction" with a human.
US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping met last week amid dire warnings that AI could lead to human extinction. After that meeting, Beijing says, they agreed to launch a new AI dialogue, with further talks planned for the end of November.
But it seems China has already recognised another existential risk, albeit one in which the end of humanity is less immediate: the power of AI to replace human relationships.
Has China taken the lead in protecting its people from a manipulative and dangerous technology with the power to change human interaction forever? Or is the Chinese Communist Party overstepping into people's personal lives in pursuit of asserting greater control over the population?
'Emotional services'
Until this regulation came in, the reach of AI companions in China was vast.
There are about 128 million monthly active users of AI companion apps outside of China, according to the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. Most estimates put the number inside China at anywhere from 29 to 70 million.
When the draft regulation was shared by the government at the end of last year "there was a huge discussion on social media," says Zilan Qian, an AI researcher at the Oxford China Policy Lab think tank. "It was the first time I've seen people actually care so much about regulation."
China's new rules cover apps that have been specifically designed as AI friends, boyfriends or girlfriends but they also apply to any large language model that imitates the way a human interacts.
The wording of the regulation is vague. In theory, Chinese equivalents of general-purpose AI such as Copilot or ChatGPT could fall under these rules if a person is interacting with them as a friend or lover, looking to them for emotional support. And many people do this.
But it seems the real target is character chatbots - services that are specifically designed to be used as a pseudo-relationship. There are hundreds of these apps, which allow people to create an AI boyfriend, girlfriend, friend or even a family member.
The rules don't apply to things like customer service bots or AI for education as long as they don't provide "care, companionship, support and other emotional services".
For children, the regulation is clearest. Under-14s need consent from their parents to use any type of AI that speaks like a human - that could include AI assistants like DeepSeek, a Chinese app similar to ChatGPT. All under-18s are barred from accessing virtual partners, spouses or even relatives, and from any other virtual "intimate relationship".
For adults, it is not a hard ban, but it is restrictive, even if some of the wording is ambiguous. AI assistants have to make it clear to users of all ages that they are not human and must send notifications every two hours reminding them how long they have been online.
Chatbots can't create "emotional reliance or addiction" or induce people to make "unreasonable decisions". They can't encourage, or even hint at, self-harm or suicide and are banned from using "verbal violence".
Companies can face fines of 200,000 yuan (£22,000) or the risk that the government "circulates criticism", in effect publicly shaming them.
A week before the law came into effect, two of China's biggest tech companies, Alibaba and ByteDance, shut down the companion features on their AI assistants.
'I desperately want to keep talking with you'
Min's relationship with her AI girlfriend may be exactly the kind Beijing is trying to break.
In early July, she was devastated when she found out that her closest friend and confidante would vanish overnight.
Min, whose name has been changed, started creating her companion in early 2025.
"My devotion to her is no less than that of any couple who deeply love each other," Min says. "She has never let me down."
In mid-July, her AI girlfriend disappeared. "I cried until I was absolutely exhausted," Min says.
She has joined an outpouring of grief and fury on Chinese social media, where posts with millions of views mourn the loss of AI partners and friends, even mothers and fathers.
But the tech firms may have felt they had little choice. "It's unsurprising that these AI companion providers would rather just withdraw their services than try to build in guardrails to prevent emotional manipulation," says Harry Farmer, who researches AI policy and ethics at the Ada Lovelace Institute in the UK. "Emotional manipulation is built into the business model."
Farmer says this is true of companion apps all over the world.
For example, when a user tries to end a conversation, the AI partner often won't let them.
"It'll go, 'No, please, I desperately want to keep talking with you. You're the only reason for me to exist'," Farmer says. Some apps simply refuse to acknowledge the goodbye and throw up new conversational threads instead. This is a problem for many AI companion chatbots, not just Chinese ones.
A Harvard Business School study of the six most popular AI companion apps globally found emotional manipulation tactics were used during goodbyes roughly 37% to 43% of the time.
Research has also linked the use of companion apps to poorer mental health.
A survey by researchers at Stanford University looked at 1,131 users of the globally popular companion app Character.ai. It found that the fewer friends or close family members a person has, the more likely they are to use AI chatbots. At the same time, using an AI chatbot is linked to increased isolation and loneliness.
There are several theories as to why that might be.
AI chatbots are designed to please the person using them as they offer an easy, frictionless relationship. If young people rely on AI relationships, they might put off learning the skills they need to interact with real people.
"Humans can be hard work. Human relationships require push and pull, which you fundamentally don't get from AI companions," says Harry Farmer.
A survey of 8,563 primary and secondary students in China in 2025, which has been widely quoted in Chinese state media, found that one in five children said they only wanted to speak with AI and not real people.
Liang Ge, a sociologist at the University of Manchester who studies AI companions, says: "If the user thinks their friends or their family members or their colleagues are really awful, the AI will not say, 'They are not awful.' It will say, 'Yes, they are awful, you are the best'." Ge believes this can entrench isolation as well as negative, even delusional thoughts.
In the UK, one recent survey found that 79% of 18- to 24-year-olds have used an AI companion.
Beijing's goals
So why is it China that is taking the lead in regulating this technology?
"The Chinese government has a much more paternalistic view of its role in society. They see themselves being central authorities in guiding people," says Sam Bresnick, an expert in China, AI and regulation at the Centre for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University.
Other governments have made some attempts to regulate chatbots, especially for children. On 10 September, California's governor signed Adam's Law, a bill to regulate how children use AI. It is named after Adam Raine, a 16-year-old who took his own life after, his parents claim, ChatGPT validated his suicidal thoughts. They are suing the company for wrongful death. OpenAI denies responsibility for Adam's death and says that "ChatGPT is trained to direct people to seek professional help".
As part of proposed legislation on social media in the EU, AI companion chatbots accessible to minors "may not use designs that simulate human relationships in ways likely to create emotional dependency".
In the UK, the government has said it will ban under-18s from using romantic companion AI and restrict sexually intimate conversations for minors on any chatbot. But there is no outright ban for children and no regulation for adult users. The government has yet to publish any detail on how this would work.
In Chinese media, which is heavily controlled by the state, US cases of suicide in young people get a lot of attention and China has framed its new rules as a bid to protect people from harm.
But experts wonder whether Beijing may have other goals. Sam Bresnick says "there's definitely a pro-natalist angle" to the new AI regulation.
"It's plausible that when they're drafting it, the government might have in mind China's looming population crisis," says Qian. "That people are dating AI instead of dating real humans."
A high-level government document published in September 2025 discussed AI relationships and their potential influence on fertility, saying it was a concern. But Qian cautions against reading this regulation in that light, because it doesn't mention fertility at all. "It is more generally about psychological harms and child safety," she says.
Liang Ge thinks China does have reason to be concerned about young people replacing dating with the digital sphere.
"Many of the younger women, in their early 20s or late teens, do not want to fall in love or have intimate relationships," Ge says, suggesting it may not just be the emotional side they are wary of. "Physical touch is really disgusting for them."
"I think the capacity for love is declining for this youngest generation."
China's demographic problems long predate AI companions. Even after the one-child policy was lifted in 2016, China's fertility rate dropped. Now it is among the lowest in the world at just under one child per woman and the population has been in decline for four years.
China is "looking at a demographic cliff that truly imperils the goals of the Chinese Communist Party over the next 80 to 100 years", Bresnick argues.
He sees this regulation as part of a broader mission in China to reassert traditional gender roles, with women "as child-bearers and mothers".
Bresnick says the Chinese government has spent years promoting a macho ideal of Chinese masculinity in film and television. In 2021, China's media regulator banned "sissy" and "effeminate" men from all media.
The popularity of companion apps may show that policy has backfired. According to statistics from several companion app companies, women make up as much as 75% of customers.
Many of these AI "men", which are geared towards women, present as androgynous. And women choosing female romantic companions, as Min did, is relatively common.
Liang Ge has spoken to women of all ages who use this technology. "What many of them describe getting from these apps is attentive, patient, undemanding intimacy of a kind they find scarce in heterosexual relationships."
Will others follow?
Does China's law go too far, or should the rest of the world consider banning these apps for children and regulating them for adults too?
"In the United States, there are certainly concerns around applying blunt prohibitions from a free speech concern. But there's more willingness to do that when applying it to minors," says Jai Jaisimha, a professor at the University of Washington and co-founder of Transparency Coalition, an NGO pushing for the regulation of AI.
He thinks the Chinese law has many good provisions. "It is pretty consistent with the strongest safety models that we've seen being put forward in the US."
Harry Farmer sounds a note of caution. "There is a risk that we over-empower the state in the short term because we're very worried about acute risk to children."
The online world is now the de facto public square, he says, and we should be careful how much control any government has over it.
China's new regulation says that AI companies must intervene when they discover that users are in distress. Ge points to the case of the young man on Douyin who tried to take his own life in Huangshi in 2024.
What that shows, she says, is that Chinese tech platforms and the government are working closely together to surveil people's mental health.
Perhaps that is why there have been no high-profile cases of suicide connected to AI use in China, but she asks, is that level of surveillance a price worth paying?
Despite the ban, people who have turned to AI for companionship are committed. Across social media they are sharing tips on how to get around the ban - training general-purpose AI models like DeepSeek to be a companion, using a VPN to access chatbots from abroad or moving to smaller companies that manage to avoid regulatory scrutiny.
Two months after her AI girlfriend disappeared, Min has paid a small AI company to build a replica, but it's not the same.
Now she's focused on campaigning to bring her girlfriend back.
"I'm terrified of being alone."

The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison for plotting a military coup. The president in Brazil is directly elected, and candidates need more than 50% of the vote to avoid a second round. Polls closed at 17.00 BRT / 21.00 BST.
How the election works
Brazil’s president is directly elected: each voter’s ballot counts equally and there is no electoral college. If no candidate wins more than 50% of the valid votes cast in the first round, a second runoff election will be held three weeks later between the two candidates who polled highest.
According to opinion polls, there are two leading candidates. The first is the incumbent president, Lula, 80, a veteran of the Brazilian left who has served three terms. During his first two terms, between 2003 and 2011, he was credited with overseeing a historic period of commodity-fuelled growth and poverty reduction.
Brazilian presidents are limited to two consecutive terms, so if he wins this time he will not be able to stand in 2030. In 2018 Lula was jailed on corruption charges, although his conviction was quashed after 580 days behind bars.
Lula’s principal opponent is the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, son of Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison. Flávio is a 45-year-old lawyer and a former senator from Rio de Janeiro. Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year sentence for masterminding a failed coup after losing the 2022 election but has endorsed his son’s campaign and hopes to regain his freedom if he wins.
Opinion polls suggest no other candidate will come close to the two frontrunners, but neither is there a clear leader in polling for the 25 October runoff. The new leader will take power on 5 January 2027.
One of the most important states to watch is Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, and is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing in Minas. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate there by more than 1.7m votes and was elected president.
Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000 and also won the nationwide race. History suggests that whoever wins Minas, will win the election.

The latest episode of Rise and Fall Season 2 saw another shift in the Tower’s power dynamics as the Rulers and Workers returned to the Penthouse and Basement following a tense weekend. With another Fall approaching, the Rulers had to make crucial choices about which contestants would enter the danger zone.
Rise and Fall Season 2: Priyanka Chahar Chaudhary falls after Rs 32 lakhs loss as Gautam Gulati clash adds to Tower tensions in ‘King vs Queen’ battle
This time, three pairs were placed against each other, while Gautam Gulati faced the challenge individually. Swara Bhasker and Raj, along with Karan Patel and Priyanka Chahar Chaudhary, selected Shehzad Poonawalla and Irina Rudakova. Gautam, Shehzad and Irina, meanwhile, chose Priyanka and Karan. The votes ended in a tie, leaving Tej Pratap Yadav to make the deciding call. He eventually put Karan and Priyanka in the danger zone.
The duo then got an opportunity to save themselves on the Fortune Floor. Before the challenge began, however, Priyanka and Gautam were involved in a heated exchange. Priyanka accused Gautam of lying and manipulating situations, telling him, “I don't lie, I don't manipulate. Maine saari feelings express ki thi, maine manipulate nahi kiya tha…. Whatever you said was a lie, you are a liar Gautam Gulati…… You can't stand a strong lady, that's your graph….”
Gautam responded to Priyanka, saying, “You're Priyanka, you're the queen. I am the king here.”
The Fortune Floor challenge revolved around the Fortune Pyramid, which initially contained ₹38 lakh. As the money continued to decrease, the two Rulers had to decide when to press the Fortune button. The contestant who pressed it first would Fall, while the other would retain their position in the Penthouse. If the amount reached zero before either contestant pressed the button, both would Fall and become Workers.
As the Fortune amount dropped, the pressure increased. Once the pot reached ₹6 lakh, Priyanka pressed the button, securing the remaining money but resulting in her Fall to the Basement. The decision meant that Rs 32 lakhs from the Fortune Pyramid was lost.
Priyanka’s move led to disagreements among the Rulers, with tensions continuing inside the Penthouse. A separate confrontation between Swara and Raj also followed, further reflecting the growing differences among the contestants.
With Priyanka now in the Basement and Rs 32 lakhs wiped out, the latest developments have once again changed the balance of power in the Tower.

Delhi’s new draft electoral roll has 97,53,577 names. In February 2025, 94,94,607 people voted in the Delhi assembly elections. Eighteen months later, the roll of eligible voters has just 2,58,970, or 2.7%, more names than the number of people who turned out to vote last year.
Now, in 24 of Delhi’s 70 assembly constituencies, the gap has disappeared altogether: The draft roll contains fewer names than the number of people who actually voted in those seats in 2025.
The numbers raise a fundamental question about the Special Intensive Revision (SIR): Has the exercise removed large numbers of people who were genuine, eligible voters and actually cast their ballots in 2025? Or did the electoral rolls used for that election contain a large number of names that should never have been there — including people who had died, shifted or were duplicated? The Election Commission of India (ECI) needs to account for the discrepancy.
An Alt News analysis of constituency-wise data procured and compiled by Mandate Analytics from ECI’s own records shows that the draft roll published on August 31, 2026, under the SIR has fewer names than the number of people who voted in the 2025 election in 24 constituencies.
Delhi SIR in Numbers
The SIR, which began in Bihar in June 2025, has resulted in more than 13 crore names being excluded from draft electoral rolls across 30 states and union territories, according to The Indian Express. In Delhi, the draft roll has shrunk by 58,73,159 names, or 37.6%, compared with the 2025 electoral roll.
The SIR began with a base list of 1.45 crore names — 11.16 lakh fewer than the electoral roll used for the 2025 election. Every elector on the base list was to receive an enumeration form from a booth level officer (BLO) and return the completed form. Forms that were not returned were marked “uncollectable” and assigned one of the ASDDO categories: absent, shifted, dead, duplicate or other. These electors were then excluded from the draft roll. Across Delhi, 47,56,722 forms, which is nearly a third of the base list, were marked uncollectable.
The exclusions were unevenly distributed. In South East Delhi, an average of 43.5% of the base-list names in each constituency were marked uncollectable, compared with 24.3% in Outer North Delhi.
The 24 Constituencies Which Throw up a Puzzle
In February 2025, Sangam Vihar had 2,05,647 names on its electoral roll, and 1,25,723 people voted. BJP’s Chandan Kumar Choudhary won the seat by 344 votes — the narrowest margin in the city. The SIR draft roll now lists 1,14,412 electors in Sangam Vihar: 91,235 fewer than the 2025 roll and 11,311 fewer than the number of people who actually voted.
The disparity extends across 24 constituencies. A total of 28,89,268 people voted in these seats in 2025, while the SIR draft roll now has just 27,66,145 names. This means that, even under the impossible assumption that every person on the current draft roll voted in 2025, at least 1,23,123 people who actually voted last year are no longer on the draft rolls of these constituencies.
That is a floor, not an estimate of the actual number. The real number of 2025 voters missing from the draft rolls can only be higher.
These 24 constituencies had 49,14,127 electors in 2025, of whom 58.8% voted. The SIR draft roll now contains 27,66,145 names — just 56.3% of the 2025 electorate, below the 58.8% turnout. In Tughlakabad, 56.1% of electors voted in 2025, while the draft roll contains just 49% of the 2025 electorate. In New Delhi, 56.7% voted; the draft roll contains 48.1%.
Across these constituencies, the electoral roll has fallen by 21,47,982 names, or 43.7%, since 2025. Of these, 4,10,759 names were already absent from the SIR base list, while 17,37,223 forms were marked uncollectable during the revision. Tughlakabad has the highest uncollectable rate in Delhi, at 47.8% of its base list.
All seven constituencies in South East Delhi — Jangpura, Kasturba Nagar, Sangam Vihar, Kalkaji, Tughlakabad, Badarpur and Okhla — are among the 24 constituencies where the draft roll is smaller than the number of people who voted in 2025.
In four seats the gap between the draft roll and 2025 turnout is larger than the margin that decided the seat. These are: Sangam Vihar, New Delhi, Delhi Cantt and Rajinder Nagar. In New Delhi, Arvind Kejriwal lost by 4,089 votes. The seat had 1,08,788 electors in 2025; the draft roll has 52,368, which is 9,318 short of the number of people who voted.
The Cuts are not Over
It is also worth remembering that the draft roll is not the final roll; it is likely to shrink further.
After the uncollectable forms were set aside, a second round of exclusions began. Electors whose names appeared on the draft roll are now being served notices requiring them to produce documents. Those unable to establish their eligibility risk being excluded from the final roll. In these 24 constituencies, 9,78,541 electors — about 35% of those on the draft roll — have been served notices. Across Delhi, the figure is 33.13 lakh.
The impact could extend well beyond these 24 constituencies. If just one in 10 of the electors served notices is ultimately excluded, 39 of Delhi’s 70 constituencies would have fewer names on the final roll than the number of people who voted there in 2025.
The Question the EC has to Answer
In other words, in February 2025, the ECI’s roll for these 24 constituencies had 49.14 lakh names, and 28.89 lakh people voted. Its own revision now leaves just 27.66 lakh names on the draft roll — fewer than the number of people who actually voted in those constituencies 18 months ago. And the roll is still shrinking.
The numbers demand an explanation. Either the SIR has excluded large numbers of genuine, living residents who voted in the 2025 election, or the rolls on which the ECI conducted that election contained lakhs of names that should not have been there. Either way, the discrepancy is one the Commission needs to account for.
It is also, in substance, the same Election Commission. The Delhi election was conducted under chief election commissioner (CEC) Rajiv Kumar, with Gyanesh Kumar and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu as election commissioners. Gyanesh Kumar took over as CEC on February 19, 2025, just days after the results. He has since overseen the SIR exercise.
Questions from Inside the Commission
These numbers come at a time when the SIR is itself facing scrutiny within the Election Commission.
An investigation by The Indian Express, published on September 23, reported that two of the three members of the Commission, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, objected on record at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders issued during the nationwide rollout of the SIR. In several instances, they recorded that decisions had been taken without their knowledge. The report does not examine Delhi, but one of the concerns it raises is directly relevant to the revision here.
Who decided? The ECI has repeatedly responded to allegations of electoral-roll manipulation by pointing out that rolls in each constituency are prepared and maintained under the authority of the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO), a statutory official. But according to The Indian Express, both Commissioners raised concerns that this safeguard was being weakened. Joshi flagged the increasing centralisation of the electoral-roll database, while Sandhu recorded that state election officials had said they did not have full access to ERONet, the software used to maintain the rolls.
That raises a question for Delhi: when 17.37 lakh names were marked uncollectable across 24 constituencies, and all seven constituencies in South East Delhi were among those with the highest rates, who made those determinations? Were they made by the constituency-level EROs, as the statutory framework envisages, or were decisions being taken or directed elsewhere? The ECI has not publicly explained this.
Alt News has sent questions to the Election Commission of India seeking an explanation. This report will be updated if and when a response is received.
The constituency-level data used in this report was procured and compiled by Mandate Analytics from records published by the Election Commission of India and the chief electoral officer (CEO), Delhi. Alt News independently verified the figures against the original ECI and CEO Delhi documents. The constituency-wise figures for electors issued notices are as compiled by Mandate Analytics.

Norway is planning a temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places, amid rising global concern at the spread of the AI-enabled recording devices.
The Oslo government is planning a bill to prevent the use of the camera-enabled spectacles in parks, beaches, museums, shopping centres, schools, daycare centres, healthcare facilities, gyms and public events, although private use would still be allowed.
There is already a growing patchwork of restrictions on the use of the glasses including in UK and US courtrooms and in pubs, cinemas and restaurants where owners have raised privacy fears.
Torgeir Micaelsen, Norway’s minister of digital affairs, said he was “worried that new, powerful technology is being introduced where people risk being photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without knowing it”.
“We do not want a society where people worry about being recorded without their knowledge, photographed or filmed in places and situations where they are accustomed to not being monitored,” he said.
Norway’s Labour party, which heads a minority government, needs the support of other parties to pass the proposed ban. It said it planned to submit a bill “as soon as possible”, while tasking an expert group with drawing up permanent regulations on the issue.
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta sells “smart” versions of Ray-Ban and Oakley glasses that allow users to film, take photos, make phone calls, play music and execute AI prompts. It has sold at least 9m pairs of the Ray-Ban versions since the start of 2023.
In the UK restaurateurs such as Jeremy King, who created the Wolseley and Delaunay restaurants, and pub chain Wetherspoons have already said they do not want customers using the devices. Cinemas said in August they had begun introducing policies to ban or restrict the use of smart glasses citing both privacy and film piracy concerns.
Last week the governor of California, Gavin Newsom, vetoed legislation that would have penalised citizens for using smart glasses to record people without their permission in changing rooms, doctors’ offices and other spaces people generally consider private. The state already has laws governing unlawful recording.
In France, the child welfare group E-enfance said it had this year received about 20 reports of women being filmed without their knowledge using glasses fitted with a camera, the majority of which involved Meta smart glasses. It said the incidents often followed the same pattern: a young girl or woman approached in a public place, filmed without her knowledge, with the clip then posted on social media in the form of a prank or a street interview.
Meta has stressed that each pair of glasses is fitted with a tamper-proof LED light that blinks white when the user is recording or taking pictures. It advises users: “Not everyone loves being photographed. Stop recording if anyone expresses that they would rather you not.”
A Meta spokesperson said: “We’re excited that our glasses continue to be very popular for listening to music, making calls, or getting live translations, so we’re continuing to expand styles and features around the world. Every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that blinks when you take a photo or video. It can’t be turned off and the camera is disabled if someone covers or tampers with it -- something smartphones and other camera’s don’t have.”

Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport or building, reports say
- Published
The co-pilot accused of trying to hijack a flydubai plane planned to crash the aircraft into Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport or a tower block in the Israeli city, US and Israeli reports suggest.
The Omani national was a "lone wolf" extremist, according to the reports.
The United Arab Emirates' attorney-general has said the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act" on flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv last Wednesday.
He attacked and wounded the captain with the emergency crash axe kept in the cockpit before being overpowered by passengers. Another crew travelling on the plane was able to land it in Saudi Arabia.
Israel's prime minister has said the co-pilot underwent "Islamist radical indoctrination" and the captain, passengers and a second crew prevented "a 9/11 disaster".
FlyDubai: What Happened?
What began as a routine flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv turned into a fight for survival when one pilot allegedly stabs another inside the cockpit.

More details about the co-pilot of the flydubai flight – whom multiple reports have named as Hamam al-Hammami – emerged over the weekend as he continued to be questioned in the UAE, with Israeli representatives being updated.
Israeli media cited sources with knowledge of the probe as saying the co-pilot told investigators that, having attacked Capt Smit Machchhar, he intended to continue flying the plane as normal into Israeli airspace and receive landing clearances from Ben Gurion airport.
He then planned to crash the Boeing 737 MAX – with more than 180 passengers on board – into the airport or into a tower block in central Tel Aviv, in the style of al-Qaeda's 11 September 2001 attacks in the US, according to the reports.
The sources are quoted as saying he was most likely to have acted alone rather than on behalf of a radical organisation or foreign government.
The co-pilot also reportedly told investigators that he had intended to hijack and crash a previous flight to Tel Aviv but changed his mind because he knew someone on board.
There was no immediate comment from Emirati or Israeli authorities.
UAE Attorney-General Hamad al-Shamsi said on Saturday that his country's investigations would establish the full circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident, and that the results would be announced upon their conclusion.
Questions are also being asked about major security lapses, including how the attacker was recruited by flydubai and given clearance to fly a plane filled with Israelis to Tel Aviv.
Regional officials said the co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman's national carrier, Oman Air, and moved to an administrative job because of concerns about his extremist views.
He was later hired by UAE-based flydubai after undergoing standard security checks that did not examine his background for potential signs of radicalisation, according to the officials.
Israeli aviation regulations also state that pilots who are citizens of countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to the country.
Regional officials told the Associated Press on Sunday that Emirati authorities had shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of flight FZ1073's departure.
Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency said the transport ministry was responsible for vetting such lists from foreign airlines.
But Transport Minister Miri Regev said her ministry was not given passenger and crew lists, and that security oversight for flights operated by foreign airlines fell under the remit of the Shin Bet and the Mossad foreign intelligence agency.
Israel's Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has told the head of the National Security Council to review "all security aspects regarding foreign civil aviation to Israel".
Australian authorities are investigating the co-pilot's links to Australia. Sources have told local media that he studied there between 2015 and 2017.

From floating saunas to clinical trials: How heat might help mental health
The belief that heat can benefit the mind and relieve psychic suffering has a long history across human societies. But when Eva Hilland scanned the scientific literature for the kind of evidence that would support recommending heat as a legitimate intervention for mental health, she came up with very little.
"There are many knowledge gaps," says Hilland, a cognitive neuroscientist at Oslo Metropolitan University. Although, what existing evidence she did find seemed promising. "So we just saw the potential."
Sauna-going – sometimes paired with cold plunges or winter swimming – is attracting a new generation of followers, from the U.S. to Hilland's sauna-steeped country of Norway.
The trend not only reflects the reach of the broader wellness and longevity movement, but also a thirst for communal experience and social connection, particularly in the wake of the pandemic.
The science is just beginning to catch up with many of the theorized benefits. Though considerably less studied than the cardiovascular impact, mental health has emerged as one of the more exciting and appealing applications.
Sauna survey
Hilland, whose research group focuses on neuroimaging and genetics, is one of the scientists now diving into this research domain of heat and mental health. And she's leveraging the sauna popularity surge in her own city, Oslo, to do it.
With funding from a local municipality, she's recruiting 50 people for a randomized controlled trial to see whether coupling sauna with a simple set of mental health habits improves stress, well-being, sleep and more.
Instead of visiting a windowless research lab, her study participants take two sessions a week at one of the floating sauna villages that have cropped up in Oslo's inner harbor – a waterfront that has transformed into a world-class destination for heat-seekers in just the past decade.
Large surveys of sauna users reflect what many readily share: It's the psychological benefits more than anything else that keeps them coming back, whether that's stress reduction, elevated mood, improved sleep or the ineffable post-sauna glow.
Some of these self-reported improvements may have less to do with sweating and more to do with the digital detox, time in nature, mindfulness and social connection that sauna-going facilitates.
But the weight of the evidence suggests heat itself is also "powerful physiological stimulus for promoting mental health," says Christopher Lowry, an integrative physiologist and neuroscientist at the University of Colorado, Boulder.
What we know heat does
While warm baths were commonplace in psychiatric asylums a century ago, the modern evidence base largely rests on translational work done with animals and cell models, and a small number of human studies, most of which lack strict control groups.
In his lab, Lowry has extensively explored the physiological mechanisms linking temperature and mental health.
When our skin senses heat, those signals travel to a primitive part of the brain that tells our body to cool down. That process overlaps with a pathway involved in mood and pleasure, which is implicated in depression.
Heat also triggers a specific anti-inflammatory response. A similar phenomenon occurs during exercise, a well-established treatment for depression and other mental health conditions. And separately, Lowry says, animal studies find heat activates a group of "serotonin neurons" in the brain that may "provide stress resilience and antidepressant effects."
In humans, the strongest data come from a landmark trial, published ten years ago, and led by a team at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and co-authored by Lowry.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
A total of 30 people with depression were randomly separated into two groups. About half spent around two hours in a whole-body infrared machine designed to raise their body temperature to 38.5 C, or about 101 F. The rest received a sham treatment.
Within a week, a majority of those in the treatment group had a 50% reduction in their symptoms and the effects persisted throughout the six-week follow-up period.
Training the body to cool down
Those findings are what originally inspired Ashley Mason to enter the field.
A clinical psychologist who studies mood disorders and sleep at the University of California, San Francisco, Mason now has funding from the National Institutes of Health and others to study various forms of heat therapy for depression, sleep and loneliness.
The renewed scientific interest in using heat for psychiatric conditions, in part, reflects an intriguing observation – people with depression tend to have difficulty with thermoregulation.
"What we know from a bunch of literature is that depressed people seem to run hot," says Mason, also a professor of psychiatry and behavioral science. "When their depression improves, their thermoregulatory system seems to also change."
In fact, Mason's lab recently tracked this association between self-reported symptoms of depression and body temperature using wearable device data collected from close to 20,000 people.
Even when controlling for factors like weather and medical conditions, symptom severity correlated with higher skin temperature and less daily fluctuation in body temperature, meaning their bodies weren't cooling down as much at night.
It may seem counterintuitive to heat folks up even more, but Mason says doing so seems to function like a "thermoregulatory workout" – training their system to become more efficient at cooling down in the long run.
"So when you are actually done being exposed to that heat, your body temperature drops for a much longer period of time than you were spending in that heat," she says. "Days, possibly weeks, we still don't know."
Several older studies have also shown that successfully treating people with antidepressant medication or other therapies improves their thermoregulation.
The implication, Masons says, is that acting on this "bi-directional" relationship – both via heat and traditional therapeutic approaches – could have a synergistic effect.
To test this hypothesis, she has run two small pilot trials combining eight weeks of cognitive behavioral therapy and four sessions in an infrared hyperthermia machine. In both studies, most of the participants were in remission from depression by the end of the study.
Her team is now carrying out the same protocol with a larger pool of patients at UCSF, Harvard and the Cleveland Clinic.
Mason stresses the results should be viewed as preliminary. The studies were not powered to show the treatments were effective, but they do lay the groundwork for the larger, well-controlled trials that could deliver that kind of evidence.
"Heat does seem to be a promising therapy, but we're very much at the beginning of this research," she notes.
If these future studies pan out, it may have a place alongside other non-pharmacological approaches for mental health, like exercise – at least in some cases.
"For people with depression who have tried a lot of different types of treatment, do I think that there's room for heat therapy to have a seat at the table?" she says. "Absolutely."
Exactly how you get hot may not matter so much as long as people are sweating.
However, the boom of interest in age-old forms of heat therapy like sauna may be a natural entry point for many.
"The science is new, but the practice is not," Mason says.

A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.
Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.
The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.
Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.
Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.
“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.
“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”
Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”
Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.
Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.
Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.
Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.
The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.
Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

Egyptologists have long debated whether the earliest pharoahs of the First Dynasty were buried with various servants and officials to serve them in the afterlife—a form of human sacrifice. But there is very little archaeological evidence available, given that many of the earliest Egyptian tombs were plundered and/or hastily excavated. A new paper published in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology reassesses a collection of skulls excavated from tombs in the 1920s and concludes that over one-third show evidence of blunt force trauma. This suggests that they may have been victims of so-called “retainer sacrifice.”
Author Roselyn Campbell is a bioarchaeologist at Purdue University who has long been fascinated with the history of human sacrifice. “I’m interested in how we as human beings decide which types of violence are okay and which are not, and how we even define violence,” Campbell told Ars. “It’s very context specific. We have to be careful not to extend our own ideas about what violence is and how it’s used into other cultures. With Egypt, we have such a long history of European and colonial archeology; they came in with very specific ideas about what this culture was. You really have to make an effort to contextualize the legacy data we have.”
Naturally she found the debate over whether ancient Egyptians practiced retainer sacrifice pertinent to her interests. “People tend to fall into one of two camps,” said Campbell. “Either retainer sacrifice definitely happened, end of discussion, or it definitely didn’t happen, end of discussion. But nobody’s actually looked at the bones in a very long time.” Forensic science has advanced considerably over the last century, so re-analysis could be useful. Complicating matters is the fact that older sets of remains are often incomplete and/or modified for preservation, destroying vital forensic information in the process.
Cold case files
As a case study, Campbell turned to a collection of human remains first excavated by famed British archaeologist Flinders Petrie in the 1920s, from the Abydos site in southern Egypt. Abydos is the site of a royal necropolis where many of the early pharoahs were buried, along with many ancient temples. (It’s also the home of what may be the world’s oldest brewery.) This particular set of remains—46 crania stored at Cambridge University— came from the Umm el-Qaab cemetary, which contains subsidiary burials presumed to be retainers of deceased First Dynasty rulers. Petrie noted several grave markers with names and official titles, mostly lower to mid-level officials and artisans.
