On 02 October 2026, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) held a protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park grounds demanding accountability from the Election Commission of India (ECI) and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Protesters raised concerns over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, alleged voter deletions, and transparency in the electoral process. Despite Mumbai Police denying permission for the gathering, thousands attended the protest and raised slogans. Police later registered an FIR against the organisers and 400–500 unidentified participants for allegedly violating restrictions on the assembly.
In this context, a video (here & here) is circulating on social media claiming that CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke was attacked at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park during this protest. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke was attacked during a protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park on 02 October 2026.
Fact: The video is from 15 June 2026 and shows Abhijeet Dipke being assaulted by unidentified individuals during a youth protest against paper leaks and unemployment in Jaipur, Rajasthan. There are no reports of him being attacked at the Mumbai protest. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video shows that the same video (here & here) has been available online since at least 15 June 2026. These posts describe it as Abhijeet Dipke being attacked in Jaipur, Rajasthan.
According to media reports (here, here & here), on 15 June 2026, Dipke was manhandled and slapped multiple times during a youth protest at Shaheed Smarak in Jaipur, Rajasthan. He had reportedly organised the protest to speak out against paper leaks and unemployment, and to demand the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. As supporters carried Dipke on their shoulders toward the stage, several people emerged from the crowd, pulled him down, and struck his face. This sparked a quick retaliatory scuffle from CJP supporters before the police stepped in and detained the suspects.
Afterwards, Dipke condemned the assault, calling it a sign of fear and cowardice from his opponents. Furthermore, there are no news reports of Dipke being assaulted at the Mumbai Shivaji Park protest
To sum it up, an old video of Abhijeet Dipke being assaulted in Jaipur is falsely shared to claim he was attacked in Mumbai.

28 bullets exchanged between two Rashid Cablewala gang hitmen and Delhi police in Usmanpur, both held
Of the 12 bullets the duo fired, one bullet each hit the bulletproof vests of two police officers, the officers said.
Two alleged hitmen of the Rashid Cablewala gang were arrested after an exchange of fire with the special staff team of the northeast police district in the Usmanpur area in Delhi in the early hours of Monday, senior police officers said.
The suspects were identified as Alu Jaseem and Mohammad Kaif, both 23 and residents of northeast Delhi’s Welcome area, the police said.
At least 28 bullets were exchanged between the raiding team members and the two men, who were allegedly involved in a case of firing multiple bullets at the house of a businessman in the Bhajanpura area over extortion demand early Friday morning, the officers said, adding the suspects suffered one bullet each in their legs.
Of the 12 bullets the duo fired, one bullet each hit the bulletproof vests of two police officers, the officers said.
How police zeroed in on the suspects
Deputy commissioner of police (northeast) Rahul Alwal said that on October 2, unidentified assailants had fired at least five bullets at the house of a businessman in the Bhajanpura area.
A case was registered in connection with the firing.
Investigation revealed that the businessman had received extortion calls but had not informed the police about them.
Through technical investigation and field intelligence gathering, two suspects were identified as the accused involved in the firing. The special staff team collected information about the two suspects.
On Sunday night, the team received information about the suspects' presence in the Usmanpur area. Accordingly, a trap was laid, and the suspects were asked to surrender after being spotted, the police said.
The shootout
“The two men took out their firearms and opened fire at the police party. They fired 12 rounds. A sub-inspector and a head constable came under fire, with bullets hitting their bulletproof jackets, but both escaped unhurt. Our team fired 16 rounds. The suspects suffered bullets in their left legs,” Alwal added.
Police said the injured were admitted to a nearby hospital, where they are undergoing treatment.

In October 2024, students at Cornell University received a campus crime alert about a reported sexual assault. At the time, it was just a campus story. Nearly two years later, on September 16, the victim, known only as “Jane Doe,” filed a civil lawsuit that brought national attention to her story. People across the country are asking what happened and why criminal charges never followed.
How did the Cornell rape case go so wrong?
A former sex crimes prosecutor explains where the Cornell case should go next.
Doe alleges that seven men drugged and sexually assaulted her at the Chi Phi fraternity house two years ago. Her lawsuit also accuses the university, fraternity and sorority organizations, and a local bar of failing to protect her.
The lawyers for several of the men have denied the allegations and any wrongdoing. Cornell says its disciplinary actions led to suspensions and expulsions for some of the young men, and that the Chi Phi fraternity remains barred from campus.
Doe went to campus police in November 2024, and the district attorney’s office reviewed her account and declined to bring charges. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has said that what she described to Cornell police didn’t meet the state’s requirements for criminal charges.
Van Houten reopened the investigation late last month while continuing to defend his original decision to not pursue charges, but it’s now out of his hands: On Thursday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul named the state attorney general, Letitia James, as special prosecutor to investigate the allegations, saying she had “lost faith” in Van Houten.
To break down why Van Houten didn’t pursue the case at the time and what should have happened instead, Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with Lauren Hersh, a former Brooklyn prosecutor who led the office’s sex trafficking unit and CEO of World Without Exploitation, about how authorities handled Jane Doe’s allegations, the limits of New York’s consent laws, and what needs to change.
Hersh also explains where she believes the case should go next and what a special prosecutor can do to investigate (the interview took place prior to James’s appointment).
Below is an excerpt of Hersh’s conversation with Noel edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
I want to start with what we know in 2024. A young woman who we know as “Jane Doe” goes to the Cornell campus police and says she had gone to a frat house while under the influence of alcohol.
At the frat house, she was given more alcohol and ketamine. Several men had sex with her while she was intoxicated. This is what she tells Cornell campus police. What, in your view, is supposed to happen next?
There are a number of things that could happen. What I would say about these cases is there is no perfect scenario of what is supposed to happen, because what is critically important is we listen to the desire of the survivor.
We want to take this at her pace. We want to be guided by her wishes. We want her to decide if she is ready to go forward, if she wants to speak to campus police, the Title IX office, if she wants to speak to the local law enforcement. There are a lot of variables here, but for me, what is critically important is that we’re listening to the survivor and what she ultimately wants to happen.
In the present day, the district attorney who was involved has said that his office reviewed Jane Doe’s statement at the time and found at the time that what she described didn’t meet the legal definition of a crime.
I think people want to understand, Lauren, how is that possible?
To be really candid with you, Noel, this is an area that seems super unclear to me because the role of the district attorney in that moment is to investigate.
When you first get a case file, you first get a victim statement, and especially with facts as horrific as these facts are, or our understanding of this six-page document that the DA read — I would never say that this is a clear-cut case where there’ll be a conviction at the end. We never know that.
What I can say with 100 percent certainty is if you get a document like that, as a prosecutor, that is a significant investigative lead. And so, as a prosecutor, what I believe to be good practice is starting to pull the layers back, trying to understand what transpired here. Interviewing the victim. That feels critical. That never happened. We now know that there are all these text messages that were shared between these boys, and the prosecutor’s now saying, “I didn’t know about the text messages.”
It’s my understanding that there were a lot of boys on that particular text thread. And so a good investigator would have gone to that fraternity house and tried to interview some of those boys, tried to understand what were the contemporaneous statements made at that time. Were there any text messages? Was there any social media activity? And I believe that had they done that in a timely fashion, they likely would have come up with these text messages at that time and not two years later.
What you’re saying is interesting because the DA has come out publicly and defended himself by saying, essentially, the details of this lawsuit, which was filed in September of this year, are different from the details in the young woman’s 2024 statement to the police.
He has used that in his defense, right? “Here’s what I knew at the time versus what this young woman is saying today.” I think I hear you saying that maybe that’s not an excuse?
You’re asking about the inconsistent statements, and I find it troubling that the DA is leading with this notion that the victim has inconsistent statements because that feels to me like here we are making excuses and blaming the victim.
To my knowledge, the DA has not yet interviewed this victim. Perhaps he’s talking about the civil complaint, which I would think is written in a way where she has worked with her lawyer to put this together. And the initial statement, the initial six-page document that the DA read, my understanding is that it is basically a summary of a conversation.
Inconsistencies come in all shapes and sizes, so it’s hard to know exactly what we’re talking about here, but it is very common for there to be some inconsistencies. That is not a dealbreaker, despite the fact that this prosecutor wants the public to believe that it is.
What do you make of the prosecutor speaking publicly in the way that he is at this moment?
I find it rather confusing. I’m not really understanding why he is doing a media tour rather than sitting in his office doing the work, interviewing this particular victim, interviewing witnesses, seeing what evidence actually exists.
It seems to me that the DA has gotten to a conclusion before he’s done the work in actually investigating the case, and it is deeply troubling. And I think the governor should consider appointing a special prosecutor because I am not certain, based on this media tour, that this DA is able to give this particular survivor a full and fair investigation of the facts.
Drugs and alcohol are central to this case, right? The young woman admits she had been drinking and she was using ketamine. Under New York law, how does that affect whether or not someone is believed to be capable of consenting to sex?
New York law is actually really problematic here. It’s a place where I believe we are desperate for a legislative fix. I think that there have been a lot of advocates who’ve been championing a correction to this voluntary intoxication loophole for a lot of years, and we’ve not been able to get it.
New York law makes it very, very hard to prosecute a person when the victim is voluntarily intoxicated, but not unconscious, and this new law would allow the prosecutors the ability to bring cases when the victim is so severely intoxicated but not physically helpless and where a reasonable person should have known the victim’s condition.
In this particular case, based on what we’re hearing, she was in a condition where a reasonable person should have known her condition. And so in this particular instance, the DA is right. This is a very, very hard case to prove in this moment, but I’m a big believer. We don’t not prosecute cases because they’re hard cases. But at the same time, we know that a change to the law is critically important.
You clearly want more investigation here. What questions do you want asked? Who do you want to be [interviewed]?
Before I say who and how and what that investigation looks like, I think it’s really important to say that when two years have passed and the DA did not investigate these cases immediately, we have a big problem on our hands.
The fact that the DA did not investigate this from the moment he found out about this, it’s really problematic because as we know, evidence disappears, memories fade. When you’re dealing on a college campus with a specific culture, there may be a narrative that takes hold. And so it’s important to talk about the time lapse and how that harms the case.
That said, I still believe that the investigation is critically important. I don’t believe that this DA is the right person to do the investigation. I think a special prosecutor should be appointed. And then I think that the prosecutor and law enforcement should be interviewing everybody who was in that fraternity on that night. Anybody who saw this victim before, saw this victim after. Were there any statements in the immediate aftermath of her leaving that fraternity? Was there an outcry witness? We know that some text messages have come to light. Are there other text messages? I suspect that there are.
I’d want to interview as many of those boys as possible to understand what was going on because some of those text messages that have come to light — one says, “Free pussy” — don’t sound like a mindset that is engaging in consensual sex.
I think it is critically important that we understand all of the correspondence of that night. I think we want to see what is out there that helps us get closer to understanding what transpired that night.
I’ve seen two lines of thinking about this. One is that this is a horrific incident that never should have happened, but it is in some ways singular. But I’ve seen another line of thinking that says, “No, this is a systemic failure. This kind of thing goes on on college campuses, and the steps that follow the outcomes are often the same.”
I wonder if you think this is a systemic failure, and if you think it is, what would need to be done to fix this problem?
That’s a big question. I do think it’s a systemic failure. I also think it’s a cultural failure. And the reason that I would say this is because I don’t think this is isolated to this specific college campus. I think that sexual assault is happening across the country on college campuses everywhere.
In terms of additional systemic failures, I’ve been working with the Epstein survivors for the last year and a half, so I’ve seen so many systemic failures, so many prosecutorial failures, so much failure with law enforcement. I think that this is yet another example of prosecutorial failure.
I think the law enforcement failed this young person — the fact that there’s no investigation that happened immediately in the aftermath of this incident, no investigation. We just continue to fail survivors all over the place, and we have to start doing better.

This is going to be an age of flux for the world, with conflicts and tariff volatility making it turbulent, External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar said on Monday (October 5, 2026), underlining that responding to the challenges emerging out of the “choppy waters” is the task at hand.
“I'm very confident that we will rise to the challenges,” Mr. Jaishankar said during an interactive session at the 5th Kautilya Economic Conclave in New Delhi.
The flagship event's theme was ‘Resilience in an Age of Flux’.
Mr. Jaishankar shared the dais with former Foreign Minister of Singapore, George Yong Boon Yeo, during the closing session of the three-day conclave.
The Minister was asked how he saw the challenges ahead amid the geopolitical uncertainties.
“We know that this is going to be an age of flux, as you call it. And it is going to be turbulent and volatile, with uncertainties. We are seeing two major conflicts; we are seeing other frictions. As I said, there is the pressure of non-market factors; there is tariff volatility,” Mr. Jaishankar said.
“So, taking all of these into account... Yes, these are choppy waters,” he said.
The Minister, however, said that as India's record shows, “we have been able to rise to the challenges, whether it was Covid, or the challenge of a double conflict today”.
“The challenges of energy, food, fertilisers… We need to factor them into our thinking, plan and respond – that in a sense is the task before us. And I'm very confident that we will rise to the challenge," he said.
Mr. Jaishankar also spoke about championing the voice of the Global South.
“The Global South expects India to articulate on the world stage,” he said.
According to the Minister, New Delhi maintains that dialogue and diplomacy are the way forward to resolve the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
On reforms needed for the United Nations and other multilateral institutions, Mr. Jaishankar said, “The UN is gridlocked,” adding that a few countries were resisting its reforms.

Why protecting home values is Beijing’s new priority
With resale transactions outpacing new home sales for the first time, stabilising the existing housing stock has become vital
Official figures published by the National Bureau of Statistics in September reveal that secondary market home transactions have surpassed new residential builds in volume. Nationwide registered resales reached 549 million square metres, signalling that housing demand in China has not vanished. Rather, it appears to have structurally migrated.
This marks a departure from the previous growth model. For a quarter of a century, following the end of the old welfare housing system in 1998, China’s property market operated on a high-velocity loop: developers acquired municipal land, pre-sold unfinished apartments, collected buyer cash and funnelled those advances into their next projects. That mechanism turned residential construction into the primary economic engine of the country.
That engine is now losing momentum. What is emerging is not merely a smaller version of the old market but a different market altogether. The centre of gravity is shifting – from developers selling a promise of tomorrow to households trading the homes of today.

- Ninja Theory has begun layoffs after two deals to save the UK studio fell through amid the "XBOX Reset."
- Multiple employees took to LinkedIn to speak about the Xbox layoffs, which made their positions redundant.
- Previously, Xbox VP Matt Booty revealed they were exploring "other paths forward" for Ninja Theory.
Around two weeks ago, Xbox announced that Senua developer Ninja Theory faces potential closure as part of the ongoing “XBOX Reset” restructuring plan after two deals to save the studio fell through over the summer. Fast forward to October 5, 2026, and Ninja Theory has begun layoffs, making employee positions redundant.
Reporter Chris Kerr on BlueSky spotted the Ninja Theory layoffs, with multiple studio employees announcing their departure from the UK studio on LinkedIn.
Performance capture technician Rachel Kimber wrote on LinkedIn, “Ninja Theory has been some of the best years of my life, but sadly it is time to say goodbye. I can’t express enough the amazing people I have been able to work with over the last 4 and a half years. It has been such a pleasure, and I have made friends for life.”
Meanwhile, Ninja Theory’s gameplay programmer Katrin Mair spoke about the harsh effects of the Xbox layoffs, saying, “It’s incredibly sad knowing that we won’t get to finish what we were working on. Principal programmer Stefano Prosperi wrote, “Now, with Ninja Theory facing closure and all of us facing redundancy, it’s difficult to process the idea that this chapter may be coming to an end.” So, it’s an incredibly difficult time for Ninja Theory, as the studio faces layoffs and a possible closure.

What are emotions, really? And why do we have them?
Simply put, emotions are intangible responses to what we see happening around us. They arise spontaneously, without conscious thought.
Emotions allowed early humans to efficiently dodge dangers as they explored the world around them. While the world and our lives in it are very different today than the way they were for our ancestors, our emotions haven’t changed.
Despite being so fundamental to our survival as a species, however, scientists are still piecing together how emotions arise in our brains. In a study recently published in Science, in fact, scientists have just reported mapping the brain-wide activity patterns that trigger emotions.
The team found that once an emotion was set off, it outlasted the trigger that sparked it in the first place. If this sounds familiar, it’s because this is what you feel when you accidentally stub your toe, burn your hand, and even when you enjoy your favourite flavour of ice cream.
In all these examples, there is incoming sensory information that prompts an emotional response while the good or bad feeling lasts even after the body part has been reflexively pulled back or after the ice cream is finished.
Stories hidden in blinks
In the new study, scientists led by Karl Deisseroth at Stanford University examined how emotions emerged in response to unpleasant (but not painful) sensory stimuli.
The participants were subjected to an eye puff assay: a machine called a tonometer blew light puffs of air into their left eye in specific sequences. Each puff lasted about 60 ms, the gap between puffs was 3-8 s long, and the entire session lasted 5 minutes. The scientists varied the gap between puffs so that participants didn’t reflexively tense up for the next puff they knew was coming.
Also read: Making the brain transparent
During the entire duration, a high-speed camera recorded the way participants closed their eyes and their behavioral and subjective responses.
As expected, repeated puffs of air to the eye elicited reflexive blinking as participants instinctively pulled back from the tonometer. They also kept the eye closed for certain durations or squinted or blinked rapidly during the gaps. As part of their subjective reports, the participants said this experience was “unpleasant” and “annoying”.
The scientists recruited a separate group of participants who were, at the time of the study, inpatients at the Stanford university hospital and had electrodes planted in their brains to check for epileptic seizures. Members of this group who consented to participate underwent the same eyepuff assay. The scientists found that these participants’ behavioural responses were consistent with those of the previous group. They also blinked reflexively and kept their eyes closed for (relatively) long periods.
The real story emerged in the brain activity patterns.
Enter: ketamine
Each puff causes a signal to be broadcast throughout the brain, like a “breaking news” alert, followed by a slower, more persistent signal. In this second phase, based on data from the electrodes in the brains of participants, scientists found that specific circuits in the brain were activated, which were linked to the generation of an emotional response in the individual.
To confirm this possibility, the scientists administered ketamine to some of these participants and had them redo the eye puff assay. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved ketamine’s use as an anaesthetic and at lower doses as an antidepressant. Ketamine also induces short-term dissociation: i.e. for a brief period, it alters subjective perceptions. By injecting it, the team could separate a person’s reflexive response from the emotional one.
The scientists found that being subjected to air puffs in the eye when a person was on ketamine changed neither the initial reflexive behaviour nor the initial burst of neural activity in the brain. However, it caused the subsequent slower brain response to dissipate much faster, so much so that the volunteers no longer described the experience as annoying but as a “tickling of the eyeball”.
Consistent with this ‘weaker’ subjective experience from ketamine, the participants’ behaviour also changed. They didn’t blink or close their eyes between consecutive air puffs. Instead, they held their eyes open even though they knew more puffs were in the offing.
Ketamine is known to block a sensor in the brain whose job it is to integrate signals coming from different corners. This means in the participants injected with ketamine, the brain may not have integrated the various signals into a coherent emotional response.
Of mice and men
Even though vertebrates have brains of vastly different sizes and complexity, the overall ‘brain plan’ is highly conserved. (The brain plan is akin to the building plan of a house or apartment.) To zero in on those systems responsible for emotions and which have survived evolution, Deisseroth’s team repeated their experiments with lab mice. The mice went through the eyepuff assay, had their brain activity measured with surgically planted electrodes, and had ketamine injected.
The team noticed the same patterns in mice as they had in humans. Injecting ketamine substantially changed the spiking activity in some neurons but not others. Only those neurons (or brain regions) coordinating the second phase — the slower response after the burst — were affected by ketamine. The initial burst didn’t change in any way, just as with the human participants.
The scientists could also study the neural activity following a puff in greater detail in the mouse model. They found that the fast/reflexive responses corresponded with a sharp rise in activity in some of the midbrain regions. This included the thalamus, where incoming sensory signals converge before being relayed onward, and the periaqueductal grey, which is involved in emotional behaviours.
They also found that the second phase of neural activity corresponded with activity in the brain’s emotional centres (described by the umbrella term ‘limbic regions’) and the frontal cortex. Again, as expected.
Then they dissected the brain activity patterns by stages, focusing on how quickly activity in brain regions shot up after the eyepuff and how long it took to fade away. They noticed that activity patterns in most of the pertinent regions increased at an explosive pace right after the eyepuff — but the rate of decrease was more interesting.
A pattern appears
The patterns in different regions slowed at different rates, fading first in the midbrain regions and last in the frontal cortex. The thalamus was active both in the first and the second phase. Considering the thalamus is the brain’s coordinating centre for all sensory signals, it makes sense that it would be active in the first phase. Incoming sensory signals go on to higher brain regions from the cortex. So it also served the role of handing off the baton, so to speak, and thus essayed a sort of bridging role across timescales.
The new study is the first to report this sort of differential pattern across different parts of the brain vis-à-vis emotions. At this point, it is not possible to say with any certainty what the implications are for the brain’s cortical and mid-brain areas.
With computational models of neuron firing activity in the mouse and the mouse’s behaviour following the eye puff assay, the team found that the timescale of neural activity was an important factor that shaped the emotional response.
Indeed, if the sensory signals dissipate before the brain has a chance to integrate the information, the person won’t be able to learn the lesson: “protect yourself from that obnoxious thing”. On the other hand, if brain activity is more strongly coupled to the fast and slow phases that Deisseroth & co. observed, such activity also lasts longer than normal, causing its own problems. Over-stabilised brain states have been correlated with depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder, all of which cause people to experience uninterrupted or mistimed thoughts and emotions.
Beyond the binary of health and disease, the fast and slow phases of brain activity highlighted in the study could reveal the fundamentals of information processing in the brain. People differ in how their brains process information about their environment — in turn a product of their genetic makeup and their upbringing in their formative years.
First steps
Why do we have emotions? For now it may be more gainful to flip the question: what would happen if we didn’t have them?
In the absence of an instinctive reaction that our emotions afford us, the brain’s response would be based entirely on risk-benefit analyses, which can be very time consuming. Over time we’d struggle to make decisions both big and small. What should I wear today? What should I make for dinner tonight? What should I study? Whom should I marry? Purely rational thought would turn such questions into never-ending decision-making exercises with no final answer.
The new study has revealed what happens in the brain in the first seconds when an emotion takes root. One hopes future studies will reveal the specific information encoded by this primal circuitry, how they encode different emotions, and how they evolve with time.
Dr. Reeteka Sud is a neuroscientist by training and senior scientist at the Center for Brain and Mind, Department of Psychiatry, NIMHANS, Bengaluru.

What to expect from school protests rattling France's government
High school students in France are expected to continue their protests this week, challenging President Emmanuel Macron's government
PARIS -- After a weekend lull, high schoolers in France are expected back at the barricades this coming week in their protest movement that is rattling the government of President Emmanuel Macron.
A key question is whether violence on the margins of the demonstrations will worsen, blurring the lines between protest and rioting, and whether Macron's government will ratchet up the already muscular response by police. According to the interior minister, officers made more than 5,000 arrests last week, 85% of them minors. Hundreds have been injured.
A test of the movement's endurance and appeal will come Tuesday, when the influential CGT labor union is urging workers to demonstrate, too.
Here's what to know:
Protests first erupted in the Paris region in mid-September. Teachers and students mobilized against a lack of staff at a lycée, or high school, in Creteil, in the southeastern outskirts of the French capital. From there, class strikes, blockades and demonstrations spread to other Paris suburbs and then nationwide, with protests even in high schools of smaller towns.
Hundreds of schools have had to close because of damage or attacks that targeted staff, according to the education minister. More than 170 pupils and 65 staff members have suffered injuries, he says.
From the outset, pupils focused on perceived inequalities in the school system, saying that teaching, facilities and opportunities for advancement aren’t as good for students in disadvantaged neighborhoods — despite the promise of France's national motto: “Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.”
Placards held up by the first protesters in Creteil read “Too many inequalities, we’re disgusted,” “Education is a right, not a privilege,” and “Sorry to bother, it’s for our future,” according to photos posted by Clémence Guetté, the district's lawmaker at the National Assembly, France's parliament.
Pupils elsewhere complained that during summer heat waves, they roast in classrooms without air-conditioning, and they freeze in winter. French media broadcast videos of scampering rats, collapsed ceilings, leaks, broken furniture and other woes filmed in dilapidated schools.
"The public needs to know that conditions for studying are no longer what they were for us,” said Sophie Bordy, a 50-year-old literature teacher in Paris. "It has deteriorated significantly.”
Still, spending on education is one of the costliest items in the state budget that Macron’s government is proposing for 2027. It earmarked 65.5 billion euros ($74 billion) for schools, more than the 63.4 billion euros for defense.
Pupils also complain of long hours. In high schools, classes often start at 8 a.m. and can last to the early evening. French high schoolers’ compulsory school hours are among the highest in Europe, according to European Union figures.
“I see the teachers more than my family,” read one young girl's placard photographed by Le Parisien newspaper.
Guetté, the lawmaker who posted photos of herself meeting with the first protesters in Creteil, bullhorn in hand, is a rising star of the far-left France Unbowed party. Other France Unbowed lawmakers and elected officials also quickly identified with the protests, meeting with pupils and backing their demands.
France Unbowed leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon urged party members and supporters to protect pupils from the police, by putting themselves in between the two sides.
Mélenchon has denounced what he called the “savagery” of police officers who have liberally used tear gas and their batons to break up crowds. Police riot-control projectiles are suspected in some facial injuries that young protesters suffered.
Critics of Mélenchon accuse France Unbowed of stoking and manipulating the pupils for political gain. Mélenchon, a fiery anti-capitalist, says his party supports the movement but isn’t organizing it and wants it to be non-violent.
Mélenchon, 75, is making his fourth run for the French presidency and is wooing young voters. They tended to vote less than other age groups in the last presidential election in 2022 but could potentially help Mélenchon qualify for the decisive second-round runoff in May — a success that has always escaped him — if he can mobilize them to turn out.
“What we want is for this country’s young people to emerge from this episode with their heads held high, having won something and learned something, and to remember it when they cast their ballots,” Mélenchon said Thursday.
——
Associated Press journalist Oleg Cetinic in Paris contributed.

IPO-bound study abroad platform Leverage Edu is targeting ₹600 Cr in revenue in FY27, up over 60% from the ₹372 Cr it reported in FY26, sources told Inc42. Quick Answer
You can get Microsoft 365 for free through an eligible Education plan, free web and mobile versions of Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and other apps, or a 30-day Microsoft 365 trial with full desktop apps and 1 TB of OneDrive storage.
Microsoft 365 (formerly Office 365) is a subscription service that gives you access to various Microsoft products. This includes productivity apps like Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and OneNote; 1 TB of OneDrive cloud storage; and tools like Teams, Forms, and Loop.
As of writing, a paid subscription starts at $1.99 a month or $19.99 a year for Microsoft 365 Basic and goes up to $19.99 a month or $199.99 a year for Microsoft 365 Premium. Whether getting a subscription is justified depends on which of the included apps and services you use and how much.
If you’re not too sure about that and don’t want to buy a subscription right away, you can get Microsoft 365 for free using the following methods. Which method to pick depends on whether you’re a student/educator and your requirements.
Get the Microsoft 365 Education Plan
Microsoft 365 Education is a special plan for students and educators that provides free access to Microsoft 365 apps and services. You need a valid school, college, or university email address to be eligible. You’d have one if you’re a student or educator at an accredited institution with a Microsoft Education license.
To check if you qualify, visit the Microsoft 365 Education portal, type your institution-issued email address, and hit Next. If you’re eligible, you’ll be prompted to log in with the same email address. Or you may receive a verification link in your inbox. Subsequently, you’ll be able to use the Microsoft 365 apps within the browser or download them to your devices, based on the plan your institute offers.
Microsoft 365 Education is currently available in three plans: A1, A3, and A5. Your institute will most likely offer an A1 plan since it’s free, though some may offer an A3. The major difference between them is that A1 is web-only, whereas A3 supports downloads, so you can use the apps even when you’re offline.
If you don’t have an institute-provided email address or it isn’t eligible for the Education plan, you can get Microsoft 365 for free using the next method.
Also See: 11 AI-Powered Tools With Student Discounts
Use Microsoft 365 for the Web or Native Mobile Apps
Unless you have advanced needs — creating and running macros (VBA) in Excel, multi-device installation rights, or fully offline mode — you don’t really need a Microsoft 365 subscription. The online version of Microsoft 365, which offers access to basic versions of its apps, along with 5GB of free cloud storage, should serve your needs just as well.
All you need for this method is a Microsoft account and a web browser. In your preferred browser, visit the Microsoft 365 online portal and sign in with your Microsoft account. Create a new Microsoft account if you don’t have one.
Next, click the app launcher icon in your dashboard and select the app you want to use. This will open the app in a new browser tab, where you can create a new document or work on an existing one in your OneDrive storage. Any changes you make to the document are automatically saved to the cloud. Keep in mind, though, that the app’s functionality halts completely when you lose the internet connection.
Just like Microsoft 365 for the web, Microsoft also offers mobile apps for many of its productivity apps. So, if you just want to work on a Word, Excel, or PowerPoint document, you can download their mobile apps on your phone or tablet and use them. Just note that these apps offer limited functionality, similar to the web version. However, unlike their web versions, mobile apps support some offline functionality, allowing you to view a cached version of the document or edit local documents, even without an active internet connection.
Get the Microsoft 365 Free Trial
Microsoft offers a 30-day free trial to Microsoft 365. This trial gives you full, unrestricted access to the service, including complete offline capabilities and the ability to download desktop apps to your PC or Mac. You also get 1 TB of OneDrive cloud storage.
A free trial is great for someone who wants full-blown access to Microsoft’s productivity suite for a brief period. It also makes sense for those who want the Microsoft 365 service without committing to an upfront payment.
To subscribe to a 30-day Microsoft 365 free trial, you need a Microsoft account and a valid payment method. Open a browser and go to the official Microsoft 365 free trial page. Click the Start Free Trial button, and log in with your Microsoft account when prompted. If you haven’t taken a free trial with this account previously, you’ll be asked to add a valid payment method. Complete the checkout process. You now have complete access to Microsoft 365.
Set a reminder to cancel the subscription before the 30 days are up. If you forget, Microsoft will convert the trial to a monthly or annual subscription and charge you for the same on your added payment method.
Identify Your Use Case to Find the Right Method
You can use any of the above methods to get Microsoft 365 for free. However, not all of them offer the same level of access. As such, it’s important to identify your use case before choosing a method.
For example, if you want a full-blown Excel experience for a few weeks, the free 30-day trial makes more sense. Meanwhile, you might want to subscribe to the Microsoft 365 Education plan if you’re a student or educator and want desktop access to productivity apps for a longer period. Or use their mobile apps on your phone or tablet if you only need to view or maintain a few Excel sheets.

“Rendering Doom in a database is obviously a bad idea,” Lukas Vogel writes in a lengthy blog post explaining how exactly he managed to render Doom using an SQL database.
OK, that’s not entirely accurate. The SQLDoom project uses a small Python client to handle input and output, drive the game’s timing, and display each frame to the screen. Behind that, a series of CedarDB tables tracks the game geometry and state, while about 1,300 lines of SQL queries spread across 89 common table expressions implement the game logic and generate 35 bitmap framebuffers per second.
In this, SQLDoom is a major improvement over Vogel’s previous DoomQL project, which last year set out to build “a multiplayer Doom-like shooter entirely in SQL.” Unfortunately, that effort ended up with raycasting-based, grayscale ASCII graphics that were more akin to the simplistic 90-degree-angled maps of Wolfenstein 3D. The newer SQLDoom, on the other hand, generates full-color 640×480 frames that look like they could have come from the original Doom executable.
It’s all just data, man
Converting Doom‘s classic WAD files to a relational database was relatively simple and straightforward, Vogel writes, because of the way the original game broke levels down into vertices, lines, sectors, and so on. Even Doom‘s famous binary-space partition trees can be broken down into SQL using a sort_key for objects that’s pre-computed for each position at load time. With this set in your table, a simple “ORDER BY” statement can determine every frame which parts of walls to display and which to ignore, vastly improving performance.

'I've lost my peace' - Cape Verde hero Vozinha on newfound fame
- Published
Cape Verde's heroic World Cup goalkeeper Vozinha says he craves the "peace and tranquillity" of the life he led before he shot to fame.
The 40-year-old shot to global prominence in June when he almost single-handedly kept Spain at bay as Cape Verde drew 0-0 with the European champions on their World Cup debut.
Vozinha's follower count on social media sky-rocketed over the course of the game, from about 50,000 to more than one million.
But his fame shot up even further when Argentina needed extra time to beat Cape Verde in the round of 32.
Vozinha says his life was easier before his World Cup heroics.
"I've lost my peace and tranquillity," he told the Observer., external
"I no longer have any privacy, or at least much less than I used to.
"Now I go out, I go to a restaurant, and there's always someone who wants to take a photo with me or asks me for an autograph. Or, worse, someone is filming me.
"That's what has changed most in my life, and I don't think there's anything I can do about it."
Vozinha's mother became part of the fairytale too. After he revealed that she had could not afford a visa to watch his World Cup debut, US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries announced that the visa fee had been waived.
Now Vozinha has revealed that his mother is visited on a daily basis by fans wanting to talk or to take photographs with him.
"A lot of people want to be famous and have a public profile, but they only see the positive side of that reality," said Vozinha.
"To be honest, if I were offered the life I have today or the life I had before, I'd choose the one I had before."
His World Cup performances for Cape Verde, a West African island nation with a population of 525,000, earned Vozinha a nomination for men's goalkeeper of the year at the Ballon d'Or awards.
"It's nice to feel like a kind of ambassador, but I want to make it clear that what we achieved was a collective effort," Vozinha said.
"We made history and the best news would be if we could harness that momentum to develop our country and improve the living conditions of our people."

The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial.
The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court.
Johal’s nine-year detention on alleged terrorist offences, has been a cause of diplomatic tension between the UK and India, but campaigners have claimed the British government has not been active enough to secure his release or, alternatively, a full trial.
The campaign group Reprieve says his case has never come to full trial largely because of the inability of the Indian government to assemble credible witnesses to back their claim that Johal transported £3,000 to France to fund a multinational extremist plot involving targeted killings in the Punjab in 2016-17.
On Thursday morning, the high court in Delhi instructed the Indian government to release Johal by 2.30pm Indian time, giving government officials three hours to comply or find themselves risking contempt proceedings. In the end, he was released in the late afternoon wearing a red T-shirt to be greeted by friends, family and flowers.
Documents shown to the court by Johal’s lawyers on behalf of his father-in-law as petitioner revealed that messages from the prison to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking permission for his release had been left unanswered.
His lawyers in their petition stated he had met all the bail conditions yet “the detainee has nevertheless not been released, and is being held in custody without the authority of any court, pending a ‘clarification’ sought by the jail from the Ministry of Home Affairs”.
The petition added that no clarification from the ministry had been forthcoming, explaining: “Every day of such detention is a continuing violation of the detainee’s fundamental rights under article 21 of the constitution of India.”
Johal has been detained by Indian authorities since 4 November 2017. He is facing eight charges of terrorism in the federal court, but had been cleared of largely similar charges by a Punjab court. He claims any initial confessions he gave were extracted under torture.
The bail terms last week imposed 11 conditions, including surrender of passport, a personal bond of 500,000 Indian rupees (£3,930) with two sureties, fortnightly reporting to the investigating officer, prior intimation of any change of residence and a ban on travelling to the Punjab. He was also restricted from talking to media about the case directly or indirectly.
The Indian government has alleged the Khalistan Liberation Force undertook the killings and Johal had “complete knowledge of the conspiracy” and was a KLF member.
His Dumbarton-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “There have been so many setbacks and disappointments in the last nine years that I didn’t dare to believe it until I saw Jagtar walking out of the prison gates with my own eyes. The last two weeks have been torture – knowing that Jagtar had been granted bail, but the authorities were refusing to let him out. I’ll sleep well tonight, knowing that he’s not behind bars.
“Tomorrow morning, the fight continues, because he’s still on trial and facing the death penalty for something he didn’t do, trapped in a sham legal process designed to punish him for standing up for human rights”.
Reprieve’s deputy executive director, Dan Dolan, said: “While tonight is the first night in almost nine years that Jagtar Singh Johal is not caged in a prison cell, he still has the threat of a death sentence hanging over him. It should also be noted that, despite bail being ordered, the prison refused to release Jagtar until his family brought a habeas corpus petition and a judge warned the jail they’d be found in contempt of court”.
The UK Foreign Office is understood to have been supporting recent calls for his release on bail after last week’s court order, as have two campaign groups in the UK Redress and Reprieve.

Prem* is a young mathematics graduate from a village in Jharkhand. He was known as an energetic and supportive young person. Children from the village often approached him when they had difficulties with mathematics. When he was selected for a job with the Indian Railways, it was expected to be a moment of happiness. But the thought of leaving his parents, friends, village and the life he shared with them was difficult for him.
In the weeks following the job offer, Prem began having sleepless nights, worrying about how he would cope with a new life and new responsibilities. Gradually, he stopped talking to his family. He began to feel helpless and worthless, lost interest in everyday life and reached a point where he attempted to end his life.
What helped was having people around him who could understand not only what he was going through, but also the world he was coming from. A neighbourhood facilitator working in a community-based organisation was able to sit with him, listen to his worries and share his dukh-sukh. They understood why leaving his parents, friends and village felt so difficult and gave him space to talk about the fears he was carrying.
The support was not about asking him simply to adjust or move on. It helped him think about what mattered to him, what he wanted for his future and how he could remain connected to the people and place that were important to him while taking up the new opportunity. He eventually wrote to the department asking for another opportunity to join. He was invited again and went to work, while continuing to receive support.
Prem’s experience highlights that what looks like a positive life event from the outside can sometimes become overwhelming. A suicidal act can often happen suddenly, during a moment of intense crisis. But the distress behind that moment may have been building for much longer.
For Adivasi communities, distress can be shaped by circumstances that may never appear in a psychiatric consultation.
When distress is accumulates
A recent study in Jharkhand examined psychosocial distress and help-seeking among Adivasi Ho adolescents. It found that distress was often linked to family conflict, pressure around education and work, financial hardship, violence, separation and loss, and difficulties in relationships. Some adolescents withdrew and stopped sharing what they were going through; for some, this included thoughts of self-harm or suicide
These accounts do not offer a single explanation for suicide among Adivasi communities. They show how distress can accumulate across everyday life — in family conflict, having to leave school temporarily or reduce schooling to help with agricultural or household work, substance use, untreated illness, violence, displacement, loss of livelihood, lack of mentorship, identity-related stigma and self-doubt, or the erosion of community and belonging.
When communities are disrupted
Belonging is an important part of suicide prevention. Stereotypes, exclusion, humiliation, discrimination and pressure to hide one’s identity can affect how people see themselves and how connected they feel to society. Historically, Adivasi communities stayed together. But modern development, alongside education and employment opportunities, have in some cases, uprooted Adivasi people from their culture. Mainstream schools do not teach Adivasi children in their own mother tongue; their history is woefully under-represented in the school curricula.
Sandip Sing, a radiologist from the Munda community practising in rural West Bengal and a first-generation learner, says, “There is a rapid transition in accessing and navigating educational and professional spaces, often amid gaps in resources, networks, and institutional familiarity. Bridging these gaps can be challenging, particularly with unfamiliar systems.”
Many educated Adivasis may also have had fewer opportunities to engage with their community’s history, culture, language and traditions, and may have complex or evolving relationships with their Adivasi identities. This matters for mental health because belonging itself is a source of strength. When people are uprooted without finding a new sense of belonging, distress can deepen.
This does not mean that development itself causes mental illness or suicide. The concern is what happens when rapid social change is accompanied by displacement, loss of livelihood, cultural disconnection and weakening social support.
Collective strength, mentoring
The strength of Adivasi life also lies in ways of expressing emotions and sharing knowledge. Songs and dances are not simply cultural performances; they are ways of expressing emotions, maintaining connection and making sense of life. The Adivasi dance itself is a powerful metaphor. People dance in a chain, holding one another. The village headman, Majhi Baba, dances alongside everyone else. An 80-year-old and an eight-year-old can dance together. There is no hierarchy; the strength is in the circle. For suicide prevention, this collective strength matters.
Young people also need places where they can be themselves without constantly having to explain or defend who they are. Lilibiti Saren, a medical officer from the Santhal community working in tribal areas of Bankura, West Bengal, notes that she often finds young people in these communities lacking direction. “There is a need for proper mentorship,” she says.
Locally organised Adivasi youth spaces can help. Such spaces can offer young people opportunities to speak in their own language, share experiences, learn from peers and elders and explore what Adivasiyat — identity, history, relationships and belonging — means to them.
Access and pathways in care
Clinical care remains essential. A person experiencing suicidal thoughts may need assessment for depression, substance use, trauma, psychosis, previous attempts, suicidal intent, access to means and immediate safety. Treatment and follow-up can save lives.
But access to mental health care is itself a major challenge in many Adivasi areas. Services are often limited, distant and unevenly available.
And even when services are available, the pathways into care may not be optimal. An Adivasi person with lived experience of mental healthcare says: “I felt like the psychiatrists and the psychologists were not speaking to me. They were judging me for what I had done and they were trying to find symptoms instead of trying to understand me, my pain and my situation.”
This raises an important question: are our mental health systems listening as carefully as they are diagnosing?
When formal services are scarce, difficult to reach, or experienced as unfamiliar or judgmental, people may seek support elsewhere—including from family, community networks, faith healers or indigenous systems. These spaces may offer something that the formal system does not: familiar language, relationships, cultural understanding and a sense of belonging.
Adivasi mental health therefore cannot be treated simply as another category within rural health. Representation matters — from schools to healthcare institutions and policy making.
Models that could work
In Adivasi communities of Jharkhand, particularly among the Ho, Munda and Santhal communities, Madait refers to a tradition of voluntary help and collective support for someone who needs it or is in distress. It reflects an understanding that some difficulties are too large for one household to manage alone.
This may be a useful way to think about mental healthcare too. The question is not simply how services can be delivered to Adivasi communities, but how communities themselves can shape, participate in and lead the care they need.
The same principle can be seen in Dukhu-Sukhu Baithaki — community support group meetings where people experiencing mental health difficulties and their families can meet, share experiences and support one another. This model works in West Singhbhum, Jharkhand, where people living with mental health conditions come together each month. These spaces do not replace professional care. They bring community knowledge, relationships and mutual support into the process of recovery.
Education without a knowledge of one’s roots; development that comes with displacement and mental healthcare that does not see or hear the people who need help is no longer enough. For suicide prevention, we must ask not only, “What is wrong with the individual?”, but also, “ Where is the community support? Where is the system that understands them?”
Perhaps suicide prevention in Adivasi communities must begin there — not by doing things for Adivasis, but by doing them with Adivasis.

Brazil heads to runoff as Bolsonaro leads Lula in first round of presidential election
Liberal Party makes major gains as the right strengthens grip on Congress

Brazil’s presidential election will go to the second round after far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly outpolled incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva but failed to secure the majority needed to avoid a runoff.
Mr Bolsonaro took an early lead as the South American nation began reporting results on Sunday afternoon in the first round of a tight election, following a campaign dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling.
The field of 13 candidates had been led by two clear frontrunners – Mr Lula da Silva, 80, who was seeking a fourth term, and Flavio, the 45-year-old son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
With 99.9 per cent of the votes counted, Mr Bolsonaro had won 47 per cent, compared with 45.1 per cent for the incumbent. Mr Bolsonaro received 56.1m votes to Mr Lula da Silva’s 53.8m.
They will now contest a 25 October runoff.
Early results had shown southern states leaning towards Mr Bolsonaro reporting faster, while votes from Mr Lula da Silva’s northeast stronghold were tallied slower.
Mr Bolsonaro-aligned politicians won several key races, including three seats for members of his family. As many as 34 of the 54 newly elected senators are from the right or the far-right.
Mr Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party emerged with the largest number of governors, senators and federal deputies elected so far, putting it in a strong position to wield influence in Congress.
The runoff will determine whether Brazil joins a wider wave of electoral gains across Latin America by right-wing candidates aligned with US president Donald Trump, or whether Mr Lula da Silva will secure another term despite tensions between his government and Washington over trade and security.
Despite growing worries over Brazil's public finances and sluggish economic growth, the campaign had offered meagre policy debate, as both leading candidates skipped the major TV debates.
Addressing his supporters, Mr Bolsonaro said that the result pointed to “the end of an era” for the ruling Workers’ party.
“Lula has fought seven presidential elections. He’s worried about power. I am worried about the future of Brazil,” he said.
While polls right up until Saturday showed Mr Lula da Silva would likely lead the first round but not avoid a runoff, Mr Bolsonaro told journalists earlier in Rio de Janeiro he was confident he could win the presidency in the first round, citing voters’ frustration with his chief opponent.
He was counting on "a protest vote from people who would otherwise vote for another candidate but are opposed to Lula", he said. "I hope it’s enough to secure a victory in the first round."
Thaise Lima, a 41-year-old lawyer on her way to vote in Sao Paulo, said her main goal was to get the Workers' Party out of office.
"I don't think Flavio is the best candidate, but I might decide to vote for him in the next few minutes," she said, adding that she wished psychiatrist and author Augusto Cury were a more viable candidate.
Fernando Tempel, 49, a management consultant, told Reuters he was voting for Mr Bolsonaro despite initially planning to vote for Romeu Zema, the former governor of Minas Gerais state.
On the other hand, Mr Lula da Silva’s allies had warned that the Trump administration might refuse to recognise election results if he won, pointing to an aborted effort to send US officials to Brazil.
"What is at stake is the future of Brazil," the president said earlier after voting in Sao Bernardo do Campo, in Sao Paulo state.
Mr Trump has not formally endorsed a candidate, though he had hosted Mr Bolsonaro at the White House and praised him publicly.
Speaking after the results, the incumbent president said: “We have just had a lesson in Brazilian democracy. The result is often unexpected. We can never get everything we want. I confess to you that I was convinced I was going to win the election in the first round. But we have a second round.”
“From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign,” he added, “and in a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil.”
Cristiano, 34, a doctor in Brasilia who voted for the president and preferred to withhold his surname told Reuters: “I'm a little worried about everything that's been happening recently, including internationally. I feel this election has had a lot of outside influence, more than in previous elections.”
"We are confident in our President Lula, who will fight for national sovereignty," said Pedro Palacio, 45, who was voting in Brasilia alongside his wife, Andreia, and their two sons and two dogs, all of whom wore outfits supporting the president.
Earlier, Brazil's electoral court chief Kassio Nunes Marques said in a press conference that “teams monitoring international risks have not identified any risks whatsoever”.
It was reported on Wednesday that Brazilian intelligence officials had briefed a French and German delegation on alleged US and Russian interference before the election. The US has rejected claims of interference in Brazil's affairs.
Despite falling inequality and unemployment, Mr Lula da Silva has struggled to win over voters grappling with high living costs, heavy household debt and the threat of street crime and more pervasive gang activity.
Mr Bolsonaro had sought to capitalise on cost-of-living concerns, while Mr Lula da Silva had moved to ban online gambling and, as the race tightened, expanded welfare and proposed fresh debt relief for families.
Rising spending and public debt above 82 per cent of GDP have stoked fiscal concerns that Brazil's next president will need to address. The government lowered its economic growth forecasts for this year and next to 2.0 per cent and 2.3 per cent respectively.
"I voted for Brazil to start growing again," said Marciano de Souza e Silva, a 52-year-old public servant in Brasilia and former Workers’ Party voter who moved right, voting for Jair Bolsonaro in 2018 and 2022 and Flavio on Sunday.
"The best social program is one that encourages people to start businesses, to actually produce real wealth," he said.
Overshadowing the policy debate, a scandal surrounding the now-defunct Banco Master has engulfed much of Brazil's political class and renewed public anger over corruption.
Daniel Vorcaro, who ran the bank, was arrested earlier this year and accused of a multibillion-dollar fraud scheme. The investigation has probed the banker's ties to figures from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes to Mr Bolsonaro, who is being investigated for money laundering tied to the case by the federal police.
The candidate has denied any wrongdoing, although he confirmed raising millions of dollars from Vorcaro to make a movie about his father.
The banker's connections to Mr Moraes, widely perceived as an ally of the president, plunged the court into crisis a month before the vote, creating fresh problems for the president. Mr Moraes has said the case against him is politically motivated for his role in the conviction of the elder Bolsonaro.
Congress has gained greater influence in Brazilian politics since the impeachment of former president Dilma Rousseff, an ally of Mr Lula da Silva, in 2016, raising the stakes of those legislative races.

Forced to call him 'Dad': Sexual abuse of disabled residents that shocked South Korea
- Published
"I was hurting inside, so I came to tell my story."
These were Seo Mi-hyeon's first words to the police.
Seo, who has an intellectual disability, struggles to form long sentences and can only communicate through brief words and gestures. But her memories of the abuse inflicted upon her were clear.
She was one of three residents at a state-run care home in South Korea who were sexually assaulted by the home's director, in a case that has shocked the country and raised serious questions about state care for the disabled.
Earlier this month, a court in Seoul sentenced the director - who has only been identified by his surname Kim - to 15 years in prison. Kim is appealing the conviction.
The court had heard that some residents were made to call the director "Dad", which prosecutors said illustrated the unequal relationship between Kim and those in his care.
The ruling came nearly two years after Seo, who is in her 40s, first disclosed the abuse to her mother.
We have changed Seo's name and the names of another victim in this story to protect their identities.
'I just endured it'
Seo first began living in Saekdongwon, a care home for the intellectually disabled, in 2016.
The institute, located in the city of Incheon, is fully subsidised by the state and still houses some 33 residents, although it has been asked to close down in light of this case.
According to Seo, the abuse began shortly after she began living there, with Kim visiting her at night or in the early hours of the morning to rape her.
Speaking through her lawyer Ko Eun-young, Seo said there was no adult at the facility she could speak to about the abuse, adding that she felt that other staff members would not help her. The care home has not responded to this allegation.
That was her life for almost 10 years, until the case came to light in February 2025, when Seo suffered a head injury.
She said it happened one of the times Kim tried to sexually assault her. She had blocked him with her hands, causing him to throw a glass at her.
Her lawyer told the court that the care home took Seo to hospital and informed her mother about the incident only after the wound on her head had been stitched up.
According to Seo's lawyer, Seo's mother had asked to see CCTV footage to establish how her daughter had been injured, but the facility refused, saying they were not authorised to release it.
As a result, her mother brought her home and decided to withdraw her from the facility. It was only after Seo was told that she would not have to return to the home that she disclosed the sexual abuse to her mum, who then reported it to the police.
"I thought it was safe to speak because I was told I didn't have to go back to Saekdongwon," Seo told the BBC via her lawyer.
When asked how she had managed on her own for so many years, she said: "I just endured it."
A police investigation into Seo's account was then widened to other residents.
They found at least two other alleged victims, including Lee Mi-Na, who said that she was also raped by Kim.
Earlier this month, a judge found all three victims' testimony credible.
He was sentenced to 15 years in jail for raping Lee and Seo, five years less than the original sentence prosecutors were asking for. He has denied all allegations and has since appealed the ruling.
For the third victim, Kim was found guilty of a lesser charge of sexual violence, with the judge saying the charge of rape against her was dropped as they could not find conclusive evidence that "force or threats [were used] that rendered the victim unable to resist".
A joint response committee made up of disability rights and other civic groups have criticsed this ruling, saying a victim's ability to resist an assault should not impact the verdict they receive.
The committee has also criticised the investigation process, saying there was a failure to identify more potential victims.
In November last year, following the initial allegations of abuse, local authorities from Ganghwa County had commissioned a team from Woosuk University to conduct an in-depth assessment of Saekdongwon's residents.
The report, which was submitted to the court as evidence, found indications that many more residents - at least 10 - could have been sexually assaulted by Kim.
But during the trial, the court did not address this finding.
According to local media reports, police had struggled to establish details of alleged abuse when interviewing residents, because most of them had severe disabilities and faced difficulties communicating. Some residents reportedly gave answers unrelated to the questions or did not respond at all.
Kim has not responded to allegations that he may have abused more residents.
Jeon Ji-su, the professor who led the Woosuk research team, told the BBC that investigators had accepted "only the accounts of people who could describe the abuse in complete sentences".
But activists said that this reliance on verbal testimony meant the police failed to recognise residents with greater communication difficulties as victims.
"If victims express their experiences differently from the way we expect, shouldn't the state make a greater effort to hear their voices?" said Baek In-seong, of Hansahoe, a counselling centre for survivors of sexual violence with disabilities.
Police have said that "while there may have been shortcomings in individual instances, these should not be taken as representative of the investigation as a whole".
Rights groups have also criticised others who have sought leniency for Kim.
Ahead of the verdict, a total of 13 petitions seeking leniency were said to have been submitted to the court. One of them, from a social welfare organisation, asked the court to take into account the defendant's "contribution to the welfare sector".
Welfare advocacy group Gyeol condemned the petitioning organisations, saying: "Past service in the welfare sector does not exempt anyone from accountability."
The judge's ruling on Kim's conviction stated that his offence was "particularly reprehensible" because "despite his professional duty to protect and support [the victims'] rights and interests and prevent abuse, he exploited the imbalance of power" with his victims to "gratify his own sexual desires".
Public scrutiny and protests
The case has shocked many in South Korea and raised questions about why the abuse was not prevented in the first place. More shocking is that it happened despite a move in 2011 to strengthen laws to protect people with disabilities from sexual assault.
That was the year a fictional film called Dogani, based on a true story of sexual abuse at a school for deaf children, premiered. Amid intense public scrutiny and protests, the school in question was shut and tougher laws were passed as a result.
These included more specific categories of sexual offences against disabled people, harsher penalties for offences committed by facility directors and employees, and the removal of the statute of limitations for some rape offences involving disabled victims.
But in the case of Saekdongwon, the abuse persisted despite regular regular inspections by Ganghwa County, the local authority responsible for overseeing the facility.
A county official told the BBC that such inspections focused largely on paperwork, and that residents were interviewed only when specific issues arose.
The official said there had also been an external monitoring team but it had received no reports from staff, and expressed regret that the authorities had not examined the situation more closely.
Jo Ha, a representative from the national council of a counselling centre who has supported some Saekdongwon victims, said some families she had spoken to had suspected there was abuse but felt unable to raise their concerns.
Leaving a facility would mean the family has to take on all care responsibilities, as finding alternative placements is difficult.
One survey conducted through a national association of parents of people living in residential facilities for those with disabilities found that around six in 10 people who secured a place in a residential facility had waited at least three years, highlighting the difficulty of accessing appropriate care.
Professor Kim Yoon-tae, the head of Woosuk University's Institute of Cognitive Science, points out that such facilities exercise great control over residents' actions, from what they eat to where they sleep in addition to their access to healthcare and even whether or not to grant they could go outside.
And while Saekdongwon is "a landmark case" because of the scale and duration of the abuse, it is also not an isolated incident, added Jo.
In 2023, an appeals court upheld an eight-year prison sentence for a worker who raped or sexually assaulted two women with intellectual disabilities at a facility in Yeongcheon the previous year.
In a separate case in Anseong, a care home worker was recently sentenced to six years in prison for repeatedly raping a female resident with a disability in 2022.
"The violence women with disabilities experience is not an individual problem," Jo said. "It is structural violence, shaped by overlapping layers of gender, disability, institutionalisation, poverty and social isolation."
- South Korea jails care home head for sexually assaulting disabled residents 
  - Published2 September
'We want to live in peace'
Since the case came to light, South Korea's prime minister has ordered the formation of a cross-government response team, calling the incident "a grave matter that calls into question the very reason for the state's existence".
In April, the government said it had inspected 1,507 residential facilities for disabled people nationwide and identified 33 suspected cases of abuse. So far investigations have been opened into eight of them.
The government also said it would strengthen targeted inspections based on risk factors, as well as joint inspections involving local authorities, police and disability rights advocacy agencies.
Ganghwa County has ordered Saekdongwon to close and the local government has revoked the licence of the foundation that operated it.
However, the closure has been deferred until the remaining residents have been relocated and arrangements for independent living have been completed.
The local government has said it will draw up individual independent-living support plans for all 33 Saekdongwon residents. That process is still under way.
Saekdongwon has filed an administrative lawsuit challenging the revocation of its licence. It has yet to comment on Kim's conviction.
Asked what had changed most since leaving Saekdongwon, Seo said: "I just feel at peace. I'm happy every day."
She also said the best thing was being able to eat and sleep when she wanted.
What she wanted most now was "to cut ties with the director completely and never have anything to do with him again".
But, Seo added, people with disabilities still need somewhere they could feel safe.
"I hope there can be a facility without sexual violence, where disabled people like us can live in peace."

Congo’s Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.
The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday (October 1, 2026). They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases, making up for nearly half of the confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
Congo announced an outbreak on May 15, caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine.
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.
A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources.
Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation’s 17th Ebola outbreak.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country’s government for reasons ranging from how it’s managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.
