Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
- Published
Rebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said its decision to relocate was made because of concerns about risks to civilians.
Two residents in Mekelle told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF forces have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services appear to have resumed in parts of the city.
Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and federal government forces alongside allied fighters in parts of Ethiopia's northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.
The development marks a major shift in the conflict and raises concerns among observers that the fighting could further destabilise the Horn of Africa, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries.
The US Department of State called for "restraint" and "dialogue" on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting about the conflict in Egypt on Sunday with leaders from some of Ethiopia's neighbours.
- How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia 
  - Published2 days ago
Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides.
However, in the last six months there has been a worsening of relations, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement.
Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.
The civil war was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
On Friday, neighbours Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with each other after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting a new rebel alliance - an allegation that it denied.
Ethiopia has also accused Egypt of supporting the rebels, leading to the expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, which Cairo responded to by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period.
The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

Members of the Rajaka community staged a protest at the Gandhi statue near the Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation office in Visakhapatnam on Monday demanding inclusion of the community in the Scheduled Castes list.

Unannounced protest on Gurugram’s Sohna Road triggers hours-long traffic jam
Some students staged a sit-in outside the State Council of Educational Research and Training office over some admission issues
An unannounced student protest on Gurugram’s Sohna Road triggered a traffic jam along a nearly three-kilometre stretch on Monday afternoon, with an ambulance remaining stuck for over 40 minutes. Paramedics and motorists watched helplessly as tightly packed cars, trucks, and motorcycles filled every inch, making it impossible for the ambulance to move.
Desperate two-wheeler riders tried squeezing through narrow footpath edges, only to block lanes. The jam choked key arterial roads, from the busy Rajiv Chowk underpass and junction past Tau Devi Lal Sports Complex up to Civil Lines and the District and Sessions Court.
An HT spot check found bumper-to-bumper traffic for over two to three hours. “We had not moved an inch in nearly 40 minutes,” said a commuter in his car en route to Old Gurugram. “Inside the underpass, the trapped exhaust fumes and blaring horns were suffocating. The worst part was seeing an ambulance siren wailing right behind us with nowhere to go.”
Gurugram traffic police officers said some students staged the unannounced sit-in outside the State Council of Educational Research and Training office over some admission issues. “The traffic police were prompt in diverting traffic to ease the congestion. Our teams were deployed on the ground continuously to monitor the situation,” said Gurugram traffic police spokesperson Vikas Verma.
Traffic police personnel took nearly three hours to regulate and implement diversions to gradually ease the bottleneck and restore normal vehicular flow.

On Sept. 28, 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump held an event at the White House to announce the planning of a new steel plant in Iowa. Joining him in the Oval Office for the event were several Iowa state leaders and officials.
Afterward, some social media users claimed Trump insulted Iowans during the event. For example, an X post (archived) displayed a video clip apparently recorded at the event and asserted, "Trump claims the federal government can 'supersede' Iowa and calls Iowans 'troubled people.'"
In the clip, Trump can be heard saying this: "And we can supersede the state, right? If we can supersede the state, it's good. Otherwise, it will never be good. They're very — they're really troubled people."
Users shared other posts claiming Trump called Iowans troubled people on Instagram (archived) and Threads (archived). Snopes readers searched the site and emailed us asking whether the claim was true.
It was not true. While the video clip is real and unedited, it omits important context that proves Trump didn't call Iowans "really troubled people." Trump was actually referring to Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz and other Democratic leaders in that state.
The remark came immediately after an exchange in which Trump asked how Walz was treating the opening of a new iron mine in Minnesota. Given that this context was omitted, we have rated the clip miscaptioned.
Videos and transcripts of Trump's remarks at the event were uploaded online by C-SPAN and Roll Call. The conversation that led to Trump making the "troubled people" comment begin at about the 6:20 mark in the C-SPAN video and 6:07 in Roll Call's Vimeo video.
At that time, John Jovanovic, the Trump-nominated chairman and president of the Export-Import Bank of the United States, begins describing the opening of an iron mine in Minnesota that is meant to supply the Iowa steel plant (emphasis ours):
JOVANOVIC: Thank you, Mr. President. So, what we're really talking about today is America's economic security. And Mr. President, it's your plan in action, but it all starts mining more in America. The mine you mentioned is the first mine opened in America in 50-plus years focused on iron ore. EXIM financed it, but most importantly, it's found on the Iron Range in America, which for 145 years has been the most prolific iron ore deposit in the world. It helped build America. It helped win two world wars. You're helping resurrect it, Mr. President, with this first iron ore mine. That is why this plant is possible, because we are creating one American supply chain. And what you see again here today, Mr. President, is private capital flowing in to rebuild America and to build America's future, so we can assure that the warfighter of tomorrow in America is always well-equipped and that everyday Americans have what they need when they need it most. And this is what it's going to take to continue to deliver the American dream, Mr. President, for another 250 years.
TRUMP: And how is the governor treating you? Because I freed up the iron ore in that place, and I absolutely won the election, but they wouldn't — they cheat like hell. But how is the governor treating you? Because I freed it up and then they closed it, and the people were devastated because it is the finest iron ore in the world, they say. So how is the governor and these other people that don't — I mean, it's one of the worst-run places I've ever seen. How are they doing?
JOVANOVIC: You know, Mr. President, we were there only 10 days ago, actually, to initiate the mine. We set off 1.3 million pounds of explosives that put it into operation and that will be the iron ore that feeds this plant and to make steel in America the —
TRUMP: And we can supersede the state, right?
COMMERCE SECRETARY HOWARD LUTNICK: Yes.
JOVANOVIC: [unintelligible, cut off by Trump]
TRUMP: If we can supersede the state, it's good. Otherwise, the state will never be good. They're very — they're really troubled people. Thank you very much; great job you're doing, too, by the way. Secretary Lutnick, please.
The mine Jovanovic referred to is owned by Mesabi Metallics in northern Minnesota, where part of the American Iron Range is located. Mesabi Metallics is the same company investing in the steel plant in Iowa.
Local news reports on the fraught history of the mine suggest its struggles have largely been tied to the parent company of Mesabi Metallics, Essar. The India-based company first started work on the mine and an accompanying steel mill in 2007 before shuttering its plans for the mine in 2015 and filing for bankruptcy in 2016. Essar still owes Minnesota more than $22 million in infrastructure debt, according to Iowa news channel KWQC.
As Jovanovic said, Trump administration officials were at the opening of the iron mine in Minnesota about 10 days earlier. If Trump's concern was about opening the mine, he'd have no reason to call for the federal government to "supersede" Minnesota. According to Essar itself, Minnesota State Auditor Julie Blaha said in 2024, "After years of uncertainty, it's encouraging to see Mesabi Metallics breathing new life into this major mining operation."
While the context makes it clear that Trump was referencing Walz and his administration in Minnesota, not Iowans, Snopes reached out to the White House to seek confirmation on whom exactly Trump believed to be "really troubled people." We'll update this story if and when we receive a response to our question.
For further reading, Snopes recently investigated a claim asserting Trump's renaming of "artificial intelligence" to "super intelligence" is a play to profit off of .SI domain names.

COVID-19 made the weaknesses in our pandemic preparedness at national and global levels painfully clear. But a new study highlights that even at the first, local steps of an outbreak with pandemic-potential, we are worryingly underprepared.
Health officials in New York set up a regional test of healthcare facilities to identify and respond to a patient with a mystery infection that could pose a pandemic-level threat. But things didn’t go well. Overall, responses were slow, appropriate use of personal protective equipment was spotty, and only 60 percent of facilities passed the basics of the test—an overall failing grade.
“These drills identified needs for health care workers and health care facility staff member training to achieve earlier identification, masking, and isolation of potentially infectious febrile patients,” the officials wrote in the study, which was published in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.
The drill centered on “professional patient actors,” who staggered into healthcare facilities feigning expected symptoms of an H5 bird flu infection—a virus type thought to have pandemic potential. The actors wore makeup to look unwell, used eye drops and petroleum jelly to mimic having conjunctivitis (aka pink eye), and had a fake cough. They complained about feeling weak and feverish and reported taking a Motrin (fever reducer) before coming in. When questioned, they said they hadn’t traveled out of the country and, if asked about any sick contacts, would respond, “Does a sick bird count?” They would tell a sad tale of trying to save a sick duck they found in a park. In the story, the duck doesn’t make it, and the now-ill patient didn’t wear any gloves while handling it. The chatty actor would tell this story without prompting.
To pass the test, a healthcare facility needed to mask the patient and put them in an isolation room. Ideally, the masking would occur within a minute or less of the patient walking in, and isolation would occur in 10 minutes or less. For this drill, both masking and isolation were enough to pass, regardless of timing.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

A video showing a man with a disability being assaulted by a group of men is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that it shows a Muslim being harassed in India. Let us verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals showing an old handicapped muslim being harassed by a few men in India.
Fact: The viral video is scripted content from a YouTube channel called Muklesur Bhaijaan 2.0, which regularly posts similar videos on social media. The channel’s bio states that it shares scripted content. We also found several other videos on the channel featuring the same elderly man. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of the key frames from the viral video led us to a YouTube channel named Muklesur Bhaijaan 2.0, where the same video was uploaded and published on 15 December 2025, with the description ‘ak muslim chacha ko mara chapri na | #shortsvideo bike rider | bike rider vs chapri.’
We noticed that he regularly uploads similar fight videos. His YouTube bio also states that he uploads riding vlogs and scripted videos.
The old man shown being harassed in the video has appeared in several other similar videos published by the same channel (here, here, here). Factly had previously debunked a similar claim featuring the same old man seen in the viral video.
To sum up, the video showing an old disabled man being assaulted by a few men is scripted, not a real incident.

Nobel medicine prize goes to 3 scientists for research into brain activity
STOCKHOLM — The Nobel Prize in medicine was awarded Monday to three scientists working on the mechanisms the brain uses to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells.
Karl Deisseroth, 54, Peter Hegemann, 71, and Georg Nagel, 73, have carried out research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. They are based at universities in Germany and the United States.
The Nobel committee lauded their work, writing on X that the method "is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain's mysteries."
The Nobel Assembly said Deisseroth is based at Stanford University in California, while Hegemann is at Humboldt University in Berlin and Nagel at the University of Würzburg in Germany.
Thomas Perlmann, the secretary of the medicine committee, said he was able to reach all three winners by phone Monday.
The prize was announced at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, kicking off Nobels week.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million).
Last year, the prize went to three scientists researching the immune system.
Monday's medicine prize is followed by the physics prize on Tuesday, chemistry on Wednesday and literature on Thursday.
After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Oct. 12.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

Our skin, hair and nails require adequate protein, energy, vitamins and minerals for growth, repair and normal functioning. When deficiencies are significant or prolonged, some may become visible. But many of these signs also overlap with hormonal disorders, chronic illnesses, dermatological conditions, stress, poor sleep and other factors. So when and how do you know if there is a nutritional deficit?
What the signs can indicate
Iron deficiency, particularly when it progresses to anaemia, can cause pallor of the skin and mucous membranes, and may be associated with diffuse hair shedding. Spoon-shaped nails can also occur with iron deficiency. Vitamin B12 deficiency may cause hyperpigmentation, particularly over the knuckles, as well as changes in the tongue and oral mucosa.
Zinc deficiency can affect skin integrity and hair growth, while inadequate protein intake can affect hair structure and growth and, in severe cases, cause marked changes in the skin and hair. Vitamin C deficiency can result in bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Dry or scaly skin may be associated with inadequate vitamin A, essential fatty acids or zinc.
Cracks at the corners of the mouth can occur with iron, vitamin B12, zinc or riboflavin deficiency. A smooth, red and sore tongue, or glossitis, can be associated with deficiencies of vitamin B12, iron, folate or niacin.
Ramya Subburaj, senior clinical dietitian and head of the department of dietetics, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, said these signs should be viewed as clues rather than proof of a deficiency. “There is considerable overlap between nutritional and non-nutritional causes,” she said, noting that a person with hair loss should not assume that poor nutrition is necessarily responsible.
What ‘ferritin face’ really means
Terms such as ‘iron-deficiency face’ and ‘ferritin face’ circulating on social media are not recognised medical diagnoses. Iron deficiency can cause anaemia and pallor, but there is no specific facial appearance through which low ferritin can be diagnosed.
Ferritin is a protein that stores iron and its level is used to assess the body’s iron stores. Low ferritin can occur before iron-deficiency anaemia develops. However, it does not produce a distinct facial appearance.
Pushpa Gnanaraj, senior consultant, dermatology, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, said pallor associated with anaemia may be visible in the skin, lips, gums or inner eyelids because of reduced haemoglobin. But dullness, dark circles or changes in facial appearance are not specific to low iron stores.
Vinitha Krishnan, chief clinical dietitian, nutrition and dietetics, SIMS Hospital, Chennai, said any changes associated with depleted iron stores are generally subtle and non-specific. Similar features can occur with inadequate sleep, stress, dehydration, allergies, ageing, thyroid disorders or other nutritional deficiencies.
A proper history and clinical examination are therefore important. Depending on the symptoms, investigations may include a complete blood count, ferritin and iron studies, vitamin B12 and vitamin D. Thyroid testing, zinc assessment or other investigations may be considered when clinically indicated. Dermatological conditions such as eczema, psoriasis, fungal infections, autoimmune disorders and pigmentary diseases may also need to be ruled out.
Correcting deficiencies
When a confirmed nutritional deficiency is responsible for a symptom, correcting it can lead to improvement. The timeline, however, depends on the nutrient involved and the severity and duration of the deficiency.
Pallor and some symptoms associated with iron deficiency may begin to improve within weeks of appropriate treatment, while mouth ulcers and glossitis can also improve after the underlying deficiency is corrected. Hair shedding and thinning generally take longer to recover because hair grows slowly; improvement may take several months. Nail changes can similarly take months to grow out.
Reshma Aleem, senior clinical dietician, Rela Hospital, Chennai, said the extent and speed of recovery depend on whether the deficiency is mild, moderate or severe and on how effectively it is corrected.
Fixing the basics
A varied diet remains the foundation. Adequate protein, pulses, whole grains, vegetables, fruits, nuts and seeds, along with eggs, dairy, fish, lean meat or fortified foods according to dietary preference, can provide a range of nutrients.
Experts caution against taking supplements based only on a social-media checklist. Excessive intake of some vitamins and minerals can itself cause adverse effects and may interfere with the absorption or metabolism of other nutrients. More importantly, treating an assumed deficiency can delay the diagnosis of the actual cause.
The appropriate approach is to investigate persistent changes, confirm a deficiency where indicated and then correct it with dietary measures or supplementation under clinical guidance.

Poland's antitrust regulator accuses Google of unfair market practices
The penalty could be up to 10 percent of Google’s annual revenue.
A Polish regulator said that Google isn't playing by the rules when the tech giant displays articles from local media publishers in Google Search, Google News and Google Discover. Poland's Office of Competition and Consumer Protection, abbreviated as UOKiK, said that Google leaned on its dominant market position and failed to provide necessary data when negotiating compensation with the country's news publishers.
Tomasz Chróstny, president of UOKiK, said in a press release that there were rules that clearly laid out what info Google was required to provide to publishers to figure out proper compensation and that the company still failed to do so. The agency could hit the company with a fine amounting to up to 10 percent of Google's annual revenue, according to Chróstny. We reached out to Google for comment and will update the story if we hear back.
Like the UOKiK, the European Commission previously opened an antitrust investigation against Google, looking at if the company offered appropriate compensation for articles used in its AI Overview or AI Mode features. Prior to Google, the Polish authority also accused Apple of using its App Tracking Transparency feature of creating unfair competition in the personalized ads market.

Hospitals across the State are up against a shortage of drugs for treating non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Several commonly prescribed drugs for blood sugar management (metformin), hypertension (telmasartan), and cholesterol (atorvastatin) are in short supply in hospitals, even as authorities have assured that these will be back in stock within a week.
“It is not as though we are running short on all drugs. But NCD drugs are medicines that people should be taking without fail as a matter of routine and disruptions in its supply can be worrying. We anticipated this shortage last month and moved fast to make local purchases so our patients do not miss the medication,” the medical officer at a family health centre in Thiruvananthapuram said.
“NCD drugs are in short supply but we have not had any issues because our hospital management committee has adequate funds, apart from the substantial resources that our block panchayat sets aside every year for purchasing drugs, for making local purchases. If a substantial amount of drugs has to be purchased, then we float a tender. However, there are also health institutions in smaller panchayats which might be struggling to make local purchase because of insufficient funds,” the superintendent at a taluk hospital in the suburbs said.
Ideally, when a patient registered at the NCD clinic of a particular healthcare institution comes for review, the hospital should have at least 30 days’ stock of the NCD drugs for the patient to take home. In the present situation, many hospitals are not able to ensure that.
Medical officers said this year, the Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) released only the drug supplies of the first quarter and that the second quarter release of June did not happen at all which led to the shortage of some drugs, including NCD drugs.
The KMSCL purchases around ₹700-800 crore worth of medicines every year for supplying to around 8,000 government healthcare institutions. In its last procurement exercise, 180 items reportedly received no bids, while suppliers quoted higher prices for another 171 items. This resulted in re-tendering and delays in placing fresh orders.
According to sources, the supply orders given in January-March, for some 18 non-bidder drugs, were cancelled by the new government because the prices quoted were considered far too high, which triggered the present shortage. However, fresh procurement orders have been placed and the supplies are expected to arrive within a week, it was pointed out.
The fact that the KMSCL owes over ₹2,200 crore to various pharma firms, for drugs purchased for hospitals as well as the drugs purchased by hospitals for patients under the Karunya Arogya Suraksha Padhati, has not helped the situation. The massive delays in payment is one of the reasons why many pharma forms do not respond to tenders floated by the KMSCL.
Health Minister K. Muraleedharan had directed that the procurement procedures for the next financial year begin in October itself and that the entire process be completed by the end of December.
He also directed that middlemen be removed from the tender processes and that agencies dealing directly in imported medicines also be allowed to take part in tenders. He said a comprehensive overhaul was under way at the KMSCL
According to sources, there are also efforts to form a consortium with medical service corporations of other States so that common purchase tenders can be floated, which might likely bring prices further down.

బ్యాంకులకు వారానికి ఐదు రోజుల పని విధానం అమలు చేయాలని బ్యాంకు ఉద్యోగ సంఘాలు చాలా కాలంగా డిమాండ్ చేస్తున్నాయి. ఈ డిమాండ్పై సెప్టెంబర్ 2026లో యునైటెడ్ ఫోరం ఆఫ్ బ్యాంక్ యూనియన్స్ (UFBU) దేశవ్యాప్తంగా నిరసనలు చేపట్టింది. వీటిలో పెన్షన్ ప్రయోజనాలను మెరుగుపరచడం, పాత పెన్షన్ విధానాన్ని (OPS) తిరిగి అమలు చేయడం, పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న వేతన సమస్యలను పరిష్కరించడం వంటి డిమాండ్లు ఉన్నాయి. సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 చివర్లో మూడు రోజుల బ్యాంకు సమ్మెకు పిలుపునిచ్చారు. అయితే, ఇండియన్ బ్యాంక్స్ అసోసియేషన్ ఈ అంశాలపై చర్చించేందుకు అంగీకరించడంతో సమ్మెను వాయిదా వేశారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, ఆర్థిక మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ జారీ చేసినట్లు చెబుతున్న ఒక గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్ సోషల్ మీడియాలో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) వైరల్ అవుతోంది. ఇందులో అన్ని ప్రభుత్వ రంగ బ్యాంకులకు ప్రతి శనివారం సెలవు ఉంటుందని, ఈ నిబంధన వెంటనే అమల్లోకి వస్తుందని కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం ప్రకటించినట్లు పేర్కొన్నారు. ఈ పోస్ట్లో చేసిన వాదనను ఇప్పుడు పరిశీలిద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ప్రభుత్వ రంగ బ్యాంకులకు ప్రతి శనివారం సెలవు ఉంటుందని ఆర్థిక మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ జారీ చేసిన గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్.
ఫాక్ట్: PIB ఫ్యాక్ట్ చెక్ ప్రకారం, ఆర్థిక మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ ఇలాంటి నోటిఫికేషన్ను ఏదీ జారీ చేయలేదు. సోషల్ మీడియాలో వైరల్ అవుతున్న గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్ OpenAI టూల్స్ను ఉపయోగించి AI ద్వారా రూపొందించినది. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్ట్లో చేసిన వాదన తప్పు.
ముందుగా, ఇలాంటి నోటిఫికేషన్ ఏదైనా విడుదలైందా అని తెలుసుకోవడానికి ప్రభుత్వం యొక్క అధికారిక e-Gazette పోర్టల్ను పరిశీలించాము. అయితే, అక్కడ దీనికి సంబంధించిన ఎలాంటి రికార్డు కనిపించలేదు. అలాగే, ఈ విషయంపై భారత ప్రభుత్వం నుంచి ఎలాంటి అధికారిక ప్రకటన కూడా వెలువడలేదు.
తర్వాత, వైరల్గా మారిన గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్ చిత్రాన్ని OpenAI కంటెంట్ డిటెక్షన్ టూల్ను ఉపయోగించి పరిశీలించాము. ఈ పరిశీలనలో, ఈ గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్ OpenAI టూల్స్ను ఉపయోగించి AI ద్వారా రూపొందించినట్లు తేలింది.
అదనంగా, ప్రభుత్వ ప్రెస్ ఇన్ఫర్మేషన్ బ్యూరో (PIB) ఫ్యాక్ట్ చెక్ ఈ విషయంపై స్పష్టత (ఆర్కైవ్) ఇచ్చింది. ప్రభుత్వ రంగ బ్యాంకులకు ప్రతి శనివారం సెలవు ప్రకటిస్తూ ఆర్థిక మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ ఎలాంటి నోటిఫికేషన్ జారీ చేయలేదని సోషల్ మీడియాలో వైరల్ అవుతున్న గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్ నకిలీదని నిర్ధారించింది.
చివరిగా, వైరల్ అవుతున్న గెజిట్ నోటిఫికేషన్ AI ద్వారా రూపొందించబడింది; అన్ని శనివారాలను బ్యాంకులకు సెలవులుగా ప్రభుత్వం ప్రకటించలేదు.

Bellingham unlocks new level and potential to be 'one of the greatest'
- Published
Just a year ago, Jude Bellingham's place in the England squad was up in the air. Now he is being talked about as having the potential to be one of football's "greatest of all time".
The Real Madrid man was left out of Thomas Tuchel's Three Lions squad in October 2025 and his place at the World Cup was called into question, with the German head coach saying Bellingham wouldn't get star treatment.
But Bellingham did of course make the squad for the World Cup and was arguably his team's standout performer, finishing as England's top scorer with seven goals as they reached the semi-finals and finished third.
He has already shown that he is world class with starring performances for club and country, but the way he helped England to dismantle Croatia 7-0 in the Nations League on Saturday looked like someone perhaps reaching a new level.
The 23-year-old was instrumental in Rijeka, scoring as well as registering a hat-trick of assists. He even ended the match wearing the captain's armband as England inflicted the heaviest defeat in Croatia's history.
"Bellingham can go on to be one of the greatest players of all time," former Manchester United and Republic of Ireland midfielder Roy Keane said on ITV after the game.
"At this moment in time, he is an amazing footballer. The package – his running power, his delivery, his goal threat. The way he is progressing as a player, I still think there is a lot more to come from him."
Bellingham, recently voted England's player of the year for the second year in a row, is now "nailed on as the 10" for the future, former England defender Matt Upson told BBC Radio 5 Live.
Keane added: "He has been fantastic in possession, but what he does out of possession lifts all these other players.
"If you have a player that good in your team, who is amazing in possession and he's playing for Real Madrid and doing brilliant things, but his work rate off the ball... that will just inspire other players. He is a huge leader for them."
'Push for next level or other teams will catch up'
England's front four will share praise for the way in which they demolished the Croatian backline.
Record goalscorer Harry Kane scored twice, as did Bukayo Saka, with Anthony Gordon scoring and assisting too.
And Kane will be back in the spotlight on Tuesday when he can equal Peter Shilton's all-time England men's appearance record against the Czech Republic at Wembley.
In moving to 89 goals for his country, the 33-year-old again showed how irreplaceable he is for England, but, when he was rested with 20 minutes to go, it was Bellingham who took the captain's armband.
And that highlighted the younger man's importance as a leader within the squad.
Bellingham was also directly involved in more than two goals in an England game for the first time, and he became the first player to record three assists in a game for the Three Lions since Trent Alexander-Arnold against San Marino in November 2021.
It was Bellingham's performance in front of goal that impressed former England striker Ian Wright.
"When Bellingham is on the pitch, he is always driving forward and going again and again," Wright said.
"He was involved in everything. His athleticism, his technical ability, his intensity. He never lets up, the way he gets in the box, he is always in there unmarked. He is always in there."
Bellingham showed every aspect of his game against Croatia and Tuchel was asked by BBC Sport if he had gone to another level.
"Yes, at the moment it seems like it, and you always need to," Tuchel said.
"It's like you can never stand still. You have to develop and you have to push for the next level, otherwise other teams will catch up."
Tuchel, who said the performance was a way to "move on" after the disappointment of England's World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina, said that he "adjusted some things" following the tournament, giving players, including Bellingham, "a lot of responsibility".
Saka was part of the front four and Bellingham assisted his first goal with a high quality cross.
"He was amazing tonight," Saka said of Bellingham.
"He deserved player of the year and he deserved man of the match tonight too. He was special.
"[I'm] happy to play with him and happy to have him in the England team."

Lucknow, October 5: Uttar Pradesh has achieved a historic milestone in implementing the 'Pradhan Mantri Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana' by installing more than 8,76,500 rooftop solar plants and surpassing Gujarat in cumulative installations. With this, UP has secured first position in the country in cumulative rooftop solar installations under the scheme. This achievement is the result of continuous, coordinated efforts under CM Yogi's leadership to take solar energy to every section of society.
For the past several months, the pace of rooftop solar installation under the 'Pradhan Mantri Surya Ghar Yojana' in UP has remained consistently high. Regular district-level reviews, inspection and monitoring of metering at the DISCOM level, banking follow-up, vendor coordination, and resolution of pending cases are being prioritized.
Under the scheme, UPNEDA has also impanelled more than 8,000 vendors, employing more than one lakh people, and this direct impact is reflected in the national ranking of districts. A total of 15 districts of the state are among the top 100 in the country, with Lucknow ranking first and Varanasi tenth.
The state's installed rooftop solar capacity has crossed 2,942 MW. At a standard of 4.5 units per kilowatt per day, this capacity can generate more than 1.32 crore units of clean electricity every day. At an equivalent value of Rs. 6.50 per unit, this electricity is equivalent to more than Rs. 8.5 crore per day and more than ₹3,100 crore annually. This provides relief to lakhs of families on electricity bills while also strengthening the state's energy economy.
One of the biggest features of rooftop solar is that it does not require large tracts of land for electricity generation, as it is installed on house rooftops. Based on the standard of 4 acres per MW, the current rooftop solar capacity installed in the state saves more than 11,700 acres of land. In this way, installing solar plants on house rooftops and other available building structures reduces the need to use large tracts of land, allowing that land to be used for other commercial activities.
Based on the clean electricity generated through rooftop solar, the state is estimated to reduce CO₂ emissions by more than 34 lakh tonnes annually. In tree-equivalent terms, this environmental benefit matches the carbon absorbed in one year by more than 15 crore trees. This tree equivalence is an estimated environmental comparison.
Pradhan Mantri Surya Ghar Yojana has created a large-scale green job ecosystem in the state. Through more than 8,000 UPNEDA vendors, more than one lakh direct employment opportunities are being generated in areas related to the sale, design, engineering, installation, electrical work, commissioning and after-sales service of solar systems. At the same time, the scheme's employment impact is not limited to vendors and installation.
The scheme has also created many indirect employment opportunities in areas such as logistics, transportation, warehousing, packaging, loading and unloading, material supply, structure fabrication, surveying, site assessment, customer service, repair, and maintenance. In this way, the scheme has created a new market for green skills and green jobs for the youth in the state.
Under this scheme, Uttar Pradesh has received more than ₹5,722 crore in central subsidy and more than ₹2,000 crore in state subsidy. With direct financial assistance from the Central and State governments reaching beneficiaries, rooftop solar has become more accessible to domestic consumers.
Rooftop solar is now not only a means of environmental protection, but also an effective tool for reducing household electricity expenses, achieving energy self-reliance, and strengthening household economic empowerment.
With more than 8,76,500 rooftop solar plants, an installed capacity of more than 2,942 MW, more than 1.32 crore units of clean electricity every day, the impact of saving more than 11,700 acres of land, potential annual carbon savings of more than 34 lakh tonnes, more than 8,000 vendors and more than one lakh direct employment opportunities have now made the Pradhan Mantri Surya Ghar Yojana the foundation of a comprehensive green economic transformation in Uttar Pradesh. Under the guidance of CM Yogi Adityanath, Uttar Pradesh has presented an effective model to the country by linking rooftop solar with public participation, employment, industry, energy savings and environmental protection.

In late September 2026, an image spread online claiming to show a herd of wild bison surrounding a hiker. According to a Facebook post (archived) with the image, the wild bison were protecting the "stranded hiker" from a wildfire:
A wild bison herd formed a tight circle around a stranded hiker during a wildfire, and firefighters say the formation was the only reason she wasn't overtaken by the flames.
Rachel had been hiking a remote section of the reserve when the wind shifted without warning, turning a controlled burn nearly six miles away into a fast-moving wildfire cutting off her only route back to the trailhead. She had no cell signal, no clear path around the advancing smoke, and less than twenty minutes before the fire line would reach her position on an open grassy ridge with nowhere to shelter.
That's when the bison found her.
A herd of nearly thirty animals, moving away from the fire themselves, suddenly changed direction as they passed her position, slowing and gathering into a tight defensive ring around her exact spot on the ridge, facing outward, the way herds typically only form when protecting newborn calves from predators.
Rachel said she didn't understand what was happening at first, terrified she was now trapped between fire and a wall of two-thousand-pound animals. But the herd held its formation as the fire's smoke rolled over them, and she realized, watching the ash fall around the massive bodies surrounding her, that their sheer size and the churned, trampled earth beneath the herd was creating a wide buffer of bare ground the flames couldn't easily cross.
The fire burned around the herd's position rather than through it. When air support finally spotted the unusual circular formation from above and redirected a rescue team, they found Rachel unharmed at the center, the herd only breaking formation and moving on once the helicopter's rotors got close enough to disperse them.
Wildlife officials say bison herds have never been documented forming protective circles around a human being before, only around their own young. They have no explanation for why this herd made the exception.
(Facebook user "Wonder Paws")
The above image is fake, and the story accompanying it is not true. The image contains numerous signs it was generated using artificial intelligence. There also was no available evidence of bison legitimately protecting a hiker in this manner.
The first sign that the image was artificially generated was visible in the top portion showing the circle of bison. Several of them are facing outward but also appear to have heads on both sides of their bodies. The hiker is also not visible in the top portion. Furthermore, the bison in the lower portion of the image, showing the alleged rescue, appear to be copy-and-pasted versions of the same animal. Some bison in the lower portion also appear to have heads on both sides of their bodies.
The post appears to have first ben shared by a Facebook account that has a history of posting AI-generated material.
The "photograph" was allegedly taken in August 2025, according to the timestamp at the top left. We looked for evidence of news coverage around that time about a rescue involving a woman named Rachel and found no reporting from trustworthy outlets such as The Associated Press and Reuters. The story in the post also did not contain information that would be included in legitimate reports about such an incident, such as the specific location of the wildfire.
The image and accompanying story are an example of AI slop: low-quality content that's easy to create thanks to AI tools. Such content overwhelms social media feeds, leaving users unsure of what's real and what's not.
For further reading, Snopes has covered numerous examples of AI slop.

In short:
Spain's prime minister has called an early election for November 29.
The announcement follows nationwide protests after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her Madrid apartment.
Mr Sánchez leads a minority government that recently failed to pass proposed housing relief measures in parliament.
Spain's prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has called an early election as the country grapples with a housing crisis.
In a televised address to the nation, Mr Sánchez said the election would be held on November 29.
"We need to renew people's support," the prime minister said.
"We need to mobilise and win a much larger progressive majority in parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain."
The leader also acknowledged having made mistakes and falling short of campaign promises.
"I also know that part of that social majority is dissatisfied today," he said.
The announcement comes after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his government as tens of thousands gathered in Madrid over the weekend to demand affordable housing.
Protests were sparked by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid from her apartment of more than 70 years by an investment firm.
In response, tent cities have been erected in Madrid, Barcelona, Seville and even the tourist mecca of Palma de Mallorca, in the Balearic Islands.
Over the past decade, the average rental price per square metre in Spain has almost doubled, reaching 15.10 euros ($24.62) per square metre in August, according to real estate portal Idealista.
The Bank of Spain estimates that the country of about 50 million people is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.
Social housing in Spain makes up less than 2 per cent of the housing stock, according to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development data.
Measures proposed by Mr Sánchez's minority government, including automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants, were voted down by opposition parties in Spain's parliament.
He also planned to stop "vulture funds" from buying in bulk and then reselling properties at higher prices, and to introduce a new tax on seasonal rentals.
Opinion polls suggest a coalition led by the conservative People's Party (PP) with the support of the conservative Vox party is the most likely outcome in Spain, ushering a far-right party into central government for the first time since the return of democracy after the death of dictator Francisco Franco.
Still, Mr Sánchez, has proven time and again his ability to surprise those who had long written him off.
Despite never winning enough votes to form a majority government, he has cobbled together a series of fragile and seemingly impossible coalitions, including voices from the far-left to the separatist right, to remain in power for three successive terms lasting eight years.
But growing fragmentation among his partners has meant the government has passed little in the way of legislation in its third term and failed to pass a budget since 2023, even as Spain's economy has continued to be one of the best-performing in the developed world.

I was born and raised in Mexico, but I spent most of my financially independent adult life in New York and London.
Living abroad made me second-guess a lot of the norms related to money and dating that I'd long internalized — for instance, the expectation that in a heterosexual relationship, men should just pay for everything.
For years, though, I was single, so I never had to decide how I'd actually split finances with another person.
Things changed when I entered a serious relationship. Funny enough, my partner's background is remarkably similar to mine: She is also Mexican and has built much of her adult life abroad.
Given our similarities, I was curious to see how we'd approach money as a couple.
We seemed pretty in sync until we decided to move in together
At first, we set an expectation that we'd go 50/50 on things like date nights and groceries.
We had similar salaries, neither of us expected the other to fund our lifestyle, and dividing shared expenses down the middle felt like the simplest solution. This system felt like a breath of fresh air after growing up with the idea that men should always pay for everything.
Then, several months into our relationship, we decided to move in together.
Suddenly, we had to agree on how much of our monthly income we were comfortable putting toward rent. She wanted to find a slightly more expensive place in a better location, with more space — a home we genuinely loved.
I, on the other hand, felt like we could find a more affordable spot and save money for things like flights and nice dinners.
The conversation made me realize: Our main difference isn't how much we earn, or even how much we spend, but what we want our money to do for us. Once we found a place and moved in together, the same tension started appearing everywhere.
What feels worthwhile to me can feel unnecessary to her, and vice versa
I am much quicker to spend on travel and experiences. Paying for a flight somewhere new, a weekend away, video games, or even Pokémon cards can make perfect sense to me. I tend to judge a purchase by the enjoyment or experience I expect to get from it.
My partner is more willing to spend on her well-being: our home, clothes, cleaning, and things that make everyday life nicer. For her, anything that would improve our apartment is obviously something worth buying.
I can look at the same thing and wonder whether we need it at all. I am sure she has had exactly the same reaction to some of my purchases.
This has caused friction, because our equal-split system started to feel unfair when one of us had to pay for something we didn't want. Even when it came to things we both enjoy, such as eating dinner together, she would rather buy ingredients to cook our meal at home, whereas I'd rather splurge on going to an upscale Italian restaurant.
We are not a classic saver-and-spender couple. We are both willing to spend. We just have different ideas about what deserves our money.
With time, we stopped trying to make every expense perfectly equal
Eventually, we began thinking about our finances in categories. There are things we need, things I care about, things she cares about, and things we genuinely enjoy together. Seeing our spending this way made it easier to separate shared decisions from personal preferences.
We created a joint savings account, which gives us a place to put money toward some goals that belong to both of us — like theater tickets or a new TV — as well as expenses like rent. With our separate accounts, we each pay for our own priorities, like plane tickets for me and house plants for her.
As our circumstances evolved, we also moved beyond a rigid 50/50 split and began dividing shared costs proportionally according to income.
However, we try to still be flexible and not keep score. For example, I don't drink. If we order wine at dinner, I could insist that we exclude it from my half of the bill, since technically, that might be more precise.
I do not think a relationship works if every amount has to be allocated perfectly, though. Sometimes I contribute toward something she enjoys, and she does the same for me. Compromise is part of the point, and love is the center of everything.
We still don't agree on every purchase, and I don't think we need to. What matters is knowing what belongs to me, what belongs to her, and what we want badly enough to build together.
Our next shared project is already waiting: a dog.

The Trump administration is facing growing questions over its decision to abandon a fraud and bribery case against the Indian billionaire Gautam Adani after he promised to invest $10bn in the US.
For the second time this year, two Democratic senators have demanded attorney general Todd Blanche answer questions about the US Department of Justice department’s handling of the case – and raised concerns over its judgment under Donald Trump.
In August, a federal judge in New York agreed to drop the fraud case against Adani, one of the richest people in the world, at the request of prosecutors, despite having concerns about “irregularities” in the “highly unusual” decision. It has become the latest example of judges raising eyebrows at Trump administration prosecutors for pushing to dismiss criminal cases.
Now, more than a month later, senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal are asking Blanche to clarify whether people close to Donald Trump were involved in that decision.
It comes aftera New York Times report revealed that Adani, represented by one of Trump’s personal lawyers, admitted to offering a $10bn investment in the US to resolve the criminal case. The federal judge overseeing the case determined the investment played no role in the DoJ’s decision to abandon the case.
“These fresh details continue to raise concerns about the judgment of the DoJ, and the extent to which the DoJ is willing and able to prosecute white-collar criminals under President Trump,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in a letter sent on Wednesday, and seen by the Guardian.
Adani was indicted in 2024 in New York for allegedly participating in a bribery and fraud scheme in which he paid Indian officials to secure a contract for one of his companies. He denied the allegations.
Prosecutors suddenly moved to dismiss the case against Adani in May after he hired a new legal team, led by Robert Giuffra Jr, and offered to invest $10bn into the US.
Following the news, Warren and Blumenthal sent a letter to Blanche in June requesting information about the fraud case and raising concerns about whether the justice department dismissed the case in exchange for Adani’s investment.
However, the senators did not receive a response. Since then, new details about the case have emerged, including allegations that Boris Epshteyn, a member of Trump’s personal legal team who also served as an informal adviser, helped Adani.
Another report claimed Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son, met with Adani in November 2025, before the case was dropped. A spokesperson for Trump Jr said earlier this year that the conversation “had zero to do with DoJ’s actions in this case”.
A spokesperson for Epshteyn denied being involved in Adani’s “arguments, advocacy or efforts” to the Wall Street Journal in June. Epshteyn was never hired by Adani or his company, the Adani Group, nor did he maintain a relationship with Adani, the spokesperson added.
The Guardian has asked Epshteyn for comment.
The Democratic lawmakers are now asking the DoJ for more information about Adani’s alleged investment offer, including a list of employees who were present when the offer was made, the terms of the offer, when the offer was made and where.
They also want to know whether the DoJ employees knew Epshteyn was allegedly working on behalf of Adani, or if Epshteyn had any contact with DoJ employees regarding Adani, among other questions.
“We are also concerned about the involvement of two of President Trump’s personal lawyers in this case, and the extent to which they reveal potential political influence and special treatment for well-connected insiders at the DoJ,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in their letter.
The Democrats also want to know if Trump Jr, or any person working on behalf of Trump Jr., had contact with a DoJ employee regarding Adani.
Warren and Blumenthal requested responses no later than 5 October. The Guardian has asked Blanche’s office for comment.

Bellamy bemoans new schedule after Denmark loss
- Published
Craig Bellamy suggested the new four-match international window had counted against Wales after Sunday's Nations League defeat against Denmark.
His side failed to build on Thursday's win over Norway as they were deservedly beaten thanks to a second-half Rasmus Hojlund penalty.
It was a third loss in four games played inside 10 days as part of the newly elongated international break.
Head coach Bellamy said his injury-hit squad paid the price for the heavy workload he feels benefits the bigger nations and "puts a real stress" on countries like Wales.
"Physically, I completely agree with the ones who don't like [the new window]. It makes no sense," he added.
"Four games at this type of level… for the other nations, we know who they are because I was in the room when they all voted for it.
"I was one of the ones who wasn't [voting for it], because we know it's a complete disadvantage to us."
Traditionally, international sides have played six games across three windows - all of which have featured two fixtures - in September, October and November.
But for the first time this year, the September and October breaks were merged.
Wales' hopes of coping with the new schedule were not helped by a string of injuries, with stars such as Karl Darlow, Joe Rodon, Dylan Lawlor and Harry Wilson missing the entire camp and David Brooks dropping out of the squad after defeat by Portugal in the opening game.
Bellamy said Dan James was not fit enough to play against Denmark after he was left on the bench at the Cardiff City Stadium, and acknowledged Ben Davies probably should have been rested after he was withdrawn late on.
"If we have a few injuries, which we had more than one or two, they miss four games," said Bellamy.
"We can deal with two, do you understand? And then the squad will get really tested. The intensity of the squad, the athleticism, really I think [the four-game break] is designed for the elites.
"[They can] say, we can go, we can go, we can turn over these games really, really quickly and we can change, we can change [the team] like for like because we have the numbers. So, it puts a real stress on a lot of us."
Ward did 'incredibly' to keep it level before penalty
Wales rarely looked like scoring against Denmark, who came close to breaking the deadlock on a couple of occasions before Hjolund's 75th-minute winner.
"On Thursday [against Norway] we were on the front foot so we're able to shorten distance," Bellamy added.
"Today, we just couldn't work it well enough, couldn't get the energy up enough to be able to have a bigger say in the game."
Danny Ward made fine saves from Hojlund and Gustav Isaksen to keep Wales level but it was the goalkeeper's error, and foul, which led to the penalty.
Bellamy, though, suggested the game had not swung on Ward's mistake, adding: "Obviously it's the decisive moment, but he made two incredible saves before that.
"I thought Denmark with the physicality were able to just crank it a little bit. You see their runs are really menacing, so I felt they were knocking on the door. He did incredibly well to keep it 0-0 to that time."
Despite defeat, Wales climbed to third in Nations League Group A4 courtesy of their head-to-head record against Norway after the Norwegians were beaten 2-1 in Portugal.
Wales play Norway in Oslo next month before completing the campaign with a home game against Portugal three days later.

Apple says it is changing its macOS privacy settings to stop third-party app developers from misusing them to access message histories.
Friday’s announcement comes two weeks after tech columnist Jason Aten said that Meta’s new general-purpose AI agent Muse sent him an unsolicited notification referencing a thread between him and a co-worker over Apple Messages. Aten said he never granted Muse permissions to read his messages and had assumed they were off-limits. Social media last week blew up with masses of people who agreed and said the incident showed that AI assistants given access to calendars, emails, messages, shopping accounts, and other resources are akin to a skill saw or other power tool. While potentially useful, they can do real damage if not used carefully.
He said/she said
Meta CTO David Singleton joined the fray with a rebuttal that appeared solid. For Muse to access Apple Messages, a user must manually give it two privileges. One is full-disk access, a macOS system-level permission. The other is to enable a Messages connector setting in Muse.
“The Messages integration in the Muse Mac app is opt in,” Singleton said. “Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled.”
Singleton’s implication was clear. Muse could have read Aten’s Messages communications only if he had enabled both settings, and if so, the columnist had only himself—and certainly not Meta—to blame.
Earlier this week, I spoke to macOS security expert Patrick Wardle, who questioned Singleton’s denial. His reasoning: “From a technical point of view, with FDA (full-disk access), any (non-root file), is readable, browsing history, browser cookies, chats, etc etc etc.” I asked Meta how Muse couldn’t read messages when the app had full disk access, while every other app with that privilege could. Meta PR’s only response was to requote Singleton saying: “The Messages integration in the Muse Mac App is opt-in. Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled.”

Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion – but he does not always feel like it.
This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.
But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.
While the other regional champions in the German fourth division were promoted to the nationwide 3. Liga, "Lok" faced a play-off against a representative of the Regional League Bavaria, Wurzburger Kickers. Ziane scored, but an injury-ravaged Leipzig lost 3-1 on aggregate.
"Euer System ist krank," read a simple protest banner displayed by the 2,000 travelling supporters – "your system is sick".
"It's the worst thing – injury aside – that you can experience as a footballer," Ziane tells BBC Sport.
"Catastrophe doesn't cut it. It doesn't make any sense. If they really wanted to change it, they could do tomorrow."
But it's not that simple.
Germany's football pyramid has a bottleneck.
Beneath the Bundesliga, 2. Bundesliga and 3. Liga, the fourth tier is split into five regional divisions (North, West, Southwest, Northeast and Bavaria), each of which produces a league champion.
So far, so good. But with only four teams being relegated from the 3. Liga each season, the sums don't add up.
An unsatisfactory solution is currently in place: the champions in the West and Southwest go up automatically while a third automatic promotion spot is rotated among the other three leagues in a three-year cycle. The fourth spot is allocated via a play-off between the winners of the remaining two leagues.
One champion always misses out and, increasingly, it's the champion from the Regional League Northeast, covering the territory of the former eastern German Democratic Republic (GDR).
In addition to Lok Leipzig's triple tragedy, former serial GDR Oberliga winners Dynamo Berlin fell short in 2022 and Energie Cottbus drew the short straw in 2023. This season, there is only one eastern German club in the 3. Liga: Hansa Rostock.
The struggles of the regions' football clubs are, to some degree, a result of continuing socio-economic disparities between east and west, which were also reflected in the success of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in recent state elections.
Even in 2026, not one of the 40 leading companies listed on Germany's DAX stock exchange is based in the former east (outside Berlin). Salaries remain lower, unemployment remains higher and the population is older and shrinking as young people move west.
The reason that automatic promotion spots are handed to the champions in the West and Southwest is simply because there are more men's football teams registered in those jurisdictions - because more people live there.
It is an argument that Ziane is tired of hearing.
"In that case, you might as well give us the automatic promotion spot because we attract bigger crowds," he says.
Indeed, the average attendance in the Regional League Northeast last season (3,125) was around twice as high as that in the other leagues. Lok Leipzig themselves had the fourth highest (6,352). More than 11,000 attended the local derby against city rivals Chemie Leipzig.
"Unfortunately, you don't get any points for tradition, crowds and history," says 39-year-old Lok chief executive Toni Wachsmuth, who does not have access to sponsors with the same financial firepower as his counterparts further west.
"The [western] leagues do have better economic foundations but everyone agrees that the current system is nonsense. Everyone needs to compromise but some officials are clearly putting their own interests and positions above the general good of German football."
It comes as little surprise, therefore, that the latest push for change has come from the east, with clubs launching a new campaign in March 2025 with the slogan: "Meister mussen aufsteigen!" – champions must go up!
Their proposal: a reduction from five leagues to four, with the precise geographical borders to be determined anew each season with the help of artificial intelligence, taking into account factors such as distance of travel to away games and attractive derbies.
They call it the compass model. Because it can go in all directions. In return, the Regional League Northeast is prepared to compromise by giving up its emotional attachment to the territory of the former East Germany.
"I want to get away from this east-west debate," says Tommy Haeder, the 35-year-old chief executive of Chemnitzer FC and figurehead of the reform campaign. "We've had a change of generation. Many older officials have retired and been replaced by younger people who don't have this nostalgia for the GDR."
Haeder also emphasises the benefits that a fairer promotion system would bring for German football as a whole, arguing that eastern clubs would be better equipped to continue nurturing youth talent.
"It's not in the interest of talent development when young footballers from Chemnitz are torn away from their homes and families at the age of 10 to join academies in Hamburg, Dortmund or Stuttgart," he tells BBC Sport.
"The compass model is a model in which every region sacrifices a little bit to solve a much bigger problem. We're organised, we have a plan, we've made suggestions. Now it's up to the federations to act."
The campaign has since gained the support of more than 80 clubs across Germany, from east to west and up and down the pyramid.
Union Berlin, who were playing in the fourth tier as recently as the 2000s, became the first Bundesliga club to officially back the initiative, with club president Dirk Zingler saying: "The current set-up contradicts our understanding of sporting competition."
Borussia Dortmund president – and Bundesliga chairman – Hans-Joachim Watzke added his influential voice, stating: "Champions must go up and we think the compass model with four regional leagues is the best option."
Support also has also come from Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose who, drawing on his past as both a player and coach at Lok Leipzig, said: "I know what it's like for clubs trying to work within their means, or lack of means, at that level. Everything is on a knife edge.
"You have to give the clubs and their fans the belief that their efforts and sacrifices will be rewarded with promotion."
Momentum was growing before a key vote at the end of June when, after months of discussions, clubs were finally set to vote on the compass model – but the ballot descended into farce when, at the last minute, the regional federations conducting the vote announced two key changes:
Suddenly, the four new leagues would consist of only 18 teams rather than 20 (thus making the compass model less attractive because 10 more teams would miss out), and a stipulation was added that a majority be reached in each of the five regions for the model to pass.
An overall majority (50.9%) in favour of the compass model was still reached (including 60.9% in the West, 61.5% in the North and 76.3% in the Northeast) but the Southwest voted for an alternative option in which the northeastern league would be dissolved and its clubs reallocated, while the Southwest and West would simply remain the same.
"The move from a functioning system to a complex, insecure and economically riskier model without an obvious benefit doesn't make any sense to me," Robert Lempka, chief executive of Regional League Southwest side FSV Frankfurt told local public broadcaster Hessischer Rundfunk this summer. "I find it unsettling that an untransparent algorithm should decide a club's future."
The Bavarians, meanwhile, voted vaguely for "further talks", with Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) President Christoph Kern telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper in August: "We've gathered our clubs together on several occasions and none of the suggested models have majority support. I'm not prepared to simply give up the Regional League Bavaria like that."
For Haeder in Chemnitz, the vote was "an absolute catastrophe – completely amateurish". And he's not alone.
This season, protests have erupted across German football. In the Regional League Northeast, almost every game has begun with a delay as players have simply refused to play for the first minute.
On the opening day, Lok Leipzig supporters, their team still stranded in the same division, threw hundreds of plastic trophies on to the pitch, symbolising the worthlessness of their club's back-to-back titles.
Down in Bavaria, Bayern Munich's ultras attended a reserve team game in the regional league and produced an intricate choreography criticising the Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) for what they perceive to be an unco-operative stance.
"You've taken us for fools long enough," read a banner beneath a display depicting BFV officials using a magnet to pull a compass needle towards them. The ultras then set off red pyrotechnics which turned the compass needle back in the direction of the fans.
And before the international break, fans of clubs across the Bundesliga used their platform to call for reform with co-ordinated banners reading: "Clubs and fans betrayed! Champions must go up! Compass model now!"
The compass, it would appear, may finally be pointing towards a resolution after the German Football Federation (DFB) announced the convening of an extraordinary general meeting on 18 December.
"[The issue] must be resolved," said President Bernd Neuendorf. "The compass model received the most votes and offers the best chance for a concentration of elite performance and therefore better development of talent."
Any changes would only be implemented in the 2028-29 season – too late for Ziane who, now 34, has embarked on his 13th season with Lok Leipzig. Back-to-back champions, but still in the fourth division.
"You can never completely get over it because, at our level, the 3. Liga is probably the pinnacle. Promotion with my hometown club would have been the most wonderful thing in the world for me," he says before heading out for training.
"It's a shame that we have to force ourselves to remember what we've achieved. It's so hard to win this league and we did it twice in a row! You can't take that for granted."
