Some 20 years ago, Mary-Claire King was asked to hold a seminar at the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm.
The invite, the geneticist soon learned, was code for: You are being considered for a Nobel Prize. She traveled to Sweden, held the seminar, then spoke about her work with interested experts who she later understood to be the prize committee.
She couldn’t have been too surprised: Her work has saved hundreds of thousands of lives, and changed cancer therapy.
In 1994 and 1995, King, then a professor at the University of California, Berkeley, showed that breast and ovarian cancer could be hereditary, and identified that mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes dramatically increased the risk of developing breast and ovarian cancer.
There is actionable power in this knowledge: Women who test positive for the mutations can have preventive mastectomies, or get their ovaries and fallopian tubes removed. Many have decided to do so, and preventive surgeries have reduced cancer mortality for thousands of women.
Naturally, when Nobel Prize predictions are made, King’s name is often on the list. Ahead of this year’s announcements, starting with the medicine and physiology prize on Monday, STAT spoke to her about what it feels like to be a finalist of sorts in the highest-profile intellectual competition in the world. Now 80 and at the University of Washington, she also talked about her work, her advice to young women scientists, and her favorite mantra — which she invented.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length.
So, the Nobel announcement is next week.
Oh, my God, it’s next week already. I can’t believe it.
Your name has been among the possible winners for many years. Do you have a routine? Do you set an alarm to check the winner?
I think if it were at any time other than truly the middle of the night, I might. But I’m on the Pacific Coast, so it is the middle of the night.
It’s not worth setting an alarm for 2 a.m. in the morning?
It’s not that it’s not worth it! It’s just that it’ll still be there, and the chances of any one year are extremely low.
Still, it’s hard to predict.
That’s true. The year that Katalin Karikó won [with Drew Weissman for work that led to the mRNA Covid vaccines], I think, was the most predictable. I mean, she saved the planet, it’s hard to argue that anything else could have surpassed that. It was the world’s largest experiment. But my guess would be GLP-1 this year.
It must be an interesting process. It’s certainly a tiny filter, and there’s a lot of stochastic features involved.
Do you remember the first time that you heard your name among the possible winners?
It was when they invited me to the Karolinska Institutet to give a seminar. They were very open about saying that they do this with people who are under consideration, and that anyone in this position should bear in mind that these things take years to sort through, and they just want to have the information and be able to talk to us personally.
I had a lovely time. I gave a seminar. I interviewed with what I’ve now recognized in retrospect are the members of the committee, and it was fine. There was no feedback.
That was the first time I realized that it was even a possibility.
What were the discussions like?
It varies a lot within the course of the visit. I think it’s largely about the personality of the individual and their belief in the work and their knowledge about the work. In my case, the individual discussions ranged from totally fascinating with someone who totally understood the work … and then another person who was very open about being skeptical about how genetics could possibly solve such a problem. He was extremely polite, absolutely delightful, and charming — but very skeptical.
In a way it’s like going for any other interview: You just have to be prepared for a variety of levels of skepticism and questioning. It was an interesting experience.
What does it feel like to know your work is so impactful that not only does it get noticed by the Nobel Committee, but becomes common knowledge?
I don’t think that scientists are necessarily aware of how important the positive impact that we have on other people is. It just boosts you. It just makes you feel so much stronger and so much more confident and so much more able to continue in rough patches, of which there are of course many.
It’s been a half-century now that I’ve been working on this, and I think when it comes up it’s more like a secret handshake. Thousands of women, or their husbands, fathers, brothers write to me for clarification, for information. It’s a huge network of women all over the world, multiple languages which I don’t speak, and we work together on this.
I got a letter a few years ago, which I’ll treasure forever, from a woman. It was a physical letter, just a note on a little piece of paper and with a photograph of her and her daughter. She said, “My mother died of breast cancer when I was 14. It was way before testing. I’ve since discovered I have a mutation in BRCA1. I’ve had the necessary surgeries. I have not had breast or ovarian cancer. As you see, my daughter just graduated from high school: I thought you’d like to know.” What can you say? I was in tears. I’m in tears telling you about it.
So that’s it, it’s a secret handshake, and we all know what it means, and we can help each other out.
You went into a line of work that didn’t have many women in it, and did work that benefited, first and foremost, women. You encouraged female scientists, and advocated for greater diversity in the field. What do you think of the state of women in research now?
An enormous amount has changed for the better. We are a far greater proportion of the research pool. We’re a far greater proportion of senior faculty. We’re a far greater proportion of policymakers in the health arena.
What hasn’t changed is that the time of a woman’s life when she has small children is the same as the time of her life when her career is getting off the ground, and until we accept that responsibility as a society and have structured high-quality subsidized childcare, it’s not gonna be equal. It’s simply not.
But over the years, generation after generation, what I tell younger women is that careers are long, and children grow up quickly. So it’ll be OK if you just do what you can now. But as one physician-scientist said to me, “All that’s true, but while they’re growing up, there’s a lot going on [in the lab].”
What is your advice for young scientists — perhaps women — looking to make a big discovery, something that can change the course of medicine, as you did?
What’s most important is picking problems that are important to you. That will, for many of us, be problems that are important to many people — but they have to be important to you, they have to involve ways of thinking and experiment approaches that appeal to you, that you like doing every day.
I think that’s the way to go because these things have a way of growing. What begins as a small problem becomes a larger problem and a larger problem and a larger problem, and if you still like it, and if it still seems plausible, stick with it and and accept the encouragement from people who care, both people who might be affected by it and, especially at the beginning, people that you see every day, that are right there in the lab with you.
When did you start realizing how major your discovery was going to be for medicine?
It was quite abrupt, because the whole time I was working on the problem, it was a 17-year period. I came out of evolutionary biology and genetics, and then when it was clear that that way of thinking applied just fine to proving that breast cancer was inherited, and furthermore there was a gene, and furthermore, here’s where it was — that was a huge creative leap. And as soon as that happened, all sorts of people who cared about breast cancer from a medical perspective as well as genetics realized its importance. And that’s when I did too.
You have done a lot of work since the BRCA discoveries. What is it like, emotionally and intellectually, to continue doing research after you’ve found something this big?
It’s something I think about a lot. One can apply the same way of thinking with new tools to problems that are as old as people but haven’t been tackleable before. My favorite mantra — which I confess to having invented — is, genetics is a way of thinking, genomics is a set of tools, so then problems that one can tackle are ever more challenging. The kinds of approaches that we can use now are just fabulous. We can ask genetic questions that we could not have asked even a decade ago, or three years ago.
And then, within the area of inherited predisposition to cancer, where do I see myself having a long-term niche? I think that’s in two ways. One is a kind of public-facing way. But the other is in what I’m really good at, which is figuring out how to use genetics in really tricky areas, and we still do that a lot.
When this [the BRCA discovery] clearly became a major issue in medicine, and far greater than I would have ever guessed, Bernie Fisher, who was the father of modern breast cancer treatment, said to me: “You’re not going to be able to control this. You need to, on the one hand, let it go, but on the other hand, be there for people when they have questions.”
What are you working on now in your lab?
I have a nice group, and we’re all all involved in all our projects. We’re working on de novo mutations in schizophrenia, we’re working on expanding repeats in bipolar disorder, we’re working on cryptic mutations, structural variations leading to inherited predisposition to breast and other cancers. We’re working on congenital abnormalities.
It’s a wide swath.

Finding information from the National Institutes of Health about human health, disease, and biomedical research is about to look a lot different. On Monday, the NIH will unveil a new version of its website that shifts attention away from individual institutes and centers and towards eight thematic hubs focused on health, research, data, clinical studies, rare diseases, technology, cancer, and grants.
Agency officials say the redesign — which is part of an ambitious project to consolidate the NIH’s digital footprint — is intended to streamline what was a sprawling and fractured information ecosystem, requiring users to understand the NIH’s organizational structure, into an intuitive experience that more closely reflects what type of information people seek out most often.
The goal, said Amanda Fine, NIH deputy director for public affairs, is “to make trusted NIH information across the agency easier and faster to find.”
The beta version, which was soft-launched this week, is still under development and will continue to evolve in the coming months, NIH officials told STAT. Some functions, including search, do not yet appear to be operational. During this transition period, NIH’s existing websites will remain available. They will be sunset on a rolling basis “as critical and mandated content is verified and redirects are put in place,” Fine told STAT.
Researchers who study science communication and science misinformation say the overhaul is a welcome development. “It was badly needed,”said Kathleen Hall Jamieson, a professor of communication and former director of the Annenberg Public Policy Center at the University of Pennsylvania. “Trying to find something on the old website required the skills of an Egyptologist.”
Over the past few decades, the NIH’s digital footprint had ballooned to include more than 700 separate websites — often with different, non-connecting backend architectures and hosting platforms — stretching across millions of webpages. Information was duplicated across five or six locations, sometimes appearing in slightly different configurations. Its potential for creating confusion became apparent during the Covid-19 pandemic, when the public turned to the NIH and other federal science agencies for guidance and information about the fast-moving public health crisis.
“It became a dramatic illustration of a dysfunctional website whose dysfunction wasn’t evident pre-Covid,” said Hall Jamieson.
Spurred by the pandemic, the NIH began to develop its first-ever five-year strategic communications plan in 2022 under President Biden. Working groups made up of more than 70 staffers from communications offices spread across NIH’s 27 institutes and centers came up with a plan to streamline the hundreds of NIH-owned websites to just one per institute. This massive undertaking was set to be phased over five years, starting in 2025.
That plan, which was never published but which was obtained by STAT, was scrapped when the Trump administration came in and fired hundreds of communications staffers as part of a government-wide reduction in the federal workforce. As a result of the layoffs and mass cancellation of contracts in early 2025, millions of NIH websites have been effectively frozen for nearly 18 months. That created a sense of urgency for the remaining dozen or so communications employees tasked with pushing forward website consolidation under the new administration.
Fine said her team worked to develop a data-driven process to better understand the path people take to NIH websites and how they navigated them once there. That helped them identify where people were getting stuck and the most highly sought after and frequently accessed information. The content on the new site is taken directly from health information from existing NIH websites, Fine said.
The consolidation, once complete, will reduce the number of NIH-owned websites from more than 700 to a single, fully connected web environment.

Son of Zambian bishop detained in post-election raid fears for his father's safety
The son of detained Zambian opposition politician Bishop Trevor Mwamba has told the BBC he is concerned for his father's safety after the former Bishop of Botswana was detained along with 10 other opposition figures by authorities.
Eno Mwamba said his father, who is leader of the United National Independence Party, has been charged with treason following President Hakainde Hichilema's disputed election victory.
The opposition politicians have been held since a raid by security forces on 14 August.
Opposition leader Brian Mundubile, head of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), had gone into hiding after disputing the election result, but has since also been detained by the authorities.
The government accuses the opposition of planning an armed insurgency and have charged the detained politicians with treason. They have denied the charges.

ICC will unseal warrants for 4 Taliban leaders wanted on gender persecution charges
The International Criminal Court says it is unsealing arrest warrants against four senior Taliban leaders on charges of crimes against humanity
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- The International Criminal Court said Monday it will unseal arrest warrants against four senior Taliban leaders, accusing them of the crime against humanity of gender persecution against women, girls and members of the LGBTQI+ community in Afghanistan since the Taliban seized power in 2021.
The court said in a statement that warrants were issued in July and September last year for the Taliban's supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, and the head of Afghanistan’s Supreme Court, Abdul Hakim Haqqani. Also wanted are Education Minister Habibullah Agha and Minister of Higher Education Neda Mohammad Nadim.
The existence of the warrants against Akhunzada and Haqqani was revealed last year, but the warrants remained sealed. With the Taliban in control of Afghanistan and the court having no police force to execute warrants, the prospect of any of the suspects being arrested is remote.
Since they took back control of the country, the Taliban have barred women from jobs, most public spaces and education beyond sixth grade. Last year, Akhundzada banned buildings from having windows looking into places where a woman might sit or stand.
The Associated Press approached the Taliban for a reaction to the court's announcement.
Former ICC chief prosecutor Karim Khan announced in January last year that he had requested warrants for Akhunzada and Haqqani, saying that his applications "recognize that Afghan women and girls as well as the LGBTQI+ community are facing an unprecedented, unconscionable and ongoing persecution by the Taliban.”
The four suspects are charged with persecution on gender grounds against “girls, women and other persons nonconforming with the Taliban’s policy on gender, gender identity or expression; and on political grounds against persons perceived as ‘allies of girls and women,'” the court said Monday. Full details of the unsealed warrants were not immediately released.
Judges who issued the warrants said that the four suspects, “acting on behalf of the Taliban,” implemented a government policy that “resulted in severe violations of fundamental rights and freedoms of the civilian population of Afghanistan, in connection with conducts of murder, imprisonment, torture, rape and enforced disappearance.”
The judges said that the Taliban “specifically targeted girls and women by reason of their gender, depriving them of fundamental rights and freedoms” including education, privacy and family life and the freedoms of movement, expression, thought, conscience and religion.
“In addition, other persons were targeted because certain expressions of sexuality and/or gender identity were regarded as inconsistent with the Taliban’s policy on gender,” the judges said.
Rights groups applauded last year when the court issued sealed warrants for the two senior Taliban leaders.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Uttar Pradesh state capital Lucknow is witnessing severe flooding after two decades as the water level of the Gomti River continues to rise. Landmark locations across the city, including Hanumant Dham, the Gomti Nagar riverfront, Prayag Sthal, and Faizullaganj, have been partially submerged. At Hanumant Dham, the temple domes, a ride, and nearby vehicles were inundated, prompting authorities to close the area for prayers. The Gomti Nagar riverfront has also been shut for visitors due to the alarming water levels. Lucknow Municipal Corporation Commissioner Gaurav Kumar stated that the civic body and district administration have deployed over 70 boats, set up temporary and permanent shelter homes, and organised medical camps. SDRF and NDRF teams have been mobilised to evacuate residents who are stranded, while food, medicines, and ration supplies are being delivered by boat to those choosing to remain on upper floors. A round-the-clock control room has been established to respond to distress calls within one to two hours.
Thousands of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf workers and supporters have launched a march towards Islamabad from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, demanding the release of former Prime Minister Imran Khan. The march follows the failure of government talks aimed at averting protests in the capital, prompting authorities to impose heavy security deployment and bar demonstrations. Imran Khan has been imprisoned since 2023 on charges spanning over a hundred cases, which his supporters describe as false and politically motivated. Family members have raised serious allegations regarding his health, alleging denial of medical care, custodial torture, and loss of vision in his right eye. Demonstrators insist the protests will continue unabated until Khan is released.
An India Today special report on 'India First' examines the foiled mid-air attack aboard Flydubai flight FZ1073 bound for Tel Aviv. Details from interrogation reports reveal that Omani co-pilot Fiam Al-Hammami planned a Nine Eleven-style attack targeting Ben Gurion International Airport or skyscrapers in Tel Aviv. UAE authorities have officially termed the incident an act of terror. The transcript features testimony from Captain Smith Machchhar, who recounted being struck from behind while the co-pilot was supposedly praying. Despite severe head injuries and blurred vision, Machchhar opened the cockpit door, allowing crew and passengers to overpower the attacker. Experts Wing Commander Sharad Panicker and Dr. Wael Awad analyze severe security oversight, questioning how Oman Air's prior derostering of Hammami for radical ideology was not flagged by Flydubai or Israeli intelligence. Aviation experts highlight transponder squawk codes and insider threat mitigation frameworks to prevent future cockpit hijackings.
Congress party student wing National Students' Union of India staged a symbolic demonstration on Raisina Road towards Jantar Mantar against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the Bharatiya Janata Party. Protesters lay down on the road portraying dead bodies to signify individuals allegedly deleted from voter rolls under the Special Intensive Revision drive. Demonstrators claimed names of thirteen crore voters were purged, accusing authorities of declaring living citizens as deceased. Protesting members demanded the immediate resignation and criminal proceedings against Gyanesh Kumar, also citing media reports regarding internal lack of consultation among election commissioners. Delhi Police and paramilitary personnel deployed multiple layers of barricading near Kerala House and Jantar Mantar to halt the student march.
Thousands of fish have died in the historic Banganga tank at Malabar Hill in Mumbai during Pitrupaksha rituals carried out since 26 September. The immersion of worship items and ritual offerings following Pind Daan Puja is suspected to have raised pollution levels in the water, depleting dissolved oxygen and causing large-scale fish deaths. A foul smell from the decaying fish prompted the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation to begin clearing dead fish, pumping out contaminated water, and removing pollutants. Additionally, the BMC D ward convened a meeting with local priests, Banganga Trust representatives, and residents to establish preventive measures against water pollution during Pitrupaksha.

India recorded 3,832 new leprosy cases among children in 2025-26, including 37 who had Grade-2 disability (G2D) at diagnosis — an indicator of delayed detection. The child caseload was 91.6% higher than the National Leprosy Eradication Programme's (NLEP) target of 2,000 cases for the year.
The figures, from the latest NLEP annual report for 2025-26, come even as India pursues the National Strategic Plan for Leprosy 2023-27, which seeks to interrupt transmission at the district level by 2027. Under the roadmap, a district is considered to have interrupted transmission after reporting zero new indigenous child cases for five consecutive years.
The NLEP's programme objectives include zero disability among new child cases and a national G2D rate of less than one case per million population. The roadmap projects 1,000 child cases and a G2D rate of 0.5 per million for 2026-27.
The appearance of children among newly detected cases matters beyond the absolute number. The World Health Organisation (WHO) considers new cases among children below 15 years an indicator of recent transmission, while G2D among newly detected patients indicates delayed diagnosis.
The WHO also says disabilities among newly detected child cases signal both delayed detection and ongoing transmission.
India recorded 63 children with G2D in 2019-20, followed by 35 in 2020-21, 41 in 2021-22, 55 in 2022-23 and 45 in 2023-24. The continued detection of children with G2D contrasts with the NLEP's objective of zero disability among new child cases.
The latest numbers therefore raise a fundamental epidemiological question: if India is working to interrupt transmission by 2027, why are children still developing leprosy, and why are some reaching diagnosis only after visible disability has appeared?
India detected 91,783 new leprosy cases in 2025-26, according to the Union Health Ministry. The prevalence rate was 0.56 per 10,000 population, and 1,945 patients had Grade-2 disability at diagnosis, accounting for 2.12% of all newly detected cases. The national G2D rate was 1.34 per million, above the NLEP's target of less than one case per million.
According to the WHO's latest global update, India reported the world's largest number of newly detected leprosy cases in 2025, with 91,783 cases, followed by Brazil with 22,901 and Indonesia with 16,292. Together, the three countries accounted for 78.3% of all new cases reported globally. The WHO notes that, although the update is for 2025, India reported data for April 2025 to March 2026.
India also reported the world's largest number of new child leprosy cases in the WHO's 2025 global update, with 3,832 cases.
The WHO figures and the NLEP figures refer to the same reporting period for India — April 2025 to March 2026 — although the WHO presents India's data in its 2025 global table. The WHO table records 3,832 child cases and 37 child cases with G2D for India.
Dr. Kabir Sardana, Professor and Head of Dermatology at ABVIMS-Dr. RML Hospital, Delhi, attributed the continuing burden partly to gaps in case detection.
"Data points to the fact that there is poor detection, which is why we are seeing more children with leprosy," he said.
The Health Ministry identifies high-endemic and hard-to-reach areas as priorities for intensified case detection. The NLEP emphasises active case detection, household contact surveys and focused campaigns, along with special plans for hard-to-reach areas. The programme also identifies stigma and discrimination as continuing concerns.
The WHO says prolonged, close contact with untreated cases allows transmission to continue, while the disease's long incubation period makes interruption difficult. New child cases are considered an indicator of recent transmission, although the presence of a child case cannot by itself establish when or where the infection occurred. The WHO notes that symptoms can appear years after infection.
Leprosy, or Hansen's disease, is a chronic bacterial infection caused mainly by Mycobacterium leprae. It primarily affects the skin and peripheral nerves. Transmission occurs mainly through prolonged, close contact with an untreated person. The disease is curable with multidrug therapy, a combination of antibiotics provided free through public-health programmes.
Children and household contacts are particularly important to surveillance because a new child case can indicate ongoing transmission within a community. However, the presence of a child case cannot by itself establish when or where the infection occurred. The average incubation period is about five years and can be considerably longer.
India's child caseload has fallen substantially from a decade ago, but the decline has not been linear. The country detected 11,365 children with leprosy in 2014-15, 11,389 in 2015-16 and 11,770 in 2016-17. The number fell to 10,287 in 2017-18, 9,227 in 2018-19 and 7,859 in 2019-20.
Child detections fell sharply during the COVID-19 period, reaching 3,753 in 2020-21, before rising to 4,107 in 2021-22. They fell again to 2,363 in 2022-23 and 2,335 in 2023-24, before rising to 3,832 in 2025-26. Changes in reported case numbers also reflect the intensity and reach of case detection, making it difficult to interpret the trend as a direct measure of transmission alone.
The Health Ministry has identified high-priority States and districts where the burden remains concentrated. Twenty-three districts in Chhattisgarh, 21 in Jharkhand, 18 each in Maharashtra and Odisha, and 10 in Madhya Pradesh had a prevalence rate above one case per 10,000 population, according to the Ministry.
These figures identify districts with prevalence above the elimination threshold; they should not be read as meaning that these are the only States or districts with continuing transmission.
For a disease that is curable, and for which early detection and treatment can prevent the progression to disability, the continued detection of children — including some already showing Grade-2 disability — highlights the tension between programme targets and what is still being detected in communities.

Making politics 'fun, trendy, sexy': How Gen Z could shape Kenya's next election
- Published
Ademba Allans is making it "cool" to vote in Kenya.
The student journalist turned civic mobiliser launched a voter registration drive on social media earlier this year, using snappy selfies infused with music and humour to target young people.
The result astonished him and many observers of Kenyan politics – by the time the registration period ended, 2.6 million new voters across the country had signed up. He is aiming to get another 2.3 million on board in the next round.
"It was the Gen Z way of doing politics," he tells me. "Fun, trendy, sexy, fashionable. Because of how we created the hype around it, people had the fear of missing out. Everybody wanted to be involved."
Gen Z, the term used to describe people born in the late 1990s and early 2000s, burst onto the scene two years ago with mass protests that forced the government to retreat on a widely unpopular tax bill. But their victory was followed by a police crackdown that killed and injured dozens of demonstrators.
Now many young Kenyans are planning to move from the street to the ballot box, angry with a political establishment they accuse of corruption and police brutality.
And they have the numbers to make a difference - more than 30% of voting-age Kenyans are younger than 35.
Polls suggest President William Ruto is looking vulnerable.
[The youth] just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created"
But can Gen Z convert a decentralized digital-led rebellion into organised political power?
"These youth-led movements are a wild card, in that they are unpredictable," says political analyst Tom Mboya.
"They don't require much in the way of resources and can pop up at any time. The finance bill protests were political in nature, but the movement has not been tested at an overtly political level. So if they decide to support a candidate, then he's likely to do fairly well."
One of the strengths of the digitally savvy Gen Z activists is that they have been able to mobilise outside the party structures and ethnic allegiances that anchor Kenyan politics.
Allans has been careful not to advocate a particular candidate or party – emphasising leadership rather than politicians, marshalling a new force, he says, outside traditional tribal voting blocs.
"There has never been a case where there is a bloc that is not affiliated to any person or any party. They just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created," he says.
"It's more of a swing vote because you cannot tell who we are going to vote for."
Ruto and his United Democratic Alliance (UDA) are facing strong head winds with less than a year to go before the August 2027 vote.
More than three-quarters of respondents to a survey conducted in June felt the country was moving in the wrong direction, with two-thirds saying their personal economic situation had worsened since Ruto was elected in 2022.
But analysts argue that the president does not necessarily have to be popular to win. He is a master political organiser with the resources of the state, they say.
Ruto's political rivals are also fragmented, and it is not yet clear whether they can form a united opposition to take him on.
One man who has captured the attention of many Gen Zs is Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has emerged as the leader of a movement called Linda Mwananchi (Protect the Citizen), which is getting strong support from disaffected young people.
Sifuna first caught their attention when he tried to stop police from shooting at protesters who were storming parliament during the 2024 demonstrations.

Now he is championing a "people-led" movement that promotes the protection of human rights and rule of law as enshrined in the constitution.
He has yet to officially declare a run for the presidency, but is already on the road rallying support. The BBC caught up with him on a recent trip to Meru county in central Kenya, a region that voted strongly for Ruto in the last election.
"Young people want us to create an environment where everybody feels that they can compete fairly," he told me before starting out on his raucous road show.
"We need to absolutely dismantle the system so that everybody has a fair chance at life, a fair chance at education, a fair chance at employment, and the opportunities to grow themselves.
"This election in 2027 is when this theory that the young people are advancing will be put to the test," he said. "Our challenge as a leadership is to ensure you have a compelling message that then encourages people to come out, let them see the vision for the new country."
Ruto also had a compelling vision for the country when he came to power in 2022.
He promised to transform the economy from the bottom up, with a focus on lifting the marginalised. His government has since introduced changes including landmark reforms that widen access to public healthcare, but many young people felt betrayed by his austerity measures and tax hikes.
"I'm here to participate in a revolution change that we want a new Kenyan youth leader who knows the common problems that are facing the young people," 23-year-old Brandon Muremi told the BBC.
I found him in a relatively quiet corner of the final stop in a hectic day of a "rolling rally" – Sifuna's convoy visited four locations, sometimes blocking traffic as he and local politicians climbed on top of their vehicles and delivered rousing speeches at ear-splitting volumes.
They promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths"
"We are looking for a leader who sticks to his plans, not just talking the promises that he makes," agreed Conrad Mutangili, a 19-year-old mechanical engineering student who had come out of curiosity.
"We are looking for somebody who can actually accomplish and actually bring to the people what they are talking about," he said. "Because they promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths."
"We want immediate results," said a 22-year-old computer science student, Yvonne Kileme, acknowledging that the results of government projects may be more long-term. "And one thing that we want as youths is employment, employment, employment, employment."
Ruto argues strongly that his government is delivering jobs, and says the high rate of youth unemployment is a problem that predates his presidency.
He has reached out to Gen Z with various programmes that offer grants and loans to small business and youth-led enterprises, technology hubs and digital work opportunities.
The national youth leader of Ruto's UDA, Kariuki Ngunjiri, told the BBC he was confident of winning the election with an overwhelming majority.
"The president is a listening president and he's been able to now come down to the youth, get what their concerns are, give them jobs, and that has absolutely, even for the party, given us a head start," he said.
"We are not worried about the social media buzz because we are people who actually engage the young people on real, actual, tangible development. What you see mostly on sponsored hashtags and sponsored headlines does not really concern us."
He was speaking as a senior sports official promised to expand the stadium-building programme with another venue, at a packed UDA town hall meeting in Kangema, about 100km (60 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi.
Like so many others, 23-year-old Shintah Mutahi was job hunting.
"I came to listen to what they were saying," she said, "maybe find an opportunity for a job. I think they can give me a chance, they should just be given some time to do that."
John Kiragu, a local UDA youth leader, said he understood the grievances that had driven young people to protest.
"There have been challenges," he said, "but now the government is really trying hard to consolidate the youth. The government is implementing programmes that will really uplift their lives."
Kiragu told me he was involved in a programme to deal with youth alcoholism – a real problem in this region. Many of the young men who attended the morning town hall meeting were already drunk on a cheap local liquor.
The captain of the local football team, Calvin Ware, also turned up to hear the stadium announcement. He said he had heard similar promises many times before, especially before elections, and this one was not going to influence his vote.
"We have already made our mind," he said. "The whole government should go home. We want to build a new Kenya, new youth, new people, fresh people from all over the country, and we are not basing on tribal [allegiances] or anything else. We just want a change, a change, and a change. Nothing else."
As we were speaking, we heard a loud cheer – the event had ended and people were lining up to receive cash handouts – 350 Kenyan shillings, about $3 (£2.20).
It is common practice to pay people to attend political meetings in Kenya, and politicians can use much larger sums to try and influence votes.
"More so than many other parts of the world, money talks in an election here," says political analyst Mboya. "The cost of politics is significantly higher than in other parts of the world."
Less than a year to Kenya's election, it does feel like politics might be changing, that the race could be shaped by youth disillusionment with the political establishment. But while the Gen Z movement has rejected the "old politics" based on ethnic group and money, those have been the building blocks that win elections in Kenya.
Nobody yet knows what the energy of Gen Z voters will mean at the ballot box.

When I started collecting physical media in 2009 at 13 years old, CDs still dominated the market. Big-box retail stores had music sections with rows and rows of sealed jewel cases, and it was normal to spend $25 on a deluxe album or a box set.
Less than a decade later, streaming had taken over. Vinyl records outsold CDs for the first time in 2022. The Compact Disc began to feel like an afterthought.
But now the CD is enjoying a surge in popularity thanks to cultural shifts like the rise in K-pop, the backlash against the streaming platforms’ policies, and Gen-Zers driving hand-me-down cars without Bluetooth connectivity. When I walked into a record store in July and found a deluxe CD for Madonna’s new album, Confessions II, on sale for $34, more expensive than some of the vinyl pressings, it finally felt like the format was officially back. (And yes, I bought it.)
According to 2026 data from the entertainment industry research firm Luminate, K-pop groups like BTS, Enhypen, and ATEEZ contributed to an overall 16 percent increase in CD sales so far this year, thanks to collectible editions that encouraged fans to buy multiple copies of the groups’ albums. This seems to be the major shift between the old way of buying music and the new normal: CDs are looked at more as merch—collectibles that support the artist—than as necessities to hear the songs. According to the same Luminate report, if K-pop were taken out of the data, disc sales would’ve still increased 6.7 percent.
Though the numbers show solid growth, CDs are nowhere near as hot as they used to be. The music industry sold 16.3 million discs in the first half of this year, a paltry number compared to the CD’s heyday around the turn of the millennium, when annual sales topped 900 million. Still, their collectible physicality has brought them back into fashion.
There really is no right or wrong way to collect CDs. If you keep a CD in its packaging, it will be protected for years to come. But here are some tips if you want to elevate your collecting experience and get more out of your collection, whether you’re new to the format or rescuing an old box of discs from the garage.
Get a CD Player
It might seem that owning a CD player is the obvious first step to collecting CDs. But according to Luminate’s report, only half of millennials and Gen-Zers that collect CDs have a player. Luckily, finding a good CD player is easier and more budget-friendly than buying a record player.
You might even have a CD player without knowing it; a Blu-ray player hooked up to a nice sound bar is a convenient set up to play CDs, since most Blu-ray and DVD players can handle audio discs. Even your Xbox can play them, though the disc drives on Sony PlayStation 4 and 5 consoles weirdly cannot play CDs.
If you need a CD player, the first thing to consider is what kind you want. A personal portable player lets you take your music anywhere. If your record player setup includes a stereo receiver, chances are it has a CD input that you can use to hook up a hi-fi player for at-home listening. This will give you the best audio from your discs. These component players can still be found at big-box retail stores or online music shops like Turntable Lab or RETROSPEKT that specialize in hi-fi systems.
Del Bravo Record Shop, one of the oldest record stores in Texas, has seen an increase in demand for personal CD players that it ships out of its San Antonio store. “They’ve been flying off the shelves,” says Jessica Campa, Del Bravo’s sales associate and social media manager. “We’ve also had about a 12.6 percent increase in CD sales so far this year.”
Bluetooth CD Players are the latest advancement; they let you connect wireless headphones or speakers. If you love the hunt, a thrift store or flea market can be a great place to find a CD player at a great price. Just be sure to test that it works before paying for it. Record stores sometimes keep a variety of used or new CD players as well, depending on their specialty.
The Record Store Is Still Your Friend
Independent record stores are the go-to place to get exclusive vinyl, and many of them still carry CDs. While online shops like Amazon seem like a convenient way to buy these small discs, record stores often receive promotional goodies like posters or stickers that they throw in for free along with your purchase. Oftentimes indie stores will get autographed albums during an artist’s release week to encourage shoppers to come into the store to buy the disc. These are often sold at the regular retail price and not up-charged.
Of course, record stores are great places to buy used discs, and most of the time, the discs are inspected by the staff and you can expect them to play properly and without skips. Stores sometimes even have listening stations so you can preview the used discs.
Track Your Collection
Knowing what music you already have is a great way to prevent accidentally acquiring doubles when you’re out shopping. Thankfully, you don’t need to rely on an Excel spreadsheet. Discogs, an online marketplace and music database for collectors, is well known among vinyl aficionados, but it’s just as helpful as a tool to keep track of your CDs. Not only does the free mobile app feature a barcode scanner that will show you the exact pressing of a CD, it will also show you the current market value of it, in case you come across a rare find in the wild or something that could be overpriced. You can also look up different versions of a CD to find that rare version, like the Japanese pressing with the extra tracks. Discogs will show you a list of the users who own that particular disc who’d be willing to sell it to you for a fair offer.
Inspect Thrifted and Stored CDs
Found that box of old CDs in the garage? Scored a 75-cent copy of Santana’s Abraxas at the thrift store? Be sure to not only check if the disc is actually in the case, but inspect the bottom of the disc—CDs are read by a laser that moves underneath the disc as it spins—for any scratches, discoloration, or spots, which could be a sign of disc rot.
Disc rot is exactly what it sounds like, the deterioration of the reflective layer where a CD’s music data is stored. Sometimes it’s caused by manufacturing defects, but usually it’s the result of improper storage. Over time, heat and humidity can turn these once seemingly indestructible pieces of media into unplayable garbage.
You can score some great finds when thrifting for CDs, but you never know the conditions the discs were stored in before they hit the discount shelf, so learn to spot the most common problems and be discerning. You may even want to bring a portable player with you when you shop so you can test your finds—with the seller’s consent, of course.
Invest in Proper Storage
Similar to a vinyl record, the best way to store a CD is vertically, in its original sleeve, jewel case, or digipack. Any solid shelf makes a good home, but used furniture stores or Goodwill shops will often also have dedicated CD shelving, made of wood or metal, specially designed to fit rows of jewel cases.
About those jewel cases: If they’re damaged or missing pieces, they don’t do as good a job protecting the CDs or artwork inside from spills or scratches. Go the extra step and invest in replacements for cracked jewel cases or damaged interior spindle trays.
If you listen on the move and like to take your discs in the car, a classic CD wallet or CD book is your best solution. You load your disks into the wallet’s plastic pouches and store the jewel case and the artwork somewhere safe, either on the shelf or in a box.
The demand for these nostalgic book-style cases has only increased over the years. “We stocked some recently,” says Steven Alejandro, who has been the general manager at Hogwild Records for over 30 years. “And then the supplier ran out, and now they don’t have any more to sell.”
If you’re lucky to find a case, or you’ve repurposed your parents’ old CD wallets, remember not to leave the case in a hot car, in the sun, or anywhere near a heat source for an extended time.
Keep Your CDs and CD Players Clean
The best way to maintain a physical media collection is to keep everything clean. Found your dream player at a garage sale? Chances are it hasn’t been properly maintained in 20 years. CD players do need to be cleaned every once in a while to ensure the laser lens is free of any debris or fingerprints that can impact playback and audio quality.
On the actual disc, fingerprints, dust, and anything else stuck to the bottom surface can cause audible skips during playback. It's best to use a microfiber cloth and, if necessary, a cleaning solution for extremely dirty CDs. Don’t wipe the disc in a circular motion. Always wipe the disc from the center outward, starting at the hole and pulling the cloth gently toward the outer edge of the disc.
Final Tip
Enjoy your CDs! Rip the contents to your hard drive if you need to, but they sound great when you just give them a spin. There’s a joy in collecting music, because while online streams may be temporary, the physical media we have will always be something we truly own and the actual definition of on-demand.

On 02 October 2026, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) held a protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park demanding accountability from the Election Commission of India (ECI) and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Protesters raised concerns over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, alleged voter deletions, and transparency in the electoral process. Despite Mumbai Police denying permission for the gathering, thousands attended the protest and raised slogans. Police later registered an FIR against the organisers and 400–500 unidentified participants for allegedly violating restrictions on the assembly (here, here, and here).
In this context, two videos are circulating on social media (here, here, and here) claiming to show the CJP protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai. Let’s verify the truth behind these videos in this article.
Claim: The videos show the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai on 02 October 2026.
Fact: The videos do not show the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest at Shivaji Park on 02 October 2026. The first video was recorded at CJP’s protest at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, while the second video shows the Tiranga Vijay Rally jointly organised by Shiv Sena (UBT) and Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) at Shivaji Park on 26 July 2026 . Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
Upon closely reviewing the viral videos, we noticed ‘Delhi Police’ written on the barricades. This indicates that the videos were recorded in Delhi, not Mumbai, as claimed in the viral posts.
We then conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to the same video uploaded on the Facebook page ‘Indian Sawarn Samaj News’ on 08 August 2026. The video was uploaded with a caption stating that it shows a CJP protest in Delhi demanding the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan. This confirms that the viral video predates the CJP protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai on 02 October 2026.
We also geolocated the high-rise building visible in the viral video to Jai Singh Marg, Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, Delhi. A comparison of the building in the viral video with its appearance on Google Maps Street View can be seen below.
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) began its protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 06 June 2026, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged irregularities in NEET-UG 2026. The protest continued for several weeks and was called off on 25 July 2026 following Pradhan’s resignation and government assurances on some of the protesters’ demands.
Video 2
We conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to the same video uploaded on the Facebook page ‘Mumbai Explore’ on 26 July 2026. The caption states that Dadar celebrated a memorable victory with grand celebrations. This confirms that the viral video predates the CJP protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai on 02 October 2026.
According to reports, the Tiranga Vijay Rally was held at Shivaji Park on 26 July 2026, one day after Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned. It was jointly organised by Shiv Sena (UBT) and Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS), led by Uddhav Thackeray and Raj Thackeray. The rally was originally planned as a Tiranga Morcha demanding Pradhan’s resignation, but after his resignation on 25 July 2026, it was turned into a victory gathering celebrating the student movement. Thousands of people attended, carrying the national flag and posters (here, here, and here).
We found multiple posts (here, here, and here) on the official Shiv Sena (UBT) social media handle featuring the rally. The stage, banners and other visual elements seen in these posts match those visible in the viral video, confirming that the viral video shows the Tiranga Vijay Rally held at Shivaji Park in July 2026, not the CJP protest held there on 02 October 2026.
To sum up, none of these viral videos shows the CJP protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park on 02 October 2026.

Hurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region of Mexico, the latest system in a Pacific hurricane season that has been notably active in recent months. On 22 September, a measurement of 892 millibars was registered for Hurricane Polo, making it the second-most intense hurricane on record in the east Pacific. It is fuelled by exceptionally warm waters across the Pacific Ocean, providing favourable conditions for the system to maintain its considerable strength.
Polo is expected to turn towards the west-north-west, before taking a more north-westerly trajectory on Saturday. It has maximum sustained winds of around 150mph, with even stronger gusts occurring within the most intense parts of the hurricane. Hurricane-force winds extend outward for approximately 40 miles from the centre, while tropical storm-force winds reach as far as 125 miles. These powerful winds, combined with torrential rainfall and dangerous seas, could have significant impacts. Although some fluctuations in intensity are possible over the coming days, Polo is expected to remain powerful as it tracks north-westwards.
In India, a deep 988-millibar low-pressure system – a tropical storm in this case – is centred along the east coast, bringing widespread and potentially disruptive weather conditions to Odisha and surrounding areas. The system is producing heavy rainfall across the region, with the latest forecast models suggesting totals could exceed 200mm in some locations over a 24-hour period. Rainfall rates are expected to be particularly intense at times, with hourly totals potentially exceeding 30mm in the heaviest downpours. Such intense rainfall could cause significant surface water and localised flooding, particularly in low-lying areas and places with poor drainage. Strong and gusty winds are also affecting coastal parts of Odisha. Winds are forecast to reach around 50-60mph, creating hazardous conditions in exposed areas and potentially causing disruption to travel, infrastructure and power supplies. Authorities have closed numerous schools across the affected districts for safety reasons.
Meanwhile, in Iberia, the relentless heat of summer is extending into meteorological autumn, with temperatures rising into the high 30s celsius on 23 September. Alvega, in Portugal, recorded a maximum temperature of 41.7C, smashing many July records from previous decades.

A popular national footwear brand recently published a collaborative Instagram post with a fraternity, despite two former members being recently accused of disseminating nonconsensual intimate images of a fellow college student.
On September 25, HEYDUDE, a viral shoe brand that was acquired by Crocs in 2022, posted a photo on its Instagram account promoting shoes that appeared to be UF versions of the brand’s popular “Wally” loafer, a lightweight slip-on sneaker with a foam insert.
“@heydude called, @thetachiflorida answered,” the caption read, alongside photos of Theta Chi members clowning around and wearing orange-and-blue sneakers. The brand also posted a video on its TikTok account outside of the Florida fraternity house with the caption “wtf is any shoe besides a HEYDUDE?”
The post led to backlash in the comments section, with many questioning why the brand would choose to work with the fraternity. “#CancelHeyDude,” one person wrote. Another chimed in: “I would boycott if I wore fucking ugly shoes but I don’t so I can’t.”
As WIRED previously reported, two former members of the UF chapter of Theta Chi, Kamran Ahmed and Brendan Pitfield, allegedly used anonymous burner accounts with the handles "Steve 'SC’ Cumfull" and "Arnie_Grape16" to disseminate a nonconsensual intimate video of Maddie Kowalski, then a 19-year-old UF student. One of the "Steve 'SC' Cumfull" posts on X identified Kowalski by her full name and sorority affiliation.
According to affidavits from the Gainesville Police Department, the posts accumulated thousands of views. Kowalski’s name went viral on X, causing her “widespread public humiliation and significant emotional distress,” according to the affidavit. Ahmed and Pitfield are currently being charged with sexual cyberharassment, a first-degree misdemeanor punishable by up to a year in jail and a $1,000 fine. Kowalski is also suing both men for financial damages in Florida Northern District Court. Through their attorneys, Pitfield (who has entered a plea of not guilty) and Ahmed did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Though no other Theta Chi members have been charged, a screengrab of Instagram comments from an account linked to Ahmed appears to show fellow members referencing his alleged burner name. Some comments also appear to reference a cryptocurrency in Kowalski’s name, that the police affidavit alleges Ahmed promoted on X. When reached for comment, Theta Chi CEO Michael Mayer previously told WIRED that the alleged behavior described in the affidavit is “reprehensible” and “completely contrary to Theta Chi’s ideals.”
The charges against Pitfield and Ahmed, as well as WIRED’s reporting on the case, sparked an outcry on the UF campus. On September 15, a group of students advertised a protest outside the Theta Chi fraternity house, circulating a flier demanding that the chapter be removed from the UF campus. “They need to be held accountable,” the flier reads.
On YikYak, the anonymous campus forum, there have also been calls to “boycott” or “nuke” Theta Chi, according to screengrabs reviewed by WIRED. Some anonymous YikYak posts appeared to suggest that the September 15 protest was broken up by campus police outside of Theta Chi: “Cops nuked the theta chi protest good job UF,” one reads. “Typical.” Blake Trauschke, the assistant director of public affairs for UF, tells WIRED that while “there were calls and social media posts for a protest,” she was on site and “none emerged.” She clarified that, as standard UF practice, university police were present “to ensure the safety and security of all.”
Founded in 1856, Theta Chi has established more than 246 chapters at colleges and universities across the country, and it has more than 250,000 initiated members nationwide, according to the organization’s website. At UF specifically, Theta Chi has 190 active members, according to the UF Interfraternity Council.
When asked about the post with HEYDUDE, a representative for Theta Chi tells WIRED Ahmed and Pitfield are no longer members of Theta Chi Fraternity. “If it is determined through the legal process that the defendants are guilty of the alleged behavior described in the complaints, Theta Chi will support the maximum allowable penalty under the law and the permanent expulsion of the student offenders from the University of Florida,” the spokesperson says.
In mid-September, the Cornell Sun published the names of seven Cornell University students who a former student alleged gang-raped her in 2024 at a Chi Phi frat house; In September, the Jane Doe filed civil cases against them. The revelation has sparked widespread criticism of frat culture on social media. The content creator and activist @bluraybeyond, who has also posted about the Kowalski case, made a Reel calling out HEYDUDE for posting with UF Theta Chi, writing in a caption “@heydude what the actual heck is your problem #maddiekowalski.” “HEYDUDE is sending the same message we're seeing out of Cornell and the DA's office: Survivor experiences [are] unimportant to us,” she tells WIRED. She believes the company “has chosen to reward sexual [exploitation] with a lack of accountability and free PR swag.”
After seeing the collab post with HEYDUDE, Kowalski tells WIRED she and her mother emailed the company to ask why they had decided to work with the UF chapter. She says they did not hear back.
In a statement to WIRED, a HEYDUDE spokesperson says the company “has no affiliation, sponsorship, or ongoing partnership” with UF Theta Chi, and that the post was part of a larger “HEYDUDE Tailgate Tour” visiting various locations, including frat and sorority houses, across the country.
“We were unaware of the allegations made against” members of the UF Theta Chi chapter “when the tour was planned,” the spokesperson says. “Our company does not support this alleged behavior and takes allegations such as these very seriously. We will re-evaluate future stops for the remainder of the tour.”
As of Friday morning, the post was still up.

Poor diet, sedentary habits, and prolonged screen use are contributing to metabolic disorders among young people at increasingly younger ages, said Challa Suresh, Scientist ‘G’ and Director Grade, Head of the Cell Biology Division, AcSIR Coordinator at the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition, at an oration organised by Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education and Research recently.
Delivering the Prof. S.P. Thyagarajan Endowment Oration on ‘The Modern Lifestyle Paradox: Why are Young People Developing Metabolic Disorder Earlier?’, Prof. Suresh stressed the importance of nutritious food and healthier lifestyle habits in preventing lifestyle-related illnesses.
He advised young people to choose wholesome, nutrient-rich foods, and limit processed and packaged foods, which he linked to rising obesity. He also called for reducing screen time, noting that prolonged use of digital devices encourage sedentary behaviour and affect memory and overall well-being.
The event was attended by university officials, academicians, clinicians, researchers, and students.

A decade ago, actor Deepika Padukone said in an ad campaign: ‘My body, My choice.’ But, in reality, when it comes to older people, society often wrests that agency from them. Last week, as the world observed both International Day of Older Persons (October 1) and Gandhi Jayanti (October 2), Mumbai-based Sumira Roy’s documentary film Bhangaar (Obsolete), raised the question of dignity in death and the right to die for the elderly.
The yet-to-release Marathi film, which won the National Film Award for Best Non-Feature Film last month, was screened by the Kriti Film Club in Delhi NCR.
Bhangaar trains the lens on Narayan and Iravati Lavate, an octogenarian Maharashtrian childless couple, who petitioned for active euthanasia in 2018. Iravati succumbed to cancer in 2023, Narayan lives in an old-age home. His eyesight and memory, too, have deserted him. After the news of the National Award came in, Roy wanted to share the moment with Narayan. She rang up Prakash Joshi, the brother of Iravati, who also appears in the film. Joshi told her that due to Narayan’s present old-age health and impediments there of, nothing would register with man.
While Nilesh Maniyar and Shonali Bose’s documentary A Fly on the Wall (2024) is also on the same subject and travels with Chika Kapadia to Switzerland for his last days, Roy’s documentary shows how only privilege can afford that right.
Monisha Advani, Bhangaar’s producer and partner, Emmay Entertainment, calls the film personal, “My late mother was a Maharashtrian and while growing up, the frugality of my maternal grandparents’ lives somewhere was mirrored in the Lavates. Sumira has given me the opportunity, in a private way, to pay tribute to my familial pedagogy."
Excerpts from an interview with director Roy:
You are from an advertising background; how, when and why did you transition into filmmaking and documentary films at that?
Since I’ve been a student, I’ve been passionate about films and documentary films and had even sat for the FTII entrance examination. But the women in my family were against me going to Pune and feared the casting couch in the film industry. Years later, when I went to Japan for work, I did a postgraduate course in Japanese cinema, theatre and painting. I was just hooked on when I saw [films by Yasujirō] Ozu and all the greats there. So, I thought, there’s a roundabout way to do films through advertising films. There’s a great amount of discipline in ad films; you shoot minimally and you have only 30-40 seconds to tell your story. Ad films [at Ogilvy and JWT] also gave me a lot of exposure to a lot of things that you need in documentaries. For instance, understanding human behaviour. And then, in documentaries, I learnt how to listen… to people’s stories. I went on foreign location shoots and for post-production. All that’s helped me now. In 2011, I left advertising and started two agencies, mainly for production. I was a little bit jaded and cynical, trying to do these falsehoods to make people buy things they didn’t need.
Did the Central Board of Film Certification raise any objections in Bhangaar?
Only to the title. The censor board didn’t like the word bhangaar [obsolete] and called it insulting. I had to keep going back to explain to them that the word is what Narayan uses [in life and in the film]. It’s his, not mine. After some time, they agreed but asked me to carry a disclaimer in Marathi at the start of the film that this is the character’s interpretation of the title. That was fine by me.
There seems to be a thematic continuity between your documentaries Last DaysLast Shot (2017) and Bhangaar. Tell us about the earlier film.
I have an idea, and then I make a film. I don’t just go and make documentaries, because I’m not an activist or an investigative filmmaker. As Narayan says in the film [Bhangaar], the day you’re born is the beginning of death. He echoes the Myth of Sisyphus when he says there’s no purpose to life; it’s absurd. I am drawn to existentialism, and like diving into the interior of minds.
For my earlier film, I was interested in exploring the philosophy of moksha and nirvana. I went to Banaras [Hindu] University, and walked around in the gullies and ghats. People would pop out from the woods to say, ‘Come listen to my poem.’ There, I found a Bengali poet-artist who had gone to Japan and become famous. He returned to Varanasi with his Japanese wife [they ran the Kumiko Guest House]. By the time I shot him, he looked like Rabindranath Tagore. He was about 80 or 81. He told me his idea of moksha: to dissolve the ego. Then I met a 26-year-old Dom in Harishchandra Ghat cremation ground, who [told me he] hardly got a chance to light the fire, and couldn’t make money with it. So, he bought a camera and started shooting the relatives of the dead. He said from his experience that a good person’s corpse burns faster than a sinner’s.
What drew you to Iravati and Narayan Lavate’s story?
It’s a personal reason. My long-widowed mother was quite active in life. She’d drive, have a social life, her body and mind intact. A year before she passed away, she started saying, ‘I want to die with dignity.’ I was a documentary filmmaker, but I never listened to her nor asked her what she meant. I was petrified of her dying. [After] she passed away, I was stricken with grief and regret. I came across the Lavates’ story in Mid-Day; they asked for the right to die together with dignity. That struck me, and I went to meet them in their 12x12 room in a Mumbai chawl, to get closure for what I hadn’t done with my mother. They taught me so much about Marathi literature and theatre. Narayan looked like Picasso to me. He knew the Constitution by heart. I asked, how could they want to die. He said, ‘It’s time to go.’
They had this fixed spiel they would rattle to the media/news channels. They would do the same during our initial days of shoot. I just told them not to look at the camera and go about their days. I had to be a fly on the wall and filmed them over four years. Afterwards, they forgot there’s a camera. My DOP is brilliant because it was a boot camp for her, with no lights, no space to set up the camera. The aerial shot of them playing cards was shot from atop a washing machine.
In India, the elderly population is growing rapidly even as the birth rate declines. What did your research throw up about ageing and caregiving?
The elderly are growing three times faster than the population of the youth. Palliative care exists only for the rich. There’s no geriatric care and no focus on what is going to happen to the elderly population. All of us are in some stage of caregiving. We are either watching our parents or grandparents.
Gandhi spoke of self-rule. Swaraj is not just political self-rule but also the rule/autonomy over oneself. Does that idea of self-determination versus duty get complicated when it comes to an older person’s choice to die?
Loss of personhood and loss of autonomy, which older people fear, is exactly why they [Irawati and Narayan] asked for it [active euthanasia]. We do not connect with our families. Our conversations revolve around whether they have taken their medicines, if the oxygen tank is running low, if the nurse administered the injection. That’s our only conversation with them. The elderly feel like they are [outdated] machines. We have moved away from joint families to nuclear families. As a society, we have forgotten how to respect someone who has lived longer than expected. We keep talking about Gen Z and loneliness, but loneliness is far worse among the older generations. We hardly talk about it. Even our films don’t.
We’ve read about the Aruna Shanbaug case. This year, the Supreme Court gave its landmark judgment permitting passive euthanasia for Harish Rana who was in a vegetative state for over 13 years. What has been the impact of the Lavates’ petition?
Narayan and Iravati are the pioneers of this, at least in our country, or in South Asia. The courts are getting more and more petitions since. The press doesn’t cover many of these.
Bhangaar (Obsolete) screens on October 1 at the India Habitat Centre, Delhi, and on October 4 at Museo Camera, Gurugram at 4.30 pm.
