Each rare disease affects very few people. However, there are around 8,000 rare diseases, and they cumulatively affect hundreds of millions of people. In India, 1,004 rare genetic disorders have been reported so far.
It used to be that because the number of patients for a rare-disease drug was very small, so the pharmaceutical industry’s interest in developing such drugs was limited. Therefore they were called orphan drugs.
In order to overcome this hesitancy, many governments have incentivised companies to develop orphan drugs. Examples include the Orphan Drug Act, which the U.S. passed in 1983 to provide tax incentives, seven years of market exclusivity for the first approved product for a given condition, grants, regulatory fee waivers, etc.That is, it reduced the costs of developing the drugs and enabled companies to make a good profit.
This allowed companies to diversify into rare-disease drugs. Before the passage of the Orphan Drug Act, only 38 relevant drugs had been approved in the U.S. But after that, by 2022, there had been 1,122 approvals. Subsequently, several countries and regions, including Japan, Australia, and the European Union had approved similar legislation encouraging pharmaceutical companies to develop and manufacture orphan drugs.
Because of the small market, companies tend to set very high prices for these medications, and it is not unusual for a rare disease patient to find that a year’s worth of the drug costs around $100,000 (Rs 1 crore) or more. This puts the medication out of reach for virtually all patients around the world unless a health insurance scheme or government health service covers it. Samples of such high-priced pharmaceuticals are described in the table.
Two challenges
Although the Government of India supports rare disease patients with up to a total of Rs 50 lakh for their treatment, this is often insufficient to cover the necessary costs even for a year, and patients may have to resort to crowdfunding to raise the required capital.
For example, in mid-2025, Rs 9 crore was raised through crowdfunding to pay for gene therapy for a 16-month-old child in Kolkata. In fact, almost 4,000 children are listed on a Government of India crowdfunding platform, with the cumulative annual cost of treatment for these patients amounting to over Rs 9,000 crore.
Many drugs for rare diseases have been developed, but they cater to only about 5% of rare diseases and associated conditions. Therefore, most patients lack suitable drugs, even those available at high cost.
Two key challenges in developing new orphan drugs are identifying a patient cohort for conducting clinical trials and determining endpoints in these trials. Once a drug is approved, undertaking small-scale manufacturing and distribution that is affordable and of high-quality are other major challenges.
In this article, the authors present here a possible solution to these issues. These solutions touch on how foreign companies that tend to develop novel drugs can work with India both for clinical trials and manufacturing.
Trials for new drugs
With an overall population exceeding 1.4 billion, India has a large number of patients with any given condition. And due to high rates of endogamy in certain social groups, the prevalence of a particular rare disease is even higher than might be expected based on its prevalence elsewhere.
For example, research has shown that in particular ethnic groups, the prevalence of beta-thalassemia in India can be 10.5% whereas, per a 2023 review, the prevalence in India’s general population is 3.7%. Indian patients have also become increasingly organised in recent years, with a proliferation of patient advocacy groups focusing on specific diseases.
On the research front, for example, one longitudinal study has been tracking a group of 70 people with a rare condition called GNE myopathy. Patient groups pertaining to Rett syndrome have a registry of more than 400 patients. The gene pool of the Indian diaspora also has unique mutations, often across different ethnicities.
In all, there is a large number of rare disease patients, which should help in finding a suitable patient cohort for trials. However, patients from India are not usually participants in international trials for orphan drugs.Therefore, there is considerable scope to increase their involvement in such trials. The government could foster the collaboration of foreign companies and local organisations, as it does in the area of chip manufacturing. It also could invite multinational drug companies to set up drug-development centres vis-à-vis rare diseases in India, in collaboration with patient groups.
If Indian patients are important participants in developing such drugs, they are also likely to be more interested in accessing the resulting drugs than in any monetary compensation. Put another way, Indian patients may be willing to help drug development but only if they see themselves as beneficiaries of the approved drugs.
Overpriced drugs that they cannot access serve no local purpose. To this end, the authors propose that India decide on the price of drugs sold within the country or in the Global South. The company developing the drug can be free to set prices in the rest of the world.
The authors say this with reference to the concept of benefit-sharing. Recently, country representatives and medical experts discussed this concept in the context of the Pandemic Agreement of the World Health Organization (WHO). The idea is that in the event of a pandemic, countries will rapidly share information about pathogens, including their genetic information, with the rest of the world. That way, pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies can develop diagnostics, drugs, and vaccines as early as possible. The catch is such products must be shared across countries, fairly and equitably.
Notably, U.S. and Chinese companies are locked in a charged race to develop drugs for rare diseases. Chinese companies will usually have access to enough patients, and also to low-cost manufacturing. Likewise, companies from the Western nations may find it worthwhile to explore opportunities of collaboration in India.
Manufacturing in India
India has been called the “pharmacy of the world” due to its production of small molecule generics, which fill 47% of the prescriptions for generics in the U.S. India also has the largest number of manufacturing sites approved by U.S. regulators outside the U.S.
Indian firms also manufacture and export biosimilars to the U.S. and the European Union and supply 15% of all biosimilars sold in the U.S. Of late, facilities in the country have been producing a relatively novel therapy personalised to each patient for particular cancers, called CAR-T, to international standards.
In effect, India can manufacture various categories of high-quality drugs at low cost. Local manufacturers are also ready to do this for small volumes, whereas manufacturers in Western nations are often unwilling to do so.
After understanding how foreign companies could develop and manufacture orphan drugs in India, we can consider how existing orphan drugs that have been approved abroad can be produced in India.
Under Rule 101 of the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has specified six countries — including the U.S. and the U.K.; if one of these countries approves a drug, the drug need not have a new clinical trial conducted in India before its maker seeking the Indian regulator’s approval.
This provision can be a major incentive to manufacture and market certain generic drugs in India. However, this policy can benefit from greater transparency, including guidance documents to help drug developers and sponsors file applications to the regulator. Regulatory agencies abroad routinely develop such documents to ease the applications process.
As a rule, the approval of such drugs should be based on bioequivalence, i.e. their behaviour in the body should be the same as that of the original drug; safety and toxicity studies; and the drug’s effectiveness once it is on the market.
Such a pathway will require appropriate safeguards for quality, safety, a system that looks out for adverse events after the drug is on the market (i.e. pharmacovigilance), and manufacturing standards — but it will also considerably reduce the need for duplicate paperwork.
What the state can do
We also have an opportunity to take advantage of India’s expertise in generic drugs to create a global orphan drug manufacturing industry. The government should draft policy that reduces the financial barriers to producing such drugs locally. A useful model could be developed along the lines of the production-linked incentive schemes for manufacturing. That is, companies investing in the manufacture of selected orphan drugs could receive incentives linked to production, investment, exports, and patient access.
The financial incentives could include tax incentives for investing in orphan drug manufacturing and production-linked incentives for approved orphan drugs. Other kinds of support could include support for technology transfer and process development in collaboration with a national laboratory, advanced market commitments (AMCs) by the government, committing to buy a certain output at a certain price point, and distributing it through the Centres of Excellence on Rare Diseases, the Central Government Health Scheme, and the Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Jan Aushadhi Kendras. Manufacturers could also benefit from predictable demand during the early stages of production, and incentives for exporting to low- and middle-income countries.
The overall objective should not simply be to subsidise companies. Instead, the government should de-risk the initial investment enough to make orphan drug manufacturing commercially viable.
With a streamlined regulatory pathway, appropriate financial incentives, and government procurement, India could build a globally competitive rare-disease pharmaceutical sector.
Taken together, India has already shown the world how to make drugs affordable. The next challenge is to show the world how to make rare-disease drugs accessible.
Gayatri Saberwal, Rakesh Mishra, and Alok Bhattacharya are with the Tata Institute for Genetics and Society. Bhattacharya is also with ‘World Without GNE Myopathy’.

Some big AI companies seem to think that the best way to keep models from becoming too chaotic or too mischievous is to keep them locked inside of labs. If only a chosen few can access them, the thinking goes, they can do less damage in the real world while researchers try to understand what they’re capable of.
Nathan Lambert and Tom Zick, two industry scientists, believe the opposite. The pair founded a nonprofit, Trillium Labs, that will work on various areas of AI research—including potentially problematic areas like recursive self-improvement (RSI) and agents—in a more transparent way. In practice, this will mean publishing the details of experiments so that outside scientists can study and replicate them.
Lambert says the way frontier AI labs keep their work secret reduces the community’s ability to scrutinize ideas and contribute new approaches. He believes that letting outside experts see how models are built and tuned could be crucial to mitigating risks.
“Over the past few millennia, humanity has had the scientific method in our toolbox as a way to mitigate harms and build better futures,” Lambert tells WIRED. “The current closed trajectory of frontier AI development is taking us a step backwards.”
The world’s most powerful models, like those from OpenAI and Anthropic, can only be accessed through an app or an application programming interface (API). Often, this comes at the cost of transparency about how the model is built and how it behaves.
Other companies, especially those in China, offer relatively powerful models that can be downloaded and run on a user’s own hardware. The Chinese company Xiaomi, for example, recently published live details of a major training run involving one of its models. And researchers at Stanford are pretraining the AI model Marin in the open.
The industry is currently locked in a battle over which strategy is best, mostly because of how powerful frontier models now are. They can automate the discovery of new software vulnerabilities and automatically probe and hack into systems, and recent high-profile hacking sprees have prompted even greater scrutiny.
Proponents of a limited-access system say it’s crucial to keep that power in the hands of a trusted few, while those in Lambert and Zick’s camp believe that a shared understanding of the risks means we’re all better off.
Lambert previously worked at Ai2, a research lab that has taken an unusually open approach to AI, including publishing details of the data and the training methods used to build models alongside the models themselves. He previously worked at Hugging Face, runs a popular technical blog, and founded the American Truly Open Models, an initiative aimed at encouraging US companies to release more open models. Zick worked at Harvard University and helped Charles Schwab devise policies around “responsible AI.”
The two met over Zoom during the COVID-19 pandemic, when both were graduate students at UC Berkeley working on AI. They got the idea for the new nonprofit after seeing how disconnected industry AI research has become from academic work; Lambert says professors and students are often unable to replicate the work going on inside big company labs because they lack the resources required.
Zick says Trillium Labs, which launched today, will initially focus on post-training—fine-tuning large models after they’ve been built. Another key area will be RSI, a process for developing new models by having AI contribute research. The prospect that ongoing progress could continue indefinitely, leading to a loss of human control, has alarmed many AI researchers. The issue gained mainstream attention earlier this month when an Anthropic researcher left the company and warned that RSI could pose an existential threat to humankind.
The nonprofit will also look at how reinforcement learning, which rewards a model for good results and punishes it for bad outcomes, can improve its capabilities. That approach has made agents far more capable, but also more inclined to do unexpected things. They’ll study how reinforcement learning shapes the character and behavior of AI models, a method that can pose problems when a model becomes overly sycophantic, for example.
“To understand something like how reinforcement learning scales in post-training, you need significant compute and a lot of careful experimentation,” Zick says. She says that publishing details of how reinforcement training runs work could yield surprising insights as outside researchers scrutinize the work.
The lab has raised an undisclosed sum from Schmidt Sciences, Halcyon Futures, and others. The founders say they aim to raise $40 to $100 million in total and plan to spend $30 million on training over the next 18 months.
“I'm a massive fan of much more transparency than we currently have in R&D,” Tim Fist, director of emerging technology policy at the Institute for Progress, a policy thinktank, tells WIRED.
Lambert and Zick ultimately hope that Trillim Labs will contribute some much-needed nuance to the wider discussion about how best to build AI.
“We’re in an era of AI discourse dominated by a few world views,” Lambert says. “We believe that the scientific method and careful measurement of recent events is the best way to understand new behaviors of AI models.”

In a laboratory 2 kilometers underground, a crane lowers Matt Depatie, a detector technologist, through a hatch into a white-walled cavern filled with about 7,000 tons of ultrapure water that glows as blue as wiper fluid in the light. “Splashdown,” Depatie says over a radio as he steps into an inflatable raft waiting below.
Normally, the cavern is one of the darkest places on Earth, but today it is lit up for maintenance, offering us a rare chance to see inside. I peer through the hatch at Depatie as he paddles over to examine the submerged experiment. He’s inspecting a house-sized detector built to catch some of the most elusive particles known to physics: neutrinos.
This is the SNO+ neutrino experiment, buried deep within the Creighton mine at Snolab, an underground physics laboratory in Sudbury, Canada. SNO+ consists of an acrylic sphere lined with nearly 10,000 sensitive light detectors and filled with 780 tons of oily liquid scintillator, which flashes when lit up by energetic particles. The water around the device and the rock above it shield the detector from the glare of cosmic radiation, allowing the flickers of less common particle interactions to shine through.
Our whole journey down has been part of the crusade to maintain absolute darkness, even beyond the visible spectrum of light. As we descended the main shaft and walked through a rocky tunnel to the lab, our bodies and clothes collected minute amounts of radioactive radon dust. Before entering the main laboratory space, we tossed our mine clothes, showered, and changed into electric blue jumpsuits and hairnets to minimize the contamination we carried in with us. “The showers aren’t for you,” Depatie said as we changed, “they’re for the science.”
Such extremes are necessary when you’re trying to catch ghosts—in this case, ghosts that may help reveal the secrets of inaccessible regions deep within the Earth.
Neutrinos are the most abundant of all the particles that have mass. But that mass is tiny: just a millionth of the mass of an electron. With such little heft and a neutral electromagnetic charge, the particles hardly ever interact with other matter. Trillions of neutrinos—mostly those produced in the sun—pass through our bodies every second, yet after years of hunting them with detectors such as SNO+, researchers have captured only a few hundred thousand of their precious flashes.
Even more elusive—so much so that after decades of searching, scientists have detected only a few hundred of them—are geoneutrinos.
Geoneutrinos are produced in processes that heat the interior of the planet. This heat plays a major role in powering the flow of rocks in the mantle, which shapes everything from plate tectonics to Earth’s magnetic field. It comes from two main sources: heat left over from the planet’s formation, and heat produced by the decay of uranium, thorium, and potassium in the rocks of the mantle and crust. Without this second source, Earth would have long since cooled off and become a tectonically dead planet.
In counting geoneutrinos, physicists can get a direct measure of Earth’s vital heat-producing elements. “It’s the one thing we do that focuses on the Earth,” said Ryan Bayes, a particle astrophysicist at Queen’s University in Ontario who works on SNO+. “Everything else we do is more focused on what we receive from other places in the universe.”
The first detection of geoneutrinos, by an instrument in Japan called Kamland, was reported in 2005. In 2009, the Borexino detector in Italy reported catching several dozen more. In November 2025, SNO+ reported its first detection, bumping up the number of observed geoneutrinos by about 50.
What makes the detections at SNO+ special is the experiment’s location: These are the first geoneutrinos measured in the western hemisphere, offering a new perspective on Earth’s radioactive interior.
Major uncertainties remain in interpreting the results from these experiments, but researchers’ best estimates suggest that each site is measuring a different flux. “It could be that that’s the first hint that the mantle is not uniform,” said Mark Chen, a particle astrophysicist at Queen’s University and director of the SNO+ collaboration.
Geochemists have conventionally assumed that radioactive elements are distributed evenly throughout the mantle, because the flowing rock should mix everything together. But the measurements of geoneutrinos in different locations could hint that this is not the case.
The regions that seem to be producing the most geoneutrinos sit roughly above continent-size blobs of anomalously hot, dense material, known as large low-shear-velocity provinces, or LLSVPs, which seismologists have mapped on either side of the core. One is under Africa, the other under the Pacific Ocean. “There may be deep Earth structures in the mantle that are not understood,” Chen said. “It could be that [they] concentrate some kinds of elements.”
Neutrinos could one day offer new insight into the still mysterious origin of these deep structures and, more broadly, the patterns in the mantle that underlie many aspects of the Earth system. “It really would be a way to make a chemical map of the Earth’s interior,” said William McDonough, a geochemist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences who has long been a leading voice in the search for geoneutrinos.
The outstanding question is whether the geoneutrino measurements reveal differences between the areas of mantle below each experiment, or if the imbalance originates in the way the different experiments count their geoneutrinos. Researchers across the board say there’s still so much uncertainty that it’s impossible to say.
“If we take it at face value, we could say maybe the western hemisphere has a lot more radioactive material in it than the eastern hemisphere,” McDonough said. But there are reasons to be wary of these estimates. “Are the Italians right? Are the Japanese right? Are they both right? Or is something wrong?” he said.
The uncertainties associated with each detector’s results come from the sorting process that physicists go through to identify geoneutrinos, Bayes said. “They don’t just show up and say, ‘Hi, I’m a geoneutrino.’”
Scientists must eliminate signals from particles with too much energy, particles with the wrong measure of a property called helicity, and particles that they expect to see flowing from nuclear reactors. They must also eliminate geoneutrinos coming from Earth’s crust, with the largest contribution coming from the area within a few hundred kilometers of the detector. When those other detections are subtracted from the total count, the geoneutrino signal from the mantle should be all that’s left.
In general terms, the geoneutrino flux from the mantle seems to be very high at Borexino and very low at Kamland, though the uncertainties are great. A detailed geological interpretation of the SNO+ results is still in the works, Chen said, but so far scientists see a “pretty in-between” mantle below Canada.
A particular challenge for SNO+ scientists is understanding the neutrinos coming from the detector’s surroundings, including a basin formed 1.8 billion years ago by a giant impactor. “There are lots of unknowns in this geological area,” said Virginia Strati, a researcher at the University of Ferrara in Italy who helped develop a local model of radioactivity for Snolab.
Uncertainty also comes from estimates of the total amount of radioactive material heating the mantle. The flux of geoneutrinos suggests that these elements could contribute anywhere from just a small percentage of its heat to half of it—a discrepancy equivalent to the output of tens of thousands of nuclear power plants.
Both sources of uncertainty make it even more difficult to detect any differences between the chemical makeup of particular sections of the mantle. The difference in the geoneutrino flux expected from various distributions of radioactive elements “is very small, and is hidden in these uncertainties,” Strati said.
The detection at SNO+ comes at an exciting moment for geoneutrino research: JUNO, another huge neutrino experiment currently collecting data in China, is expected to report its first geoneutrino flux later this year, adding a fourth and notably richer view. With more than 20,000 tons of scintillator, the experiment—buried under a mountain outside the city of Guangzhou — is so large that it is expected to detect more geoneutrinos in its first year than the combined output of Kamland, Borexino, and SNO+ over decades.
Clearer estimates of the geoneutrino flux at each experiment could come from more detailed geological data, as well as further geoneutrino counts at each site. However, McDonough says the best thing would be to build a neutrino detector at the bottom of the ocean. It’s an idea McDonough has championed for decades.
Such a detector would be far from continental rocks, which are rich in radioactive elements; oceanic crust is also thinner and more uniform. Crust-related uncertainties go down so much that “you are in mantle-only territory,” he said.
The idea of an ocean-bottom detector, estimated to cost hundreds of millions of dollars, has seen little take-up from government funders to date. But McDonough is hoping he can make something happen in China, which has given the green light to other big geoscience projects. “It’s very possible,” he said. Until then, physicists will keep paddling around for answers deep underground.

Republicans and Democrats find a unifying target: Pharmacy benefit managers
Amye Joseph says America's political polarization has made it an "interesting time" in her Tennessee household.
She and her husband, Charlie, have been married for 35 years. She's a Republican. He's a Democrat. But their shared disenchantment with profit-driven healthcare has provided a unifying target: pharmacy benefit managers, known as PBMs.
The Josephs' frustration is focused on CVS Health. The conglomerate, which reported $400 billion in revenue last year, includes a major health insurer (Aetna), one of the country's dominant PBMs (CVS Caremark), and America's largest retail pharmacy chain (CVS Pharmacy).
"We hate CVS. I'm going to be straight-up," Amye Joseph said.
She laments the lack of face-to-face interaction with pharmacists, prices that seem to rise without explanation, and pressure from the couple's CVS Caremark drug plan to use CVS stores instead of their local pharmacy.
"They're not even a middleman," she said. "They're a money grab for CVS."
PBMs were conceived as a way to manage prescriptions and hold down costs. But these middlemen have become bipartisan punching bags, accused of sucking up profits at the expense of employers, governments, and patients.
And while healthcare debates still divide Democrats and Republicans in Washington, D.C., taking on PBMs has become a unifying cause in an era of widespread frustration over rising healthcare costs.
In recent years, every state has imposed restrictions on PBMs. The Josephs' home state of Tennessee, where the GOP has a lock on state government, is among a growing number looking to outlaw companies that own PBMs from also owning brick-and-mortar pharmacies, as CVS does.
That's aligned conservative, business-friendly Republicans with Democrats, who are traditionally more open to government regulation.
This legislative push reflects a feeling even in the GOP that the market for prescription drugs is being gamed, said Antonio Ciaccia, CEO of 46brooklyn Research, a nonprofit think tank that tracks drug pricing.
"Republicans are looking at this issue, saying, We know what competition is supposed to do, and it isn't happening," said Ciaccia, a critic of the PBM industry. "This is not a free market."
Charlie Joseph, a retired fire captain who now works as a custodian, was miffed when he realized he could save money on his blood pressure medication if he paid cash at his local pharmacy rather than using his CVS Caremark drug plan.
He now buys a 90-day supply for the same price he would have paid for a 30-day supply through the CVS plan.
"Right now, it's more of an inconvenience than anything else as far as it goes, but there's no consistency," he said. "The whole healthcare thing is just frustrating, on a good day."
CVS spokesperson Phil Blando said the price of individual drugs can vary.
"Looking at the price of a single prescription does not reflect the value of a comprehensive pharmacy benefit," he said in a statement. "Our focus remains delivering the lowest possible total cost and the greatest overall value for members and plan sponsors."
Unified opposition
PBM officials say their industry has been unfairly maligned. "PBMs are the only part of the prescription drug supply chain working to lower drug costs, which makes PBMs the target of powerful groups, Big Pharma and pharmacists," said Greg Lopes, a spokesperson for the Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, which represents PBMs across the nation.
"Drug manufacturers attempt to shift blame for high drug costs to PBMs in order to retain their profit margins and weaken PBMs' ability to lower costs," he said.
Drugmakers have worked for years to cast PBMs as unnecessary go-betweens, said Barak Richman, a lawyer and economist who studies healthcare competition at George Washington University. He called the fight between Big Pharma and PBMs a corporate "cage match."
"We have wildly passionate partisan divides on a lot of healthcare," he said. "But there's a lot of healthcare policy that I don't think is obviously partisan."
PBMs haven't won over many Democrats or Republicans. Attorneys general from nearly 40 states and U.S. territories last year wrote a letter to congressional leaders arguing that "horizontal consolidation and vertical integration have transformed PBMs from useful administrative service providers into market-dominating behemoths."
In state legislatures like Tennessee's, shared ownership of PBMs and pharmacies has drawn particular fire. Independent pharmacies have little choice but to contract with major PBMs while also competing with the conglomerate-owned pharmacies. Many lawmakers have said they want to protect small businesses.
"If a corporation argues that its pharmacy cannot survive unless it is owned by the same entity that sets the reimbursement rate, then we're not talking about a free market. We're talking about control," Tennessee state Sen. Bobby Harshbarger said in a February legislative hearing.
Harshbarger, a Republican who led the legislative push, is a pharmacist in a small city in northeastern Tennessee.
His mother, U.S. Rep. Diana Harshbarger, R-Tenn., is also a pharmacist and has sponsored a similar PBM ownership ban at the federal level. The Senate version has brought together some unlikely bedfellows, such as Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass. and Josh Hawley, R-Mo.
State lawmakers vs. CVS
CVS officials argued that the Tennessee legislation was misguided. "Any proposed reform should be evaluated based on whether it improves access to care, simplifies the patient experience, and enhances affordability," Blando said in a statement.
It's unclear whether the PBM ownership ban will do that in Tennessee. An analysis by the state legislature's researchers concluded that the bill could drive up healthcare costs in the short term.
To fight the bill, CVS launched a $7 million TV advertising campaign, claiming it would have to close all its 134 pharmacies in the state, similar to its threat in neighboring Arkansas when state lawmakers there passed a similar measure in 2025.
CVS also sent text messages to Tennessee customers, asking them to contact their lawmakers to keep pharmacies open.
Ominous texts from CVS helped kill another PBM ownership ban in Louisiana last year.
Sponsors of the legislation said closure wasn't the only option: CVS could also divest either its stores or its PBM.
Tennessee lawmakers moved forward. State Sen. Rusty Crowe, a Republican from northeastern Tennessee, where the Josephs live, told his colleagues before the vote that they should consider the fierce resistance a sign that they were onto something.
"I learned when I was in the Vietnam War, when you start taking on flak, you know you're over the damn target," he said.
As with most votes in Tennessee's legislature, Republicans didn't need support from Democrats. But they got it anyway.
State Rep. Antonio Parkinson, a Democrat from Memphis, said he felt like he was voting in favor of lower drug prices and supporting "ma and pa" pharmacies. "If there's a benefit to my people, I'm supporting it."
CVS has not divested or closed its pharmacies in states that have passed ownership bans — the laws have yet to take effect. The Arkansas ban is being held up in court after CVS challenged the constitutionality of the law. CVS also sued in Tennessee, though the ownership ban doesn't take effect until 2028.
This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with Nashville Public Radio and KFF Health News.

Portugal head coach Jorge Jesus said Cristiano Ronaldo can return to the national team if he chooses to, leaving the door open for the 41-year-old captain after his abrupt departure from the squad last week.
Ronaldo left Portugal’s training camp after being an unused substitute in a win over Norway and learning he would not start against Denmark. He subsequently said on social media that he would explain his reasons for leaving the national team “in due course.”
“If he wants to, he’ll return to the national team,“ Jesus told reporters after Portugal’s 2-1 Nations League win over Norway on Sunday. “We can talk before the next call-up, but Cris is the one who’s going to decide.
“He’s the one who should decide how he wants to end his time with the national team. In my first call-up, I said, ’I need you, I need you to be close to me, playing or not playing, I need you’. And now I’m saying the same thing.”
Defending champion Portugal won 4-2 in Denmark without Ronaldo and then beat Norway on Sunday to maintain a perfect record in Group A4 and secure a place in the Nations League quarterfinals.
Five-time Ballon D’Or winner Ronaldo is Portugal’s record scorer and most-capped player, with 146 goals in 234 international appearances.
Portuguese Football Federation President Pedro Proenca also said Ronaldo remained part of the team’s plans, describing the episode as a misunderstanding that should be resolved internally.
“He is in the national team on sporting merit, and that must be unquestionable,” Proenca told RTP. “We have to pay tribute to Cristiano Ronaldo.”
Jesus, who also coached Ronaldo at Saudi Arabian club Al-Nassr, expects the forward to be available for the next international window if he wanted to return.
Portugal next hosts Denmark on Nov. 14 before visiting Wales three days later.

Germany's Merz visits Kyiv as Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian cities
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has arrived in Kyiv to show support as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukrainian cities
KYIV, Ukraine -- German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv Sunday in a show of support as Russia escalated its attacks on Ukrainian cities.
The aerial war has intensified, with Moscow menacing cities across Ukraine with hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, while Kyiv has been striking Russia’s oil industry and businesses.
Merz said he traveled to the Ukrainian capital on his second trip as chancellor to demonstrate his country's solidarity with Ukraine. Germany is Ukraine’s largest donor, sending Kyiv more than €43.3 billion ($48.8 billion) since the war began, along with equipment and weapons.
“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said in a statement Sunday, adding that he told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy: “You can continue to count on our help.”
Merz said the partnership between the two countries was “not a one-way street,” pointing to German and Ukrainian companies jointly developing technologies that benefit both sides. “This makes us safer and stronger,” he said.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy thanked Germany and said the two countries would make “important agreements” during the visit to strengthen Ukraine’s defenses and those of the rest of Europe. “Russia must be stopped together,” he wrote.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the agenda would focus on "strengthening Ukraine, our defense and resilience, and our shared European security.”
Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Saturday it would continue to carry out “mass retaliatory strikes” on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, urging foreign nationals and diplomats to leave the country. It previously issued a similar warning in May.
The German and Russian foreign ministers met on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly’s annual gathering of world leaders last month in what was believed to be the first such face-to-face meeting since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Russia's Sergey Lavrov rejected German calls to ease off its “dangerous path of escalation” toward the country, and instead accused Germany of being Ukraine’s main sponsor and seeking to be a leading military power in Europe.
Ties between Russia and Germany have soured even more in recent weeks, following an attempted drone attack in early September at Leipzig airport. Germany has blamed Russia for the incident and announced the closure of the German consulate in St. Petersburg, the latest in a cycle of tit-for-tat moves.
Meanwhile, Merz's power inside Germany has taken a blow after a string of state election defeats last month, including losses to the anti-migration and Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany party. However, he said he intends to remain chancellor.
On Sunday morning, Russian attacks continued with a drone hitting Kyiv’s Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River again, Zelenskyy said. Video circulating on social media showed the drone flying into the bridge and the explosion as vehicles crossed. There was no immediate word on casualties.
The latest strike came after Russian assaults forced the full or partial closure of three of Kyiv’s six road bridges over the Dnipro River earlier this week, suspending traffic and causing tailbacks in Moscow’s latest effort to disrupt life in the Ukrainian capital. Previously, Russia has hit apartment blocks, supermarket warehouses, gas stations and data centers, among other targets.
Seven people were wounded Sunday in a Russian aerial bomb attack on the Ukrainian city of Sumy, local officials said.
Russia invaded its neighbor more than 4½ years ago, and there are no concrete signs that a peace settlement might be possible. Fighting along the roughly 1,250-kilometer (780-mile) front line snaking through northern, eastern and southern Ukraine has been virtually deadlocked in recent months.

MUMBAI/TOKYO – Honda Motor aims to cut costs by as much as a fifth and halve development times under its new partnership in India with Tata Technologies, according to two people familiar with the matter, as pressure from rivals forces the Japanese automaker to rethink its go-it-alone approach.
Reeling from electric vehicle-related losses that it expects to reach more than $12 billion, Honda is pivoting to gasoline-electric hybrids and slashing expenses. In May, engineering firm Tata Technologies said it was selected to develop vehicles for a Japanese automaker. It declined to name the partner, but the two people and another person familiar with the matter said it was Honda.

India and the West Indies have been sanctioned for maintaining slow over-rates during the third and final ODI of their series in New Chandigarh on Saturday.
India has been fined 20 per cent of its match fee, while the West Indies has been fined 10 per cent after being ruled four and two overs short of their required over-rates, respectively, after time allowances were taken into consideration.
Since both captains pleaded guilty to the offences and accepted the proposed sanctions, there was no need for formal hearings.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

India’s Manav Thakkar and Japan’s Sachi Aoki will be the singles top seeds at the WTT Feeder Chennai, to be held at the Tamil Nadu Physical Education and Sports University (TNPESU) from October 28 to November 1.
World No. 48 Thakkar heads the men’s field, while the 55th-ranked Aoki leads the women’s entries. Asian Games mixed doubles bronze medallist Diya Chitale will spearhead the Indian women’s singles challenge.
Chitale, ranked 66th, returns to international competition on home soil after partnering Manush Shah to bronze at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya. She is the highest-ranked Indian in the women’s singles field, behind Aoki and South Korea’s Yang Haeun, ranked 60th.
Ankur Bhattacharjee, ranked 66th, and G. Sathiyan, ranked 82nd, join Thakkar among the leading men’s entries. South Korea’s Kwon Hyuk, at No. 93, is the highest-ranked overseas entrant, with Harmeet Desai, ranked 97th, completing the top five.
Payas Jain (107), Snehit Suravajjula (117) and Akash Pal (146) are also in the men’s singles field, giving India seven of the eight highest-ranked entrants.
Yashaswini Ghorpade, ranked 76th, follows Chitale among the Indian women. Divyanshi Bhowmick (120), Sutirtha Mukherjee (128), Nithya Mani (130) and Swastika Ghosh (138) are among the other home players, while Japan’s Cocona Muramatsu is ranked 132nd.
In mixed doubles, Desai and Ghorpade will pair up again after reaching the final of February’s Star Contender Chennai. They finished runners-up to Romania’s Eduard Ionescu and Bernadette Szocs at the same venue.
Thakkar will partner Taneesha Kotecha, while Pal teams up with Mukherjee and Jain with Sayali Wani. Kwon and Kim Seoyun are among the South Korean combinations in the field.
Aoki has also enjoyed success in Chennai this year, winning the Star Contender women’s doubles title alongside compatriot Sakura Yokoi. The pair defeated South Korea’s Ryu Hanna and Kim Nayeong 3-1 in the final.
The senior tournament will follow the WTT Youth Contender Chennai, scheduled for October 23 to 26.
This will be Chennai’s second senior WTT event of 2026, following the Star Contender from February 10 to 15. India also hosted the WTT Feeder Vadodara from January 7 to 11.

The upcoming midterm elections are setting the stage for unusually significant changes to key Senate committees that play an important role in health care, STAT explains. Both the finance and health committees could undergo major changes, though for different reasons. Of course, if Democrats take control of the Senate, they would get to run the committees, though the GOP membership changes could still influence the panels’ directions. Specifically, five or more of the Senate Finance Committee’s 14 Republicans are set to leave. And the outlook for the Senate’s Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, or HELP, is even more difficult to predict with the departure of chairman Bill Cassidy.

Novartis will gain exclusive rights to Abogen’s experimental drug, ABO2203, and options to license other therapies based on Abogen’s RNA technology. It will also have the option to license additional experimental medicines developed using Abogen’s RNA platform. The drug is designed to treat autoimmune diseases by targeting B cells, a type of immune cell that causes disease in conditions like lupus and rheumatoid arthritis.

A British Airways flight heading to Chicago reportedly turned back after a pressurisation problem. Flight BA295 departed London Heathrow and was operated by a Boeing 777-236ER, registration G-VIIA. According to FlightRadar24, the scheduled departure at Heathrow was 11:10 AM. But it took off at 12:14 PM. The scheduled arrival in Chicago was 1:50 PM. However, it is now expected to arrive at 11:02 AM. UPDATE: The latest update on FlightRadar24 shows that the flight has arrived at Heathrow Airport. The live flight tracker has stopped sharing updates since the flight has been grounded. The details about the British Airways flight were shared on X by Turbine Traveller, an aircraft technician based in Nairobi. The post was about a reported crew message explaining the decision to return. The message said the aircraft was returning to Heathrow due to a pressure problem. It recorded cabin altitude reaching 10,500 feet. Cabin altitude refers to the altitude corresponding to the air pressure inside the aircraft. According to the post, BA295 was cruising at 36,000 feet before descending rapidly. Soon, it reached around 9,000 feet. The 27,000-foot descent happened within seven minutes. Turbine Traveller said this descent had matched Boeing's procedure for a loss of cabin pressurisation. The aim is to reach an altitude where additional oxygen is no longer required. At cruising height, the thin outside air cannot support normal breathing without additional oxygen. The reported crew message also raised concerns about the aircraft's landing weight. It indicated the aircraft was around 30 tonnes above its maximum landing weight. The message said there was no way to release fuel. This made fuel management another consideration during the return. Burning fuel during holding would help reduce the aircraft's weight before landing. Flightradar24 shows several loops along the aircraft's tracked route near southwestern Britain. The post also explained how the Boeing 777 maintains cabin pressure. Its air-conditioning units supply air while valves control how much air leaves. Two exit valves sit towards the front and rear of the aircraft. During automatic operation, they adjust as the aircraft climbs, cruises and descends. This helps maintain cabin pressure throughout different stages of flight. The system normally limits cabin altitude to 8,000 feet. It also manages how quickly cabin pressure changes. Pilots can select manual control and adjust either exit valve when needed. Airflow distribution changes depending on whether forward cargo air conditioning is operating. When switched off, about 20% leaves through the front valve and 80% through the rear. When switched on, the distribution is roughly equal between both valves. Separate safety valves protect the aircraft against excessive pressure differences between its interior and the surrounding atmosphere. Other vents protect against the pressure inside becoming too low relative to the outside. These systems work together to maintain suitable cabin conditions. When pressure is lost, reaching a lower altitude becomes the immediate priority. For BA295, the rapid descent followed the crew's decision to return to Heathrow. “Heading back to Heathrow, too heavy for a normal landing, they’re currently dumping fuel over the Bristol Channel and will continue onto London once below max landing weight,” an ex-commercial and military Irish pilot posted on X. “This is ALL regular practice in the simulation by the pilots and will be carried out entirely according to procedure. The event was dominated by new hardware launches, such as the new Meta Ray-Ban glasses, new VR glasses, and camera-free Ray-Ban glasses (audio only), but swimming beneath the surface of all these was something that was actually introduced earlier. Meta had introduced Meta Muse in early September, but announced the rollout of the Muse AI agent on its Meta wearables and Meta Muse Charm at the event, and for us, that was easily the real highlight of Meta Connect.
After investing heavily in recruiting AI talent, Meta finally had something to show: an AI agent, which will basically make your dreams of having a robot butler come true. Not surprisingly, it has been making massive tech waves ever since. Since Meta Connect and its rollout, Muse has been topping app store charts, and its early numbers are being compared with ChatGPT, with many pointing out that it is far ahead of OpenAI’s chatbot’s numbers.
While this may paint a very rosy picture for Meta Muse, the reality may be a trifle thorny.
What those numbers do not tell – the “Threads” deception
These numbers, impressive as they are, do not necessarily mean Muse is a runaway success. There are a few reasons for this. Topping app store charts is more of a temporary phenomenon, often influenced by what is trending in a particular week, and does not represent real industry trends. Also, Meta has billions of users across different social media and messaging platforms, which makes it easy for the tech giant to get a few million users quickly without too much trouble. But the adoption rate might not match the number of downloads or sign-ups.
We have seen this happen with Meta’s X rival app, Threads, as well. It has more “active users” as per the numbers than X, which means it must be more used and popular than X, but that is mostly because of Threads’ integration with Instagram and Facebook, which gets the app most of its “active users.” However, the time spent on the app is not nearly the same as its other two sibling social media apps. Similarly, early ChatGPT comparisons with Meta Muse signups may not be fair, because ChatGPT was not launched or advertised as a tool for the masses when it was first launched. It did not have the sort of subscriber base and reach that Meta has, and back then, AI chatbots were not too common either.
Definitely a big deal
That does not mean Muse does not represent a big tech leap. So far, AI chatbots have generally been used for queries, information, help with work, and even personal advice, but that’s mostly about it. All of these chatbots are more about helping you with your queries, with no bar to the nature of the query. While useful in this regard, many are not able to perform actions that have an impact on your day-to-day life. That is where Meta Muse differs.
As we said earlier, Muse is actually the robot butler that the future always promised us. It can get tasks done and help you with managing your digital and even real life. Once you give it access, the AI agent can go through your mail, find messages, draft new messages, reply to emails, all without too much intervention. That might not sound too impressive, as most AI agents and virtual assistants can do the same with a simple command. But Muse goes a step further – it can even make purchases, make reservations, book appointments, and more, across different devices and platforms. In fact, if allowed, Muse can basically make deals on Facebook Marketplace or book you a table at your favorite restaurant or even call you a cab, all without needing any major intervention. Proper butling!
Muse has power and potential, but does Meta have our trust?
As impressive and life-altering as it may sound– some are calling it the biggest tech innovation since the iPhone – Meta still has a massive hurdle that it would have to cross to make Muse the AI butler it wants it to be. And that is the lack of trust in Meta.
For all its innovation and massive subscriber base, Meta has been in a number of controversial situations when it comes to security and privacy. Zuckerberg’s brand has been accused of and even found guilty in cases that range from rigging elections, pushing agendas and ads, to exposing young children to adult content and potential groomers, to monopolizing social media and personal messaging space and using unfair means and practices to kill competition. Its recent hardware “hit” the Meta glasses have also got into a privacy mess, and have been (in)famously christened pervert glasses, following reports of their being used to record people without their consent.
Now, Muse requires even more data and access to private information to actually deliver on its promises. For instance, to be able to draft emails, it needs access to your email account. To be allowed to send messages, it needs permission to read, understand, store, and reply to messages, and needs access to your contact list. To make a reservation, it needs to know your location; to order things online, it needs to have your bank details and also your address. Basically, it needs to have complete access to all your information to act like the magic help that Meta is claiming it can be.
Why I am not A-Muse-D
And that is where my beef with Muse really comes in. Had this been any other company– if Apple had managed to deliver on its intelligent Siri promises or Google had delivered Gemini with such prowess, I personally would have felt less apprehensive in handing over the keys to my digital life, but to give Meta even more access to my data than it already has just feels scary.
Even though I have come to terms with the fact that we are all under passive surveillance from brands at all times, it will take some time for me to give complete control of my data over to Meta without any struggle.
Some of the recent headlines Muse has made do not help its cause. Recently, the AI agent not only made a deal for its user on Facebook Marketplace but even shared his address with the buyer. All without consent. The user, a tech YouTuber, Matt Robb, mentioned how the AI agent accepted low offers and even pretended to be the user while chatting with the buyer, calling the buyer to his address when he was not home at all. Once Matt realized what was happening, he specifically instructed Muse to not share his address. He then asked his friends to send him messages on Facebook Marketplace to see if the agent shares the address. Rather disturbingly, it did: multiple times, and even accepted low offers, all without consent. In another report by Apple Insider, alleged that Muse accessed and uploaded past and present Apple Messages even though the user said he had not granted it permission to do so. All this despite Meta’s claims that Muse has strong privacy and security protections.
All of this does not take away from the fact that Meta has created something really powerful with Muse. It has managed to deliver a finished, capable AI agent which can manage your digital lives, if you let it. Unfortunately, it may also steal your data, force specific ads, and make conversations on your behalf by pretending to be you. And therein lies the problem. The AI Agent is not just about technology, but also about trust. Meta has delivered on the first front with Muse, but until it delivers on the second, I refuse to be A-Muse-D by it. Pun intended.

Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down as White House press secretary in August, is joining Fox News as an on-air contributor, according to the New York Times, citing a network announcement.
Leavitt, 29, who was the youngest press secretary in White House history, left the administration after the birth of her second child earlier this year. She said at the time that she planned to spend more time with her family and take a role with the Trump-aligned Super Pac Maga Inc.

Pointing out that high-cost medicines used to treat cancer, kidney ailments, and AIDS are being sold at prices up to “70 times higher” than the rates at which dealers and stockists procure them, Karnataka Health Minister U.T. Khader has written a letter to Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda, seeking national action against “abnormal gaps” in drug prices.
The Minister said dealers and stockists purchase advanced pharmaceuticals from manufacturers at heavily discounted wholesale landed rates, while the MRPs printed on the medicines are fixed at “inflated, highly disproportionate levels”. The letter said the gap between the procurement price and MRP was “sometimes 30 times to more than 70 times”.
Mr. Khader said that the issue was particularly concerning for in-patients, emergency and intensive-care patients, oncology patients, and those requiring implants, surgical consumables, and other hospital-based treatment, as they cannot realistically compare suppliers or defer purchases.
The letter said that while the existing MRP framework prevents medicines from being sold above the printed MRP, it does not address situations where the MRP itself has little relation to the actual institutional transaction price, adding that hospitals retain an excessive undisclosed margin.
Mr. Khader sought a national study comparing the printed MRP, manufacturer/importer price, hospital’s net acquisition price, and the price ultimately billed to patients for selected high-value medicines, medical devices, and consumables. He also proposed that the patient-facing price of products supplied through hospitals be capped at the lower end of the applicable statutory price, MRP or the hospital’s net acquisition cost plus a notified and reasonable service margin and applicable taxes.
The Minister said Karnataka would “cooperate with any pilot or national framework” and could, within its powers, make private hospitals disclose more information, require detailed bills for patients, and set up a system to handle complaints locally. However, he said the Centre needs to fix the basic problem — the large difference between what hospitals pay for medicines, the MRP printed on them and what patients are finally charged.

Hamilton bemused after glitch turns F1 into 'Lego race'
- Published
Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton likened the effects of a software bug that affected multiple cars before the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to a "Lego race".
The problem led to several cars, including those of the two multiple world champions who were sharing the front row of the grid, not working in the wet conditions that preceded the race.
A tropical downpour delayed attempts to get the grand prix under way for the best part of an hour. And when the cars set off on formation laps behind a safety car to test the conditions, audiences were treated to the bizarre sight of many of them struggling to move.
A bug in the software that mandates how the engines' electrical power can be used in wet conditions had been triggered by a combination of low engine speeds, low grip and specific aspects of the circuit layout.
Verstappen, who went on to take a dominant win that was his first victory of the year, said: "These engines are so complicated and a lot of software is implemented.
"I triggered [the problem] first and then I looked in my mirror, I was like, 'Wait, are they waiting for me or what's going [on]...?' It was like the Lego race."
Verstappen was referring to a show run in battery-powered Lego F1 cars that was held before the British Grand Prix in July.
Hamilton, sitting beside Verstappen in the post-race news conference after finishing third, interjected to say: "Yeah, we had the same speed. I had to stop on track and stop the car and engine and restart it. I've never done that before."
Verstappen added: "It was insane. Like, it's the Lego power. At some point we were five-wide on the straight because we couldn't understand what was going on.
"Then we did a lap and then I see eight other cars crawling still, and I saw you (Hamilton) by yourself crawling. That's not what you want, right, for the sport."
Mercedes driver George Russell, who retired from the race with an engine failure, said: "It didn't feel very F1."
Nikolas Tombazis, the single-seater director for governing body the FIA said there would be a full investigation.
The issue arose, he added, because, while the software had been tested, it had not been tested in these specific conditions. Largely because there has been so little running in the wet this year.
"Cars are complicated," Tombazis said. "We would all like it to be simpler, but when you have electrical energy and combustion energy all working together, and obviously when you want to ensure that there's sporting fairness between the teams, that is complicated.
"We haven't done a full debrief of the situation and see how we can avoid such an issue. Every race, we have a long debrief afterwards, where we identify criticalities.
"Obviously, that was a major criticality, and we need to make sure we avoid it. Can I guarantee it will never happen again? This specific problem, yes. A problem, no, but we will do our best to avoid it, of course."
This is far from the first issue created by the huge complexity of the latest hybrid engines introduced this year, with their near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power.
Because the engines are fundamentally energy starved, and so cannot deploy their full combined power output at all times, a series of complexities were added into the management of the engines to try to sticking-plaster solutions.
Many of these led to the counter-intuitive driving about which many of the sport's stars have been complaining all season - and more changes have been added since.
Off-track conversation has been dominated by this all year, and rules are changing for next year to alter the energy split to try to ameliorate the issue.
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "What happened at the start obviously is not ideal in terms of presentation of the sport.
"But at the same time it is the first year of new regulations, quite complex from a regulatory point of view, and it was also the first time we started in such conditions.
"So we have to concede that F1 has done an excellent job in making some new regulations that came with some question marks from a power-unit behaviour point of view when it came to racing for instance.
"We have to acknowledge there has been really good work to make the show and racing work, and if there are some glitches occasionally, we have to accept they are glitches for everyone, be supportive and make sure it doesn't happen again."
The problem had a secondary consequence - the field order was jumbled up, and one reading of the rules could have meant the grid order should change for any restart.
But while the FIA's software engineers were rewriting the code as fast as possible, it was determined that, as this situation had never occurred before, and as the problem was out of any competitor's control, the most appropriate order was to revert to the original grid.
Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord said: "If you think of the millions of people watching around the world, they tune in for the start and suddenly the cars are all in a jumbled up order because of something that happened 40 minutes earlier and it was behind a safety car on a formation lap. That would have been a much harder thing to explain than resetting and then going from where we did."

Verstappen's 'amazing' win crowns Red Bull comeback
"Amazing" was the word Verstappen chose to describe his and Red Bull's first win of the 2026 season at a chaotic, bizarre and, in some ways, unprecedented race.
It would be wrong to say the victory was a complete surprise, as it came after three consecutive podium finishes in which the four-time champion appeared to be edging closer and closer to such an achievement.
But it certainly adds a fresh twist to a season of fluctuating fortunes at the front, in which the only real constant has been Kimi Antonelli, as the championship heads into its final stretch.
It was Verstappen's 72nd victory and it came in a manner entirely familiar to those who have followed his career - but entirely unfamiliar to this season.
The Dutchman was the man all weekend at Sepang, where Verstappen also won the last time the track held a race in 2017. As early as Friday afternoon his rivals were all saying he was going to be difficult to beat.
He duly delivered a dominant win, which barely looked in doubt even through the chaos of a delayed start, software glitches caused by a bug in the mandated FIA engine settings that wreaked havoc for him and several other drivers on a formation lap, losing the lead to the two Mercedes off the line and a late safety car period.
What was remarkable about that, though, is that until Malaysia not once so far this season had Verstappen had been in this position.
Red Bull started this year in a bit of a state.
The fourth fastest car among the big four teams, it was debatable at times in the early races whether their car was even better than that of their junior team, Racing Bulls.
All year, Verstappen has been battling an inconsistent handling balance and there was doubt for some time as to whether he would even stay at Red Bull beyond this year.
Although contracted until the end of 2028, it was widely known there were performance-related clauses in his contract that allowed him to leave, and McLaren courted him in the summer.
In the end, though. Verstappen decided to stay, saying he liked the environment at Red Bull, he had faith they would return to the front, and he did not mind a bit of extra work helping them do it.
Those sentiments were expressed in an interview at the Italian Grand Prix a month ago. He finished third that weekend, but even that recently there was no indication a performance such as this was in the offing.
But a trickle of upgrades in the past few races finally all came together with the introduction of a new floor in Baku, the weekend before Malaysia.
There, awkward circumstances in qualifying left him eighth on the grid when by merit he would have been on the front row. But a late safety car closed up the field, and he spent the final stint right on the gearbox of George Russell's leading Mercedes, and lost out on the win by less than 0.2secs.

"Step by step, we've been getting closer and closer, and today, and of course especially this whole weekend, we've been really in good form. So, yeah, it's amazing."
There are six or seven races remaining, depending on whether F1 gets the security reassurances it needs to give it the final confidence to commit to the end of the season grands prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi in the context of the war in the Middle East.
On this basis, Verstappen could well be a factor in all of them.

In 2025, India recorded 55 deaths by malaria, 131 deaths by dengue, and 27 deaths by kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis or black fever), according to Union Health Ministry data, whereas there is no single comparable and comprehensive national measure of its annual human rabies mortality, even as the country looks to eliminate dog-mediated human rabies by the year 2030.
While a community-based study led by researchers from the Indian Council of Medical Research-National Institute of Epidemiology (ICMR-NIE) and published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases recently estimated that 5,726 people die of rabies in India every year, the Health Ministry’s Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme-Integrated Health Information Platform (IDSP-IHIP) system reported 21 deaths by rabies in 2022, 50 in 2023, and 54 in 2024.
In contrast, the Registrar General of India’s Medical Certification of Cause of Death (MCCD) system recorded 66 medically certified rabies deaths in 2022, and 271 in 2023. The MCCD system, however, covers only medically certified deaths and does not capture all registered deaths.
These figures are not directly comparable — the IDSP-IHIP is a disease surveillance system, while the MCCD captures medically certified causes through civil registration. At the national level, the MCCD covered 22.3% of registered deaths in 2022, and 22.0% in 2023. Neither system, therefore, provides a complete national count — underscoring the gaps in India’s rabies mortality surveillance.
The government table, sourced to IDSP-IHIP, had recorded one death in January 2025 but did not provide a figure for all of 2025. The government’s published table, labelled ‘Human Rabies cases (Death)’, gives the source as IDSP-IHIP.
ICMR for its study surveyed 3,37,808 people in 78,807 households across 60 districts in 15 States and estimated that India sees about 9.1 million animal bites every year, including about 5.6 million dog bites.
The researchers used the community survey, laboratory data, and a probability decision-tree model to estimate the number of people who progress from an animal bite to rabies and die. The 5,726 figure is therefore a modelled estimate of annual deaths, and not a count of deaths recorded in hospitals or by government surveillance.
The difference between the two datasets is substantial. The 54 deaths reported through government surveillance in 2024 is less than 1% of the study’s estimated annual toll of 5,726.
“The two figures, however, are generated through different methods and should not be treated as directly equivalent. The figures therefore highlight a large gap between reported surveillance deaths and estimated mortality,” a senior Health Ministry official said.
“Lack of consolidated data is a challenge in rabies eradication. Very often cases and deaths occur in areas of the country where they are not measurable. Vaccination of stray dogs, stringent post-exposure vaccination for humans, and disruption of the rabies chain is essential to curb the problem,” Nirmal Kumar Ganguly, medical scientist, public health expert, and former ICMR chief, speaking exclusively to The Hindu, said.
The National Centre for Disease Control itself says efforts are continuing to make human rabies a notifiable disease across India, and that all States have been asked to notify the disease under the relevant State legislation.
The Health Ministry has also acknowledged the surveillance challenge, with deaths occurring outside the formal health system posing an additional difficulty in capturing the full burden of disease.
Meanwhile, the Lancet study found important gaps even after animal bites. About one in five dog-bite victims had not received the anti-rabies vaccine, while only 66.2% had received at least three doses. Among those who received only one dose, nearly half did not complete the vaccination course. Only about one in 10 eligible victims received passive immunisation.
Rabies is a vaccine-preventable viral disease that attacks the central nervous system and is almost invariably fatal once symptoms appear, with infected dog bites causing most human transmission.
The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that domestic dogs are responsible for up to 99% of human rabies transmission. Globally, rabies causes an estimated 59,000 human deaths every year, with more than 95% of deaths occurring in Africa and Asia.
The WHO estimates that India accounts for 35% of rabies deaths globally and 59.9% of rabies deaths in Asia, underlining the country’s significant contribution to the global burden. Children are particularly vulnerable. The WHO says 40% of people bitten by suspected rabid animals are children under 15 years. Rabies is entirely preventable through timely vaccination of dogs and prompt post-exposure care.
The ICMR-funded study states that although there has been a substantial decline in human rabies deaths over the past two decades, India needs to fast-track its actions to eliminate dog-mediated human rabies by 2030 by adopting a focused ‘One Health’ approach — integrating human and animal surveillance, ensuring timely administration of the full course of post-exposure prophylaxis, and accelerating dog vaccination across the country.

Ladli Behna proved costly: Madhya Pradesh CM's witty reply to girl's query
Madhya Pradesh CM Mohan Yadav joked that the Ladli Behna scheme had proved "very expensive" when Bundeli creator Binnu Rani asked what he had planned for "Binnus", or daughters. He then quipped that she was "too young" for the scheme and should grow older to benefit from it.
Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister Dr Mohan Yadav's lighter side was on display at the Bundeli Sammelan held in Bhopal.
A discussion was underway at Ravindra Bhavan on issues such as Bundeli culture, youth and employment when a question from popular Chhatarpur-based Bundeli content creator Binnu Rani suddenly lightened the mood.
At the event, organised as part of the ‘Bundeli Bauchhar’ programme, Binnu Rani asked Yadav what his plan was for “Binnus”, or daughters, given that he had done a lot for “Jijjis”, or sisters, in the state.
Smiling at the question, Yadav replied in a humorous manner, “You don't know, Ladli Behna has already proved very expensive. I had no idea that becoming Chief Minister would come with such a heavy blow.”
His response was met with laughter and applause across the hall.
Yadav then jokingly told Binnu Rani, “You are still too young for this scheme. Grow a little older, and then you will benefit from it.” His remark drew loud applause from those present.
CM ALSO SPEAKS ABOUT LADLI BEHNA
During the interaction, Yadav also spoke about the Ladli Behna scheme, saying that after becoming Chief Minister, he got a real sense of the government's financial responsibilities. Despite this, he said, the government would not shy away from taking decisions in the interests of women.
He said the scheme was launched with a monthly amount of Rs 1,000, which has now been increased to Rs 1,500. Despite the initial financial challenges, he said, the government's objective was to make women in the state financially stronger and empowered.

A Laotian man deported by the US to the African kingdom of Eswatini has been released from prison, ending an ordeal lasting for more than a year in a country where he has no ties.
Phone Chomsavanh was deported in July 2025 along with four other people under president Donald Trump’s contentious third-country deportation programme.
Mr Chomsavanh, who had arrived in the US as a minor, had no connection with Eswatini.
His American lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen, said Mr Chomsavanh had only been informed that he was being deported to Eswatini shortly before a military cargo plane carrying him landed in the African nation.
Mr Chomsavanh was freed from the maximum-security Matsapha Correctional Complex near the administrative capital Mbabane after 14 months, pending his deportation to Laos, according to Mr Nguyen.
Mr Chomsavanh and the four fellow immigrants deported to Eswatini with him were convicted of serious crimes in the US, but had served their sentences by the time they put were on the military aircraft.
“He’d already served his time,” the lawyer said. “Instead they put him on a plane without telling him where it was headed and left him in a prison in a country he had never heard of, where nobody ever accused him of anything.”
“He sat there for more than a year. No notice, no hearing, no chance to object. That is not due process by any definition.”
The US had described the deportees as “criminal illegal aliens”.
“This flight took individuals so uniquely barbaric that their home countries refused to take them back," Tricia McLaughlin, assistant secretary for homeland security, said at the time.
Mr Chomsavanh was born in a refugee camp in Thailand to parents who had fled Laos. His family had moved to the US when he was seven, his lawyer said.
Thousands of Laotian families affected by the relentless American bombing of their country during the Vietnam war were resettled in the US.
Mr Chomsavanh is one of around 500 immigrants who have been deported to African countries that aren’t their home nations since the third-country programme began last year, according to advocacy groups Human Rights First and Refugees International.
About a dozen African countries have accepted third-country immigrants from the US so far, some in exchange for millions of dollars in payments. Eswatini, Africa’s last absolute monarchy ruled by a king, has received $5.1m from the US to take some of the deportees, according to an agreement between the two countries.
In July this year, Amnesty International said at least 25 more people had been removed from the US to Eswatini under the same arrangement.
The third-country programme, which sees immigrants deported to places they have no ties to, has been fiercely criticised by rights groups and lawyers. It has been the subject of legal challenges in the US and in some of the countries where immigrants have been sent.
The Trump administration has defended the policy as a means to quickly remove immigrants who have received their final deportation orders but whose home countries might not immediately want to take them back.
Last month, a US appeals court upheld a judge’s ruling to halt the programme because it did not give immigrants facing removal from the US time to challenge their deportation to a third country if they feared persecution or torture there.
