A video showing Indian Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that he said Major Rajendra Pratap drank cow urine for 40 days to quench his thirst during the 1965 India-Pakistan war and urged modern soldiers to continue the practice. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Indian Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth stated that Major Rajendra Pratap drank cow urine for 40 days to quench his thirst during the 1965 India-Pakistan war and urged modern soldiers to continue the practice.
Fact: The viral video has been digitally altered. The original footage shows COAS General Dhiraj Seth visiting a mega cataract surgery camp in Tangdhar, Kupwara district, where he interacted with patients and army veterans. The audio promoting the consumption of cow urine was not part of the original video and has been falsely attributed to him. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led to reports from several media outlets with similar visuals (here, here, here, here). According to the descriptions, the video shows Chief of the Army Staff (COAS) General Dhiraj Seth visiting a mega cataract surgery camp organised by the Indian Army in Tangdhar, Kupwara district. He is also seen interacting with patients and army veterans.
After verifying these reports, we could not find any mention of General Dhiraj Seth talking about cow urine during his interaction with patients or army veterans.
Further, we analysed the audio using AI detection tools Hiya and Resemble AI, which indicated that the audio is likely AI-generated and may involve voice impersonation.
We also found that on 27 September 2026, the Indian Army’s official Fact Check handle clarified that the video had been digitally altered. It stated that genuine footage of the Army Chief had been manipulated and falsely attributed to fictitious statements that were unrelated to the original event.
To sum up, this video showing COAS General Dhiraj Seth promoting the consumption of cow urine has been digitally manipulated.

How to turn on Developer Mode on your Chromebook
It's easy, but it's also a little risky.
Chromebooks have earned their reputation as affordable, secure and simple machines over the years. Most owners never venture beyond the Play Store, downloading apps and calling it a day. But much like Android power users, Chromebook owners can take things one step further and unlock a completely different experience by turning on Developer Mode.
Developer Mode strips away many of ChromeOS' built-in protections and gives you full control over the system, which may or may not be a good idea depending on your technical knowledge. Still, you get root access, kernel modifications and the ability to install software that was never on the Play Store. It's a powerful tool, so it's not something you should use without understanding what you're getting into.
So what exactly does Developer Mode do? When does it actually make sense to use it? How do you enable this feature? We'll dig through everything and discuss what changes once Developer Mode is on and whether it's something you need as you use your Chromebook as your everyday computer.
What is Developer Mode on a Chromebook?
Developer Mode is a system setting that gives you more control over how your device operates, relaxing ChromeOS' "verified boot" protections. Normally, ChromeOS runs on a locked-down system. It double-checks itself on every boot, reverting automatically if something looks tampered with and sandboxing every app and webpage so problems can't spread. Developer Mode tears down most of those protections.
As with most systems, once Developer Mode is enabled, you gain full system access. That means you can change the ChromeOS kernel and core files. The trade-off is security. With Verified Boot relaxed, your Chromebook no longer has some of its default defenses against malicious tampering. Lest you forget you made this move, there'll be a visual reminder in the form of a warning screen on startup that reads OS Verification is OFF or You are in Developer Mode. The warning times out after 30 seconds with a warning beep, so there's no way to say you didn't know. It's not a sign of danger, but it's a signal that your system is running without a safety net.
When would you actually need Developer Mode?
Let's be honest here: Developer Mode isn't something the average Chromebook owner needs to think about. Most day-to-day tasks like shooting emails, browsing, streaming, editing documents and so on work just fine within the safety brackets provided by stock ChromeOS.
That said, there are situations when enabling Developer Mode is needed. For instance, while modern ChromeOS includes built-in support for running Linux apps in a secure sandbox, deeper system-level modifications still require Developer Mode. You'll need it if you want full root shell access to the OS, need to load custom Linux kernels or plan to run alternative operating systems. Developer Mode is also required for advanced system tweaks like firmware modifications and boot flag changes.
Also, if you want to quickly double-click and install APK files directly through the native ChromeOS Files app without touching the command line, Developer Mode is required. It's worth noting that ChromeOS now allows you to sideload APKs securely without Developer Mode by enabling Android Debug Bridge inside the official Linux environment. If that's the reason you're looking into Developer Mode, you might want to try this out first.
Of course, Developer Mode is also going to be a feature that actual developers building or debugging apps for ChromeOS might use. If none of these apply to you, there's a strong chance you should leave your Chromebook alone. Note that school- or work-managed Chromebooks usually have Developer Mode blocked by the administrator.
How to turn on Developer Mode
If you still want to turn on Developer Mode, then you need to follow a few steps. One important thing to know is that switching between Normal and Developer Mode wipes all local user data.
- Let's boot the system into Recovery Mode. Press and hold Esc + Refresh + Power simultaneously to do this on a standard Chromebook laptop.
- From the Recovery screen, press Ctrl + D and confirm the prompt that pops up asking whether you want to turn OS Verification off. The system will then reboot.
- Next, you'll see one of two notifications: "You are in Developer Mode" or "OS Verification is OFF" (the exact wording can vary by device). Press Ctrl + D to start the transition right away, or just wait 30 seconds for the beep and it will begin on its own. This is when the local data gets wiped. The process can take up to 15 minutes, so do not interrupt it.
Developer Mode transforms a Chromebook from a simplified, locked-down device into a system that's a lot easier to customize. The cost, however, is your device's security — one of the things that make ChromeOS appealing in the first place, especially for people who were hoping to get an affordable Chromebook to use as their daily driver. For developers or Linux enthusiasts, however, it's a genuinely useful tool. If you decide to enable it, back up your files first, keep your device plugged in and follow the steps carefully.

Torrential rain and potentially damaging flooding are forecast in eastern Spain over the coming days, as cold upper air moves over the warm, humid surface air of the Mediterranean Sea, fuelling violent, slow-moving thunderstorms near Spain’s east coast. The weather pattern, known as a Dana, occurs most often in autumn.
Models show more than 100mm of rain could fall across the region on Friday, with 200-300mm possible in some areas. Cities including Valencia and Castelló de la Plana, are most at risk. Valencia has experienced several damaging floods in recent years. Catalonia has now put three towns under lockdown and Valencia has shut schools for nearly half a million children.
Meanwhile, heavy rainfall in Nepal last week resulted in 542 disaster incidents and left 27 people dead between 24 and 27 September, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Of the recorded incidents, 304 were related to landslides while 87 were linked to flooding.
During this extremely wet period, 186 meteorological sites recorded more than 100mm of rainfall, with Dedhgaun, in Lumbini province, recording 544.2mm. Nearly a million people received SMS flood warnings, and 2,000 people living in high-risk areas were relocated.
This heavy rainfall also affected the Gandak River in Bihar, north-east India, which reached a record water level of 91.25 metres on Tuesday, 0.35m metres above the previous record, set only in 2024, according to the water resources department. So far, 169 seepage points along the embankments have been repaired, with teams deployed across several sites along the river as the embankments continue to face heavy water pressure.
Strong winds, heavy rainfall and coastal flooding have hit the north-east US as a very deep area of low pressure developed into a nor’easter on Saturday. Such storms are named due to the north-easterly winds typically affecting coastal areas. This was the first nor’easter of the autumn and winter season, bringing gusts of up to 74mph (119km/h) and waves rising to 3 metres.
The storm left approximately 200,000 people without power, inundated the streets of New York City and killed one person when a tree fell in Brooklyn. However, the storm also uncovered a piece of history as the wreckage from the Warren Sawyer, a three-masted ship destroyed in 1884, washed ashore on Nantucket, off Cape Cod in Massachusetts.

Swyer syndrome is a rare condition in which a person is born with XY chromosomes, the combination usually associated with males, but their reproductive organs develop along a typically female pattern. The person typically has female external anatomy and a uterus and fallopian tubes.
The condition often goes unnoticed during childhood and comes to light during adolescence, when puberty does not progress normally or menstruation does not begin. It can also be diagnosed later during investigations for infertility. Here’s all you need to know about Swyer syndrome.
What is Swyer syndrome?
Swyer syndrome is a rare difference of sex development, medically known as 46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis. According to the US’ Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center, a person with the condition has a 46,XY chromosome pattern, but the gonads do not develop into functioning testes. Instead, they remain as small, non-functioning structures called “streak gonads”. The person generally develops female external genitalia, while the uterus and fallopian tubes are usually present. The condition is estimated to occur in about one in 80,000 people,
Swyer syndrome results from disruption of the genetic pathway involved in testicular development during early embryonic development. The SRY gene, located on the Y chromosome, plays an important role in initiating this process. However, an SRY mutation is not found in every person with Swyer syndrome.
What are the symptoms?
Swyer syndrome may not be apparent during childhood and often comes to light during adolescence, when puberty does not progress normally. One of the most characteristic signs is primary amenorrhoea, meaning that menstruation does not begin.
Delayed or incomplete development of secondary sexual characteristics can also prompt investigation. Because the streak gonads do not produce sufficient sex hormones, spontaneous breast development may be limited. The condition can sometimes remain undiagnosed even when a person reaches adulthood.
How is Swyer syndrome diagnosed?
Diagnosis usually involves looking at the person’s chromosomes, hormone levels and reproductive anatomy. Karyotyping, a test that examines the number and structure of chromosomes, typically shows a 46,XY pattern in Swyer syndrome. Blood tests generally show evidence of gonadal failure, including low levels of sex hormones and elevated levels of hormones such as follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinising hormone. Ultrasound or MRI can be used to examine the uterus and the gonads.
Genetic testing can be used to investigate the underlying cause, including variants in SRY and other genes involved in gonadal development. However, not finding an SRY mutation does not exclude Swyer syndrome. In some patients, even more extensive genetic testing may not identify the precise molecular cause.
Can Swyer syndrome be treated?
There is currently no treatment that can change the 46,XY chromosome pattern or turn the streak gonads into functioning ovaries. However, the effects of Swyer syndrome can be effectively managed. Hormone replacement therapy, usually involving oestrogen and subsequently an appropriate progestogen regimen when indicated, is used to induce and maintain puberty, support development of secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone health.
The streak gonads also need to be assessed because they carry an increased risk of gonadoblastoma, a type of germ-cell tumour. Decisions about gonadectomy and its timing are now generally individualised according to the underlying diagnosis and tumour risk.
Fertility is another important consideration. Because the streak gonads cannot produce eggs, people with Swyer syndrome cannot conceive using their own eggs. However, if the uterus is present and sufficiently developed, pregnancy can be possible through IVF using a donated egg or embryo. Research shows that patients with Swyer syndrome can have successful pregnancies following endometrial preparation with hormones and IVF using donated eggs. Following pregnancy and delivery, continued hormone replacement is important for maintaining bone health.
In other words, Swyer syndrome itself cannot currently be reversed, but its effects can be managed. Hormone replacement can address the absence of normal gonadal hormones, removal of the streak gonads can reduce the risk of tumours, and assisted reproductive techniques can make pregnancy possible for some patients.

Russian lab worker dies of ‘unknown’ virus as hundreds placed in quarantine
Emergency quarantine protocols are in place in Irkutsk after a suspected laboratory accident

Russian health authorities have reportedly placed hundreds of people in quarantine in Siberia following the death of a laboratory worker who was exposed to an “unknown” virus.
The 28-year-old victim was an employee at the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov, a town near the regional capital of Irkutsk, according to reports.
Prior to her death, she reportedly told medical personnel that she had accidentally broken a test tube containing live biological samples while working inside the facility.
She was subsequently hospitalised with severe pneumonia of "unknown origin," placed on a ventilator, and died shortly after on Thursday.
State consumer safety watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said that emergency sanitary protocols were immediately enacted following a case involving "pneumonia of unknown etiology" at the facility.
Since, Rospotrebnadzor has maintained that the broader situation in the Irkutsk region remains stable.
At least 197 people suspected of having direct or indirect contact with the technician have been placed under medical isolation, according to independent regional news outlet Liudi Baikala. More than 100 of those individuals are currently being monitored in hospital wards.
At the same time, local authorities have instituted strict quarantine measures across the district, targeting the Shelekhov District Hospital, a nearby maternity facility, and a local aluminium plant.
Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev urged residents to remain calm, writing on Telegram that an anti-epidemic commission convened to address a "suspected case of a particularly dangerous infection."
While his public statement did not acknowledge the worker's death, Kobzev stated that all identified close contacts remain asymptomatic and have tested negative.
Russian law enforcement agencies have reportedly opened a criminal investigation into potential workplace health and safety violations resulting in the lab worker’s death.
Former Rospotrebnadzor head Gennady Onishchenko downplayed the threat in comments to state news agency TASS, stating that the infection in the Irkutsk region is "most likely not the plague, but even if confirmed, there will be no spread of this disease."
He added that widespread transmission remains unlikely, noting that cooler seasonal temperatures would help contain potential spread.
Because the facility specialises in dangerous pathogens, the incident has drawn speculation it could be pneumonic plague – one of three variants caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
Unlike bubonic and septicemic plagues, which generally pass to humans via flea bites or contact with infected animals, pneumonic plague attacks the lungs directly and can easily spread from person to person through airborne respiratory droplets.
According to guidelines from the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, patients infected with pneumonic plague typically experience rapid onset fever, headaches, and physical weakness, alongside severe respiratory distress such as shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing, and watery or blood-tinged mucus.
While the World Health Organisation (WHO) warns that the disease carries a high mortality rate if untreated, it remains highly manageable with early antibiotic administration and standard infection control measures.

From Patagonia vests to Rolex Submariners, the finance world is full of status symbols and fashion flexes. Wealthy Swiss investors have one of the weirdest: a blue briefcase filled with roughly 10 pounds of chocolate.
Lindt shareholders who vote at the Swiss chocolatier's annual meeting in Zurich every April receive a "Schokoladekoffer" or "chocolate suitcase."
The briefcase is free, but a Lindt voting share costs around 78,000 Swiss francs, or more than $94,000. The shares have traded as high as 132,000 Swiss francs — north of $150,000 — within the past year.
"Nobody rationally spends around 100,000 Swiss francs on a share because they want 3kg of free chocolate," Thierry Borgeat, the cofounder and chief investor of Swiss asset manager arvy, told Business Insider by email on Monday. "But that is exactly what makes it fun."
"It's a flex — but a very Swiss kind of flex," Borgeat continued. "You don't buy a Ferrari or a flashy watch to show people you have money. You own one registered share in a 180-year-old Swiss chocolate company, attend the annual meeting, and then quietly walk through Zurich carrying three kilograms of chocolate in a blue suitcase."
Borgeat recalled that when he worked in wealth management, clients and private bankers would bring their sweet hauls to the office after the annual meeting and share their bars and truffles.
Doing so "had the convenient side effect of letting everyone know that you owned a full Lindt registered share," he said.
Borgeat noted the "quirky tradition has become so exclusive" because Lindt has been an "exceptional long-term investment," resulting in its shares becoming "extraordinarily valuable over time."
Lindt stock climbed from around 3,600 Swiss francs in April 1995 to 132,000 at its peak last October, a 36-fold increase. But it has slumped in recent months as record temperatures have sapped sales, and historically high cocoa prices have inflated the chocolatier's costs and crimped its profits.
Why Lindt rewards its investors
"We consider this a thank you for their efforts," a Lindt & Sprüngli spokesperson told Business Insider about the company's yearly gift to voting shareholders.
"The box contains a variety of Lindt products such as Excellence bars and Lindor truffles, but we don't reveal what's exactly inside because it's meant to be a surprise for our shareholders," the spokesperson added.
Lawrence Cunningham, the director of the Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware, said the gift boxes were "good marketing and a thoughtful gesture."
"It thanks shareholders for showing up and puts the company's product in their hands," he said, adding that it also fosters goodwill.
The buzzy phenomenon is reminiscent of Berkshire Hathaway's annual meeting. Every May, thousands of shareholders from across the world fly to Warren Buffett's hometown of Omaha, not only to see the legendary investor in person, but also to load up on discounted wares from Berkshire's many businesses, including boxed-chocolate maker See's Candies.
Borgeat said he can "definitely see the similarities" between Berkshire and Lindt as "companies that become more than just investments — they create a sense of identity and community among their shareholders."
"Berkshire has Omaha and See's Candies," he continued. "Lindt has Zurich and the blue chocolate suitcase."

Inside Djibouti refugee camp for thousands fleeing Houthi advance in Yemen

The BBC's Frank Gardner visited a refugee camp in Obock, a small port town where officials are preparing for the arrival of up to 10,000 refugees.
The UN International Organisation for Migration said people were travelling on overcrowded boats and arriving with very limited food and water.
The crossings were sparked by an offensive by the Iran-backed Houthi movement to take control of a key island and seize the strategically important port of Mokha.

Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?
- Published
The pilot who was stabbed on an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday has been identified as Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar.
Capt Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, forcing the plane to divert to Saudi Arabia.
The captain, who has been hailed as a "true hero" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was taken to a hospital in Tubak City, north-western Saudi Arabia, where he remains in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Riyadh.
Writing on X, Netanyahu said Capt Machchhar "saved the lives of 174 people" and prevented "a catastrophic mid-air disaster".
What do we know about Capt Machchhar?
Capt Machchhar joined Flydubai in 2022 - he was an experienced pilot by then, having worked at Indian airline SpiceJet since 2011.
He has more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile.
His former employer SpiceJet issued a statement calling Machchhar a "hero" who had saved "countless lives".
Last year, Capt Machchhar spoke about how he started flying and his experiences as a pilot on a podcast called Bona-Fide Banter.
Aviation, he said, was "never a childhood dream". When he was around 19, he joined a management course, planning to work with his family's business. But then he came across an aviation seminar and "the bug bit [him]," he added.
Machchhar also spoke about how, when he wore his pilot's uniform, he was "no-nonsense" and thought "about work 100%". But unlike his younger days, he added, he now placed a greater value on having a healthy work-life balance and spending time with family.
"Give personal life equal importance - it will help you fly longer," he advised.
He also detailed challenges he had faced in the air, including when a passenger went into early labour and the crew worked together to ensure the baby was born safely.
"In aviation terms, I was lucky to grow up with people who helped me be the pilot that I am today," he said, crediting senior pilots with teaching him how to face stressful situations.
At the time of the conversation, Capt Machchhar said that no plane he'd flown had had to make an emergency landing. He had, however, faced medical emergencies and minor aircraft issues causing delays.
He said delays were "not my problem. As long as you're walking out of the aircraft [safely], that's what I want."
Indian social media has been awash with praise for Capt Machchhar since his identity emerged, with commenters calling him a hero. Snippets from the podcast have also gone viral.
What happened on the Flydubai flight?
Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the United Arab Emirates at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time) en route to Ben Gurion Airport in Israel.
The flight was carrying at least 150 people, with Netanyahu saying "almost all" passengers were Israeli.
Data from flight tracking website Flightradar24 shows the plane made a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia around two and a half hours after take-off, dropping more than 17,000ft (5,000m) in less than two minutes at around 05:21.
Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code, which indicates a hijacking.
At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.
Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.
Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots.
But speaking on Wednesday after the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane.
He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".
The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in north-eastern Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data.
The stabbed pilot, who is in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia, was later identified as Capt Machchhar.
Modi and Trump praise Capt Machchhar
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Machchhar "showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others" despite being seriously injured.
"His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy," he wrote in a post on X, adding that he hoped for the pilot's speedy recovery.
Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar praised the pilot's "extraordinary courage and remarkable presence of mind, even in the face of grave danger".
Speaking to reporters at the White House, US President Donald Trump said that "the pilot was in very bad shape" but had the sense to open the cockpit door during the attack.
"Amazing, in a way he was a hero, to open the door. He was able to fall back and get the door open."

India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote.
The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.
Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted in tens of millions of people being deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal.
Opposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured into resigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy.
Last week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru.
The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said, at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?”
Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy.
“Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.”
Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said that the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”.
“We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said.
The election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls.
Anger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try and stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed.
Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights.
Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election commission office in Delhi next week.

Spotlight on new coaches as road to Afcon 2027 begins
- Published
Just eight months on from the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) - and with the world still waiting to find out the ultimate destination of the title - the road to the 2027 tournament begins in earnest.
The 48 sides still in contention will play two rounds of qualifying in this extended international window, which gets under way on Thursday.
Two more matches follow in November, with the groups reaching their denouement with the final two fixtures in March.
The top two in nine of the 12 groups will progress to the 24-team finals in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.
Preparations for the tournament in East Africa may be lagging behind but, with the three hosts all guaranteed qualification, there is only one spot on offer in their respective groups. That means a second-placed finish may potentially not be enough.
Several managerial changes have occurred since the last Afcon in Morocco and this year's Fifa World Cup, while several star players have hung up their boots. Here's what to keep an eye on in the first two rounds of action.
- Senegal appeal date set after Afcon win overturned 
  - Published24 July
Big names in the dugout
Among several coaching changes, two in particular have caught the eye.
Herve Renard, the only man to win Afcon with two different nations, has returned to the Ivory Coast job some 11 years after leading the West Africans to the title.
The 57-year-old Frenchman starts his second stint with the Elephants at home against Ghana on Thursday in what is the standout match in the first round of fixtures.
In the opposing dugout, the experienced Carlos Queiroz is back at the helm after leading the Black Stars to the last 32 at the World Cup. However, Tottenham's Mohammed Kudus is among a number of players to withdraw from his squad.
Patrick Vieira is another high-profile arrival, as the 1998 World Cup champion with France takes charge of Senegal, the country of his birth.
The former Arsenal midfielder, 50, describes the role as "an absolute dream" yet he will begin with two away games against Mozambique and Ethiopia because Dakar is getting ready to host the 2026 Youth Olympics.
- Africa prepares for historic Olympic moment at Dakar 2026 
  - Published23 July
Other new arrivals
Cape Verde were one of the great stories of the 2026 World Cup, pushing Argentina all the way in the last 32 before the debutants lost 3-2 after extra time.
Long-serving coach Bubista has since resigned from the Blue Sharks hotseat, with his former assistant Humberto Bettencourt stepping up.
He will begin his reign in Mali on Friday before hosting Rwanda on Tuesday.
Algeria, Tunisia and South Africa have also changed coaches since the World Cup.
The Tunisians have turned to former Esperance and Renaissance Berkane boss Moin Chaaban as they aim to move on from their disastrous World Cup campaign which saw Sabri Lamouchi dismissed after one game and Renard fail to orchestrate a revival.
Pitso Mosimane has been reappointed by South Africa some 14 years on from his last spell in charge - which saw Bafana Bafana miss out on the 2012 Afcon - and Brahim Hemdani has taken over Algeria after Vladmir Petkovic's departure.
Meanwhile, Afcon legend Claude Le Roy has returned at the age of 78 after signing on for a second stint with Congo-Brazzaville.
The Red Devils have not appeared at the finals since 2015, while Frenchman Le Roy is aiming to coach at a record-extending 10th edition of the finals.
Burkina Faso have turned to ex-Comoros boss Amir Abdou and, after a stint with Libya, 2021 Afcon-winning coach Aliou Cisse has his first competitive matches in charge of Angola.
The former Senegal boss starts with a tough away assignment in Egypt.
An era ends
Some big-name players have called time on their international careers since the World Cup, with several of them former Afcon winners.
Senegal are looking for a new number one after Edouard Mendy hung up his goalkeeping gloves.
The 34-year-old helped the Teranga Lions become champions at the 2021 and 2025 tournaments - even if the latter title is still disputed at the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
Wing wizard Riyad Mahrez, who captained Algeria to the trophy in 2019, has quit international duty while Ivory Coast will have to cope without midfielders Seko Fofana and Jean-Michael Seri.
Ellyes Skhiri has also called time on his international career and will not be involved as Tunisia aim to reach a record-extending 18th consecutive Afcon.
Meanwhile, Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang has stepped back from Gabon duty, saying he felt "humiliated" by his treatment after their exit at the previous tournament.
The 37-year-old was excluded from the national team set-up after their group-stage exit. That sanction was later lifted, but Aubameyang ruled himself out of Sebastien Migne's Panthers squad despite his fine start to the season with Deportivo La Coruna.
Return of the Red Sea Camels
Elsewhere, Eritrea are back in the group stage of Afcon qualifiers - for the first time since the build-up to the 2008 edition - after seeing off Eswatini 4-1 on aggregate in the preliminary round in March.
Chad, Djibouti, Mauritius, Sao Tome and Principe and Seychelles are the other five nations already eliminated.
However, seven Ertirea players absconded after the away leg of their tie which was held in South Africa.
Occurrences of Eritrean sportsmen and women failing to return home to what is a one-party state and a highly militarised society has long been an issue, and was part of the reason for the East Africans withdrawing from qualifying for both the 2023 Afcon and 2026 World Cup.
Yet the Red Sea Camels, who have been drawn alongside Kenya, South Africa and Guinea in Group D, are now largely relying on talent drawn from the diaspora.
Just three home-based players have been named in the squad for their opening two fixtures, which see them take on the tournament co-hosts in Nairobi on Saturday before a 'home' game against Bafana Bafana in Cairo on Tuesday.

A rumor spread in late September 2026 that CNN television host Anderson Cooper built a free hospital for homeless people. According to the claim, the journalist opened the Anderson Cooper Homestead Medical Center in New York, complete with 250 beds, 120 apartments and a range of additional services — all at zero cost to patients.
Snopes readers searched our website and emailed us about the claim, with one reader asking, "Did Anderson Cooper build a free hospital for homeless people in New York?"
Several Facebook users shared the rumor. The posts generally featured the same image allegedly showing Cooper cutting a ribbon in front of a building with a sign reading, "Anderson Cooper Medical Center."
(Jeannette Piña via Facebook)
According to the posts, Cooper said of the hospital, "This is the legacy I want to leave behind." The facility allegedly cost $142 million, with the Anderson Cooper Foundation raising all funds from anonymous donors over an 18-month period — complete with no public fanfare or announcements until opening.
In short, the rumor is false. No evidence suggests Cooper opened a free hospital for homeless people. The claim is nothing more than "AI slop," spam-type content generated using artificial intelligence tools that has, in recent years, deluged social media with untrue stories, as well as fake images and videos, usually featuring public figures.
CNN spokesperson Shimrit Sheetrit said via email that the rumor is false.
Researching the claim
Searches of Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo uncovered no news media outlets reporting that Cooper opened a hospital. Even if a famous person secretly raised funds to open a hospital without publicity, news organizations would at some point publish articles about the facility's existence. Officials would eventually launch a website or use other online means to alert homeless people of the project and its offerings. No such information has been published or shared.
The story in the posts is inconsistent with the AI-generated images accompanying it. For example, the text in one post refers to the hospital as "Anderson Cooper Homestead Medical Center," while the image features a sign reading, "Anderson Cooper Medical Center." A different post (archived) contains other fake images of Cooper wearing completely different clothes at the supposed opening, with the different facility name, "The Anderson Cooper Center." The posts also say there was "no ribbon" and "no fanfare" at the supposed opening, despite the images containing both a ribbon and a crowd.
This claim possibly originated from a post on a Facebook page called The Silver Voice, which links to an external website hosting an advertisement-filled article. That website's domain name appears to be at least partially in Vietnamese, a language that often appears alongside "AI slop" website content, as Snopes has previously reported.
The heartwarming subject matter about Cooper's purported grand act of kindness resembles glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental." Creators of such content capitalize on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up stories, profiting from advertising revenue on external websites to which the posts link. (Snopes has also previously reported on this business strategy.)
AI-generated content and similar rumors
A scan of the Facebook posts' text with AI detection tool Pangram displays the results, "We believe that this entire text is AI," and, "100% of this text is AI." A scan of one of the post's images returns the same result.
Snopes doesn't depend solely on AI detection tools, which vary in reliability, and instead considers the tools' results as one of several data points toward judging an image's authenticity. With Pangram, we bear in mind the platform's strong performance in third-party and internal evaluations, as well as some criticisms of the tool.
Reporters at fact-checking website Lead Stories previously reported on many other celebrities being named in similar "AI slop" stories about them opening free hospitals for homeless people.
Snopes also previously addressed a false claim that first lady Melania Trump and her son, Barron Trump, opened a hospital for homeless people, and a similar rumor about late-night host Stephen Colbert and his wife, Evelyn McGee-Colbert. The latter also features an AI-generated image that resembles the fake photo of Cooper.
For further reading, we previously reported about numerous fabricated stories that circulated online following the deadly Texas flash floods in July 2025, as well as how those false accounts show signs of originating in Southeast Asia.

Yemen's government declares major military campaign against Houthis
In short:
Yemen's government has announced a major military operation against Houthi rebels holding the nation's capital, Sanaa.
The Houthis have held the city and vast parts of Yemen's north-west, where most of the population live, since 2014.
They have withstood a series of attacks by Saudi Arabia, the UAE and their Western allies over the years.
Yemen's Saudi-backed government says it is launching a major military campaign to recapture all areas of the country controlled by the Iran-backed Houthis.
The internationally recognised government's armed forces would press the offensive "until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia", Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address.
A military spokesperson later called on the Houthis to lay down their weapons.
The Houthis, known formally as Ansar Allah, have held Yemen's capital Sanaa and parts of the north-west since 2014.
They have so far withstood a series of attacks over the years by Saudi Arabia, the UAE and their Western allies.
The movement launched a surprise offensive last month, capturing the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and some 150 kilometres of coast on the Red Sea, giving the Houthis new leverage over the international shipping route.
That advance also opened a new front in the wider US-Israeli war against Iran, which began in February.
Houthis say they struck Saudi Arabia
As the Yemeni government, known as the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), made its announcement, the Houthis said they had launched missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and the Khurais area.
They claimed the attacks caused major fires and were in response to 50 Saudi-led air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.
Loading...
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Mr Alimi said the decision to launch the military campaign came after all chances of de-escalating the conflict were exhausted.
New front in Middle East war
The US is already providing intelligence to support Riyadh's operations in Yemen, while some regional and European nations are providing defensive military aid to the kingdom.
The US war on Iran has decimated a layer of Iranian military and political leadership, but has also entangled Washington in a new engagement in the Middle East.
Yemen has been mired in conflict for years, with an array of local armed groups backed by competing regional and international actors.
After a popular uprising that was part of the Arab Spring movements in 2011, the Houthis, an armed group of Zaidi Shi'ite Muslims, captured Sanaa.
The government has controlled the south and east of the country since the Houthi takeover.
Saudi Arabia entered Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition in support of the PLC, but failed to defeat the Houthis.
A truce agreed between the warring parties in 2022 largely held until this year.
Houthis at the front door
The Houthis have maintained the initiative on the ground since seizing control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in their lightning offensive last month that saw government forces collapse.
Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia.
In the past 48 hours, the Houthis have also made gains against near Yemen's Taiz, military sources said, advancing on the last road between the city and Aden.
Houthi control over the Taiz-Aden road would lead to an effective siege of the city, Yemen's third-largest, inhabited by hundreds of thousands of civilians.
The city is important not just for its strategic location; Alimi is from the region, and a siege of Taiz would amplify an already-dire humanitarian situation in the country.
Three in four families in parts of Yemen are going hungry from the impact of the surge in fighting, which has displaced tens of thousands of people and disrupted supplies to millions, the World Food Programme said last week.

Martin Brundle's verdict on Bahrain GP software 'chaos' and how track tricked Ferrari and McLaren into wrong tyre choice
Sky Sports F1's Martin Brundle delves into the talking points from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, assessing the chaos caused by a software glitch, a major tyre-choice drama, and Max Verstappen's return to the top step of the podium for Red Bull
Monday 5 October 2026 18:50, UK
The Bahrain GP in Malaysia was one of the crazier races I've seen in F1. Eventually, this collaboration of lateral thinking which ensured a Grand Prix took place on a great track we have missed in F1 for nine years, was a huge success.
I want to say straight away that I know from meeting numerous fans over the weekend, particularly at the airport on Monday morning, that a great many people suffered very long delays getting out of the venue and back to their bases.
Road systems became gridlocked and transit buses blocked. While the event was necessarily hurriedly assembled, this was still disappointing, and I want to add my personal appreciation to those fans in Malaysia.

At least those I spoke with said they thoroughly enjoyed the race and spectacle, many of whom would also have got as wet through as I did on the grid walk.
That weather cell and deluge popped up literally just as the cars headed to the grid, and as the 'easy up' shelters were positioned over the cars and wet tyres feverishly wheeled out, the standing water around the track was such that the start procedure was suspended.
When the rain eased, and with pleasing urgency, it was declared that there would be two formation laps behind the Safety Car and then a proper standing start.
'Chaos' before the start as software glitches in wet
That was all fine until we started seeing a number of cars travelling very slowly and then stopping altogether, except for the Safety Car which continued at normal pace, increasingly out by itself.
Those still running were wary of the regulations and reluctant to pass very slow cars. Many of the six Ferrari-powered cars seemed affected, some Red Bull Powertrains and a McLaren Mercedes too. Given this was the first time many of the all-new 2026 cars had run in wet conditions, there was clearly an unexpected issue.
It turned out to be FIA software settings. All cars must run a standard FIA 'brain' for many essential functions to ensure parity and abide by regulations, which couldn't compute with cars travelling at such increasingly slow speeds, shutting down power delivery.
Cars were eventually spread out all over the track in two and then three tranches. Drivers at the side of the track effectively having to hit the control/alt/delete to restart their motors. It was chaos and the Safety Car was about to lap many cars which should have been diligently following it.
The only option was to abandon the whole thing and recover to the pits, at which point the Safety Car was bizarrely mid pack rather than at the front.
The next problem was to unravel the problem and regulations; would those who fully stopped and lost position, like Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari, be obliged to start from the position they arrived back in the fast lane of the pits?
Although it took 40 minutes all told, which actually conveniently allowed the rain cell to clear the district, a smart and fair decision was made that the restart would be in original grid order. Furthermore, the FIA quickly found the issue, rewrote some code altering key power unit operating parameters which are in place for starting procedures when the car is under 50kph, and flashed that 'patch' to all the cars, not all of which had experienced problems, such as the Aston Martins.
Anyway, it worked, even though cars would now be travelling faster behind the Safety Car on pit exit with much better track conditions, and teams and drivers by then knew what to look out for.
'Sponge-like' surface catches out Ferrari and McLaren
This track, often doused mid-race with a cloudburst, used to dry out remarkably quickly, but temperatures had been much lower on race day than during practice and qualifying. The pit lane was bone dry, and, on television pictures, so was the pit straight and many other areas. Which tyres to use for the new standing start, more than an hour and a half after the original time slot, was the next dilemma.
It looked like slick dry tyres to me, and several thought so too, like Ferrari, McLaren, Audi and Aston Martin. As soon as the cars left behind the Safety Car it was clear there was much more spray than expected, and areas such as turns three and five were still quite wet.
Some like Oscar Piastri at McLaren and Audi recognised immediately that the right tyre was the intermediate with the light water grooves. Others like Hamilton and Lando Norris decided to stick with it and hope for fast improvement. Charles Leclerc did too but contact on the first racing lap broke his front wing and he had to pit anyway, so they also fitted intermediates. Despite that long stop, in no time at all he'd caught Hamilton's sister Ferrari and passed him, such was the painfully slow pace on dry tyres.
The track surface was heavily worn in places, and the extreme weather in these parts clearly take their toll year-round. There had been no time, and no appetite either given the one-off aspect of this event, to resurface it. The nature of the asphalt, and sometimes over-60 degrees Celsius surface temperature, had been stressing the dry tyres throughout practice and qualifying with heat degradation.
Now, in a situation which George Russell described over his radio as 'weird', the track wasn't drying anything like as fast as expected. I believe that the old asphalt, with billions of tiny pockets of water in the surface, acted like a sponge.
Verstappen seizes control as Hamilton fights back
Out front it was a thrilling battle between the two Mercedes of Kimi Antonelli and Russell, and Max Verstappen's Red Bull, who were all on intermediate tyres. Max had looked the favourite to win this race for three days such was his pace.
It would be nine laps before the leading slick-tyred car of Norris was faster than the intermediate-shod cars, and by then the slick runners were over a minute behind. Importantly, Hamilton had resisted the call to change onto intermediates based on the fact that he'd taken the pain and there was no point in pitting now.
Just at that moment Valtteri Bottas spun off his Cadillac deep into the gravel at turn 13 and there was a Safety Car deployed. It was perfect timing for the leaders as they could ditch their now overheating inters during a pit stop that would cost 18 seconds rather than 26 given the pack on track were at Safety Car speeds.
Crucially the full (not virtual) Safety Car would stay out for a good while and this allowed the slick runners to close back up and negate the huge time losses they had thus far suffered, even if they had plenty of traffic between them and their natural rivals up front who had chosen the right tyres. This was a key reset for the race.
Hamilton didn't pit and preferred track position to fresh rubber. He would impressively run his starting soft compound dry tyres for 31 laps, and it would pay dividends.
Championship leader Antonelli had been going along nicely in the lead, and there had been some quality overtakes between him and team-mate Russell. On dry tyres the natural speed of Verstappen, and his wily restarts, would put him into a lead which he would never be seriously challenged despite some more dramas to come.
The fast-starting Racing Bulls had been going along very nicely in the hands of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad, who had started at the very back due to power unit penalties. Esteban Ocon had similarly been running in sixth in his Haas, and Carlos Sainz had fast-started his Williams into the top 10 too. But as the track fully dried, while it was a three-horse race out front, the usual suspects in the form of the two Ferraris and two McLarens made their way forward.
Isack Hadjar had been running in a solid fourth place in the second Red Bull, having shown decent speed again all weekend, and, given he would suffer a relative loss of power in the closing stages, he could have well have done without what happened next.
Russell engine failure 'sums up his season'
Alex Albon's Williams would grind to a halt on the exit of turn three on lap 42 of 55, albeit well parked next to a service road. The car wouldn't easily move though and so a vehicle and marshals would have to emerge from behind the barriers, meaning a full Safety Car was called again in order to control the pack to give space to recover the Williams.
Over the next couple of laps most cars would stop for fresh, albeit mostly used tyres, in order to have decent grip for the restart and closing stages. This Safety Car of course also packed the whole field back up again.
It took an age to let the three lapped runners unlap themselves, as per the flawed regulation, especially as the third of whom, Sergio Perez, was a long way behind the Safety Car even before he could unlap himself.
Then two things happened. Russell's Mercedes had a power unit failure despite the Safety Car speed. It's not so unusual for something to fail when not being fully loaded, and incredibly painfully for him and his fans, he pulled over to the side of the track and retired. That image sums up his whole season of bad luck, and the pain may well continue in Singapore if he has to take fresh power unit elements.
As the pack behind him were trying to work out what was going on and if they could legitimately pass George's car under Safety Car rules, everyone slowed quite dramatically on the approach to turn one. Lando was sailing along warming his tyres, minding his own business, and in the glare of the sun failed to notice he was catching the pack at great speed.
At the back of that particular train of cars was his team-mate Oscar Piastri, and if Lando had smashed into him then it would have been a shocker for the team in terms of results in the race and spare parts and costs. He swerved left to miss Piastri, skidded down the kerb and took a long trip through the gravel losing several places in the queue, with no rights to pass them back under the Safety Car. He would end up ninth, and with Red Bull first and fifth, this leaves McLaren just 18 points ahead in the Constructors' Championship in third place.
Verstappen made another great restart to lead and Antonelli gave the best chase he could, but the Red Bull was too fast. Behind, after a great drive, Hamilton passed Hadjar for what was third place after Russell's demise, and Leclerc in the second Ferrari did the same thing for fourth place. It was a solid and important result for team boss Fred Vasseur too, who's taken a lot of media pressure recently.
Lawson and Lindblad finished a fine seventh and 10th for Racing Bulls, and it was a welcome eighth for Fernando Alonso. His Aston Martin had been more competitive than of late, perhaps due to the layout of the track and also how the track surface affected aerodynamics, even holding off the recovering Norris on the last lap.
'A victory that has been shaping up'
It was the seventh time this year that Verstappen has been voted the fans' driver of the day, but the first time he's won a race this season and of course the impressive first victory for the all-new Red Bull-Ford power unit. It was a victory which has been shaping up for a few races now and very well deserved for the team.
Through all this, championship leader Antonelli kept his head along with speed and consistency, and by finishing ahead of his two main championship rivals in Russell and Hamilton, yet again increased his championship lead to 84 points.
It seems Qatar and Abu Dhabi will now take place as scheduled which adds another 50 points available, but if Kimi didn't show up in Singapore, Austin, or Mexico, he'd still lead the championship with four races to go.
It was a long afternoon and the race completed with just 12 minutes remaining before it would time out. In fact, it finished a full three hours and twenty minutes after the initial start time.
Let's see what challenges Singapore can throw at the teams and drivers this weekend.

On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.
Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.
Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.
Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled had no money for an operation. For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it.
After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery.
Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries.
“I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said.
“The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.”
On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu.
“Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.”
Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition.
When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.”
The Guardian investigation into the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack.
In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according to research by New America, a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town.
“We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].”
With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed.
She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said.
“I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.”

Milt Windler, one of the four leaders of Mission Control who in 1970 directed the round-the-clock efforts to bring the Apollo 13 astronauts back to Earth safely, has died at the age of 94.
Windler died on Thursday, surrounded by his loving family, according to a brief notice posted online.
Named a NASA flight director in 1968 after working on recovery operations during the Mercury and Gemini programs, Windler also led a shift of flight controllers for the Apollo 8 first circumlunar flight and Apollo 10 lunar landing dress rehearsal, as well as the second, third and fourth moon landings — Apollo 12, Apollo 14 and Apollo 15. He then served as a flight director for all three crewed missions to the United States’ first space station, Skylab.
“Apollo was such a rapid pace that I don’t think people had the chance to think about it very much. It has only become more clear to me later on that we were making history,” said Windler in a 2006 oral history interview for the University of North Texas. “You’d do a mission and then you’d immediately turn around and get ready for another mission.”
“It was not [a] time for reflection,” Windler said.
Maroon Flight
Each flight director chose a team name (at first colors). As the seventh person to be appointed to the position — and one of the first two to be selected from outside of the flight operations team — Windler became “Maroon Flight.”
On his first mission at the flight director’s console, Windler was assigned to the third shift, putting him at the head of the operations control room when it was time to send the first humans beyond Earth orbit. The trans-lunar injection, or TLI, burn placed Apollo 8 crew members Frank Borman, Bill Anders and Jim Lovell on a trajectory to advance the United States ahead of the Soviet Union by becoming the first nation to orbit people around the moon.
Realizing this, Windler, working with his wife, Betty, and other flight controllers’ spouses, secretly prepared a batch of small red and blue flannel banners, each with the numeral “1” in white at their center. He planned to distribute the flags to the members of his Maroon team to wave at TLI as a not-so-subtle message to their space race adversaries.
“However, it was decided that this display was inappropriate, especially since the mission was only half over,” wrote Windler in a 2020 letter accompanying one of the flags that had since been acquired by a collector. “Consequently, the flags were never displayed during the mission and American flags were used at the time of a successful landing on Earth.”
Later, Windler and all of his colleagues in Mission Control were provided with a dramatic reminder about why you do not celebrate until the crew has stepped onto their recovery ship. For Apollo 13, Windler was named lead flight director.
“What that meant was you did the ascent — the liftoff from Earth, I should say, the launch — and you did the lunar surface activity,” he told the UNT interviewer. “But then, of course, after we lifted off from the Earth, when we got more toward the moon, why, the whole mission changed.”
Flight director Milt Windler, Maroon Flight (at left) looks on as the director of flight crew operations Deke Slayton displays a makeshift “mail box” as devised to adapt square command module carbon dioxide scrubbers with the round receptacles in the lunar module on board the crippled Apollo 13 spacecraft in April 1970.
Credit:
NASA
Flight director Milt Windler, Maroon Flight (at left) looks on as the director of flight crew operations Deke Slayton displays a makeshift “mail box” as devised to adapt square command module carbon dioxide scrubbers with the round receptacles in the lunar module on board the crippled Apollo 13 spacecraft in April 1970.
Credit:
NASA
An explosion tore through the Apollo 13 service module, crippling the spacecraft and venting the crew’s oxygen supply into space.
Instead of overseeing the third time humans had walked on the moon, Windler — together with Gold Flight, Gerry Griffin — polled the flight controllers in the room to develop three options for when, where and how long to fire the lunar module’s engine to put the Apollo 13 spacecraft on a path back to Earth.
It would not be the last time Windler was involved in re-planning a mission already underway, but not because something had gone awry. As flight director during the Skylab missions, the challenge was working with emerging scientific events.
“We had to come up with a system that would allow us to plan in real time and accommodate the science people. If something interesting happened on the sun, which it did several times, then we needed to be able to schedule the ATM [Apollo Telescope Mount] work,” he said in 2006.
“We invented a way of flight planning in real time, or cycles,” said Windler, where one day the science people talked about what they wanted to do, and the ‘Science Czar’ got with them and said, ‘All right, then, we need these particular objectives for tomorrow.’”
After the Skylab missions ended, Windler went to work on the space shuttle and the development of the remote manipulator system or “Canadarm,” the winged orbiters’ robotic arm contributed to the program by Canada. He then retired from NASA and joined private industry to work on what would become the International Space Station, consulting on the operations aspect of the orbiting laboratory, and later, as modules were produced, on some of the verification procedures.
‘Pay more attention’
Born on Jan. 10, 1932 in Hampton, Virginia, Milton Windler graduated from Virginia Tech (Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University) in 1954 with a degree in aeronautical engineering. He joined the U.S. Air Force’s Reserve Officers’ Training Corps (ROTC) while still in school and then worked for the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA), NASA’s predecessor, before serving in the Air Force for four years.
Windler rejoined NACA at Langley Research Center in Virginia and was there for its transition to becoming a NASA facility. He relocated to Houston, Texas, just as the Manned Spacecraft Center (today, Johnson Space Center) was being established.
Milt Windler stands with fellow flight directors Glynn Lunney, Gene Kranz and Gerry Griffin for President Richard Nixon’s presentation of the Presidential Medal of Freedom to NASA’s Apollo 13 mission operations team on April 18, 1970.
Credit:
NASA
Milt Windler stands with fellow flight directors Glynn Lunney, Gene Kranz and Gerry Griffin for President Richard Nixon’s presentation of the Presidential Medal of Freedom to NASA’s Apollo 13 mission operations team on April 18, 1970.
Credit:
NASA
As a member of Mission Control during the Apollo 13 mission, Windler and his fellow flight directors and controllers were awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by then-President Richard Nixon in 1970. Windler was also honored with NASA’s Exceptional Service Medal.
Milton and Betty (née Selby) Windler had three children and eight grandchildren. A memorial service will take place in the coming weeks at the family’s former church in Friendswood, Texas.
“If I did it again, I’d probably try to do something more about trying to pay more attention,” said Windler. “Apollo was — well, all of [the missions] were … bang-bang-bang. You couldn’t enjoy, really, in a way you couldn’t savor it, like maybe it would have been better to have done.”
Robert Pearlman is a space historian, journalist and the founder and editor of collectSPACE, a daily news publication and online community focused on where space exploration intersects with pop culture. He is also a contributing writer for Space.com and co-author of "Space Stations: The Art, Science, and Reality of Working in Space” published by Smithsonian Books in 2018. He is on the leadership board for For All Moonkind and is a member of the American Astronautical Society's history committee.

A Delhi-based makeup artist has revealed how much she earned from makeup bookings in a single week, saying she made ₹4.5 lakh through bridal and party makeup assignments. She explained how several wedding and party makeup assignments added up to the substantial weekly income. Momina's week started with a booking worth ₹63,000, for which she created three different makeup looks. She then took up a wedding makeup assignment that paid ₹73,000. She also provided party makeup services for members of the client's family. The entire booking brought in ₹2.2 lakh, according to her breakdown. She ended the week with another bridal makeup appointment, for which she charged ₹37,500. On the eve of Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Cairo last month, the city authorities were busy removing a 66-metre-long mural from the esteemed guest’s line of sight.
Depicting the Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti, the painting was among 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for Xi’s arrival and was painted by volunteer youth group Rasmet Basma, in Tahrir Square.
But it drew a furious reaction for depicting the two historical figures with dark skin – angering those Egyptians who saw it as reviving Afrocentric claims about the Pharaohs’ origins. The artwork vanished under fresh paint just hours before Xi landed.
Now, Ahmed Moussa, the 22-year-old founder of Rasmet Basma, has admitted it was asked by the Cairo governorate to paint over its work, which had been prepared in just five days in late August.
The team used the AI programme ChatGPT to generate the designs, which volunteers then painted on to the wall.
Moussa said Cairo’s deputy governor and the head of the district had visited the site throughout the process and were impressed by the murals – until controversy began to build on social media.
“We used a golden-bronze tone that cast a kind of shadow on the faces at night, so they appeared dark-skinned,” Moussa said.
“We acknowledge our mistake in not consulting specialists in archaeology and art.”
Afrocentrism is a political movement asserting that ancient Egyptian civilisation was black African in origin and population.
One user asked whether anyone involved had “even seen what Nefertiti actually looked like”, while others accused Afrocentric groups of appropriating the images to claim Egyptians endorsed their theories.
Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, said the volunteers should not have been allowed to paint a city site as significant as Tahrir Square without expert oversight, and that the public outrage was justified.
“Claims linking ancient Egyptian civilisation to sub-Saharan Africa are nonsense,” Hawass said.
“Temple carvings from the late period show Egyptian kings depicted alongside captives from parts of Africa, Libya, Syria and Palestine, with the king himself not shown as dark-skinned,” he said.
This is just the latest episode in a long-running debate over the complexion of ancient Egyptians. In 2023, a Netflix documentary provoked discussion after casting a dark-skinned actor as Cleopatra, and a similar dispute flared in June 2024 after a guide reportedly gave an Afrocentric perspective of Egyptian history in Cairo’s Egyptian Museum.
Monica Hanna, an Egyptologist at the American University in Cairo, labelled Afrocentric claims “pseudoscience”. She said Egyptian society had always been ethnically diverse, from Nubian communities in the south to Mediterranean populations in the north.
“Egyptians were never one skin colour,” she said. “We are not snow-white, or the colour of cream.”
Walid Mahmoud, an AI researcher and expert in African anthropology, said AI tools such as ChatGPT reflected whatever information was most widely shared online, rather than what was factually accurate.
They were built by companies in the US and Europe, he said, and the content they generated could shape how those audiences saw themselves.
“That’s why we should never simply accept what it produces, especially when it comes to cultural identity and heritage,” Mahmoud said.
Mostafa Eissa, an art critic, said AI should remain a tool, never a decision-maker in its own right.
“I favour using technology without abandoning the human element within the artist,” he said, warning that letting such tools substitute an artist’s own skill risked emptying a work of its originality.
