- The claim that male students who were accused of raping a female student at Cornell University were fired from their jobs or expelled from Cornell is still under investigation.
- Snopes readers asked us to determine what happened to each of the seven accused, including whether the university penalized them or their employers fired them.
- A spokesperson for Cornell said via email that the university issued suspensions for some students and expelled others but did not specify which students received which penalties. Cornell did not respond to our specific questions about each student.
- Using the university database, social media posts, a lawyer's statements and college news reporting, Snopes was able to determine that at least one of the accused was still a student on campus. Three others were alumni at the time of the September 2026 lawsuit, while the remainder have an undetermined status at the university.
- Snopes has also reached out to most of the accused students using emails from the college database. We will update this report if we get more information.
In September 2026, a lawsuit brought against Cornell University and seven of its male students alleged the men drugged and raped a 20-year-old female student in October 2024. The story spread online along with claims that the accused students faced little or no consequences, though some allegedly lost their jobs or were expelled.
As Snopes previously reported, the lawsuit named seven male students as defendants: Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar. According to the lawsuit — filed on behalf of the plaintiff, identified only as Jane Doe, on Sept. 14 — the drugging and multiple assaults occurred the night of Oct. 19, 2024, into the early hours of Oct. 20 at the Xi chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity.
According to Doe's lawsuit, Cornell temporarily suspended the accused students on Nov. 8, 2024, (Page 29) but they were given the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by writing an essay to the university. Cornell has denied that the students only had to write essays as a disciplinary measure.
Posts on X, Facebook and Instagram claimed two of the accused students, Sarabia and Ingalls, lost their jobs at Wells Fargo and Data Annotation Tech, respectively. Jane Doe's attorney also reportedly claimed two of the students were expelled from the university, without naming them.
Snopes emailed a spokesperson for Cornell University to determine the enrollment status of each of the accused students. The university declined to respond to specific questions about the accused, directing us to its official statement. The statement says that students were expelled and/or suspended but would not identify which students:
Temporary suspensions and other restrictive measures were issued when the conduct was reported. Chi Phi, Xi Chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus. Following the university's Title IX investigation, sanctions including expulsions and suspensions were issued by a hearing panel comprising trained faculty and staff. Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students, and the university is therefore unable to make a public statement regarding any other disciplinary response.
Below we break down everything we know about the education and employment status of each of the seven accused students. We will update this story as we learn more.
Diego Sarabia
Student newspaper The Cornell Daily Sun and Cornell's online directory say Sarabia is an alumnus from the class of 2025. 
Gossip outlet TMZ reported, citing anonymous sources, that Sarabia is no longer employed at a Wells Fargo bank branch in Charlotte, North Carolina. It was not possible to independently verify this ourselves. According to the report, Sarabia had worked at the branch since 2022. Wells Fargo has not publicly commented on the story as of this writing.
Snopes has contacted several Wells Fargo representatives to learn more about Sarabia's role, employment status and the circumstances around his alleged termination. The company has not responded to our queries.
Snopes has also reached out to Sarabia through an email address in the student directory.
Matthew Ingalls
On Sept. 30, Data Annotation Tech responded to the claim that it had employed one of the accused. The company, which hires independent contractors to train artificial intelligence models, said on Instagram (archived) that one of the accused was blocked from its platform in May 2024, long before the lawsuit.
According to its Instagram post, which does not name Ingalls, the claim that the company employed one of the accused is "incorrect." It continues, "He has had no access to our platform or our company at any point since then."
We contacted Data Annotation Tech to learn more about whether Ingalls, specifically, had ever been a contractor or employee there.
The Daily Sun reported that Ingalls was a member of the class of 2027. Cornell's online database initially listed Ingalls as a student but his college affiliation as "not applicable." When Snopes returned to the directory on Oct. 2, his name had been removed.
Snopes has reached out to Ingalls through an email address in the student directory.
Gillio Lopes
The Daily Sun reported that Lopes was a member of the class of 2027 and was still listed in the directory as a student in the College of Arts and Sciences. Snopes was unable to confirm the directory listing.
Footage shared online purported to show a woman confronting Lopes on Cornell's campus in late September 2026. Lopes' lawyer confirmed the veracity of the footage to TMZ, saying:
What has emerged today only reinforces how dangerous it is to rush to judgment. The contemporaneous texts and other evidence now being reported show a far more complicated and evolving factual picture than the one initially presented to the public.
[…]
Due process exists for precisely this reason. Publicity is not evidence. Repetition is not proof. An accusation cannot be allowed to become its own proof. He is entitled to have the evidence tested through the legal process—not by headlines, social media, or people confronting him in public or threatening his family.
Snopes has reached out to Lopes' lawyer, Andrew Miltenberg, to learn more.
Winston Lee
The Daily Sun reported that Lee was a member of the class of 2027 and was still listed in the directory as a student in the College of Arts and Sciences.
Some social media users claimed (archived) Lee was still on campus and had changed his name to Jay Lee. As of this writing, Snopes was unable to independently verify this claim.
Snopes was unable to determine Lee's status via the student directory or to find contact information for him.
Scott Kretzschmar
The Daily Sun reported that Kretzschmar is an alumnus from the class of 2026. When Snopes first looked at the student directory, it listed him as a student, but his college affiliation was "not applicable." When Snopes returned to the directory on Oct. 2, his name had been removed.
Snopes has reached out to Kretzschmar through an email address in the student directory.
Johnathan Newell
The Daily Sun reported that Newell was a member of the class of 2027. When Snopes first looked at the student directory, it listed a "Jonathan Newell" (with a different spelling) as a student, but his college affiliation was "not applicable." When Snopes went back to the directory on Oct. 2, there was no record of a Johnathan or Jonathan Newell.
Snopes has reached out to Newell through an email address in the student directory.
Scott Norris
The Daily Sun reported that Norris is an alumnus from the class of 2026. Cornell's online database initially listed him as a student but his college affiliation as "not applicable." When Snopes returned to the directory on Oct. 2, his name had been removed.
Snopes has reached out to Norris through an email address in the student directory.

- The claim that a Russian oligarch close to President Vladimir Putin paid for Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding in May 2026 is still under investigation.
- The investigative newsroom ProPublica reported on Sept. 14 that Umar Kremlev, a Russian boxing and sports betting mogul, "bankrolled" the wedding of the U.S. president's son with an undetermined six-figure sum.
- Trump and his wife, Bettina Anderson, said on Instagram that Kremlev had paid for two days of celebrations after the couple's private May 22 wedding. The couple described the post-wedding festivities as "an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend" that was "never intended to be our wedding weekend."
- ProPublica's reporting raised questions about a potential political conflict of interest because Kremlev has previously benefited from Russian government contracts to his companies and Trump has previously advised his father on political appointments.
- Days after ProPublica's reporting, President Donald Trump said his son had paid back Kremlev. This claim remains unproven as of this writing.
- Snopes could not independently view and verify sources that substantiated either ProPublica's or Anderson and Donald Trump Jr.'s claims about what exactly Kremlev paid for in relation to their wedding. Therefore, we leave this claim unrated.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have contacted the Trump family, the White House and Kremlev's press office for further comment on ProPublica's reporting and are waiting for responses.
In September 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that a Russian oligarch close to President Vladimir Putin paid for Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding that May.
Trump, U.S. President Donald Trump's oldest son, married the socialite and model Bettina Anderson in the Bahamas on May 22, followed by two days of festivities.
One Threads user who shared the claim about the funding of Trump's wedding wrote:
A Russian oligarch who is close to Putin paid for a good portion of the wedding between Donald Trump Jr. and Bettina Trump. Let's say it again for the people in the back of the class: THERE. IS. A. RUSSIAN. ASSET. SITTING. IN. THE. WHITE. HOUSE.
Similar claims circulated on X (archived), Facebook (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers also contacted us about the rumor.
The claim circulated after the independent newsroom ProPublica published an investigation that found Umar Kremlev, a prominent figure in the Russian boxing and sports betting scenes, paid an undetermined six-figure sum for a lavish island party in connection with Anderson and Trump's wedding. The couple appeared to confirm this payment from Kremlev as "an extraordinarily generous wedding gift" in a statement on Instagram (archived).
However, while the newlyweds appeared to confirm that Kremlev had paid for celebrations that took place directly after their Bahamas wedding, they did not appear to accept ProPublica's claim that Kremlev had "bankrolled" the wedding either in whole or in part.
Kremlev's payment presented a potential conflict of interest, ProPublica's reporting claimed, because of the Russian's reported proximity to Putin and Trump's position as a "political power center" as an adviser to his father. It was unclear at the time of this writing exactly how close Kremlev was to Putin, though Russian reporting found his businesses had benefited from government contracts.
After ProPublica's reporting, the U.S. president claimed (archived) that his son paid back Kremlev for the celebrations. This claim is unproven.
ProPublica's investigation was based on interviews with at least three people "familiar with the event" and records reviewed by the outlet.
We contacted ProPublica to independently verify the sources that formed the basis of their investigation. A spokesperson said, "ProPublica doesn't comment on sourcing beyond what we put in our stories, but we do want to flag that Donald Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Anderson, have since confirmed the payments."
Because Snopes could not independently view and verify sources that proved either ProPublica's or Anderson and Trump's claims about what Kremlev paid for in relation to their wedding, we leave this claim unrated.
We contacted The Trump Organization and Kremlev to verify statements given to ProPublica and seek further comment on the outlet's reporting. We await replies to our queries.
The statement
Anderson and Trump wrote on Instagram on Sept. 14, 2026:
Don and I got married privately on Friday, surrounded ONLY by our family. It was intimate, deeply personal and one of the most beautiful days of our lives.
The weekend that followed had actually been planned well in advance as a fun weekend with friends. It was never intended to be our wedding weekend. When our original wedding plans changed, we simply decided to get married before it and arrived at an already planned weekend as newlyweds.
Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding. It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful.
It's unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from. Friendship doesn't require a political motive. Generosity doesn't automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift.
While the statement (signed: "With love and gratitude, Don & Bettina") did confirm Kremlev had paid for a "fun weekend with friends," the couple appeared to distinguish between the wedding itself and Kremlev's reported gift of a preplanned event that was "never intended to be our wedding weekend."
According to ProPublica's reporting, Kremlev was not present at the couple's wedding ceremony, but they had their first dance on the island he allegedly rented "for around $100,000 a night." It was unclear how that detail aligned with Anderson and Trump's statement that claimed the celebrations paid for by Kremlev were unrelated to the wedding.
Uncertainties remain over Trump-Kremlev friendship
Though Anderson and Trump described Kremlev as a "dear friend," ProPublica reported that the men "appeared to have met only recently." Kremlev's press office reportedly told ProPublica they met "a couple of years ago." In 2025, Trump spoke at an event hosted by the International Boxing Association, of which Kremlev has been the president since 2020.
A spokesperson for Trump reportedly told ProPublica that he and Kremlev bonded over a love of boxing and the outdoors and that Kremlev did not talk about "political matters" with his American friends.
That could well be true, given that ProPublica reported that Kremlev spoke "limited English."
Though it was unclear exactly how close Kremlev was to the Russian president, reporting by the Russian independent newsroom Proekt found that Kremlev rose through the Russian boxing and sports betting worlds in large part due to being awarded government contracts for his businesses. Kremlev said in a February 2024 interview that he would not describe himself as a friend of Putin's but praised the president's work ethic.
Kremlev received a government award from Putin in April 2026 for his services to sport.
The next month, Kremlev's Telegram account (archived) showed he visited China at the same time as Putin, days before Anderson and Trump's wedding, though Kremlev's press office said he was not part of Putin's official delegation on the trip.
Trump family had 'no clue' about 'dear friend' Kremlev
Though Anderson and Trump described Kremlev as a "dear friend," two other members of the Trump family did not appear to know who the generous gift-giver was.
A spokesperson for Eric Trump reportedly told ProPublica that he had "absolutely no clue" who Kremlev was.
Donald Trump reportedly told The New York Times on Sept. 14 that he, too, did not know who the Russian benefactor was.
Four days after ProPublica published its reporting, on Sept. 18, the president told reporters at the White House that he had "heard" that his son paid back Kremlev for what the newlywed couple initially described as a wedding gift. He did not say whether paying back Kremlev had always been the plan or whether it was sparked by ProPublica's reporting.
At the time of this writing, neither the White House nor Donald Trump Jr. has publicly proved Kremlev's money was repaid, nor have they returned queries from Snopes about the alleged payment.
During the same news conference, the president appeared to play down the significance of Kremlev being Russian and but also appeared to muddle Anderson and Donald Trump Jr.'s distinction that Kremlev's celebrations were not part of their wedding.
Donald Trump called Kremlev's celebrations a "wedding party" and suggested that it was a normal thing to give to newlyweds. He said, "I've given, well, I don't know, maybe he didn't do a background check, but I've given, I've given wedding parties for numerous people."
The president later repeated, "I have to say, though, you know, giving a wedding party is pretty common."
Reporting sparks bipartisan calls for investigation
ProPublica's investigation into Kremlev's alleged payments raised immediate concerns on both sides of the political divide.
Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the lead Democrat on the House Committee on Oversight and Reform, wrote in a Sept. 14 letter to Donald Trump Jr. that the committee was investigating the "numerous ways in which you have sought to enrich yourself and your family on the basis of your proximity to President Donald Trump."
Garcia wrote that, to this end, "your ties to your self-described 'dear friend' Mr. Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch responsible for bankrolling your May 24, 2026, wedding celebrations in the Bahamas, may be the most serious allegation against you to date."
Sen. Eradicating Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection early could become an important strategy for preventing gastric cancer, Nobel laureate and gastroenterologist Dr. Barry Marshall said, stressing the need for wider testing, appropriate treatment and confirmation that the infection has been cleared.
Dr. Marshall, who shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Robin Warren for their discovery of H. pylori and its role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, said the bacterium should no longer be regarded only as a cause of ulcers.
“H. pylori is much more than an ulcer organism. If the infection persists for many years, it can cause chronic inflammation in the stomach and increase the risk of gastric cancer. That gives us an opportunity because this is a potentially preventable cause of cancer," Dr. Marshall told PTI.
Dr. Marshall was in India to attend the World Congress of Gastroenterology (WCOG 2026) in the national capital.
Held in India for the first time, the four-day event, which concluded on October 3, brought together around 3,000 delegates from 61 countries to discuss the changing global burden of gastrointestinal and liver diseases, including H. pylori infection, gastric cancer prevention, early diagnosis and treatment.
His comments come amid renewed global focus on population-based H. pylori "screen-and-treat" programmes for gastric cancer prevention.
The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) working group has recommended such programmes in populations where the benefits are expected to outweigh potential harms.
Dr. Marshall said the priority should be to identify infected individuals and ensure they receive effective eradication therapy.
"If we can find the infection before there has been extensive damage to the stomach, we have a much better chance of preventing the chain of events that can eventually lead to cancer," he said.
However, rising antibiotic resistance is emerging as a major challenge to this approach, he highlighted.
A 2026 review in Gastroenterology noted that increasing antimicrobial resistance is threatening the success of established H. pylori treatment regimens, while concerns also remain about the effects of repeated antibiotic exposure on the microbiome.
"We cannot simply keep giving the same antibiotics and expect the same results. Resistance varies between countries and even between regions, so treatment needs to take local resistance patterns into account," Dr. Marshall said.
The IARC guidance similarly emphasises antibiotic stewardship, treatment based on local resistance patterns and follow-up testing to determine whether eradication has been successful.
Dr. Marshall said India, where H. pylori infection is common, has an important role to play in generating evidence on local bacterial strains and antibiotic resistance.
"India has a very large population with H. pylori, so it is an important setting for research. We need to understand which strains are circulating, what antibiotics are still effective and how we can make testing and treatment accessible," he said.
According to the IARC guidance, Indian recommendations have included bismuth-containing quadruple therapy in areas with high clarithromycin resistance, highlighting the importance of regional resistance patterns in treatment decisions.
Dr. Marshall also stressed that successful treatment should not be assumed simply because symptoms improve.
"Treating the patient is only half the job. We should confirm that the bacterium has actually been eradicated. Otherwise, the patient may continue to carry the infection and remain at risk," he said.
He said non-invasive testing could make detection easier and help expand screening.
Dr. Marshall has also invented PYtest, a C14 urea breath test that provides a 15-minute, non-invasive and quantitative method for detecting current H. pylori infection using a breath sample from the patient.
The patient-friendly test could help Indian doctors detect active H. pylori infection through a quick diagnostic procedure.
PYtest is available in India through Pylorium Diagnostics, part of Trimed Australia, founded by Dr. Marshall and headed by Bhanu Rahoni in India.
The need for prevention has gained urgency as gastric cancer remains a major global health burden, with the highest incidence concentrated in several Asian regions.

'I don't even know if my parents are alive' - the war heroes jailed 25 years ago
- Published
Hanna Petros Solomon breaks down in tears as she recalls how she and her siblings effectively became orphans 25 years ago when their father was arrested in Eritrea and jailed without trial. Their mother was subsequently detained - and no-one has heard from either of them - or of them - since.
"He had a towel on his shoulders like a sportsman," she tells the BBC about the last time she saw her father when she was 10 years old, and he had gone out for a jog.
"He used to work out every morning."
Her parents met when they both fought in the long liberation war that saw Eritrea gain independence from Ethiopia in 1993.
Her father Petros Solomon had been one of the senior leaders during the war and is regarded by many as a national hero for his critical role.
After independence, he had served as defence minister, then foreign minister and had been heading the fisheries ministry when his troubles began.
That was in May 2001 when he and 14 other high-profile politicians signed an open letter to President Isaias Afewerki calling for the implementation of a constitution that was ratified after independence and demanding national elections. They became known as the G-15.
Isaias, the leader of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) which had fought against Ethiopia, did not take the criticism well.
Unbeknown to Hanna, her father had been dismissed as a minister, though he still went out early to get some exercise each day.
It was not until a few days after 9/11 - when the world was distracted by the al-Qaeda attacks on the US - that the country was to discover the full extent of Isais's displeasure in what became a watershed moment in Eritrea's history.
In the early hours of 18 September, the security forces positioned themselves outside the homes of 11 senior government officials in the capital, Asmara, on the president's orders.
Petros was picked up by security agents as he left in his tracksuit.
The family had no idea what had happened to him. Hanna and her three siblings went to stay with their paternal grandmother as their mother, Aster Yohannes, was away studying in the US.
It was only some days after Petros had disappeared that things became clearer, says Hanna about the painful memories.
"My classmates told me that my father sold out his country.
"That is when I understood how serious the situation was, and how people framed my dad and his colleagues who fought for the independence of their country. I was hurt."
In the US, Aster was shell-shocked by what had happened - and was in a very bad way. She asked government officials if they could issue the children with passports - but they refused, telling her to come home.
After agonising about the situation for two years and reportedly receiving assurances from government officials, she packed her bags to return.
Hanna and her siblings desperately wanted her back - but they were also worried.
"I told her on the phone: 'What if they arrest you?'" Hanna remembers.
"She insisted nothing would happen to her, saying: 'I haven't done anything wrong, and am only coming to raise my children.'"
Hanna says she learned later that President Isaias himself had promised Aster that she would be safe. But while the family waited at Asmara International Airport on 11 December 2003, she failed to emerge through arrivals with the other passengers.
Their hopes began to wilt along with the flowers they had brought: "It was a long, long wait. Eventually we gave up and went back home.
"First we called to the US, friends and relatives told us they saw her off at the airport."
Then ominously an official called from the airport asking Aster to collect her luggage. That is when they realised she had arrived in the country but would not be coming home.
All pleas and requests for information fell on deaf ears in the months that followed. Instead Hanna's grandmother was warned by authorities to stop inquiring.
The family later heard that Aster was being held in the infamous jail known as Karshelli in the heart of Asmara.
Hanna's father is believed to be detained, with the others arrested on 18 and 19 September 2001, in the remote, hostile and highly secretive prison known as Ela-Ero, located in eastern lowlands north-east of Asmara. Accused of treason, none of them has ever been brought to trial or allowed to see their relatives.
At around the same time, the government also shut down all the fledgling independent newspapers and detained their editors and journalists - also believed to be imprisoned in Ela-Ero.
The Eritrean government - including its embassy in the UK - has not responded to the BBC's request for comment regarding the whereabouts of the prisoners or whether or not they are alive.
Hanna, like many thousands of young Eritreans fleeing conscription and in search of better opportunities, left the country - travelling secretively over the border without a passport.
Now 35 years old, she is married and lives in the US, working as a trauma specialist - but still feels traumatised herself by how she lost her parents.
As she stares at old pictures of her parents, she worries her memories will fade of the happy times before their arrest - the laughter, the family gatherings, the birthday parties: "My dad always wanted to gather people in the house, they were good days."
She also hankers after her mother's "unmatched" egg and potato sandwiches.
On trips down to the coast when her father was the minister of fisheries, Hanna remembers him organising singing competitions in the car: "He would ask us to sing one by one and whoever won would get a present."
One of his favourite songs included the lyrics: "I had a sweater, a blue sweater, that my sister took" - which reminded him of his sister who was also a freedom fighter and had been killed during the war.
She also has memories of her mother loving music - playing and singing hits by Abba, Dolly Parton and Whitney Houston.
Until her father's arrest, Hanna remembers September as being full of hope with its three big Orthodox Christian festivals, including the Geez New Year. Now the month brings her no joy.
Ibrahim Sherifo knows exactly how she feels. Both his parents, who were senior members of the ruling People's Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ), were among the G-15 people arrested 25 years ago.
He was 13 years old at the time
"For me 18 September 2001 is a dark day, but not only for me, it is a dark day for Eritrea and its people, because it is the day when law and democracy was detained," he tells the BBC.
He is now 38 and living in exile in the Netherlands, where he was granted asylum, and is pursuing an MA in political science - following in his father's footsteps.
His dad Mahmoud Ahmed Sherifo was the local government minister and de facto deputy president before his detention.
Ibrahim was with his mother, Aster Fissehatsion, staying with her sister when he remembers security agents knocking on the door early in the morning and taking her away in her pyjamas.
Worried about his father, Ibrahim immediately ran to his nearby house but was told he had already been picked up when he had gone out for exercise.
Both Hanna and Ibrahim say they are forever grateful to the friends and family who offered them care and supported them as they grew up without their parents, despite the risks.
They are also proud of what their parents stood for and daring to call for reforms.
"They had conscience and couldn't observe idly while what they fought for what had been hijacked by Isaias and his coterie," says Ibrahim.
"As a family, we should be informed whether they are alive or not," he adds, accusing the government of wanting to erase all memory of the political prisoners.
Hanna also wants the plight of the many others whose relatives have disappeared over the years to be heard too.
Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down"
Human rights groups, including the UN, consider the G-15 prisoners of conscience and have been calling for their release.
President Isaias, now 80, has still not implemented the country's first constitution - approved in 1997 - and remains in power without ever holding an election.
Hanna recalls that on the eve of her father's disappearance, she had a "bad feeling" - and had crept into his bed and tied his legs to her own with string while he slept.
"In the morning he woke up to find he was tied up and to release himself he pulled my legs and I woke up. I begged him not to leave but he assured me that he would return [after his run]."
Describing the years of sorrow since, she says it is like living in the deep sea.
"Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down.
"Sometimes you lose hope and you are out of breath."
Asked what she would say if she could get a message to her parents, she replies: "Don't worry about us.
"Like you survived the struggle through sheer steadfastness, we hope you can pull through this too and return to us."

Siri can index more of your personal data — here's how to limit it
If you’re concerned about Apple’s new digital assistant, here’s how you can restrict its access to your data.
With the release of iOS 27, Apple has finally begun rolling out its long delayed redesign of Siri. You'll need to join a waitlist before you can get Siri AI, but once you gain access to the new digital assistant, you're likely to find it's a significant leap over its predecessor. Engadget's Mat Smith found the new Siri much improved when he tested it on the iOS 27 beta, thanks to its ability to deliver smarter, more personalized responses.
However, there is a downside worth mentioning. Apple partnered with Google to train the new large language models that power Siri AI's features. And as with any AI system, the new Siri requires a great deal of data to work at its best, and that data comes from you(r phone).
How does Siri AI access data from your apps?
The reason Siri AI can provide a more personalized experience is thanks to a framework called App Intents that allows Apple Intelligence tools, including Siri, to access data from the apps on your Apple devices. When you enable Siri AI on your iPhone, iPad or Mac, Spotlight and Siri are unified under a single interface. By default, when you ask Siri a question, it will search through your Apple apps, including Notes and Messages, to pull information that might be relevant to your prompt or query. If a developer has chosen to support App Intents, Siri will be able to scan through their apps too.
Siri AI relies on a combination of on-device models and Apple's Private Cloud Compute (PCC) infrastructure, meaning the assistant will sometimes offload your data to a remote server for processing. Apple says it does not store any data sent to its PCC servers after processing a request, and that it can't even see the data. Still, you might feel uncomfortable about sharing data regardless. Thankfully, there are ways you can control what Siri can index.
Restrict Siri AI's access to content inside your apps
As mentioned, Apple has left it up to developers to decide if Siri AI can access the data people generate inside of their apps. That means as long as they allow iOS 27's Spotlight tool to index the contents of their apps, Siri AI can in turn access and surface that information for you as a user. However, you still have control over the process, and can ultimately decide to restrict Siri from accessing your apps. To do so, follow these steps:
- Open the Settings app.
- Scroll down and tap Apps.
- Select the app you want to restrict Siri from accessing.
- Tap Search.
- Toggle off Show Content in Search.
After you disable Show Content in Search in relation to a particular app, Siri won't pull information from that app, even if you ask it to do so directly. For example, if you disable indexing of Messages, and ask Siri to summarize a series of messages from your friend, the digital assistant will tell you it can't find those messages.
In the Apps settings menu, you may have noticed a collection of options grouped under "Apple Intelligence & Siri." For the purposes of this guide, you can leave those alone; they don't have privacy implications. Instead, they primarily control where iOS might suggest an app for you. For instance, if you disable the "Suggest App" option, you won't see that specific app among the "Siri Suggestions" iOS generates when you access your iPhone's search shade. The "Learn from this App" option sounds nefarious, but it merely allows iOS to see how and when you're using your apps so that it can tailor when it surfaces those apps for you.
On-screen awareness
Even after you restrict Siri's ability to search through your apps, you can still get it to help you with situations requiring contextual knowledge on a more ad-hoc basis. A feature called on-screen awareness allows Siri to read the contents of screenshots and images. This can be useful from an accessibility standpoint, or if you want Siri to summarize a lengthy article or message thread. Just note if you snap a screenshot and ask Siri to interpret it, it might be sent to the company's PCC servers.
Ensure you're not sharing Siri recordings with Apple
By default, Apple won't collect or use the data from your interactions with Siri to train future versions of the virtual assistant. But as part of your iPhone's setup process, you might have accidently opted into sharing your Siri recordings and transcripts with the company. Either way, it's worth checking to confirm your Siri data isn't being used for model training.
- Open the Settings app.
- Tap Privacy & Security.
- Scroll down and select Analytics & Improvements.
- Disable Improve Siri & Dictation if turned on.
Disable Siri AI altogether
One final option worth mentioning is that you can revert to the older version of Siri. This gives you a way to continue using apps like CarPlay with your voice while limiting your privacy exposure. Unintuitively, however, you'll find the option to do this hidden inside the Screen Time section.
- Open the Settings app.
- Tap Screen Time, followed by Content & Privacy Restrictions.
- Enable Content & Privacy Restrictions.
- Tap Siri.
- Under Allowed Siri Version, select Siri Classic.
Alternatively, you can disable Siri entirely by following the steps below.
- Open the Settings app.
- Tap Siri.
- Scroll down and select Turn off Siri.
If you want to restrict any other part of the Apple Intelligence suite, Apple has helpful support page on the topic.

It's been five years since James Bond was on the silver screen in No Time to Die. For fans of the secret agent, the wait has been arduous, made even harder by the fact that Amazon, which now owns the franchise, still hasn't chosen a successor to Daniel Craig, let alone started filming Bond's resurrection.
But if it's seemed like a long haul for fans, just think how it has felt for Omega, which counts on a steady stream of Bond action to regularly inject lots of lovely cash into the company via watch releases linked directly to the films. Omega's last official Bond film tie-in watch was the titanium No Time to Die Seamaster prematurely launched back in 2019, ahead of the film’s then Covid-delayed release in 2021.
Considering that Swatch Group’s net profit collapsed by almost 90 percent to $32 million in 2025 (though, thankfully, things look rosier so far this year), we shouldn't be surprised that Omega isn't bothering to wait for Jeff Bezos to put his white cat down and proceed with world domination. As there's no new Bond or Bond film to work with, Omega has decided to launch 007-themed watches anyway—not just one, but an entire collection totaling six Seamaster Divers.
You can hardly blame the brand. When Omega first strapped a Seamaster to Pierce Brosnan's wrist in 1995's GoldenEye, it reportedly saw a 20-fold sales increase. In 2012, Omega's then-president Stephen Urquhart even told Variety that Omega’s sales “look like a stock market chart” that peaks during promotion of Bond films, then sinks afterward. “The films have had a very marked influence on sales,” Urquhart conceded.
The new “James Bond and Spectre” collection is themed around good and evil, with three watches bearing the “007” symbol of James Bond, and three the octopus-like motif of Spectre, the fictional global terrorist organization in the series.
The six Seamaster Diver 300M watches share the same movement. However, the two non-limited stainless-steel editions are the core pieces, available individually at $8,600 each—one with a blue aluminum dial dedicated to James Bond, and the other black for dastardly Spectre fans. Both come on a brushed mesh bracelet.
The James Bond edition has a grade 5 titanium bezel, while the Spectre edition boasts a black ceramic bezel ring to match the dial's blackened grained finish.
The remaining four Seamasters are split across two limited-edition numbered sets—one dedicated to Bond, the other to Spectre—capped at 77 boxes each. At a cool $89,800 per pair (Omega won't sell them individually), you get one stainless-steel model on a brushed mesh bracelet, and a second in platinum-gold on leather.
Each set comes in a presentation box with an additional NATO strap, strap-changing tool, cuff links, a cord bracelet, a loupe, a leather travel pouch and card holder, and papers. In the James Bond set, the strap keepers are engraved with 007; in the Spectre set, the strap keepers carry the Spectre emblem.
This collection is not the first time Omega has sought to leverage its Bond connection without a film peg. Back in May of this year, Omega unveiled the Seamaster Diver 300M Chronograph “007 First Light,” a new 44-mm chrono tied to 007 First Light, a James Bond game developed by the same studio responsible for the Hitman franchise. Originally designed as an in-game gadget, Omega turned it into a production model.
Back in 2012, there was the Seamaster James Bond 007 50th Anniversary watch with a red number 50 on the bezel. In 2019, there was an On Her Majesty's Secret Service edition Seamaster to mark 50 years of the 1969 film, limited to 7,007 pieces. Then, in 2022, Omega released a Seamaster to coincide with 60 years of Bond movies.

A hot tip to battle performance anxiety? 'Pretend flush' a mistake down the toilet
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
In 2012, psychologist Cindra Kamphoff was running a marathon. Then at Mile 22, her self-doubt started to kick in. She remembers telling herself, "This is dumb. Why am I doing this?"
Life Kit
Beat performance anxiety with these quick tips
But Kamphoff, who works with top athletes on how to overcome performance anxiety — including from the Minnesota Vikings and USA Track & Field — was prepared. She had written positive phrases on her arm that she could read when she needed a boost during the race: "I'm strong, I'm fast, I'm fit, I'm ready."
This is just one of many techniques that Kamphoff shares in The Confidence Habit: 7 Core Practices to Transform Self-Doubt to Self-Belief, published in September. The book offers creative ways to manage fear and negativity — like pretend-flushing your mistakes down the toilet — before, during and after a high-stakes task.
These tools can be applied to any situation, whether it's a race, work presentation or a job interview. The goal is for people to "be their best in the moments that matter most to them," she says.
Kamphoff, who has a PhD in sport and performance psychology, shares four tools you can try today.
Move on quickly with "learn, burn, return"
Maybe you fumble the ball in a big game or forget the lines in your school play and can't stop thinking about it afterward.
If you make a mistake during a high-stakes moment, Kamphoff says it's important to move on quickly.
She suggests a tool she calls "learn, burn, return" to build back your confidence and keep your goals in reach. Try this if you fumble mid-performance, or as a way to reflect after the event.
Learn: Ask yourself, what did you learn? Use this prompt: Next time, I will _____.
Burn: Think of a motion or a cue you can use to remind yourself to move on quickly. Kamphoff says you can snap your fingers, say "that fast" or "you might literally pretend to flush a toilet."
She taught the toilet flush move to former Minnesota Vikings player Adam Thielen, who used it after he fumbled during a playoff game in 2020. He then went on to catch a 43-yard pass over his head that helped the Vikings win the game.
Using the same motion or phrase every time you "burn" helps your brain strengthen new neural pathways when it comes to moving through anxiety, she says.
Return: Now it's time to build yourself back up. Remind yourself, "you got this, you're doing the best that you can," says Kamphoff.
Speak to yourself powerfully
How you talk to yourself matters, Kamphoff says. According to the American Psychological Association, self-affirmations, even in small doses, can have lasting effects on our self-esteem.
When Kamphoff wrote positive messages on her arm to motivate her during her marathon, they worked because she was giving her brain evidence that she could be successful.
As Kamphoff repeated these phrases during her race, her pace picked up. She ended up not only winning the race in her division, but running her last four miles the fastest out of any part of the marathon.
To make what Kamphoff calls a "power phrase," choose a statement that starts with I will, I can or I am. Then ask yourself, How am I at my best? What does that look like? What does that feel like?"
Kamphoff chose phrases that reminded her of her love for running — and that she had trained for hundreds of miles to run the race.
Set gold, silver and bronze goals
Instead of focusing on one perfect outcome, set a range of goals for yourself. Kamphoff recommends creating a "gold, silver and bronze goal," she says.
Let's say you're running the mile in track. Your bronze goal might be running a time you're generally happy with, your silver goal might be to run a personal best, and your gold goal might be to win the race.
This can help decrease anxiety and increase confidence by removing the pressure of one ideal performance and shifting focus to the present moment. Especially because "an outcome is something you can't control," she says.
Fact-check your self-doubt
If you're feeling overcome with negative thoughts right before a job interview or a big test, ask yourself three questions:
- Is that thought true?
- Is that thought serving you?
- What would be a more empowering statement? 
This method is similar to other frameworks, like acceptance commitment therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy. It can pause negative thoughts and help you get back to the present moment.
For example, if you walk into a job interview thinking, "If I don't ace this, I'll never get another job," this exercise can challenge that thought. And it can help you find a more positive, grounded alternative: "Even if I don't get this job, I know I'm capable of success and that there are better opportunities for me."
Remember, she says. Confidence is a choice you get to make.
"You get to decide in the moment, are you going to be confident?" she says. "Many times the action of confidence comes before the feeling, and it's a skill."

LJP (Ram Vilas) chief Chirag Paswan is set to contest the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly election, with the party preparing for all 403 seats.
NEW DELHI: Chirag Paswan once described himself as Prime Minister Narendra Modi's "Hanuman". Six years later, the LJP (Ram Vilas) chief offered another approach of his politics: "I can stand up to my government ... I am in the alliance but I am not the BJP."This distinction becomes relevant as he prepares to take his party into the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly election. LJP(RV) has announced that it will contest the polls and is preparing for all 403 constituencies, while leaving open whether it will eventually contest alone or as part of an alliance.
We want this to take the form of a legal right for the youth. Wherever exams are cancelled, students should receive reimbursement for their travel expenses, arrangements for their accommodation, and provisions for their food. We have firmly presented this stance of the party on the floor of the House as well.
Chirag Paswan
The UP move comes after a significant change in Chirag Paswan's political position. In 2020, the undivided LJP broke with the NDA in Bihar, contested 135 seats and targeted Nitish Kumar's JD(U), while maintaining its support for PM Modi. Its slogan captured the strategy: "Modi se bair nahi, Nitish teri khair nahi." The party won only one seat, but its 5.66% vote share had a measurable impact on the results.Since then, LJP(RV) has moved from being a marginal alliance partner to a more consequential NDA component.
It won all five Lok Sabha seats it contested in Bihar in 2024, giving Chirag Paswan a 100% strike rate, and in the 2025 assembly election it contested 29 seats under the NDA arrangement and won 19. The BJP and JD(U) contested 101 seats each, while LJP(RV) secured 29.That progression provides the context for the 403-seat announcement. Chirag Paswan now has five Lok Sabha MPs, 19 MLAs in Bihar and a Union cabinet position. The question is whether that political weight can be extended beyond Bihar.
The 403-seat gamble
The latest phase of the UP push took shape in September, when Paswan launched his party's youth outreach in Prayagraj. At the "Youth Bole Toh" programme, he spoke about education, employment, skills and greater youth participation in politics, and announced plans for a National Youth Commission.On September 28, he made the electoral plan explicit: "There is no doubt that LJP (Ram Vilas) will contest the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections."The following day, he said the response in Prayagraj had strengthened his confidence in the UP plan. LJP(RV) MP Rajesh Verma subsequently said the party was preparing for all 403 seats, while making clear that the eventual alliance arrangement would be decided later.
Chirag Paswan on law and order in Bihar.
The 2020 flashback
The 2020 Bihar assembly election was the debut test of Chirag Paswan's leadership. His father, Ram Vilas Paswan, had just died a few days ago.The LJP won only one seat but emerged as a significant factor in 54 constituencies where its vote total was greater than the victory margin. In 25 seats where JD(U) finished second, LJP's vote exceeded the winning margin. Chirag was explicit about the objective, saying after the election: "My main idea in the election was to make the BJP stronger. I am happy with the impact I have had in this election."The BJP finished with 74 seats in that election, ahead of JD(U)'s 43 for the first time. The episode demonstrated that LJP did not need to win seats itself to affect the relative strength of its larger alliance partner.The 2025 Bihar election showed the other side of the equation. LJP(RV) was no longer operating as a spoiler outside the alliance. It contested 29 seats as an NDA partner and won 19, converting its electoral relevance into representation inside the alliance.UP could now test both models: LJP(RV) as an alliance partner with an electoral base of its own, and LJP(RV) as a potential vote-splitter in constituencies where even a few thousand votes can decide the outcome.
The Dalit arithmetic
The potential constituency is significant, but far from straightforward.The BSP won no seats in the 2024 Lok Sabha election in UP and polled around 9.4%. At the same time, the SP expanded its support among Dalit voters as part of its broader PDA coalition. A Lokniti-CSDS post-poll analysis showed a sharp difference between Jatav and non-Jatav Dalit voting patterns, with the BSP retaining much stronger support among Jatavs than among non-Jatav Dalits.For Chirag Paswan, the challenge is therefore larger than taking the Paswan identity from Bihar to UP. Pasis, Valmikis, Khatiks and other non-Jatav communities have distinct political histories and local calculations. Whether LJP(RV) can persuade sections of these voters that it is a credible political vehicle will determine whether its UP expansion produces votes or merely an organisational footprint.The impact could also vary by constituency. A modest LJP(RV) vote could matter in a close BJP-SP contest if it draws disproportionately from one side's potential support base. But unlike Bihar in 2020, there is no single obvious target. The BJP, SP, BSP and Congress have overlapping social coalitions, making the direction of any vote transfer harder to predict.
Why UP and why now?
The UP expansion also fits Paswan's attempt to establish LJP(RV) beyond its Bihar base. The party has already demonstrated that it can operate outside the state: in the 2023 Nagaland assembly election, it contested 16 seats, won two and finished runner-up in eight, securing more than 8.6% of the vote.But UP is on a different scale. A credible organisation here would give Chiag Paswan a political presence in the country's largest state and potentially strengthen his position in future NDA negotiations.
Chirag Paswan asked CEC to address recent SIR controversy.
His recent conduct suggests that maintaining an independent identity is part of that calculation. He has criticised the Bihar government's handling of law and order while remaining part of the NDA, and questioned the Election Commission over concerns surrounding SIR before welcoming its subsequent clarification.
The UP experiment, therefore, would not simply be about how many seats LJP(RV) could win. It would be abot whether Chirag Paswan can build an influence outside Bihar to make his party a more consequential NDA partner, while retaining the political independence he summed up in his own words: "I am in the alliance but I am not the BJP."

1 dead, 1 injured after Telok Blangah Heights incident; man to face murder charge
Police said the man is believed to have acted alone and there is currently no evidence to suggest that it was a religiously motivated attack or an act of terror.
SINGAPORE: A 32-year-old man will be charged with murder on Wednesday (Oct 7), police said on Monday.
The police received calls for assistance in the vicinity of Block 61 Telok Blangah Heights at about 6pm on Monday and responded to the scene within 10 minutes.
Upon arrival, officers found a 73-year-old man lying motionless and a 53-year-old man injured on the ground floor of the block.
Both men were taken to Singapore General Hospital, said the Singapore Civil Defence Force. The 53-year-old man was conscious when taken to hospital, the police said.
The 73-year-old man subsequently died.
The 32-year-old man later called the police to surrender and was arrested in the vicinity.
Police said the man is believed to have acted alone and there is currently no evidence to suggest that it was a religiously motivated attack or an act of terror.
He will be charged with murder under Section 302(1) of the Penal Code. The offence of murder carries the death penalty.
Police investigations are ongoing.

For nearly five months, the family of Indian sailor Mohammed Tanweeruz Zaman lived in distress, going from office to office and contacting every authority they could think of as they desperately sought his release after he was taken captive aboard the MT Honour 25. But when they were told that Zaman had been killed during a rescue operation, their ordeal took a darker turn. The family says the injuries they saw on his body raised serious doubts about the official account of his death and led them to believe he may have been tortured while in captivity. “We felt that he had been held captive and tortured. To us, it did not look like the injuries were the result of crossfire or a rescue operation,” Zaman’s nephew Raja Altaj Khan told LiveMint in an exclusive interview. Zaman, the sole breadwinner of his family, had been working aboard the fuel tanker when it was hijacked off the coast of Somalia on 21 April, according to Khan. After the vessel was seized, Zaman managed to get access to a phone and contacted his family, Khan said. “After a few days, the pirates gave him access to their phone so that he could call his family and inform them that the ship had been hijacked. They wanted the kidnapped crew members to convey the information to their families and the authorities,” Khan said. The family said that they immediately contacted the shipping company and authorities, including DG Shipping and the International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF). “After that, we started communicating with the pirates. They would give us instructions and make demands. During the negotiations, they initially demanded $7 million,” Khan said. According to Khan, the ransom demand was eventually reduced to $1 million after months of negotiations. “The negotiations had already been going on for around five months. The ship owner was Somali and told us that he was trying to negotiate with the pirates. Eventually, the ransom demand came down to $1 million,” he said. The family alleges that the company ultimately did not pay the $1 million ransom. Khan said ITF Europe advised the family that experienced negotiators and competent authorities should handle the negotiations. “But the ship owner said that they would deal with the matter themselves,” Khan said. For months, the family had little information about Zaman’s condition or whereabouts. “There were always delays in receiving information. We would get updates only after a long time. All of this was extremely shocking and distressing for our family,” Khan said. The family also approached various authorities, including the Ministry of External Affairs, seeking Zaman’s release. “We pleaded for Zaman’s release. We approached various authorities and offices, but received no response. The only response we received was from Lok Bhavan (West Bengal), which told us that our representation had been forwarded to the Ministry of External Affairs,” Khan said. Then, in September, the family received news that Zaman had been killed. Khan said his last conversation with the ship’s captain was on 16 September. The family continued receiving updates through the captain’s wife. “On 29 September, I received a call from the captain’s wife, who used to give us updates from time to time. She told me that a rescue team had reached the ship and that five people had died. Zaman was the only Indian among them,” he said. “The news was extremely distressing for my mother, who is Zaman’s sister. I immediately video-called the captain. During the call, he told me that Zaman had been killed,” Khan said. According to Khan, the family was told that a pirate had opened fire during the rescue operation. “He told us that when the rescue operation was taking place, everyone was on the deck. When we asked how Zaman had died, he said that one of the pirates had suddenly started firing at the people, and Zaman was killed,” Khan said. “We asked for confirmation and requested photographs and videos because we wanted to be absolutely certain that it was Zaman,” Khan said. The captain eventually showed Zaman to the family during a video call, Khan said. “The captain sent us photographs. Initially, we thought they might be AI-generated, given how advanced AI has become. After repeated requests, the captain showed Zaman to us on a video call. He pointed out the injuries to his right arm and showed us what appeared to be a gunshot wound,” Khan said. What the family saw in the photographs and video deepened their doubts about how Zaman died. “After seeing the video, we felt that he had been held captive and tortured. To us, it did not look like the injuries were the result of crossfire or a rescue operation,” Khan said. “In the video, we could see serious injuries to his arm and leg. There were other wounds, bruises and black marks on his body,” he added. LiveMint has reviewed the photographs and videos shared with the family. The material shows multiple visible injuries on Zaman’s body, including wounds and extensive marks on his arms and legs. The family said it subsequently approached Indian authorities for answers. “After seeing the photographs and videos, we approached the embassy, but we were told that they had no information about what had happened. We then went from office to office — from the shipping company to DG Shipping — trying to get some confirmation,” Khan said. After Zaman’s death, the family’s demands have changed. They just want his body brought back to India. “After he was killed, we continued approaching different offices because we wanted to bring his body back. Even now, we have not received any clear assurance from the government or the authorities. From the ministry, we have received no information. Nothing,” Khan said. “Now, we are simply pleading with the authorities to bring his body back to us. We want him to be handed over to his family. When he was alive, nobody could bring him back. We do not know whose mistake it was, but our request now is very simple — please bring him home,” he said. “He was an Indian citizen, and we believe the authorities have a responsibility to help us bring him back. We are asking everyone for help,” Khan added. The MT Honour 25, a Palau-flagged oil tanker carrying around 18,500 barrels of oil, was hijacked off Somalia’s northeastern Puntland region on 21 April, according to media reports. The Puntland Maritime Police Force later retook control of the vessel and apprehended 16 suspected pirates, according to reports. Zaman was among those reported killed during the incident. FlyDubai attacker intended to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport, investigation finds
Motive behind midair attack aboard FlyDubai plane remains unclear
TEL AVIV, Israel — An ongoing investigation into last week's midair attack on a FlyDubai plane has found that the co-pilot who tried to take control of the flight intended to crash it into Israel's Ben Gurion International Airport, a person familiar with the matter but not authorized to speak publicly told NPR.
The plane was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv and was intending to land at Ben Gurion midmorning on a busy weekday. The co-pilot attacked the plane's captain midflight with an axe and attempted to take control of the plane.
It is believed that the co-pilot likely acted alone, the source said.
Authorities in the United Arab Emirates — which is leading the main investigation into the incident, with help from Israeli officials — and in Israel have deemed the attack an attempted terrorist attack, although the motive is still being investigated.
The commercial flight had 172 people on board, according to the airline, the majority of whom were Israeli. All passengers and crew were safe and accounted for after the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. They were flown to Tel Aviv late Wednesday.
Investigators said that the co-pilot carried out the attack with what's called a crash axe — a lightweight emergency tool stored in the cockpit to break through panels or jammed doors in the event of a crash.
The aviation tracking site Flightradar24 said data shows at one point the plane descended more than 14,000 feet, or nearly 3 miles, in under 30 seconds — way faster than normal.
The pilot was able to open the cockpit door during the attack, and passengers rushed in and subdued the attacker, while another pilot who happened to be on board helped land the plane, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who spoke to the injured pilot as he was recovering in the hospital.
Both the pilot and the co-pilot are alive and have been transferred to the UAE for questioning.
Attacker is an Omani national
The co-pilot is from Oman, according to Israeli officials. Omani and Emirati officials have not confirmed that publicly.
The detail of his nationality is raising questions in Israel about how he was allowed to fly a plane heading to Ben Gurion, as Israel does not allow pilots from countries it doesn't have diplomatic relations with to fly in its airspace. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Fox & Friends that Israel checks the background of pilots flying routes into the country, and that the attacker must have gotten through a "loophole."
Officials from Israel's Ministry of Transportation and security services have traded accusations over the lack of oversight and vetting of the pilot. Meanwhile, several of Netanyahu's political opponents have said the security breach is a failure on the prime minister's part and have called for a larger investigation.
Netanyahu announced late Sunday that there will be a formal examination into the security situation around "foreign civil aviation into Israel," but did not provide further details.
A politically tense time in Israel
National elections in Israel — which will determine whether or not Netanyahu will remain prime minister — are just weeks away. It's the first such national election since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which sparked the war in Gaza.
Polls in Israel show that the race is tight, and analysts say the FlyDubai attack would likely not change Israelis' attitudes on how they will vote.
Netanyahu has been campaigning largely on the idea that he alone can protect Israelis from the external threats that Israel faces, while his opponents have pointed to what they see as major security failures under his leadership — including the Oct. 7 attack.

New Delhi: Indians rely heavily on private two-wheelers for getting to work, while buses and trains dominate longer overnight journeys, according to the first-ever all-India National Household Travel Survey (NHTS) released by the National Statistics Office (NSO) on Monday.
Two-wheelers accounted for 42.6% of workers travelling to fixed workplaces, making them the largest single mode for regular work travel. By contrast, buses accounted for 55.8% of household overnight journeys and inter-city railways for another 17.7%, together accounting for 73.5% of such travel.
Conducted between July 2025 and June 2026, the survey provides a nationwide picture of how, why and how frequently Indians travel. It is intended to provide an evidence base for transport infrastructure planning, public transport routes and service scheduling.
The survey covered 14,274 villages and 10,377 urban blocks, collecting information from 492,023 households and 2.03 million people across the country. It is the first dedicated national survey to comprehensively capture household travel behaviour, including modes, purposes, frequency, duration and expenditure.
The NSO defined travel for the survey as a trip involving a distance of at least one kilometre. Trips shorter than one kilometre were excluded.
Public transport assumes greater importance when Indians travel overnight. Buses accounted for 55.8% of household overnight journeys, while inter-city railways accounted for 17.7%. Cars made up 15.1% and two-wheelers 8.8%.
Rail use was significantly higher among urban households. About 22.7% of overnight journeys by urban households were undertaken by railway, compared with 14% among rural households, highlighting the continuing importance of rail for longer-distance mobility from cities.
Overnight travel also remains driven overwhelmingly by social and religious requirements rather than tourism. Social, communication and religious activities accounted for 70.2% of overnight household trips, with the share broadly similar in rural and urban India.
Tourism-related travel, including culture, leisure, sports and tourism, accounted for 7.4% of overnight trips, rising to 9.3% in urban areas. Travel for self-care and maintenance accounted for another 6.5%.
Patterns differ considerably by purpose. Among students travelling to educational institutions, walking was the most common mode, accounting for 37% of trips, followed by buses at 29.5% and bicycles at 15.8%.
The survey found that 66.4% of students aged six years and above travelled more than one kilometre daily to attend their educational institution. The proportion was 65.6% in rural areas and 68.1% in urban areas.
Young people aged 15-29 had the highest regular participation in education-related travel. Among this age group, 79.1% of rural students and 73.3% of urban students undertook daily trips to educational institutions.
Travel times were relatively short for most students and workers. About 87.6% of students reached their educational institutions within 30 minutes, while 83.4% of workers reached their fixed workplaces in less than 30 minutes.
Commuting nevertheless represents a recurring household expense, particularly in cities. The average monthly expenditure on travel to a fixed workplace was ₹785 per worker, but the figure was substantially higher in urban areas at ₹1,044, compared with ₹612 in rural areas.
Students spent an average of ₹443 a month commuting to educational institutions. Urban students spent ₹617, against ₹361 for rural students.
The survey also shows a gender gap in work-related travel expenditure. Male workers spent an average of ₹835 a month commuting to fixed workplaces, compared with ₹533 for female workers.
For other within-day trips unrelated to education or employment, two-wheelers remained the most widely used mode at 32.2%, followed by walking at 24.9%, auto-rickshaws at 18.9%, bicycles at 12.6% and buses at 8.5%.
The government said the NHTS would help identify gaps in existing transport systems, assess accessibility, optimize routes and improve service frequency and scheduling. The data is also expected to support regional transport planning and infrastructure investment by providing a more detailed understanding of where people travel, when they travel and why they travel.

SCO condemns Winnipeg Sun, mayoral-candidate CEO for column questioning deaths at residential schools
Column published days after National Day for Truth and Reconciliation; Kevin Klein disavows responsibility
A column questioning the deaths of children at residential schools has led the Southern Chiefs' Organization to condemn the Winnipeg Sun and express concern that the newspaper's CEO is running for mayor of the Manitoba capital.
On Oct. 4, the Sun published a column entitled "Grave misdirection: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence," suggesting the deaths of Indigenous children at residential schools have been mischaracterized.
"Each death is a tragedy, but none is evidence of an atrocity," the column states, citing as examples the death of one child from bronchitis and another by lightning.
The National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation documented the deaths of at least 4,200 Indigenous children over the course of 165 years at Canada's residential schools. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada defined the deaths and widespread abuses within residential schools as cultural genocide.
The publication of the column four days after the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation led to a formal statement of condemnation from the Southern Chiefs' Organization, which represents 33 Anishinaabe and Dakota First Nations in Manitoba.
"Survivors and their families should not be forced, yet again, to prove what happened to them or defend the children who never came home," SCO Grand Chief Jerry Daniels said in a statement. "Thousands of children died while attending residential schools. Children were forcibly removed from their families and Nations, stripped of their languages and cultures, and subjected to systems of abuse, neglect and assimilation.
"These are not allegations or political talking points. They are part of Canada's documented historical record."
The co-author of a book about residential school denialism called the column disgusting because, he said, it perpetuates the notion the deaths of thousands of children who were forcibly removed from their families is less horrific because many died of disease, malnutrition and neglect as opposed to murder.
"A lot of people will say, oh, it was just tuberculosis. Lots of kids died of tuberculosis in the early 20th century," said University of Manitoba history professor Sean Carleton, the co-author of Truth Before Reconciliation: Confronting Residential School Denialism.
"That, in fact, is true, except for the fact that, you know what spreads tuberculosis faster? Overcrowding, poor nutrition. Lack of proper sanitation, overwork. All of these issues that were known to be systemic to the residential school system."
Carleton said the column perpetuates what he describes as far-right misinformation about First Nations making claims about mass graves or clandestine murders.
"This is a distraction tactic. It's an attempt to move the goalposts, to make it extremely difficult for Indigenous nations, to explain the complicated nuanced understanding of what we already know, thanks to church and state records, that at least 4,000 children died in these institutions for a variety of different reasons," he said.
As criticism of the column mounted Sunday, the editor-in-chief of the Klein Group, the company that owns the Winnipeg Sun, dug in her heels. Heather Klein defended the column in a followup entitled "Disagreement is not denial."
The Southern Chiefs' Organization also criticized her husband, Klein Group CEO Kevin Klein, the candidate who is running for Winnipeg mayor.
Daniels called it "deeply concerning" someone seeking public office provided a platform for someone to use residential schools and the deaths of First Nations children as the basis for political commentary.
"Winnipeg is home to a large and vibrant First Nations population. Anyone asking to lead this city has a responsibility to understand the history of residential schools and the ongoing responsibilities of reconciliation," Daniels said.
Kevin Klein said in a statement he is not responsible for the content of the Winnipeg Sun while he runs for mayor.
"From the day I entered the race for mayor, I stepped away from every editorial decision at the Winnipeg Sun, and I have kept that commitment. The paper stands on its own," the mayoral candidate said.
Heather Klein alone is responsible for the content, he said, adding he does not assign stories, edit copy, approve pieces or stop them from running.
"Any suggestion otherwise is reckless and without foundation," he said.
Other mayoral candidates criticize Klein
Several mayoral candidates also criticized the newspaper CEO-turned-candidate.
Mayoral candidate Noah Redden said in a statement there is a difference between upholding freedom of speech and tolerating hate speech.
Redden called residential school denialism inflammatory and said Klein needs to explain to Winnipeg's Indigenous population why his newspaper echoed attacks on residential school survivors.
Incumbent mayoral candidate Scott Gillingham told reporters Sunday he's spoken to enough Indigenous families in Winnipeg to hear first-hand the impact of residential schools.
"What is not deniable in my mind is the impact, the lasting, devastating impact of residential schools on our country," said Gillingham, who attended TRC Day events in an official capacity on Wednesday.
Klein said Friday he did not attend TRC Day events but called the national holiday important.
"Canadians ought to know what took place in the residential school system and what it has meant for Indigenous families and communities ever since," Klein said Sunday in a statement.
"The wrongs of the past should not be forgotten. As a father and a grandfather, I cannot begin to imagine the pain those families carry."

Call it Imperfect Woman. The trend of streaming limited series becoming ongoing ones continues with Apple TV ordering a second season of thriller Imperfect Women. Taking a spinoff approach, it will follow one of the limited series’ three titular characters, Eleanor, played by Kerry Washington.
Imperfect Women, based on Araminta Hall’s novel, revolved around best friends Eleanor and Mary (Elisabeth Moss) as they tried to solve the murder of the third member of their friends group, Nancy (Kate Mara), seen in flashbacks.
Washington and Moss executive produced the original installment in addition to starring and will also both executive produce Season 2.
There is no second Imperfect Women book so there is no source material for Season 2. Instead, it is based on an original story from series creator Annie Weisman and Justin Hillian. The two will serve as co-showrunners on the second season, which will change locations from Los Angeles, where Season 1 was set.
Watch on Deadline
In Season 2, Eleanor (Washington) returns to her hometown roots in the affluent black enclave of Martha’s Vineyard, only to find that beneath it’s idyllic surface, lie secrets and scandals that threaten to upend everything she thought she knew about her past.”
For now, there are no plans for Moss’ Mary and Nancy’s widower Robert (Joel Kinnaman) to be in the second installment which picks up on the Eleanor’s flash-forward scene in the finale, which resonated with fans. It showed her moving away from the toxic dynamic of her relationships and enjoying a new life on a yacht with a new love interest.
While cast deals are still being worked out, expected to return as part of the new Eleanor-centered installment are Leslie Odom Jr., who plays her brother, and Sheryl Lee Ralph, who plays their mother.
As for the lingering question over Mary and Robert’s ambiguous glance at the end of the finale as the two were seen celebrating the birthday of Mary’s daughter together, that may be answered in Season 2 with a reference of the characters’ status.
“We were thrilled to see how deeply these women and their stories resonated with audiences around the world, and I’m so excited to step back into Eleanor’s shoes,” Washington said. “She’s intelligent and strong, but she also finds herself navigating complicated and sometimes messy situations. We at Simpson Street along with our incredible partners at Apple and Love & Squalor Pictures can’t wait to explore a fresh chapter for her and share where this story takes us next.”
The long list of limited series that have been picked up for additional installments include Apple TV’s Reasonable Doubt, Netflix’s Untamed, Squid Game, The Beast In Me and Beef, HBO’s Big Little Lies, The White Lotus, True Detective and Task, HBO’s Good American Family and FX’s Shōgun.
Imperfect Women is a co-production between 20th Television and Apple Studios. The second season is created, co-showrun and executive produced by Weisman and Hillian, and executive produced by Washington for her Simpson Street banner alongside Pilar Savone. Moss and Lindsey McManus, who initially optioned the book, via their production company Love & Squalor Pictures are executive producers alongside author Hall.
“After a wildly entertaining first season, driven by the performances of Kerry, Lizzie and Kate, we jumped at the opportunity to expand the world of Imperfect Women through Kerry’s fan favorite character of Eleanor,” said Matt Cherniss, Apple TV’s head of programming. “Annie and Justin’s thrilling new story felt like an exciting and natural next chapter. We can’t wait for fans to experience it.”

Salah out of Egypt game because of artificial turf
- Published
Egypt have left Mohamed Salah out of their Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against South Sudan because the match will be played on artificial turf.
The former Liverpool forward, now with Turkish club Trabzonspor, has not travelled with the squad to the capital Juba for Tuesday's game.
The 34-year-old started Friday's goalless draw with Angola in Cairo but was substituted by coach Hossam Hassan after an hour.
"The Egypt national team's technical staff, led by Hossam Hassan, has decided to rest Mohamed Salah for the match against South Sudan scheduled for 29 September because of the playing surface," the Egyptian Football Association (EFA) said.
"It was agreed between the national team's technical staff and Mohamed Salah before the Angola match that he would not play against South Sudan, and the technical staff preferred this approach in order to protect the player," it added.
There is a perception of increased risk of injury on artificial surfaces despite technological improvements, though studies have shown, external there is no evidence of a greater risk of injury.
Salah left Liverpool at the end of last season after nine years during which he made 442 appearances and scored 257 goals, winning nine major trophies.
In six Turkish Super Lig games for Trabzonspor this season he has seven goals and two assists.
