Rows of hardware and car-part shops line Garstin Bastion Road, with faded signs crammed together above their shutters. By day, the street is one of Old Delhi’s busiest commercial thoroughfares. But as dusk falls, GB Road, as it is known locally, transforms into one of the city’s most notorious red-light districts.
An estimated 2,800 sex workers live and work in brothels that occupy the upper floors of the dilapidated buildings, their entrances tucked behind narrow stairways and unmarked doors. Women sit on plastic stools beneath the stairways, calling out to men passing on the street, while others watch from windows above, their eyes following the movement below before customers are directed upstairs.
The challenges the women of GB Road face are numerous and well documented – from health risks to abuse, debt to poor sanitation. Now they face a new struggle: India’s controversial electoral reform process. The Election Commission’s special intensive revision, or SIR, is a nationwide exercise in which electoral rolls have shrunk by more than 58 million voters across the 13 states covered in the first two of three main phases. In Delhi, covered in the third phase, the scale of exclusion is the highest recorded as a percentage: 4.76 million names – 33% of the city’s previous electorate – do not appear on the city’s draft roll published on 31 August.
The government says SIR is meant to “purify” the electoral rolls by removing ineligible voters, including alleged undocumented migrants, but critics have accused Narendra Modi’s government of using it to target minority voters and reshape electoral rolls in ways that could benefit his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
On GB Road, the proportion of those excluded is even higher. Data shared by officials overseeing about 1,300 voters in the area show that about 650 were sex workers on the previous electoral roll. Of these, at least 500 have either been marked as “shifted”, meaning they have moved home or location, or have been unable to establish their eligibility because of missing documentation – more than three-quarters of the sex workers on the local roll.
One of them is 36-year-old Beauty*, who has lived on GB Road for more than two decades. She got her first voter ID in 2008. At the time, the address where she lived and worked as a sex worker and verification by a government official called a booth-level officer (BLO) were enough to put her on the electoral roll. She voted in previous elections.
But under the new rules, voters had to establish eligibility by proving their link to the relevant previous electoral roll or by producing prescribed documents such as a passport, birth or education certificate – a paper trail Beauty struggled to reconstruct. Trafficked at 16 and brought to the brothels of GB Road, she has no contact with her family. She does have an Aadhaar card, India’s biometric identity document used widely to establish identity and access government services, with her GB Road address. But Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship and does not, by itself, establish eligibility to vote under the SIR process.
She tried to get a copy of her matriculation certificate, which is evidence of schooling, from the village in Rajasthan where she grew up. One of her regular customers of the past 10 years – a man she refers to as her husband, agreed to help track down the old record but failed.
“If I had the papers to show my father’s birth certificate, or even my own matriculation certificate, then I could prove who I am,” she says. “But how can I go back to my village to ask for these things when my trafficking has brought so much shame to my family that they no longer accept me?”
Now Beauty has lost hope – and, for now, her vote. Her name was left out of Delhi’s recent draft electoral roll. For her, the voter ID had meant more than a piece of identification. Sex workers, she says, are accustomed to being treated as immoral, degraded and less worthy than others.
“We all shit. That is what makes us equal as human beings. Voting is the same in the realm of rights. When I stand in that queue, nobody is more or less than me. It reminds me that whatever people think about my work, I am still equal to everyone else.”
Beauty is not alone in struggling to prove her eligibility. The SIR requirements have exposed the precarious paper trails of women across GB Road, a roughly 1.5km stretch running between two of Delhi’s historic landmarks, Ajmeri Gate and Lahori Gate.
Of the nine sex workers interviewed for this story, none had successfully completed the SIR process: six said they had never received the enumeration form distributed by BLOs to verify voters’ details and collect information for the electoral-roll revision, while the remaining three were unable to meet the documentation requirements.
According to Kiran Deshmukh, a sex worker and coordinator at the National Network of Sex Workers (NNSW), many have spent years, even decades, in Delhi but possess few documents establishing their family histories or links to earlier electoral rolls. “Some were trafficked as children and lost contact with their families; others never attended school or have moved between rooms and brothels without leaving a stable documentary trail,” says Deshmukh. “It is impossible in such circumstances to prove such rigid eligibility requirements under SIR.”
The process is so cumbersome that even people who are literate and have institutional and organisational support can struggle to establish their eligibility. “The process of receiving the enumeration form, knowing when you have not received it, reaching out, then trying to create a paper trail is so daunting that the entire burden of proving your eligibility is placed on the citizen to protect their own constitutional right,” says Deshmukh.
Sagrika Rajora, a researcher and member of Voter Adhikar Manch, a citizens’ collective, argues that the burden falls particularly heavily on people whose lives do not fit neatly into the categories used by the verification process. “To identify people of such marginality is a tedious task. These categories of ‘shifted’ become an easy way forward for booth-level officers, when finding people on the ground is already time-consuming.”
BLOs are often drawn from occupations such as auxiliary nurses or health workers, adding electoral duties to already demanding jobs. Some have raised concerns about the workload and unrealistic timelines of the exercise. Yet, Rajora says, there has been little effort to streamline the process to ensure that “no eligible citizen is left out”, the aim outlined by the Delhi chief electoral officer, Ashok Kumar.
“There is so much discretion vested in one BLO. Even if you leave citizenship aside and talk only about voter rights, the entire process of delivering and collecting these forms depends on that one person. There are no grounds for entrusting one person with such a huge responsibility without any accountability at all,” Rajora says.
“It is not surprising that sex workers are among those being excluded. When people have lives that are so complex and mobile, you are going to be untraceable, absent from the system. These are the people for whom such a verification system is simply not designed to work.”
The gaps also cause problems for workers’ children when they reach adulthood. “Children may not possess documents establishing parentage in the manner expected for verification. Some are raised by relatives, guardians or members of the community, while others grow up in institutional care, making conventional family records difficult to establish,” says Deshmukh.
For 23-year-old Dinesh*, whose mother was a sex worker, the problem is not abstract. His mother died three years ago, but she never had a birth certificate. Without one, obtaining her death certificate became nearly impossible, leaving Dinesh with little documentation through which to establish his maternal lineage.
When Dinesh submitted his enumeration form, he relied on his matriculation certificate as proof of his identity. But the booth-level officer pointed out that it did not have his father’s name. “If my mother gave birth to me, why do I need a man’s name on any official certificate?” he asks.
Dinesh says his name is missing from the draft electoral roll. He is still unsure why, but suspects the absence of his father’s name may have been a factor.
The NNSW has written to the chief electoral officer seeking special measures to ensure that sex workers and their children are not excluded from the SIR. But the joint chief electoral officer, Balram Meena, told The Hindu there was no separate process for sex workers. “If their mapping can’t be done and there are no documents either, their names will be removed as per the process.”
The fear of losing the vote is not only about voting rights. In West Bengal, where the SIR has already been completed, the BJP government has used lists of voters deleted during the exercise to scrutinise eligibility for welfare schemes. The BJP chief minister, Suvendu Adhikari, says welfare programmes will continue under a “transparent process”, but adds: “No deceased person, illegal infiltrator, or non-Indian individual will be allowed to avail benefits meant for citizens of the state.” The government has excluded about 3 million beneficiaries from its new Annapurna Bhandar welfare for women scheme, using SIR deletion data in its verification process.
In Delhi, the next stage of the SIR process – issuing notices to those whose eligibility or previous electoral-roll details could not be established or matched, and dealing with claims and objections – has now begun and will continue until 29 October. Those excluded from the draft roll can challenge their omission. But Dinesh says he does not intend to.
After years of being asked to produce documents that his family never had, he is unsure what more he can submit to prove that he exists.
“Even if my mother were alive today, I don’t think that would be enough to prove anything. She never had the documents they are asking for. So how am I supposed to get those documents now, especially after her death?”
* Names have been changed. Workers and residents did not permit any photography during the Guardian’s visit

The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'
- Published
"I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk."
"I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her."
Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township.
"Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am."
At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust.
At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve.
He raises his fist.
"We are men!" he shouts.
The group clap and cheers. Some sip bottled beer.
"Listen guys," Bra Steve says. "We must stand together to fight against gender-based violence and femicide."
Bra Steve is the local organiser of Father A Nation, a non-profit that works with men and boys to promote positive masculinity and help end violence against women.
The group's meeting comes as South Africa grapples with renewed anger over renewed cases of femicide and violence against women.
The discovery of the bodies of 12 women over three months, in the city of Ekurhuleni, near Johannesburg has reignited questions about the scale of what many people see as being a crisis of violence against women.
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has acknowledged that his government has not done enough and announced measures he hopes can make women feel safer.
The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
In that period, according to the South African Human Rights Commission, 569 women were killed, an average of six a day, and 1,052 others survived attempted murder.
A report in 2022 by the Human Sciences Research Council found that more than 35% of South African women experienced physical or sexual violence, many from their own intimate partners.
For Bra Steve, part of the solution to the crisis is helping men to understand the issue and take responsibility for their actions.
"We are a lost generation," he says. "We must restore dignity to the men around here."
Amongst the group of men outside the tavern is Zizipho Mtwesi, the project co-ordinator of Father A Nation.
Reflecting on recent weeks, he says more should be done.
The latest measures announced by Ramaphosa, including better street lighting and a review of unsolved cases, are too little, he says, and too late.
"When I think about all of these recent murders in Johannesburg, I get angry. Why do we have to wait for this to happen for us to act?"
He looks around and gestures at the meeting. "We are trying to reach men before things like these murders happen again."
Craig Wilkinson is the founder of the group. "We get men to talk, to process their feelings," he explains.
"And as they do, this healing takes place. And the second phase is teaching and training positive masculinity.
"We ultimately hope that this will eliminate the scourge of gender-based violence."
He stands up, moving into the centre of the group, calling out to the men.
"You as a man are a powerful force for good," he tells them. "You choose what kind of man you want to be. Women need to be safe."
Father A Nation operates across South Africa, teaching healthy masculinity and running training programmes across dozens of schools and colleges.
Mystery surrounds the spate of murders which has sparked South Africa's latest moment of soul-searching about the safety of its women.
Police have not ruled out potential links between some of the Ekurhuleni deaths but have not said they are investigating a serial killer. Suspects in some of the cases have appeared in court.
But the spate of deaths has sparked new concerns and in Organic Market some women are more fearful than ever.
Outside a nearby shack Linkie listens with interest as she cleans clothes in a large metal bucket.
"We are not safe when we are outside our place," she says.
"We are afraid when we see a car behind us when we walk. We feel afraid. We feel scared. What if this guy's going to kidnap me or do something to me?"
It is a feeling shared by many women here. In the local hair salon, sporting a mane of thick pink braids, is Providence Maseko.
She comes to the door to speak to Bra Steve.
"Safety here is very bad," she says, "Maybe you are the serial killer. How do I know who to trust?"
Bra Steve laughs. "We must talk about these things," he urges. "Come to our meetings and we can learn to trust each other."
Maseko tells me that she now takes an e-hailing taxi everywhere in the hope that it is safer.
Back at the tavern, the men's meeting is wrapping up.
"As we try to stop gender-based violence," says Zizipho, "each and every man needs to know that they need to play a part in this.
"And if they wouldn't allow these things to happen to their own daughters or own mothers, they mustn't allow it to be done to someone else's daughter, which is their wives or their girlfriends."
Mathekga is impressed with what he has heard.
"I would love them to keep on practising what we have learned, because we no longer have role models," he says. "Our fathers and our uncles, they are there in prison. We must now become role models and help make this country better."

Oura Ring 5 vs. Apple Watch Series 12: Which smart health wearable is right for you?
There's a clear winner.
Once niche, health and fitness wearables have become pretty commonplace. It's not that everyone is suddenly into running and weightlifting. Rather, Fitbit helped popularize simple, affordable wristband trackers, and Apple integrated health sensors into the Apple Watch, snaring millions of iPhone owners and inspiring copycats. The benefits of health tracking are also tangible — it's not hard to find anecdotes in the wild from people who say a wearable helped them go from sedentary to fit, or even saved their life.
In recent years, the supremacy of bands and smartwatches has been challenged by smart rings. These provide many, if not all, of the same tracking benefits, but in an even more compact form factor. Some people may also prefer them for their more stylish or "professional" look, though that's extremely subjective.
Starting around the $400 price point, the Oura Ring 5 competes directly with Apple's latest flagship, the Apple Watch Series 12. There are arguments for both devices, although issues like platform support, workout intensity and your willingness to spring for subscriptions will probably dictate your path. This is a case where aesthetics should definitely not rule the day.
The pros and cons of the Oura Ring 5 and Apple Watch Series 12
The Oura and the Series 12 gather much of the same health data, including metrics like sleep, steps, estimated calorie burn and heart rate (including variability). They also provide tracking related to menstrual cycles, though Oura claims to go a step further in women's health, providing insights related to pregnancy and menopause. They further share Readiness scores, which synthesize various factors to gauge whether you should push for that new squat PR or take it easy.
From there, though, the devices actually diverge pretty sharply. Naturally, the biggest difference is that the Series 12 has a touchscreen, available in 42 and 46mm sizes (the latter costing $50 extra). It's about more than checking the time or health data — in tandem with 64GB of storage and Apple's S11 processor, the Series 12 can handle many tasks without needing to pull out your iPhone, from Apple Pay and notifications to navigating off-road trails. Cellular models (starting at $500) can handle some online functions without Wi-Fi, whereas an Oura has no choice but to talk to your phone. You'll have to pull out your phone to see any of your Oura's data or control its settings — the company is even discontinuing its web interface.
Speaking of which, it's time to talk about platforms. While both devices sync with Apple Health, only the Oura supports Android's equivalent, Health Connect, for one very obvious reason: The Series 12 requires at least an iPhone 11 running iOS 27 or later. If you own an Android phone from the likes of Google, Samsung, Motorola or others, your time is going to be better spent pitting the Oura against Google's Pixel Watch 5 or Garmin's many alternatives.
It's also worth noting that the Series 12 is miles ahead when it comes to workouts. The Oura mostly detects activities automatically and stores your data in its app, and it may not always register them accurately or at all. Manually launching one is more reliable, but either way you'll have to grab your phone to see any real-time data. Conversely, while you have to launch many Series 12 workouts yourself, that gets you real-time stats on both your phone and your wrist. Often, it's tracking data that the Oura simply can't, such as running cadence or your precise GPS location. The Oura can only link GPS data from your phone. Incidentally, any smart ring is a bad choice for weightlifters, since you're liable to grind down its shine with the knurling on barbells and dumbbells.
One area where the Oura triumphs is battery life. Realistically, any non-Ultra Apple Watch should be charged every day, possibly even twice per day if you want to do sleep tracking. The Oura can potentially last six to nine days straight. That's far more convenient, and it reduces the gaps in your data as well.
The elephant in the room and final thoughts
While we could talk about the color and material options for the two products, those are mostly cosmetic. Far more significant is the products' reliance on subscriptions, or the lack thereof. Strictly speaking, you don't need an Oura Membership to use the Ring 5. Without one, however, you lose access not just to a lot of coaching insights, but to basic things like 24/7 heart rate tracking, blood oxygen levels and integration with third-party apps like Strava. Apple supplies similar content at no extra cost, since its real goal is to hook you into its broader ecosystem. Taking full advantage of the Oura Ring 5 is going to cost you an additional $6 per month or $70 per year.
The bottom line is that iPhone fans will likely find the Series 12 to be the better deal, as it gets them a multipurpose wearable that can subscribe to various services, but at least isn't dependent on them. It's inherently superior if you take fitness seriously or want to do anything without your phone in your pocket.
The Oura wins by default for Android users. Otherwise, it arguably is a niche product, intended for people who just want an overall picture of their health and prefer to have their wearables fade into the background the rest of the time. An Apple Watch is meant to be a constant companion and draw your attention, which might not suit your lifestyle.

- Alexa D’Agostino, one of the writers of GTA 6, discussed creating Lucia in an interview with Love magazine.
- The writer's mother inspired her while penning Lucia's character.
- She believes Lucia can stand tall alongside the likes of Arthur Morgan and Niko Bellic.
Ahead of GTA 6‘s release, Alexa D’Agostino, one of the game’s writers, discussed how the team brought Lucia Caminos to life. In a recent interview, Alexa said that an undeniably real woman like Lucia can stand tall alongside previous Rockstar Games protagonists such as Arthur Morgan from RDR2 and Niko Bellic from GTA 4.
In an interview with the French fashion magazine Love, Alexa D’Agostino opened up about creating Lucia Caminos for GTA 6. Surprisingly, Alexa revealed that her mother served as an inspiration for GTA 6’s Lucia. She explained that writing Lucia felt natural because the character was relatable, and the way she was raised by her mother also helped shape the character.
“When it came to writing Lucia, I thought of the women I know, my mother was an immigrant who grew up in New Jersey, close to Lucia’s hometown of Liberty City. I thought about the way she raised me: rowdy, kind, but not to take any sh*t. I related a lot to Lucia and writing her came very naturally to me.” Alexa said.
Furthermore, Alexa talked about how Lucia Camino, one of the main characters in GTA 6, is a fully fleshed-out person in the game. She described Lucia as a ‘perfectly imperfect-with clichés,’ but believes that’s what makes her an undeniably real character in GTA 6.
As everyone knows, Lucia Caminos is the first protagonist in the history of GTA games. With a genuinely well-written woman character in hand, Alexa believes that Lucia can join the ranks of RDR2’s Arthur Morgan and GTA 4’s Niko Bellic:
“When you are focusing on writing a fully realized person with their own wants, you’re going to get something perfectly imperfect-with clichés, but also undeniably real. That’s how you get a woman that can stand tall next to the likes of Arthur Morgan and Niko Bellic.”
Rockstar’s writers have already proven that they can deliver strong, compelling female characters with Sadie Adler in RDR2. Now, Lucia has all the potential to become one of the greatest characters ever created by Rockstar Games.

Imran Khan supporters march in Pakistan to demand his release after talks failed
ISLAMABAD — More than 5,000 supporters of imprisoned former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan began a dayslong march toward Islamabad on Sunday to demand his release, after talks between the government and the opposition fell through.
The looming showdown threatens to deepen Pakistan's political uncertainty at a time when the country is also grappling with a surge in militant attacks.
Khan is current Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's main political rival and has been imprisoned since 2023 on corruption and other charges that he and his party say are politically motivated. Despite his imprisonment, he retains a substantial and passionate support base, keeping him at the center of Pakistan's turbulent political landscape.
The demonstrators, traveling in a convoy of trucks, buses and cars, departed from Lakki Marwat district in the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where Khan's party holds power. Organizers have planned overnight stops along the route as the caravan makes its way toward the capital. Sohail Afridi, the province's chief minister, and a staunch Khan supporter is leading the march.
Speaking from a specially designed container truck emblazoned with a large portrait of Khan, he expressed confidence in the movement's ability to press its demands and bring the political standoff into the heart of the capital.
Authorities have erected roadblocks, using containers, at the entrance to Islamabad and inside the city.
Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party, or PTI, and the federal government were in talks to postpone the march but failed to reach a resolution. Gohar Khan, the party's chairman, said negotiations remained deadlocked after two rounds.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi blamed Afridi for the failure of the talks, warning that he would be held responsible for any loss of life during the planned march.
Sharif's government urged postponement of the march, citing a surge in militant attacks by the Pakistani Taliban in the northwest. His government has accused PTI of sympathizing with the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan.
The organizers now vow to reach the capital after rallying with hundreds of thousands of Khan supporters.
Besides Khan's release, protesters are demanding his transfer to a hospital and permission for his family to visit him. Officials say he is in good health and receives regular family visits but maintain that meetings with the imprisoned former leader cannot be used for political purposes.
The march was originally scheduled for Sept. 27 but was postponed after party leaders said authorities blocked key approaches to Islamabad, including Attock Bridge, a major crossing for convoys from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Previous protests by Khan's supporters have turned violent, including one in 2024 in which security personnel and civilians were killed.
Khan, a former cricket star, was ousted in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022. Sharif returned to office after the February 2024 election, which Khan's party says was rigged to deny it victory. The government denies the allegation.

Riaz reported from Peshawar, Pakistan. Associated Press writers Ishtiaq Mahsud in Dera Ismail Khan and Rasool Dawar in Peshawar contributed to this report.

‘Brain fog’ is used to describe a feeling of mental slowness, difficulty concentrating, finding words, remembering information or processing things as quickly as before. But it is not a medical diagnosis, and persistent cognitive difficulties should not automatically be attributed to brain fog.
What brain fog feels like
Brain fog is a subjective description of changes in cognitive functioning. People may feel that their thinking has become slower or more effortful, that they cannot concentrate on a task, lose their train of thought, struggle to find words or read something without absorbing the information.
“Brain fog is basically a subjective feeling that you are cognitively slow, that you are mentally slow, that you are not able to do your daily activities as quickly or as deftly as before,” says Srividhya S., associate consultant, department of neurology, Rela Hospital, Chennai.
It is different from the occasional forgetfulness that occurs when a person is tired, distracted or stressed. Forgetting where the keys were kept or briefly forgetting a name, for instance, does not by itself indicate a cognitive disorder. Tiredness is also not the same as brain fog. Fatigue is primarily a feeling of reduced physical or mental energy, while brain fog refers more specifically to difficulties with attention, memory, processing or mental clarity.
T. Swathi, consultant, neurology, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai, says people with brain fog are often aware that they are not functioning as efficiently as before. This also distinguishes it from some memory disorders, where relatives may be the first to notice changes such as repeated questions, difficulty managing regular tasks or getting lost in familiar places.
Health factors
The causes of brain fog can be varied, and more than one factor may be involved. Poor or inadequate sleep is a common contributor. Sleep apnoea can also disrupt sleep repeatedly without the person being aware of it.
Stress, anxiety and depression can affect attention and processing speed. Other possible contributors include thyroid disorders, diabetes, anaemia and nutritional deficiencies such as vitamin B12 and folate. Migraine and hormonal changes, including those during pregnancy, the postpartum period and menopause, can also be associated with cognitive symptoms.
Medicines should also be considered. Sedatives, some sleeping medicines, antihistamines, anticholinergic medicines and some anti-seizure drugs can affect alertness or cognitive function. Alcohol and dehydration may add to the symptoms.
“Brain fog has several possible causes and can be due to more than one,” says Arulselvan V.L., senior consultant in neurology, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai. “It is crucial to not think that all brain fog is neurological.”
Cognitive difficulties can also occur during or after infections. A recent systematic review of 47 studies involving more than 25,000 people with long COVID estimated the pooled prevalence of brain fog at 30%. However, various studies use different definitions and assessment methods. There is so far no comparable prevalence estimate because brain fog is a symptom description and not a defined medical diagnosis.
When tests are needed
There is no fixed duration after which every case of brain fog requires investigation. Persistence, progression and its effect on daily functioning are important.
Doctors advise evaluation when symptoms continue despite adequate sleep and lifestyle measures, recur frequently or gradually worsen. Repeatedly forgetting important information, struggling with previously familiar tasks, difficulty following conversations or unusual changes in work performance are also reasons to consult a doctor.
Symptoms lasting for several weeks without an obvious explanation, particularly when they affect work, studies or relationships, should be assessed. New symptoms such as persistent fatigue, weight changes, breathlessness, tingling, low mood or excessive daytime sleepiness can provide additional clues.
Evaluation usually begins with a detailed history. . A neurological examination may then be performed.
Depending on the history and examination, doctors may check blood counts, blood sugar, electrolytes, thyroid function, kidney and liver function and nutritional markers such as vitamin B12.
A brief cognitive assessment may be useful when there are concerns about memory, attention or language. Brain imaging such as an MRI is also not routinely required for uncomplicated brain fog. It may be considered when symptoms are progressive, the neurological examination is abnormal or there are other features suggesting a structural or neurological cause. A sleep study or EEG may be considered in selected cases.
Certain symptoms, however, require prompt attention rather than being attributed to brain fog. Sudden difficulty speaking, facial drooping, weakness or numbness on one side, sudden problems with vision or balance, seizures, fainting or severe confusion can indicate an acute neurological problem such as stroke. A sudden, severe or unusual headache also requires urgent assessment.

Washington, Oct 5: President Donald Trump on Monday corrected an earlier post on social media in which he referred to Brazil's presidential election as India's to claim that the electoral process in the US was “corrupt”.
In a glaring factual error, Trump, in a post on Truth Social on Sunday, claimed that “125 million people voted in India’s Presidential elections and the results came out shortly after the vote closed”.
Trump then used the faster counting example to target Democratic-run cities and states such as Detroit, Philadelphia and California.
"In Detroit, Philadelphia, California, and numerous other US Cities and States, the results, with much smaller numbers, will often take weeks to Rig, I mean, calculate," Trump said.
“Voting in America is CORRUPT,” Trump said, referring to the weeks taken for the counting of votes in elections in US cities and states.
Later, he corrected himself to say that "25 Million People voted today in the first round of Brazil’s Presidential Election. The results came out shortly after the vote closed, on the SAME DAY!"
Brazil, not India, went to the polls on Sunday for the first round of its presidential election. The South American country recorded 125.27 million valid votes, according to its electoral authority, while results started coming in from 5 pm, when voting closed, and were updated as ballots were counted.
Brazil, alphabetically the first part of the acronym BRICS, attended a summit of the grouping in New Delhi last month and the two nations met each other in a FIFA international friendly football match in Kolkata on Saturday -- though neither fact could reliably be cited to explain the mix-up by the US President who handed over the sport's biggest prize in New Jersey in July.
India's citizens do not directly vote for their President, who is elected by an electoral college formed by members of Parliament and state assemblies. The incumbent Droupadi Murmu assumed office in 2022.
Brazil's election on Sunday featured incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. With neither candidate securing a majority, the two will face each other in a run-off on October 25.

In the 53rd episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu, Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, and Athira Elssa Johnson, Senior Reporter, discuss medicine pricing, drug safety and dengue surveillance.
The episode examines the Supreme Court’s concerns over the difference between the supply price and maximum retail price of essential cancer medicines. In one instance, the court was told that a cancer drug with a price to retailer of about ₹2,700 carried a maximum retail price of ₹27,000. The Bench described the difference as “broad daylight dacoity”.
The discussion also covers the court’s concerns about hospitals requiring patients to buy medicines from their own pharmacies, its suggestion of a uniform 16% margin and questions around generic prescriptions and the implementation of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order.
The episode also covers the risks of indiscriminate painkiller and antibiotic use, including kidney disease and antimicrobial resistance. While prolonged or inappropriate use of painkillers can cause kidney-related complications, unnecessary or incorrect antibiotic use can make infections harder to treat. The discussion highlights the importance of appropriate prescribing and responsible medicine use.
The final segment focuses on a Dengue Early Warning System being developed by researchers at the Institute of Advanced Virology in Keralam. The system combines disease surveillance data with rainfall, temperature and humidity to generate weekly, district-level forecasts using machine learning.
Trained on six years of data, from March 2020 to February 2026, the system aims to help health authorities anticipate increases in dengue transmission. If validated, the forecasts could support earlier surveillance, mosquito-control measures, healthcare preparedness and public alerts. The system is still under development and evaluation.
The episode ends with a fun fact about dengue mosquito eggs, which can remain dormant for months in dry conditions and hatch when water becomes available. Even seemingly dry containers can harbour eggs that may contribute to future mosquito populations.
The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

In 2016, the American Academy of Pediatrics issued a policy statement urging doctors to offer medications for opioid use disorder to adolescent and young adult patients who needed them.
New national data show that more young people with an opioid use disorder diagnosis did start receiving addiction medications like buprenorphine and methadone, but the increase was small. And the number of young people who stayed on medication for six months — already quite low — may have actually decreased.
“There have been some real positive changes, and then there have been some really catastrophic changes,” said Scott Hadland, the chief of adolescent and young adult medicine at Mass General Brigham for Children.
Hadland’s latest paper, published Friday in JAMA Network Open, offers a national perspective on the continuity of addiction care among young people. Researchers analyzed Medicaid enrollment and insurance claims for people ages 13 to 25 who were diagnosed with an opioid use disorder between 2016 and 2023. Out of nearly 230,000 young people over that period, about half initiated treatment by seeing a clinician, and about a third had at least two appointments in the first month. Of those youth engaged in care, about 1 in 6 received some medication. But just 1 in 32 continued with medication for six months.
As with the general population, overdose deaths skyrocketed among young people beginning around 2019 and into the early 2020s. For those age 19 and under, poisonings including overdose rose to the third-leading cause of death.
“I have had patients die as recently as this past month here in Massachusetts, from overdose,” Hadland said. “And so the stakes here are really, really high.”
Medications for opioid use disorder, specifically buprenorphine and methadone, are highly effective treatments that are also relatively cheap and easy to deliver. Yet adults often struggle to get these medications, and for minors, it can be nearly impossible. Federal law requires minors to have two documented “failed” attempts at recovery without medication before they can start methadone, and even then, many of the specialized clinics that provide it won’t accept minors. Buprenorphine is easier for doctors to prescribe, but recent research shows that few residential treatment facilities for adolescents actually offer it.
“Once you turn 18, a whole bigger field of people are open to helping you,” said Sivabalaji Kaliamurthy, a child and adolescent psychiatrist who treats addiction. “And it’s just a number if you think about it.”
In Hadland’s study, fewer than 10 minors received methadone over the entire period — a number so low that researchers had to suppress the specific number and categorize it as “not defined” to protect people’s privacy.
While there are dozens of studies showing the safety and effectiveness of these medications, very few focus specifically on young people. That means doctors don’t have a definitive answer for families when asked how long their child might need to stay on the medications, or what the long-term effects might be. Still, existing research and clinical experience are clear that the longer someone is on the medication, the better they do.
Kids often don’t want to hear that, Kaliamurthy said, and families can be apprehensive about such an open commitment. On top of that, young people also face the same structural barriers that hamper adult care: For example, the study found that Black young people and other racially minoritized groups had worse attrition through the stages of care than their white peers.
Kaliamurthy found the number of young people initiating treatment after diagnosis to be promising, but he and others agreed that more work needs to be done to prevent attrition over time.
“It doesn’t matter how good the treatment we have actually is if we haven’t created a clinical environment that is appealing, safe, compassionate, and nonjudgmental,” said Sarah Bagley, an internist and pediatrician at Boston Medical Center who provides addiction treatment to adolescents. “That engagement piece is everything, because without it, nothing.”
For Bagley, it’s important to continue advocating and doing research around young people as a distinct population. “Because it is different taking care of young people compared to adults,” she said. They have different systems organizing their lives, like school and parents.
Primary care physicians and pediatricians who have longstanding relationships with patients and families need to feel comfortable prescribing buprenorphine, addiction doctors said. And over time, interest from generalists in understanding and treating opioid use disorder does appear to have increased, Bagley said.
Hadland sees it, too. Where he used to feel like he was pitching his pediatric colleagues and professional organizations on the importance of understanding addiction treatment, now there appears to be active demand for such knowledge. On the day the study was published, he traveled to the AAP’s annual conference, where he’ll give a plenary talk on the big stage about addiction and the potency of the drug supply. To him, that signals a cultural shift that will, hopefully, equip more doctors to help young people struggling with addiction. Because currently, he said, the pediatric workforce is not keeping up.

Kerala Health Minister K. Muraleedharan on Saturday (October 3, 2026) denied reports of a shortage of medicines in government hospitals and alleged that pharmaceutical companies were behind claims highlighting such a crisis.
Speaking to reporters, Mr. Muraleedharan described the reports as a “media creation” and maintained that adequate stocks were available in government hospitals.
“There is no crisis at all. There is sufficient stock of medicines. If needed, you can ask the Superintendent or anyone whether there is medicine stock or not,” he said.
He alleged that some pharmaceutical companies were attempting to create an impression of a shortage and accused sections of the media of highlighting their claims.
“Some pharmaceutical company representatives have come out with sticks and swords. And to highlight that, some big and small TV media people have also stepped out,” he said.
Reiterating that medicines were available in sufficient quantities at government hospitals, Mr. Muraleedharan said he would not be intimidated by such allegations.
“There is adequate stock of medicine. Furthermore, if any pharma company people come out brandishing sticks and swords, I am not someone who gets scared seeing that. That is all,” he said.
On the spread of infectious diseases, Mr. Muraleedharan said the number of cases reported so far was lower than during the corresponding period last year.
“Compared to last year, that many cases have not been reported. So far, infectious diseases haven’t been reported in such numbers,” he said.
On the proposed All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) in Kerala, the Minister rejected Union Minister Suresh Gopi’s allegation that the State government was not cooperating with the Centre.
He said Mr. Gopi was unaware of the facts and that the Principal Secretary of the Health Department had already submitted a report to the Centre on the matter.
“If he asks for it, I can show him a copy. Then why unnecessarily blame the State Government?” Mr. Muraleedharan said.
He said Mr. Gopi was keen on establishing AIIMS at a particular location.
“However, we don’t have any such preferences. Our only demand is that Kerala should get an AIIMS,” he said.
On cases of alleged medical negligence, Mr. Muraleedharan said the Health Department had not received any direct complaints.
“If we receive a complaint about anything, we will investigate it. There is no doubt about that,” he said.
Sabarimala preparations
Mr. Muraleedharan, who also holds the Devaswom portfolio, said preparations for the upcoming Sabarimala pilgrimage season were progressing.
A meeting chaired by Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan would be held at Pampa on October 17 to review the arrangements, he said.
“The government is providing full support to the Travancore Devaswom Board. Therefore, what we expect is that things can be conducted without any issues,” he said.
The Sabarimala pilgrimage season begins on November 17.

A decade ago, the biggest demographic concern gripping the globe was population overgrowth. Cut to 2026, and the demographic worry has shifted to the other end of the spectrum: declining birth rates. In developed economies such as Germany and Japan, fertility rates have fallen well below the replacement rate of 2.1 births per woman. The demographic imbalance is resulting in a growing shortage of workers to support the ageing population. Such countries are increasingly looking overseas, particularly to talent pools in parts of South and Southeast Asia, to fill blue-collar jobs. Plugging this supply-demand mismatch is the opportunity that upGrad cofounder Mayank Kumar is betting on. While helming the upskilling giant, Kumar felt that the local blue-collar ecosystem remained “under-penetrated and under-represented”. But the domestic opportunity was harder to monetise, as workers in these segments were less willing to pay large amounts for training. Kumar found this gap especially stark in the nursing profession when he travelled to Germany and visited nursing homes. This pushed him towards building a system that could train workers in one country and move them into jobs in another. To realise his new idea, he joined forces with Ayush Mathur, a former colleague, to incorporate BorderPlus. Founded in 2025, BorderPlus is building what it calls a vertically integrated talent mobility platform that trains workers, matches them with overseas employers, and then handles everything from language and skills training to visas, documentation and relocation. Kumar focuses on sourcing and developing talent, while Mathur works on building demand among overseas employers. Backed by Owl Ventures, CaratLane founder Mithun Sacheti and OYO founder Ritesh Agarwal, the founders raised $7 Mn last year within a month of its launch. But how does BorderPlus play the cross-border mobility game? Controlling The Talent Pipeline BorderPlus wants to control the entire journey of moving a skilled worker overseas, including sourcing, training, employer interviews, placement and visa processing. For placements in Germany, its model starts with sourcing candidates through direct applications and college partnerships. After multiple rounds of screening, they enter language and finishing-school programmes before being introduced to overseas employers. Once selected, BorderPlus handles documentation, qualification recognition, visas and relocation. This allows BorderPlus to monetise beyond recruitment. Candidates initially pay ₹10,000 for the first month of the programme and, after clearing the subsequent screening, another ₹1.9 Lakh. However, Kumar says that the startup derives the bulk of its revenue from successful placements. Recruiters pay BorderPlus around €8,000-€12,000 (₹8.7 Lakh to ₹13 Lakh) per successful placement, equivalent to roughly three months of the candidate's salary. The startup then uses this revenue to cover expenses related to visas, examinations, documentation, translations and flights. The structure helps fund a recruitment cycle that typically lasts eight to 15 months. Kumar says upfront collections cover a large portion of the company's working-capital requirements, while the business generates a gross margin of around 70% per candidate. The economics also give BorderPlus an incentive to be selective. Only 30-40% of applicants are accepted into its full-time finishing schools, according to Kumar. He says this is because the business makes most of its money when a candidate is successfully placed, rather than simply enrolled. With an examination pass rate of more than 90% for its selected candidates, the startup is betting that hospitals and recruiters will return to the platform if it can consistently deliver language-ready and qualified candidates. Moving Beyond Germany BorderPlus is now moving beyond its core market, Germany, and has recently begun expanding into the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and Japan. However, around 90-95% of its business still comes from Germany, according to Kumar. The startup claims that it has built a network of 80-90 hospitals and care homes in Germany, giving it a direct employer base. It also operates eight finishing school locations across India, the Philippines and Brazil with more than 50 physical trainers. Around 70% of its candidates are from India, while the remaining 30% come from markets such as the Philippines, Brazil and North Africa. Women also make up roughly 70–75% of the candidate pool. On the employer side, it has completed around five acquisitions in Germany to gain access to existing hospital and care-home relationships, with two more acquisitions underway. The startup is also looking to expand its physical presence in Germany, where it currently has offices in Düsseldorf and Frankfurt. The startup is also looking to go beyond its current three markets. It plans to roll out its services across English-speaking markets such as the US, UK, Australia, New Zealand and Canada. Nevertheless, Kumar expects Germany to still account for around 70% of the business next year, with Japan and the Middle East making up the remainder. Once those markets are established, BorderPlus plans to foray into the English-speaking markets. It also plans to extend its employee mobility network beyond healthcare to other areas like hospitality, kindergarten teaching, retail and last-mile delivery, manufacturing and construction, and logistics and trucking. BorderPlus has already started working on hospitality. Meanwhile, Kumar says one or two additional sectors could be tested in the near term, with a more concerted push planned for the next financial year. But the startup does not intend to stop at merely expanding its footprint. Leveraging AI For Revenue Extraction Beyond geographic and sectoral expansion, BorderPlus is also trying to build a second layer to its business through NursePlus, an AI platform designed to support nurses after they move to overseas markets. While the startup’s core business is still talent placement, Kumar sees NursePlus as a way to extend the relationship beyond the point of recruitment. NursePlus has three components: Learn, Ask and Do. Learn uses conversational simulations to help nurses practise local languages, cultural nuances and 1,000 hours of clinical scenarios before they arrive in their destination country. Ask is an AI assistant trained on local medical literature, compliance requirements, insurance guidelines and hospital protocols. Do focuses on documentation, allowing nurses to have their responses transcribed, translated and formatted for electronic health records. Kumar claims this can save nurses anywhere between 15 minutes and an hour on certain documentation tasks. Unlike the placement business, NursePlus follows a B2B subscription model, with hospitals and other employers paying for the software once the nurses have joined them. BorderPlus had around 100-150 subscribers in August, with pricing at roughly €30 per month. This allows BorderPlus to also have recurring revenue streams from the same worker after they have entered the workforce. Kumar believes AI could eventually contribute 5-30% of the startup’s revenue, while accounting for a considerably larger share of EBITDA because of the software's scalability. The same infrastructure could be adapted across countries and professions by changing the underlying language, regulatory and workplace context. This fits into BorderPlus' larger ambition to build a repeatable talent-mobility infrastructure rather than a Germany-focused nursing recruitment business. The Scale-Up Challenge Kumar expects the startup’s revenue to at least triple in the current financial year, adding that BorderPlus could achieve $10 Mn in annualised revenue run rate by the last quarter of the current financial year. On the operating side, BorderPlus is targeting around 1,000 placements across Germany, Japan and the Middle East in FY27, including 700-800 in Germany. Despite its grand plans, it is yet to be seen whether BorderPlus’ talent-mobility model can scale into a venture-sized business. For BorderPlus, the biggest test will be whether it can replicate its Germany playbook without any hitch. Revenue concentration also remains a risk as Germany still contributes 90-95% of the business, while the newer Japan and GCC corridors are only beginning to scale. The startup is also exposed to the usual risks of cross-border hiring, including immigration and visa policies, shifting attitudes towards migrant workers and recruitment cycles that can stretch for 15 months. At the same time, expanding physical training infrastructure across new source markets and professions could make the model operationally heavier. BorderPlus’ answer is diversification, technology and deeper employer relationships. But the jury is still out on whether BorderPlus can turn its Germany-focused nursing recruitment business into a repeatable global talent powerhouse.

Eight organisations from different parts of the world have come together to form the Global Alliance for Diabetic Foot Survival and Limb Preservation. This was announced at the Diabetic Foot Society of India’s (DFSI) national conference held in Bengaluru on Friday, October 2, 2026. The founding organisations also signed a joint declaration calling for diabetic foot ulceration to be recognised as a global public health priority.
The eight organisations are the DFSI, King’s College London, the International Association of Diabetic Foot Surgeons, D-Foot International, the Pan African Diabetic Foot Study Group, the American Limb Preservation Society, the International Federation of Podiatrists and the Podiatric Surgeons’ Society.
A 2023 review cited in the alliance proposal estimated that about 18.6 million people worldwide are affected by diabetic foot ulceration annually. It reported a five-year mortality of about 30% following a diabetic foot ulcer and over 70% following a major amputation.
The proposed alliance will focus on research, workforce training, comparable data collection and advocacy with the World Health Organization and national governments to secure greater policy recognition of diabetic foot disease.
The proposed framework also emphasises the involvement of people living with diabetes, those who have experienced foot ulcers and people living with amputation or disability in decision-making and programme design. It envisages regional demonstration programmes, a common measurement framework and an annual report on progress.
The DFSI Scientific Committee is proposed as the alliance’s interim secretariat, with a governing council representing the founding organisations overseeing strategy, finances and activities. The members are expected to meet within 30 days to discuss governance, collaboration, resource mobilisation and implementation.

'It's a nightmare.' Former refugee, professor on Trump's new Medicaid policy
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Mustafa Rfat has been getting frantic phone calls recently from refugees with disabilities. As of Oct. 1, refugees are losing access to Medicaid across the country because of H.R. 1, the Trump administration's major budget bill Republicans passed last summer.
"I spent these past two weeks just talking with so many of them, literally just terrorized by the reality that their children with disabilities are losing coverage," he says. "For example, a father is a refugee with disabilities, with two kids with disabilities, and he's just confused how he's going to get the medication."
Rfat is a professor of social work at the University of Nebraska at Omaha, and his research focuses on refugees with disabilities, an experience he knows firsthand.
When he arrived in the U.S. as a refugee from Iraq in 2011, the chronic condition that affects his spine was severe. "I was in a very bad situation," he says. "I couldn't walk. I was in so much pain. I missed my medications for a long time. I didn't see a doctor. So it was a very, very difficult and vulnerable situation."
As he moved from Alabama to Illinois to West Virginia trying to find housing and continue his education, Medicaid was a lifeline, Rfat says. "I had to climb this big mountain of acclimating into the culture here, learning English, dealing with the traumas of the war, the loss of family members, the challenges that I faced, being alone with a disability," he says.
"I was determined and in this determination, Medicaid was the big factor that made my dreams come true." In fact, he says one of the specialists who treated him wrote his first reference to apply for college. He has since become a U.S. citizen with a family, a doctorate, and a job as a professor.
Now, he's trying to help refugees with disabilities facing the challenges of navigating life in the U.S. without that lifeline. As of Oct. 1, refugees are among the groups that will lose Medicaid coverage.
Hundreds of thousands will lose coverage
Only a small portion of legal immigrants have been eligible to enroll in Medicaid, including refugees and asylum seekers. Because of the changes to "Alien Medicaid Eligibility" in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that Republicans passed last summer, an even smaller subset now have access. An estimated 280,000 people will lose Medicaid in October, according to an analysis by KFF Health News.
That includes immigrants admitted to the U.S. on humanitarian grounds who are waiting to be approved for a green card, explains Ben D'Avanzo, senior strategist at the National Immigration Law Center.
"The people who are losing Medicaid and CHIP [the Children's Health Insurance Program] are among some of the most vulnerable immigrants — people who have experienced violence in their own homes or on their journey, who may have physical and mental conditions, who are fleeing persecution and war," he says. "These are people who we have long, in the United States, welcomed, and populations who have had very strong, historic bipartisan support."
Rfat points out that refugees are more likely to have serious health conditions than other groups. "More than one third of them have at least one type of disability — this is what the research tells us," he explains. In refugee camps and during war access to doctors and medication is difficult, and simple conditions can become serious and complex.
That was his own experience with an inflammatory condition called ankylosing spondylitis. "By the time I arrived in the U.S., a lot of doctors told me, 'You are one of the worst cases that we are seeing,'" he says. "And that is the case for a lot of refugees that come here."
In a statement to NPR, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services wrote that they are enacting the law passed by Congress working with states to accurately implement the policy. They did not respond to a follow up question about the effect of the policy on refugees with disabilities.
"Once these changes take place, these groups of immigrants will be left with very few options for affordable, comprehensive coverage," says Drishti Pillai, director of immigrant health policy at the nonpartisan health research organization KFF.
"They could still buy full price coverage from ACA marketplaces, but that is often unaffordable," Pillai says. "Employer-sponsored coverage is also an option, but many immigrants, especially those who are on Medicaid, don't work in jobs that don't offer employer-sponsored coverage, such as jobs in construction, agriculture, food service."
She says a few states are creating their own coverage options for these groups, but many have tight budgets and are facing even bigger Medicaid cuts in January. Most states have also opted in to allow Medicaid to continue to cover pregnant women and children who would otherwise be losing coverage.
D'Avanzo points out that the categories of people losing coverage now will eventually become green card holders who are eligible for Medicaid.
"So these are people who are going to put off preventative care, who are not going to treat their chronic conditions, who are going to forgo important medication," he says. "And then when they are Medicaid eligible again in the future, once they've received their green card, they're going to be needing much more specialized care and much more costly care."
Hope for change
Mustafa Rfat is headed to his alma mater Washington University in St. Louis, Missouri this weekend to meet with a few dozen refugees with disabilities and share some of his recent research. He says the loss of Medicaid and food benefits will hang over the event.
"It's a nightmare for the community," he says. He hopes Congress will reverse course.
He's decided to devote part of the event to teaching about civic engagement. "To understand the importance of voting when they become citizens, to understand the importance of being aware of the policies, being aware of who their representatives are, how to communicate with their representatives," he says.
"These are new Americans," he adds. "These people are going nowhere. By making their health and well-being worse, it's not going to benefit anyone."

Shefali Shah has generally kept her personal life away from the public eye, but the actor has now reflected on her first marriage and divorce in her memoir-in-essays, The Audacity of Being. In a recent interaction, she spoke about her decision to write about the experience and explained that the book does not focus on specific individuals or details of what led to the separation.
Shefali Shah breaks silence on writing about her first marriage and divorce with Harsh Chhaya: “I’ve written about it very respectfully”
Speaking to The Indian Express, Shefali clarified that she was not interested in revealing private details about her former relationship. “I’m not naming anyone in the book. I’m not even getting into what happened or didn’t happen. I’m just talking about what happens on a general scale when people get married and nobody’s prepared for a divorce,” she said.
The actor also discussed how people often enter marriage with certain expectations about their future together. According to her, couples may approach marriage with “the idea of a happily-ever-after”, but things can change when a relationship begins to fall apart. Shefali said her writing focuses on the emotional and practical reality of dealing with the end of a marriage rather than placing blame on either person.
Addressing why she chose to write about her first marriage and divorce, she said she did not feel there was anything that needed to be hidden. “There was nothing to really hide about. I think I’ve written about it very respectfully. I’m just talking about any marriage falling off the brink. There’s an entire thing about when you realise your marriage is falling apart. So it’s, I think, about the failure of a relationship.”
Shefali was married to actor Harsh Chhaya. The two got married in 1997 and divorced in 2001. She has largely refrained from discussing the relationship publicly. She later married filmmaker and producer Vipul Amrutlal Shah, with whom she has two sons, Aryaman and Maurya.
On the professional front, Shefali has appeared in films including Waqt: The Race Against Time, Dil Dhadakne Do, Jalsa and Darlings. She also received international recognition for playing DCP Vartika Chaturvedi in the Netflix series Delhi Crime, which won the International Emmy Award for Best Drama Series.

President Donald Trump is promising more payments to voters just ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections — this time, to more than 20 million seniors, giving them $90 each to help pay for Medicare premiums.
The announcement, made late Friday night by Trump on social media, comes after the president last month said about 1 million people would get rebate checks of $500 for Affordable Care Act premiums. He has also promised on the campaign trail to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections.
That pledge — which would require approval from Congress — would likely cost more than $1 trillion, adding to the deficit and worsening inflation.
Trump highlighted his $5,000 promise at a rally in Vandalia, Ohio, on Saturday night, and told supporters that 70,000 families in the state would receive the ACA rebates “within the next couple of days.” He also reminded voters about the $1,776 payments to military members, announced in December — though he mused that they should have been timed better.
“Maybe I should have waited a year,” he said. “To be honest, I said that. Should I wait for before the election?”
Polls show Americans increasingly blame Trump for the high cost of gasoline and groceries with just 17% approving of his handling of inflation. Trump has sought to shrug off concerns about affordability, saying the economy is booming.
The White House said the $90 payments for seniors will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, established by Congress in 2008 as flexible funding to improve program operations and payments to health care providers.
Medicare Part B enrollees can expect to receive a one-time payment in October, either through direct deposit or by check, the White House said. Total monthly costs for the program — which covers costs like doctor’s visits, ambulance services and lab tests — start around $200 and vary with income.
To be eligible, seniors must be living in the U.S. and not be already receiving premium assistance from Medicaid or paying adjusted monthly premiums based on income, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage, a private plan alternative to traditional Medicare coverage, are not eligible for the payment. More than half of eligible Medicare beneficiaries have Medicare Advantage, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF.
Previous administrations have not used the Medicare Improvement Fund in this way, although Congress has periodically taken out money from the fund to pay for other priorities, said Larry Levitt, KFF’s executive vice president for health policy. For example, $20.74 billion was used for the creation of the Affordable Care Act in 2010.
“The Medicare Improvement Fund language is quite broad and gives substantial discretion to the administration,” Levitt said.

The decision by the U.S. Coast Guard to end the search for the crew and passengers of a medical transport jet out of Hamilton means it's likely that the four Canadians and two Bermudians on board didn't survive, says the company that operated the jet.
Latitude Air Ambulance issued a statement late Sunday night, saying hope of finding survivors from the downed Gulfstream G100 aircraft appeared to be gone.

"It is with profound sadness that we acknowledge the decision by the United States Coast Guard to conclude active search and rescue operations and transition to recovery efforts," Latitude said in its statement.

Latitude said its thoughts are first and foremost with the families, loved ones, friends, and colleagues of the people on the jet.

From the edge of extinction, two captive-bred Great Indian Bustards released into wild in Rajasthan
The release marks a new phase in the conservation programme, with experts set to track whether captive-raised birds can survive and reproduce without assistance
Not very long ago, the Great Indian Bustard (GIB) ranged across a vast swathe of India, from Punjab in the north to Tamil Nadu in the south. Today, fewer than 150 remain in the wild, confined largely to pockets of Rajasthan’s Jaisalmer and Kutch in Gujarat.
The decline has been driven by two major threats.
Grassland loss emerges as a major threat
The first was the loss of its grassland habitat. Dry grasslands, the natural home of the bustard, were often classified as wasteland, leaving them vulnerable to takeover by government agencies and encroachment. The resulting neglect degraded the habitat, reducing the prey base and depleting water sources.
The second, and more recent, threat came with the rapid expansion of high-voltage transmission lines and windmills across the bustard’s remaining habitat. Unlike many other birds, bustards have excellent peripheral vision to detect predators but relatively poor front vision. When flying, they can fail to detect overhead power lines and collide with them, often fatally.
Also read: Ten captive-bred Great Indian Bustards to be released in Jaisalmer on Oct 3-4
“Degradation of grasslands along with hunting contributed in a major way in decline of the GIB population. Their habitats have shrunk to less than 10% as compared to 1960s. In the last two decades, the high voltage lines connecting wind mills and solar farms to the grid in western Rajasthan and Gujarat overlap with Bustard traditional homes, and is a reason for death of large number of bustards,” said MK Ranjitsinh, former Union environment secretary.
Supreme Court relaxes restrictions on overhead power lines
In 2021, the Supreme Court banned laying of overhead new power transmission lines in 99,000 square km area of GIB habitat in Rajasthan and Gujarat to save them. Years later, the SC relaxed the guidelines by reducing the area to about 14,000 square kilometers and providing more time to lay the underground lines.
In 2016, the Government of India started a project to revive Rajasthan’s state bird, the Great Indian Bustard, through captive breeding in Jaisalmer. By June 2026, the captive population had reached 98, of which 38 were born through artificial insemination.
On Sunday, that effort entered a new phase when two captive-bred GIBs were released into the wild at the Desert National Park, at Sam in Jaisalmer.
“With this, we have entered a new era of GIB conservation,” said Ashok Singh, assistant conservator of forest at Jaisalmer.
Also read: Rajasthan: 3 Great Indian Bustards born naturally; experts cite reduced stress
Rewilding training prepares birds for life outside captivity
But releasing a bird is one thing. Making it survive in the wild is another. The birds underwent extensive rewilding training at a specially designed facility costing ₹9.25 crore at the GIB Conservation Breeding Centre at Ramdevra.
Inside the tunnel, captive-bred birds are exposed to natural sunlight, temperature variations and airflow and were made to hunt the prey — insects and other natural foods — and find water, Singh said.
If they survive, the experts from Wildlife Institute would monitor their reproduction in wild to revive the GIB population. “If that happens, we could say that the project was successful,” said an expert from the Wildlife Institute.
Also read: Gujarat: Great Indian Bustard chick sighted in wild for 1st time in decade
First release to guide future conservation efforts
The information gathered from the first release will be important in determining how future captive-bred GIBs should be trained and released. It will also help scientists assess whether birds raised in captivity are capable of establishing themselves in the wild without prolonged human assistance, said WII official Mahesh Gurjar.
He added that use of artificial insemination is considered an important development because it provides conservation scientists with an additional tool for breeding birds and managing genetic diversity in a species whose wild population has fallen to critically low levels.
If the experiment works, the officials said the next destination could be Kutch. Already, a first chick has hatched in March 2026 after a fertile egg was moved about 770 km from Rajasthan. The chick has survived beyond the critical first three months in the wild, a landmark for restarting breeding in Gujarat’s isolated population.
Also read: Rajasthan: 9 critically-endangered Great Indian Bustards spotted together in wild
Gujarat steps up habitat restoration at Naliya
In Gujarat, officials said that the habitat restoration work at Naliya has started and about 11 sq km of invasive Prosopis juliflora, with 30 km of predator proof fencing covering 15 sq km, has been done. As per the Gujarat Action Plan for GIB Conservation, a target of release of 30 birds and 200 to 500 sq km of secure grassland has been set. In future, the GIB can be introduced in new habitats in states such as Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh, officials said. “That will all depend on how the captive bred GIBs survive in the wild,” a senior environment ministry official said.
Sumer Singh Bhati, who has followed bustards in western Rajasthan for over a decade, said, “The real test is not just producing birds in captivity. That is easier than making them survive in the wild. There is a need to create a landscape where bustards can survive after release and flourish. Improving the habitat and putting all transmission lines below the ground would be key to revive the bustard population in the longer run,” he said.
