There are very few horror games that truly make you rethink every decision while encasing you in this unbearably odd feeling that everything is going down the gutter. Silent Hill has always been one such franchise that thrived in peaking our uneasiness with out-of-the-box storylines.
And they have done it yet again with Townfall, crafting one of the most visually appealing brain twisters that completely leaves you stunned by the end of it. But even the best stories can have their fair share of terrible moments in direction, and Townfall has them plenty. So, before you decide to play Silent Hill Townfall, here’s our in-depth review.
A Hauntingly Beautiful Town Hides a Messy Story
Silent Hill Townfall is undoubtedly one of the best visually stimulating games I have played this year. The game’s atmosphere completely hooks you from the very first minute, and the shift to first-person only heightens the uneasiness so common in the franchise.
The game takes place in St. Amelia, a fictional coastal fishing town where something awful happened. How do I know? Well, the very first second you step into the town square, you see placards filled with protest signs or messages about deceased loved ones. The very first feeling you have when entering the town is that something terrible happened, but what?
That’s what you, as Simon, need to investigate. However, Simon is not a detective; he himself is part of the puzzle. We find him on the shores of St. Amelia, with an IV line hooked into his hand, and having completely lost his memory. We control him into the town, which has now been encapsulated in the Silent Hill classic “Fog.”
Silent Hill Townfall’s biggest strength is its visual storytelling. The atmosphere completely hooks you from the get-go and never eases its grip. It uses many normal events to create a sense of realism and unease at the same time. One example is how players have to dial ‘100’ on a working telephone to save the game. The same telephone can be used to dial other numbers, which gives story clues.
Simon has a CRTV that catches frequencies to show ‘memories,’ also acting as a quest guide. It also helps reveal monsters around Simon. Similarly, other playable characters, like Zoe, have similar instruments that are very rooted in reality, while also acting supernaturally. It almost made me remember the camera in Fatal Frame II Crimson Butterfly remake.
Another example is how Simon uses a scalpel to cut open ‘chests’ inside doors to unlock them. The first time I saw it, I definitely had a knee-jerk reaction and couldn’t stop speculating about the connection between medical patients and St. Amelia.
The game also masterfully changes colors to emphasize a change in pacing or story importance. Many times, the world starts to flash red, while other times it remains a silent gray. Along with the creepily composed music that continues to make you feel unease, the game creates the perfect horror background for us.
That is until the first monster shows up, and the game changes from an investigative horror to a poorly made stealth game.
Townfall Has the Fun Sneaking Out the Back Door
Unlike Silent Hill f, which had too many combat scenarios, Townfall instead fully relies on sneaking around. Normally, this makes sense in a horror game, especially as sneaking only heightens the fear. However, Townfall takes this to an annoyingly high degree, making it feel highly repetitive and annoying.
I already had enough of sneaking around by the end of the third act, especially because of how terribly unfun it felt. The sneaking did not add anything new. It followed the same pattern we have already seen in hundreds of games, like running around monsters in circles by crouching, or using environmental items to distract enemies.
It’s the same thing, overdone to an annoying degree that I forgot which genre I was even playing at one point. Some entire acts only had sneaking. For example, the entirety of Act 2 and most of Act 3 had very few puzzle scenarios and investigation. Instead, the map was simply filled with mindless monsters that had the same running pattern that you had to run circles around by figuring out their movement pattern.
You may be wondering why sneak when we can fight. Yes, you can fight the monsters in Silent Hill Townfall, but doing it feels much worse than sneaking around. The combat mechanics in the game are terribly designed, boiling down to only blocking and hitting enemies with a plank.
At one point, you do end up having a gun, and that does make combat a bit quicker; however, it never feels enjoyable until the very end. The combat of Silent Hill Townfall requires absolutely zero skill. It was more of a hassle fighting the monsters than sneaking or running away to a safe place.
Compared to that, Silent Hill f was a much better experience and even felt justified having so many enemies to fight through due to the decent combat mechanics.
A Little Too Puzzling
One of my favorite gameplay features about the Silent Hill franchise is puzzles. The franchise has time and time again showcased its strength in crafting some incredibly well-made puzzles. Silent Hill f included some very well-made Japanese-centric mind twisters, so I had big hope from Townfall as well.
Sadly, Silent Hill Townfall fell quite short in that regard as well. The game does have some good puzzles, but some had overly complicated solutions that felt unfair. For example, the Shorefront Shop puzzle required that players find a code to open the locker.
But unlike finding a normal code, the game makes you look at five completely different things around the shop to come up with a code, like ‘three for three hands of a clock’. The only clue you have in this puzzle is a CRT recording that showcases the different elements around the room, which end up having the codes, in a very vague way.
Now, some of the elements do have a clear number, like 5 on a poster of 5 reasons to wash your hands. But things become dicey when you have to count fingers shown on a poster to find the number ‘6.’ Why a locker code would have a number based on the amount of fingers displayed on a wall poster is beyond me.
Even though I figured the puzzle out after spending a huge chunk of my time thinking about it, the solution at the end did not leave me satisfied at all. This is true for many other puzzles in the game. Either they are too easy to solve, or they are so overly complicated that the solution makes zero sense.
Performance: St. Amelia Has Problems but My PS5 Doesn’t
Silent Hill Townfall is one of the most visually appealing games in the franchise, and it ran seamlessly on my base PS5. The game gave a constant 60 FPS throughout on Performance mode; however, it did lock at 30 FPS in Quality mode. The upside is that shifting from Quality to Performance did not lead to a huge difference in visual quality, making the change much less bitter.
As already mentioned earlier, Townfall is a very graphically stimulating game. It perfectly uses the new first-person view to immerse players in the heart of all the trouble in St. Amelia. Although there is never much to look at in Silent Hill games due to the omnipresent fog, Townfall does a fairly great job of presenting every location with clarity.
Although St. Amelia is a small town, it never feels like you are roaming around the same place due to the change in colors and tone, which also brings fair changes to the map. Overall, I had zero qualms with the performance on my PlayStation 5 and did not run into any bugs for the entire 12-hour playtime.
Verdict: A Great Silent Hill Story with Some Seriously Loud Problems
Silent Hill games have always been about storytelling, and Townfall has one of the best story designs in the franchise. I cannot emphasize enough how good the storytelling is in this game, especially through the use of old-school technology like pages, telephones, and CRT recordings. Till the very end, I was unable to guess what was happening, and it was the only thing that kept me playing the game.
However, I do not see myself replaying Silent Hill Townfall due to the sheer amount of senseless sneaking I’ve done in it. Even though the game has multiple endings and it’s always best to play multiple playthroughs of any Silent Hill game, I cannot see myself going through the same ordeal of running circles around mindless monsters for hours.
Townfall also falls drastically behind when it comes to puzzle imagination, and that creates a much worse gameplay loop. More puzzles and less sneaking would have hugely upgraded my experience of the St. Amelia, and I expect the same feeling from others as well.
Overall, Silent Hill Townfall has one of the best story designs and a visually stimulating world, but its tiring stealth gameplay and poorly made puzzles make it hard to recommend to die-hard fans, as well as to those new to the franchise.

Capitals' Alex Ovechkin, 41, announces NHL retirement after this season
'Let's make the playoffs, have fun,' says league's all-time leading goalscorer
Alex Ovechkin said Monday his 22nd season in the NHL will be his last, beginning the farewell tour for the longtime Washington Capitals captain who holds the league's career goalscoring record.
Ovechkin addressed teammates in Arlington, Va., to deliver the news before the team posted a message from him on social media.
"It's sad, but it is what it is," Ovechkin said in his dressing room address. "It's hard, but let's enjoy it and let's do some special things this year."
Ovechkin signed a one-year contract this past summer and turned 41 on Sept. 17. All signs pointed to this being the end, and he said he and his family decided as much in recent months.
"I love this game so much, but I know in my heart it's the right decision," the Russian star said in a statement released before the Capitals' home opener Wednesday night.
Ovechkin broke Wayne Gretzky's goals record in April 2025 and entered this season at 929. The front office acquired Jordan Kyrou and Alex Tuch in trades and signed fellow forward Boone Jenner and defenceman Vincent Desharnais in free agency to add around a young core in the hopes of making another long playoff run and contending for the Stanley Cup.
"Let's make the playoffs, let's have fun and enjoy the moment because times fly," Ovechkin told the team. "For young guys who are first year or experienced guys, I remember that moment, and enjoy the time. Because times fly. It seems like yesterday I was here my first year."
Speaking to reporters later Monday, Ovechkin said this was the right time to announce his decision, two days before the home opener.
- Why Alex Ovechkin is the greatest goalscorer who ever lived
- Ovechkin to decide hockey future after season, with health biggest factor
"I'm not 20 years old," he said. "I want to play with my kids when they're growing up. Play hockey, play soccer, play basketball. I want to be healthy enough to do that kind of stuff."
Ovechkin has spent his entire career with Washington, winning the Calder Trophy as rookie of the year in 2005-06, the Hart Trophy as MVP three times and leading the NHL in scoring nine times. He was playoff MVP in 2018 when he led the Caps to the first Stanley Cup championship in franchise history.
Will live in Russia post-NHL career
There's been speculation Ovechkin could receive an unfriendly reception on the road after he appeared in an ad for a party aligned with Vladimir Putin during the off-season. But there wasn't much sign of that during the first two games of the season — at Carolina and at Tampa Bay.
When addressing the fallout from that last month, Ovechkin confirmed he'd be going back to live in Russia when he retired from the NHL.
In Washington's season-opening win over the Hurricanes, Ovechkin had 12 minutes 46 seconds of ice time, the lowest of his career in a game when he wasn't injured or ejected.
Monday was 21 years to the day after Ovechkin made his debut with the Capitals.
"It's been pretty good career, pretty good 22 seasons," he said. "Obviously the goal that we have, to bring a Stanley Cup to D.C., we did it."
Although the Capitals have designs on making the playoffs this season, within a couple hours of Ovechkin's announcement, tickets for Washington's regular-season home finale against Pittsburgh on April 4 were going for a minimum of $825 on StubHub. With D.C. hosting college hockey's Frozen Four next year, the Capitals finish the regular season with three straight road games, wrapping up April 10 at Philadelphia.
The Capitals missed the playoffs in 2025-26, but Ovechkin played all 82 games and scored 32 goals. He's reached 30 in every season of his career except 2020-21, when he played only 45 games.
Long before he broke through during the Capitals' Stanley Cup run, Ovechkin had rejuvenated hockey in Washington, and he'll retire as one of the city's most accomplished athletes in any sport. The Capitals drafted him No. 1 overall in 2004, and he and Pittsburgh's Sidney Crosby became stars almost immediately in 2005 when the league emerged from missing a season because of a lockout.
Ovechkin's combination of goal-scoring skill, physicality and boundless energy made him an instant hit, and he scored a career-high 65 goals in his third season, which earned him the first of his Hart Trophies.
Washington's penchant for post-season heartache, which existed long before Ovechkin showed up, followed him for a while as well. The Capitals won the Presidents' Trophy three times with the league's best regular-season record, falling short in the playoffs each time before a Washington team that merely won its division finally went all the way in the playoffs.
In four post-season meetings between Crosby and Ovechkin — 2009, 2016, 2017, 2018 — the winner won the Stanley Cup each time. Washington's home opener Wednesday is against Pittsburgh.

A woman in the remote Siberian region of Irkutsk has died of plague, a regional official said Friday, as a Russian media outlet reported dozens were under quarantine.

The plague is an infectious disease caused by bacteria.
Pneumonic plague is highly infectious and can be fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization.

Why Canada is preparing for a (long shot) US invasion
- Published
Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion.
Noting the risk was low and the likelihood highly improbable, he told the New York Times he had a responsibility to consider all possibilities as the US-Canada relationship is redefined under the Donald Trump presidency.
"That's just risk management," Carney said.
Trump's global tariffs and his often-repeated desire to make Canada the 51st state has led Canada to war game an attack by the Americans.
In 2025, the US president said it was "highly unlikely" that the US would ever use force against Canada. Instead he said, he would continue to exert economic pressures to obtain political aims.
"President Trump has done more than anyone to protect the great people of Canada," the White House told the BBC in a statement this week.
Military experts who spoke to the BBC also think an invasion is a long shot, pointing to the multiple ways the two countries work together on defence.
But the issue is clearly weighing on Canadians' minds.
In January, after the US captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a Leger poll suggested that over 30% of Canadians believed that a US invasion was likely.
Why it is unlikely to happen
A war between Canada and the US would be complicated and almost difficult to imagine, said Lt-Gen Christopher Coates, a former military officer of 34 years with the Royal Canadian Air Force who held various senior positions.
"I was involved in military operations for my whole career, and we never considered the possibility that there would be a military attack coming from US territory," he told the BBC.
Coates, who had served on Nato missions, noted that Canada and the US collaborate on many aspects of military defence.
They are both members of the north Atlantic defence alliance, which mandates members to defend a fellow member-nation should they be attacked.
The two countries also conduct joint Arctic defence missions under the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD), and frequently share intelligence.
Because of this, Coates said he believes an attack by the US on Canada would not begin with an armed assault, but rather with more discreet means like cyberwarfare.
Not always the best of friends
After World War II, Canada and the US became natural allies for the latter part of the 20th Century, and have become heavily integrated economically, militarily and culturally.
But it wasn't always this way. In fact, a core tenet of Canada's identity is its resistance of US expansionism in the 18th and 19th Centuries, said Tim Foran, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum.
"Fear of the United States is foundational to the political project that is Canada," he said.
Canada was formed as a collection of British North American colonies who remained loyal to the British Crown when the colonies in the modern-day US rebelled.
Before the formation of Canada, the US had attempted to invade British North American colonies, taking control of Montreal in 1775 and nearly conquering Quebec City.
In the war of 1812, the Americans invaded what was known then as Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime colonies repeatedly, resulting in a stalemate. During that war, British troops famously burned down the White House in retaliation.
Foran said that at the time, the colonies that later became Canada relied on Great Britain and its Royal Navy for its defence, as well as indigenous peoples who served as generals in major battles.
Canada again contemplated war with the US post-World War I in response to its growing power and influence.
It drafted a plan that was informed by secret trips to border cities made by Canadian army generals, who would pose as tourists and snap photos of bridges and highways for intelligence.
They also spoke to local residents to better understand their enemy.
A war was an unlikely scenario then, said Andrew Burtch, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum with expertise on Canada in the 20th Century, but the Canadians still wanted to be prepared.
"That's part of what militaries do," he said. "They envisage all sorts of different scenarios."
What a US invasion could look like
Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.
He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way.
"It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.
Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.
So what would it be like if it happened?
The first phase of a war could be quite short.
According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a week
Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.
Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.
The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.
The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.
He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.
Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada's defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers.
An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either.
Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt.
"I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada," he said.
"They would see it as an illegal and immoral order."
Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together, and share a mutual respect.
But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation.
"You would see a a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela," he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro.
Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that "pound for pound" Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.

World Contraception Day on September 26 offers an opportunity to look closely at a part of family planning that receives very little attention: contraception for men. The key question here is why the range of methods available to men and women remains so different.
Women today have options including oral pills, injectables, implants, intrauterine devices and permanent sterilisation, though access and affordability to safe and reliable contraception in our country continues to remain a major challenge. For men, the practical choices are still largely limited to condoms for reversible contraception and vasectomy for permanent contraception. Male and female reproduction are governed by the same broad hormonal axis, yet the biology, anatomy and mechanics of preventing conception create very different problems. Understanding those differences helps explain why a male equivalent of the pill has remained elusive.

The setting for perhaps the country’s biggest exercise in public debate was quintessential rural India: fields of green paddy, a pond, a temple. On a normal day, as dusk falls in the village of Ajgara, in Uttar Pradesh, people gather beside the pond to chat about the price of crops, the weather, or the theft of a goat.
But for more than a month, metaphysics and ethical dilemmas replaced the usual topics. Is it permissible to use deceit to defeat an evil enemy? Is a lie justified to save a life? What is the nature of reality?
The debating tournament was the brainchild of Abhishek Pandey, district magistrate of Pratapgarh district in Uttar Pradesh. When he took up the post two years ago, he knew the area was rich in archaeological treasures connected to the ancient Indian epic, the Mahabharata.
Throughout the text, Yudhishthira, one of the central characters, debates the nature of human existence. In Ajgara he answers a string of philosophical questions to save the lives of his four brothers.
Pandey, 35, like most Indians, grew up on this story and was proud of the intellectual depth of the dialogues. When he attended Oxford University on a fellowship, he admired the debating society, which has a 200-year-long history. But India’s tradition of sophisticated public debate is much older, going back more than 3,000 years.
Pandey started to question why the tradition had not survived. “Indians have celebrated certain traditions for centuries,” Pandey says. “Why have we ceased to celebrate the legacy of debate and questioning?” Was it possible to revive this noble tradition, particularly when it was a vital component of a democracy?
He decided that the annual fair held in Ajgara in September would be a good time to stage the event. In the run-up to the fair, Pandey and his team arranged 1,500 debates across the district.
Age and education were no bar. The youngest participant was a 10-year-old schoolboy, the oldest an 80-year-old farmer. In debating for and against a motion, participants were judged on reasoning and moral clarity.
The overwhelming public response dumbfounded Pandey. Thousands of people participated in multiple rounds, and were whittled down to eight finalists – two women and six men.
While villagers milled around, enjoying the food, watching folk theatre, buying local crafts and taking a ride on a ferris wheel, a silence descended inside the debating tent.
The finale of the Great Ajgara Debate 2026 on 17 September lasted about six hours.
One topic was women’s rights. A finalist, Vivek Singh, argued that women might have equality on paper but society’s expectations of them impeded the exercise of these rights.
Another, Prajjwal Shukla, 24, argued that the real question was not what role society assigned to women but who had the authority to make those choices. Whether a woman chose a career, household responsibilities, or both, should be her choice and hers alone, he said.
“What amazed me the most was not the intellectual quality of the debates (which was great), but the atmosphere. Everyone listened respectfully, patiently, without interrupting. No one got personal. People sat for hours,” says Pandey.
Marx’s adage that history repeats itself, first as tragedy and then as farce, is a perfect description of how debate in India has descended from the sublime to the farcical.
In television studio debates everyone shouts at the same time. No one can finish a point. Personal abuse and gibes fly while the anchor whips them into ever greater frenzies.
Sadhana Dwivedi, one of the two women to progress into the last round of the Great Ajgara Debate, despises this new format.
“People need to learn to listen, to understand there may be value in another person’s point of view,” she says. “In a democracy, it is crucial for all opinions to be aired so that we can get to the truth.”
The turnout was a good demonstration of the thesis posited in economist Amartya Sen’s book The Argumentative Indian that India had a rich tradition of questioning authority and entertaining heterodoxy.
It is only in recent years that dissent has been suppressed, notably by the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party, which values conformity.
“It’s ironic, because the BJP wants to recreate a Hindu state but is not even acquainted with the traditions of ancient Hindu civilisation, such as that of debate and being open to different ideas,” says author and commentator Parsa Venkateshwar Rao Jnr.
At the end of the tournament, the eight finalists were garlanded and driven around in an open-top car to much cheering, feted as “intellectual heroes”. The winner was Shukla, who is preparing to sit exams to enter the civil service.
“I can’t believe I am the winner of a debate that took place at the exact same spot as in the Mahabharata all those centuries ago. I participated just because I wanted to hear other people’s thoughts,” he says.
Pandey is still processing the public enthusiasm. “My deputy asked me if we should get some police deployment because the turnout everywhere was so big, but I laughed and said no. That would be a sad affair.”
He hopes to spread the event across other Indian states and perhaps nationwide. “We have to inculcate a culture of debate. It’s the hallmark of a democracy.”
Meanwhile, he has planted his flag. The inscription on the stone slab he has installed at the site reads: “The Great Ajgara Debate. First Debate 3152 BC: Yudhishthira. Second Debate 2026: Prajjwal Shukla.”

You should avoid using a screen protector on your MacBook — here's why
Putting on a screen protector may have unintended consequences.
Putting a screen protector on expensive electronics is second nature for any experienced technology user, and in almost all cases is the smart choice for your device. Considering how much a new MacBook costs, it's a natural assumption that this same logic would apply. However, putting a screen protector on your MacBook can actually do more harm than good.
There are a lot of theoretical boons that come along with using a protector on your MacBook, especially if you're frequently transporting it from place to place. Fancier ones that boast privacy from prying eyes can be particularly appealing for anyone who frequently uses their laptop while out in public. A laptop is different from a phone, though, and in practice screen protectors really aren't that necessary — it's closed when on the move, and you aren't nearly as liable to drop it since it's used on a sturdy surface instead of one-handed. More so than that, though, the cons simply outweigh the benefits.
Why you shouldn't use a screen protector on a MacBook
From a purely aesthetic point of view, a screen protector on your MacBook can visibly dampen the display you spent good money on. A protector can scatter more light and reduce overall clarity, and with such a large surface area, the chances you're sticking one on with zero air bubbles is slim. However, the much bigger threat is to your screen's overall health, particularly the anti-reflective coating that sits on the top layer of the screen. It's something imperceptible so long as it's not damaged, but a screen protector can ruin it. When it comes time to replace your screen protector, peeling off of the adhesive can leave the coating cracked, peeling and frankly pretty ugly to look at.
Depending on the thickness and material of the screen protector, it can also stop your laptop from closing properly or cause damage to the screen even deeper than this top layer. A MacBook is designed to close with a very small gap between the screen and keyboard, and a thick glass screen protector can bridge that gap. If that's the case, the force of closing your laptop even a bit too hard could have a ripple effect from the base into the screen.
If you absolutely must get a screen protector for your MacBook, there are a few safe alternatives. There's the UltraThin Magnetic Privacy Screen Filter from Kensington, for example, which is sold on Apple's official website. Its magnetism prevents any of the dangers associated with adhesive, and its thinness eliminates the chance of force-based damage.
Other accessories can also be harmful
There are many useful MacBook accessories, but a screen protector isn't the only one that can be harmful to your computer. Many others that sound like safeguards can also be a detriment, like a hardshell case. A heavier hardshell case can wear out the MacBook's hinge, and depending on its design can also trap heat against your computer. To make sure your hardshell case is safe, make sure it's very lightweight and has vent cutouts. It's also important it doesn't stop your laptop from closing fully, as Apple warns any accessories that do so pose a risk of damaging your screen by disrupting the "tight tolerance" between screen and base.
In that same vein of preventing your laptop from closing properly, keyboard and webcam covers pose a similar risk. Over time, a keyboard cover can even leave permanent marks on your screen, since the microscopic gap between screen and keys no longer exists. A webcam cover can also potentially damage the screen due to disrupting the tight tolerance, as well as make a very useful feature, the ambient light sensor, no longer work. Apple recommends that if you must use a keyboard cover, remove it before closing your laptop, and if you need to use a webcam cover, make sure it's not thicker than an average sheet of printer paper.

New Delhi, Oct 5: The country's largest airline IndiGo on Monday announced a hike in fuel surcharge for domestic and international flights in the wake of rising jet fuel prices.
The revised charges will be effective from October 6, and the move will push airfares higher.
The quantum of the hike ranges from Rs 100 to Rs 350 for domestic flights depending on distance. The hike in surcharge has also been effected for international flights.
This is the second time since April that the carrier has increased the fuel surcharge, which was introduced in March.
The fuel surcharge will be Rs 375 for routes with distance up to 500 kilometres and Rs 600 for flights having distance between 501 and 1,000 kilometres.
The amount will be Rs 900 for routes with a distance of 1,001 to 1,500 kilometres and Rs 1,150 for a distance of 1,501 to 2,000 kilometres.
The statement said the fuel surcharge will be Rs 1,300 for flights having a distance of more than 2,000 kilometres.
For SAARC region flights, the fuel surcharge varies from Rs 1,000 to Rs 3,000 and Rs 6,000 for Africa flights and Rs 10,000 for Europe services.
The fuel surcharge will be Rs 5,500 for flights to Southeast Asia, GCC and the Middle East, and North and East Asia, as per the statement.
Jet fuel accounts for around 40 per cent of an airline's operating costs.
IndiGo said ATF prices have remained volatile in recent months, especially following the geopolitical situation in the Middle East.
According to the airline, the continuous rise in fuel prices, with the latest month-on-month increase exceeding 14 per cent, has taken ATF costs to levels that are amongst the highest in the last decade.
"Given that Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) makes up a significant share of the airline's operating costs, this rise is expected to impact airlines' cost structures and network economics, including those of IndiGo," it said in a statement on Monday.
In view of the situation, the airline said it has marginally recalibrated its fuel charges across its domestic and international flights.
While offsetting the increase in fuel costs would have required a significantly larger increase in fuel charges, a measured and relatively modest adjustment to minimise the impact on customers has been made, the airline said.
Regretting the additional burden the revised fuel charges would have on travellers, the airline said the decision reflects the sustained increase in operating costs and evolving market environment.
The airline also said it would continue to monitor the situation and make relevant adjustments as and when appropriate.
IndiGo operates over 2,200 flights daily.
On October 1, ATF prices were hiked by a steep Rs 16 to Rs 137 per litre from Rs 121 for domestic airlines. The revision came after the jet fuel prices were raised by Rs 6.28 per litre, or 5.46 per cent, in September, following a Rs 5 per litre increase in August.
In April, Air India announced revisions to fuel surcharges while Akasa Air started levying a fuel surcharge from March 15 amid the spike in ATF prices.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with claims that it allegedly shows the Chief of the Army Staff, General Dhiraj Seth, dancing with Supreet Sapra, described as the wife of an Army major. The video features a purported CNN headline stating, “Indian Army Chief Dhiraj Seth Spotted Dancing with Army Major’s wife Supreet Sapra,” giving the impression that CNN published the video. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth dancing with Supreet Sapra, the wife of an Army major.
Fact: The video has been digitally manipulated to make it appear as though Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth is dancing with Supreet Sapra. CNN has not published any report or headline matching the one shown in the viral video. The original video, shared in March 2026, features a different man and woman dancing at a gathering. Supreet Sapra has also clarified that she is not an Army major’s wife and that the woman shown in the viral video is AI-generated. The Indian Army’s fact-check wing has also confirmed that the video is digitally manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but found no credible reports carrying the viral footage on CNN’s official website or any report or headline matching the one circulating with the video.
Upon closely reviewing the viral video, we noticed several inconsistencies. Though the man and woman appear to be dancing while holding glasses, the liquid inside them does not move or splash naturally as they dance. In one frame, the man’s ear and cheek area also appear smudged, while the faces of people in the background appear heavily blurred. The man’s face remains almost completely frozen with a wide smile throughout the video, further raising signs of AI manipulation.
We then ran the video through multiple AI detection tools, including DetectVideo AI and Meta AI’s verification platform. Both assessed the clip as likely AI-generated and detected AI signatures in the video.
The viral video contains an inset photograph showing a woman with a different man wearing a defence uniform. To learn more about the photograph, we conducted a reverse image search, which led us to an Instagram post (archived) by @sufimeranaam, dated 22 February 2026, featuring the same image. Newschecker contacted the account user regarding the viral video. She identified herself as Supreet Sapra and said, “I am Supreet Sapra, but I am not a major’s wife. My husband retired four years ago. The woman in the video is AI-generated, so apart from the name, everything is misinformation.”
Further investigation led us to an Instagram post (archived) by Rhythm Gupta, shared on 11 March 2026, with the caption, “Always dancing weirdly.” The video features a man and a woman dancing at a gathering. Their dance movements, the way they hold their glasses, and the song playing in the background are the same as those in the viral video. Although the background differs in colour and certain visual details, the overall setting and arrangement of elements are similar, and the movements of people around the dancing pair also closely resemble. This indicates that the viral video was likely manipulated using the earlier footage to make it appear as though the Army Staff chief was dancing with an Army major’s wife. Comparison of screengrabs from the viral clip and the Instagram video can be seen below.
The Indian Army’s fact-checking wing also clarified in an X post (archived) on 29 September 2026 that the viral video is digitally manipulated and fake.
To sum up, this viral video of Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth dancing with Supreet Sapra, the wife of an Army major, is AI-manipulated.

South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
- Published
South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikaners - he is "a born Afrikaner" himself.
"Is he talking about us?", Roelf Meyer remembers thinking, when he first heard President Trump say it.
His response to the US president's claim is blunt.
The notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist, he told the BBC, adding that his identity gave him the legitimacy to say so.
Meyer was one of the chief mediators to end white-minority rule known as apartheid in South Africa in the 1990s. He was appointed ambassador to the US in April, after diplomatic relations between the US and South Africa plummeted.
In an interview with the BBC, Meyer said the facts about violence in South Africa had been misrepresented and he never got a clear answer about where this "misdirection of information" was coming from.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.
Since last year, nearly 13,000 refugees were admitted to the United States and all but three were South African.
Among them was Lielie, the name she uses publicly, who moved with her family to Texas from South Africa, where they had lived on her stepfather's farm, growing macadamia nuts and bananas.
Despite walls around the house, an electric fence, and eight bull terriers, she said she felt "fear the whole time" and that on three occasions she saw people entering her property.
"Nothing was stolen, we weren't harmed, but there are friends of my husband, people that lived around us, they were brutally attacked," she said.
She said since moving to the US under the Trump administration's refugee pathway her life had changed, she felt safer walking around, and "my kids can actually play outside".
The Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday.
In a statement to the BBC, a White House spokeswoman said: "President Trump has provided a lifeline for Afrikaners, who are being raped, maimed, killed and driven off their property across South Africa.
"While the South African government and many in the media have brushed off the horrific lived experiences of this community, the Trump administration continues to process applications for refugee status because the president has a humanitarian heart."
SJ Du Venage, who lives on South Africa's west coast, has been trying to move to the US under the new scheme.
Du Venage is a council member of the Freedom Front Plus, a right-wing Afrikaner party, and argues that there is a "political drive towards killing white people, and killing the farmers on the farms".
"There's absolutely an agenda to wipe us out here," he says.
- Race policies or Israel - what's really driving Trump's fury with South Africa? 
  - Published23 February 2025
- Is there a genocide of white South Africans as Trump claims? 
  - Published2 June 2025
- Do Afrikaners want to take Trump up on his South African refugee offer? 
  - Published15 May 2025
An Afrikaner lobby group is holding a vigil on Saturday with thousands of white crosses on Washington's National Mall to commemorate what it says are victims of "farm attacks".
Claims of genocide against white South Africans have been discredited by every political party in the country, including by those representing Afrikaners.
"I'm an Afrikaner from South Africa myself," Ambassador Meyer said, "and I can say that I've never experienced something of that kind."
Meyer said he would like to have a conversation with Trump about the reality of the situation, saying that as a "born Afrikaner", he has the "legitimacy" to speak about the subject.
The ambassador helped negotiate an end to apartheid on behalf of the National Party, which was responsible for it, with now-president Cyril Ramaphosa also a key negotiator for the African National Congress party.
He said the "trust" between the two men was one reason President Ramaphosa appointed him to help mend US-South Africa relations, as well as "the fact he also saw the value of me being an Afrikaner".
"But I'm not here to represent the Afrikaner only," Meyer says.
Last week, the Trump administration announced visa restrictions for those South Africans who it said were responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white people. It also warned of further punitive actions if South African leaders did not address the issue.
Police data shows the majority of victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black. Farm violence, often motivated by robberies, is an issue but represents a smaller number of homicides in the country.
While no politician disputes that crime is a problem in South Africa, many experts say this does not qualify as "persecution".
Larry Bartlett, the former director of the US Refugee Assistance Programme, said it could even be "unlawful" to appropriate a programme defined in law for people who "really have no chance to go home".
He said white people who were unlikely to qualify as refugee in law were taking scarce opportunities meant for those fleeing war or ethnic cleansing.
The programme has its critics among Afrikaners in South Africa too.
"Why single out the white Afrikaner to say this group qualifies to flee to the US? This country suffers gender-based violence. Why not single out women?" Rudi Swanepoel, a pastor from Johannesburg told the BBC.
Swanepoel thinks it is not persecution but a "loss of privilege" that is causing some Afrikaners to feel aggrieved.
"To use the metaphor of a cake, 30, 40 years ago the white people of South Africa controlled the cake," he says. "Since democracy came, the obvious reality was we had to now start sharing that cake and those privileges."
Alongside "rural safety", the Trump administration has raised other concerns about South Africa, including targets for companies to increase non-white employment and a law allowing the state, in exceptional circumstances, to expropriate land without compensation. These are aimed at redressing historic racial inequality.
Meyer wants Trump's executive order against South Africa, which underpins the refugee pathway, revoked.
He said South Africa had never prevented people from leaving and had addressed all the US concerns, stressing that the land expropriation law is awaiting a court judgement.
"South Africa has challenges with the prevention of crime and with the combatting of crime," he said.
But he added: "It's a problem all around. It's not rural. It's not farm attacks only. If you look at the total picture, the huge levels of crime in the black townships of South Africa are the biggest concern, proportionally, far more than anything else."
He said he would encourage the US to help South Africa with resources on combatting crime, including by providing equipment to speed up reaction times.
Meyer also has a message for Afrikaners protesting against "farm attacks" by laying white crosses in Washington.
"It doesn't help us to raise a voice outside, if we are not committed to doing something inside the country," he says.

Russian report says Siberian plague institute worker fell ill, died of unknown cause
Russian authorities say a staffer at a plague research institute in Siberia contracted pneumonia of an unknown cause, and local state TV reported the woman died last week
Russian authorities have quarantined a hospital and are monitoring contacts of an employee at a plague research institute in Siberia who contracted pneumonia of an “unknown” cause. Local state TV said the woman died last week.
Russian authorities said they found no evidence that her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with. But the case has raised alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
The woman worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk, southeastern Siberia. A state TV station in Irkutsk reported Monday that she died last week in a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside Irkutsk.
The hospital has been placed under quarantine, Mayor Maxim Modin said Friday, no longer admitting or discharging patients, and its laboratory halted carrying out routine tests. The hospital's outpatient clinic kept operating as usual, he said.
Anna Popova, head of Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Irkutsk and met with Gov. Igor Kobzev and other officials on Friday.
Kobzev said everyone who came into contact with the woman is under medical supervision. He didn’t identify the infection and called it a suspected case of “a particularly dangerous infection.”
Rospotrebnadzor was implementing “a full range of anti-epidemic measures,” he added.
Rospotrebnadzor said Sunday the woman was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” and said “extensive” testing found “no microorganisms associated with the patient’s professional activities.”
The agency also said it didn't uncover any incidents at the institute “involving pathogenic microorganisms."
Two people who were in contact with the woman tested positive for a virus that causes a common cold and two others for COVID-19, the agency said, adding that others who were tested were all negative.
Independent local news outlet Lyudi Baikala quoted sources it did not identify as saying the woman died from pneumonic plague and that several Irkutsk hospitals were placed under quarantine.
Asked Monday to comment on the case, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the public and media should follow official statements from Rospotrebnadzor, rather than "rumors or speculation.”
The Irkutsk Aluminum Plant in Shelekhov required staff to wear masks as a precaution, its director Artyom Fominykh said Saturday on Telegram, calling for calm and adding: "Better be safe than sorry.”
The World Health Organization describes pneumonic plague as a less common but severe form of plague — a disease caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals and their fleas.

One of India’s earliest ecommerce marketplaces has finally trotted onto D-Street. After a relatively muted 4.93X subscription to its IPO, Snapdeal’s parent AceVector is all set to make its stock market debut on Monday. AceVector’s ₹420 Cr IPO, which opened on September 25 and closed on September 29, comprised a fresh issue of ₹287 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of around ₹133 Cr, with shares priced in the ₹30-32 band. The company's IPO response is a far cry from its once-lofty standing in India’s ecommerce race. At its peak, the company was valued at $6.5 Bn, backed by heavyweight investors, including SoftBank Group, Alibaba Group and Foxconn. Then, as Amazon poured billions into building its India business and Flipkart emerged as a formidable rival, the ecommerce battle grew increasingly intense. Snapdeal eventually stepped away from its ambition of competing across the broader market and shifted its focus to affordable fashion, home and beauty products, catering to shoppers in Tier II and Tier III India looking for low-priced goods rather than premium brands. But is value commerce really working for it? Let’s find out in this edition of Inc42 Markets. How AceVector Makes Money Snapdeal is only one part of AceVector’s portfolio. The company has two other businesses: Unicommerce, an ecommerce enablement software business, and Stellaro Brands, its consumer-brands arm. According to an expert tracking the consumer internet sector, Snapdeal has grown its net merchandise value and customer base of value-conscious shoppers, but its scale remains quite modest compared with larger ecommerce platforms, especially Meesho. The expert added that Snapdeal may not be generating enough revenue per transaction to cover customer acquisition, technology and logistics costs. Unlike an inventory-led retailer, Snapdeal operates an asset-light marketplace. Sellers own and list products, while Snapdeal facilitates discovery, transactions and associated services. It earns money through seller-related marketplace fees, advertising and marketing services, freight and collection fees, and charges for return shipments. This structure limits the need to purchase and hold inventory, but leaves the company dependent on transaction volumes, seller participation and the economics of fulfilling orders. The marketplace revenue rose to ₹293.7 Cr in FY26 from ₹249.9 Cr in FY25. Net merchandise value (NMV), the value of delivered merchandise after excluding cancellations and returns, increased 25.7% to ₹1,093.1 Cr, from ₹869.6 Cr in FY25. In FY24, NMV stood at ₹633.3 Cr, even as marketplace revenue remained relatively flat between FY24 and FY25 before rising in FY26. The gap between NMV and revenue is important. NMV measures the value of merchandise transacted on the platform; it is not the amount Snapdeal earns. In FY26, marketplace revenue was roughly 26.9% of NMV, down from 28.7% in FY25. Meanwhile, marketplace marketing and business promotion expenses climbed to ₹84.4 Cr in FY26, from ₹63.2 Cr in FY25 and ₹58.5 Cr in FY24. The company’s ecommerce enablement arm, Unicommerce, has emerged as a significant growth driver within the group. Its SaaS revenue rose 51.6% to ₹204.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹134.8 Cr in FY25, compared with Snapdeal’s marketplace revenue growth of 17.5% during the same period. The business provides order, inventory and warehouse management software through Uniware, alongside shipping and logistics automation through Shipway and marketing automation through Convertway. Its acquisition of Shipway Technology added to this portfolio, extending its services across more stages of the ecommerce lifecycle. Meanwhile, AceVector’s consumer brands business, housed under Stellaro Brands, remains smaller but expansion-heavy. It operates Rangita, a women’s ethnic wear brand sold online and through an omnichannel retail network. Stellaro’s revenue from operations rose to ₹12.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹11.4 Cr in FY25. What Does Snapdeal Offer Beyond Brand Recall? Snapdeal has been in the game since 2010, one of the early players that helped open the floodgates to online shopping in India. According to Karan Taurani, executive vice president at Elara Capital, Snapdeal has an edge in terms of brand recall. He said the company has remained relevant through multiple changes in its business model, from deal-led discounting to a broader marketplace and, more recently, a value-commerce platform. “Its longevity gives it an established identity among consumers, but that alone may not be enough to sustain growth in a market where customer acquisition, transaction frequency and operational efficiency are increasingly important,” Taurani said. He is of the view that Snapdeal’s focus on value-conscious shoppers does give it a clear customer segment to serve, but it also operates in a crowded market where affordability is not exclusive to one platform. Meesho, which has built a much larger marketplace around value-conscious consumers, is a key example. In FY26, Snapdeal clocked an NMV of ₹1,093.1 Cr, while Meesho’s marketplace raked in ₹41,560 Cr. This is a staggering 38X scale gap. The gap also extends beyond merchandise value to the number of customers and transactions each platform handles. Snapdeal reported 12.16 Mn annual transacting users and 25.98 Mn delivered units in FY26. Meesho reported 264.29 Mn annual transacting users and 1.71 Bn delivered units. Therefore, Snapdeal’s central challenge is scale, even in its value segment. Snapdeal Has AI Tools But Is There A Real Competitive Edge? At a time when Meesho has an extensive technology stack, including AI-led tools, Snapdeal is trying to take steps in a similar direction. Snapdeal recently introduced a multi-solution AI suite aimed at making fashion discovery more personalised, visual and conversational for Indian shoppers. The suite brings together AI-powered recommendations, conversational search, image-based discovery and customer experience tools across the marketplace. According to its RHP, 72.69% of orders in FY26 were placed without users entering a search term. The company attributes this to its recommendation engine and personalised product feeds, which use browsing history, product interactions and other data to tailor the shopping experience. Overall, its tech stack supports processes such as seller onboarding, catalogue ingestion and fraud detection. AI-supported customer service is available through channels including calls, WhatsApp, IVR and in-app support. Snapdeal may have added AI to the shopping cart, but that does not necessarily give it a competitive edge. Recommendation engines, conversational search and AI-powered support are increasingly becoming standard ecommerce features. For Snapdeal, AI is currently an ongoing bet. What it needs to solve immediately is the puzzle of scale. Temperamental traits and adverse experiences during childhood may together offer clues to vulnerability to major psychiatric disorders, a transdiagnostic study by researchers at NIMHANS has found.
The study, published recently in the Journal of Affective Disorders, examined 1,162 adults, including 532 people with psychiatric disorders, 457 unaffected first-degree relatives (FDRs) and 173 healthy controls. The participants were drawn from 393 multiplex families - families in which multiple members had been diagnosed with psychiatric disorders - involving schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and alcohol use disorder (AUD).
The researchers examined four broad dimensions of adult temperament - negative affectivity, extraversion/surgency, effortful control and orienting sensitivity - along with adverse childhood experiences (ACEs).
“Our findings suggest that temperament does not map onto psychiatric disorders in a simple, one-to-one manner. Rather, different combinations of temperamental characteristics are associated with different disorders, and some of these characteristics are also seen among unaffected family members,” said Srinivas Balachander, corresponding author and one of the lead researchers of the study.
Temperament shared within families
Using data from the erstwhile Accelerator programme for Discovery in Brain disorders using Stem cells (ADBS) project, (funded by the Department of Biotechnology and Pratiksha Trust), now known as the Rohini Nilekani Centre for Brain and Mind, at NIMHANS, the researchers found evidence of familial sharing across all four temperamental domains.
This was observed despite considerable variation in the psychiatric diagnoses within the same families. The finding is of interest because temperament is known to have a substantial heritable component, although the study did not directly establish that the temperamental characteristics observed were caused by specific genetic variants.
“In our study, considering the significant within-family heterogeneity in terms of different diagnoses, there was still a significant degree of shared temperament,” Dr. Balachander said.
Among affected participants, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder were associated with lower extraversion/surgency and orienting sensitivity. OCD was associated with higher negative affectivity and orienting sensitivity, along with lower effortful control and extraversion/surgency. Participants with AUD showed higher negative affectivity and orienting sensitivity and lower effortful control.
Some of these patterns were also observed among unaffected first-degree relatives. Relatives of people with schizophrenia showed lower extraversion/surgency, while relatives of people with OCD showed higher negative affectivity and lower effortful control.
“These findings are particularly interesting because some temperamental characteristics were evident even in individuals who did not have the disorder but belonged to families carrying a higher degree of familial risk,” Dr. Balachander said.
Childhood adversity and alcohol use disorder
The researchers also examined whether adverse childhood experiences altered the relationship between temperament and psychiatric disorders.
The clearest evidence for an interaction between temperament and childhood adversity emerged in alcohol use disorder. The overall ACE score was significantly associated with AUD, and interactions between childhood adversity and two temperamental domains - extraversion/surgency and effortful control - were also observed.
“Childhood adversity appears to add another layer to the relationship between temperament and psychiatric vulnerability. In our study, the evidence for this interaction was particularly apparent in alcohol use disorder, rather than uniformly across all four disorders,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers, however, cautioned against interpreting the findings as evidence that a particular temperament or childhood experience causes a psychiatric disorder.
The study was cross-sectional, meaning that the assessments were made at one point in time. The adult temperament measures were self-reported and could be influenced by current illness, treatment, illness duration or an individual’s perception of their own past Reports of childhood adversity may also be affected by recall and measurement biases.
Testing the findings
To examine whether the findings extended beyond the genetically enriched family sample, the researchers tested their statistical model using an independent community-based cohort from the Consortium for Vulnerability to Externalizing Disorders and Addiction (c-VEDA).
The analysis included 2,485 adults aged 18 to 23 years for whom the relevant temperament, ACE and psychiatric assessments were available.
The model showed an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.822 for alcohol use disorder, 0.742 for bipolar disorder and 0.752 for OCD. Its performance for schizophrenia was close to chance level, with an AUC of 0.526.
“The external validation gives us some indication that the associations identified in the family-based sample may extend to community populations for some disorders. However, the findings for schizophrenia did not replicate well, which is an important limitation and needs further investigation,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers said the findings point to the need for prospective studies that follow unaffected family members over time. Such studies could help determine whether particular temperamental characteristics precede the onset of psychiatric illness or are partly consequences of illness and its treatment.
“Temperament and childhood adversity may eventually become useful components of broader risk assessment frameworks, but we need prospective longitudinal evidence before we can say that they have predictive or preventive value,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers said that studying temperament alongside childhood adversity could eventually provide a more nuanced understanding of psychiatric vulnerability than considering family history alone. However, they stressed that the present findings do not establish that these measures can predict who will develop a psychiatric disorder.
The researchers said continued longitudinal follow-up of the cohort would be important to establish whether the observed temperamental patterns have value in identifying individuals at increased risk before the emergence of clinically significant symptoms.

When the government officials arrived in Tarluvada last year, they came with abundant promises.
Google, one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech companies, would soon be bringing a “golden opportunity” to this tiny village in south India: a $15bn AI datacentre.
The project, being built in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, is set to be Google’s largest “hyperscale” AI datacentre outside the US and would, officials said, make the village of Tarluvada into a world-famous tech hub. Jobs, usually scarce in this impoverished community, would become bountiful, real estate prices would soar and compensation for any land would be generous.
Few in the village – which sits on a dusty unpaved road and is surrounded by farms and forest – had even heard of AI or knew what a datacentre was. Yet it did not take long for local jubilation over Google’s arrival to turn to suspicion.
Just as protests have erupted globally over AI datacentres – from California and Texas to Scotland and Australia – communities in Andhra Pradesh, too have been gathering in opposition to the project, fearing that the people will end up bearing a crippling environmental and economic cost.
“We have learned that America does not want the problems of datacentres and so now Google is bringing them here,” said Tarluvada’s village head, BRB Naidu, who admitted he was torn about whether the datacentre would bring prosperity or ruin to their community. “Many in the village are very worried. But the government has refused to answer our questions.”
Pointing up to the nearby hillside – where bulldozers recently stripped the land bare of trees to ready it for Google’s mega AI campus – Naidu adds: “The work just continues every day.”
The state government, which is allied with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s party, have been accused of trying to obfuscate the true scale of the vast AI hub being built in Andhra Pradesh, to push the project through at lightening speed and avoid more stringent environmental scrutiny. Google has partnered with the Adani Group, one of India’s largest and most politically powerful conglomerates with a reputation for getting approvals through quickly, to build the project.
Publicly it was announced as a 1GW project – already a larger energy requirement than most AI datacentres. In its response to the Guardian, Google referred to it only as an unspecific “gigawatt scale AI hub”, that was “comparable to other projects”.
But state environmental clearances reveal that permission has been granted for it to be more than double that size – 2.51GW; the power equivalent of two large nuclear reactors at full output. Over a year, it amounts to upwards of 30% of the current energy consumption of the whole of Andhra Pradesh, a state home to more than 55 million people.
Activists fear that meeting the datacentre’s vast energy demands will lead to seismic environmental consequences for the region, including driving up fossil fuel emissions. While Google has pledged to help generate “new, clean energy” to power its AI hub, currently 75% of the country’s electricity grid is run on coal.
The state government argues AI datacentres will be essential to India’s growth and long-term digital competitiveness. According to the government of India’s Economic Survey 2025–26, India generated nearly 20% of the world’s data but hosts only about 3% of global datacentres.
But locals and activists say that building one of the world’s largest AI datacentres in a region of India already struggling with issues over extreme heat, water, land, forests, power shortages and environmental regulation comes at a heavy cost.
Google’s project will in fact encompass three separate datacentres around the state capital of Vizakhapatnam. One other site nearby to Taluvada is a few metres from reserve forest, a drinking water reservoir and a wildlife sanctuary home to endangered species such as leopards.
Despite the AI datacentre’s expansive footprint, the state government issued environmental clearances to Google in just nine days, with no public consultation.
Three petitions challenging the state’s quick approval of the project have now been filed to India’s National Green Tribunal (NGT), the country’s top environmental court. The petitions allege that government’s assessment of the risks to the environment and water supplies were “grossly inadequate, scientifically unrealistic, and misleading”. A public litigation has also been filed in the Andhra Pradesh high court.
“This datacentre will be unprecedented in scale but there was no public hearing and no substantial evaluation of the ecological damage or the economic cost for local communities,” said VS Krishna, an activist with Human Rights Forum, the organisation which filed the NGT cases.
Krishna alleged that their campaign to protest against the datacentre had been met with a deliberate silencing, including videos and social media pages being taken down. The government did not respond to this allegation.
“We just have to look at the protests happening across the world to understand how environmentally catastrophic this will be,” Krishna added.
In Tarluvada, temperatures regularly soar to about 45C during the summer and there are concerns the datacentres – documented emitters of heat – could make this even worse. The mass deforestation required for the project – more than 100 acres, could drive up temperatures even more. In response to the Guardian, Google said the project would have “no expected impact” on the local community.
The strain on water supplies in this already water-stressed area has also been a cause of concern. In similarly water-stressed cities in the US, datacentres have been accused of exacerbating drought while polluting the water supply. Google said this project would use air-cooling instead of water, and would therefore have no impact on local drinking water supplies.
Venkat Surynarayana, 40, a farmer in Tarluvada, said that when officials had initially come to measure land for the datacentre “they never mentioned anything about risks of pollution or water or heat, they didn’t even tell us what the project was.
“We are sick with worry since we learned about the problems a datacentre can bring. This area can not afford to be any hotter. What if this makes our land dry and worthless? What will happen to my crops and my livelihood?”
Surynarayana claimed attempts to get answers from the local administration had been met with police threats and protesters such as himself had been routinely detained. “When we raised our voices, they ignore us and then they shut us down,” he said. “But if this is not stopped, it could be the end of Tarluvada.”
For the state government of Andhra Pradesh, the deal struck with Google to build this vast datacentre on its turf is a source of enormous pride, part of a wider policy to make the state into India’s most advanced and affluent tech hub. “Artificial intelligence is becoming foundational infrastructure for the global economy,” said Sribharat Mathukumilli, a local MP with the ruling state government, who rejected the environmental concerns.
The subsidies and incentives they offered to Google, from decades-long tax breaks and discounted land to access to cheap electricity and water, are estimated to amount to 220bn rupees ($2.2bn) over 20 years.
“Our objective is not simply to host a datacentre, but to create an AI and digital ecosystem,” said Mathukumilli. Late last year, the state granted permission for another 1GW AI datacentre, to be built by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries.
Google insisted the design choices of its AI datacentre have been tailored to local conditions and that it had “engaged deeply” with local communities, claiming it would generate thousands of jobs around Vizakhapatnam.
But swathes of villagers in Tarluvada allege they were forced to give up land for the project against their will, and say they have not been given all they were promised in return.
“No one will tell us the truth about this project,” said T Applaraju, 40, who was one of the 520 local families in Tarluvada who recently had land taken back that the government had allocated to him 20 years ago. He claims he was given no notice that his land was to be taken until April this year, when security guards working for the Adani Group erected fences and blocked locals from entering the plots they had farmed for years.
“They took land that we thought belonged to us, it’s a big shock,” he said. “Why are Google building this here and not in America?”
The state government claims no lands were forcibly taken and that it gave “generous compensation” to those who were eligible. The Adani group says that all necessary legal approvals were given. But many of the 47 farmers from the impoverished Dalit community who were compensated for their land are also unhappy.
One farmer, P Venkat Rao, alleged he was pressured by the government into giving up his only acre of land against his will. He received $40,000 in compensation, but said the government’s promise to give them a replacement piece of land and one job per family had not materialised. Without land to farm, Rao described the compensation as “worthless”.
“I am a farmer, without my land I am nothing,” he added. “They have taken my livelihood and broken their promises.”
