New-age tech stocks remained under pressure this week, with 47 stocks declining as benchmark indices recorded their eighth consecutive weekly fall. Moneyview’s market debut this week took the number of new-age tech companies under Inc42’s coverage to 66. Despite the addition, their combined market capitalisation fell to $153.61 Bn from the $166.6 Bn commanded by 65 companies last week. Shares of Moneyview made their debut on Thursday (October 1) at ₹55.6 on the BSE, nearly 64% above the issue price of ₹34. The stock closed at ₹54.03, down 2.8% from the listing price but 58.9% above its issue price. Of the 65 stocks under Inc42’s coverage at the end of last week, 47 fell between 0.08% and 20.1% this week. Eighteen stocks gained between 0.17% and 22.55%. Turtlemint led the losers, falling 20.1% to ₹69.75, while PB Fintech declined 15.66% to ₹983 following IRDAI’s proposed changes to insurance commissions. ESDS was the second-biggest loser, falling 18.54% to ₹1,431.70 after announcing its Q1 FY27 results on September 24. However, it remained more than 91% above its listing price. Swiggy, Fractal, Menhood, and IndiaMART touched fresh lows during the week. Eternal, Lenskart, Ather Energy, Paytm, and Nykaa also declined this week. SME-listed Zappfresh led the gainers, rising 22.55% to ₹60.49 after hitting an all-time low of ₹47.10 on September 25. RentoMojo, Meesho, BlackBuck, and Go Digit also gained, while Aequs, Kissht, Nazara, SEDEMAC, and Zelio touched fresh highs. The stock markets were closed yesterday on account of Gandhi Jayanti. Beyond stock movements, the week saw GST notices, stake sales, and expansion plans across listed new-age tech companies. Here’s a closer look at the key developments. GST Notices Put Companies In Focus Kissht’s NBFC arm, Si Creva, received a GST show cause notice involving ₹44.06 Cr over alleged input tax credit discrepancies and tax shortfalls for FY23. This comprises ₹22.03 Cr in tax, ₹19.83 Cr in interest, and ₹2.2 Cr in penalties. The company said it would contest the notice. WeWork India received a ₹11.01 Cr show cause notice over alleged excess input tax credit utilisation arising from differences between its annual returns and audited books. Urban Company faced a ₹3.05 Cr demand over alleged incorrect input tax credit claims and tax shortfalls for FY23. ideaForge received a ₹109.17 Cr GST demand and penalty for allegedly paying 5% instead of 18% on drone sales between January 2022 and March 2024. It plans to appeal, citing a 2025 government clarification that drones attract 5% GST, and expects no immediate material financial or operational impact. Stake Sales And Purchases TPG, through NewQuest Asia Fund IV (Singapore), sold 40 Lakh Shadowfax shares at ₹284.03 apiece for ₹113.6 Cr, following its ₹202 Cr exit from FirstCry on September 25. SBI Mutual Fund bought 1.18 Cr Swiggy shares for an estimated ₹300.6 Cr, raising its holding from 4.7% to 5.12%. MobiKwik cofounder and CFO Upasana Taku bought 1.07 Lakh shares for ₹2.1 Cr in two September transactions, increasing her stake from 10.11% to 10.24%. RateGain Names New CFO RateGain appointed former Optum India executive Chetan Garg as CFO, effective Monday (September 28). Garg, who also held senior finance roles at Whirlpool, will oversee global finance operations, capital allocation, and risk management. SEDEMAC Reports Record Unit Sales SEDEMAC’s quarterly sales of control-intensive electronic control units (ECUs) rose 37.5% to a record 14.53 Lakh units in Q2 FY27 from 10.56 Lakh units in Q2 FY26. Trailing 12-month sales rose 44.2% YoY to a record 45.97 Lakh units. Cumulative sales of its sensorless ISG+EFI ECUs crossed 1 Mn units in September, 23 months after launch. AceVector Heads For Listing Snapdeal parent AceVector will list on Monday (October 5), after its ₹420 Cr IPO was subscribed 4.93X. Several OFS participants booked losses. SoftBank’s sale fetched substantially less than the acquisition cost of its shares sold, while returns varied across Nexus Venture Partners’ investment vehicles. BlackBuck, LEAP India Back Subsidiaries BlackBuck invested ₹22 Cr in wholly owned subsidiary TZF Logistics Solutions, subscribing to 34.08 Lakh shares at ₹64.55 apiece. The rights issue will support expansion, working capital, and compliance with RBI requirements for its prepaid payment instrument licence. Separately, LEAP India incorporated packaging manufacturer Vimprotech after its board approved two wholly owned subsidiaries on Tuesday (September 29). Vimprotech will receive an initial ₹4.03 Cr investment. The second proposed subsidiary, Total International Packaging Solutions, will provide returnable packaging pooling services to automotive and manufacturing businesses, with an initial ₹1.65 Cr investment. Now, let’s take a look at the broader market trends this week. Benchmarks Extend Losing Streak The aforementioned developments unfolded against a weak market backdrop, with rising US bond yields, foreign investor selling, and crude oil concerns weighing on sentiment. The Sensex fell 2.69% to 71,909.70, while the Nifty 50 declined 3.11% to 22,421.95. Midcap and smallcap indices also declined around 3.5% each. Despite the fall in indices, domestic fundamentals remained resilient, with industrial production growth accelerating to 8% YoY in August. Domestic triggers ahead include the RBI’s policy decision, September services and composite PMI readings, and Q2 FY27 earnings, starting with TCS and DMart. Religare Broking’s SVP of research Ajit Mishra expects caution to persist, with bond yields, crude prices, geopolitical developments, and RBI policy providing direction. Against this backdrop, here’s a closer look at Aequs’ rally and Turtlemint’s continued decline. Aequs Rallies On Fundraise Plan Aequs gained 11.66% to ₹274.90, taking its gains over the listing price to 96.36% and market capitalisation to $1.92 Bn. Its board approved a ₹650 Cr preferential warrant issue to promoter-group entity Mellwood Trustee Services on September 25. Proceeds will support aerospace and consumer capacity expansion, including the Hosur facility, subsidiaries, and joint ventures. Inside India's forest villages, where a dangerous mix of crises led to 32 child deaths
- Published
Warning: This article contains details some readers may find distressing
At about 3am one morning in May, Bamita Markam began convulsing.
The three-year-old had spent days with a high fever and angry red sores on her body. Her mother, Koushila, had first taken her to a doctor, who prescribed an ointment.
Bamita seemed to recover, then became ill again. A faith healer, called to the house in Matla village, gave her syrups and tablets. Nothing worked. By dawn, Bamita was dead.
"She cried a lot," Koushila recalls. "She convulsed all night." The family tried to make her drink water. At one point she vomited blood. They buried her in a jungle after midday.
Bamita's death was one of at least 32 child deaths recorded since May in a cluster of remote villages in Balaghat district in India's Madhya Pradesh state, officials say. The victims ranged from babies just three or four months old to an 18-year-old, and most were Baiga, one of India's 75 "particularly vulnerable tribal groups", external.
Officials attribute the deaths to mainly measles and malaria, possibly aggravated by malnutrition and delays in treatment.
They believe eight to 10 deaths were associated with measles, roughly another 10 with malaria, with several children suffering more than one infection. The precise cause of every death is less certain.
"I have never seen an outbreak like this. My father was a two-term lawmaker, and I have served three terms, but neither of us has seen so many children die in such a short time," Sanjay Uikey, who has represented the area since 2013, told me.
But disease is only part of the story. In remote, forested parts of Balaghat, where Maoist insurgency once took root, reaching a health centre can be a challenge in itself.
In the monsoon, the terrain can make that journey harder. Paddy fields glow against red earth and low, forested hills. Narrow dirt tracks wind between fields and mud homes, often becoming slippery and impassable in heavy rain.
The countryside is lush, but the homes are sparse. Most Baiga houses have low mud walls, rough timber and bamboo, and tiled or thatched roofs patched with plastic against the rain.
Some homes are accessible only by these tracks. Doctors investigating the deaths have travelled through the mud in tractors. On a recent visit, we walked nearly 2km (1.2 miles) uphill to reach some of the more remote homes. The surrounding jungle was dotted with the graves of children who had died.
The nearest state hospital, a 100-bed facility in Birsa, is about 70km away. For families without vehicles, reaching it can mean muddy tracks, a makeshift bamboo stretcher or a motorcycle - and a day's lost wages.
When Bamita became seriously ill, the family did not get her to hospital. It was raining heavily. The tracks were muddy and slippery, and the family had no way of transporting her.
"If I was able to take her to hospital she might have lived," Koushila says.
Her other daughter, Ankita, keeps asking what happened to her sister. The six-year-old has been told what many children in these villages are told: "Mata aa gayi" - the goddess has arrived.
For some Baiga families, some illnesses - like chicken pox - are seen as the arrival of a disease goddess, who must be appeased rather than treated. Families perform a seven to nine-day ritual of bathing and offering cool water and neem leaves to the local disease goddess. Many believe that treating the patient before the ritual is completed could cause death.
For weeks, such beliefs shaped how families responded to sick children. Then the scale of the deaths began to emerge.
On 21 July, Parshuram Dhurwey, a local village council chief, heard that two children in the same household in Bondari village had died. The next morning, he heard of another death. He called local officials and went to the area.
They found a grim picture.
"Every other child was sick," Dhurwey says. "They had fever, they had rashes. Many were undernourished."
When government medical officer Nimish Gautam arrived, he found severely dehydrated children. The first case he saw was a teenage girl with several days of fever and rash, whose blood sugar appeared dangerously low. Her family refused to let the health team examine her properly.
"Police were brought in to persuade them to take her to a health centre. The family still refused," Gautam told me. "They said if we took her for treatment, she would die. So we kept her under observation, and she recovered."
In one village, Dhurwey says, officials forcibly entered homes and took five seriously ill children to hospital. All recovered.
By the time the outbreak became unmistakable to local authorities, children had already been dying for weeks. By September, Dhurwey says, 10 children aged about 18 months to 14 years had died across the four villages in his council - Adori, Kundekasa, Bondari and Usri.
The symptoms were frighteningly similar and frustratingly non-specific: fever, rashes, weakness, dehydration and, in some cases, seizures. Some children had scabies, fungal infections or bacterial skin infections alongside suspected measles and malaria. In a district where malaria is endemic, external, fever could mean several things at once.
Sagnibai of Bondari lost two children within 24 hours. Her daughter, Lamnin, 12, died on 26 June. Her one-year-old son, Sahil, died the following day. A local healer told the family it was Mata. They also had no money or vehicle to take the children to a doctor.
Her husband, Samaroo Dhurwey, remembers nights in which the children's bodies seemed to be "on fire". They could not digest food. They died at home.
Mahasingh Parte of Matla village lost two children - a six-year-old girl and a four-year-old boy - within two days of each other. The family followed a faith healer's instructions. "He said don't take them to hospital," Parte recalls.
Parte is a landless farm labourer who earns about 200 rupees ($2; £1.58) on a good day, he said. Work is scarce in the monsoon, and although a small primary health centre is just 5km away, he had never been there. Poverty and remoteness had stacked the odds against his children.
The question of what was making children sick became harder to answer as the deaths mounted.
An investigation by the ICMR-National Institute for Tribal Health Research (NIRTH) tested 10 samples collected from the affected villages on 7 August. Six tested positive for measles; four were negative.
Measles is highly contagious, causing high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by a rash. Most children recover, but malnutrition can make measles far more dangerous, external, increasing the risk of pneumonia, severe diarrhoea and dehydration, and inflammation of the brain. The infection also weakens the immune system, leaving children vulnerable to other infections. Malaria can compound that risk.
But doctors cautioned that malaria did not necessarily follow measles, and not every fever and rash was measles. Instead, several infections and vulnerabilities collided.
"Sometimes there is no single factor behind the deaths," Gautam said. "There are malnourished children and there's zero health education and hygiene at home."
The Baiga villages are not entirely disconnected from modern India. Seasonal migration takes families to other states for chilli picking and other work. Children watch reels on smartphones, while many families have minimum single-bulb solar-powered electricity, bank accounts and, in some homes, piped water.
Yet malnutrition remains widespread, with children often poorly fed. A five-year-old who died recently of measles weighed around 5kg.
Gautam believes malnutrition is driven by early marriage and motherhood, with some girls becoming mothers at 16 or 17, when their bodies are still developing.
Closely spaced pregnancies, premature births and low birth weight can follow, while young mothers struggle to breastfeed and care for their children. Diet is another problem: many families rely heavily on rice and lentil soup, with too little protein and dietary variety. Studies on Baiga households have found widespread nutritional deficiencies, compounded by poor uptake, external of public services.
The gap between services on paper and on the ground was stark: the state response came weeks after deaths began, while health teams struggled to reach and persuade families.
Once the outbreak was recognised, health workers began door-to-door screening in affected villages. Mobile medical units carrying oxygen, nebulisers, suction equipment, malaria tests and medicines visited more than 20 affected villages.
One mobile doctor, Neeraj Sharma, says teams routinely saw more than 50 patients a day, about half of them children. They conducted 10 or more malaria tests daily, sometimes finding two positive cases a day.
More than 6,200 patients - mostly children - were eventually treated at home, according to Gautam. More than 630 were referred to district hospitals. About 600 returned home, while around 30 remain admitted.
Vaccination became an emergency response. Although official records suggested 90-95% coverage in some areas, health workers found children without records and families reluctant to vaccinate.
Authorities therefore offered the measles-rubella (MR) vaccine to all children under 15, regardless of recorded status. Of about 40,000 children identified in Birsa, roughly 27,000 had been vaccinated, Gautam said. Of the area's 180 villages, some 67 are predominantly Baiga and among the most vulnerable.
But vaccination is only one part of the protection children need. There are wider questions about whether basic nutrition and other health services are reaching those most at risk.
A 2024 audit by India's Comptroller and Auditor General found "serious irregularities", external in Madhya Pradesh's distribution of take-home rations meant to supplement the diets of children aged six months to three years, pregnant women and lactating mothers, including problems with beneficiary identification, production, transport and distribution.
The outbreak has now subsided. Officials say the last child death was more than two weeks before their late-September assessment, while teams continue visiting villages. In Kundekasa, a medical camp that once saw about 120 children a day was seeing fewer than 10.
Back in Matla, Bamita's mother speaks about the child who would ask for money for snacks, play with her sister and run inside whenever cars approached because vehicles frightened her.
"I had hope she'd study and make something of herself. I never regretted I didn't have a boy," Koushila says.
Then she looks at Ankita, the surviving sister.
"I want more kids," she says. "I feel alone. Ankita is alone. She keeps crying for her sister."

While most Americans may think the Iraq War is long over, it wasn’t until last week that the last U.S. troops departed, ending a long and painful experience for both nations that began with the U.S. invasion in 2003.
The residual force of around 2,500 had been in Iraq to help fight the Islamic State terrorist group for the past dozen years — a tiny fraction of what was once an occupation force of nearly 200,000 U.S. and coalition troops. There was a break in the U.S. presence from 2011 until the rise of ISIS in 2014 made a return necessary, but this time feels final.
About 4,500 Americans died in Iraq since 2003, around 3,500 in combat, and more than 30,000 were wounded. Hundreds of thousands of Iraqis were killed and wounded. The cost to the U.S. is estimated at around $1.7 trillion. A lot of blood and treasure. Most historians and military analysts consider the conflict a disaster, calling it a “war of choice” and placing it alongside obvious failures such as Vietnam and Afghanistan.

Access to genomic testing and matched treatments remains profoundly unequal within and between countries, according to a new commission by The Lancet Oncology.
It has also identified substantial inequalities in cancer genetic testing research, reporting that only 2 per cent of biomarker-based cancer trials are conducted in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), compared to almost 81 per cent in high-income countries.
An international team of authors of the commission has warned of a "paradox of success" -- the rapid expansion of precision oncology has increased cost and complexity faster than the benefits it delivers at a population level.
Global spending on cancer medicines is estimated to have risen by around 75% over the last five years, reaching approximately USD 252 billion in 2024, and is projected to reach USD 441 billion by 2029, they have said.
The researchers analysed global data on clinical trials and genomic datasets, and conducted a survey of national cancer programmes.
The team estimated that seven to eight million (70-80 lakh) people with cancer worldwide need standard-of-care molecular testing every year.
However, the coverage remains far from universal, particularly in LMICs, it has said.
For example, an estimated 3.14 lakh women with ovarian cancer are eligible for BRCA -- the breast cancer gene -- testing annually, yet around half do not receive it, a gap driven largely by a low testing coverage in LMICs, the researchers have said.
To help health systems respond, the commission has proposed a framework for prioritising which molecular tests and matched therapies to implement, alongside a system-readiness assessment tool.
It has also set out a workforce-competency framework and principles for responsible data-sharing.
The commission has also put forth 10 core recommendations for an equitable, effective and responsible integration of precision oncology into cancer control and universal health coverage, and a phased implementation roadmap.

"This is for her - we just want to live and go running and come back home without having to think that it may be one of us", said Nonhle Mpohlo.

The ASUS ProArt PZ14 is a powerful 2-in-1 Windows tablet for creators, with a sharp 3K OLED display, strong Snapdragon X2 Elite performance, excellent battery life, and full desktop apps. However, its high price, weak touch experience, and some ARM app limits hold it back.
People still debate why the tablet category exists. Some people believe they can replace laptops, while others see them as glorified smartphones with bigger screens.
I agree with both statements, as tablets are extremely portable. They are thinner, lighter, and easy to carry anywhere, and they can also convert into a laptop on the go, with the added advantage of a stylus for note-taking, sketching, or even marking up PDF files. Not to mention, they’re also great for watching movies and other entertainment.
But they are extremely limited in software capabilities despite hardware that can run fully native desktop applications. But Apple’s software limitations are also a deal-breaker for many. On the other hand, it runs the full Windows 11 OS on tablets without limitations. But it isn’t optimized for tablets.
For most people, or for creative work, the iPad is the first choice. But I recently got a chance to review the ASUS ProArt PZ14, which is a 2-in-1, tablet-first Windows device designed for creative work that is portable and offers an excellent OLED screen, solid performance, solid battery life, and is capable of running fully native applications, and comes with a keyboard and a pen out of the box for all your creative work and note-taking. I have been using the ASUS ProArt PZ14 for the past two weeks. In this detailed review, you will find out whether the ASUS ProArt PZ14 breaks tradition by doing things differently. Or is it just another tablet in the debate? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Design and Build: Lightweight and practical, but the design is an acquired taste
ASUS ProArt PZ14 is a tablet-first Windows PC. The keyboard detaches completely from the tablet, and all components, including the processor, sit on the back of the display.
As a result, it carries all the weight. ASUS includes a magnetic case in the box that you can attach to the back of the tablet to use as a stand and to hold the ASUS Pen 3.0. I wouldn’t recommend attaching it without the case because, while you’re holding the tablet, the magnets are not strong, and it can easily fall off, which it did. But hopefully, thanks to the build, it survived accidental falls.
Thanks to the matte finish, the back of the tablet isn’t a fingerprint magnet either, but stains are visible if you look at it a certain way, and they wipe off easily with any standard cloth.
An ASUS design choice on the back can be a hit or a miss depending on your perception. Right off the bat, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 doesn’t look like a tablet. It felt like a very niche tablet designed for a specific purpose. It has a single rear camera. Thankfully, there is no bump, and it comes with a lot of stickers, which indicates it is more than just a tablet.
You get ProArt branding at the top in the center. Overall, the fit and finish are solid, but the looks can be hit or miss based on your perception. I wish it looked more like a tablet.
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 comes with dual speakers, with one on each side The power button is on the top in landscape and on the right in portrait, which is convenient for landscape use but less convenient in portrait.
And you can find the volume-down and volume-up keys on the right as well, making it easy to control with your right hand. The SD Express 7.0 card reader and two USB4 Type-C ports are on the left side.
The look changes entirely from the front. It comes with a 14-inch 3K OLED display with a 144Hz refresh rate and minimal bezels, similar to the iPad Pro, but wider overall. At the top, you get an 8MP IR front camera with no privacy shutter.
The tablet weighs just 790 grams, making it lightweight and easy to use, but the larger display is hard to hold for long periods when using it as a tablet. The tablet has rounded corners on the back, which make it easy to hold for long periods, and the textured finish on the front half provides better grip. The matte finish makes it less slippery.
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 also has an IP52 rating. ASUS officially claims that it is tested to MIL-STD-810Hstandards . So you have the military standard, but don’t drop-test it like other laptops.
When I first held the ASUS ProArt PZ14, the back finish felt like plastic. However, ASUS claims the chassis uses an aluminum alloy. The sides feel very solid.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Display: A gorgeous 3K OLED made for creators
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 display is one of the best-looking, and if there is one reason to choose this tablet, it’s this display. Whether you are a business user, a graphic designer, or someone who wants to casually watch movies and play games, it delivers a great viewing experience.
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 comes with a 14-inch 3K OLED display. It comes with a 144Hz refresh rate for a smooth experience. The 14-inch display is a sweet spot. On your desk and used with the keyboard, it is a sweet spot and a perfect middle ground between the 13.6-inch and 15-inch laptops, but it feels very large in hand when you hold it and use it as a tablet.
The OLED display is one of the best I have seen on a tablet, matching premium, high-quality displays with 100% DCI-P3 color gamut and PANTONE validation. The blacks look deeper, and colors are represented very accurately, making it a good choice for designers and photographers who want to edit images accurately. The touch response is also fast, but Windows is the one to blame. It makes interactions less convenient, which I will cover more in the OS section.
The display also supports a stylus. ASUS includes the ASUS Pen 3.0 out of the box. Writing and drawing on the display feels faster and more fluid. But because of the glass finish, it feels slippery while taking notes. You can apply a matte-finish screen protector for a better typing and note-taking experience on this tablet. After the iPad Pro, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 provided the best note-taking experience, even better than the Apple Pencil in some cases.
ASUS, being extra generous, added the pencil-scribble sound while taking notes. Well, thank you, ASUS, for looking at those tiny details to enhance the user experience. But it sounds so artificial.
Next, this 16:10 aspect ratio is perfect for watching content. I watched three episodes of Better Call Saul (season 4) on Netflix, and the experience was better on the ASUS ProArt PZ14 than on my iPad Pro.
With 3K resolution and 243 pixels per inch, it is also one of the sharper displays. It looks sharp even when you zoom in on minor editing details.
However, if you often read web pages, blogs, or docs on this tablet, while it looks fine when using it in laptop mode, as soon as you pick it up and use it as a tablet, you are holding a massive tablet, and 16:10 feels very wide when you put it close to your eyes, which means you need to move your head to read the text. Also, portrait mode isn’t appealing either, with that 14-inch massive screen making it hard to read and scroll. With this large form factor, using it with a single hand is almost impossible. You can try if you want.
Overall, the display is one of the ASUS ProArt PZ14’s biggest strengths. Whether you’re watching content, editing, or designing, everything looks incredible on this massive screen.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Keyboard and Trackpad: Laptop-like typing, but better suited for a desk
ASUS also provides a keyboard out of the box. Unlike with the iPads, which you need to buy separately and are also expensive. Fortunately, the typing experience is as good as on thin-and-light laptops. However, if you’re used to mechanical keyboards or longer key travel, you might find it hard to type at first, but you can eventually get used to it.
Also, there are a few things that you need to know: the keyboard completely detaches from the tablet, which means it doesn’t have a hinge that holds the display and keyboard together. A small magnetic attachment on the bottom of the tablet connects to the keyboard.
You can just hover the tablet over the keyboard, and it attaches magnetically. However, the magnet isn’t as strong, so it can also detach easily. And since there is no strong hinge holding the keyboard and tablet together, you cannot place it on your lap and type on uneven surfaces, where the tablet takes the full weight and could tip back.
Fortunately, ASUS also included a full touchpad, and again, it’s almost like using the touchpad on a regular thin-and-light laptop. The speakers are very loud. They have rich sound. There is no headphone jack.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Specs and Performance: Snapdragon X2 Elite delivers plenty of power
Under the hood, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 runs on the Snapdragon X2 Elite X2E-88-100 processor. My variant has 32GB of LPDDR5X RAM and a 1TB M.2 NVMe PCIe 4.0 SSD. That’s a large configuration by current standards.
Qualcomm is trying too hard to become a name for its PC processors after it conquered Android phones. The processor offers very solid performance. Tasks feel faster, and it compares with some of the best in the industry right now, including the Intel Core Ultra 7 series and Ryzen AI Max+, among others. In comparison, in Geekbench single- and multicore scores, Snapdragon X2 Elite has produced very good numbers.
You can see the benchmarks of the ASUS ProART PZ14 from third-party testers.
The tablet also offers a dedicated performance mode that provides extra power when needed. This results in smooth day-to-day performance; whether it’s opening apps, touch interactions, gaming, or uploading files, everything feels smoother on this tablet
The built-in SD Express 7.0 card reader delivers strong sequential read and write rates, including 730 MB/s sequential read speeds. So if you are a creator who copies videos and files to and from the tablet, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 won’t consume your time.
However, while the processor is solid in CPU performance, the GPU is still weaker on Snapdragon processors, and the same is true of the Snapdragon X2 Elite. It comes with an integrated Qualcomm Adreno GPU. That performs decently; however, it’s not as good as Radeon or Intel Arc GPUs.
Because of this, it might not excel at higher-end applications or even gaming. It can offer decent performance, but not top-tier.
While the GPU might not be the most powerful, the NPU performance is significantly better. The Snapdragon X2 Elite includes a Qualcomm Hexagon NPU rated up to 80 TOPS. This lets you offload a few AI tasks locally for better performance. For instance, if you are a creator, you can run AI models locally.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 also comes with a fan. Under load, the tablet tends to get a bit warmer, and the fan kicks in.
Overall performance is impressive for such a thin and light device. Daily use, such as browsing the web, watching movies and shows, and running a few high-end software applications, feels faster and handles every task without breaking a sweat.
Moreover, while compatibility with popular ARM apps on Windows has improved over the years since Qualcomm announced Snapdragon X Elite, some older programs and plug-ins still aren’t natively compatible with Windows on ARM, and some run via x86 emulation.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Battery Life: Easily lasts an entire workday
The battery life is incredible on this tablet, and Windows on ARM has already proved it. The ASUS ProArt PZ14 comes with a 75Wh four-cell lithium-ion battery. ASUS also offers a 68W USB-C charger in the box.
Even in performance and non-performance modes, battery life stays consistent. On average, I got around 12 to 14 hours of battery life with light to medium use and about 10-11 hours with heavy use, including gaming. With light use, just using the browser, I even got two days of battery life.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Windows 11 Experience: Full desktop software, but a poor tablet interface
Now let’s address the elephant in the room: Windows 11. I would say having Windows 11 is both the biggest strength and also the biggest weakness of this tablet. The ASUS ProArt PZ14 ships with Windows 11 or Windows 11 Pro out of the box, depending on the configuration. My unit comes with Windows 11 Home.
No matter which version you are on, Windows 11 isn’t optimized for the touch interface. In Windows 11 touch mode, it feels like a desktop and has very small buttons, menus, and toolbars.
If you primarily want to use the ASUS ProArt PZ14 as a tablet, and you’re used to iPad Pro-type interaction, you will definitely find it hard to use day-to-day. Fortunately, using the pen minimizes this. However, if you primarily use your hands, keep that in mind.
Also, this tablet has a core Windows problem. The biggest problem is the annoying Windows updates. They are still an issue even after Microsoft promised to reduce those interruptions. Unfortunately, I haven’t been able to set up the tablet from scratch because it’s a pre-owned unit, and someone else has already set it up for me, so I was saved from dealing with lengthy setup processes.
Another big limitation of Windows running on ARM is limited app support. While app support has improved significantly since I first reviewed the Snapdragon X Elite laptop, most popular applications are now natively available on Windows on ARM, but a few legacy applications still use Prism emulation, which affects performance and misses core features. However, if you mainly want to use it as a creator tablet, most creator apps are natively available on Windows, and a few games are also natively supported on Windows on ARM.
But the biggest advantage is that, since it runs on Windows, you can run full desktop-level software without any limitations. You can multitask with multiple windows. If you want better multitasking and portability at the same time, this is something you should get.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Ports and Connectivity: USB4 and SD Express are useful, but some ports are missing
Despite its tablet form factor, ASUS has included decent port support on the ASUS ProArt PZ14. It comes with two USB 4.0 Gen 3 Type-C ports that support up to 40 Gbps, which can be used to connect external SSDs, docks, and even an external monitor.
It also includes an SD Express 7.0 card reader, which is excellent for transferring video and photos from your cameras. There’s no HDMI port, which I miss, but you can easily work around it with external peripherals. The camera quality is also good, much better than the webcam quality on other ASUS laptops I have tested. The rear camera is also decent in good lighting, which you can use to scan documents quickly. The tablet also supports Wi-Fi 7 or Bluetooth 6.0.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Verdict: A powerful Windows tablet for creators on the go
So, that is everything that you need to know about ASUS ProArt PZ14. With its excellent display, tablet-first design, portability, battery life, and solid performance, it is a great pick for anyone who wants a powerful tablet on the go.
The 3K OLED display also makes it a great option for entertainment whenever you want to watch content or even play games. Overall, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 is a great option for a creator-first experience and for anyone who values portability and wants an all-in-one tablet that can replace a conventional laptop and a tablet at home. However, the tablet costs Rs 2,69,990 for 32GB LPDDR5X RAM. It is expensive.

- Lightweight and highly portable
- Strong Snapdragon X2 Elite performance
- Excellent battery life
- Keyboard and ASUS Pen included

- Poor Windows touchscreen experience
- Weaker GPU performance
- Some ARM app compatibility issues
- No headphone jack

'I reduced my running because of urine leaks' – Commonwealth finalist Korir
- Published
Naomi Korir's career on the track reached a high point in August when she finished fifth in the final of the mile at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
But things could have been very different for the Kenyan middle-distance runner.
The 28-year-old was born with fistula, a medical condition in which abnormal openings develop between organs and can lead to uncontrolled leakage of urine or faeces.
While Korir loved athletics as a child, it initially forced her to rethink any plans to be a runner.
"I played most of the sports activities: football, netball, athletics, even rugby," she said.
"But it was difficult because [of] the training, and the urine is flowing continuously. It's bad.
"I reduced my running to shorter distances to reduce the leaking.
"I began doing 100m hurdles."
Despite the challenges, Korir's love of sport also offered a form of escape and belonging.
"I could do it because I loved it," she explained.
"Because most of the people could avoid me, I did a lot of activities just to pass time and not to feel that I'm excluded."
Three surgeries and a second chance
The charity Doctors Without Borders estimates that 500,000 women live with fistula globally.
Some develop a fistula after childbirth while for others, like Korir, it is congenital.
Access to good obstetrics, or to simple surgery, means that the condition has all but disappeared in some countries, but it remains a problem in sub-Saharan Africa, where high quality medical care can be hard to access.
Korir was born with genitourinary tract fistula - an opening between bladder and vagina which caused her urine leakage.
Surgery was required, but her first two operations failed to solve the problem.
In August 2013, a third operation finally brought relief for the then 13-year-old.
The procedure was carried out in her home town Eldoret by the Gynocare Hospital, which specialises in fistula, obstetrics and reproductive health.
"It's a difficult condition to live with every day," Gynocare director Caroline Mabeya told BBC Sport Africa when discussing the stigma and isolation women with the condition suffer.
"They are ostracised in the society. That's the psychological torture that they face with the fistula."
The hospital has treated patients from across East Africa since opening its doors in 2011. Its work extends beyond surgery, with a post-operation programme designed to help women rebuild their confidence.
"We offer free treatment for these women at Gynocare because most of them are very poor," Mabeya explained.
"When they come into the facility, they are crushed, they have low esteem. So, there's a huge amount of effort that is put in to make them at least be strong enough to be reintegrated and get back into the community."
'A champion in sport'
For Korir, successful surgery offered a second chance, both on the track and in the classroom.
As well as allowing her to run properly again, she continued her education through Gynocare's Beyond Fistula programme.
"I have a family in GynoCare, a fistula home," she said.
"That is where I schooled after my surgery until I finished my secondary level."
In 2019, Korir began competing professionally and two years later was part of the Kenyan duo which claimed a silver medal in the 2x2x400m mixed relay alongside her partner Ferguson Rotich at the World Relays in Poland.
A year later she went one better, bagging gold as part of Kenya's 4x400m relay team at the African Championships in Mauritius.
The mile at this year's Commonwealth Games was her first appearance in major global final.
"I'm giving hope to young women maybe who have lost hope," she said of her achievements.
"They need to come back again in living and enjoying life."
Mabeya says Korir's transformation makes her a powerful example to the women currently receiving support at Gynocare.
"She makes them realise that you can actually pull yourself out of these struggles and still make it in life and succeed.
"Naomi actually is one of those patients that inspires us to continue working very hard, because we struggle with this condition and these women. The work is not easy."
As a young girl, Korir sang in church and played the keyboard, convinced that music was a more likely career than athletics.
"But now I'm in different career and I'm so happy," she beamed.
And with the World Championships in Beijing next year and the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, Korir believes there is another chapter to write.
"I know I'm a champion in life, because conquering fistula alone is being a champion.
"Now I'm looking forward to be a champion in sport."

Military aircraft carrying 32 people crashes in southern Nigeria

A military aircraft carrying 25 passengers and seven crew members has crashed in southern Nigeria, triggering a frantic search and rescue operation, according to authorities.
There was no immediate information on casualties.
Nigeria’s Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo said in a statement that the aircraft was on a routine mission to Lagos when it crashed in the Igbokoda area of Ondo state.
The Nigerian Air Force identified the aircraft as an ATR-42. It was not immediately clear to what extent the aircraft was damaged.
“Search and rescue operations, in coordination with relevant authorities and emergency response agencies, are currently ongoing,” air force spokesperson Ehimen Ejodame said.
Locals told The Associated Press that the aircraft crashed near a river and that part of it was sinking in the water.
“We heard something like a thunder strike,” said Akinbulejo Pius, a witness. “The plane cleared some trees. We found some body parts, some clothes and shoes.”
Mr Keyamo said the aircraft first disappeared from radar at around 9 am local time, and that it was found to have crashed close to a naval base.
The Nigerian military has in the past used the ATR-42 for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), alongside for transporting personnel and supplies.
Writing on X, Mr Keyamo said: “I regret to inform the general public that Air Traffic Controllers have informed me of the disappearance of a military aircraft with tail number NGR 931, enroute Lagos from Benin at 0913 hours earlier today. All efforts to raise the aircraft on radio proved abortive.
“Subsequently information however confirmed that the military aircraft has crashed close to the Naval Base in Igbokoda, Ondo State. The wreckage has been located and search and rescue operations are ongoing.
“Preliminary information suggests that there were 25 passengers and 7 crew members on board.

Brazil’s presidential election is going to a run-off after boost for right-wing Bolsonaro. What happens next?
The runoff will determine whether Brazil joins a wider wave of electoral gains by right-wing candidates aligned or whether Mr Lula da Silva will secure another term

On Sunday, 4 October, 2026, Brazilians didn’t just vote against President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. They buried a political project that had been on life support for almost a decade.
That project is the Nova República, the “New Republic”. It was born in the mid-1980s from the debris of a 21-year military dictatorship, and written into the country’s 1988 Constitution. For a generation, Brazilians called it the democratic pact, and it rested on three commitments.
The first was social. The New Republic embraced pluralism and made Brazil’s diversity part of its national identity rather than a problem to be managed.
The second was institutional. In a fragmented multiparty system, no one governs alone, so consensus was the engine of policy. That consensus came from free and fair elections, but also from coalitions that let federal, state and municipal governments carry out a shared agenda, and a working balance among the president, Congress and the Supreme Court.
The third was about policy: keep the economy stable, use social programs to reduce one of the world’s starkest inequalities, and widen popular participation in politics.
For roughly 30 years, the pact held well enough. Its results were uneven, but they were real: hyperinflation tamed, tens of millions of Brazilians lifted out of poverty, and power transferred peacefully at least between the two main parties of that era, the Workers’ Party (Partido dos Trabalhadores, PT) and the Brazilian Social Democratic Party (Partido da Social Democracia Brasileira, PSDB).
The first assault
Many on the left claim that the New Republic started to crumble with former left-wing President Dilma Rousseff’s impeachment in 2016. Her removal was allegedly plotted to preserve the elitist and corrupted structures that the new pact had not fixed.
But it was former president Jair Bolsonaro’s victory in the 2018 election that represented a frontal assault on each of Brazil’s democratic commitments. The now jailed politician presented himself as an outsider despite having spent 28 years in Brazil’s Congress, and put Christian nationalism in place of pluralism ahead in his agenda.
He recast the consensus-building system as elite corruption, and the coalition politics that had kept Brazil governable became, in his telling, the source of its rot. He promised to fix the economy by getting the State out of the way of businesses and individuals, all in the name of freedom.
Bolsonaro, however, delivered little. Once in office, he discovered he had to govern inside the pact he had campaigned against. Congress had to be bargained with, courts had to be obeyed, and governors had their own power bases. Those constraints help explain why so many of his voters felt let down.
It also helps explain why, after losing to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva the 2022 election, he plotted a coup to stay in power. A leader who cannot bend the rules may come to believe he has to break them.
The restoration that wasn’t
After governing Brazil for two terms between 2003 and 2010, Lula returned to power in 2023 promising to save Brazilian democracy. Instead, his third term became the clearest proof that the New Republic could not be saved.
The institutional balance that had sustained the system was gone. Congress, which now controls a large share of the federal budget through earmarks, held the Presidency hostage, while the Supreme Court increasingly filled the vacuum by legislating from the bench.
Lula’s attempts to move his agenda forward stalled again and again. His economic record was respectable, but not transformative: decent growth and low unemployment that never translated into a visible improvement in most people’s lives.
Public security, consistently among voters’ top concerns, went largely unaddressed. In fairness, under Brazil’s division of powers most policing belongs to the states, and the federal government can only do so much.
But voters generally don’t care about the letter (or the spirit) of the Constitution. They want results.
Then there is Lula himself. At 80 years old and four decades in public life, he had become the most recognizable face of the New Republic. That made him a convenient target. Many Brazilians merged their frustration with the political system into frustration with Lula, and for some, into outright hatred.
A swan song
So if Lula’s defeat is confirmed in the runoff to be held 25 October, and the odds of reversing this Sunday’s first-round results are slim, it will be more than a personal loss or a setback for the Workers’ Party, which has governed Brazil for nearly 18 of the last 24 years.
It will be the swan song of a political project that promised to build a new country out of authoritarian ruins and could never fully deliver what it promised: political stability, economic prosperity and social justice.
The frustration that decided this election is the frustration of that unmet promise.
None of this means that the 56 million Brazilians who voted for Flávio Bolsonaro, one of former president’s Jair Bolsonaro sons, reject democracy. Some do. They are nostalgic for a largely imagined past, when the middle class was stronger (and much smaller), when Christian family values prevailed, and when imposing order counted for more than the rule of law.
But the larger lesson of 4 October is different. Millions of Brazilians want a different kind of democracy: less pluralist, built on a different idea of what democracy is for. Above all, they no longer believe the New Republic can answer the challenges of the world they live in.
The old is dying
Italian Marxist philosopher Antonio Gramsci (1891-1937) famously observed that crisis comes when “the old is dying and the new cannot be born.” Brazil now stands at that crossroads.
Unlike his father, Flávio Bolsonaro would take office with a rare alignment of political forces. Sunday’s results suggest his allies will hold close to a quarter of both the Chamber of Deputies, Brazilian Congress’ lower house, and the Senate, a solid base in a Congress where coalitions are rented rather than built. He would also be able to appoint four of the Supreme Court’s eleven justices during his term.
Jair Bolsonaro spent four years fighting the institutions. His son may get to reshape them.
That does not make Flávio the new thing Gramsci was waiting for. He most certainly isn’t. He is a career politician with several corruption charges and the heir to a family brand, more continuity of the last decade’s backlash than a break from it.
On top of that, given Flávio’s desire to become Donald Trump’s preferential ally in South America, Brazil may make significant concessions to the U.S. down the road, giving up on some of the country’s riches, such as oil or rare earth minerals, to secure a privileged place in the new hemispheric order. But one is left to wonder what this place actually means - and recent events in the neighborhood suggest it is not a respectable one.
In any case, Flávio Bolsonaro’s victory upends Brazil’s political landscape. Brazilians who disagree with his platform, whether on the left, in the center, or on the democratic right, can no longer count on the old pact to protect them or to bring them back to power. They will have to learn how to navigate this new game, domestically and internationally, if they want a comeback anytime soon.
The New Republic is over. The question for Brazil, and for everyone who has watched it as a bellwether for democracy in the Global South, is what will replace it, and whether the new rules will finally lead Brazil into the future. If Brazilians do not want this future to look like a dark and distant past, they must understand that the fight is not over.

A purported Dainik Jagran newspaper clipping (here & here) claims that the Rajasthan High Court has given a judgment that provides for six months of imprisonment and a ₹50,000 fine for any candidate who fails to secure at least 100 votes in the Sarpanch elections. Let us verify the authenticity of the claim made in this post.
Claim: A Dainik Jagran newspaper clipping claims the Rajasthan High Court has ordered a six-month jail term and a ₹50,000 fine for Sarpanch candidates securing under 100 votes.
Fact: The viral newspaper clipping is an AI-generated fake image. The Rajasthan High Court has given no such judgment, Dainik Jagran published no such report, and Indian electoral laws contain no provision imposing jail time or fines for low vote counts. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
First, an initial search confirmed that the Rajasthan High Court has not issued any such judgment regarding low vote counts in Panchayat elections. Additionally, we found no news reports published by Dainik Jagran corroborating this matter. Moreover, no such law, Court order, or judicial mandate exists under the Election Commission of India or Indian electoral statutes (such as the Representation of the People Act, 1951) penalising candidates with imprisonment or fines purely for receiving a low vote count. Under current election rules, the only major consequence for a poor electoral performance is the forfeiture of the security deposit, which applies if an unelected candidate fails to secure more than one-sixth of the valid votes polled.
Further, we ran the viral newspaper clipping through the OpenAI content detection tool, which confirmed that the clipping is an AI-generated image created using OpenAI tools. Earlier, we debunked a similarly fabricated clipping that falsely claimed a woman gave birth to puppies in the United States.
To sum it up, the viral newspaper clipping is a fabricated AI-generated image, and there is no legal provision or court order mandating jail time or fines for securing low votes in a Sarpanch election.

On Sunday, President Donald Trump raged at Fox News for not broadcasting his rallies.
It was a surprising turn given that Fox remains the most-watched news outlet in the United States and many of Trump’s most devoted fans still watch it.
“Sad to see that Fox & Friends (Sunday) is not covering our packed house and incredibly enthusiastic (beyond!),” he said. “These Election Rallies were representative of what is really happening with our great Republican Party.”
On one hand, Trump griping about Fox News is not that surprising. He’s clashed with Fox News ever since his first campaign for president when he famously criticized debate moderator Megyn Kelly, saying “you could see there was blood coming out of her eyes, blood coming out of her wherever.” He recently criticized host Shannon Bream for displaying outdated photos of his planned ballroom. And Trump understands something about the id of the Fox viewer more than the executives of the network do.
In the grand scheme of Trump’s attacks on the press, this appears, to borrow a Trumpism, like “small potatoes.” Trump banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House premises and is still trying to stiff-arm their coverage.
But a look at the data shows that Trump is in real trouble, including in the states where he’s barnstorming. And the more Trump becomes unpopular, the more he is likely to lash out at Fox since he feels he can influence it the most.
On Saturday, he visited Ohio. On paper, this should be a bank shot for Trump. He turned it from a perpetual swing state to a solid red state. His endorsement of JD Vance in the 2022 primary paved the way for him to become a senator and his running mate in 2024.
Now? Vance’s replacement in the Senate, Jon Husted, is floundering. A New York Times/Siena College poll released Saturday showed former Sen. Sherrod Brown beating Husted by three points. And the Republican candidate for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, is not doing much better. The same poll shows Democratic Amy Acton beating Ramaswamy by four points in the Buckeye State.
Then there is Texas. This might be where Trump’s hubris could cost him more than anything. In May, he chose to endorse ultra-MAGA Attorney General in the primary runoff against incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn.
But Paxton’s numerous scandals, which led to the Texas state House impeaching him before the state Senate acquitted him, have proven to be an albatross. Paxton’s estranged wife, whom he allegedly cheated on, had to cut an ad this week saying “it’s about getting the whole team across the finish line,” and “that’s why I am voting the Republican ticket on November 3rd.”
And despite pouring millions of dollars into Texas, Democrat James Talarico has a slight lead. If he wins, Talarico would be the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Texas since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988. Even more alarming, polling is now showing that Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who is seeking a fourth term, is now in a competitive race with Democrat Gina Hinojosa.
Even in blood-red Kansas, incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall is in a competitive race.
Trump continues to say this is all a matter of branding, rather than actual anger about his policy on tariffs and the war in Iran, which has only driven prices up.
Furthermore, Trump’s ability to touch on subjects that anger voters has dulled. He’s pushed back on voters’ anger about data centers and AI, fully embracing both and attempting to dub the latter “Super Intelligence.”
But people aren’t buying it. Trump continues to bleed support, and surveys show Democrats are more motivated to turn out than Republicans, as is usually the case in midterm elections with the minority party.
And as time progresses and Trump enters the twilight of his time in politics, expect Fox to be more forward-looking. It will likely have to begin focusing on whatever outrageous comments from Democrats they can amplify while also giving special attention to the 2028 Republican candidates.
Trump may not like it, but the currents of politics are moving away from him. And they are forces stronger than him. Not even Fox can defy them.

A US marine stationed on Japan’s southern island of Okinawa is accused of murdering a Japanese woman and has been arrested on suspicion of murder, police said on Sunday.
The suspect allegedly “killed [a] 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha and stole her wallet” as well as her backpack, local police told news media outlets.
Citing police, NBC News reported that the suspect charged in the case was identified Lance Cpl Devin Jacob Ballard, 20. Anna Yagi was identified as the victim.
Ballard denied the allegations, police said, according to NBC.
Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drunk-driving accidents by US personnel have long sparked protests on Okinawa. The island bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70% of US military facilities in Japan.
US ambassador George Glass posted on social media that he had spoken with Japan’s foreign ministry and Okinawa’s governor, offering “sincere condolences to the victim’s family” and pledging cooperation into the investigation of her death.
The Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said Japan had lodged a protest with US authorities and called the crime “exceptionally brutal and vicious”.
The government has urged the US “to provide maximum cooperation with the investigation, enforce stricter discipline among US military personnel, and take thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of similar crimes,” Takaichi said.
Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.
Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage and asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station where he was arrested, NHK reported.
“We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened,” Yagi’s brother said through local police, according to the Asahi Shimbun daily newspaper. “My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter.”
The US has about 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.
Crimes committed by US personnel in Japan have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.
“Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen,” Japan’s defense minister Shinjiro Koizumi said.
In June 2025, a Japanese court sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton – then 22 – to seven years in prison after being convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
Earlier, in 2017, former US marine and civilian military base worker Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, US forces in Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated American marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.
According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since Okinawa was returned to Japan from the US in 1972 after the second world war.
The number of arrests in a year hit 80 in 2024, the highest in 20 years.

Tamil Nadu is recording around 200 cases of dengue a day. Fresh cases are being reported in places including Chennai and its neighbouring districts and cities such as Coimbatore and Madurai.
Officials of the Directorate of Public Health (DPH) and Preventive Medicine said the caseload remained steady and was not at outbreak proportions. A. Somasundaram, Director of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, said cases had not risen exponentially, with the numbers remaining broadly steady. “We are seeing nearly 200 cases a day. The numbers are not doubling or tripling, which usually happens in an outbreak. Right now, there is a static trend in the number of dengue cases, and we are expecting the cases to decline soon,” he said.
Cases are being reported across cities including the Chennai belt (Tiruvallur and Kancheepuram), Coimbatore, and Madurai. This could partly be due to a “natural bias” with these areas having more hospitals and testing facilities, Dr. Somasundaram said.
“We have specifically instructed staff to increase the number of tests for dengue for better surveillance and patient management. This is so we don’t miss a case, and when samples are tested, we can identify pockets of cases or clusters, which are likely to bring about an outbreak,” he said. There are over 4,500 government and private laboratories in the State, he added.
Surveillance measures to identify Aedes mosquito breeding pools are continuing, but the number of pools detected has started to decline as a result of source reduction measures. The mosquito density is slowly coming down, the official said. About 25,000 Domestic Breeding Checkers (DBC) have been engaged across the State, with 20 persons covering one block.
Dr. Somasundaram said while preventive measures had been intensified, they had been holding daily monitoring meetings with District Health Officers via video conferencing. “We are analysing the case trend, whether increase or decrease or static, and number of laboratory tests conducted. We are also monitoring fever triaging, patient management, and discharge policy. Patients are being categorised as having mild, moderate, or severe symptoms and treated appropriately. Right now, the severity of infections is less. Fogging operations and source reduction measures, along with work taken up by DBCs, are being supervised. We are also looking at creating awareness among the public,” he said.
With October and November being crucial months, he said, there could be intermittent or heavy rain and people should ensure that their household environment is clean. “Avoid storing water unnecessarily. If you have too, keep containers closed properly,” he added.

The era of generative AI has upended technology supply chains, and there is one ironclad rule in 2026: If it has memory or storage, it’s getting more expensive. Even devices with years-old tech inside are still apparently subject to that unwritten rule. Nvidia has just announced that the Shield TV Pro is getting $100 more expensive, effective immediately.
The most recent version of the Shield streaming box debuted in 2019, running Android TV with AI upscaling and hardware decoding for almost any type of media. While it ran an aging Tegra X1+ processor, that was (and still is) fast for a TV media streamer. The device launched at $199.99, with a non-Pro variant at $149.99. The non-Pro Shield has since been discontinued, but the Shield TV Pro lives on at the new $299.99 price.
Nvidia has confirmed that you can blame AI for the higher Shield TV pricing. “Starting October 2, SHIELD Pro will be priced at $299. The cost of components, including memory, has increased substantially across the industry,” a spokesperson told Ars.
When Ars Technica talked to Nvidia’s Andrew Bell earlier this year, he framed the Shield as a passion project, but it looks like passion projects still have to pay the bills at Nvidia. In that interview, Bell explained that Nvidia still actively manufactures the Shield and sells every unit it makes. Without a stockpile of pre-AI hardware to sell, new Shield TV units are subject to the same supply chain constraints as today’s smartphones and computers.
Nvidia isn’t a victim here, though. As a key player in AI hyper scaling, the company is more responsible than most for the sky-high cost of components. It has also become one of the most valuable firms in the world thanks to its market-leading AI accelerators and GPUs. As a consequence, we’re seeing new products launch at higher prices than their predecessors, and many end up getting more expensive during their lifetimes. Game consoles have been particularly affected, with Nintendo, Microsoft, and Sony all bumping the prices of their current-gen hardware. The PS5 Pro, for example, has gone from $699.99 at launch in 2024 to $899.99 today.
Stock of the Shield TV Pro has been slim for the last few months, probably because it became too expensive to manufacture new units with component prices rising so quickly. At $300, it will make sense for Nvidia to churn out more devices. However, this higher price will cause an already niche set-top box to be even less appealing to people who just want to stream Netflix.
Unless you need the Shield’s extensive codec support or Plex server capability, it makes more sense to get a cheaper streamer. The Shield is still out of stock on Nvidia’s store, but it’s available at the new price from Best Buy.

An explosive and newly partially unsealed court filing alleges that the US Department of Homeland Security built up dossiers on ICE observers—including their photos, license plate numbers, and other information—and stored them in a system called the Investigative Case Management database, which was built by Palantir.
Palantir did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
A spokesperson for DHS calls the case “meritless” and says that “the underlying lawsuit is based on the lie that there is a database of ‘domestic terrorists’ run by DHS.”
Plaintiffs allege in the filing, which is heavily based on documents produced by the government and depositions of DHS agents, that agents had a practice of intimidating protesters and observers. They did this, the filing says, by doing drive-bys of the observers’ homes and, in the case of at least one observer, requiring that she be referred to secondary inspection any time she tries to cross the border until at least January 2027.
"The government is treating people who exercise their First Amendment rights and seek to hold it accountable as criminal suspects, and that's what we're asking the court to stop,” says JoAnna Suriani, an attorney at Protect Democracy who is representing ICE observers in the case.
The filing focuses on agents’ conduct during “Operation Catch of the Day,” an immigration enforcement surge in Maine this past January. It is part of a proposed class action brought in federal court in Maine by four observers: Elinor Hilton, Colleen Fagan, Polyxenia Pantos, and Carlyn Williams. It was filed under seal in September, and a redacted version was made public Friday.
In particular, it describes how one DHS agent, referred to as “Agent J.C.” in the filing, used the Investigative Case Management (ICM) database, which the government describes as the case management system the ICE component Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) uses to document its investigations, to flag observers.
According to the filings, J.C. created ICM records on at least six observers; the government puts the number of people at eight. He labeled two people he filmed at a Home Depot parking lot with “Threat to Law Enforcement, Professional Protestor,” according to the filing, and sent photos of them and others to a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer so he could run a facial recognition search on them using an app called Mobile Query.
On January 20, Pantos briefly watched and photographed an arrest in Portland, Maine, standing a few car lengths away beside their spouse's car. Hours later, per the filing, J.C. ran the car's plate and pulled a report on the owner—Williams—from Accurint, a LexisNexis database for law enforcement, which listed her address, phone numbers, and cohabitants. J.C. then allegedly circulated her photo to his team, asking, “Was this the protestor.” Another agent, per the filing, replied that it didn’t match the woman he had dealt with at the scene; J.C. then told colleagues he was "adding them in ICM now."
According to the legal filing, that afternoon, J.C. called Williams on her cell phone, identifying himself only as "the Department of Homeland Security." According to Williams, he told her she "should encourage" her spouse, Pantos, "not to do anything like that in the future because people who are doing things like that might get added to a domestic terrorism watchlist." J.C. testified in a deposition that he warned Williams she would be arrested if she “continue[d] to do this.” Government attorneys asserted in a court filing that he denied referencing a “domestic terrorism watchlist.”
According to documents produced by the government, Williams’ ICM record says that she was the registered owner of a vehicle used to “interrupt ICE arrests” and that her driver’s license photo matched a video of "aggressive woman [who] interject[ed] herself into an arrest." According to a 2016 DHS privacy assessment, ICM automatically shares the subject records agents create with CBP’s TECS system, where they act as "lookout records" for screening travelers at the border.
ICM is the system used by HSI agents to create and track case files. ICE awarded Palantir the contract to build ICM in 2014, and the system is built on the company’s Gotham software, which ICE says was customized specifically for operational needs. In 2022, ICE awarded Palantir a new five-year ICM support contract initially valued at up to about $96 million. In 2025, the agency added nearly $30 million to that contract to develop a new platform called “ImmigrationOS.”
Todd Lyons, the former acting director of ICE, wrote in an April letter to Rep. Maxwell Frost, the Florida Democrat, that ICE “does not maintain any kind of database of U.S. citizens protesting ICE activities.” He also said DHS isn’t keeping a “separate, standalone database” of people it hasn’t arrested or detained.
The government’s motion to dismiss argues that these were isolated incidents and that DHS policy prohibits this conduct. It says J.C. made records on people he believed were “potential threats to law enforcement” and “did not attempt to nominate any individuals to the terrorist watchlist.”
Attorneys for the observers say that DHS’s efforts have had a chilling effect on their First Amendment rights. According to the motion, Pantos stopped all ICE observation work after J.C.’s phone call to Williams, who briefly continued to observe ICE activity and then stopped all together too.
The observers are asking the court to order that Williams’ records be archived, to bar DHS from using the information it collected about the plaintiffs against them, and to prohibit agents in Maine from threatening observers with watchlists or following them to their homes.

The story so far
The groundwater resources of Kerala have been under severe stress due to changes in rainfall pattern following climate change, high population density as well the fact that approximately 62% of the population relies on groundwater from an estimated 6.5 million open wells for their domestic needs. The State’s fragmented wastewater management system and the unscientific construction of septic tanks and pit latrines at homes close to shallow and open wells have resulted in persistent faecal contamination of ground water in the State, which has been documented by several studies.
A 2024 study in the Journal of Environmental Management reported that 7.4% of the State’s population could be making do with poor quality of groundwater and estimated that 0.59 million people in 252 local self government bodies in the State could be continuously exposing themselves to health risks from consuming ground water from wells which may not be chlorinated regularly.
And the latest report on E.coli contamination comes from Pala, where a water quality assessment conducted in flood-affected areas along the Meenachil river detected E. coli bacteria in 67% of the samples, raising concerns over the safety of drinking water sources in and around Pala.
Researchers attributed the spike in bacterial contamination to the recent floods, which may have allowed contaminated surface water to enter water sources.
How is contamination taking place?
It is a dangerous combination of high population density, unplanned urbanisation with hundreds of septic tanks and wells sitting close to each other in small plots and the State’s natural hydrogeological features that allow surface pollutants to reach the water table quickly. In recent years, unpredictable and heavy rainfall has been adding to the State’s woes, as oversaturation of the soil and the overflow of drainage systems can quickly allow pollution and microbial contamination to infiltrate ground water.
Environmental scientists explain that groundwater is drawn mostly from shallow, unconfined aquifers, which are recharged directly by rainfall and surface infiltration. In most areas the local water table might be sitting just below the level of the river bed and it naturally leaks water downwards to recharge the underlying unconfined aquifers. If rivers are polluted, then all groundwater resources in the surrounding area would also be carrying the same pollutant.
What is the extent of groundwater contamination in Keralam?
A community-level GIS study of 449 households in an urban area of Thiruvananthapuram in 2018 had reported that most of the wells were in an intermediate-high contamination risk state, with more than 77% of wells having a septic tank within 7.5 m radius. Coliform contamination was prevalent in 73% of wells, and the groundwater was predominantly acidic with a mean of 5.4, rendering it unfit for drinking.
This picture could be true for the rest of the State also. Because of the State’s unique geography and highly dispersed, continuous rural-urban settlement pattern, just about 5-6% of major urban zones are connected to a centralised pipe-based sewerage network system. The State’s sanitation strategy relies heavily on onsite sanitation systems, with individual household septic tanks and soak pits for sewage disposal.
Unscientific construction of these household sanitation systems has rendered much of the groundwater resources unsafe for human consumption, unless properly treated.
What are the health impacts?
Safe drinking water is one of the crucial social determinants of health. It is thus unfortunate that a State which has made enviable strides in developing its public health sector has paid little attention to ensuring that people have access to safe drinking water. While people in urban areas have to a large extent, access to treated water supply, in many rural areas of the State serviced by local small water supply schemes, water distribution lines often run close to sewerage lines and even small breaks in the pipelines can lead to the contamination of drinking water
Recurrent outbreaks of water-borne diseases like Hepatitis A, Shigellosis and norovirus outbreaks have been the bane of the State in recent years, especially in the northern districts of the State, indicating the scale and impact of groundwater contamination. Hepatitis A in particular has been taking a heavy toll on the State since the last three years, with significant mortality and in many instances, leaving people with severe morbidities
Epidemiological studies conducted by the ICMR and Health department into amoebic meningoencephalitis, which has emerged as a significant public health problem in Keralam in recent times, has traced the infection to the use of non-chlorinated well water which has high concentration of E.coli, in which free-living amoeba thrive
What is the sewerage infrastructure status?
To modernise sewerage infrastructure, the State is executing projects under the AMRUT 2.0 Mission, a Central initiative aimed at ensuring universal access to safe water and reliable sewerage connections across urban areas. The CAG’s 2025 report stated that at the closure of the AMRUT Mission (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation), Kerala’s overall achievement was just 11.25% and only 0.13% households got sewerage connections.
Keralam’s geography, population density, lack of vast tracts of uninhabited land means that many proposed treatment plants end up being close to residential areas, which triggered huge public protests. Such protests led to the cancellation of multiple approved septage treatment plant projects in many parts of the State. There are also reports about the State’s financial crunch affecting project payments leading to delays in implementation

The Tony Awards Administration Committee has announced its Nominating Committee for the 2026-27 Broadway season, with former Washington Post chief theater critic Peter Marks and playwrights José Rivera and Migdalia Cruz among the new members.
Each Broadway season, the Nominating Committee attends all eligible productions and convenes to vote on that year’s Tony Award nominees. This year’s committee consists of 65 members who will serve staggered three-year terms.
New additions to the committee include Bonnie Becker, Keith Bunin, Bruce Coughlin, Migdalia Cruz, Scott Farthing, Wendall Harrington, Daniel K. Isaac, Mia Katigbak, Joyce Ketay, Michael Kooman, William Ivey Long, Khady Kamara Núñez, José Rivera, Linda Shelton, Rona Siddiqui, Pearl Sun, Sanaz Toossi, Allyson Tucker and Sam Willmott.
Popular on Variety
Presented by the Broadway League and the American Theatre Wing, the Tony Awards are the highest honors in live theater. The upcoming Broadway season will feature productions including “Paddington: The Musical,” Dolly Parton’s “Dolly,” Lin-Manuel Miranda’s “Warriors” and Jamie Lloyd’s “Evita,” starring Rachel Zegler.
At last season’s Tonys, “Schmigadoon,” a comedy about a couple who become trapped in a magical town, won best musical. “Liberation,” an exploration of feminism and social change, won best play. Arthur Miller’s “Death of a Salesman” won best revival of a play, while “Ragtime” won best revival of a musical. Acting honors went to John Lithgow (“Giant”), Lesley Manville (“Oedipus”), Joshua Henry (“Ragtime”), Caissie Levy (“Ragtime”), Laurie Metcalf (“Death of a Salesman”) among others.

Daniil Medvedev defaulted for hitting spectator with ball as Novak Djokovic reaches another China Open final
Six-time champion Novak Djokovic moves to 33-0 at Beijing tournament after Daniil Medvedev defaulted for hitting spectator around left eye in semi-final; Medvedev to lose all points and prize money; Djokovic, who fended off 16 of the 18 break points he faced, plays Alex De Minaur in final
Monday 5 October 2026 15:30, UK
Daniil Medvedev was defaulted for hitting a spectator with a ball as Novak Djokovic took his impeccable record at the China Open to 33-0 and moved one win away from a first title of 2026.
Medvedev accidentally struck the fan while trailing 7-5 5-3 and three points from defeat in Monday's punishing semi-final in Beijing, during which Djokovic saved 16 of the 18 break points he faced.
Medvedev will now lose all points and prize money eared from the event.
