Djokovic, 39, won the China Open six times in seven years between 2009 and 2015 but had not returned prior to this campaign.
The Serb, who secured a come-from-behind quarter-final victory over world No 2 Alexander Zverev on Sunday, will meet Alex De Minaur in Tuesday's final as he looks to clinch a 102nd career title and first since the Hellenic Championship little under a year ago.
Speaking on court afterwards, Djokovic, defaulted at the 2020 US Open for hitting a line judge with a ball, said: "It is a bit of a shock, to be honest. I am sorry for the person.
"I didn't see what happened and I hope the person is not badly injured. I also feel sorry for Daniil as I know exactly how it feels to be disqualified in a big match.
"I'm sure he didn't want to do this intentionally."
Djokovic reached the Australian Open final in January, losing to Carlos Alcaraz in four sets, but has struggled for fitness and form since and dropped out of the world's top 10, although this run in Beijing has returned him to that elite level.
The 24-time Grand Slam champion, who has played just eight tournaments this year, revealed an ongoing medical condition that has led to fatigue and vomiting on court, with the issue exacerbated in hot and humid conditions.
Djokovic added: "It was a gruelling battle that I definitely didn't want to take to a third set. It was looking like that. It is always a big battle with Daniil, so hard to play him when he is feeling the ball in slower conditions with his big serve.
"I always believe in myself and felt I played really well in training bit obviously it is different in an official match.
"My draw wasn't favourable, very tough matches from the beginning, but it makes the run the final sweeter. Something about Beijing keeps me going."
In the women's event, Britain's Sonay Kartal saw her WTA Tour comeback end in the third round with a 6-4 6-1 loss to Alina Charaeva - the player who dumped out world No 1 Elena Rybakina at the weekend.
The Beijing event was Kartal's first WTA tournament since March after a stress fracture of the back and she picked up wins over Andrea Lazaro Garcia and Wang Xinyu before falling to Armenia's Charaeva.
Iga Swiatek, reached the fourth round after rallying from a set and 5-2 down to beat Donna Vekic 4-7 6-7 (7-0) 6-2.

It's the perfect time to be cooking asparagus.
Blossoms and hay fever concerns aside, spring is really about asparagus season. A time for asparagus lovers to rejoice and an annual opportunity for sceptics to get onside.
From one-pot pasta to a crunchy green salad, these four recipes will help you embrace those delicious green spears while they are affordable.
One-pot pasta with asparagus, tuna, lemon and capers
With a cooking time of just 15 minutes and minimal prep, this one-pot pasta recipe from Heidi Sze combines about two bunches of asparagus and a lot of staple ingredients.
Lemon and capers will help brighten the dish and either tinned or cooked salmon fillet could be substituted for the tuna, she says.
Spring onion, corn and asparagus galette
Hetty Lui McKinnon's galette recipe is an unfussy and adaptable vehicle for your favourite spring vegetables.
The corn could be replaced with fresh peas, podded broad beans, green beans, thinly shaved fennel, broccoli, or crunchy sugar snap or snow peas, Hetty says.
And it can be enjoyed either warm or at room temperature, making any leftovers a potentially perfect work lunch candidate.
Crunchy green salad with sauce gribiche
Another recipe from Hetty Lui McKinnon, who says this salad is "high on texture and assertive with spring vibes".
If you're not familiar with sauce gribiche, it brings together vinegar, cornichons, capers, mustard and chopped hard-boiled eggs.
"The iconic French sauce is part chunky vinaigrette, part punchy mayonnaise," according to Hetty.
Quiche with goats' cheese, asparagus and a hint of lemon
This quiche recipe from Thalia Ho is simple to assemble and includes beginner-friendly pastry.
Asparagus, lemon and goats' cheese is a tried and tested flavour combination, but Thalia says "you can play around with the filling, depending on taste, craving and what's available".

Relative humidity is a simple concept as weather phenomena go – but it has significant, far-reaching consequences for how we must take care of ourselves on a hot or wet day.
Letting the wind flow freely is the secret to cooling our cities
Humidity is the amount of moisture in the air around us, and there are three ways to track it. The most common of them is absolute humidity: the mass of water vapour in a given volume of the air and water vapour mixture, expressed as kg/m3. The second is specific humidity, equal to the mass of the moisture divided by the mass of air. It is expressed as a dimensionless number (but sometimes also as grams per kilogram, among other similar units.)
The third way is relative humidity: it is important because it factors in the amount of vapour that air can hold at different temperatures. Determining its value is a bit more complicated: it is the vapour density of the air divided by the saturation vapour density at the dry-bulb temperature.
Why does relative humidity matter?
On a hot day, our body uses sweat to cool itself. Sweat is released via our skin to the surface. There, the liquid evaporates. When water changes phase from liquid to vapour, it absorbs heat from the surface on which it lies. So when sweat evaporates, it absorbs heat from the skin, cooling it.
The higher the relative humidity of air, the more it is filled with moisture. When air already contains a lot of moisture, it won’t easily accept more. This means that the sweat on your skin can’t evaporate. At the same time, the body keeps sweating because it is still expecting to cool itself.
As a result, if the relative humidity is high, you can sweat on a hot day even when you are sitting still – while your body also keeps accumulating heat. This can quickly become dangerous.
A relative humidity of 30-60% is generally considered to be comfortable. Environments that have lower levels than this typically use humidifiers to increase the humidity. When the level is higher, a fan will help move the air around you and help sweat evaporate better.
In both cases, drinking water is important.
What does relative humidity imply physically?
Warmer air can hold more moisture than cooler air. So at the same absolute humidity, the relative humidity of warmer air will be lower than that of cooler air. It is like saying two vessels can hold the same amount of water – just that the bigger vessel will be less full than the smaller vessel.
This is why, for example, while Chennai had an absolute humidity of 70% at 2.30 pm on April 23, its relative humidity was lower, around 60%, because it had an ambient temperature of 32 C.
The change in the capacity for moisture as the air warms is also non-linear, meaning it doesn’t increase by the same amount as the air warms. For example, the difference as it warms over 20º C from -20º C to 0º C is small, but there is an enormous improvement in its vapour-carrying capacity as it warms over 20º C from 30º C to 50º C.
How do you measure relative humidity?
There are a few ways to measure relative humidity. One is to conduct a simple experiment with household items; another is to use maths; a third is to use an app or device.
Experiment
For the experiment, you need two mercury thermometers, some cotton, rubber bands, and access to cold water.
First, make sure both thermometers show the same reading, say, under a fan. Next, soak some cotton in cold water and wrap it around the bulb of one of the thermometers with a rubber band. Hold this thermometer under the fan, such that water from the cotton evaporates, and record the thermometer reading after five minutes. Hold up the other thermometer in the air and record its reading after five minutes. You will thus have the wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperatures, respectively.
Next, subtract the wet-bulb temperature from the dry-bulb temperature to get the temperature difference. Finally, use the relative humidity chart (see below) to get the relative humidity value. For example, if the difference was 6 C and the dry-bulb temperature was 28 C, the relative humidity would have been 59%.
A psychrometer is a device that has two such thermometers plus a chart to get the final reading. Modern, electronic psychrometers can calculate the relative humidity directly.
For a rough sense, the lower the wet-bulb temperature, the drier the air is, and the less relatively humid it is.
Mathematics
There are two mathematical ways (among others) to estimate the relative humidity, one simpler and one a bit more involved.
The first way is to divide the actual vapour pressure by the saturated vapour pressure. The vapour pressure is the amount of moisture that air contains. The ‘saturated’ value is the maximum possible amount. The formula (below) requires the dew point (Td), which you can obtain from a weather website.
RH = (e/es)*100
e = 6.11 x 10((7.5 x Td)/(237.3 + Td))
For es, use the same formula but replace Td with T, the actual temperature.
The second way is to calculate relative humidity starting from the specific humidity, pressure and temperature, using the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.
App
If you prefer software: Search for “hygrometer” in your phone’s app store to locate some options. (A hygrometer is an instrument that measures humidity.) Note that the app will only work if your phone has a sensor that can sense humidity.
If you like hardware, psychrometers and devices called hygrometers are available in physical as well as online stores.
Why does the wet-bulb temperature matter?
This said, a more direct way to understand the implications of the relative humidity for your wellbeing is in the form of the wet-bulb temperature (a.k.a. the adiabatic saturation temperature). It is the lowest temperature a surface – like your skin – can reach when water evaporates from it. The wet-bulb temperature is equal to the dry-bulb temperature when the relative humidity is 100%.
A wet-bulb temperature in an environment of 32-35º C or higher can be quickly lethal, even if you are not doing any physical activity or are in the shade. (At least one study has shown that even a wet-bulb temperature of more than 29º C can be dangerous.)
The climate crisis is rendering heatwaves more common, more frequent, more spread out, and more potent over the Indian subcontinent. As a study published in May 2022 put it:
“Whether today’s most impactful heatwaves could have occurred in a pre-industrial climate, traditionally a central focus of attribution research, is fast becoming an obsolete question. The next frontier for attribution science is to inform adaptation decision-making in the face of unprecedented future heat.”
One way to adapt is to keep an eye on the relative humidity, drink lots of water, and cool yourself.

- The higher the relative humidity of air, the more it is filled with moisture. When air already contains a lot of moisture, it won’t easily accept more.

Edtech major PhysicsWallah’s wholly owned subsidiary FinZ Finance has agreed to sell a ₹95.79 Cr loan portfolio to Auxilo Finserve, taking forward the company’s retreat from direct student lending announced four months ago. FinZ signed the deed of assignment on Saturday (October 3), with the transition of the loans and associated borrowers expected to conclude within 60 days, PhysicsWallah said in an exchange filing yesterday. The portfolio represents a substantial portion of FinZ’s loan book. The filing also pegged the consideration for the transaction at ₹95.79 Cr. “As the principal business activity of FinZ Finance is lending, the proposed transaction constitutes a substantial reduction in its lending operations and is expected to result in partial/piecemeal closure of its lending operations,” the company said. PhysicsWallah said the sale forms part of a broader strategic realignment to optimise capital allocation and focus on its core business. Lending would instead be facilitated through established, regulated third-party NBFCs to reduce balance sheet exposure and credit risks. Founded in 2017, Mumbai-based Auxilo Finserve is an RBI-registered NBFC that provides education loans and financing to students and other stakeholders in the education sector. Unwinding The Lending Push The transaction follows PhysicsWallah’s decision in June to reverse its direct student lending strategy, shortly after approving a ₹120 Cr capital infusion into FinZ Finance in May. The proposed investment put pressure on the company’s shares and raised concerns about its capital allocation priorities. Announcing the reversal, cofounder Prateek Maheshwari said feedback from partners indicated that the company should focus on its education business and leave lending to NBFCs with established underwriting capabilities. Under the revised model, the edtech company would operate as a technology platform connecting students with lending partners, with financing tailored to their learning lifecycle and academic progress. It said this would improve affordability and accessibility while making financing more scalable and better integrated into its student ecosystem. At the time, PhysicsWallah said FinZ’s future strategic direction would be decided subsequently, subject to board and regulatory approvals. FinZ commenced business operations in February 2026, according to the latest filing. It reported negligible operating revenue and ₹1.35 Cr in other income in FY26, taking its total income to ₹1.35 Cr, or 0.04% of PhysicsWallah’s total income. Its net worth stood at ₹60.3 Cr as of March 31, representing 1.18% of PhysicsWallah’s net worth. As Inc42 previously reported, PhysicsWallah’s lending push raised questions about the potential conflict between driving student enrolments and maintaining lending discipline when the same group controls both education and financing. The concerns also reflected the sector’s experience with BYJU’S, whose use of third-party loans to finance courses drew allegations of mis-selling and coercive recovery practices. Meanwhile, PhysicsWallah’s operating revenue rose 24.4% to ₹1,054 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹847.1 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Its net loss narrowed 30.5% to ₹88.3 Cr from ₹127 Cr in Q1 FY26. However, the loss widened 27.8% from ₹69.1 Cr in the preceding quarter. Shares of PhysicsWallah were trading 6.12% higher at ₹127.50 on the BSE at 13:42 IST.

Amid increasing state-sanctioned censorship of digital content across platforms like Meta and X, activists, journalists, cartoonists, artists, opposition politicians and others critical of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government and its policies have faced sweeping content restrictions and takedowns in the last few months. The latest to face such censorship are those raising concerns over the establishment of large-scale data centres in Visakhapatnam.
The port city in Andhra Pradesh is witnessing a massive digital infrastructure push, with investments of up to ₹1.25 lakh crore planned over five years (2026–30) and more than 2,000 acres of land earmarked for data centre projects. In October last year, Google and Adani formally announced an AI hub project in Visakhapatnam. By December 2025, 308 acres at Tarluvada, 120 acres at Adavivaram and 160 acres at Rambilli had been identified for the project. In January this year, reports indicated a much larger expansion involving Google, Sify, Reliance and CtrlS.
In April, the state government and Google laid the foundation stone for the Google Cloud India AI Hub at Tarluvada village. The facility, spread across 266.6 acres, is expected to draw 1 GW of power and is reportedly Google’s largest data centre outside the United States.
The projects are expected to make Visakhapatnam a major eastern data and subsea-cable hub, providing direct routes for Indian data to the US, South Africa, Singapore and Australia. Officials say this could reduce reliance on existing routes through Chennai, Kochi and the Red Sea, while shifting high-value technology activity from expensive metros to other cities.
But local influencers and journalists have raised concerns about the environmental and ecological impact of this rapid expansion of data centre infrastructure in Visakhapatnam and beyond.
ALSO READ: Government orders trigger sweeping Instagram censorship days after CJP protest
Why the Data Centres are being Opposed
The Stop Dirty Data Centre campaign, led by over 60 individuals, formed to “oppose the setting up of 6.5 GW of AI data centres”, lists over 10 proposed data centres spanning across over 2,500 acres of land in Visakhapatnam. Besides the Tarluvada facility, the list mentions two other major Google-Adani Hyperscale data centers: At Rambilli village consuming 1 GW of power across 174.8 acres, and at Adavivaram-Mudasarlova consuming 512 MW of power across 165.40 acres of land. All three are currently under-construction.
It is important to note that Adavivaram-Mudasarlova is around 120 metres from the Mudasarlova reservoir — a critical drinking water source for the city; it also lies near the Kailasagiri-Kambalakonda forest landscape. The Tarluvada site is located 1.53 km from the Kambalakonda Wildlife Sanctuary and about 450 metres from its notified Eco-Sensitive Zone (ESZ) while the Rambilli site lies on the Anakapalli coast and is surrounded by forests.
As most of these sites lie on coastal regions, close to wildlife sanctuaries, forest areas and ESZs, opponents of this expansion project have flagged the disproportionate energy and land usage, large-scale hill cutting, deforestation, and further water depletion in an already water-scarce zone — Visakhapatnam’s water demand already exceeds supply by around 70 million litres per day. They also cite the massive impact on climate, biodiversity, wildlife sanctuaries, coastal ecosystems, and residential areas as serious detrimental effects.
“If fully built, the proposed AI data centers capacity could consume as much as the entire electricity currently used by the state of Andhra Pradesh,” states the campaign website. “Vizag is already severely water stressed and cooling these data centers could take up almost half of city’s supply based on estimates; the proposed land allocation is roughly equivalent to more than 700 cricket grounds, and is present in eco-sensitive regions; hyperscale AI facilities can significantly increase regional greenhouse gas emissions through backup Diesel Generator (DG) sets, solid waste, and more,” it adds.
Critics also highlighted the lack of transparency and public awareness around the setting up of these data centres, demanding that these projects be undertaken in consultation with locals and not unilaterally by the state and corporations. “In a brazen act of environmental lawlessness, forest land at the site [for the Adavivaram-Mudasarlova data centre] was cleared by the project proponent over several months even before environmental clearance was obtained,” alleges a petition initiated by the campaigners.
Citizen Movement Flagging Environmental Concerns Blocked
Against this backdrop, on September 19, the Instagram account of the Stop Vizag Data Centre campaign was banned in India under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000.
One of the founders, Deeksha Vanguru, told Alt News that they did not receive any prior notification. While the account was restored on September 27, nine of their posts critical of the data centre expansion, which were restricted over the last two months, remain unavailable in India.
“Our page was apparently blocked due to a local government request, we appealed to Meta and it was restored due to that request being either expired or reversed. However, our reach has been affected and posts are getting shadowbanned. We had to open a backup account in the meanwhile because we did not want to stop our fight. We are still fighting for the restoration of our nine posts,” Vanguru said.
“We started this as a citizen group in July this year. Most of us are born and brought up in Visakhapatnam and we couldn’t sit and watch the destruction of our home. We wanted to ensure that voices of the farmers, fishermen, villagers, and common citizens are heard. Initially, there was a small-scale mobilisation of citizens, but it needed more youth anger, therefore we turned the campaign into a social media project,” she added.
ALSO READ: Content creators decry Instagram censorship, call restrictions a ‘digital emergency’
“A big concern around AI data centres globally is the consumption of fresh water, and India is already going into a phase of water scarcity. The 10 data centres together are going to consume 200 MLD of water, which is 50% of the city’s daily water supply. The DGs will require constant air conditioning because they claim to be using advanced air cooling, thus the energy strain on the grid will be extremely high. Due to the constant running of generators and ACs, there could be overheating. The whole thing is going to be concrete, which will increase the land surface temperature and reduce night-time cooling. The average night-time temperature in Visakhapatnam has alreadt gone from 23-24 degrees to around 28 degrees,” she said.
Vanguru alleged there was no transparency while these data centres were being set up.
“The government hasn’t held any public consultation with either the farmers or the people of Vizag living close to these sites. In fact, environmental clearances for a 600-acre project, now broken up to escape scrutiny, was given within nine days. On April 9, the environmental clearance request was filed and it was received on April 18. There was no Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) because these projects haven’t been categorised as Category A projects (considered to have greater potential environmental impacts and are appraised by the Union environment ministry and require an EIA) but as Category B2 projects, which means buildings and construction. The way the government has gone about this is as if they’re building malls,” she said.
Further, Vanguru claimed that these data centres had nearly nothing to offer to the locals, even in terms of job creation, which she said was one of the upsides of an industrial construction. “When we checked the environmental clearances, the number of permanent jobs being created was only 1,725. The rest are all construction jobs and temporary jobs. These temporary and construction jobs are being positioned as skilled jobs, but in India, the government definition of skilled means blue-collar jobs. So it keeps people in the same worker or employee cycle and doesn’t really help uplift people from poverty,” she added.
Original Reportage on Dalit Displacement Blocked
After the Tarluvada data centre’s construction began, independent journalists Shamsheer Yousaf and Monica Jha began reporting the ground realities of the construction in early January, as part of the Dirty Data project undertaken by the Environmental Reporting Collective (ERC).
A 2-minute long Instagram reel posted by ERC in collaboration with Yousaf, which features interviews of Dalit farmers in the village who are faced with imminent displacement, was blocked in India on May 22 under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act with no prior notice. In the reel, which garnered 2.6 million views and 46,000 shares, several farmers say that they were granted the land over 50 years ago by the Congress government and have since cleared forests to build homes and farms, which is their only form of subsistence — all under threat as the same land has been allocated to the Google-Adani data centre.
View this post on Instagram
The reel formed part of a 5-minute-long video published on Dirty Data’s website alongside the report, ‘As data centers arrive, India’s poorest face displacement, health risks’ by Yousaf and Jha. Yousaf wrote to the Union ministry of electronics & information technology (MeitY), seeking the blocking order, reasons for the action, restoration of the reel and a personal hearing in order to appeal or respond. He also wrote to Meta’s grievance officer in India.
ALSO READ: Meta restricts posts by Indian Youth Congress, AAP, Opposition leader
Upon not receiving any response from either authorities, on June 30, Yousaf and Jha moved the Delhi high court with a writ petition. A month later on July 23, the petitioners were given access to the blocking order which revealed the authority behind the restriction as the director general of police (DGP), CID, Andhra Pradesh.
‘Procedural Lapses, Unconstitutional Takedown’
In a report, the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), whose lawyers are representing the petitioners, highlighted certain procedural lapses in the blocking order and claimed that the takedown was “unconstitutional”. The order names one Mr. Vemireddy Prabhakar Reddy, alleging that the video “spread misinformation” against him. However, this individual does not feature anywhere in the reel or any of the journalists’ reportage on the data centre issue; he is also not known to either of them.
IFF had then sent a legal notice to the principal secretary, home department and the DGP-CID, Andhra Pradesh, flagging this discrepancy and violation of the provision of the IT Rules, 2021. “…there have been several procedural lapses which violated Rule 14 of the IT Rules, 2021..the Petitioners were not served with any notice…never afforded an opportunity to submit a response/defend themselves…provided with a copy of the blocking order…[the takedown] directly affected [the petitioners] right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution,” the report read.
On September 10, the reel was restored. Yousaf found out through a notification this time, that the restriction was lifted as the “local legal requirement or government request that has now expired or been reversed” — similar to Vanguru’s case.
Local Influencers, HRF Silenced
In the same vein, several local influencers reported that their reels critical of the data centres were being arbitrarily taken down. Malla Gnanesh, who runs the page @vizag_blogger, told News Meter, that a reel he posted on May 28 titled ‘Vizag Welcoming Google Data Centre — At What Cost?’ was restricted in India on May 31. In the reel, Gnanesh spoke about the massive loss of green cover due to the construction of the data centre at the Adavivaram-Mudasarlova region.
Another account, @vizagmowa, also posted a reel on the negative environmental impact of the same data centre such as massive deforestation and water depletion due to its proximity to the Mudasarlova reservoir. This reel was withheld in India on May 30 with the same Section 79(3)(b) notification. Both reels remain restricted till date.
Human Rights Forum on June 1 published a statement condemning the rampant restrictions. Four of HRF’s own Instagram posts were blocked in India on May 31 and June 25, again under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act.
Speaking to Alt News, Vijayawada state coordinator of HRF, Rohith Gutta, stated: “We have moved the Andhra Pradesh high court with a writ petition against the unlawful restriction on September 28, demanding the blocking order, the reason for the action and the immediate restoration of our posts,” he said.
ALSO READ: Instagram censorship puzzle: Alt News post survives only after ‘Burhan Wani’ is removed
He mentioned that all four posts were critical of the date centre expansion. The two posts blocked on May 31 publicised an online petition seeking transparency and accountability regarding the proposed data centre projects; demanded an immediate stoppage of all ongoing site activities at the proposed sites in Adavivaram and Mudasarlova villages of Visakhapatnam Rural mandal.
The next two blocked on June 25 showed a protest in the city against the construction of all three data centres; questioned how the Adavivaram data centre received environmental clearance despite being located within an ESZ, close to the Mudasarlova reservoir. One of the these posts directly asked: “Should a Resource-Guzzling, Intensely Polluting Data Center be Located near a Reservoir? On its Catchment?”
“The restrictions imposed on HRF content by Instagram do not appear to be isolated incidents but form part of a broader pattern,” the Forum wrote while highlighting the restrictions imposed on Yousaf and Jha’s work with the ERC. The Forum also put out another statement condemning the restriction of the Stop Vizag Data Centers account.
Speaking about the ordeal, Rohith told Alt News, “The restrictions have not deterred us from speaking up against the data centres, however, it is a painful experience. We received no prior notification all four times and when we searched for the reason, it was only a vague message repeated word for word four times. It feels like you are legally violated because your work is banned without explanation. Now, blocking of posts is akin to being arrested digitally. We are living through times of ‘social media arrest’ and they [the authorities] have blocked all means to fight it.”
Alt News has reached out to Meta’s grievance officer in India and Kumar Vishwajeet, the principal secretary, home, Andhra Pradesh government. This article will be updated if and when we receive a response.
It is worth noting that the opposition to the projects has also spilled onto the streets, with residents, activists and environmental groups staging protests in Visakhapatnam over concerns around water consumption, deforestation, displacement and the environmental impact of the projects.

Inside The Dalal Street Startup Ride Indian startups had gained a reputation for being “loss making” by prioritising growth at all costs and market share over immediate profitability. The trend of putting scale ahead of the bottom line was at its peak amid the funding boom of 2020-22. While prioritising growth is not wrong for startups, especially at early stages, the start of funding winter in 2022 gave a reality check to the Indian startup ecosystem. Subsequently, startups started pushing for profitability. Giving further wings to the aggressive profitability push was the ambition to list on the exchanges. While new-age tech companies look to turn profitable before filing their draft IPO papers, those that cross the line manage to stay in the green, data shows. About 60 of the 73 new-age tech companies are currently profitable. In terms of profits, Groww now leads the pack of new-age tech companies, posting a net profit of ₹2,083 Cr in FY26. Prominent internet companies Paytm and Eternal trail Groww in terms of profitability, raking in profits of ₹553 Cr and ₹366 Cr in FY26, respectively. It is pertinent to mention that these companies have been listed on the bourses for years now, with Info Edge making its public market debut in 2006. While these companies trace their origin back to the 90s, a large majority of the new-age tech stocks under Inc42's purview are about a decade old. From a broad perspective, Inc42 data reflects that the median time taken for a startup to get listed on the bourses is 11 years. While listing for 18-year-old ixigo and 19-year-old Fino Payments Bank came relatively much later, ArisInfra's IPO materialised within four years of its operations. Meanwhile, the new-age tech companies that have made their public market debuts this year generally turned profitable right before their public market debuts. For instance, eyewear major Lenskart reported a net profit of around ₹297 Cr , a significant turnaround from a ₹10 Cr loss in FY24. The company maintained profitability in FY26, raking in a PAT of ₹494 Cr in the fiscal. Urban Company also reported its first consolidated net profit of approximately ₹240 Cr for FY25, it returned to the red in FY26. For the full year FY26, the company reported a net loss of ₹234.8 Cr against a net profit of ₹239.8 Cr in previous year despite seeing a revenue growth of 36% YoY to ₹1,555.5 Cr Sectors Driving India’s Startup IPO Boom The startup sectors producing the most number of listed companies is proportional to the private funding trends witnessed in the Indian startup ecosystem. The three most funded sectors, fintech, ecommerce and enterprise tech, also house the highest number listed startups. The dominance of the fintech and ecommerce sectors on the bourses is expected to continue as the likes of PhonePe, Zepto and OYO would soon be making their public market debuts. Delhi NCR Home To Highest Number Of Listed Startups While Bengaluru continues to be the startup capital of India, Delhi and its neighbouring cities Gurugram and Noida account for the most number of listed new-age tech companies. Overall, the Delhi NCR region is home to 25 listed new-age tech companies, ahead of Bengaluru's sixteen and Mumbai's thirteen. While fifteen companies, including Eternal, Delhivery, and Lenskart, call Gurugram their home, Awfis, EaseMyTrip, MapmyIndia and E2E Networks are from Delhi. Noida on the other hand is home to six listed new-age tech companies, including Paytm and IndiQube. Delhi NCR contributes $112.2 Bn in the cumulative $178 Bn market cap of new-age tech companies. How did retro consoles handle graphics before modern GPUs?
Graphics chips could draw but not compute, until the Xbox arrived.
Console graphics came from bespoke, fixed-function chips for more than two decades, until the original Xbox burst onto the scene in 2001 with a PC GPU inside. Those of us who played on early consoles like the NES will have come across some familiar quirks with those fixed-function chips: When too many Goombas lined up on the same row in Super Mario Bros., for example, some of them would start to flicker. That's the NES's graphics chip hitting its hard limit of eight sprites per scanline; the chip drops anything past eight, and the game alternates which ones.
In the NES, it was the Ricoh 2C02 Picture Processing Unit that rendered game graphics. A pretty rudimentary chip, it couldn't run any code. Instead, it took tile artwork from the cartridge and a couple of lookup tables from memory and turned them into a TV signal, one scanline at a time. That arrangement — a dedicated picture generator fed by the CPU — is how most consoles rendered their graphics from the late 1970s into the 2000s.
When Microsoft's first Xbox came out in November 2001, it didn't look much like any console before it. Instead, it was built around an Intel Pentium III and a graphics chip NVIDIA made specially for it, based on the GeForce 3. The GeForce 3 had only been announced that February, and it was the first GPU that let developers program their own pixel and vertex shaders.
Sprites and scanlines
The NES' Ricoh 2C02 worked from about 10kB of memory. That's broken down into roughly 8kB of tile shapes stored on the cartridge and 2kB of RAM in the console holding a background map or two. Separate small memories inside the chip tracked things like the position, shape and orientation of up to 64 sprites. Its output was 256x240 pixels, built from 8x8 tiles.
As the CRT TV's electron beam swept across each line of the screen, the 2C02 worked out which 8x8 tile belonged at each spot. It then cross-referenced this with which sprites were sat on that line and decided which pixel to show. This took place in step with the beam, so the CPU couldn't safely rewrite the picture while it was being drawn.
Unlike the NES, the earlier Atari 2600 made the CPU also handle graphics. Because its Television Interface Adaptor had no frame buffer, the processor had to feed new values to the chip for every scanline drawn by the beam. Just five years earlier in 1972, the Magnavox Odyssey had no processor or memory, period, drawing its dots and lines with discrete diode-transistor logic. All of these machines were designed around a CRT, which is partly why retro games look better on old CRT TVs.
The PlayStation 2's custom silicon shared the load
Sony showed off the PS2's chips in March 1999. The CPU was the Emotion Engine, a 128-bit design Sony built with Toshiba, and graphics went to a separate chip called the Graphics Synthesizer. In the final consoles, the two ran at about 295 MHz and 147 MHz.
The Graphics Synthesizer didn't do any geometry work, though. By the time a triangle reached it, it had already been placed within the frame, and all the chip had to do was fill it in with color and texture. The geometry work happened back on the Emotion Engine, in two vector units. The CPU could give VU0 odd jobs, while VU1 mostly ran the 3D transforms that turned a game's models into on-screen triangles. Sony and Toshiba's engineers said a single vector unit could manage 85 million of those transforms a second. While no two consoles were the same, many early 3D consoles similarly shared the graphical load across multiple chips.
Interestingly, Sony had used the term GPU for the 1994 PlayStation's Toshiba-designed graphics chip. That's five years before NVIDIA marketed the GeForce 256 as the world's first GPU. But the working definition of a modern GPU, a chip that runs small programs written by the game, only came with GeForce 3 in early 2001.
The original Xbox and everything after
NVIDIA and Microsoft signed their Xbox deal in March 2000, and five days later, Bill Gates took to the stage and announced the console. It would use an Intel Pentium III-class processor, a custom NVIDIA graphics processor, 64MB of memory shared by both and an 8GB hard drive. The finished box was unveiled at CES 2001 and then went on sale that November.
But consoles didn't make the switch to PC-style hardware all at once. The Nintendo GameCube launched the same month with a PowerPC processor from IBM, and every major console used one for the next decade: the Xbox 360 dropped Intel for three PowerPC cores from IBM in 2005, the PS3's Cell chip was built by Sony, Toshiba and IBM around a PowerPC core and the Wii and Wii U both ran updated versions of the GameCube's IBM chip.
The graphics side had already gone PC-style, with the 360's ATI chip and the PS3's NVIDIA one, but the processors hadn't. That changed in 2013, when the PS4 moved to eight AMD processor cores and a graphics design taken from AMD's Radeon PC cards. Today's PS5 and Xbox Series X each run eight AMD Zen 2 cores alongside AMD RDNA 2 graphics on the same chip as the CPU. Ultimately, designing graphics chips from scratch for consoles stopped making sense once off-the-shelf GPU architectures fit a console's budget.

Telangana tea seller sets himself ablaze outside police station, cops cite dispute with grocer over cigarettes
The 55-year-old tea seller walked to the polcie station with a bottle of petrol and a matchbox and allegedly set himself ablaze.
A 55-year-old tea stall owner in Nizamabad district of Telangana reportedly attempted suicide by setting himself on fire in the premises of a police station in this district on Monday.
While the police said that the man was allegedly upset over being threatened by two local reporters, some local residents and political activists in Bheemgal town held protest seeking action against a Sub-Inspector of Police, who had booked a petty case against the tea stall owner, news agency PTI reported.
The 55-year-old man reportedly walked to the police station with a matchbox and a bottle of petrol on Monday morning. He then set himself ablaze outside a police station and some police personnel and people present there intervened and extinguished the flames after which he was taken to a hospital.
What the police said
Police cited an alleged rivalry with a grocery shop owner as a cause of the distress for the tea stall owner, which may have prompted him to take the extreme step. Police said the owner of a grocery shop had sent two reporters to threaten the middle-aged man after he recently stopped buying cigarettes and other material from his shop.
The police had registered a petty case against him for running his tea shop during late-night hours and he was asked by a Sub-Inspector of Police to pay the fine in court. The case was registered as part of routine enforcement duties, The Times of India quoted police officials as saying.
Nizamabad Police Commissioner P Sai Chaitanya said there was no fault on part of the police in the issue.

An OpenAI publicist tried to change the topic of CEO Sam Altman’s interview with Vanity Fair’s Mark Guiducci after the editor brought up a ChatGPT user’s suicide. When Guiducci confronted Altman about the incident, the publicist warned Guiducci about running out of time, saying she’d like to “move on” to another topic.
OpenAI PR tells journalist to ‘move on’ while asking Sam Altman about a ChatGPT user’s suicide
‘These are some of the hardest questions that we face or that anybody developing this technology faces,’ Altman said.
The interruption came shortly after Guiducci asked Altman if he knew who Laura Reiley is, a journalist who wrote an essay for The New York Times about her daughter’s conversations with ChatGPT before she took her own life. “Her daughter committed suicide after speaking to ChatGPT. ChatGPT did not tell her to kill herself—,” Guiducci said just before the publicist interrupted him.
“Mark, we have two minutes left. I want to be respectful, but I’d like to move on and talk a little bit about the future and what’s coming,” the publicist said. Even after Guiducci explained that he’s going to finish the question and then “go back to what we were talking about,” the publicist pushed back. “We really actually have to walk out the door in one or two minutes,” she said.
Despite the pushback, the interview continued with Guiducci asking Altman whether the company planned to use conversations with ChatGPT to shape policies surrounding its response to a user’s mental health crisis. “These are some of the hardest questions that we face or that anybody developing this technology faces,” Altman said. “You know, should we release people’s private data and some of their hardest moments to researchers? I think probably not without their consent. Or I should say, not without their consent.”
When reached for comment about the interruption, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said: “The interview was running over, which is why we ultimately asked to schedule even more time to continue the conversation after Sam addressed this critically important topic.”

North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, a day after it rejected Seoul’s accusation of its mines wounding soldiers.
The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at about 6.30am towards the East Sea – also known as the Sea of Japan – and flew more than 700km (434 miles), the South Korean military said. Seoul and Washington were analysing the test for details, it added.
Japan’s coast guard, citing the defence ministry, said the object may have been a ballistic missile and appeared to have come down, warning ships to take precautions.
South Korea’s military said it heightened its monitoring of any further missile tests and would share intelligence with the US and Japan. The South Korean presidential office’s national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation.
Pyongyang’s Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of ruler Kim Jong-un, issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the demilitarised zone – the heavily guarded buffer between the two Koreas.
South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier. Kim Yo-jong responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” and ridiculing Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch”.
Kim also warned that Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast – remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.
South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that injured three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide buffer zone that stretches across the Korean peninsula.
The missile test might be an attempt by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister’s statement, said Cheong Seong-chang, vice-president at the Sejong Institute in Seoul, a research centre on North Korean affairs. North Korea might also have tested a new type of missile, he added.
North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Some came after North Korea protested against joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.
North Korea has ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its “primary foe”.

The EC said the Bihar SIR order was unanimously approved by the Commission and later upheld by the Supreme Court in its May 27, 2026 judgment.
NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Monday issued a “fact check” amid the controversy over reported changes to Form 6, calling Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi’s claim that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar had “changed Form 6 illegally and unilaterally” misleading.In its response, the EC said the order for the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Bihar, issued on June 24, 2025, had received the unanimous approval of the Commission and was subsequently upheld by the Supreme Court in its judgment dated May 27, 2026.The poll panel also cited its Press Note No. 120 dated September 26, 2026, pointing to point 1(iii), which states: “The declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Hon'ble Supreme Court.”
The EC's response came after Rahul alleged in a post on X that the CEC had changed Form 6 “illegally and unilaterally”, citing the recent Supreme Court observation.EC officials also clarified that Form 6 itself had not been changed, but that a declaration had been attached to the form under the Bihar SIR order, as quoted by PTI.The clarification came after the Supreme Court said it had not approved any modification to Form 6 used by the EC during the SIR exercise in various states.
“Any modification to Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let's be clear. When records are produced, we would like to see who has modified it,” a bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant and comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said.
Form 6 is the application used by eligible voters for inclusion in the electoral roll.The declaration was attached to Form 6 during the Bihar SIR, which began with the EC's June 24, 2025 order. The declaration sought additional details, including information about the applicant's parents.According to EC officials, the form itself remained unchanged, while the declaration was a separate document attached to it for the SIR exercise. Outside SIR, the forms prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 apply.The declaration was later withdrawn from the EC's online portals.The online version of Form 6 and the declaration also used a single OTP for both, rather than requiring separate OTP verification, which had led to suggestions that the declaration was part of Form 6.The EC also rejected claims that it had withdrawn its September 26 press note and shared the document to show that it remained available.

Turning artificial intelligence research into real-world tools isn’t always straightforward, despite the remarkable progress in recent years ranging from self-driving cars to large language models. Systems that perform well in controlled lab settings often fall short when deployed in homes, in hospitals or on city streets.
Vision-based systems, for example, hold promise for improving safety, monitoring health and aiding rehabilitation. For example, a camera-based system could help a clinician assess a patient’s gait or rehabilitation progress.
In the future, an assistive robot in an older adult’s home might need to recognise when the person is struggling to stand or reaching for an object. But a major challenge is ensuring these robots perform reliably beyond the lab, particularly in messy, unpredictable or low-visibility conditions.
As a computer scientist who studies AI systems designed to understand human behavior – especially through visual cues like body movements and interactions with objects – I see three main challenges to taking AI from the lab to the real world: generalisation, human behavior and resources.
Challenge 1: The generalisation gap
Most AI vision systems are trained on well-lit, high-quality images, often from curated sources like motion capture studios or daytime recordings. But when these systems are deployed in real-world settings, such as in a dimly lit home, hospital room or nighttime street, they often struggle. This is not because the technology is flawed, but because the data used to train it cannot fully represent the enormous variability of the real world.
Take human pose estimation, for example. This task involves detecting key points on a person’s body, such as joints, to understand how they’re moving. The result resembles a digital skeleton that represents the positions of a person’s arms, legs and other body parts. Pose estimation has been studied for health and rehabilitation applications, including measuring a person’s gait, monitoring rehabilitation exercises and assessing movement patterns associated with the risk of falling. In well-lit environments, modern AI models do this with impressive accuracy. But in low or uneven lighting, performance can drop sharply. That’s because the model has learned from clean, consistent data and isn’t prepared to generalise to tougher conditions.
Would collecting more nighttime training data solve the problem? More labeled data would certainly help, but collecting it is especially difficult. When a person’s joints are hard to see in an image, they are also hard for a human annotator to label accurately. Low light can also obscure visual information rather than simply make an image darker, and nighttime conditions vary with cameras, shadows, glare and other sources of noise. Collecting and manually labeling examples that cover all these conditions is therefore difficult and expensive.
We’ve been working to close this gap by developing AI systems that perform better in low-light scenarios. One method we use is unsupervised domain adaptation, where a model trained on well-lit, labeled data is adapted to handle low-light settings, without needing manual body-joint labels for the low-light images. This helps bridge the “domain gap” between clean training data and the messier world where these systems are actually used.
In our 2026 study on low-light human pose estimation, we generated realistic low-light training images and designed the system to balance uncertain visual evidence with its learned knowledge of human body structure. The method substantially improved performance on two low-light benchmarks, although the broader challenge is far from solved.
Challenge 2: Human behavior
Another major hurdle is the sheer variety of human behaviors, especially when people interact with objects. In computer vision, this is known as human-object interaction detection. Teaching an AI system to recognise actions like cutting a tomato or passing a basketball requires not just object detection, but an understanding of context and intent.
The real challenge is scale. The number of objects is large, and the ways humans interact with them are even greater. You can sit on a chair, carry it, drag it or stack it. Each is a distinct interaction. A cup might be used for drinking, washing, pouring or handing something to another person. An assistive robot would need to distinguish among these actions to respond appropriately. It’s simply not feasible to collect and label data for every possible combination.
In my research, we study how an AI system can detect interactions it has never seen during training. Researchers call this a generalisation-to-unseen-classes problem, and it’s a key challenge for building models that don’t just memorise patterns, but can adapt to new situations. Our work has explored how foundation models can help recognise previously unseen interactions. In a more recent study, we used large vision-language models, models that combine computer vision and natural language processing, to identify the parts of an object that support particular actions, without training the system on labeled examples for that specific task. This matters in areas like assistive robotics and safety monitoring, where AI needs to respond intelligently to behaviors it wasn’t specifically trained on.
This challenge is different from the low-light problem. In low-light pose estimation, the system is trying to recognise a familiar type of movement under unfamiliar environmental conditions. In human-object interaction detection, the action-and-object combination itself may be new. Both are generalisation problems, but they require different solutions.
Challenge 3: The resource gap
Even when researchers know how to make models more robust, applying those improvements isn’t always easy, especially in academic or smaller research settings. Today’s most powerful AI systems depend on massive computational resources in the form of data centers that contain huge numbers of specialised computer chips.
These are often too expensive for university labs or public-sector researchers, and the computing power needed to train leading models has continued to rise. According to the 2026 AI Index Report, the technology industry produced more than 90% of the notable AI models introduced in 2025.
At the same time, a model developed using large computing clusters may ultimately need to operate in a clinic, school, robot or home device, which means running on much smaller hardware. Such systems may also need to respond quickly without continuously sending sensitive data to the cloud. This mismatch creates a widening gap between what’s possible in theory and what’s practical in deployment. Bridging that gap requires not just better models, but more efficient algorithms and open-source tools that broaden access to advanced AI.
Why it matters
These challenges aren’t just academic. They affect how and whether AI tools can be trusted in the real world. Imagine a fall-detection system that fails at night, a workplace safety monitor that misses a crucial action or a robot that misunderstands what a person is doing because it’s never seen that exact interaction before. These aren’t just minor bugs – they’re breakdowns in trust, usability and sometimes even safety.
AI systems are being deployed in homes, hospitals, factories, vehicles and other everyday environments. If they can’t adapt to different environments or recognise new human behaviors, their usefulness becomes limited and their risks amplified. That’s why researchers are increasingly focusing not just on accuracy in ideal conditions, but on robustness, generalisation and real-world readiness.
Looking ahead: Closing the gap
Closing the gap between lab-trained AI models and messy, unpredictable real-world environments won’t happen overnight, but it’s possible. In my research, we’ve explored techniques like using augmented data to simulate challenging conditions and help models adapt. We’ve also worked on enabling AI systems to better generalise to new, unseen situations by using knowledge from foundation models to distinguish unfamiliar interactions from similar ones encountered during training.
Ultimately, I believe that making AI systems more reliable in everyday settings is a challenge worth solving, not just to improve gadgets and apps, but because AI has the potential to support human well-being, whether that means safer streets, smarter healthcare or more secure homes.
Bo Wang, assistant professor of Computer and Information Science, University of Mississippi

In September 2026, a rumor (archived) circulated online that water levels in Wyoming's Yellowstone Lake dropped 11 feet between Sept. 26 and 27.
For example, a Facebook user wrote on Sept. 29:
YELLOWSTONE NATIONAL PARK - Scientists are investigating after portions of Yellowstone Lake reportedly dropped nearly 11 feet overnight when an unknown underground channel opened beneath the lake bed.
Rangers first noticed the change Sunday morning after several docks were found sitting completely above the waterline. Geologists believe shifting rock beneath the lake may have opened a previously sealed underground passage, allowing millions of gallons of water to drain into Yellowstone's extensive subterranean geological system.
The rumor also spread on X and Threads (archived, archived).
The rumor originated from the Facebook page Casper Planet, which described its content as satire. The page's About section read, "Snews that doesn't matter directly to your Snews feed. Did we say this is satire? Well it is, names/locations are made up."
In addition to Casper Planet's own declaration of the satirical nature of its content, we found no reporting from reputable sources on Google, Yahoo or DuckDuckGo (archived, archived, archived) that supported the Facebook page's claim about Yellowstone or cited the "geologist Dr. Aaron Keller" who featured in Casper Planet's post.
The image that Casper Planet used to illustrate the satirical story was fake. The highly regarded Pangram artificial intelligence detection tool found the image to be "fully AI." Open AI's Verify scanner found that someone had generated the image using Open AI's tools.
Though Casper Planet did note on its page that its content was satire, it did not say so on the actual post. Shares of Casper Planet's posts on X and Threads contained no indications (aside from the nature of the content) that the story was satire.
The United States Geological Survey's water level readings from the Yellowstone River at its inlet into Lake Yellowstone did not show an 11-foot drop in water levels between Sept. 26 and 27. The USGS found that water levels between 9 a.m. on Sept. 26 and 9 a.m. on Sept. 27 varied by inches, not feet.
Snopes has previously investigated other satire claims shared by Casper Planet, including whether an ancient city appeared under Wyoming's Horse Peak Mountain or whether Wyoming wolves mauled a Colorado man who tried to join their pack.
Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

BUNIA, Congo — Congo’s Ebola outbreak has killed more than 4,000 people, authorities said, as they struggle to contain what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
The latest figures released by the Health Ministry on Thursday showed that 4,018 people have died among 8,300 cases recorded since the outbreak was declared in eastern Congo on May 15.
Some health workers, meanwhile, gathered at the epicenter in Ituri Province to demand payment for wages owed them. The protesters, who included surveillance team members, waved placards saying, “No money, no data!” and “No payment for months.”
Some of the workers haven’t been paid for August and September, said Biongi Beiza, one of the protesters in Bunia, Ituri’s capital. “There is no explanation from the administration,” he said.
Congolese authorities did not immediately address the issue. Front-line workers have gone on strike several times since the outbreak began, further hampering efforts to contain the disease.
A senior U.N. official said an Ebola-hit displacement camp housing a transit center for infected patients was burned by soldiers earlier this week as they were looking for weapons in Kigonze, on the outskirts of Bunia, forcing 19,000 people in the camp to flee.
Creating such transit and treatment centers has been a struggle, requiring money and staff, all of which are in short supply, said Julien Harneis, the U.N. senior Ebola coordinator. “When we lose a center, that means we lose capacity, we lose investment, and we have to start again. And above all, it means that people do not get access to the care that they really need,” Harneis said.
Infected aid worker evacuated to the Netherlands
An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement.
The worker arrived in the Netherlands late Thursday on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement.
“The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country,” MSF said.
At least 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus.
Mobile labs are helping detect cases quickly
One way local authorities have tried to contain the outbreak is through mobile laboratories. In Butembo, an Associated Press journalist watched a medical team operating one such lab near an Ebola treatment center on Thursday.
Test results that used to take 72 hours can now be obtained in six hours with the mobile labs, said Lota Kalubi, a doctor at the treatment center.
The labs have also made it easier to get to locations usually difficult to reach, said Michel Ngimba with the National Institute of Biomedical Research in Butembo. “So we can go, if today we have an emergency, for example, in Katwa, we can start up the vehicle, and we can move the lab to Katwa,” said Ngimba.
Insecurity and community resistance are hampering containment efforts
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm about the virus’ rapid spread into new health zones, stretching limited resources. The current outbreak is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which killed 11,000 people, WHO has said.
The number of newly confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hot spots, Africa CDC said on Thursday. While the spread of the disease has slowed in some areas, it has accelerated in others.
Confirmed cases fell from around 850 cases and 470 deaths a week in mid-July to an average of 490 cases and 230 deaths in September.
A Congolese politician was beaten to death earlier this week in one of the emerging hot spots after defending government measures to deal with the outbreak, highlighting tensions and mistrust in communities.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach that involved working with local leaders to educate people about the virus, but those efforts face resistance from residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country’s government for reasons including how it’s managed past Ebola outbreaks and chronic corruption.
— Dieudonne Dirole and Ope Adetayo
Adetayo reported from Lagos, Nigeria. Sebastien Kitsa Musayi in Butembo, Congo, Chinedu Asadu in Abuja, Nigeria, and Mike Corder in the Netherlands contributed.

Health-focused restaurant chain True Food Kitchen, which has counted Oprah Winfrey and former Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz among its backers, has filed for bankruptcy.
The Phoenix, Arizona-founded chain filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in a Texas court on Sunday and is pursuing a court-supervised sale of the business as part of its restructuring proceedings.
True Food Kitchen also closed 12 of its restaurants on the day it filed, cutting its footprint to 34 locations across 14 states. Those eateries remain open and are serving customers as usual, the company said.
The company's Chapter 11 court filings say it is about $42 million in debt and cites management turnover and the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic as reasons for its bankruptcy filing.
True Food Kitchen's "growth was accompanied by a number of operational challenges," a court filing in the bankruptcy case said.
"The Company experienced significant management turnover, which resulted in frequent changes to expansion strategy, brand direction, and menu offerings," said the filing.
It added, "Under successive leadership teams, the Company invested capital outside its core market areas and in new product lines and restaurant concepts that were ultimately unsuccessful and outside of the Company's core mission and menu."
The filing said that while many True Food Kitchen outposts are profitable, several have struggled with low foot and vehicle traffic, and others have been affected by "changing market forces and demographics," leading to revenue losses.
True Food Kitchen was founded in 2008 by wellness author Andrew Weil and restaurateur Sam Fox, who wanted to serve both delicious and healthy food for an anti-inflammatory diet.
In 2017, the company spun off from Fox's restaurant group as FRC Balance, LLC. A year later, Winfrey made an undisclosed equity investment in the company and also joined its board of directors.
"When I first dined at True Food Kitchen, I was so impressed with the team's passion for healthy eating and, of course, the delicious food, that I knew I wanted to be part of the company's future," the media mogul said at the time.
A spokesperson for True Food Kitchen told Business Insider on Monday that Winfrey is no longer on the board, but remains a "minority investor." Representatives for Winfrey did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Chapter 11 filing.
Meanwhile, in a statement Monday, True Food Kitchen CEO Jeff Chandler called the company's bankruptcy filing the "best path forward to simplify the business and focus on what we do best: delivering craveable, health-forward food and genuine hospitality."
"We are confident this step will help us build a stronger True Food Kitchen for the future," he said.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday (September 29, 2026) expressed concern over the sharp disparity between the prices charged to retailers and consumers for essential medicines, particularly cancer drugs, observing that steep mark-ups placed an enormous burden on taxpayers and amounted to “carnage”.
A Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta questioned the Centre on why the 16% retailer margin provided for under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013 should not be applied uniformly to essential medicines to curb steep mark-ups over the price to retailer (PTR).
“Why not keep the 16% margin on MRP, which is prescribed in the DPCO, on everything? ... Ultimately, the loser is the taxpayer. This is carnage, as simple as that,” the Bench remarked.
The observations came while the top court was hearing petitions filed by advocate Kishan Chand Jain and paediatric surgeon Sanjay Kulshrestha, seeking its intervention to regulate the prices of drugs, medical equipment, and generic medicines, and make them more affordable.
Justice Mehta pointed, in particular, to the nearly ten-fold mark-up on an essential cancer drug, which was supplied to retailers for around ₹3,000 but sold to consumers for ₹27,000. He questioned who ultimately benefited from the nearly ₹24,000 difference. “You tell us why this difference... Where does this chunk of money go? Ten times...” Justice Mehta remarked.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, acknowledged the concern and said the government would have to find a way forward while “balancing equities”. He, however, said it was private hospitals, rather than pharmaceutical companies, that benefited from the steep mark-ups. “The pharma company is not the gainer. The gainer is the private hospital,” the Solicitor General submitted.
The Bench also flagged the practice of private hospitals insisting that patients purchase medicines from their in-house pharmacies, leaving them with little choice to procure the same drugs at lower prices elsewhere.
It also pointed to the impact of such inflated prices on public finances, observing that when treatment is covered under government-funded health schemes such as Ayushman Bharat, the cost is ultimately borne by taxpayers.
“Suppose the patient is taking treatment through government services... The government doesn’t pay, the taxpayer pays. This affects a larger section of society,” the Bench remarked.
Mr. Mehta sought time to place before the court details of the existing mechanisms governing drug pricing and assured the Bench that he would make his submissions on the next date of hearing. The Bench accordingly posted the matter for further hearing on October 12, 2026.
The petitions have sought directions to make drug formulations more affordable by curbing alleged overpricing of essential medicines by pharmaceutical companies and retailers. They have also sought stricter enforcement of price controls under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013 to prevent violations of the prescribed pricing mechanism and disproportionate profit margins across the drug supply chain.
Earlier, the top court had described the wide difference between the price to retailers and the MRP of medicines as “dacoity”, while drawing attention to the financial distress faced by patients struggling to meet treatment costs.
“The MRP is 10 times the rate at which it is provided to the retailers. If this is not extortion, then what is it? People sell their houses, ornaments to get treatment,” the Bench had remarked.

Trump says data centers are the future — deal with it
President Donald Trump has asked Ohioans to consider the money they allegedly could make if they allow data centers in their communities

President Donald Trump tried to sell Ohioans on data centers during a recent rally in the Buckeye state, asking his supporters to consider the cost of China gaining an advantage over the U.S.
During a visit to Vandalia, Ohio — just north of Dayton — Trump asked the Ohioan workers to consider the U.S.'s supposed AI race with China when they form their opinions on data centers, The Hill reports.
“There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” he said.
Trump recently made the curious decision to rename AI to "super intelligence" and has opposed moratoriums on data center construction as well as calls from AI developers like OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei to slow down AI research due to safety concerns.
The president insisted that data centers would provide Ohio with economic benefits for local communities.
Critics have argued that data centers do not typically create many local jobs, drive up energy prices, and produce noise, light and traditional pollution.
Sen. John Husted, who is currently facing a re-election challenge by Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown, has faced criticism from Ohioans over his role in bringing data centers to the state while he was serving as its lieutenant governor.
Husted introduced a bill that aimed to address the concerns over data centers by forcing large power users to bear more of the costs of their energy use, but that bill was blocked by Senate Democrats.
Brown has used Husted's ties to data centers as a point of attack in his campaign.
“Sen. Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centers in Ohio,” Brown said in a social media post. “Now, he’s making Ohioans foot the bill.”

In early October 2026, after the Tennessee Department of Correction failed to execute death row inmate Christa Pike on Sept. 30, 2026, a claim circulated online that Pike's execution team had been all female.
Pike was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death in 1996 for the killing of her Jobs Corp training program classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. She also was convicted of attempted first-degree murder in 2001 after attacking another inmate.
The department halted Pike's execution in the evening of Sept. 30 after she appeared to survive receiving two doses of the sedative pentobarbital. Pike was taken to a hospital and her lawyers said on Oct. 1 that she was in critical condition, The Associated Press reported.
Some social media users appeared to suggest that there was a connection between the failed execution and the alleged all-female lethal injection team. One X user wrote (archived), "I'm just going to say it, I think that the all-female execution team botched this on purpose."
I'm just going to say it, I think that the all-female execution team botched this on purpose.
— Cassandra MacDonald (@CassandraRules) October 1, 2026
The claim also circulated elsewhere on X (archived). Snopes readers searched our site for more information about the rumor.
At the time of this writing, conflicting claims circulated about whether an all-female team had carried out Pike's botched execution.
Speaking at a news conference after the execution attempt, Pike's lawyer Randy Spivey appeared to confirm that her execution team had all been women by saying that the team he saw at the execution was "consistent" with a reported request Pike made for an all-female team.
However, local media in Tennessee reported that Dr. Mark Fowler, a man who also was involved in the botched execution of Tony Carruthers in Tennessee in May 2026, administered the lethal injections or "oversaw" Pike's attempted execution.
When reached by Snopes via phone on Oct. 2, Fowler would not comment on whether he was involved in Pike's attempted execution. The Tennessee Department of Correction also declined to comment on whether Pike had an all-female execution team.
Given the lack of confirmation from official sources to settle conflicting claims, we leave this claim unrated.
The Tennessee Department of Correction had not confirmed at the time of this writing exactly what led to the failure to execute Pike. Therefore, it was impossible to say whether an all-female team affected the outcome of the execution.
Snopes contacted reporters for WSMV and WVLT, the two local news stations that reported Fowler's apparent involvement in Pike's attempted execution, to ask how they knew Fowler was present. We also contacted lawyers for Pike for the latest update on her health and case. We await replies to our queries.
The New York Post reported in September 2026 that Pike had requested an all-female execution team "citing past sexual abuse." Pike reportedly also said that if her request was not possible she would prefer to be executed by hanging.
Snopes contacted lawyers for Pike to access a copy of this reported request and await a reply. Spivey appeared to acknowledge the existence of the request when he responded to a question about it during a news conference (archived) after the failed execution (at 33:41):
MODERATOR: We have a question from Heather Derell. Was she granted the all-female execution staff she requested?
SPIVEY: I want to be careful with that because I understand the rules around identifying that, and I will say that I think what TDOC has said is that they would make every effort to comply with that, and what I saw was consistent with that.
At a news conference on Oct. 1, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said (at 0:54, archived) he had called for a "thorough and comprehensive and third-party review and investigation into the protocol" at the execution attempt. Lee also said that the state's last planned execution of the year would not take place while that investigation was ongoing.
Pike appealed to Lee for clemency and to have her death sentence converted to life in prison without the possibility of parole on Sept. 14. Lee rejected that appeal on Sept. 28.

Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets. The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership. Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. “Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership. Building on the momentum, fourteen new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Of these, ESDS Software Solution, Klassroom, RentoMojo, SEDEMAC, Kissht, LEAP India and Shiprocket made a bumper debut on the bourses. Nevertheless, the IPO pipeline remains strong. Twenty six startups have already filed their DRHPs with SEBI, while over 25 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO, Razorpay and Zetwerk alone could raise over ₹34,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs. However, recalibration is likely to define 2026 as investors are expected to prioritise strong fundamentals, profitability and low cash burn when backing new-age tech companies. “IPO-bound startups in 2026 will be increasingly defined by their ability to demonstrate predictable cash flows, sustainable unit economics, and operational discipline rather than headline growth alone. Public market investors will place greater emphasis on governance, capital efficiency and long-term value creation, favouring companies that balance scale with financial prudence,” Orios Venture Partners’ managing partner Rehan Yar Khan told Inc42. There are other challenges as well. Average retail subscription levels are moderating, while foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are pulling back in droves, reflecting caution amid geopolitical tensions and muted secondary market performance. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has further complicated the situation. Yet, the overall outlook remains bullish for new-age tech IPOs. Maturing business models, deeper domestic capital pools and an evolving regulatory framework favouring transparency position India as a leading startup IPO hub.
