Nobel Prize awarded for revealing inner workings of the brain
- Published
US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and his German colleagues Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work in the field of optogenetics.
Their research has helped scientists learn more about the inner workings of the brain, to better understand how the human mind works.
The Nobel Committee, external praised the trio for laying the foundation of a new era in neuroscience by revealing how to switch on and off neural circuits behind "specific memories, feelings, and behaviours relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders".
In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method to try to restore sight in people with visual impairment.
'Absolutely wonderful'
"Optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain," the Nobel Assembly said.
"Every day brings new discoveries, helping to solve one of humanity's great mysteries: how our incredible brain works."
The winners said it was "absolutely wonderful" to get the award, and that it was an honour to share the accolade with friends.
The three men will also share the £900,000 (12 million Swedish kronor) prize money.
What is optogenetics?
Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, explained: "Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of."
Before, the inner workings behind feelings, behaviours and bodily functions were more of a mystery to scientists.
Optogentics is a way to illuminate brain pathways, using a special protein borrowed from algae that scientists use to control cell electrical activity using light.
In the early 2000s, Hegemann and Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, the algal protein with unique properties.
Deisseroth worked out how to use this light controlled protein to switch on nerve cells in the brains of mice.
Researchers have since been able to study nerve cells and pathways in animals to see and discover more about what they do.
The Nobel Committee said: "Using light, researchers are now able to switch individual neural circuits on or off in the brain. They can bring memories to life, create feelings, drive behaviours and study the types of neurons that are involved in various psychiatric and neurological disorders."
That is providing important insights into how the nervous system interacts with various cells in other areas of the body, such as in the heart and gut, the committee added.
Restoring people's sight
Researchers have also taken "the first steps" towards using optogenetics as a medical treatment, the committee explained.
In ongoing clinical trials, scientists have been working to restore vision in people who have become blind due to retinitis pigmentosa, a disease that destroys the eye's rods and cones.
By inserting a special protein in the damaged region of the eye, the patient regained some vision when wearing special glasses emitting light. This switched on the therapeutic algae proteins.

Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?
- Published
Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army.
Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict.
There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted.
This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago.
Why has fighting broken out now?
It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray.
The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions.
This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting.
This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation.
The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray.
Who are the TPLF?
For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government.
It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades.
At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population.
When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence.
Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century.
The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine.
An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022.
Why has the peace deal faltered?
There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray.
The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army.
Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991.
When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa.
The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum.
For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms.
The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy.
But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy.
This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions.
Who is backing the TPLF?
A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies.
Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army.
Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power.
So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside.
TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated.
Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests.
What is the government's position?
As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country.
It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies.
During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out.
Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports.
Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force.
What do we know about the bombing in Tigray?
Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces.
The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify.
Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war.
This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces.
The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks.
What is being done to stop the fighting?
The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks.
It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently.
The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict.
The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume.
The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated.
Could the fighting spread?
Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia.
The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia.
The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily.
There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government.
The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters.
The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis.

Mamata Banerjee sends notice to SSKM Hospital for allegedly leaking her medical reports
This comes days after Adhikari said that Banerjee faked her leg injury while releasing a five-year-old medical report
Former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee served a legal notice to the Institute of Post Graduate Medical Education & Research (IPGMER) authorities in Kolkata seeking an explanation on how the medical reports of her leg injury ahead of the 2021 state assembly elections reached present CM Suvendu Adhikari.
This comes days after Adhikari said that Banerjee faked her leg injury while releasing a five-year-old medical report which purportedly said that there was “no evidence of fracture/dislocation” on Banerjee’s leg.
“You are called upon to inform me or my client that whether any medical records pertaining to my client has been at all placed before the chief minister (Adhikari) and if so placed, then kindly intimate or my client the due process of law adopted by the department of radio-diagnosis while placing the said records before the chief minister,” the notice sent by Arka Kumar Nag, Banerjee’s counsel, read.
On March 10, 2021, hours after filing her nomination from the high-profile seat of Nandigram where she contested against her protégé-turned-rival Adhikari, Banerjee alleged that unidentified men attacked her. The Criminal Investigation Department (CID) started a probe into the incident then.
She claimed to have fractured her leg and campaigned over the next two months, even holding a road show on a wheelchair with a plastered left leg. Even though the Trinamool Congress (TMC) won the assembly elections, Banerjee lost to Adhikari in Nandigram.
“The findings of the department of radio-diagnosis in the Bangur Institute of Neuro-Sciences at IPGMER (popularly known as SSKM hospital) on March 11, 2021 stated that there was no evidence of fracture or dislocation,” Adhikari told reporters at the state secretariat on Saturday.
The legal notice was sent to the Manimoy Bandyopadhyay, director of IPGMER and two other senior officials of the hospital.
“If it is identified that no due procedure of law was followed while placing the medial records of my client before the chief minister (Adhikari), then it shall be the legal liability of your office to initiate necessary steps in accordance with law against politically motivated officers of your institution involved in causing such delinquency and breach,” the notice stated.
Bandyopadhyay, refused to respond to calls and messages sent to him.
“She is committing a mistake. I asked the authorities to send me the notice through the state health department. She had ordered a CID probe into the incident. I would ask her not to dig further. If I make the X-Ray plates and MRI reports she would not be able to come out of her house. The documents were not with the SSKM hospital authorities. If needed I would reveal from where I got the documents,” Adhikari told media at the state secretariat on Monday.

SC refuses to restrain Gyanesh Kumar, says can't pass order based on news report
The SC bench made it clear that any decision found to have been taken contrary to the statutory requirements governing the ECI could subsequently be injuncted.
The Supreme Court on Monday declined to pass any interim order restraining chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar from functioning over allegations that he took several decisions unilaterally despite objections from the two other election commissioners (ECs), saying it could not proceed on “assumptions” without first verifying the facts.
A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued notices to the Election Commission of India (ECI), the Union government, the CEC and the two ECs on a petition filed by social activist Rakesh Kumar Singh. Track Gyanesh Kumar news live updates here.
The bench, however, made it clear that any decision found to have been taken contrary to the statutory requirements governing the functioning of the poll panel could subsequently be injuncted.
Senior advocate Vikas Singh, appearing for the petitioner, sought the immediate suspension of Kumar. Alternatively, he urged the court to direct the Election Commission to take only unanimous decisions until the next hearing.
Singh relied on the 1993 amendments to the election law to contend that, as far as possible, decisions of the Commission were required to be taken unanimously. He also referred to the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, particularly Section 18, which provides for majority decision-making in case of a difference of opinion.
“There is a distinction. The unanimity relates to transaction of business and allocation of work, while functioning can be by majority,” Singh submitted.
The bench, however, questioned him on what had changed from the 1993 legal position.
Also Read | Supreme Court issues notice to Centre, poll panel over CEC Gyanesh Kumar's functioning; no interim order
Singh said the 2023 law had also introduced Section 16, which conferred a level of immunity on the CEC and election commissioners that was “unheard of”, including protection extending beyond their tenure.
“A protection while in office is understood,” the bench observed.
Singh, however, pressed for an interim order suspending Kumar, saying the credibility of the Election Commission was at stake.
“We are facing a very grave situation. We have been known in the world for conducting free and fair elections but here the CEC’s working…” he said.
The bench cautioned against acting on allegations before receiving the ECI’s response.
“Let us not have an authentic information about the averments made by you,” it said.
When Singh pressed for immediate intervention, saying “the country will burn” without an interim order, the bench said it could annul a decision subsequently if it was found to be unlawful.
Singh then proposed that, until the matter was heard next, the three members of the Commission should be required to take only unanimous decisions.
The bench pointed to Section 18 of the 2023 Act and said the statutory scheme itself contemplated unanimity where possible and majority decision-making in case of disagreement.
Court questions reliance on media reports
The bench also refused to proceed merely on the basis of media reports.
“You have come here on the basis of a news report, which can be 100% correct, partially correct or partially incorrect. We cannot pass any order on the basis of a newspaper report,” the bench said.
“If correctional requirements are there, we can issue those orders in future. We cannot pass any orders on the basis of any presumption. We are calling upon all ECs and they will present all facts before us,” it added.
The bench said the Election Commission was bound by the statutory requirements governing its functioning and warned that it would intervene if it found that the law had not been followed.
“There is a mandatory law and we will expect them to follow them. If we find they have not followed the law, our powers are known to everyone,” it said.
Singh argued that the court could not undo an election or an elected government later and therefore needed to intervene immediately.
The bench said it would first issue notices and examine whether the decisions had been taken in accordance with Section 18.
“If we find out that some decisions were taken either unanimously or without majority, as provided under Section 18, we will injunct those decisions and say these decisions cannot be implemented,” it added.
When Singh said several of the disputed decisions related to the ongoing special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and had allegedly been taken unilaterally, the bench cautioned against assuming the factual position.
“We cannot put the cart before the horse. You want us to assume all these decisions were unilateral. We are issuing notices and they will respond. We expect them to respond to the notice and respond fairly,” it said.
The court identified the central issue in the petition as the interpretation of Section 18 of the 2023 Act and whether its requirements had been followed in the decisions under challenge.
What is the petition based on?
The petition is based substantially on allegations contained in an investigation by The Indian Express, which reported that ECs Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections to aspects of the functioning of the Election Commission between October last year and August this year.
The report also raised questions about changes in the digital systems used for electoral rolls and the information sought from prospective voters through Form 6, besides decisions relating to the SIR exercise.
The Election Commission has disputed the allegations, maintaining that the decisions were unanimous and that the communications from the two election commissioners concerned administrative issues relating to an officer deputed to the poll body, rather than policy decisions.
The ECI has also maintained that there was no change to the statutory Form 6 itself and that additional information was sought through an addendum.
Separate plea over Form 6
In a separate but related matter listed before the same bench, the Supreme Court also issued notice on a petition filed by advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi challenging alleged modifications to Form 6 on the ECINet/ERONet portal, including requirements relating to ancestry and declarations concerning the last SIR.
Senior advocate Menaka Guruswamy, appearing for Tripathi, referred to the manner in which the SIR was conducted in Delhi and alleged that two new conditions had been added to the voter-registration process.
The bench, however, made an important clarification.
“Any modified Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let’s be clear. When record will be produced, we would like to see who has modified,” the bench said.
Guruswamy said the alleged changes had wider implications, pointing to the number of electors affected during the SIR in Delhi and West Bengal and claiming that 16 lakh appeals were pending before appellate tribunals.
The bench, however, said the prayers in Tripathi’s petition appeared to be “jumbled up” and asked counsel to examine them.
Guruswamy said she stood by the prayers in the petition, while adding that the plea had also challenged the manner in which the Election Commission was functioning as a national constitutional institution. She sought that the matter be tagged with Singh’s petition.
The court then directed that Tripathi’s petition be tagged with the matter concerning Singh.
The two proceedings therefore bring before the Supreme Court, in separate forms, questions over the functioning of the Election Commission, the decision-making framework under the 2023 law and alleged changes to the electoral-roll machinery, at a time when the SIR exercise has triggered intense scrutiny over the inclusion and exclusion of voters.

Allegations that the son of the Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell” that launched drone attacks on fuel storage facilities and power stations in western Libya have upended plans for the Tripoli-based government of national unity (GNU) to continue cooperating with Haftar on a plan to unify the country.
Saddam Haftar, the deputy commander of the so-called Libyan National Army (LNA), has increasingly been seen by the US as an important figure in its plans to unify Libyan security, judicial and political institutions.
But a round of drone attacks in August worsened electricity blackouts in the west of the country, putting intense popular pressure on the GNU led by the prime minister, Abdul Hamid Dbeibah.
Libya has been split between the east, dominated by Haftar, and the west, governed by the GNU, since the fall of Col Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, leaving the oil-rich country at the mercy of corruption, militia, migrant traffickers and myriad external actors.
Donald Trump’s Africa adviser, Massad Boulos, has hatched a plan to unify the two Libyan governments in which Haftar from the east would take on the role of president and a member of the Dbeibah family from the west would become prime minister.
Boulos has insisted he is not trying a quick fix that entrenches family elites in Libya. “It’s not about families or names,” Boulos said when asked about the reported Haftar-Dbeibah deal, before adding: “At the end of the day, those are individuals that have to be in one position or the other.”
But the drone strikes, it is claimed, were prompted by Haftar’s anger at Dbeibah apparently stalling on the Boulos merger plan and by Tripoli allegedly encouraging tribes in southern Libya to attack and kill his forces.
Over more than five days in August, drones attacked the Zawiya oil station and fuel storage facilities in western Libya. The drone strikes hit the gasoline-storage tank at the Zawiya oil complex, west of Tripoli, causing a large fire and the tank’s collapse. The tank held approximately 4.5m litres of fuel when it was struck, according to Libya’s National Oil Corporation.
On 5 September, three Libyans and one Spanish citizen were arrested in southern Tripoli by the GNU for their alleged role in a plot that was intended to include an attack on Tripoli airport. It was thought the whole group involved five Spaniards and four Libyans. The three arrested Libyans were allegedly affiliated with the Tareq ben Ziyad brigade, an LNA formation. Information that has emerged from interviews about the plot, and Saddam Haftar’s alleged role, not just in Libya, has been described as a goldmine, capable of weakening Khalifa Haftar.
Sources in the GNU said the alleged plotters were working for Saddam Haftar. “No formal decision has been made, but in light of what has been discovered it is impossible to work with Saddam,” the sources said.
The claims not only damage Saddam Haftar’s role in the Boulos plan but also the parallel UN sponsored 4+4 talks involving the main four political institutions in Libya that led to an August agreement to stage elections within two years. The deal endorsed by the UN security council overcomes previous obstacles to elections, and had been backed by the main actors capable of delivering the change.
Walid Ellafi, minister for state for political affairs in the UN-backed Libyan GNU and an enthusiast for elections, said: “Our support for the 4+4 process is rooted in its role as a UN sponsored framework offering a new approach to achieving practical results that pave the way for elections and institutions whose political legitimacy derives from the will of the people – not as a political settlement that overlooks violations or sets aside the rights of those affected.”
He opposes an elite east-west political deal that brushes aside longstanding grievances such as the displacement of 9,000 families in Benghazi during the 2014 war.
The allegations about the sabotage operation may intensify a power struggle between the three sons of Khalifa Haftar in the east.
Saddam Haftar is seen as his father’s most likely heir, possesses the most resources, enjoys the backing of the United Arab Emirates and has so far dominated the political tracks. But his brothers, Khaled and Belqasim – more allied with Egypt than the United Arab Emirates – have recently started to challenge his dominance.

Indian police accused of sexually harassing journalists at protest
- Published
Three female journalists have accused police officers in India of sexual harassment during street protests in the capital Delhi.
The claims were made on Saturday after the force detained scores of young people calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner.
In a post on social media, Delhi Police said its New Delhi District had received the complaint, and it had been transferred to its crime branch for a "fair and impartial" inquiry.
Thousands of protesters gathered in Delhi and Mumbai cities for a third day on Sunday demanding that Gyanesh Kumar step down over large-scale changes to voter rolls.
The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.
Videos online show people being physically dragged away from the Jantar Mantar protest site in central Delhi.
The accusations by the women journalists include inappropriate touching by some police.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said women fear for their safety and the home ministry must "answer for this".
"Police dragged me by my hair," Aahna Singh, an activist and student at Jawaharlal Nehru University told Reuters news agency during the protests.
She said the police were resorting to "brutality".
The Press Club of India has demanded immediate action on the complaints against police officers, saying it was "shocked and dismayed" by the treatment of journalists.
"Behaviour of this kind cannot be normalised in a democracy. Journalists must be allowed to work freely, without fear, and document those who gather to raise various issues," it said in a statement.
The protesters say the voter-roll revision will benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.
It says the last revision was done nearly a quarter of a century ago and the voters' list needs to be updated to account for those who have died, left the country or are registered in more than one place as they've moved to a new address.
But the exercise has been mired in controversy from the start with the opposition parties accusing Kumar of manipulating voters' list to favour the BJP during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.
The protesters have included supporters of the influential Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) that began as an online satirical movement.
The pressure group recorded its first major victory in July when it forced the then Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign after weeks of protests calling for education reforms.
The CJP called for the latest protest after a report in The Indian Express, external said that Kumar's two fellow election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had formally objected at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders they said had been issued without their knowledge.
The differences were reported to be mostly over the controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year.
The Election Commission has defended its way of working and said in a statement that "differing views" were part of the "decision-making process" and that all the decisions were taken unanimously.
But the revelations sparked a furore, with opposition leaders demanding Kumar's resignation.

Leh, Oct 5: In a significant step towards strengthening early childhood care and education (ECCE) and improving foundational learning among children, Ladakh Lt Governor Vinai Kumar Saxena on Monday inaugurated Saksham ICT Labs established across 100 Anganwadi centres in the Union Territory.
Saxena inaugurated one such lab physically at the Anganwadi centre at Government Primary School, Killibuk, Thiksey, while the others were inaugurated virtually, a Lok Bhavan spokesman said.
Of the 100 Saksham ICT Labs, 50 have been established in Leh and 50 in Kargil, marking an important milestone in the administration's efforts to create stimulating, inclusive and technology-enabled learning environments for children at the grassroots level, the spokesman said.
The initiative has been undertaken under Mission Saksham Anganwadi & Poshan 2.0 to strengthen ECCE and is aligned with the 'Poshan Bhi Padhai Bhi', Aadharshila Curriculum and the ECCE framework of the Ministry of Women and Child Development, he said.
He further said the ICT facilities will provide children with age-appropriate digital and audio-visual learning content, including stories, rhymes, poems and songs, while supporting language and communication, colours, shapes and pre-number concepts, as well as cognitive, creative, physical and motor activities.
Speaking on the occasion, the LG said the future of Ladakh is closely linked with the quality of learning and development provided to its youngest generation.
He emphasised that the 100 Saksham ICT Labs are not merely about introducing technology into Anganwadi centres, but about creating a new learning experience where technology, creativity, participation and joyful learning come together.
"Technology must be used to make learning more engaging, joyful and meaningful for our children. These Saksham ICT Labs will complement play-based learning and help strengthen the foundations for their future," Saxena said.
He stressed that children learn best when they are encouraged to explore, ask questions, play and learn through experience. The ICT facilities, therefore, will complement the existing play-based and activity-based pedagogy, making learning more engaging, interactive and child-centred.
The LG said technology should not replace children's imagination or human interaction, but should provide them with new opportunities to explore, express themselves and develop their curiosity.
He emphasised that the objective is not to make children passive consumers of digital content, but to use technology as a tool that encourages participation, interaction and experiential learning.
The ICT Labs will support children in developing their language and communication skills through stories, rhymes, poems and songs, while helping them understand colours, shapes and basic numerical concepts, the spokesman said.
He said a range of cognitive, creative, physical and motor activities will also contribute to the holistic development of children during their crucial formative years.
The initiative has been enabled through convergence between the Social & Tribal Welfare Department and the Information Technology Department, with ICT equipment being provided by the IT Department, the spokesman said.

Nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals repatriated from Malaysia as UN warns of risks
Nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals have arrived in the country’s largest city after being sent back from Malaysia
YANGON, Myanmar -- Nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals who were sent back from Malaysia arrived in the country’s largest city on Sunday, despite warnings from the United Nations refugee agency and rights groups that conditions for return remain unsafe.
Myanmar has been in turmoil since the military seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi on Feb. 1, 2021, triggering widespread opposition and plunging large parts of the country into conflict.
The returnees, including 86 women, have been convicted of staying illegally and other immigration violations in Malaysia, according to reports from Myanmar state media. They were transported from Malaysia aboard two navy warships and a hospital ship last Tuesday. They arrived in southern Yangon early Sunday, Nay Lin Tun, a regional government minister, said.
The returnees are among 5,000 Myanmar nationals who will be repatriated in stages from Malaysia, where 10,388 others were being held at immigration detention centers, according to Malaysia’s Home Ministry.
The U.N. high commissioner for refugees and rights groups have criticized the repatriation, saying the security and humanitarian situation in parts of Myanmar remains volatile and returnees could face persecution and forced military conscription in an active war zone.
“Under international law, the Government of Malaysia is obligated to uphold the principle of non-refoulement and prevent the return of individuals to situations where they face a real risk of persecution, torture, or other serious human rights violations,” Kelley E. Currie, the U.N. special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, said in a statement on Thursday. “In my assessment, the risk of refoulement in the present circumstances is substantial.”
It was unclear if any of the returnees included minority Muslim Rohingya, who are facing persecution in Myanmar and have been denied citizenship.
Myanmar Foreign Ministry official Han Win Aung told The Associated Press that the repatriation involved “genuine citizens.”
Malaysia is home to about 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the UNHCR, including about 126,000 Rohingya who make up one of Southeast Asia’s largest refugee communities. Despite hosting them, Malaysia is not a party to the U.N. Refugee Convention and treats refugees as undocumented migrants.
Min Aung Hlaing, the leader of Myanmar’s military-backed government who was sworn in as president in April, is expected to visit Malaysia this month to discuss the refugee and migrant issues.

Trump unveils 'Super Intelligence Force' to oversee AI policy

US President Donald Trump says he has created a new taskforce focused on artificial intelligence, which will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.
The "Super Intelligence Force" will work to ensure that the US continues to lead in the technology's development and will coordinate the government's engagement with the public, Trump posted on Sunday.
It comes after the president signed an executive order on 29 September to rename AI as Super Intelligence, after previously saying the word artificial made it sound "fake".
Trump also said last week that he would set up a board to oversee AI safety after top tech bosses signed what he described as a "morally binding" pact.
"The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump wrote.
Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Undersecretary of Defense for Research, Engineering Emil Michael and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor will also be part of the taskforce.
It will report directly to the president and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.
The taskforce's chief, Clayton, took office as the US national intelligence director in August after Trump's original choice, Bill Pulte, was rejected by lawmakers.
On AI, Clayton has previously said: "When something's both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it."
Clayton previously served as US attorney for the Southern District of New York, overseeing several prominent cases, including the drug trafficking case against former Venezuelan President Nicholas Maduro.
The announcement of the taskforce follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry, including executives of OpenAI and Anthropic, to tighten regulation of the technology.
In an interview published on 4 October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of AI justify accepting some of its risks and argued that the technology should remain accessible to the public.
"The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency," Altman told Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded.
Over the weekend, a former leader in OpenAI's Safety Systems team wrote in an article for the Atlantic magazine that he had left the firm because its culture was "broken".
"As [OpenAI] sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed," wrote David Robinson, who was involved in safety and transparency reporting.
The BBC has contacted OpenAI for comment.
Last month, the ChatGPT-maker pulled the release of its latest AI model due to safety concerns.
Its AI models have come under scrutiny after a series of cyber security incidents involving its technology, including an unauthorised breach of Australian government systems.

Would you put money on whether Covid-19 originated from a lab? How about whether some of the footage from the Apollo 11 moon landing was actually filmed on Earth?
Verifact Markets, a new startup that bills itself as a “prediction market for disputed facts,” is betting that people will be eager to weigh in on questions like these. The company’s premise is so quirky it sounds like something a couple of philosophy and economics majors dreamed after too many bong rips in their dorm room: Instead of wagering on the future, why not trade on stuff that already happened?
When Verifact Markets launched on Friday, some of the initial topics traders could take a position on included whether Jeffrey Epstein died by suicide and whether insurance behemoth State Farm “intentionally delayed” claims related to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires. The featured market during beta testing was, indeed, about the origins of Covid-19. (As of writing, the market is still open, with “true” priced at 76 cents and “false” at 32; the majority of participants had put money on the pandemic beginning at Wuhan Institute of Virology.)
Verifact Markets is being funded and incubated by Positron Capital Management, the family office of tech investor Peter Wokwicz. He envisions the startup as a way to settle debates over hot-button issues like the amount of energy consumed by AI data centers. “I’m excited, because nobody’s done this before,” Wokwicz says. “We’re not going to shy away from controversial markets.”
In a regular prediction market, participants buy financial instruments known as event contracts, which are pegged to whether a specific event will take place in the future. Topics range from which team will win the Super Bowl to what the price of bitcoin will be in 15 minutes to whether the US and Iran will reach a nuclear deal. Someone who buys a “yes” contract on Polymarket that the Bears will start Case Keenum next week will make money if that happens. Similarly, someone who bets “no” on Kalshi that it will rain in Miami tomorrow will lose money if there’s a downpour.
Each prediction market has its own rules about how it resolves events, and sometimes things can get messy, like when Polymarket bettors tussled over whether Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky actually wore a suit, or when Kalshi traders revolted over how the platform settled a market on whether Iran’s supreme leader would leave power.
Verifact Markets’ setup is even messier. That’s by design, since the platform focuses specifically on scenarios where people disagree on what took place. It lists markets for past events that it considers “disputed” and lets its customers wager “true” or “false” on whether they really happened. People can also submit “evidence” for or against their position, and the company plans to offer rewards for credible documentation that helps resolve markets. If Verifact Markets determines that there’s enough evidence to make a call, it does so. If it still can’t tell, the company will “expire” a market and pay out users based on its calculation of the odds at the time.
According to Verifact Markets chief executive and cofounder Rodrigo Aquino, the markets themselves won’t determine whether something is true or false. That means even if all of the customers in a given market voted “true,” that won’t necessarily make it so. Trading prices will be factored in alongside other evidence and documentation that is submitted to the company by users. It is also planning to launch its own research system, which Aquino describes as “patent pending.” When I ask Aquino how the system works, he keeps the answer impressively vague: “We are analyzing, multi-dimensionally, a multitude of data points,” he says, noting that the process is “very mathematical, very quantitative” and also “very secretive.”
When I point out that credibly determining how the Covid pandemic started would be a massive news story, resolving a mystery that has eluded scientists for years, Aquino remains upbeat. “It’s doable,” he says.
Verifact says that it is currently in talks with market makers about providing liquidity. Right now, the project is so small that it is being bootstrapped by Positron Capital Management. There are a number of ongoing lawsuits in the US over whether prediction markets should be considered financial instruments or gambling, but it’s hard to discern how Verifact would factor into that debate because of its rather odd business model.
For the time being, the company is only offering its markets to people outside of the United States as it looks for the most viable legal path forward domestically, as it is not a licensed exchange in the US. But Wokwicz claims he purchased a regulated financial exchange in the last year and intends to roll Verifact into it when he can. Like Polymarket’s decentralized product, Verifact Markets is “on-chain,” and participants can make trades with stablecoins, a class of cryptocurrencies tied to the price of the US dollar and other fiat currencies.
Verifact Markets is part of a wave of startups interested in resolving the facts about disputed news and historical events. One of the most recent entries was the short-lived Peter Thiel–funded project Objection (later rebranded as The Primary), which aimed to determine whether specific media stories were accurate. But before the truth-adjudication stuff really got off the ground, The Primary pivoted to publishing news and a scoreboard for ranking journalists.
For now, there are very few details about how Verifact Markets will ultimately determine whether something is true or false, even though its entire value proposition rests on the idea that it’s uniquely positioned to do so. It's an extremely tall order, made even taller by all the other details that haven’t been worked out yet, like how the project will make money—it doesn’t plan to charge fees at launch. Wokwicz isn’t focused on that sort of thing, at least not yet. “What I'm looking forward to most is just some of the very unique evidence that people are going to dig up,” he says. “We're going to bring out truth—what is true and false.”
Some prediction market veterans say they are intrigued by Verifact Markets, even if there are plenty of remaining questions about how it will work. “I'll probably join just so I can keep making money off of the 2020 election for the rest of my existence,” says prominent prediction market trader Caleb Davies.

Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far
- Published
Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months.
The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police.
Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer.
The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
Here's what we know.
Busisiwe Mahlangu
Case 1
Busisiwe Mahlangu's body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July 2026, the first of a string of bodies found in Ekurhuleni within a two-month period. The 37-year-old was found naked with her hands bound with cable ties.
Police arrested a suspect, believed to be her partner, two days after her murder. He has been in police custody since then and has not been linked to the other deaths that followed.
Itumeleng Kekana
Case 2
Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was the second woman whose body was found in the same area on 3 August 2026.
The young mother disappeared in July and her body was found badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge in Kempton Park.
No arrests have been made so far.
Nomfesane Mjobo
Case 3
Nomfesane Mjobo's body was found on 26 August, also in Kempton Park.
Few details around her death have been released but like most of the victims, she was found partially or fully naked with bruises.
No arrests have been made.
Unknown woman
Case 4
Police confirmed the discovery of an unknown woman, in her 20s, on 7 September. The woman's body was found floating in a river in Olifantsfontain wearing only her underwear.
No further details have been shared about her death and no arrests have been made.
Gracious Nkomo
Case 5
Gracious Nkomo was the fifth woman whose body was discovered, again in the Kempton Park area.
Her partially clothed body was found on 10 September along a road close to South Africa's busiest airport. No arrests have been made in the 28-year-old's death.
Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo
Case 6
Elizabeth Moselakgomo was the sixth woman to be found, after a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for a daily run near her home in Kempton Park.
Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. It was the discovery of her body that really raised the alarm about the spate of killings. No arrests have been made in her case.
Unidentified woman
Case 7
Police confirmed the discovery of another body just two days after Moselakgomo was found. The body was found in Olifantsfontein on 14 September, but police have withheld her name as her family has not yet been informed.
No arrests have been made.
Dineo Motapane
Case 8
The body of Dineo Motapane, 38, was discovered on 15 September just two days after she was last seen alive.
Motapane's battered and partly burned body was found on the side of the road in Springs, another part of Ekurhuleni.
She leaves behind a young child. No arrests have been made in her case.
Jabulile Ntimba
Case 9
The body of Jabulile Ntimba, in her 30s, was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. This was the ninth body found in Ekurhuleni.
According to police, it appears Ntimba was killed because of a possible love triangle. Three people, two women and a man, were initially arrested for her grisly murder but the man was released due to insufficient evidence.
The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice.
Ntombifuthi Nxumalo
Case 10
The body of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, the 10th body found in Ekurhuleni, was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.
This has led to police believing she may have been stoned to death.
A 36-year-old man was arrested a day after Nxumalo's death after he had travelled to another province. He faces a murder charge.
Unidentified woman
Case 11
The body of a yet-to-be identified woman was found in Springs on Sunday - the 11th body found in Ekurhuleni.
The grim discovery was made by a security company patrolling the area.
The woman was found in an open field, but no further details have been shared.
No arrests have been made.
Boitumelo Gift Mashita
Case 12
Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken.
Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand.
Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies.
While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September.
The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg.
It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni.
President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience".
South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day.
Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests.

The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners.
“Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.
As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together, in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”
The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi university, by three men who posed as police officers.
Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood, after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.
Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year old were also reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by the bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.
Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.
Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say that nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic underreporting.
This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and they could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.
Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi university, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.
While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country requires a deep societal shift where men no longer feel they have ownership over women’s bodies.
“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,’ she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”
Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.
“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”
Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women; as one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.
Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old a graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender-equality initiative, said she has experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.
She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”
The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before – but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.
“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago, but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe.’”
Many of the Delhi university students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.
“Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades,” said Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for her masters in English at Delhi University. “It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”
Many on the marches said that it was no coincidence the protests took place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, which saw hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians take to the streets over education reform.
“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region.
Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.
The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”.
Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño:
‘Climate risk maps’ in China
In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees.
Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat.
In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.
Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.
Taiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke.
The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces.
Sri Lanka plans to process salterwater
El Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts of India there has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families.
The Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”.
In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets.
But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is in Sri Lanka, where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry.
Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water.
The country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable.
Tackling an agriculture crisis in south-east Asia
In south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs, disproportionately hitting the region. At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees.
During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%.
“We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore.
The Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.
“In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.”
With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says.
To prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers.
“We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” say Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.”
South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert system
South Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoes as being “boiled” in the ground.
The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours.
Officials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away.
Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoons
Japan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating.
El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised.
Japan recorded its first official “cruelly hot day” – or kokushobi – in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C.
Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons.
The public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm.
This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drowned during record-breaking rain in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo.

'He's taught us courage': Friend on Indian pilot hailed as a hero
- Published
When Captain Dharav Gosalia first heard what had happened to his old friend Smit Machchhar, he had one immediate reaction.
"I had goosebumps."
The two men have known each other since they were about 20, when they were neighbours in Ghatkopar, a Mumbai suburb, and began their flying training in New Zealand.
Machchhar was Gosalia's senior. They later spent six years as colleagues at SpiceJet, flying Boeing 737s, before their careers took them in different directions. Machchhar moved to Dubai and joined Flydubai in 2022. Gosalia went on to fly Boeing 777s for Air India.
"We have been in touch with messages," Gosalia says. "If there are some routes we have to fly, we discuss destinations and family on WhatsApp and phone."
- Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight? 
  - Published19 minutes ago
Sometimes their paths crossed in the air, too. In 2024, Gosalia was flying to London through Dubai airspace when he recognised Machchhar's voice on the radio. Machchhar was flying to Mumbai.
"We greeted each other," he recalls.
On Wednesday, Machchhar was captain of a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when another pilot attacked and stabbed him in the cockpit. The Boeing 737 Max was diverted to Tabuk in north-western Saudi Arabia, where Machchhar was taken to hospital.
He remains in a stable condition, according to the Indian embassy in Riyadh.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has called Machchhar a "true hero", saying he saved the lives of 174 people and prevented a "catastrophic mid-air disaster".
For Gosalia, however, the man at the centre of the extraordinary incident is still "Smit Mac" – the nickname used by his friends and colleagues - and a "very brilliant person".
"Outgoing person, jovial. Very jovial," he adds.
They would meet during layovers in places such as Milan and Bangkok, and play tennis-ball cricket when they were back in Mumbai. Machchhar also helped younger pilots, teaching new recruits and passing on what he had learnt.
"He is a very disciplined flier," Gosalia says.
That discipline was reinforced by years of training, including from former Indian Air Force pilots who moved into commercial aviation.
"That training gives you more focus, more discipline, and more focus on motor skills," Gosalia says.
One part of that training, he says, is known among pilots as "chair flying": rehearsing an emergency procedure while sitting in a chair, mentally running through the sequence and moving your hands to where the relevant switches and controls would be in the cockpit.
The idea is to make those movements instinctive when something goes wrong and there is little time to think.
Machchhar had plenty of experience to draw on. He had more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile.
Gosalia says the exact sequence of Wednesday's confrontation will become clearer from the aircraft's flight data and cockpit recordings. But whatever happened inside the cockpit, he says, Machchhar had to make decisions under an extraordinary kind of pressure.
"What happened to him, what he did – he was the commander on the flight," Gosalia says.
For a pilot, there are procedures for an engine failure, a fire or a loss of cabin pressure. There is no conventional checklist for another person trying to overpower you in the cockpit.
And that, Gosalia says, is where courage matters.
"How much courage plays a role? A lot," he says. "This was a threat to life."
Then comes the thought that perhaps best explains why the incident has affected him so deeply.
"Smit has taught us courage. Now we will do the same thing if something like this happens."

How Ceuta, football and Israel are shaping Morocco's election
- Published
Disillusioned young voters in Morocco were courted with viral football slogans, promises of one million jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls ahead of Wednesday's parliamentary elections.
Yet, for many young Moroccans, politics remains deeply disconnected from reality.
"I have no hope for this election. I'm ashamed of our political scene. It's a complete circus," Siham Azeroual, 32, an environmental activist who lives in the Atlas region, tells the BBC.
The outcome of the vote will decide the make-up of the next government, just weeks after 60,000 people risked their lives to cross from the North African country to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - a sign of the lack of opportunities many young people feel they have at home.
Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy where political parties compete for 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the legislative chamber.
Yet executive power remains closely tied to the crown. King Mohammed VI, the 63-year-old monarch, appoints the prime minister from the political party that comes first in the election, but also presides over the Council of Ministers - the country's most important policy-making body.
The current campaign also follows a wave of Gen Z protests that erupted in September 2025 over unemployment, healthcare and living costs.
Demonstrators chanted slogans like "freedom, dignity, and social justice" which escalated to "get out Akhannouch", a reference to current Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
More than 2,400 people faced prosecution following the unrest. Despite the crackdown, some young activists are choosing to enter the political arena.
Hamza El Kharroubi, 29, was briefly arrested during the protests. He is now running for parliament with the little-known Environment and Sustainable Development Party, which has a green agenda.
"As a young person, I don't have much hope. I joined this party because they wanted more Gen Z faces and they are allowing us to speak freely about our demands," El Kharroubi tells the BBC.
He comes from Tetouan, just 34km (21 miles) from Fnideq beach, where the migration wave to Ceuta started in late July.
Some 60,000 people crossed, both Moroccans and other nationalities. At least 100 people died in the largest migration surge to the enclave in recent history.
"We want justice for the families of those who died crossing to Ceuta. We want compensation for their families," El Kharroubi says.
He argues that the crossing was widely linked to economic hardship and unemployment.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates overall unemployment stood at 13% last year, while youth unemployment - between the ages of 15 and 24 - reached 37.3%.
El Kharroubi says his goal is not to compete with established heavyweights - but securing a voice in parliament to build toward 2031.
"As young people, we have to enter the parliament so by 2031 we have strong young politicians who can compete for a seat in the government."
Fouzi Lekjaa, head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a senior politician who works in the finance ministry, has emerged as the kingdom's newest political sensation - and a definite heavyweight.
Credited with helping the Atlas Lions - as the national men's football team is known - become global contenders, Lekjaa joined the centrist Party of Authenticity and Modernity (Pam) in July.
Videos of his campaign rallies have gone viral in the football-mad nation that is jointly hosting the next World Cup along with Spain and Portugal.
The clips show crowds chanting "Sir" which means "Go" in Moroccan Arabic - the iconic catchphrase from Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup run, when it became the first Arab and African side to make it to the semi-finals.
Lekjaa has promised to make Morocco sixth in the world in education and healthcare, to match the Fifa ranking of the men's football team.
Pam is competing against 26 other parties, including Prime Minister Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI). In its bid for a second term, RNI has renewed a pledge to create one million job opportunities by 2031.
Political expert Rachid Aourraz, from the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis (MIPA), remains sceptical about this promise.
"The slogan 'one million jobs' has become an overused electoral slogan. There is also talk of raising the minimum wage, but what is proposed cannot withstand a structural inability to create stable net jobs," Aourraz tells the BBC.
He adds that major parties "do not compete over an alternative model", but rather over how to implement public policies set by a royal vision.
Also seeking a political comeback is the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) - using anti-Israeli sentiments to woo voters.
Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 along with several other Arab countries, under the US-brokered Abraham Accords.
Led by populist former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, the PJD is campaigning heavily on a promise to end diplomatic ties with Israel. He says the normalisation was a "mistake" made by his party which led the government between 2016 and 2021.
Bilateral ties were hit during the Gaza war with weekly protests taking place in the capital, Rabat, against the Israeli diplomatic presence.
During the conflict the Israeli liaison office was closed and direct flights between the two countries were suspended.
Yet despite an outpouring of pro-Palestinian protests, with tens of thousands taking to the streets and setting ablaze the Israeli flag at the height of the war, it was announced earlier this month that Israel and Morocco had agreed to open full embassies in their respective countries.
This followed a meeting between their top diplomats and the US ambassador to the United Nations.
"We have to speak up," Benkirane told supporters at a campaign rally in Marrakesh.
"If we work hard, the king will close the Israeli embassy. The king does not like going against his own people," he added, warning of "the dangers of Israel and Zionism in Morocco".
I think young people should focus on the microscale: rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top"
More than half of Morocco's total population of roughly 38.8 million is under the age of 35 - though only 4% of the more than 15.8 million registered voters are aged between 18 and 24.
"I am not keeping up much with the campaigns - but I noticed the same faces as usual," says Hiba, a 27-year-old Moroccan living in Canada who preferred not to use her last name.
She lives in Montreal which has a large Moroccan diaspora of about 104,000 people, according to the 2016 census.
Many of last year's Gen Z protests were more vocal outside the country, where young Moroccans were able to express their anger without fear of repercussions.
Hiba, who co-organised several Gen Z protests in Montreal, says she would have considered voting had she been able to find a proxy in Morocco - which is how those in the diaspora can cast their ballot.
"Gen Z protests didn't go in vain. We achieved something. At least now we see more debates with young people on state TV," she says.
Azeroual, the environmental activist, agrees.
But having lived through both the 20 February movement in 2011 that changed the constitution and the recent Gen Z movement, she believes change must come from a multi-faceted approach.
"I think young people should focus on the microscale - rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top," she says.
Despite not being fully convinced by any political campaign, she says she will be heading to her local polling station to cast her ballot.
