In 1972, so the internet story goes, the award-winning American actor Jane Fonda traveled to Hanoi, North Vietnam, in the midst of the Vietnam War. At some point in her visit, Fonda met with U.S. soldiers being held by the North Vietnamese military as prisoners of war. While a camera allegedly recorded the meeting, the POWs supposedly managed to pass Fonda scraps of paper containing their Social Security numbers in the hopes they could be smuggled back to the U.S. to confirm they were still alive.
Instead, the story goes, Fonda handed the slips to a North Vietnamese officer as soon as the camera shut off. Three prisoners purportedly died from subsequent beatings and a fourth barely survived, living to tell the tale of Fonda's traitorous behavior.
It's a rumor that's been spreading for decades as of this writing, and we consistently receive reader mail requesting a fact check. We have in fact debunked the rumor, all the way back in 2000. This update takes a fresh look at that investigation. 
Our conclusion, however — that the specific tale about Fonda handing over the messages is false — hasn't changed in the past 26 years.
Fonda did visit North Vietnam
The story is loosely rooted in a context of truth, as many myths are. Fonda did visit North Vietnam as an antiwar activist in 1972, and, while there, she did meet with U.S. prisoners of war. She acknowledged this in a page on her website separating truth from fiction about her visit.
According to Fonda's account, she was one of roughly 300 Americans who traveled to Vietnam with the aim of ending the war throughout its course. One of her main goals was to tour and document a series of dikes and levees in the agriculturally important Red River Delta. The U.S. Air Force had reportedly bombed the dikes on purpose, possibly hoping to cause a catastrophic flood.
Upon seeing the dikes, Fonda concluded — as did some other observers — that the U.S. was intentionally bombing them. She shared her conclusion at a news conference in Paris not long after returning from Hanoi, according to contemporaneous reporting from The New York Times.
While in North Vietnam, Fonda also made statements on Radio Hanoi, a radio station that broadcast English-language propaganda aimed at demoralizing U.S. troops. "I implore you, I beg you to consider what you are doing," The New York Times reported her as saying.
The anti-aircraft gun photo
But the most likely reason the secret messages story struck such a lasting chord is because of an infamous, widely published photograph of Fonda sitting on a North Vietnamese anti-aircraft gun. As soon as the photo was released in the U.S., many began calling Fonda a traitor and referring to her by the nickname "Hanoi Jane."
Fonda has said repeatedly in the years since the picture's release that she regrets being photographed in that pose. She recalled online that the photo was taken of her on her last day in Hanoi. Exhausted from her trip, she was taken to meet North Vietnamese soldiers, Fonda said. They sang her a song in Vietnamese, and then she sang them a Vietnamese song she had memorized for the occasion. The soldiers loved it, applauding and laughing.
Amid the revelry, according to Fonda, someone led her to the anti-aircraft gun and snapped the photo without her being fully aware of what was happening.
"It is possible that it was a set up, that the Vietnamese had it all planned," she wrote. "I will never know. But if they did I can't blame them. The buck stops here. If I was used, I allowed it to happen."
The photo was published and Fonda gained a longstanding reputation in some circles as anti-American and treasonous. That reputation, deserved or otherwise, made it easier for some to believe that she might have quite literally betrayed U.S. prisoners of war by revealing secret messages entrusted to her to their captors.
Debunking the 'secret messages' myth
Since 1999, the story about the POWs' messages has generally appeared in the form of this copypasta. It is relatively unchanged from its email chain message origins in the late '90s:
From 1963-65, Col. Larry Carrigan was in the 47FW/DO (F-4E's). He spent 6 years in the "Hanoi Hilton". . . The first three of which his family only knew he was "missing in action." His wife lived on faith that he was still alive. His group, too, got the cleaned-up, fed and clothed routine in preparation for a "peace delegation" visit.
They, however, had time and devised a plan to get word to the world that they were alive and still survived. Each man secreted a tiny piece of paper, with his Social Security Number on it, in the palm of his hand. When paraded before Ms. Fonda and a cameraman, she walked the line, shaking each man's hand and asking little encouraging snippets like: "Aren't you sorry you bombed babies?" and "Are you grateful for the humane treatment from your benevolent captors?" Believing this HAD to be an act, they each palmed her their sliver of paper.
She took them all without missing a beat. . . At the end of the line and once the camera stopped rolling, to the shocked disbelief of the POWs, she turned to the officer in charge and handed him all the little pieces of paper...
Three men died from the subsequent beatings. Colonel Carrigan was almost number four but he survived, which is the only reason we know of her actions that day.
As previously stated, Fonda did meet with prisoners of war — exactly seven of them — at one point on her visit. But Larry Carrigan (a real POW), wasn't one of them. In 1999, he told Snopes editor David Emery (working for About.com at the time) via phone the rumor was a "figment of somebody's imagination" and that in fact he had never met Fonda. 
The Minnesota Star-Tribune ran an article (part 1, part 2) debunking the claim in 2005, quoting Edison Miller, who did actually meet with Fonda while a POW. "The whole email story about Jane Fonda is just malarkey," he said.
Miller told the Star-Tribune he didn't pass Fonda a slip of paper, nor, to his knowledge, did any of the other POWs who met with her that day. He said Fonda didn't ask them any questions beyond their names — which raises another point: Why would the POWs have needed to pass Fonda their Social Security numbers?
By the time of Fonda's visit in 1972, some prisoners of war released back to the U.S. had described horrid prison conditions and torture at the hands of the North Vietnamese, which later memoirs and reporting confirmed but also suggested had began to improve around 1969.
(This, in and of itself, is another discrepancy. The Star-Tribune also spoke to Mike McGrath, a former Navy pilot who ran the NAM-POWs veterans group in the late 1990s. He said there had been no known cases of U.S. prisoners of war in Vietnam being beaten to death since 1969, three years before Fonda's visit.)
Even assuming the torture had continued (and had not been documented in the following 50 years), the North Vietnamese would have wanted to maintain appearances of at least decent conditions within the prison camps. That would have included letting Fonda (and through her, the outside world) know with whom she was meeting. Fonda would have had time to memorize the names of the people she met and report them afterward — and Miller noted that she did specifically ask their names.
As one final note: The full copypasta also purported to relate accusations made by a different prisoner of war, Jerry Driscoll. According to the text, he spat at Fonda and was beaten for it when she visited in 1972. Speaking to the Star-Tribune in 2005, Driscoll not only denied those claims but denied ever meeting Fonda at all.

‘Proved misbehaviour’: Former officials serve impeachment notice against CEC Gyanesh Kumar; delegation lists 6 charges
The delegation accused Gyanesh Kumar of taking decisions in the name of the ECI without adequate consideration by the full commission.
A delegation of former civil servants and social activists on Monday moved a chargesheet and notice of impeachment against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, accusing him of “proved misbehaviour” and demanding his removal from office under Article 324(5) of the Constitution.
The move came amid reported police barricading of routes leading to the Election Commission of India (ECI) ahead of the delegation’s proposed submission.
The notice alleged that Kumar had followed a “sustained pattern of wilful disregard of law and constitutional duty, abuse of authority and conduct destructive of the integrity of India's electoral democracy”.
ALSO READ | SC refuses to restrain Gyanesh Kumar, says can't pass order based on news report
The delegation said the alleged actions had undermined the ECI's credibility and independence and asked Kumar to resign. It said that in the absence of his resignation, “We, the People of India” were serving the impeachment notice and demanding his removal.
The chargesheet contains six allegations.
What are the six charges against Gyanesh Kumar?
1. Undermining collective functioning of ECI
The delegation accused Kumar of taking decisions in the name of the ECI without adequate consideration by the full commission. It specifically cited the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), alleging that it proceeded without sufficient discussion, consultation, rule-making or recorded proceedings.
The notice also referred to reported objections by two Election Commissioners over decisions allegedly taken without their knowledge and meetings held without proper agendas and minutes.
ALSO READ | Supreme Court issues notice to Centre, poll panel over CEC Gyanesh Kumar's functioning; no interim order
2. Unauthorised changes to Form 6
The second charge relates to changes made to Form 6, used for inclusion of names in electoral rolls.
The delegation alleged that a modified version was used despite objections within the commission that the changes were “unauthorised and illegal”. It further alleged that voters whose names had previously appeared on electoral rolls were required to state that they were seeking inclusion for the first time.
3. Unlawful use of ECINET
The delegation alleged that ECINET was deployed in a way that undermined the statutory authority of Electoral Registration Officers, who are responsible for additions, deletions and corrections in electoral rolls.
It questioned the legality of the system and cited the later decision to set up an expert committee to examine its compliance with electoral laws and rules.
4. Mass disenfranchisement through SIR
The notice described SIR as an “unprecedented exercise in mass disenfranchisement”.
It alleged that the exercise placed excessive responsibility on voters to establish their eligibility and was implemented without adequate preparation, training and safeguards against wrongful exclusion.
The delegation claimed that 13.3 crore names had already been deleted from pre-SIR rolls and projected that the gap between the adult population and electorate could reach 15 crore or more.
It alleged that women, poor people, migrants, minorities and elderly voters were disproportionately affected.
5. Conduct affecting ECI's impartiality
The fifth charge accused Kumar of conduct that, according to the delegation, created an apprehension of political partisanship.
The notice cited his alleged public interventions involving opposition leaders and what it called “combative political rhetoric”, alongside decisions surrounding SIR.
“You can no longer be a referee in a game where you are widely perceived to be aligned with a player,” it alleged.
6. Breach of statutory duty
The final charge invoked Section 32(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1950.
The delegation alleged that the changes to electoral forms, alleged circumvention of Electoral Registration Officers, use of ECINET, concealment of records and failure to address known violations showed a prima facie pattern of wilful breach of official duty.
Who signed the notice?
Among the signatories are former Delhi lieutenant governor Najeeb Jung, former home secretary G K Pillai, former secretary to the Government of India Amitabha Pandey, Jayashree Mukherjee, IAS (retd), Ashok Sharma, IFS (retd), former Central Information Commissioner Yashovardhan Azad and former civil servant Ashish Joshi.
Aishe Ghosh, N Sai Balaji, Dinesh Srirangarajan, Sandeep Yadav, Amrita Johri, Anjali Bhardwaj and Yogendra Yadav are also listed as signatories.
The delegation concluded that the alleged acts amounted to “proved misbehaviour” under Article 324(5), claiming that Kumar had forfeited the “moral and constitutional authority” to remain CEC.
The allegations are contained in the chargesheet submitted by the delegation and do not by themselves establish wrongdoing by Kumar.

“In what world,” New York Gov. Kathy Hochul asked on Friday, “would the police learn from a victim that she’d been literally gang raped while she was intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney?”
The Cornell case, explained
A timeline of how a student went ignored at Cornell.
Hochul was speaking about the case of a former Cornell student who said she was raped by several members of the university’s Chi Phi fraternity in 2024. At the time, the district attorney filed no criminal charges.
The case has rocked the nation and forced a renewed reckoning over how sexual assault is dealt with in higher education. While the district attorney has defended his handling of the case, many politicians and legal experts are now examining whether certain details of the alleged victim’s account were neglected, and prosecutors have reopened the case.
Amy Wang is a staff reporter at the Washington Post who’s been covering the story over the past week. She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about what allegedly happened on the night in question, what happened afterward, and what we still don’t know.
Since the two spoke, New York state Attorney General Letitia James has also been assigned to oversee the case and said it is now “an active criminal investigation.” As new information comes to light, further legal action could be taken.
Below is an excerpt of the conversation between King and Wang, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
In October of 2024, a young woman went to a fraternity house near Cornell University’s campus. Who is this young woman, and why did she go to the frat house that night?
The young woman is only identified in documents as Jane Doe, so we don’t know her name. She was, at the time, 20 years old. She was a sophomore at Cornell. And around 11 pm on the night of October 19, 2024, this Jane Doe goes to a bar on campus, and then, after that, goes to the Chi Phi fraternity house to hang out with a friend.
She said that she was already pretty intoxicated at that point, and she’d had maybe 10 drinks in about three hours. Her friend at the fraternity house hands her a beer. After that is where she alleges that another member of the fraternity pressured her into taking drugs, specifically ketamine and marijuana, and drinking more alcohol. She alleges that two members of the fraternity assaulted her, and that one of them later sent a Snapchat message out to active Chi Phi members. The message is pretty graphic, but essentially invites them to join in, and several did.
In about three weeks, this young woman was going to go to the Cornell campus police and report what happened that night. But in the interim, what was going on? What was happening?
We now know, based on reporting by the New York Times and CBS News, this young woman was a member of a campus sorority, so she went to a member of her sorority and was trying to make sense of what happened. She was still processing it in real time. She wasn’t using, according to their reporting, the word “rape” or “assault.” And she was also seeing rumors circulating around campus about what had taken place at the fraternity house and was growing concerned about how they portrayed her.
She, in the interim, also received a text message from one of the seven men at the fraternity essentially apologizing for how things went down the other night. She is not yet accusing them of assault, but is chatting, even seeks to reassure him in that first message.
On October 22, she then makes an appointment at the campus health clinic because she had what she thought was a UTI and wanted to be tested because she told the doctor that she had gone through a traumatic experience.
According to the New York Times reporting, you could see her thinking about what happened kind of evolve over those few weeks. She at some point says that this is starting to ruin her life, and she’s sleeping and crying and she’s feeling ashamed. She’s just really grappling with what had taken place, trying to make sense of it. By November 3 is when, according to these investigative documents that were obtained by the Times, she kind of comes to this conclusion that what happened at the party at Chi Phi was assault.
She texts one of the seven fraternity members and says, “This was not consensual. I was given more ketamine than I can remember,” and that she was uncomfortable. A few days later, November 7th, 2024, according to these documents, she goes to the ER and asks for a rape kit. And the following day is when she goes to Cornell University Police.
When she goes to the police, how does she characterize what happened to the police? What does she tell them?
What she tells the police is that she believes she was assaulted, and she tells the police that it had started out as something that was consensual. And then at the end she says, “I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped.” She tells police she was extremely uncomfortable and that she kept taking ketamine in part because she thought she might black out and pass out. She had thought of at least two of the men as her friends. After the events of that night, she is then confronted with rumors that were spreading across campus, sort of depicting her as loose and blaming her essentially.
What happens after Jane Doe talks to the police? What do they do?
When she talks to Cornell University Police, they summarize what she said in a six-page statement that she then signs. And that is the statement that is submitted to the Tompkins County district attorney.
And the district attorney would be the person who would bring charges or decide not to bring charges. What does he decide?
Yes, so the district attorney decides not to bring charges in 2024 based on, he has said, the sworn statement that she signs to police.
The DA says no charges for the seven men. Were they disciplined in any way?
We don’t know exactly how each of the men were disciplined. Cornell has said that they faced a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions and suspensions. One of the details that had gone particularly viral about this is that the disciplinary measures included for some of the students to write essays. Cornell has not denied that, but it has specifically denied that the students only had to write essays as a disciplinary measure. The university has cited privacy laws and said it really can’t release any more specifics about how individual students were punished or not punished.
What did Jane Doe do after first talking to the police and then learning the DA wasn’t going to press charges?
After she goes to police, we know she remains on campus and she has to continue seeing some of these men. And she also participates in the school’s Title IX investigation, which takes place over several months and concludes at some point in 2025.
I want to ask you about the DA. He is out in public defending his decision to not press charges in 2024. How is he defending himself?
The DA is a big part of the story. This is the Tompkins County District Attorney. His name is Matthew Van Houten. And he has said that in 2024, based on the written statement from Jane Doe, they did not have what they needed to press criminal charges.
It’s important to note that we, as in the public, we’ve not actually seen a copy of Jane Doe’s sworn statement. The DA issued a press release in which he summarizes that statement. And in that summary, he describes her characterization of this as voluntary and conscious and consensual. That is at odds with some of the investigative documents that we’ve seen reported since then, including that transcript of Jane Doe’s interview with Cornell Police in which she very confidently says that she believes she was raped and even says that she was physically hit during that night.
The DA said that he did not see, before the lawsuit, the screenshot of the Snapchat message where the frat members are talking pretty crudely about the situation, and he also says he didn’t see the transcript of the interview between Jane Doe and police.
We now know the names of the seven men who were there that night. Have they said anything?
The seven men themselves have not publicly said anything, and the lawyers for three of those seven men have publicly denied the allegations. One of them says that his client went into the room, but immediately left and didn’t participate in the assault.
This is a story that is developing very quickly, and it seems like new information is coming out just about every day. What do we know about what happens next?
So there’s at least two things going on here. There is the reopened criminal investigation.
Separately, there’s the civil lawsuit that Jane Doe filed last month, and that is not dependent in any way on how the criminal investigation goes, but that will also proceed against the university, the seven fraternity members, and the fraternity itself.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Alena Beliauskaya, a 37-year-old product director based in San Francisco. The following has been edited for length and clarity.
Here in San Francisco, it seems like everyone is a startup founder.
I'm the director of product management at Wolf Games, an AI narrative games company, where I work part-time. On the side, I run 12 Scrappy Founders, a founders community in the Bay Area with paid memberships and sponsored events.
When I first moved here for my job in March 2025, I wanted to make friends, so I started going to founder events, but the interactions were so transactional. The first question everyone asks you is, 'What's your goal at this event?' So, I started hosting my own events.
I'm an outdoorsy person and love extreme sports, so I'd plan a weekend hike, a backpacking trip, or dirt biking in Tahoe and invite other founders to join me. Now, I make over $10,000 in revenue each month and take home $2,000 to $3,000 in profit.
I've worked in startups for about 15 years and am a founder
It was natural to build my network around other founders. These are the people whose lives and problems I understand best. Finding like-minded people who understand startups and also want to spend Saturday riding dirt bikes in Tahoe is worth more to me than another 100 LinkedIn connections.
At our events, there's no formal networking, and nobody pitches. People got to know each other by spending eight hours on a trail or learning to ride a motorcycle together.
I started my community group charging $0 and now earn $10,000 in monthly revenue
I didn't charge at first because we started with hiking, which doesn't cost anything. But when we started dirt biking, I usually paid out of my pocket and then asked people to reimburse me.
This hobby was starting to take up a lot of my free time, and I thought about monetizing it, but I debated at first because I thought that if I turned it into a business, I might stop enjoying myself.
I started thinking about monetization around spring this year, after so many members told me I needed to because they were getting so much value. I started rolling out memberships at the beginning of this summer.
We have over 600 founders in our community
To join, the person's startup needs to be at the seed, Series A, or Series B stage. Most members have AI startups, because that's what is happening right now. You also have to be based in the Bay Area, since events are in person.
We're all connected on Slack, and there are about 20 paid members. There are two tiers right now. General membership is $99 a month, which includes free members-only events, priority access, personalized introductions to founders and investors, and access to the private member platform and Slack community. Our core membership, which is full, costs $3,000 a year, and core members get to work with me on where the community goes next.
We also monetize working with brands that sponsor many of our events. Recently, we partnered with Red Bull. I run paid experiences like hard hikes, overnight camps, dirt-biking, go-karting, pickleball, poker nights, and roundtables.
I'm not planning to make my side hustle a full-time job
I just want to figure out how to grow and nurture this community well and have something joyful in my free time.
I invest much of my free time in this side hustle. Almost every Saturday, I spend the full day outdoors with the founders. Besides that, I spend about three to four hours a day organizing.
My advice to those wanting to start a side hustle is to find something you love. You already spend the whole day at your full-time job, and often don't have much energy left. Your side hustle should bring you joy, which will motivate you to keep going.

'Money-grab' or celebration? NFL kicks off London series
- Published
Once upon a time, tickets for NFL games in London were like gold dust.
All 43 games have been near capacity at Wembley, Twickenham and Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.
According to the NFL, its UK fanbase has swelled to 18.6 million, with 4.5 million of those considered 'avid' fans.
So in the build-up to this year's London series, why were thousands of tickets still available for two of the three games?
Next week's clash between the Philadelphia Eagles and Jacksonville Jaguars at Tottenham sold out in hours.
But the crowd for Sunday's game at Tottenham between Washington Commanders and Indianapolis Colts only reached 60,907 after ticket prices were slashed, and large sections remain unsold for the Wembley game on 18 October.
The NFL is playing a record nine regular-season games abroad this season but 19 years after the first London game, has the NFL reached a saturation point in the UK?
Why have ticket sales been slow?
Tickets to see Indianapolis beat Washington 30-13 on Sunday went on sale in July at £79-£245.
But the NFL then dropped prices twice, in late August and again last week. That meant some fans who paid £185 were sat next to fans who paid £79 a few days ago.
Some tickets were also discounted or free via the Blue Light Card and Tickets For Good platforms.
Matt Cullen has travelled from Cambridge to most of the London games and said there were two main reasons for the slow sales; a price hike and a season-ticket package being scrapped.
"I find the prices now mind-boggling," he added. "It's so far above the rate of inflation that it just feels like a money-grab. It's priced out a lot of long-term fans."
In 2019, tickets ranged from £55 to £125. According to Ticket-Compare,, external UK inflation has since risen by about 32.4% and the cheapest NFL London tickets have risen by 43.9%. The most expensive have seen a 96.5% hike.
Season-ticket packages had been available, guaranteeing seats for each London game with a discount, but they were scrapped after the 2024 season.
"It felt like a kick to the head for a lot of loyal fans who'd supported the games for a long time and spent a lot of money," said Cullen, a former season-ticket holder. "But I do understand the NFL wants to bring new fans in."
Why NFL expansion is a 'double-edged sword'
UK fans have also complained about the quality of recent match-ups in London when compared to those in the new countries where the NFL has expanded.
Australia hosted a divisional clash between the San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams last month, while the Baltimore Ravens and Dallas Cowboys played out a thriller in Brazil last week.
"It was an amazing game and we haven't had many of those unfortunately," added Cullen.
The best team coming to London this year is Philadelphia, who have reached two of the past four Super Bowls, and their game next week is a sell-out even though it was the most expensive.
The Jaguars face the Houston Texans in two weeks and Dave, another former season-ticket holder, will travel from Chorley.
"We were all gutted when they took the season tickets away," he admitted. "The way we saw it, we weren't wanted anymore because we didn't spend the money that new fans do on merchandise and we get to the stadium later.
"But it has opened it up for more fans to have the opportunity to attend so it's a double-edged sword."
'One of the greatest events for neutrals'
BBC Sport spoke to dozens of fans at Sunday's game and none of them were aware ticket prices had dropped. None seemed to care either.
American fans know the London games don't provide the same tailgating experience they get back home, but they - and the players - are still fascinated by the eclectic crowd at international games.
Fans still travel from all over the UK, Europe and the US, wearing jerseys of all the NFL teams.
"It's still one of the greatest sporting events that neutrals can go to," said Dave. "I don't think there's any other sport where you'd get tens of thousands watching teams they don't support.
"It was always a celebration of the game. People would go for the love of the sport rather than the two teams that were playing and I think that's still the same."
It sure felt like a Washington home game when they recovered a Colts fumble on just the game's second play.
The crowd produced an even bigger roar when third-choice quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis - replacing the injured Marcus Mariota - made a 47-yard touchdown pass to Treylon Burks in the third quarter.
The Commanders thought they had drawn level when Antonio Williams ran in an 87-yard score, but the touchdown was chalked off for a Washington penalty.
Indianapolis quarterback Daniel Jones then got in to seal their success, with Jonathan Taylor having run in two touchdowns for the Colts.
Biles sprinkles stardust on London opener
It is hard to imagine anyone went home disappointed, no matter what price they paid.
The stands were bathed in sunshine and fans looked like they were having the time of their life as they sang Sweet Caroline and Wonderwall in unison.
Oasis' Noel Gallagher was booed when he appeared on the big screen - no doubt because of his football allegiance to Manchester City - and former Manchester United and England striker Wayne Rooney was also among the crowd, wearing a half-and-half scarf.
Olympian Simone Biles travelled to London to support her husband Jonathan Owens, who is a safety for the Colts, and as long as stars such as those show up at NFL games, international fans will want to be there too.
"There's been a lot of anger from fans on social media about the ticket prices but it's only what they do with last-minute holidays," added Dave.
"Even though some of us fans see it as poor way for the NFL to run it, they've got a full stadium.
"We're just not used to dynamic pricing in the UK. It was the same with Oasis tickets for their reunion. We were outraged at that but we still all went didn't we."

Ben Whittaker: Conor Wallace scare raises questions over light-heavyweight's title credentials, says Matthew Macklin
Ben Whittaker beat Conor Wallace by unanimous decision in Birmingham on Saturday, despite a wobbly final three rounds for the Olympic silver medallist; Sky Sports' Matthew Macklin says Whittaker needs more fights before his shot at the IBF light-heavyweight belt which the win earned him
Monday 5 October 2026 15:50, UK
Ben Whittaker's recent scare against Conor Wallace has raised questions about whether he has the attributes needed to win a world title, says Sky Sports expert Matthew Macklin.
After controlling the fight from the start, Whittaker was troubled by a left hand from Wallace in the 10th round and then looked ragged in the 12th as he repeatedly slipped to the canvas before clinging on to claim a points win on Saturday in Birmingham.
Whittaker's victory lined up a shot at the IBF light-heavyweight belt which is held by unified champion Dmitry Bivol, but Macklin believes the Olympic silver medallist is not yet ready to challenge the Russian.

Macklin told Sky Sports: "Ben has been on a run of pretty spectacular performances, hasn't he? That said, if we're honest about the calibre of opposition, we know it's pretty low for him and where he is aiming towards being.
"All of a sudden, they stepped it up again with Conor Wallace. He boxed really well for most of the fight, but nonetheless, at the end of the fight, he struggled.
"He got caught and then struggled to shake off the effects of that shot. He recovered momentarily, but not properly. He got his head together a little bit, but was still hurt because you could see he didn't really regain control of the fight.
"I think he needs more than one [fight before Bivol], probably a few.
"While Conor Wallace is a nice boxer, you wouldn't put him in the category of your Bivols and your Callum Smiths.
"Look at the fight between Callum Smith and Joshua Buatsi, and what those two went through in that fight, and then you see how Whittaker unravelled on Saturday night, there's no way you'd say he beats those two guys.
"He has the skill, the sleekness, the speed and the savvy to mix it with those guys, but has he got the toughness, the chin, the stamina, the power, the hardness to mix it with those guys over 12 hard rounds? He hasn't shown that so far.
"That's not to say that Ben isn't tough or hard. But we can only judge him on what we've seen, and we've seen him unravel a couple of times.
"In the first Liam Cameron fight, he was unravelling and then obviously they both fell out the ring. Fair play to him, in the rematch, he came out and looked brilliant, but against Conor Wallace, he was boxing well, controlling it, but then gets nailed a couple of times and, all of a sudden, he starts to unravel.
"Fair play again, he got through it. But against a Bivol or a Callum Smith, or a Buatsi or William Hutchinson, would he have got through it against those guys? Probably not.
"I think [his trainer] Andy Lee has done a great job with him, but I also think that there's only so much you can do in the gym. You've still got to get the experience on the night, under the lights, in a real fight against real high calibre opposition.

"It's great getting the highlight-reel knockouts - it's great for your ego, for the perception of you and from a promotional point of view, to create the star quality and the hype. That's important when you're trying to build a star, but you also need to build the fighter.

"If you're not getting seasoned, if you're not putting the stuff that you're learning in the gym into practice, on the night and when you need it, it won't be there because you haven't developed it.
"By the way, I like him a lot and I want him to do well, but he hasn't been managed well in his career in terms of the opponents he's fought. He needs some proper fights."

Flávio Bolsonaro is in pole position to win Brazil’s presidential election, after a far-right tsunami propelled him to a shock first-round victory over the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, leaving progressive voters reeling.
The 45-year-old rightwing candidate received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – meaning the 80-year-old leftwinger has a mountain to climb if he is to bounce back in the second round on 25 October. Never, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot.
“Miracles are possible in politics. But I don’t see that happening,” the political scientist Miguel Lago said of Lula’s chances of snapping back. “I don’t see Flávio losing this election now.”
The far-right surge was a triumph – albeit an incomplete one – for the Bolsonaro clan and its 71-year-old patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro.
The disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula, saw four relatives elected to congress. His 44-year-old wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, won a seat in the senate, as did his second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, who is 43. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, 28-year-old Jair Renan Bolsonaro, and the ex-president’s 62-year-old brother, Renato Bolsonaro, both won seats in the lower house of congress.
Across Latin America’s biggest democracy, key congressional and gubernatorial races were also won by staunch Bolsonaristas including Tarcísio de Freitas, who was re-elected as the governor of São Paulo state, and Sérgio Moro, who was elected governor of the southern state of Paraná. Both men were ministers during Bolsonaro’s 2018-22 government.
Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) will now boast the largest caucus in the senate with 28 of its 81 seats. Combined with the seats of other hard-right parties, that number rises to 43, giving the movement an upper house majority.
Meanwhile, pro-Lula senate candidates, including the former environment minister Marina Silva, the leftwing veteran Benedita da Silva, and the centrist former planning minister Simone Tebet, suffered bitter defeats.
Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, two young Bolsonarista social media warriors, became the best-voted congresspeople in Brazilian history, securing more than 3m votes.
“We are experiencing a revolution … The far right is growing in a very consistent way, election after election,” said Lago, calling the election the worst for progressive and moderate centrist parties since the late 80s.
Lago believed Lula had managed to interrupt the advance of Bolsonaro’s populist movement in 2022, thanks to positive voter memories of his first two terms, from 2002 to 2010. Back then, a global commodities boom allowed Brazil’s first working-class president to fund major social welfare programmes that helped millions escape poverty. “But it was just an interregnum,” Lago said.
Control of the senate should allow pro-Bolsonaro politicians to approve an amnesty for their movement’s charismatic leader, allowing the former president to emerge from the Brasília mansion where he is living under house arrest and reassert his leadership of the far right.
“I think he will be freed and I think he will be very important during Flávio Bolsonaro’s [presidency],” said Lago. “Flávio will be running the country and [Jair] Bolsonaro will be doing what he has always done: leading the revolution.”
The senate majority may also help Bolsonaro’s third son, Eduardo Bolsonaro, return from self-imposed exile in the US. The 42-year-old, who has close ties to Donald Trump’s Maga movement, was sentenced in absentia to four years in prison earlier this year for coercion – the result of his lobbying the Trump administration to interfere in his father’s coup trial. Eduardo Bolsonaro reportedly hopes to become foreign minister if his brother wins the presidency.
Trump, who has been accused of trying to sway the election in Bolsonaro’s favour, has yet to comment on Sunday’s result, although writing on his Truth Social network, he praised the speed of the vote count. But the US president will be delighted by the strong rightwing showing, a major boost to his attempt to expand the conservative “orange wave” sweeping Latin America to its biggest democracy and economy. Recent years have seen a succession of pro-Trump presidents win power in the region, from Costa Rica, Honduras and El Salvador to Chile and Colombia.
One of Trump’s most enthusiastic regional cheerleaders, the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, celebrated Bolsonaro’s “historic” victory against “the communist Lula”. “The American continent belongs to citizens who want to live in freedom,” Milei wrote on X.
The prime minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, wished Bolsonaro “good luck in the final” and celebrated his “great victory”. He wrote on X: “I look forward to restoring the extraordinary friendship between Israel and Brazil.”
Speaking after Sunday’s result was confirmed, Lula put a brave face on what analysts called a catastrophic night for the left. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil,” he said, vowing to expose his rival’s “dark past”, which involves well-documented ties to members of Rio’s underworld and corruption allegations, which Bolsonaro has denied.
But the mood at Lula’s post-election event was reportedly funereal and Bolsonaro goes into the second round as the firm favourite. He is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates – Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema – who, between them, won more than 5.5m votes.
Santos quickly announced he would endorse neither candidate, considering both Lula and Bolsonaro to be “crooks”. Zema has vowed to vote against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) in the runoff, while Caiado has yet to declare his intentions.
Lula’s best hope may be convincing some of the record 33 million Brazilians who did not vote to turn out next time. “He will need to mobilise these apathetic voters who, in a sense, have already abandoned politics, which will be an extremely difficult task,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right.
Rocha has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters and identified “a great deal of voter apathy, especially among those who are not aligned with Bolsonarismo, and who could potentially vote for Lula”.
Although Flávio Bolsonaro has held political office for more than 20 years, “for undecided voters, his main positive characteristic is this idea of ‘renewal’, despite his possible involvement in corruption and with paramilitary groups,” Rocha added.
Lago believed only a dramatic shift from Lula’s campaign – such as changing the candidate, or a severe scandal involving Bolsonaro – could change the election’s outcome. But he was doubtful that would occur.

Police in Moscow detained around 60 protesters after an authorised rally descended into a rare display of anti-Kremlin dissent.
Demonstrators chanted slogans including “Freedom for political prisoners”, “For fair elections” and “Down with the Tsar” – seen as a reference to Vladimir Putin – during a Communist Party rally in the Russian capital on Sunday.
The gathering was organised by the Russian rights group OVD-Info to mark the anniversary of Russia’s 1993 constitutional crisis, but police reportedly began making arrests more aggressively as protesters shifted towards openly anti-Kremlin slogans.
It came as German chancellor Friedrich Merz announced a further €1bn in military aid to Ukraine during a visit to Kyiv in a show of support for president Volodymyr Zelensky.
The military package includes long-range strike weapons, combat drones and satellite technology, "so that Ukraine can also target Russian launch pads," Merz said at a news conference.
Berlin also pledged around €350m to help repair and protect Ukraine’s battered energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
Meanwhile, Russia hit Kyiv’s North Bridge on Sunday, the capital’s mayor said. The roadway of the bridge had already been attacked on Saturday, Vitali Klitschko said.
South Korea’s Lee threatens action against Ukraine as row over North Korean prisoners deepens
South Korean president Lee Jae Myung has threatened further action against Ukraine unless Kyiv apologises for publicly revealing the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul.
Seoul and Kyiv have been locked in an escalating diplomatic dispute since Volodymyr Zelensky announced at the UN General Assembly last month that Ukraine had handed over two North Korean soldiers captured while fighting alongside Russian forces.
Lee said the transfer was covered by a confidentiality agreement and has accused Ukraine of breaching it. Kyiv has disputed Seoul’s account of the agreement.
“If the refusal to acknowledge the facts and issue a public apology continues, we will take additional measures,” Lee said on Friday, without specifying what action South Korea could take.
Zelensky addressed the transfer again on Sunday, saying Seoul had asked Kyiv to hand over the soldiers.
“South Korea asked us to give them North Korean soldiers. By the way, according to their constitution, they are their citizens ... so we gave them these two guys,” he told reporters.
He did not refer to Lee’s demand for an apology or the South Korean president’s threat of further measures.
Moscow detains 60 protesters after chants of 'Down with the Tsar'
Moscow police detained around 60 people at an authorised Communist Party rally on Sunday after protesters began chanting anti-Kremlin slogans, according to the party and Russian rights group OVD-Info.
The rally marked the anniversary of Russia’s 1993 constitutional crisis, when a confrontation between then-president Boris Yeltsin and hardline lawmakers culminated in the military shelling of Moscow’s parliament building.
Authorities said 123 people were killed, although unofficial estimates put the death toll in the hundreds.
The Communist Party has held annual events to mark the anniversary as a symbol of resistance to reforms introduced during the Yeltsin era.
This year’s authorised gathering, however, took a more openly anti-Kremlin turn as demonstrators chanted slogans including “Freedom for political prisoners”, “For fair elections” and “Down with the Tsar”.
According to OVD-Info, protesters also chanted “No to political repression”, “Down with Roskomnadzor” and “Down with the party of crooks and thieves”.
Although Moscow authorities had approved the rally, detentions reportedly intensified towards the end of the gathering as participants began chanting more directly against the Kremlin.
Around 20 people were initially taken to Moscow’s Krasnopresnenskiy police station before the number of reported detainees rose to about 60, OVD-Info said.
Those detained were not all Communist Party supporters. They included 26 Communist Party participants, 30 members of the liberal Yabloko party and several other activists.
The Communist Party, Russia’s largest parliamentary opposition group, broadly aligns itself with the Kremlin on major national security and foreign policy issues, including Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
While it occasionally criticises the government over domestic policies, it does not directly challenge president Vladimir Putin’s rule.

Ukraine believes Russia shared jet-drone technology with North Korea, says Zelensky
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday he believed Russia may have shared jet-drone technology with its longstanding ally North Korea.
In recent weeks, Russia has sharply increased its use of jet-drones against Ukraine, which so far has no effective means of countering them other than using combat aircraft.
Earlier in the war, North Korea supplied Russia with millions of artillery shells, and it has since provided ballistic missiles that Moscow regularly uses to attack Ukrainian cities.
Asked if Russia had shared with North Korea the technology behind its latest generation of jet-powered drones, Zelensky told journalists: "Yes, of course."
"They (Russia) are sharing with North Korea all the technologies. I don't know about the ballistic and etc, but I think, yes, because North Korea helped them with missiles," he added.
South Korea and Western countries have previously voiced concerns that Pyongyang may be getting help with weapons development from Moscow in return for its help in Ukraine.
Thousands of North Korean soldiers were sent to Russia to gain combat experience in the war.
Ukrainian drones deliver new batch of food to Russian-occupied Oleshky
Ukraine's military has again used drones to deliver food and medicines to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sunday.
Oleshky, a frontline town on the Dnipro River, which separates Russian and Ukrainian forces, has been under Russian occupation since 2022.
"For months, Russia has been trying to isolate Ukrainians in Oleshky from the outside world, even obstructing the delivery of food to people facing severe shortages," Sybiha said on X.
Ukraine used heavy-lift drones to deliver food and medicines to Oleshky at the end of September.
Sybiha said that the latest delivery consisted of nearly 400 packages containing almost 4 metric tons of food and medicine.
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets told Ukrainian media last month that Russia had not agreed to Ukrainian proposals to allow civilians to evacuate from Oleshky.
The Kremlin said that Oleshky had critical problems with food and medicine supplies, but that Russia's military was working to resolve them.
Germany's Merz announces new aid for Ukraine in Kyiv as Russia steps up attacks
German chancellor Friedrich Merz announced a new aid package for Ukraine worth more than €1.3bn (£1.1bn) during a visit to Kyiv on Sunday, as Russia escalated its attacks on Ukrainian cities.
About €1bn (£84m) of the package is military aid, including long-range strike weapons, combat drones and satellite technology, "so that Ukraine can also target Russian launch pads," Merz said at a news conference.
Germany is also providing some €350m (£296m) in energy aid ahead of winter for generators, substations and repair work, he said.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky said the two countries also signed 15 agreements worth more than €8.5bn (£7.2bn), mostly covering security cooperation, weapons production and procurement, as well as a deal to expand their joint counter-drone efforts.
"This is weaponry that will help right now," Zelensky wrote on X, adding they also discussed the need for air defence, which he called "key" at this time.
One killed, six injured in Ukraine's Kharkiv, mayor says
A Russian air strike on Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-biggest city, killed one person and injured another six, mayor Ihor Terekhov said on Telegram late on Sunday.
Terekhov said an administrative building and vehicles were burning following the attack.
At least 10 multi-story residential buildings were damaged in the attack, and search and rescue operations are ongoing.
Russia has reportedly launched Banderol missiles, part of its growing use of jet-powered loitering munitions that combine characteristics of cruise missiles and drones.
The Banderol’s speed, manoeuvrability and ability to fly at low altitudes can make it difficult for Ukrainian air defences to detect and intercept.
Ukraine praises EU diplomats for refusing to evacuate Kyiv after Russian threats
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha has publicly thanked European Union Ambassador Katarína Mathernová and the EU Delegation on Sunday after European diplomats refused Russian demands to evacuate the capital.
Moscow had issued warnings advising foreign diplomats and international missions to leave Kyiv amid escalating air strikes.
Sybiha declared that the continued presence of EU missions "speaks louder than Russian threats" and demonstrates unwavering solidarity with Ukraine.
Ambassador Mathernová confirmed that all 25 EU member state embassies currently operating in Kyiv will remain open. She cautioned Moscow against violating international law, emphasising that Russia "would be wise not to test the limits" of the Vienna Convention on diplomatic relations.
Kyiv and Berlin eye LNG deal and EU access to Ukrainian gas storage
Ukrainian and German energy ministers have met to discuss importing liquefied natural gas through German terminal infrastructure.
The talks focused on routing LNG shipments to Ukraine while opening Ukraine’s vast underground storage facilities to European energy companies to help allies buffer against seasonal price shocks as the conflict is widely expected to intensify ahead of winter.
The energy discussions coincide with German chancellor Friedrich Merz’s visit to Kyiv, where Berlin pledged €350 million specifically designated for emergency repair work on Ukraine's strike-damaged energy grid.
Bosnia votes as Kremlin-backed separatist Dodik looms large over general election
Bosnians have now cast ballots in general elections overshadowed by threats from pro-Moscow Serb nationalist Milorad Dodik to dismantle the state.
Despite being legally barred from office, Dodik – who met with Vladimir Putin in Moscow just days before the vote – remains the central figure of the campaign.
Appearing alongside Russia's ambassador at his final rally in Banja Luka, Dodik declared Bosnia "dead" and an "impossible country," signalling continued Kremlin-backed pushback against the nation's EU and NATO ambitions.
Russian alignment remains a flashpoint as Moscow seeks to maintain a strategic foothold in southeastern Europe through the Serb-majority Republika Srpska.
Turnout stood at just 27 percent by mid-afternoon amid voter disillusionment and technical delays, with Western officials watching closely for potential post-election instability.

How Evans defied history to join rallying greats
- Published
For what must have felt like an eternity, Elfyn Evans feared history was repeating itself yet again.
At 3.05pm local time in Sardinia on Sunday, Evans could only stand and watch as another world rally title looked to be slipping from his grasp.
Evans was preparing in his head yet another runners-up speech - it would be his sixth - as he waited for Oliver Solberg to cross the finish line and be crowned world champion.
How could this be happening again?
Of the five previous times he had been championship runner-up, three had been decided on the final day and twice after he had taken a lead into the final event.
But at 3.06pm, for once the motor-racing gods were on his side.
With just two turns to go on the final stage of the final round and with victory in sight, Solberg somehow careered off the track into the Sardinian sand to hand Evans his first world title.
In the most dramatic of finishes, the 37-year-old from north Wales became the first British winner of the World Rally Championship (WRC) in 25 years.
Only two British men had taken the title since the WRC's 1977 inception, matching the exploits of legendary pair Colin McRae (1995) and Richard Burns (2001).
Louise Aitken-Walker was Britain's first world champion when WRC ran a women's version in 1990.
"It wouldn't by my proudest way of winning it, but it's job done," said Evans.
"It's been a difficult weekend. I felt on Friday things were slipping away. We were a bit powerless with the road position we had and Oliver was flying."
His experienced co-driver Scott Martin revealed Evans was already apologising for his stage performance as they waited for Solberg to finish.
"I've said all week that until we arrived at the beach after that last stage it was never over. How true that turned out to be," said Martin.
Evans and Martin have been consistent performers throughout the 2026 championship, through the streets of Monaco, the ice and snow of Sweden, the flowing roads of Chile, and the punishing, sun-baked gravel tracks of southern Europe.
Despite winning only two of the previous 12 events, the pair took a 21-point lead into the final race at Rally Italia Sardegna.
Solberg, whose father Petter won the 2003 title, was around one kilometre from glory only to suffer motorsport's version of Devon Loch.
"The lead up to this event gave us a bit of a buffer and we just about managed to hold on at the end. It was an incredible finish," said Evans.
"I feel for [Solberg] after he came so close and lost at the last moment. I've been in a similar situation and it will be tough for him for a few days, but he's shown he's one to watch for the future."
Born to drive
Evans, like Solberg, is also from fine rally driving stock. His father Gwyndaf was British champion, as well as runner-up four times, but the ruddy-cheeked farmer never got the break to complete on the world stage.
The curse of finishing second passed down to his son who had already turned professional by the time his father claimed the last of those near misses in 2010.
Evans clinched his first WRC stage win in Germany in 2014 and a first podium in Argentina a year later, before having to drop down to the WRC2 class in 2016.
Evans admitted that blow only fueled his determination to make it in the WRC and a first rally victory followed - in his home event in Wales - in 2017.
He has been remarkably consistent, finishing second for the title in 2020, 2021, 2023, 2024 and, perhaps most agonisingly, to Sebastien Ogier by just four points in the final race of 2025.
He appeared condemned to be one of sport's great runners-up until the late drama of Sardinia threw up one of the championship's most thrilling finishes.
There may have been a stroke of fortune about the title win, but few can deny Evans earned it.

On Friday, Amazon committed to donating more than $1 billion over the next five years to communities neighboring data centers.
In a press release, Amazon Web Services’ CEO Matt Garman said that communities would decide how to prioritize funds across “education, job training, energy affordability, water, and energy preservation, and local priorities.”
Laying out other community commitments, Amazon also promised to ensure data centers wouldn’t increase power bills or wipe out local water supplies. Regarding the latter, Amazon promised to be “water positive” by 2030, while claiming that 75 percent of projects have already met this goal.
Rolling out these commitments, Amazon seemed bent on convincing Americans that the swelling data center backlash is based on lies. Echoing Donald Trump’s claims that foreign disinformation campaigns are fueling widespread protests, Garman urged that calls for data moratoriums must end or else American frontier AI might fall behind China’s.
According to Garman, US rivals are trying to “trick us into slowing down,” and Amazon’s commitments are meant to reassure Americans that everything’s okay and that we should instead plow ahead, as Trump endlessly advocates.
However, advocates at Stand.Earth—a global nonprofit that’s been fighting for environmental protections in communities hosting data centers—told Ars that Amazon is the one being “misleading” by spreading “corporate propaganda.” Seemingly in crisis mode as billions of dollars in data center projects have been blocked nationwide, Amazon’s promised donations represent “a flailing attempt at damage control for the harm its data center build-out has already caused,” Stand.Earth said.
Most problematic, Stand.Earth suggested, is Amazon’s plan to back a power plant that experts expect will become the largest source of US climate pollution. Glaringly, Amazon’s data center commitments don’t mention the power plant and scarcely address pollution, apart from promising to exclusively rely on back-up generators that use the lowest possible emissions.

How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports
- Published
Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a better economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China.
Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%.
Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked.
Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300m (£227m) in 2020 to $100m this year, while exports rose from around $129m to $200m in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market.
The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world.
Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year.
"India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC.
More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period.
"China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI).
If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava.
On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address, external these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues".
But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC.
That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods.
To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones.
"Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava.
It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment.
Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank.
"Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production.
Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends.
China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output.
Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year.
A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava.
On the other hand, lack of access to the Chinese market remains a major challenge for Indian companies.
"Indian products face a variety of tariff and non-tariff hurdles in China that make it difficult to scale exports," says Li.
"If normalisation [of ties] continues without a serious push for reciprocal market access, India risks a situation where the political relationship improves but the economic dependency stays the same."
The long term solution to both reducing avoidable imports and improving exports performance will be to strengthen manufacturing, says Srivastava.
But that requires sector-specific industrial policy and stronger fundamentals – affordable power and credit, efficient logistics and stable regulations – areas where India still falls short.
India has also recently softened foreign direct investment rules, which could open the door to Chinese companies wanting to expand Indian investments. But these too will need careful vetting, he adds.
"Investment that merely expands distribution networks or assembles products using Chinese parts could increase imports and deepen dependence. Approvals should therefore prioritise technology transfer, local value addition, domestic component production and exports from India."
More immediately, India could focus on targeting higher exports to China in specific sectors to reduce its trade asymmetry, says Li. Sectors like pharmaceuticals could be a natural fit with China's population aging and healthcare costs rising.
"But narrowing a $112bn deficit won't come from finding niche export sectors alone," he adds.
"The key question is whether Beijing is ready and willing to make concessions on market access as part of the broader normalisation. Alternatively, India will need to find its own leverage to force that conversation."

The Sentinelese, living on North Sentinel Island in the Bay of Bengal, are one of the most isolated peoples on earth.
Part of an archipelago governed by India, it is prohibited by law to venture within 5km of their island. And when a missionary did manage to land on the beach in 2018, he was killed by bow and arrow.
Yet none of that was to deter influencer Mykhailo Polyakov, who last year filmed himself arriving on North Sentinel Island, and leaving a can of coke on the beach.
Features writer Elle Hunt documents the rise of a new breed of influencer, travelling around the world, and streaming to millions their attempts to contact the uncontacted – despite the warnings of indigenous rights groups that the consequences could be fatal, both for the social media stars and the communities they risk exposing to disease.
Helen Pidd also speaks to Ecuadorian indigenous rights activist María José Andrade Cerda about the rights and wrongs of this new world.

Effects of preventive treatment for tuberculosis could start to wane after just one year of completing the antibiotics course in high-burden settings, while the protection lasts for at least eight and 13 years in medium and low-burden countries, a study has found.
Findings published in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine show that tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) offered a strong protection during the first 12-24 months across settings with all levels of TB burden.
Consisting of antibiotic medicines that can prevent inactive TB infections from developing into active disease, TPT is considered an important public health tool for protecting individuals and countries from the deadly infectious disease.
Preventive treatment can include medications, such as isoniazid and rifapentine -- typically prescribed for four months -- and is critical for the World Health Organization's goal to end the global TB epidemic by 2035.
TPT has been shown to be highly effective, but how long this protection lasts -- and whether its duration varies by region or community risk level -- remains unclear, researchers at the US' Boston University and the University of California, Berkeley, said.
They estimated TB risk among people with TB infections in 24 countries and found that TPT offered strong initial protection, but long-term protection varied depending on the burden of TB disease in each area.
"Of 4,66,523 participants from 47 studies, we included 84,128 individuals from 44 cohort studies across 24 countries. TPT was highly protective within the first year but declined over the course of follow-up in all settings, with greater effects observed in low-burden and medium-burden settings," the authors wrote.
The results showed that high-burden countries should consider combining TPT with other interventions to achieve the long-term benefits these medications are capable of providing, they said.
Lead author Lauren Linde, an epidemiology doctoral student at Boston University's school of public health, said, "In this study, our results corroborated something that was already well-established -- TPT is highly effective at preventing TB progression among close contacts and people who have been infected with TB."
"However, our finding that the initial effect of TPT declined so rapidly in very high-burden settings strengthens the case for not placing too much emphasis on TPT in isolation from other interventions that address ongoing community transmission," Linde said.
