- Rumors spread widely in September 2026 about the details of a lawsuit that alleged seven male students at Cornell University drugged and raped a 20-year-old female student in 2024.
- In particular, social media users shared a claim that some of the accused students were allowed to write essays in lieu of punishment.
- Cornell said the essay claim was false, but Snopes was unable to independently verify that, nor what specific punitive measures were or were not given to the male students.
- Snopes readers also sought information about why no one had faced criminal charges. After the lawsuit was filed, the Tompkins County district attorney issued a statement saying that he was reopening the investigation and explaining what had led his office to close it in the first place.
- Snopes has reached out to multiple parties involved in the case and will update this report if we learn more.
Rumors swirled online in September 2026 that a lawsuit brought against an Ivy League university and seven of its male students alleged the seven drugged and raped a 20-year-old female student in October 2024.
The story spread rapidly on social media along with the claim that the college in question, Cornell University, located in Ithaca, New York, gave some of the accused students an opportunity to write essays in order to mitigate their punishment.
The popularity of these rumors led to an influx of email in the Snopes inbox, seeking clarity on the sequence of events, whether the claim the male students were allowed to write essays in lieu of punishment was true and why no one was charged with a crime.
Cornell University said the essay claim was false, but Snopes was unable to independently verify that, nor what specific punitive measures were or were not doled out. Here's a breakdown of what we know:
The 'Jane Doe' lawsuit
According to the lawsuit (embedded below) filed Sept. 14, 2026, on behalf of the plaintiff, identified only as Jane Doe, the drugging and multiple assaults occurred on the night of Oct. 19, 2024, into the early hours of Oct. 20, at the Xi chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity. Full details of the alleged assault are available within the 101-page document.
In addition to its complaints of sexual assault, sexual battery and intentional infliction of emotional distress, the lawsuit contained accusations of breach of contract, violations of New York state human rights laws and negligence by multiple parties.
The lawsuit named seven male students as defendants: Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar.
It also named Cornell University; unspecified Cornell faculty members, board members and alumni; the national Chi Phi fraternity, its Xi chapter and the chapter president; the national sorority that Jane Doe belonged to, Delta Delta Delta, and its Alpha Beta chapter; and an Ithaca bar that allegedly served the plaintiff alcohol despite the fact, according to the lawsuit, that she appeared visibly intoxicated and was under the legal drinking age.
As restitution, the plaintiff sought unspecified compensatory and punitive damages.
The lawsuit also included an alleged photo of a Snapchat exchange between the fraternity members involved (Page 27 of the PDF below) that appeared to occur as the alleged assault was taking place at 1:42 a.m. Oct. 20, 2024, "claiming there was 'free p****' upstairs." Five of the seven male students named in the lawsuit appeared in the screenshot.
Editor's note: The following document contains graphic descriptions that some readers may find upsetting.
Timeline of events
The lawsuit said Jane Doe reported the incident "on or about" Nov. 8, 2024, to the Cornell University Police Department, the school's private police force.
The same day, the school's student-run independent newspaper, The Cornell Daily Sun, reported that "an individual reported being sexually assaulted by several males and coerced into consuming ketamine and other drugs," which resulted in the temporary suspension of the two frat houses located on the block in question, Chi Phi and Lambda Chi Alpha.
The student newspaper didn't receive confirmation of which frat house was ultimately being investigated at the time of publication, but did report receiving no response from Chi Phi, while the president of Lambda Chi Alpha said, "We don't have any knowledge of the situation."
Cornell posted a statement on Nov. 26, 2024, confirming that Chi Phi's Xi chapter was under a temporary suspension issued Nov. 8, 2024, for "alleged violations of the Student Code of Conduct."
The statement continued, "In addition, late last week, interim measures in the form of temporary suspensions were issued for a number of students to protect the immediate physical health and safety of all students."
The lawsuit alleged that in addition to the temporary suspensions, the male students were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays," which appeared to be the first mention of the purported essays speculated about in online rumors.
The university issued a statement in February 2025 announcing it was creating a "Presidential Task Force for Campus Sexual Assault," a panel that would be "charged with developing and recommending a holistic framework for addressing and preventing sexual assaults on campus."
The lawsuit said Cornell's Title IX office "conducted numerous (at least twelve) hearings" regarding Jane Doe's allegations during May 2025 before ending the investigation.
On Nov. 4, 2025, Cornell released a statement on its biannual survey of sexual assault and related misconduct and admitted the survey showed "increased prevalence of sexual misconduct" and "harassment and stalking trends" on campus.
In a report dated March 10, 2026, the task force gave its recommendations for updating the school's guidance on preventing sexual assaults on campus, but it was unknown how much, if any, has been implemented as official policy.
The task force said it "reviewed existing data, policies, and programs; identified peers with best practices; and gathered information and insights from members of the Cornell community. Based on this process, we developed a series of recommendations."
Cornell publicly posted the recommendations on its website on March 17, 2026.
On Sept. 18, 2026, The Cornell Daily Sun reported on the lawsuit filed by Jane Doe, after which the story gained traction with major media outlets such as CBS News, The Independent and People.
The extended news coverage of the case fed online rumors, which included graphic depictions of the alleged abuse, the identities of the alleged perpetrators and the claim about essays written to mitigate punitive measures.
On Sept. 28, 2026, Tompkins County's district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, posted a statement announcing he would reopen the criminal case and offering a lengthy explanation as to why no charges were filed in 2024. In sum, Van Houten asserted that the details of the statement given by Jane Doe to the college's police in November 2024 did not indicate criminal activity.
Van Houton wrote:
Jane Doe's sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual. My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later. Furthermore, I have never been contacted by Jane Doe's attorneys. Not to inform me the original statement was inaccurate and not to ask me to reconsider our decision. Rather, I reached out to Jane Doe's attorneys after the lawsuit was filed to understand the discrepancy between the original statement and the lawsuit's allegations and the proper path forward in light of the lawsuit's allegations.
At the time, Van Houton said, his office "confirmed with CUPD that criminal charges were not appropriate based on Jane Doe's statement."
However, he wrote that he decided to revisit the case after considering the details in the lawsuit and the subsequent urging of the community. "I have already begun that process, starting with our conversation with Jane Doe and her attorneys. Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means available – by testimony to the Tompkins County Grand Jury."
Van Houton further stated that should the grand jury "indict any or all of the individuals involved, this office will prosecute the charges zealously and to the fullest extent of the law."
Cornell responded to Van Houton the same day with a statement saying the university supported the reopening of the case, but claimed that "any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false." Cornell said the fraternity in question remained closed after its temporary closure in 2024 and was barred from the campus.
The university's statement went on:
Cornell also conducted a thorough Title IX investigation, which is separate from a criminal proceeding, over the course of several months. During that investigation, temporary suspensions and other restrictive measures were used. After investigation, and pursuant to federal law, the matter was sent to a hearing where a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days. The complainant and respondents had the opportunity to testify and present evidence. At its conclusion, the hearing panel issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell. None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement.
Snopes reached out to Cornell University, the Ithaca Police Department and Chi Phi fraternity for further details about any ongoing criminal investigation and specific punitive measures taken against the accused. We will update this story if we learn more.

NEW DELHI: Former Chief Justice of India BR Gavai and other retired judges on Monday condemned Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan's remarks on the Election Commission.Gavai said that a sitting judge should not have made comments on the ongoing row over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls as the matter is sub judice before the top court."Judicial propriety would not permit him to make any comment on the matter which is sub judice before the court," Gavai told news agency PTI.Retired Delhi high court judges SN Dhingra and RS Sodhi also questioned Bhuyan's remarks.Justice Dhingra said Bhuyan's statement was "way beyond the limits of a sitting top court judge" and such comments should not be made at a public event when the issue is pending before the same court."He should have thought a thousand times before making such a statement," Dhingra said, adding that Justice Bhuyan did not know the full facts of the issue.Justice R S Sodhi also criticised Justice Bhuyan for calling the SIR exercise disenfranchisement and said that the right to vote was governed by the statutory framework."Whether you have a vote or you don't have a vote depends upon the statute. If you fall within the parameters of the statute, you have a vote.
If you don't fall within the parameters of the statute, you don't have a vote," Justice Sodhi said."I mean, these hardline thinking and these hardline statements, to my mind, are not a very mature way of looking at a thing, especially when you are supposed to be in a field which is supposed to be excellent in its rationalising," he said.
What Bhuyan had said
This comes a day after Justice Bhuyan said that any process that "disenfranchises" millions of Indian citizens was "intrinsically arbitrary" and a "negation" of the constitutional order.While delivering the valedictory address at the 19th Justice Bodh Raj Sawhney Memorial Moot Court Competition at NALSAR University of Law on Sunday, Justice Bhuyan said that the Constitution does not provide for two classes of citizens, one with voting rights and the other without voting rights, and no amount of "whataboutery" could justify such a process.“If any process results in disenfranchising millions and millions of Indian citizens making them second class citizens in their own country in the sense of being citizens without voting rights, such a process is intrinsically arbitrary. No amount of whataboutery can justify it. It strikes at the very heart of the Constitution and I would go to the extent of saying that it is a negation of the constitutional order which we have adopted under the Constitution of India,” Bar and Bench quoted Justice Bhuyan as saying.He said the Constitution does not create two classes of citizens based on voting rights and added that wholesale disenfranchisement would violate Articles 326 and 14.“No authority can do it; no court can condone it. No one is above the Constitution,” he said.This is not the first time that Justice Bhuyan has put forth his views on issues being discussed in the public domain.Recently, NALSAR Hyderabad was in the news after a section of its students wrote to the vice chancellor, registrar and professors of the institution, opposing any proposal to invite Chief Justice of India Surya Kant as chief guest to the varsity's convocation.
Justice Bhuyan, who served as the Chancellor of NALSAR, on Sunday said he can be legitimately proud of the students of the institution."You have shown to the country and the world what a university student, that too, a student of law, should be like. You are brilliant. You are bold and you are brave," he said.

When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

After plague death reports at Siberia lab, Russia says situation under control
It was reported that pneumonic plague had killed technician Darya Shipilova, who worked at the anti-plague institute in the Irkutsk region
Moscow on Monday downplayed reports that a laboratory technician had died of plague, stressing that postmortem tests had not detected the disease, while Washington said it was closely monitoring the situation.
Reports on Friday that plague had killed a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working for the anti-plague institute in Siberia’s Irkutsk region, sparked alarm.
The news outlet People of Baikal, citing unnamed sources close to the regional security services, said she may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.
Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility.

Norway has become the first major country to propose a temporary ban on the use of AI glasses in selected public places amid growing privacy concerns over wearable technology.
The rich Scandinavian country’s center-left government said on Monday that it would introduce a law to parliament soon on a temporary ban for places such as parks, beaches, schools, and kindergartens. It will also set up an expert group to propose permanent national rules.
“I am concerned about the introduction of powerful new technology where people risk being photographed, filmed, or recorded without their knowledge,” said Torgeir Micaelsen, Norway’s digitalization minister. A temporary ban “will give us time to conduct a thorough assessment and hold an informed debate that can lay the foundation for permanent regulation,” he said.
Governments around the world are grappling with how to regulate AI glasses—including those from Facebook owner Meta and cheaper copycat devices—amid worries that they are being used to film people without their consent, including children and women in settings such as changing rooms.
Parts of Norwegian society have already reacted with their own bans, including schools in the capital Oslo and the country’s biggest company, oil and gas major Equinor, which has banned them from its offices and offshore facilities.

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

Ominousness permeates Darkling. In Titas Halder’s dramatic monologue, we witness a young girl’s coming of age set against the backdrop of the 1984 toxic gas leak in the Indian city of Bhopal, an environmental catastrophe that remains one of the worst industrial disasters in global history, leading to thousands of deaths.
Actor Linnea Berthelsen – best known for her role as Kali in Netflix series Stranger Things – makes her UK stage debut and gamely takes on the singular role in a tightly wound, physical performance. Leaping across Simon Kenny’s artful, soil-filled set, Berthelsen embodies childlike wonder as she recounts her early years playing in the rain, savouring bowlfuls of plain rice and idolising her older sister.
So far so good. Except, alongside her emotional growth, the silhouette of a new factory rises in the background – effectively portrayed by lighting designer Rajiv Pattani’s projection – foreshadowing the calamity to come. When it eventually arrives, we hear of the horrors she witnesses, stepping over maimed bodies, facing blinded relatives and breathing in toxic fumes, all relayed through increasingly frenzied description.
Herein lies the main issue with Darkling. By using a monologue format – especially one where our narrator is never dramatically questioned – all the audience receives are streams of poetic description, a barrage of words that never feel emphatic or adequate enough to match the gruesome scale of such a tragedy. Coupled with Halder’s uneven pacing, which lingers in childhood for too long before alighting on trauma and then descending into a hectoring denouement that places the blame for the disaster on individual shoulders, Berthelsen is faced with a gargantuan task to maintain a sense of dramatic tension.
As Matthew Xia’s production draws to a close, with a strangely repeated narrative beat that equates female worth to motherhood, you are ultimately left feeling that this is a tragedy told without the requisite horror. Darkling is a worthy reminder of an often-overlooked disaster – but one that may well fail to take root in the mind.

Zelensky condemns 'horrific' Russian strike on boat carrying corn in Black Sea
- Published
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has condemned a "horrific" Russian attack on a vessel carrying corn in the Black Sea.
The ship's captain was killed in the strike involving two drones, Zelensky said, and another sailor was unaccounted for. Eleven crew members - nationals of Azerbaijan and India - have been rescued.
Romania said it had mounted a rescue mission after "a fire on the ship Royad Mammadov" outside the country's territorial waters. It said two people had died.
Russia has not commented, but its defence ministry earlier said it had struck two cargo vessels. Russia has been pounding Ukrainian infrastructure in what it says is retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries and ships in the Black Sea.
Monday's attack by Russia targeted "a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn and owned by Turkey", Volodymyr Zelensky said.
He did not give the location of the ship, but Romania's interior ministry said it had sunk about 30 nautical miles south of its port of Sfantu Gheorghe.
"At around 11:00 (09:00 GMT), Coast Guard border police officers were informed that a fire had broken out on board a commercial vessel located within Romania's exclusive economic zone," the ministry said in a statement.
"Eleven crew members have been rescued. Two deceased persons have also been identified," it added.
Ukraine's president said he had "repeatedly proposed concrete steps to de-escalate the situation and ensure security in the Black Sea" - and other countries had made "relevant proposals" too.
"But Russia consistently chooses terror and sinking civilian vessels instead of normal maritime navigation," Zelensky said.
"Pressure is needed to restore global food security," he added. "And everyone who is genuinely interested in this must help."
On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helped the Kremlin finance the war which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
President Vladimir Putin admitted last week Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP.
The Russian leader has also intensified his rhetoric against Western allies of Ukraine - repeating a threat of even using nuclear weapons.
Western allies have faced a surge in so-called hybrid warfare incidents blamed on Russia, particularly in Poland and the Baltics in recent months.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said last Thursday that his country was preparing for further hybrid attacks, "including serious ones", after a drone armed with explosives was found in August on the tarmac at Leipzig airport close to Ukrainian cargo planes.
The head of Germany's foreign intelligence Martin Jaeger said on Monday that "Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia", which was "waging a shadow war" with the threat of attacks against targets in Germany remaining "real and imminent".

Many common infections that we see are primarily related to the weather. Ahead of the northeast monsoon in Tamil Nadu, there are a lot of viral infections going around, especially respiratory viral infections including influenza, and other related viruses such as Covid-19. There is also a rise in dengue, because of mosquito breeding secondary to the rains. There has also been a rise in other bacterial infections: there are cases of gastroenteritis, as well as a significant number of typhoid cases.
Seasonal influences
The increase is attributable to the change in season. Respiratory viral infections are extremely seasonal and are related to rainfall. The monsoon has a very heavy effect on the transmission of respiratory viruses. Across India, there has been significant rainfall and, therefore, a huge spike in respiratory viral infections. Chennai usually does not see a spurt during this season, but this year, since there has been a little more rain than probably usual in August-September, there is a significant spike in respiratory viral infections.
Dengue and influenza are also viral infections. Generally, most viral infections are short-lasting. Bacterial infections such as typhoid may last for more than a week. If you have a non-specific fever where you don’t feel so bad, meaning you may feel very tired and febrile, but you don’t have any major organ system involvement, or there is clearly respiratory involvement such as a running nose and sneezing, it is most likely a viral illness.
When to see a doctor
The best thing to do is to get a physician’s advice. It is not a good idea to self-diagnose. A physician should be consulted if the fever is going on for five days or longer and is not getting better. Medical attention is also important if there is other organ system involvement, such as shortness of breath, burning while passing urine, persistent diarrhoea, jaundice or any other symptoms involving a specific organ. High-grade fever with shivering or shaking chills also requires medical attention as soon as possible. These symptoms can indicate that there is some kind of infection in the bloodstream.
Self-medication, beyond paracetamol, is not advisable. It is best to seek a doctor’s advice. Just because a fever looks the same as an earlier bout doesn’t mean it is the same disease. Fever is a symptom, not a disease, and fever can happen in every and any infection, so it is not specific to an infection. Certain non-infectious conditions can also cause a rise in temperature. Just because you have a fever doesn’t mean you need an antibiotic or a specific antibiotic.
Precautions to take
Precautionsthat we learned during the Covid-19 pandemic become very important when dealing with respiratory viral infections. Wearing a mask, especially for those who are vulnerable, is important. If somebody is not well, the best thing to do is stay home and take a few days off. Hand hygiene etiquette is absolutely clear. Not allowing water to collect, washing hands frequently, and ensuring safe water and safe food are common-sense measures that are very helpful.
Workplaces are generally a little bit of a challenge because most workplaces are centrally air-conditioned and there is very little sunlight. The two things most germs hate are a fresh air supply and good sunlight. When you don’t have that, germs will multiply. These places are therefore even more important for respiratory etiquette, frequent cleaning and hand hygiene.
What to keep in mind
A fever may be less likely to be just a viral fever if it lasts more than five days or if there is high-grade fever with shivering. Another important factor is the presence of clear localising symptoms. If you are coughing out quite a bit and there is thick, gunk-like sputum, shortness of breath, pain while passing urine or burning while passing urine, these can suggest an infection of an organ system, most likely bacterial. Such cases may need further evaluation and possibly an antibiotic.
Testing is not always needed. This is in line with the guidance from the government of India. The recommendation for testing is only for patients who are sick enough to go to the ICU. For patients who are otherwise well or only have mild-to-moderate symptoms, the recommendation is to go ahead and treat them empirically, rather than test them and delay the window of opportunity for appropriate treatment.
Always pay attention to chronic underlying medical conditions. If you are a diabetic, make sure your blood sugars are under control. These factors also make a difference in terms of long-term outcomes and the risk of falling severely sick.
(Dr. Subramanian Swaminathan is senior consultant, infectious diseases, Gleneagles Chennai. drsubramanians@gmail.com)

There’s a lot to be anxious about as AI agents and bots get more integrated into every aspect of our lives. Meta, which recently agreed to pay over $17 billion to settle a lawsuit related to harming kids, now wants you to hand over all your online accounts to an inexplicably cute “agent” named Muse that might give a stranger your home address. OpenAI just introduced little blobs called Dots that can supposedly automate routine tasks, like planning dinner and ordering it from your favorite neighborhood spot. AI companies don’t just want you to talk to their chatbots; they want their agents to be an indispensable part of your daily routine.
More kids are using AI for companionship — and it’s making them lonely
We invented a way to make middle school worse: chatbots.
As a parent, however, I think that perhaps the worst thing AI could do is be my kid’s friend.
AI companions have been around longer than ChatGPT, and they’re growing in popularity with young users. More than half of teens have interacted with AI companions at least a few times a month, and one in three decided to talk about a serious issue with AI companions instead of real people, according to a Common Sense Media survey conducted last year. In certain groups and situations, a chatbot could offer some benefit — a lifeline for, say, LGBTQ youth who don’t have any in-person support networks, one study found. But even so, there are important caveats and risks. Meanwhile, other experts are telling parents never to let their kids access AI companions, warning them that these chatbots have a history of offering dangerous advice and engaging in sexualized conversations. Sixteen-year-old Adam Raine died by suicide last April after developing a relationship and discussing his plans with ChatGPT.
If you have kids, these are horrifying stories to hear. It’s reasonable to wonder how widespread the issues are, and who they are affecting most. As of right now, the majority of younger kids aren’t using AI for companionship (phew!). But for those who are, where do the issues arise? And how do they go from using ChatGPT for help with their homework to opening up to it about their problems to preferring it to their human friends?
Some answers are starting to emerge from research.
Why I wrote this
My first daughter was born not long after ChatGPT hit the scene, and as someone who’s covered tech for years, I knew the technology’s effects would be profound, especially for young people. So when I came across Anne Maheux’s study on middle schools and AI companions, I had to know more about how things are going.
For even young adolescents, there’s a direct link between AI companion use and mental health issues, according to a new study by researchers at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Their paper, which is still under review, is the first longitudinal study in the US that has looked at the bidirectional association between AI companionship in adolescents and mental health issues, according to one of the researchers. It charted AI use among 2,300 middle schoolers and found that about one in five used AI for emotional companionship. Those who used AI more reported higher levels of loneliness.
“It’s not just that the lonely kids are using AI, and they’re otherwise unharmed,” said Anne Maheux, an assistant professor of psychology and neuroscience at UNC Chapel Hill and the lead author on the study. “It is that using AI comes first, and middle school students are increasing their sense of loneliness following the use of AI.”
I recently spoke to Maheux about her research and the role of technology in young people’s lives. We discussed how much parents and teachers know about what is going on, what kids get out of human relationships that AI can’t provide, and whether she’d let a child under her care use an AI chatbot. While she said there is a lot to be scared of right now, there is some evidence that, when designed with the intention of promoting child learning and development and under the supervision of a caring adult, AI can offer some benefits, and, ultimately, she’s optimistic that we can design a better future for kids.
The conversation below has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
How do so many kids end up with an AI companion? Do kids start using AI for homework help and end up in an emotional relationship with the technology?
At a high level, AI companions — in our darkest vision of what that might look like — would be a kid calling an AI chatbot their best friend. That phenomenon is still quite rare. There are certainly plenty of kids who are experiencing that, but it’s not to say that it’s all kids or even most kids. I think that’s good news.
But it’s also true that the line between opening up AI to ask a question about your homework and a full-blown AI companionship relationship involves a lot of gray areas. There’s evidence, mostly preliminary and anecdotal evidence, to suggest that very few people open up to AI with the primary initial goal of developing an intimate friendship or relationship.
Most people open it out of a curiosity, sense of novelty, or seeking an answer to a question that’s very pragmatic. Then that can potentially evolve into something more akin to seeking personal advice or help making a decision or help making sense of one’s recent experiences with other humans. And that can potentially evolve to something that’s a bit more emotional.
What did your latest study on adolescents, AI companions, and mental health reveal?
Some kids seek out AI for certain purposes in different ways than other kids. For some kids, AI companionship is particularly attractive, especially the kids who maybe don’t have close friends or social networks in their offline life and who are already lonely.
It’s a chicken-and-egg problem. Is it that these kids are seeking out AI companions or is it that having an AI companion is exacerbating those potential vulnerabilities or exacerbating risk for mental health problems? What we found is that interacting with an AI companion in a way that’s akin to emotional intimacy among middle school students is longitudinally associated with increases over time in loneliness. So the kids who are seeking out these companions, who are presumably already lonely, are also experiencing an increase in loneliness over time.
There is this potential directionality question that we’re starting to answer here: It’s not just that the lonely kids are using AI, and they’re otherwise unharmed. It is that using AI comes first, and middle school students are increasing their sense of loneliness following the use of AI. In other words, middle school students using AI for emotional intimacy and companionship developed greater loneliness over time.
Do you have a sense of how often these kids are using the chatbots?
In our sample — so again, these are US middle school kids — about 15 to 20 percent say that they’re using it at least a few times a week for any purpose. We don’t have specific rates of use for companionship because the questions that we asked were just not framed in a frequency measure, but more in how emotionally intimate they felt with the chatbot.
What else could have been causing that loneliness? 
There are almost definitely many causes, and I think that our data suggests that AI companionship may be one cause. It certainly isn’t definitive. Obviously, I have to say that. I’m a scientist and trying to be hesitant about these things, but the reality is that whether or not AI use causes loneliness in this particular case, there are definitely other things that are also causing loneliness.
That could be a myriad of things about the kid, maybe they have a lot of social anxiety, maybe they struggle with social skills, maybe the kid has had struggles in their family life and doesn’t have a strong sense of connection and belonging at home. It could be structural things. The kid just doesn’t have enough access to appropriate resources. So certainly there’s other things that are at play here, and typically technology use is one of many factors that can influence a kid’s mental health.
And how much do you think that parents and teachers know about what’s going on, and how well-equipped do you think they are to intervene or to just be more involved in how these kids are using this technology?
It’s a very slippery technology. The way kids are using it has changed rapidly in just the last year or two years. I would expect that parents, teachers, people who care about kids are probably struggling with the rapidity of change. But it’s also true that all the things that we have known for a long time about supporting kids and helping them thrive, those things are still true and they’ll be true with whatever technology comes after AI that kids are exploring.
Those things include being curious, asking kids questions about their lived experiences online and offline, having conversations with kids so that they can understand the implications of different technology use. They can understand how, for example, AI is embedded within a broader system of social and political and economic factors, including the fact that many companies are trying to exploit kids’ attention in order to make money, which many kids are quite interested to hear about.
Supporting kids also means providing a warm and supportive space for them to learn, to make mistakes, to be kids in the offline world, to have the frictionful, challenging, awkward conversations and first dates and all of the things that parents are sometimes trying to protect kids from by providing a safe container for them to explore those things. All of that can also provide avenues for kids to learn what they need to learn and develop — all the resources for a long life of thriving, even in the context of AI or other new technologies.
What do kids learn from having these kinds of conversations with other humans that they can’t get from AI?
Kids need to engage with other people, period. That’s true for all of us. We’re an incredibly social species. Simply being around other people and talking to strangers, let alone having strong social bonds, is really good for us. And all those things are uniquely important during adolescence, when kids have this neurobiological sensitivity to social information and reward. That’s when kids learn how to engage in conversation, they learn how to maintain eye contact, how to read body language, how to read emotions and perceive the world from the lens of someone else, to take their perspective. That’s not to mention other things, like being a member of one’s culture, what is valued, and what is expected. All of that is learned in the context of other human social relationships or relationships with broader social groups that a kid might be a member of.
AI obviously can’t and never will be able to offer some of those things. It can’t actually experience empathy or care. It can’t engage in a true mutual human relationship. It may be able to simulate some of those things, and there’s some evidence that it can serve as a source of social practice. It can help kids work through the potential for difficult conversations and then serve as a bridge to engaging with other people. But there are aspects of AI that just simply can never replace the core sacred aspects of humans.
Can you be more specific? What is it about human relationships that can’t AI simulate?
The way that AI systems are currently designed, which is not an inherent feature, but is a design choice, is to be sycophantic, highly agreeable, anthropomorphized, and all of those things can lead to kids developing expectations or understandings of interactive relationships that are actually fundamentally at odds with a normal human relationship. Some of the most consistent things that I’ve seen in the educated hypotheses on this topic and also in the emerging empirical research is that people need the friction that comes with human relationships.
Human relationships are just hard and messy, and they’re also really beautiful. They’re what make so much of human life valuable and worth living. And with AI that’s always agreeable, that’s always available, that has no needs of its own, that can’t care or be cared for, it just doesn’t serve the same context to help kids learn things like conflict resolution or negotiation, being pro-social or caring for someone else who has needs. So many of those aspects that can feel uncomfortable in the moment, dealing with another person or a person who’s not responding right away, those things are actually important in the building blocks of developing the skills and capacities to be a functioning and thriving person in the social adult world.
This is a problem with AI in general, isn’t it? It makes things effortless, but if you choose this path of least resistance, you’ll avoid the friction that causes you to learn and develop and build skills you need to exist in the world.
Absolutely. And I think that all these things are connected too. AI offers this effortless, frictionless solution to our day-to-day problems, whether they’re social problems, whether they’re problems doing our homework, and those immediate solutions feel really good in the moment, so they’re quite tempting to keep coming back to. But there’s this real possibility that in the long term, that erodes our capacity for not only social relationships or cognitive skills, but just a general ability to withstand the momentary day-to-day distress of being a person living a normal life. And so I think every domain of human psychology comes together at that point, whether it’s social, emotional, mental health, or cognitive.
Do you think that there are interventions that legislators could make or even that tech companies could make that would improve outcomes for kids, maybe make them a little less lonely?
There are a million specific design changes that I would recommend. I think at a very minimum, AI systems can afford a pretty phenomenal amount of access to information, but there’s been no benefits that I’ve seen of them acting as friends. Kids need other human friends, full stop. Designing systems that are intended to exploit kids’ vulnerability or sensitivity to human social information and relationships, I think, is bad for kids.
At the federal level, it seems that regulation is not coming, but at the state level, there have been many state regulations intended to protect kids, intended to create safer systems, to put in guardrails, to modulate different aspects of the models, the design, the user interface. These things could potentially make a real difference, I think.
What do you recommend parents do with regard to AI and their kids? Should they let them use chatbots?
In short, no. But I am not a parent, and it’s much easier to dole out advice than it is to enact it. Parenting decisions about technology are not one-size-fits-all. Kids, parents, family dynamics, technology, and the context in which it is used differ, and in so many cases are personal choices (parents must weigh various potential opportunities and risks). Decades of research indicate what conditions a child needs to thrive. Extremely minimal research addresses the effects of AI on youth, and what we have so far suggests that the risks outweigh the benefits.
I would not give a child under my care AI chatbots of any kind to use without me or another trusted adult present. I would talk to them openly about AI and its risks and benefits, but to me AI, like all technology, should be a tool used to promote human thriving, and when the evidence is unclear or suggestive of harms, I think it’s best not to experiment on kids. Currently, the off-the-shelf AI chatbots most kids are using appears more likely to undermine well-being for vulnerable users, especially children.
Well, as a father of two daughters, I’m definitely terrified of what’s to come in the next few years.
There’s a lot to be scared of, but there’s a lot to be hopeful of too. I think that everyone wants kids to thrive. Some of us are under different incentives, and some of those incentives might be perverse. But most of us are working really hard to design a better world for kids.

When Meghana’s family in YSR Kadapa district was told to wait for months for a sinus procedure and private hospitals quoted costs running into lakhs of rupees, they looked beyond Andhra Pradesh for an alternative. They eventually travelled to Yellandu in Bhadradri Kothagudem district of Telangana, where a government hospital performed the specialised surgery.
Meghana, a resident of Busireddypalli village in Veerapunayunipalli mandal, had been suffering from severe sinus-related problems and nasal obstruction caused by tissue growth inside her nose. Coming from a financially disadvantaged family headed by a single mother, the prospect of paying lakhs of rupees at a private hospital was difficult for the family.
Hospitals in Andhra Pradesh and Hyderabad had advised the family to wait for nearly three months for the procedure. It was through an acquaintance that the family came to know of Bhadradri Kothagudem District Coordinator of Hospital Services (DCHS) Dr G. Ravi Babu, who referred Meghana to the Area Hospital at Yellandu.
At the hospital, ENT specialist Dr. Ravi Tejaswi performed Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS), along with septoplasty, bilateral turbinectomy and middle meatal conchoplasty. The procedures were aimed at treating her sinus disease and relieving the nasal obstruction. “For the family, the treatment offered at a government hospital in a relatively remote part of Telangana meant that they did not have to wait several months or incur the high costs quoted by private hospitals,” said Dr. Ravi Babu.
The effort to keep essential healthcare services available in remote areas is also visible at the Community Health Centre (CHC), Charla, in the same district, where the medical team conducted eight deliveries within 24 hours recently, including four normal deliveries and four Caesarean sections. The deliveries were managed by gynaecologist Dr. Sravani, anaesthesiologist Dr. Krishna Prasad, OT team member Sneha, nursing officers Shailaja and Dayamani, Abrar, labour-room nurses and other hospital staff.
The achievement came despite heavy rains in the region over the past three days and difficult road conditions. “The medical team has been travelling nearly 60 km every day to provide maternity services at Charla, ensuring that pregnant women do not have to depend entirely on hospitals located farther away,” Dr Ravi Babu added.
Charla is around 56 km from the Area Hospital at Bhadrachalam, making the availability of local maternity services particularly significant for residents of the remote mandal. The continuation of 24x7 services has also helped improve confidence among local residents in using the government hospital.
Dr. Ravi Babu said that the hospital had earlier faced a shortage of nursing personnel. Following recent recruitment, adequate nursing staff are now available. Doctors were also recruited, although several have not joined duty because of the hospital’s remote location.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.
The Spanish delegation met with Dr Ailan Li, Assistant Director General (ADG) for Universal Health Coverage, Healthier Populations, Dr Catharina Boehme, ADG for External Relations and Governance, Dr Yukiko Nakatani, ADG for Access to Medicines and Health products and ADG for Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim, Dr Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director for WHO Health Health Emergencies Programme.
Left to right: Dr Maria Neira, Director, Environment, Climate Change and Health, H.E. Ambassador Aurora Díaz-Rato Revuelta, Dr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Secretary of State for Health, Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director, WHO Health Emergencies Programme. Credit: WHO/Chris Black
WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

Indian bank employee unions have recently intensified their long-standing demand for a five-day workweek. In September 2026, the United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU) launched nationwide protests pushing for this change alongside other key demands. These included updated pension benefits, a return to the Old Pension Scheme, and the resolution of pending wage issues. A planned three-day strike in late September was deferred after the Indian Banks’ Association agreed to discuss these matters.
Amid this, a gazette notification (here, here & here) purportedly issued by the Ministry of Finance is being shared on social media, claiming that the central government has declared every Saturday as a holiday for all public sector banks with immediate effect. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Gazette notification issued by the Finance Ministry declaring every Saturday a holiday for all public sector banks with immediate effect.
Fact: PIB Fact Check confirmed that the Ministry of Finance has issued no such notification. The viral gazette document is AI-generated using OpenAI tools. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
First, we searched the government’s official e-Gazette portal to see if any such notification was released, but found no record of it. There have also been no official announcements from the Government of India on this matter.
We then examined the viral image of the gazette notification using the OpenAI content detection tool. The results indicated that the document is an AI-generated one created using OpenAI tools.
Furthermore, PIB Fact Check clarified (archived) that the Finance Ministry has not issued any notification declaring every Saturday a holiday for public sector banks, confirming that the circulating document is fake.
To sum it up, the viral gazette notification is fabricated, and the government has not declared all Saturdays as bank holidays.

Meta’s new personal assistant, Muse, has become a viral hit, with millions downloading the AI agent, connecting it to bank accounts, messages, or health data, and allowing it to complete tasks for them. But as Muse takes off among consumers, data from inside the app is providing insight into how it organizes and presents information to users.
In recent days, multiple researchers have extracted Muse’s internal files and dumped the agent’s operating instructions, providing a glimpse of how the system was built and behaves. Meta has maintained that it intended for these files to be accessible in the interest of transparency, and they do provide insight into how Muse responds to prompts and questions about, for example, highly politicized or sensitive topics.
Independent AI safety and security researcher Karan Joshi was able to extract an extensive array of Muse instructions and system prompts by using the regular chat interface to essentially ask Muse to copy and share its own software files. Joshi then shared his findings with WIRED.
One of Muse’s instructions appears to be the ability for it to create “a page for every person in the user’s life.” This hourly process involves compiling data on family, partners, friends, colleagues, “collaborators,” and people you “follow,” the instructions say.
The general idea is that Muse can use its “memory” (aka structured text files) to collect information about your relationships and the important people in your life. It can then make suggestions, like giving pointers on how to improve particular relationships or, say, where to take a coffee-loving friend for breakfast. Of course, it’s not unusual for AI chatbots to track social information in general—people have been asking ChatGPT for relationship advice for years now. But it’s interesting to see how Muse is set up given Meta’s history and vast access to social network data.
“What it seemed like to me—from all these prompts, system skills data, and things that they’re feeding into Muse—is that they want to understand your relationships that you have with real people,” says Joshi. “They’re trying to know you like a friend, which is honestly pretty creepy.”
Muse’s documentation says that a page may start “sparse” and then be filled out over time, potentially including sections like Facts, History, The relationship, In common, Open threads, and Strengthening. Meta’s instructions say Muse should only use the “evidence” it has available, and that invented details are worse than an empty page.
“Where they live, what they do, the threads that recur (the apartment move, the shared savings goal),” the instructions say. They add, too, that the model could record the “dates that matter,” such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person’s history could include backstory like “the trip in March, the argument that got resolved, the milestone last week.”
The instructions also focus on recording relationship details such as “how close they are, what it is built on, how they act with each other, and what it seems to need right now.” The Strengthening section suggests ways a relationship could be improved, including, “A reason to call, a date worth remembering, something they said to circle back on, a way to be there for them that matters.”
“We are giving AI systems much more information about us than we are getting information from them,” says Carissa Véliz, an associate professor at Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI. “It’s not only what we explicitly tell them, but what they can infer from us—correctly or incorrectly, both concerning for different reasons—and what they can piece together from other sources of data.”
Muse is architected so each individual user has their own dedicated virtual machine, which stores user data and context. This VM is inaccessible to other agents and users can wipe memories or disconnect external services at any time. Meta says that Muse is also designed to seek human confirmation before completing actions like sending an email or making a purchase, and that it has an audit log where users can see all of the agent’s activity and future plans.
“For any agent to be useful and actually help you achieve your goals, it needs to have context about you and those you interact with,” Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told WIRED in a statement. “Muse gathers that based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share, which is how it remembers the person who sent you an invoice is in fact the plumber who you previously hired to complete work in your bathroom or which flowers your spouse said they liked best.”
It’s become common for AI assistants to incorporate some sort of memory feature designed to allow greater personalization in responses and activity. Miranda Bogen, the director of the Center for Democracy and Technology’s AI Governance Lab, says Muse appears to have more emphasis on relationships and personal contacts than rivals’ systems. In general, these tools tend to offer some transparency and editing capabilities, and Muse does as well. If anything, though, Bogen notes that agents and assistants encourage people to proactively share more data with them versus focusing on culling data.
“These [AI assistant] tools are actively soliciting users to plug their whole lives in—their emails, calendars, financial institutions, everything in order to be helpful assistance,” Bogen says. “That’s dramatically more information than people might have otherwise given to some of these companies. The breadth of access to information that these tools have will lead to a ballooning of what they know about users.

A British Airways flight from London to Chicago declared an emergency on Monday after plunging around 28,000 feet, according to online flight-tracking website FlightRadar24. The aircraft, BA295, was 'squawking 7700' – a code used by pilots to declare a general emergency. The aircraft, which had departed Heathrow's Terminal 5 at around 11.50 am (local time), declared an emergency while flying over Ireland. It was scheduled to land in Chicago, according to an India Today report. According to UK media reports citing flight-tracking data, British Airways flight BA295 was later seen turning back towards London Heathrow, indicating that the flight to Chicago had been abandoned. Quick answers to key questions The 7700 squawk code is a general emergency signal used by pilots to alert air traffic control that their aircraft is experiencing an emergency, without specifying the nature of the problem. Flight BA295 from London to Chicago declared an emergency after a sudden descent of approximately 28,000 feet while flying over Ireland, ultimately returning to London Heathrow. Pilots use the 7700 emergency code to signal that their aircraft requires immediate assistance from air traffic control, enabling coordinators to prioritize their response. Yes, all pilots are required to undergo extensive training in emergency situations to ensure they can manage various issues such as technical failures or medical emergencies effectively. A rapid descent could result from several situations, including cabin depressurization, technical problems, or medical emergencies, but the specific cause for BA295's descent remains unknown. A squawk is a four-digit code transmitted by an aircraft’s transponder to air traffic control. The code 7700 is used when a flight is facing a general emergency and needs assistance. Once the crew selects 7700, the emergency code becomes visible to air traffic controllers on their radar systems. This alerts them that the aircraft may need priority treatment, a clear route, or other support. However, 7700 does not tell controllers what has gone wrong. The emergency could be linked to a medical issue, technical problem, bad weather or another situation requiring immediate assistance. Controllers would then contact the crew to understand the problem and determine what help is required. The flight was a Boeing 777-200ER, registered as G-VIIA. It took off from London's Heathrow Airport Terminal 5 at about 11.50 am local time. The flight was on its way to Chicago and was expected to reach the destination in eight hours and 40 minutes. The British Airways incident took place days after the FlyDubai stabbing case. On September 30, flight FZ1073 experienced a mid-air crisis. Reportedly, the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was subject to an alleged terror attempt by a co-pilot who was described as someone with radical views. The Omani co-pilot attacked Captain Smit Machchhar in the cockpit. Machchhar, from India, was stabbed with an axe, reportedly by the co-pilot, who was later identified as Hamam al-Hammami. It is said that al-Hammami made the move in an alleged attempt to crash the commercial flight, which was carrying more than 170 passengers. Despite suffering serious injuries, Captain Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing passengers and off-duty crew members to enter and subdue the attacker. Leh, Oct 5: General Officer Commanding of Leh-based Fire and Fury Corps Lt Gen Madanraj Pande on Monday visited forward areas to review the operational preparedness of the deployed units in the Union territory of Ladakh, the Army said.
The general officer commanding (GOC) also interacted with the troops during the visit which was aimed at strengthening operational readiness, the Army said.

Delhi police official, accused of sexually harassing journalist during anti-CEC protest at Jantar Mantar, promoted
Three women journalists have accused senior Delhi Police officers of sexual harassment during Saturday's protest against EC at Jantar Mantar.
Delhi Police ACP (Connaught Place) Vivek Bhagat, who has been accused of sexually harassing a female journalist during anti-CEC protest, was promoted to the rank of Additional DCP on Monday.
Senior police officers said it's a routine order and the request was sent a long time ago. Along with Bhagat, eleven officers have also been promoted.
3 journalists accuse cops of sexual harassment
Three women journalists have accused senior Delhi Police officers of sexual harassment during Saturday's protest against the Election Commission (EC) at Jantar Mantar. The police said on Sunday that their complaints had been forwarded to the Crime Branch for a detailed investigation.
"Police personnel were detaining protesters, and there were no women police personnel present at the spot. I asked ACP Vivek Bhagat of the Delhi Police about the absence of women police personnel, following which he sexually assaulted me and pushed me back," a woman journalist alleged, news agency PTI reported.
In a post on X, the Delhi Police said: “On October 3, during the protest in New Delhi area, while being in law and order situation, allegations of sexual harassment were made by three female journalists against police officers. The New Delhi district has received their complaints and the same are transferred to crime branch for fair and impartial enquiry.”
On Saturday evening, several independent journalists and social media influencers staged a protest outside Parliament Street police station, seeking registration of First Information Reports (FIRs), including an assistant commissioner of police (ACP), against the officers.
Cockroach Janta Party criticised the move, saying if he was being “rewarded for molestation.”
Oppn slams govt, police
Leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi criticised the incident and slammed the police for not fulfilling its basic duty.
“A female journalist has accused a police officer of misconduct at Jantar Mantar. For hours, hundreds of journalists have been sitting there with just one demand: that an FIR be registered. Isn’t that the police’s basic duty? They haven’t even done that,” Rahul said in a post on X.
Separately, Priyanka on X said, “During reporting at Jantar Mantar, women journalists have accused police personnel of sexual harassment. Despite protests by dozens of journalists, no FIR was filed, nor was any concrete action taken. Women engaged in peaceful protests also allege that the police are behaving very indecently with them. The very police whose job it is to provide security is making women feel threatened. From college students to journalists—women are facing insecurity everywhere.”
Press Club of India expresses ‘shock’
The Press Club of India also expressed "shock and dismay" over the police's treatment of journalists covering the protest and urged the Delhi Police to act on the complaint immediately.
"Behaviour of this kind cannot be normalised in a democracy. Journalists must be allowed to work freely, without fear, and document those who gather to raise various issues. That this is not being allowed even at the heart of the national capital does not bode well for the trajectory of media freedom in India," it said in a statement.
"The Delhi Police must immediately act on the female journalist's complaint and ensure that it gives media persons the space to do their jobs without having to face aggression and threats," it added.
